a long-term exposure to high doses of aluminium and magnesium salts may lead to encephalopathy, dementia, microcytic anemiaor worsen dialysis-induced osteomalacia
The prolonged use of antacids in patients with renal failure should be avoided.

items.t: Large doses may trigger or worsen intestinal obstruction and ileus in people at higher risk, such as renal impairment or the elderly (simeticone-containing SmPC).

src.q: large doses of this product may trigger or aggravate intestinal obstruction and ileus in patients at higher risk such as those with renal impairment, or the elderly.

items.t: Phosphate depletion (with bone resorption, hypercalciuria and osteomalacia risk) with excessive doses, long-term use, or normal doses on a low-phosphorus diet. Medical advice is recommended for long-term use or if at risk of phosphate depletion (simeticone-containing SmPC).

src.q: or even normal doses in patients with low-phosphorous diets, may lead to phosphate depletion
Medical advice is recommended in case of long-term use or in patients at risk of phosphate depletion.

items.t: Porphyria with haemodialysis: aluminium hydroxide may be unsafe (simeticone-containing SmPC).

src.q: Aluminium hydroxide may be unsafe in patients with porphyria undergoing hemodialysis.

items.t: Hereditary fructose intolerance: should not be taken (contains sorbitol).

src.q: Patients with hereditary fructose intolerance (HFI) should not take/be given this medicinal product.
Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance should not take this medicine.

items.t: Sodium: one UK SmPC states less than 1 mmol (23 mg) sodium per ml, essentially sodium-free. Contains parahydroxybenzoates, which may cause allergic reactions (possibly delayed).

src.q: This medicine contains less than 1 mmol sodium (23 mg) per ml, that is to say essentially 'sodium-free'.
propyl parahydroxybenzoate (E 216) which may cause allergic reactions (possible delayed)

items.t: Tetracyclines and vitamins: antacids inhibit absorption; do not take at the same time (one UK SmPC; the simeticone-containing SmPC also names tetracyclines and vitamins).

src.q: Antacids inhibit the absorption of tetracyclines and vitamins and should not be taken concomitantly.
should not be concomitantly administered with tetracycline-containing antibiotics or any tetracycline salts
tetracyclines, and vitamins

items.t: Any oral medicine: do not take within 1 hour of the antacid; as a precaution separate by at least 2 hours (4 hours for fluoroquinolones) (simeticone-containing SmPC).

src.q: should not be taken simultaneously with other medicines as they may interfere with their absorption if taken within 1 hour
As a precaution, staggering the administration times of any orally administered drug and the antacid by at least 2 hours (4 hours for the fluoroquinolones).

items.t: Named medicines whose absorption aluminium-containing antacids may reduce include atenolol, propranolol, ciprofloxacin and other fluoroquinolones, dexamethasone and other glucocorticoids, hydroxychloroquine, iron salts, levothyroxine, lincosamides, rosuvastatin and tetracyclines (simeticone-containing SmPC).

src.q: Aluminium-containing antacids may prevent the proper absorption of drugs notably H2 antagonists, atenolol
ciprofloxacin, cyclines, dasatinib monohydrate, dexamethasone
fluoroquinolones, glucocorticoids, hydroxychloroquine, indomethacin, iron salts
ketoconazole, levothyroxine, lincosamides, metoprolol
propranolol, raltegravir potassium
rosuvastatin, sodium fluorure

items.t: Levothyroxine may also bind to simeticone, delaying or reducing its absorption (simeticone-containing product).

src.q: Levothyroxine may also bind to simeticone which may delay or reduce the absorption of levothyroxine.

items.t: Salicylates: urine alkalinisation from magnesium hydroxide can increase salicylate excretion.

src.q: Urine alkalinisation secondary to administration of magnesium hydroxide may modify excretion of some drugs; thus, increased excretion of salicylates has been seen.

items.t: Citrates: aluminium hydroxide with citrates may raise aluminium levels, especially in renal impairment (simeticone-containing SmPC).

src.q: Aluminium hydroxide and citrates may result in increased aluminium levels, especially in patients with renal impairment.

items.t: Kidney failure: should not be used (contraindicated in both UK SmPCs). No eGFR/CrCl threshold given.

src.q: Should not be used in patients who are severely debilitated or suffering from kidney failure.

items.t: Renal impairment: aluminium and magnesium levels rise; avoid prolonged use in renal failure. Very rare hypermagnesaemia after prolonged magnesium hydroxide in renal impairment.

src.q: In patients with renal impairment, plasma levels of both aluminium and magnesium increase.
The prolonged use of antacids in patients with renal failure should be avoided.
Observed after prolonged administration of magnesium hydroxide to patients with renal impairment.

hepatic.note: No hepatic impairment statements in the two UK SmPCs checked.

items.t: One UK SmPC: no clinical data in pregnancy; animal studies show no harm; use with caution in pregnant women.

src.q: For Mucogel no clinical data on exposed pregnancies are available.
Caution should be exercised when prescribing to pregnant women.

items.t: Simeticone-containing SmPC: safety not established; use only if the benefit to the mother outweighs the risks, including to the fetus.

src.q: should be used during pregnancy only if the potential benefits to the mother outweigh the potential risks

items.t: SPS: aluminium hydroxide and magnesium salts (including magnesium hydroxide) can be used during breastfeeding; no specific infant monitoring is usually needed.

src.q: Aluminium hydroxide can be used during breastfeeding.
Magnesium salts (magnesium carbonate, magnesium hydroxide, magnesium trisilicate) can be used during breastfeeding.
No specific infant monitoring is usually required.

items.t: Simeticone-containing SmPC: maternal systemic exposure is negligible, so no effect on the breastfed infant is expected.

src.q: No effect on the breastfed newborn/infant are anticipated since the systemic exposure of the breast-feeding woman to aluminium hydroxide, magnesium hydroxide and simeticone is negligible.

reproductive.note: No fertility or contraception statements in the two UK SmPCs checked.

adverseCommon.note: Neither UK SmPC lists common or very common adverse effects. Gastrointestinal effects (diarrhoea or constipation) are listed as uncommon.

items.t: Hypersensitivity reactions including angioedema and anaphylactic reactions (frequency not known; simeticone-containing SmPC).

src.q: hypersensitivity reactions, such as pruritus, urticaria, angioedema and anaphylactic reactions

items.t: Hypermagnesaemia (very rare, mainly with prolonged use in renal impairment); hyperaluminaemia and hypophosphataemia (frequency not known).

src.q: Very rare: Hypermagnesemia, including observations after prolonged administration of magnesium hydroxide to patients with renal impairment
Frequency not known: Hyperaluminemia Hypophosphatemia

items.t: Long-term use or risk of phosphate depletion: medical advice is recommended (simeticone-containing SmPC).

src.q: Medical advice is recommended in case of long-term use or in patients at risk of phosphate depletion.

items.t: Take 20 minutes to 1 hour after meals and at bedtime, or as required.

src.q: 10-20 ml three times daily 20 minutes to one hour after meals, and at bedtime, or as required.

items.t: Leave at least 2 hours between the antacid and other oral medicines (4 hours for fluoroquinolones) (simeticone-containing SmPC).

src.q: As a precaution, staggering the administration times of any orally administered drug and the antacid by at least 2 hours (4 hours for the fluoroquinolones).

items.t: Do not take other medicines at the same time as the antacid; leave at least 2 hours (4 hours for fluoroquinolone antibiotics).

src.q: As a precaution, staggering the administration times of any orally administered drug and the antacid by at least 2 hours (4 hours for the fluoroquinolones).

items.t: Tetracycline antibiotics: do not take at the same time as this antacid.

src.q: Antacids inhibit the absorption of tetracyclines and vitamins and should not be taken concomitantly.

items.t: Adults: major depressive disorder; neuropathic pain; prophylaxis of chronic tension-type headache; prophylaxis of migraine. Children 6 years and over: nocturnal enuresis after organic causes are excluded and all other drug and non-drug treatments have failed.

src.q: the treatment of major depressive disorder in adults the treatment of neuropathic pain in adults
the prophylactic treatment of chronic tension type headache (CTTH) in adults the prophylactic treatment of migraine in adults
the treatment of nocturnal enuresis in children aged 6 years and above when organic pathology, including spina bifida and related disorders, have been excluded

items.t: Enuresis: only to be prescribed by a healthcare professional with expertise in persistent enuresis.

src.q: This medicinal product should only be prescribed by a healthcare professional with expertise in the management of persistent enuresis.

items.t: Not for children and adolescents under 18 for depression or pain (long-term safety and efficacy not established). Contraindicated under 6 years.

src.q: Amitriptyline should not be used in children and adolescents aged less than 18 years, as long term safety and efficacy have not been established
In children under 6 years of age.

items.t: Start low and increase gradually. Initially 25 mg twice daily (50 mg daily); if needed increase by 25 mg every other day up to 150 mg daily in two divided doses. Maintenance: lowest effective dose. Effect usually after 2 to 4 weeks; continue usually up to 6 months after recovery.

src.q: Adults Initially 25 mg 2 times daily (50 mg daily). If necessary, the dose can be increased by 25 mg every other day up to 150 mg daily divided into two doses.
The antidepressant effect usually sets in after 2 - 4 weeks.
usually up to 6 months after recovery in order to prevent relapse

items.t: Over 65 years or cardiovascular disease: initially 10 mg to 25 mg daily, increase up to 100 mg to 150 mg daily in two divided doses as tolerated. Doses above 100 mg: use with caution.

src.q: Elderly patients over 65 years of age and patients with cardiovascular diseas e Initially 10 mg - 25 mg daily
The daily dose may be increased up to 100 mg - 150 mg divided into two doses, depending on individual patient response and tolerability. Doses above 100 mg should be used with caution.

items.t: Start 10 mg to 25 mg in the evening; increase by 10 mg to 25 mg every 3 to 7 days as tolerated. Usual dose 25 mg to 75 mg daily in the evening (once daily or two divided doses). A single dose above 75 mg is not recommended; doses above 100 mg with caution. Effect normally after 2 to 4 weeks; reassess regularly.
items.tag: Neuropathic pain, tension-type headache or migraine prophylaxis, adults

src.q: Recommended doses are 25 mg - 75 mg daily in the evening. Doses above 100 mg should be used with caution. The initial dose should be 10 mg - 25 mg in the evening.
Doses can be increased with 10 mg - 25 mg every 3 - 7 days as tolerated.
A single dose above 75 mg is not recommended.
Regular reassessment is recommended to confirm that continuation of the treatment remains appropriate for the patient.

items.t: Over 65 years or cardiovascular disease: start 10 mg to 25 mg in the evening; doses above 75 mg with caution.
items.tag: Pain or headache prophylaxis, elderly or cardiovascular disease

src.q: A starting dose of 10 mg - 25 mg in the evening is recommended. Doses above 75 mg should be used with caution.

items.t: Strong CYP2D6 inhibitor added (e.g. fluoxetine, paroxetine, bupropion, quinidine): consider a lower amitriptyline dose. Known CYP2D6 or CYP2C19 poor metabolisers: consider halving the starting dose.

src.q: a lower dose of amitriptyline should be considered if a strong CYP2D6 inhibitor (e.g. bupropion, quinidine, fluoxetine, paroxetine) is added to amitriptyline treatment
Consider a 50% reduction of the recommended starting dose.

items.t: Stopping: withdraw gradually over several weeks.

src.q: When stopping therapy the drug should be gradually withdrawn during several weeks.

items.t: Nocturnal enuresis: 6 to 10 years 10 mg to 20 mg (suitable dose form needed); 11 years and over 25 mg to 50 mg daily. Increase gradually; give 1 to 1.5 hours before bedtime. ECG before starting to exclude long QT syndrome. Maximum course 3 months; medical review every 3 months if repeated; withdraw gradually.

src.q: children aged 6 to 10 years: 10 mg - 20 mg. A suitable dosage form should be used for this age group children aged 11 years and above: 25 mg - 50 mg daily
Dose to be administered 1-1½ hours before bedtime.
An ECG should be performed prior to initiating therapy with amitriptyline to exclude long QT syndrome.
The maximum period of treatment course should not exceed 3 months.

items.t: Contraindicated under 6 years. Other indications: not for under 18 years. For enuresis, do not combine with an anticholinergic, and watch for suicidal thoughts as in depression.

src.q: In children under 6 years of age.
Amitriptyline for enuresis should not be combined with an anticholinergic drug.
the same precautions observed when treating patients with depression should therefore be followed when treating patients with enuresis

items.t: Hypersensitivity to amitriptyline or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Recent myocardial infarction; any degree of heart block or cardiac rhythm disorder; coronary artery insufficiency.

src.q: Recent myocardial infarction. Any degree of heart block or disorders of cardiac rhythm and coronary artery insufficiency.

items.t: MAO inhibitors (non-selective, MAO-A such as moclobemide, MAO-B such as selegiline): contraindicated (serotonin syndrome). Start amitriptyline 14 days after an irreversible non-selective MAOI (at least 1 day after moclobemide); start an MAOI 14 days after amitriptyline.

src.q: Concomitant treatment with MAOIs (monoamine oxidase inhibitors) is contra-indicated
Treatment with amitriptyline may be instituted 14 days after discontinuation of irreversible non- selective MAOIs and minimum one day after discontinuation of the reversible moclobemide.
Treatment with MAOIs may be introduced 14 days after discontinuation of amitriptyline.

items.t: Severe liver disease.

src.q: Severe liver disease.

items.t: Children under 6 years.

src.q: In children under 6 years of age.

items.t: Arrhythmias and severe hypotension are likely at high doses and can occur at normal doses in pre-existing heart disease. QT prolongation reported: caution with significant bradycardia, uncompensated heart failure or QT-prolonging drugs; hypokalaemia, hyperkalaemia and hypomagnesaemia raise the risk.

src.q: Cardiac arrhythmias and severe hypotension are likely to occur with high dosage. They may also occur in patients with pre-existing heart disease taking normal dosage.
Caution is advised in patients with significant bradycardia, in patients with uncompensated heart failure, or in patients concurrently taking QT-prolonging drugs.
Electrolyte disturbances (hypokalaemia, hyperkalaemia, hypomagnesaemia) are known to be conditions increasing the proarrythmic risk.

items.t: Use with caution in: convulsive disorders, urinary retention, prostatic hypertrophy, hyperthyroidism, paranoid symptoms, advanced liver or cardiovascular disease, pyloric stenosis and paralytic ileus. Narrow anterior chamber angle: acute glaucoma may be provoked.

src.q: This medical product should be used with caution in patients with convulsive disorders, urinary retention, prostatic hypertrophy, hyperthyroidism, paranoid symptomatology and advanced hepatic or cardiovascular disease, pylorus stenosis and paralytic ileus.
In patients with the rare condition of shallow anterior chamber and narrow chamber angle, attacks of acute glaucoma due to dilation of the pupil may be provoked.

items.t: Hyperthyroidism or thyroid medication: great care (arrhythmias). Elderly are particularly prone to orthostatic hypotension.

src.q: Great care is necessary if amitriptyline is administered to hyperthyroid patients or to those receiving thyroid medication, since cardiac arrhythmias may develop.
Elderly patients are particularly susceptible to orthostatic hypotension.

items.t: Surgery: anaesthetics may increase arrhythmia and hypotension risk. If possible stop several days before surgery; otherwise tell the anaesthetist.

src.q: If possible, discontinue this medicinal product several days before surgery; if emergency surgery is unavoidable, the anaesthetist should be informed that the patient is being so treated.

items.t: Suicidal thoughts/behaviour: monitor closely, especially early in treatment, after dose changes, under 25 years and with prior suicidality.

src.q: Close supervision of patients and in particular those at high risk should accompany drug therapy especially in early treatment and following dose changes.

items.t: Bipolar illness: a switch to mania may occur; stop amitriptyline if a manic phase starts.

src.q: In manic-depressives, a shift towards the manic phase may occur; should the patient enter a manic phase amitriptyline should be discontinued.

items.t: Serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic drugs (MAOIs, SSRIs, SNRIs, certain opioids such as tramadol or buprenorphine, other TCAs): can be life-threatening. Use with caution with SSRIs; observe carefully if combined.

src.q: Amitriptyline should be used with caution in patients receiving SSRIs
may lead to serotonin syndrome, which can be life-threatening condition

items.t: Diabetes: may change insulin and glucose responses; antidiabetic therapy may need adjustment.

src.q: amitriptyline may modify insulin and glucose responses calling for adjustment of the antidiabetic therapy in diabetic patients

items.t: Severe skin reactions including DRESS (mostly within 2 to 6 weeks): warn the patient; stop at once if signs appear and never restart.

src.q: At the time of prescription patients should be advised of the signs and symptoms and monitored closely for cutaneous reactions.
Amitriptyline should be withdrawn immediately, treatment with Amitriptyline must not be restarted in this patient at any time

items.t: Hyperpyrexia reported with anticholinergic or neuroleptic drugs, especially in hot weather. Abrupt stopping after long use may cause withdrawal symptoms. Lactose: not for hereditary galactose intolerance, lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption.

src.q: Hyperpyrexia has been reported with tricyclic antidepressants when administered with anticholinergic or with neuroleptic medications, especially in hot weather.
abrupt cessation of therapy may produce withdrawal symptoms such as headache, malaise, insomnia and irritability
Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: Contraindicated: MAO inhibitors (non-selective, MAO-A and MAO-B), risk of serotonin syndrome.

src.q: With MAO inhibitors (non-selective as well as MAO A-selective (moclobemide) and MAO B-selective (selegiline)) - risk of "serotonin syndrome"

items.t: Not recommended: sympathomimetics such as adrenaline, ephedrine, phenylephrine (including in anaesthetics and nasal decongestants); centrally acting antihypertensives such as clonidine and methyldopa (review all antihypertensive therapy).

src.q: Combinations that are not recommended Sympathomimetic agents : Amitriptyline may potentiate the cardiovascular effects of adrenaline, ephedrine, isoprenaline, noradrenaline, phenylephrine, and phenylpropanolamine
Tricyclic antidepressants may counteract the antihypertensive effects of centrally acting antihypertensives such as guanethidine, betanidine, reserpine, clonidine and methyldopa.

items.t: Anticholinergic drugs: avoid (paralytic ileus, hyperpyrexia).

src.q: concomitant use of these should be avoided due to an increased risk of paralytic ileus, hyperpyrexia, etc.

items.t: QT-prolonging drugs (e.g. quinidine, some antipsychotics, sotalol, halofantrine): more ventricular arrhythmias. Methadone: caution. Diuretics that cause hypokalaemia (e.g. furosemide): caution.

src.q: may increase the likelihood of ventricular arrhythmias when taken with tricyclic antidepressants
Caution is also advised for co-administration of amitriptyline and diuretics inducing hypokalaemia (e.g. furosemide)

items.t: Tramadol: higher risk of seizures and serotonin syndrome, and possible opioid toxicity (raised tramadol levels).

src.q: Concomitant use of tramadol (a CYP2D6 substrate) and tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs), such as amitriptyline increases the risk for seizures and serotonin syndrome.

items.t: Fluconazole and terbinafine raise tricyclic levels; syncope and torsade de pointes have occurred.

src.q: Antifungals such as fluconazole and terbinafine increase serum concentrations of tricyclics and accompanying toxicity. Syncope and torsade de pointes have occurred.

items.t: Strong CYP2D6 inhibitors (e.g. fluoxetine, paroxetine, bupropion): marked rise in amitriptyline levels; consider TCA levels and dose adjustment. Duloxetine (moderate CYP2D6 inhibitor): caution.

src.q: These drugs may produce substantial decreases in TCA metabolism and marked increases in plasma concentrations.
Caution is advised in the case of co-administration of amitriptyline with duloxetine, a moderate CYP2D6 inhibitor.

items.t: Diltiazem, verapamil, cimetidine, methylphenidate may raise TCA levels; strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir) may interact. Fluvoxamine: avoid.

src.q: Cimetidine, methylphenidate and calcium-channel blockers (e.g. diltiazem and verapamil) may increase plasma levels of tricyclic antidepressants and accompanying toxicity.
Clinically relevant interactions may be expected with concomitant use of amitriptyline and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ketoconazole, itraconazole and ritonavir.

items.t: Inducers (oral contraceptives, rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, St John's wort) may lower amitriptyline levels and response. The St John's wort herbal SPC says do not take it with tricyclics.

src.q: Oral contraceptives, rifampicin, phenytoin, barbiturates, carbamazepine and St. John's Wort (Hypericum perforatum) may increase the metabolism of tricyclic antidepressants
Tricyclics e.g. Reduced blood levels with Do not take with this product. Amitriptyline

items.t: CNS depressants and alcohol: increased sedation. Sodium valproate raises amitriptyline levels (clinical monitoring).

src.q: Amitriptyline may enhance the sedative effects of alcohol, barbiturates and other CNS depressants.
Amitriptyline plasma concentration can be increased by sodium valproate and valpromide. Clinical monitoring is therefore recommended.

items.t: Usual doses can be given in renal failure.

src.q: This medicinal product can be given in usual doses to patients with renal failure.

items.t: Severe liver disease: contraindicated. Other hepatic impairment: careful dosing and, if possible, serum level measurement.

src.q: Severe liver disease.
Careful dosing and, if possible, a serum level determination is advisable.

items.t: SmPC: not recommended unless clearly necessary and only after careful risk-benefit assessment. Neonatal withdrawal (irritability, hypertonia, tremor, irregular breathing, poor drinking) can follow use in the final weeks.

src.q: Amitriptyline is not recommended during pregnancy unless clearly necessary and only after careful consideration of the risk/benefit.
During chronic use and after administration in the final weeks of pregnancy, neonatal withdrawal symptoms can occur.

items.t: BUMPS: can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a specialist; not known to harm the baby. Use near delivery may cause neonatal withdrawal; hospital delivery recommended.

src.q: Amitriptyline can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a specialist.
Amitriptyline use in pregnancy is not known to harm the baby.
A hospital delivery will be recommended so that your baby can be assessed after birth

items.t: SmPC: passes into milk (0.6% to 1% of the maternal dose); risk to the infant cannot be excluded. Decide whether to stop breastfeeding or stop the medicine.

src.q: A risk to the suckling child cannot be excluded.
A decision must be made whether to discontinue breast-feeding or to discontinue/abstain from the therapy

items.t: SPS: can be used with caution, but imipramine or nortriptyline are preferred. Monitor the infant for drowsiness, poor feeding, weight gain, irritability, constipation and urinary retention. Avoid bed-sharing when sedating medicines are used (NICE, cited by SPS).

src.q: Amitriptyline can be used with caution during breastfeeding, but imipramine or nortriptyline are preferred.
As a precaution, monitor infants for drowsiness, not waking to feed or poor feeding, adequate weight gain, irritability, constipation and urinary retention
advises avoiding sharing a bed with the infant when sedating medication has been used

items.t: Fertility: reduced pregnancy rate in rats; no human data. Erectile dysfunction is common. MHRA: amitriptyline is among antidepressants linked to sexual dysfunction that may continue after stopping.

src.q: No data on the effects of amitriptyline on human fertility are available.
Citalopram, escitalopram, duloxetine, fluvoxamine, fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline, venlafaxine, amitriptyline, nortriptyline
are associated with a risk of sexual dysfunction and that symptoms may continue after stopping treatment with certain antidepressants

items.t: Very common: somnolence, tremor, dizziness, headache, dysarthria; aggression; accommodation disorder; palpitations, tachycardia; orthostatic hypotension; congested nose; dry mouth, constipation, nausea; sweating; weight gain.

src.q: Nervous system disorders Very common Somnolence, tremor, dizziness, headache, drowsiness, speech disorder (dysarthria).
Cardiac disorders Very common Palpitations, tachycardia.
Gastrointestinal disorders Very common Dry mouth, constipation, nausea.
Vascular disorders Very common Orthostatic hypotension.

items.t: Common: hyponatraemia; confusion, reduced libido, agitation; disturbed attention, taste change, paraesthesia, ataxia; mydriasis; AV block, bundle branch block; micturition disorders; erectile dysfunction; fatigue; ECG QT/QRS prolongation.

src.q: Metabolism and nutrition disorders Common Hyponatremia.
Common Atrioventricular block, bundle branch block.
Common Electrocardiogram abnormal, electrocardiogram QT prolonged, electrocardiogram QRS complex prolonged.

items.t: Serious skin reactions including DRESS (can be fatal): stop immediately and never restart.

src.q: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs) including drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), which can be life-threatening or fatal

items.t: Serotonin syndrome (mental-status change, autonomic instability, neuromuscular signs): consider dose reduction or stopping depending on severity.

src.q: If serotonin syndrome is suspected, a dose reduction or discontinuation of therapy should be considered depending on the severity of the symptoms.

items.t: Suicidal thoughts or behaviour: patients and carers should seek medical advice immediately.

src.q: to seek medical advice immediately if these symptoms present

items.t: Rare/very rare: arrhythmia, torsade de pointes, convulsion (uncommon), bone marrow depression/agranulocytosis, paralytic ileus, jaundice, acute glaucoma.

src.q: Rare Bone marrow depression, agranulocytosis, leucopenia, eosinophilia, thrombocytopenia.
Very rare Cardiomyopathies, torsades de pointes.

items.t: Overdose is dangerous (750 mg or more in an adult may cause severe toxicity); children are especially at risk.

src.q: Ingestion of 750 mg or more by an adult may result in severe toxicity.
Overdose with amitriptyline in children could have serious consequences.

items.t: Enuresis: ECG before starting to exclude long QT syndrome.

src.q: An ECG should be performed prior to initiating therapy with amitriptyline to exclude long QT syndrome.

items.t: When starting or changing dose: discuss risk of suicidal thoughts and sexual dysfunction; monitor regularly after starting (MHRA 2026).

src.q: discuss with patients when starting or changing the dose of an antidepressant or at their next review, the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviours
monitor your patients regularly after starting treatment with an antidepressant

items.t: Monitor closely for clinical worsening and suicidality; watch for skin reactions. With strong CYP2D6 inhibitors, consider TCA plasma levels. SPS: ECG, magnesium and potassium in people with non-modifiable QT risk factors.

src.q: patients should be closely monitored until such improvement occurs
Consider to monitor TCA plasma levels, whenever a TCA is to be co-administered with another drug known to be a strong inhibitor of CYP2D6.
Monitor ECG, magnesium and potassium in people with non-modifiable risk factors.

items.t: Neuropathic pain and headache prophylaxis: reassess regularly whether to continue. Enuresis: review every 3 months for repeated courses.

src.q: Regular reassessment is recommended to confirm that continuation of the treatment remains appropriate for the patient.
If repeated courses of amitriptyline are needed, a medical review should be conducted every 3 months.

items.t: Stop if: manic phase; severe skin reaction (do not restart). Consider reducing or stopping if serotonin syndrome.

src.q: should the patient enter a manic phase amitriptyline should be discontinued
Amitriptyline should be withdrawn immediately

items.t: Swallow tablets with water. Pain/headache: dose in the evening (once daily or two divided doses). Depression: two divided doses.

src.q: These tablets should be swallowed with water.
The dose can be taken once daily, or be divided into two doses.

items.t: Causes sedation: take care with driving or machines; alcohol makes this worse.

src.q: should be cautioned about their ability to drive or operate machinery
These adverse effects can be potentiated by the concomitant intake of alcohol.

items.t: Seek urgent help (NHS 111, crisis team, Samaritans 116 123) for new or worse suicidal thoughts. Do not stop without speaking to the prescriber.

src.q: You can call NHS 111, or your local mental health crisis team, Samaritans on 116 123
do not stop taking your medicine without first speaking to your healthcare professional

items.t: Know the signs of a serious skin reaction and report them at once. Effect on mood or pain usually takes 2 to 4 weeks.

src.q: At the time of prescription patients should be advised of the signs and symptoms and monitored closely for cutaneous reactions.
The analgesic effect is normally seen after 2 - 4 weeks of dosing.

items.t: Hypertension; chronic stable angina; vasospastic (Prinzmetal's) angina.

src.q: Hypertension Chronic stable angina pectoris Vasospastic (Prinzmetal's) angina

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction stated in the amlodipine 5 mg tablets SmPC.

items.t: Adults: start 5 mg once daily; may increase to a maximum of 10 mg once daily depending on response.

src.q: For both hypertension and angina the usual initial dose is 5 mg Amlodipine once daily which may be increased to a maximum dose of 10 mg depending on the individual patient's response.

items.t: Elderly: normal doses; increase the dose with care.

src.q: Normal dosage regimens are recommended in the elderly, but increase of the dosage should take place with care

items.t: No amlodipine dose adjustment is needed when given with thiazide diuretics, beta blockers or ACE inhibitors.

src.q: No dose adjustment of amlodipine is required upon concomitant administration of thiazide diuretics, beta blockers, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors.

items.t: Hypertension, 6 to 17 years: 2.5 mg once daily; increase to 5 mg once daily if blood pressure goal not reached after 4 weeks. Doses above 5 mg daily have not been studied in children.

src.q: The recommended antihypertensive oral dose in paediatric patients aged 6-17 years is 2.5 mg once daily as a starting dose, up-titrated to 5 mg once daily if blood pressure goal is not achieved after 4 weeks.
Doses in excess of 5 mg daily have not been studied in paediatric patients

items.t: Under 6 years: no data available.

src.q: Children under 6 years old No data are available.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to amlodipine, other dihydropyridines or any excipient.

src.q: hypersensitivity to the active substance, dihydropyridine derivatives or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1

items.t: Severe hypotension; shock (including cardiogenic shock).

src.q: severe hypotension shock (including cardiogenic shock)

items.t: Left ventricular outflow tract obstruction (e.g. high-grade aortic stenosis).

src.q: obstruction of the outflow tract of the left ventricle (e.g. high-grade aortic stenosis)

items.t: Haemodynamically unstable heart failure after acute myocardial infarction.

src.q: haemodynamically unstable heart failure after acute myocardial infarction

items.t: Heart failure: use with caution. In severe heart failure (NYHA III-IV) more pulmonary oedema was reported with amlodipine than placebo; calcium-channel blockers may increase the risk of future cardiovascular events and mortality in congestive heart failure.

src.q: Patients with heart failure should be treated with caution.
Calcium channel blockers, including amlodipine, should be used with caution in patients with congestive heart failure, as they may increase the risk of future cardiovascular events and mortality.

items.t: Hepatic impairment: half-life prolonged and exposure higher; start at the lower end of the dose range and use caution when starting and when increasing the dose.

src.q: Amlodipine should therefore be initiated at the lower end of the dosing range and caution should be used, both on initial treatment and when increasing the dose.

items.t: Safety and efficacy in hypertensive crisis not established.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of amlodipine in hypertensive crisis has not been established.

items.t: Strong or moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. clarithromycin, erythromycin, azole antifungals, protease inhibitors, diltiazem, verapamil): amlodipine exposure may rise markedly, with more risk of hypotension (more so in the elderly). Clinical monitoring and dose adjustment may be needed.

src.q: Concomitant use of amlodipine with strong or moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors (protease inhibitors, azole antifungals, macrolides like erythromycin or clarithromycin, verapamil or diltiazem) may give rise to significant increase in amlodipine exposure
Clinical monitoring and dose adjustment may thus be required.

items.t: CYP3A4 inducers (e.g. rifampicin, St John's wort): amlodipine levels may change. Monitor blood pressure and consider dose adjustment during and after the combination.

src.q: blood pressure should be monitored and dose regulation considered both during and after concomitant medication particularly with strong CYP3A4 inducers (e.g. rifampicin, hypericum perforatum).

items.t: Simvastatin: limit simvastatin to 20 mg daily in patients taking amlodipine (amlodipine 10 mg raised simvastatin exposure by 77%). MHRA: the 20 mg maximum applies with amlodipine 5 mg and 10 mg.

src.q: Limit the dose of simvastatin in patients on amlodipine to 20 mg daily.
The maximum recommended dose of simvastatin co-administered with amlodipine or diltiazem is now 20 mg per day.
the recommendation for a maximum daily dose of simvastatin of 20 mg applies with amlodipine at doses of both 10 mg and 5 mg.

items.t: Other antihypertensives: additive blood pressure lowering.

src.q: The blood pressure lowering effects of amlodipine adds to the blood pressure-lowering effects of other medicinal products with antihypertensive properties.

items.t: Grapefruit or grapefruit juice: not recommended (may increase blood pressure lowering).

src.q: Administration of amlodipine with grapefruit or grapefruit juice is not recommended

items.t: Tacrolimus: risk of raised tacrolimus levels; monitor tacrolimus levels and adjust its dose. Ciclosporin (renal transplant): consider monitoring ciclosporin levels and reducing its dose as needed.

src.q: administration of amlodipine in a patient treated with tacrolimus requires monitoring of tacrolimus blood levels and dose adjustment of tacrolimus when appropriate.
Consideration should be given for monitoring ciclosporin levels in renal transplant patients on amlodipine

items.t: Atorvastatin, digoxin and warfarin: amlodipine did not affect their pharmacokinetics in interaction studies.

src.q: amlodipine did not affect the pharmacokinetics of atorvastatin, digoxin or warfarin

items.t: Dantrolene infusion / malignant hyperthermia: avoid calcium-channel blockers such as amlodipine in patients susceptible to malignant hyperthermia and in its management (risk of hyperkalaemia; ventricular fibrillation and collapse seen in animals with verapamil plus IV dantrolene).

src.q: it is recommended that the co-administration of calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine be avoided in patients susceptible to malignant hyperthermia and in the management of malignant hyperthermia
In animals, lethal ventricular fibrillation and cardiovascular collapse are observed in association with hyperkalaemia after administration of verapamil and intravenous dantrolene.

items.t: mTOR inhibitors (sirolimus, temsirolimus, everolimus): amlodipine is a weak CYP3A inhibitor and may increase their exposure.

src.q: mTOR inhibitors such as sirolimus, temsirolimus, and everolimus are CYP3A substrates.
With concomitant use of mTOR inhibitors, amlodipine may increase exposure of mTOR inhibitors.

items.t: Normal dose in renal impairment (plasma levels do not correlate with degree of renal impairment). Not dialysable.

src.q: Changes in amlodipine plasma concentrations are not correlated with degree of renal impairment, therefore the normal dosage is recommended.
Amlodipine is not dialysable.

items.t: Mild to moderate hepatic impairment: no established dose; choose the dose cautiously and start at the lower end of the range.

src.q: Dosage recommendations have not been established in patients with mild to moderate hepatic impairment, therefore dose selection should be cautious and should start at the lower end of the dosing range

items.t: Severe hepatic impairment: not studied; start at the lowest dose and titrate slowly. Careful monitoring may be needed.

src.q: Amlodipine should be initiated at the lowest dose and titrated slowly in patients with severe hepatic impairment.
Slow dose titration and careful monitoring may be required in patients with severe hepatic impairment.

items.t: SmPC: safety in human pregnancy not established. Use only when there is no safer alternative and the disease itself carries greater risk for mother and fetus.

src.q: The safety of amlodipine in human pregnancy has not been established.
Use in pregnancy is only recommended when there is no safer alternative and when the disease itself carries greater risk for the mother and foetus.

items.t: BUMPS (calcium-channel blockers leaflet): no clear risks from calcium-channel blockers in pregnancy; nifedipine is the one commonly used. Others are less used and recommended only when benefit outweighs possible risk. No extra monitoring for major birth defects is needed.

src.q: There are no clear risks of taking a calcium channel blocker in pregnancy.

The other calcium channel blockers are less commonly used, and while not thought to cause problems, will only be recommended if the benefits of treating a potentially serious or lifestyle-impacting condition outweigh any possible risks.
No extra monitoring for major birth defects is required following use of a calcium channel blocker.

items.t: SmPC: amlodipine passes into breast milk (infant dose estimated at 3-7% of maternal dose, maximum 15%). Weigh the benefit of breastfeeding against the benefit of treatment.

src.q: Amlodipine is excreted in human milk.

A decision on whether to continue/discontinue breast-feeding or to continue/discontinue therapy with amlodipine should be made taking into account the benefit of breast-feeding to the child and the benefit of amlodipine therapy to the mother.

items.t: SPS: use with caution; nifedipine is the preferred dihydropyridine. As a precaution, watch the infant for hypotension (drowsiness, lethargy, pallor, poor feeding, poor weight gain). Advice applies to full-term, healthy infants.

src.q: It can be used with caution during breastfeeding, but nifedipine is the preferred dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker.
As a precaution, monitor the infant for hypotension which may manifest as drowsiness, lethargy, looking pale , poor feeding and inadequate weight gain.
Recommendations apply to full term and healthy infants only.

items.t: Reversible changes in the head of spermatozoa have been reported with calcium-channel blockers; clinical data on fertility are insufficient.

src.q: Reversible biochemical changes in the head of spermatozoa have been reported in some patients treated by calcium channel blockers.
Clinical data are insufficient regarding the potential effect of amlodipine on fertility.

items.t: Very common: oedema. Common: somnolence, dizziness, headache, palpitations, flushing, abdominal pain, nausea, dyspepsia, altered bowel habit, ankle swelling, muscle cramps, visual disturbance, dyspnoea, fatigue, asthenia.

src.q: The most commonly reported adverse reactions during treatment are somnolence, dizziness, headache, palpitations, flushing, abdominal pain, nausea, ankle swelling, oedema and fatigue.
General disorders and administration site conditions Very common Oedema Common Fatigue, asthenia

items.t: Very rare: angioedema, erythema multiforme, exfoliative dermatitis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome; toxic epidermal necrolysis (frequency not known).

src.q: Very rare Angioedema, erythema multiforme, exfoliative dermatitis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, Quincke oedema, photosensitivity Not known Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis

items.t: Very rare: hepatitis, jaundice, raised liver enzymes (mostly cholestatic); pancreatitis; leucopenia, thrombocytopenia; myocardial infarction.

src.q: Very rare Hepatitis, jaundice, hepatic enzymes increased*
Very rare Pancreatitis, gastritis, gingival hyperplasia
Very rare Leukocytopenia, thrombocytopenia
Very rare Myocardial infarction

items.t: Overdose: marked, possibly prolonged hypotension up to fatal shock; non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema may appear 24-48 hours after ingestion. Dialysis unlikely to help.

src.q: Marked and probably prolonged systemic hypotension up to and including shock with fatal outcome have been reported.
Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema has rarely been reported as a consequence of amlodipine overdose that may manifest with a delayed onset (24-48 hours post-ingestion) and require ventilatory support.

items.t: With CYP3A4 inducers: monitor blood pressure during and after the combination.

src.q: blood pressure should be monitored and dose regulation considered both during and after concomitant medication

items.t: Severe hepatic impairment: slow titration and careful monitoring may be needed.

src.q: Slow dose titration and careful monitoring may be required in patients with severe hepatic impairment.

items.t: With tacrolimus: monitor tacrolimus blood levels.

src.q: requires monitoring of tacrolimus blood levels

items.t: Oral, once daily. Food does not affect absorption.

src.q: The bioavailability of amlodipine is not affected by food intake.

items.t: Dizziness, headache, tiredness or nausea can affect driving; take care especially at the start of treatment.

src.q: If patients taking amlodipine suffer from dizziness, headache, fatigue or nausea the ability to react may be impaired.
Caution is recommended especially at the start of treatment.

items.t: Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice.

src.q: Administration of amlodipine with grapefruit or grapefruit juice is not recommended

items.t: Ankle swelling and oedema are common.

src.q: Musculoskeletal and connective tissue disorders Common Ankle swelling, muscle cramps

items.t: Essential hypertension in adults whose blood pressure is not adequately controlled on amlodipine or valsartan alone.

src.q: Treatment of essential hypertension.
is indicated in adults whose blood pressure is not adequately controlled on amlodipine or valsartan monotherapy.

items.t: Second-line combination only: for adults not controlled on either component alone. Not studied in any population other than hypertension.

src.q: is indicated in adults whose blood pressure is not adequately controlled on amlodipine or valsartan monotherapy.
has not been studied in any patient population other than hypertension.

items.t: Dual RAAS blockade, if absolutely necessary, only under specialist supervision with frequent close monitoring (see cautions).

src.q: If dual blockade therapy is considered absolutely necessary, this should only occur under specialist supervision and subject to frequent close monitoring of renal function, electrolytes and blood pressure.

items.t: One tablet once daily. 5 mg/160 mg: for patients not controlled on amlodipine 5 mg or valsartan 160 mg alone. 10 mg/160 mg: for patients not controlled on amlodipine 10 mg or valsartan 160 mg alone, or on the 5 mg/160 mg combination.

src.q: The recommended dose of Exforge is one tablet per day.
may be administered in patients whose blood pressure is not adequately controlled with amlodipine 5 mg or valsartan 160 mg alone.
may be administered in patients whose blood pressure is not adequately controlled with amlodipine 10 mg or valsartan 160 mg alone or with Exforge 5 mg/160 mg.

items.t: Titrate the individual components before changing to the fixed-dose combination; a direct switch from monotherapy may be considered when clinically appropriate. Patients on separate amlodipine and valsartan tablets can switch to the combination with the same component doses.

src.q: Individual dose titration with the components (i.e. amlodipine and valsartan) is recommended before changing to the fixed dose combination.
When clinically appropriate, direct change from monotherapy to the fixed-dose combination may be considered.
may be switched to Exforge containing the same component doses.

items.t: Elderly (65 years or over): caution when increasing the dose; when switching, use the lowest available amlodipine dose.

src.q: In elderly patients, caution is required when increasing the dosage.

When switching eligible elderly hypertensive patients (see section 4.1) to amlodipine or Exforge, the lowest available dose of amlodipine monotherapy or of the amlodipine component, respectively, should be used.

items.t: Safety and efficacy below 18 years not established; no data.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of Exforge in children aged below 18 years have not been established. No data are available.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to amlodipine, valsartan, other dihydropyridines or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substances, to dihydropyridine derivatives, or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Severe hepatic impairment, biliary cirrhosis or cholestasis.

src.q: Severe hepatic impairment, biliary cirrhosis or cholestasis.

items.t: With aliskiren-containing products in patients with diabetes or renal impairment (GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m²).

src.q: Concomitant use of Exforge with aliskiren-containing products in patients with diabetes mellitus or renal impairment (GFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m2)

items.t: Second and third trimesters of pregnancy.

src.q: Second and third trimesters of pregnancy (see sections 4.4 and 4.6).

items.t: Severe hypotension; shock (including cardiogenic shock); left ventricular outflow obstruction (e.g. hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, high-grade aortic stenosis); haemodynamically unstable heart failure after acute myocardial infarction.

src.q: Severe hypotension. Shock (including cardiogenic shock). Obstruction of the outflow tract of the left ventricle (e.g. hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy and high grade aortic stenosis). Haemodynamically unstable heart failure after acute myocardial infarction.

items.t: Sodium- and/or volume-depleted patients (e.g. high-dose diuretics): symptomatic hypotension may occur. Correct first or give close medical supervision at the start. If hypotension occurs, lay the patient supine and give IV normal saline if needed; treatment can continue once BP is stable.

src.q: In patients with an activated renin-angiotensin system (such as volume- and/or salt-depleted patients receiving high doses of diuretics) who are receiving angiotensin receptor blockers, symptomatic hypotension may occur.
Correction of this condition prior to administration of Exforge or close medical supervision at the start of treatment is recommended.
Treatment can be continued once blood pressure has been stabilised.

items.t: Hyperkalaemia: potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium salt substitutes or other potassium-raising medicines (e.g. heparin) only with caution and frequent potassium monitoring.

src.q: Concomitant use with potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics, salt substitutes containing potassium, or other medicinal products that may increase potassium levels (heparin, etc.) should be undertaken with caution and with frequent monitoring of potassium levels.

items.t: Unilateral or bilateral renal artery stenosis, or stenosis to a solitary kidney: use with caution; urea and creatinine may rise.

src.q: should be used with caution to treat hypertension in patients with unilateral or bilateral renal artery stenosis or stenosis to a solitary kidney since blood urea and serum creatinine may increase in such patients.

items.t: Mild to moderate hepatic impairment or biliary obstructive disorders: particular caution; maximum valsartan 80 mg (without cholestasis); amlodipine dose not established, use the lowest available amlodipine dose when switching.

src.q: Particular caution should be exercised when administering Exforge to patients with mild to moderate hepatic impairment or biliary obstructive disorders.
In patients with mild to moderate hepatic impairment without cholestasis, the maximum recommended dose is 80 mg valsartan.

items.t: Primary hyperaldosteronism: should not be treated with valsartan.

src.q: Patients with primary hyperaldosteronism should not be treated with the angiotensin II antagonist valsartan as their renin-angiotensin system is affected by the primary disease.

items.t: Angioedema (larynx, glottis, face, lips, pharynx, tongue) reported with valsartan, some after previous angioedema with other medicines including ACE inhibitors. Stop immediately and do not give again. Intestinal angioedema (abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea) also reported: stop valsartan and monitor until resolved.

src.q: Some of these patients previously experienced angioedema with other medicinal products, including ACE inhibitors.
should be discontinued immediately in patients who develop angioedema and should not be re-administered.
If intestinal angioedema is diagnosed, valsartan should be discontinued and appropriate monitoring should be initiated until complete resolution of symptoms has occurred.

items.t: Heart failure or post-MI: always assess renal function (severe heart failure: oliguria, azotaemia, rarely acute renal failure). Calcium-channel blockers including amlodipine: use with caution in congestive heart failure.

src.q: Evaluation of patients with heart failure or post-myocardial infarction should always include assessment of renal function.
Calcium channel blockers, including amlodipine, should be used with caution in patients with congestive heart failure, as they may increase the risk of future cardiovascular events and mortality.

items.t: Mitral stenosis or significant (not high-grade) aortic stenosis: special caution.

src.q: special caution is indicated in patients suffering from mitral stenosis or significant aortic stenosis that is not high grade.

items.t: Dual RAAS blockade (ACE inhibitor, ARB or aliskiren) not recommended; if absolutely necessary only under specialist supervision with close monitoring. Do not combine an ACE inhibitor and ARB in diabetic nephropathy.

src.q: Dual blockade of RAAS through the combined use of ACE inhibitors, ARBs or aliskiren is therefore not recommended
ACE inhibitors and ARBs should not be used concomitantly in patients with diabetic nephropathy.

items.t: Recent kidney transplant: no experience of safe use.

src.q: To date there is no experience of the safe use of Exforge in patients who have had a recent kidney transplantation.

items.t: Hypertensive crisis: safety and efficacy of amlodipine not established.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of amlodipine in hypertensive crisis have not been established.

items.t: Simvastatin: amlodipine raises simvastatin exposure (77% with 80 mg). Limit simvastatin to 20 mg daily.

src.q: It is recommended to limit the dose of simvastatin to 20 mg daily in patients on amlodipine.
the maximum daily dose of simvastatin should not exceed 20 mg when co-administered with amlodipine or diltiazem

items.t: Strong or moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors (azole antifungals, macrolides such as clarithromycin, verapamil, diltiazem, protease inhibitors): may markedly raise amlodipine exposure, more so in the elderly. Clinical monitoring and dose adjustment may be needed.

src.q: Concomitant use of amlodipine with strong or moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors (protease inhibitors, azole antifungals, macrolides like erythromycin or clarithromycin, verapamil or diltiazem) may give rise to significant increase in amlodipine exposure.
Clinical monitoring and dose adjustment may thus be required.
Caution required with concomitant use CYP3A4 inhibitors

items.t: CYP3A4 inducers (e.g. carbamazepine, St John's wort, rifampicin): amlodipine levels may vary. Monitor blood pressure and consider dose regulation during and after use, particularly with strong inducers.

src.q: CYP3A4 inducers (anticonvulsant agents [e.g. carbamazepine, phenobarbital, phenytoin, fosphenytoin, primidone], rifampicin, Hypericum perforatum)
blood pressure should be monitored and dose regulation considered both during and after concomitant medication particularly with strong CYP3A4 inducers (e.g. rifampicin, hypericum perforatum).

items.t: Potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements, potassium salt substitutes and other potassium-raising medicines: listed under 'concomitant use not recommended'; if used, monitor potassium.

src.q: Interactions linked to valsartan Concomitant use not recommended
If a medicinal product that affects potassium levels is to be prescribed in combination with valsartan, monitoring of potassium plasma levels is advised.

items.t: NSAIDs, including COX-2 inhibitors and aspirin above 3 g/day: reduced antihypertensive effect, risk of worsening renal function and raised potassium. Monitor renal function at the start and keep the patient hydrated.

src.q: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medicines (NSAIDs), including selective COX-2 inhibitors, acetylsalicylic acid (>3 g/day), and non-selective NSAIDs
concomitant use of angiotensin II antagonists and NSAIDs may lead to an increased risk of worsening of renal function and an increase in serum potassium.
Therefore, monitoring of renal function at the beginning of the treatment is recommended, as well as adequate hydration of the patient.

items.t: ACE inhibitors, other ARBs or aliskiren (dual RAAS blockade): more hypotension, hyperkalaemia and reduced renal function including acute renal failure. Not recommended.

src.q: dual blockade of the RAAS through the combined use of ACE inhibitors, ARBs or aliskiren is associated with a higher frequency of adverse events such as hypotension, hyperkalaemia and decreased renal function (including acute renal failure)
Combination use of medicines from two classes of RAS blocking agents (ACE-inhibitors, ARBs, or aliskiren) is not recommended.

items.t: Other antihypertensives (e.g. alpha blockers, diuretics) and medicines that lower blood pressure (e.g. tricyclic antidepressants): may increase the blood pressure-lowering effect.

src.q: Commonly used antihypertensive agents (e.g. alpha blockers, diuretics) and other medicinal products which may cause hypotensive adverse effects (e.g. tricyclic antidepressants, alpha blockers for treatment of benign prostate hyperplasia) may increase the antihypertensive effect of the combination.

items.t: Grapefruit or grapefruit juice: not recommended (may raise amlodipine levels and increase blood pressure lowering).

src.q: Administration of amlodipine with grapefruit or grapefruit juice is not recommended as bioavailability may be increased in some patients, resulting in increased blood pressure lowering effects.

items.t: Lithium: not recommended (raised lithium levels and toxicity); if used, monitor lithium levels carefully. Tacrolimus: monitor tacrolimus levels. Rifampicin, ciclosporin, ritonavir may raise valsartan exposure. Dantrolene infusion/malignant hyperthermia: avoid calcium-channel blockers.

src.q: Therefore, careful monitoring of serum lithium levels is recommended during concomitant use.
administration of amlodipine in a patient treated with tacrolimus requires monitoring of tacrolimus blood levels and dose adjustment of tacrolimus when appropriate.
Co-administration of inhibitors of the uptake transporter (rifampicin, ciclosporin) or efflux transporter (ritonavir) may increase the systemic exposure to valsartan.

items.t: No clinically significant interaction found between amlodipine and atorvastatin, digoxin, warfarin or ciclosporin pharmacokinetics, or between valsartan and warfarin, furosemide, atenolol, hydrochlorothiazide or glibenclamide.

src.q: amlodipine did not affect the pharmacokinetics of atorvastatin, digoxin, warfarin or ciclosporin.
cimetidine, warfarin, furosemide, digoxin, atenolol, indometacin, hydrochlorothiazide, amlodipine, glibenclamide.

items.t: Mild to moderate renal impairment (GFR above 30 mL/min/1.73 m²): no dose adjustment. Moderate impairment: monitor potassium and creatinine.

src.q: No dosage adjustment of Exforge is required for patients with mild to moderate renal impairment (GFR >30 ml/min/1.73 m2).
Monitoring of potassium levels and creatinine is advised in moderate renal impairment.

items.t: Severe renal impairment: no clinical data available.

src.q: There are no available clinical data in severely renally impaired patients.

items.t: With aliskiren: contraindicated if GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m².

src.q: Concomitant use of Exforge with aliskiren-containing products in patients with diabetes mellitus or renal impairment (GFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m2)

items.t: SPS: seek specialist advice before starting if eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73 m².

src.q: Seek specialist advice prior to initiation for patients where there is: severe or unstable heart failure renovascular disease eGFR less than 30ml/min/1.73m2

items.t: Severe hepatic impairment, biliary cirrhosis or cholestasis: contraindicated.

src.q: Severe hepatic impairment, biliary cirrhosis or cholestasis.

items.t: Mild to moderate impairment without cholestasis: maximum valsartan 80 mg (the 160 mg valsartan strengths exceed this). Amlodipine dose not established; when switching use the lowest available amlodipine dose. Use with caution.

src.q: In patients with mild to moderate hepatic impairment without cholestasis, the maximum recommended dose is 80 mg valsartan. Amlodipine dosage recommendations have not been established in patients with mild to moderate hepatic impairment.

When switching eligible hypertensive patients (see section 4.1) with hepatic impairment to amlodipine or Exforge, the lowest available dose of amlodipine monotherapy or of the amlodipine component, respectively, should be used.

items.t: Hepatic impairment raises amlodipine AUC about 40-60%; valsartan exposure about doubles in mild to moderate chronic liver disease.

src.q: Patients with hepatic impairment have decreased clearance of amlodipine with resulting increase of approximately 40-60% in AUC.
in patients with mild to moderate chronic liver disease exposure (measured by AUC values) to valsartan is twice that found in healthy volunteers

items.t: SmPC (valsartan): not recommended in the first trimester; contraindicated in the second and third trimesters. Do not start in pregnancy; stop immediately when pregnancy is diagnosed and switch if appropriate. If exposed from the second trimester, ultrasound check of fetal renal function and skull; observe the newborn for hypotension.

src.q: The use of Angiotensin II Receptor Antagonists (AIIRAs) is not recommended during the first trimester of pregnancy
The use of AIIRAs is contraindicated during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy
When pregnancy is diagnosed, treatment with AIIRAs should be stopped immediately, and, if appropriate, alternative therapy should be started.
Should exposure to AIIRAs have occurred from the second trimester of pregnancy, ultrasound check of renal function and skull is recommended.

items.t: SmPC (amlodipine): safety in pregnancy not established; use only when there is no safer alternative and the disease carries greater risk.

src.q: Use in pregnancy is only recommended when there is no safer alternative and when the disease itself carries greater risk for the mother and foetus.

items.t: MHRA: ACE inhibitors and ARBs should not be used at any stage of pregnancy unless absolutely necessary, and only after discussing risks and benefits. Stop as soon as possible on diagnosis.

src.q: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor antagonists should not be used at any stage of pregnancy unless absolutely necessary
On diagnosis of pregnancy, treatment with an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin II receptor antagonist should be stopped as soon as possible

items.t: BUMPS: ARBs are used in pregnancy only very rarely; early-pregnancy use is unlikely to harm the baby, but second/third-trimester use can cause oligohydramnios, fetal kidney damage, skull under-development, growth restriction, lung under-development and joint contractures. Extra monitoring if taken after about 20 weeks. Calcium-channel blockers: no clear risks.

src.q: ARBs are only used in pregnancy very rarely when there is no safer option to treat a serious medical condition.
Taking an ARB in early pregnancy is unlikely to harm your baby.
Taking an ARB in the second or third trimester of pregnancy can cause a number of problems in your baby
If you take an ARB after around 20 weeks you will require additional monitoring to assess amniotic fluid levels and your baby's growth and wellbeing.
There are no clear risks of taking a calcium channel blocker in pregnancy.

items.t: SmPC: amlodipine passes into milk (infant dose 3-7%, up to 15%); no information for the combination, so not recommended; prefer alternatives, especially with a newborn or preterm infant.

src.q: The proportion of the maternal dose received by the infant has been estimated with an interquartile range of 3-7%, with a maximum of 15%.
No information is available regarding the use of Exforge during breast-feeding, therefore Exforge is not recommended

items.t: MHRA (2009): ARBs not recommended in breastfeeding; prefer alternatives, especially with a newborn or preterm baby. Clarification: not absolutely contraindicated; may be prescribed if essential for the mother.

src.q: For all angiotensin II receptor antagonists, use in mothers breastfeeding is not recommended.
they are not absolutely contraindicated. Healthcare professionals may prescribe these medicines during breastfeeding if they consider that this treatment is essential for the lactating mother.

items.t: SPS (2023): valsartan and amlodipine can each be used with caution, but medicines with more breastfeeding evidence are preferred (nifedipine is the preferred dihydropyridine). Monitor the infant for hypotension (drowsiness, lethargy, pallor, poor feeding, poor weight gain) and, in younger infants, wet nappies.

src.q: Valsartan can be used with caution during breastfeeding if it is specifically clinically indicated. However a medicine from a different therapeutic class which has more evidence in breastfeeding is preferred.
It can be used with caution during breastfeeding, but nifedipine is the preferred dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker.
In younger infants, monitor for normal urine production (wet nappies).

items.t: Planning pregnancy: switch to an antihypertensive with an established pregnancy safety profile unless continued ARB treatment is essential.

src.q: Unless continued AIIRA therapy is considered essential, patients planning pregnancy should be changed to alternative antihypertensive treatments which have an established safety profile for use in pregnancy.

items.t: No fertility studies with the combination. Reversible sperm-head changes reported with calcium-channel blockers; clinical data on amlodipine and fertility insufficient.

src.q: There are no clinical studies on fertility with Exforge.
Reversible biochemical changes in the head of spermatozoa have been reported in some patients treated by calcium channel blockers.

items.t: Common with the combination: nasopharyngitis, influenza, headache, oedema (peripheral, pitting, facial), flushing/hot flush, fatigue, asthenia.

items.t: Common with amlodipine alone: somnolence, dizziness, palpitations, abdominal pain, nausea, ankle swelling. Peripheral oedema is less frequent with the combination than with amlodipine alone (mean 5.1%).

src.q: Amlodipine Common Somnolence, dizziness, palpitations, abdominal pain, nausea, ankle swelling.
The mean incidence of peripheral oedema evenly weighted across all doses was 5.1% with the amlodipine/valsartan combination.

items.t: Angioedema (airway obstruction; swelling of face, lips, pharynx, tongue) and intestinal angioedema: stop immediately and do not give again.

src.q: Angioedema, including swelling of the larynx and glottis, causing airway obstruction and/or swelling of the face, lips, pharynx and/or tongue, has been reported in patients treated with valsartan.
should be discontinued immediately in patients who develop angioedema and should not be re-administered.

items.t: Hyperkalaemia, renal failure and impairment, raised creatinine (valsartan, frequency not known); hyponatraemia (uncommon).

src.q: Investigations Blood potassium increased -- -- Not known

Hyponatraemia Uncommon -- --

vasculitis, pancreatitis, gastritis, gingival hyperplasia, hepatitis, jaundice, hepatic enzymes increased*, angioedema, erythema multiforme, urticaria, exfoliative dermatitis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome

src.q: This reaction requires amoxicillin discontinuation and contra-indicates any subsequent administration.

items.t: Ask carefully about previous hypersensitivity reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins or other beta-lactams before starting. Serious, occasionally fatal reactions are more likely with a history of penicillin hypersensitivity and in atopic people. Stop if an allergic reaction occurs.

These reactions are more likely to occur in individuals with a history of penicillin hypersensitivity and in atopic individuals.
If an allergic reaction occurs, amoxicillin therapy must be discontinued and appropriate alternative therapy instituted.

items.t: Avoid if infectious mononucleosis (glandular fever) is suspected: morbilliform rash.

src.q: Amoxicillin should be avoided if infectious mononucleosis is suspected since the occurrence of a morbilliform rash has been associated with this condition following the use of amoxicillin.

items.t: Convulsions may occur with impaired renal function, high doses or predisposing factors (history of seizures, treated epilepsy, meningeal disorders).

src.q: Convulsions may occur in patients with impaired renal function or in those receiving high doses or in patients with predisposing factors (e.g. history of seizures, treated epilepsy or meningeal disorders

src.q: Drug-induced enterocolitis syndrome (DIES) has been reported mainly in children receiving amoxicillin
There have been severe cases including progression to shock.

src.q: Hypersensitivity reactions can also progress to Kounis syndrome, a serious allergic reaction that can result in myocardial infarction

items.t: Consider antibiotic-associated colitis in anyone with diarrhoea during or after treatment; if it occurs stop amoxicillin. Anti-peristaltic medicines are contraindicated in this situation.

src.q: Should antibiotic-associated colitis occur, amoxicillin should immediately be discontinued, a physician consulted and an appropriate therapy initiated.
Anti-peristaltic medicinal products are contra-indicated in this situation.

src.q: In patients with renal impairment, the dose should be adjusted according to the degree of impairment

src.q: During the administration of high doses of amoxicillin, it is advisable to maintain adequate fluid intake and urinary output in order to reduce the possibility of amoxicillin crystalluria.

items.t: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction can follow treatment of Lyme disease; it is common and usually self-limiting.

src.q: Patients should be reassured that this is a common and usually self-limiting consequence of antibiotic treatment of Lyme disease.

items.t: Not suitable for some infections unless the pathogen is known or very likely to be susceptible, particularly UTIs and severe ear, nose and throat infections.

src.q: This particularly applies when considering the treatment of patients with urinary tract infections and severe infections of the ear, nose and throat.

items.t: Urine glucose: use enzymatic glucose oxidase methods (false positives with chemical methods). May distort oestriol assays in pregnancy.

src.q: It is recommended that when testing for the presence of glucose in urine during amoxicillin treatment, enzymatic glucose oxidase methods should be used.
The presence of amoxicillin may distort assay results for oestriol in pregnant women.

src.q: This medicinal product contains sorbitol. Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance should not take this medicine.
May increase the risk of jaundice in newborn babies.

If co-administration is necessary, the prothrombin time or international normalised ratio should be carefully monitored with the addition or withdrawal of amoxicillin.

If the duration of penicillin is short (up to 10 days), consider using with caution and advise to monitor for signs of toxicity.

src.q: Probenecid Concomitant use of probenecid is not recommended.

src.q: For patients with a creatinine clearance of less than 15 ml/min/1.73 m2 (equivalent to serum creatinine of greater than 600 micromol/litre), the oral dose should be 25 mg daily or 50 mg on alternate days

items.t: Haemodialysis: 50 mg orally after each dialysis, under hospital supervision (marked falls in blood pressure can occur).

src.q: Patients on haemodialysis should be given 50 mg orally after each dialysis; this should be done under hospital supervision as marked falls in blood pressure can occur.

hepatic.note: No hepatic dose advice in the UK atenolol tablets SmPC (no significant hepatic metabolism stated in 5.2).

items.t: SmPC: use with caution. Crosses the placenta; associated with intra-uterine growth retardation; weigh benefit against risk, particularly in the first and second trimesters.

src.q: Caution should be exercised when Tenormin is administered during pregnancy or to a woman who is breast-feeding.
Administration of Tenormin to pregnant women in the management of mild to moderate hypertension has been associated with intra-uterine growth retardation.
requires that the anticipated benefit be weighed against the possible risks, particularly in the first and second trimesters

items.t: BUMPS: can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor; no concern about birth defects; babies may be smaller; extra growth scans may be offered at around 32 and 36 weeks.

src.q: Atenolol can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor.
There are no concerns that beta blockers cause birth defects, stillbirth or preterm birth.
Women taking atenolol may be more likely to have a smaller baby.
you may be offered extra scans at around 32 and 36 weeks to check the growth of your baby.

items.t: SmPC: use with caution. Significant accumulation in breast milk; breastfed neonates may be at risk of hypoglycaemia and bradycardia.

src.q: There is significant accumulation of Tenormin in breast milk.
Neonates born to mothers who are receiving Tenormin at parturition or breast-feeding may be at risk of hypoglycaemia and bradycardia.

items.t: SPS: use with caution; labetalol, metoprolol or propranolol are preferred. Monitor the infant for bradycardia or hypoglycaemia (drowsiness, lethargy, poor feeding, poor weight gain); risk of accumulation, especially in neonates.

src.q: It can be used with caution during breastfeeding, but labetalol, metoprolol, or propranolol are preferred if clinically appropriate..
There is therefore significant risk of accumulation of atenolol in breastfed infants, particularly neonates, resulting in increased risk of adverse effects.

reproductive.note: No fertility or contraception advice in the UK atenolol tablets SmPC. BUMPS: no increased risk expected if the father takes atenolol.

items.t: Common: bradycardia, cold extremities, gastrointestinal disturbances, fatigue.

Vascular disorders Common Cold extremities
Gastrointestinal disorders Common Gastrointestinal disturbances

Rare Hepatic toxicity including intrahepatic cholestasis

treatment in an intensive care ward

items.t: Heart rate: reduce the dose if symptomatic bradycardia with resting pulse below 50-55 bpm.

src.q: the pulse rate drops to less than 50-55 bpm at rest, the dose should be reduced.

items.t: Diabetes: patients should monitor blood glucose carefully.

src.q: Diabetic patients should be advised to carefully monitor blood glucose levels.

items.t: During withdrawal: follow patients, especially with ischaemic heart disease.

src.q: Patients should be followed during withdrawal, especially those with ischaemic heart disease.

items.t: Oral, usually once daily as a single dose.

Most patients respond to 100 mg daily given orally as a single dose.

items.t: Do not stop suddenly; the dose is reduced gradually.

items.t: Dizziness or tiredness may occur occasionally; take this into account for driving.

src.q: it should be taken into account that occasionally dizziness or fatigue may occur.

items.t: Management of hypertension (the 50 mg/12.5 mg strength: particularly suited to older patients).
