The management of hypertension, particularly suited to older patients.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restrictions stated in the UK SmPCs.

items.t: One tablet daily. Little or no further fall in blood pressure with higher doses; add another antihypertensive (e.g. a vasodilator) if needed.

src.q: Adults One tablet daily.
There is little or no further fall in blood pressure with increased dosage and, where necessary, another antihypertensive drug, such as a vasodilator, can be added.

items.t: One tablet daily (adults and elderly). If blood pressure is not controlled, a small dose of a third agent (e.g. a vasodilator) may be added.

src.q: Adults One tablet daily. Elderly One tablet daily.
Where hypertensive control is not achieved, addition of a small dose of a third agent e.g. as a vasodilator, may be appropriate.

items.t: Elderly: dose requirements are often lower; older patients not controlled on low-dose single-agent therapy should respond to one 50 mg/12.5 mg tablet daily.

src.q: Elderly Dosage requirements are often lower in this age group.
The elderly with hypertension who do not respond to low dose therapy with a single agent should have a satisfactory response to a single tablet daily of Tenoret.

items.t: Not recommended in children; safety and efficacy not established.

src.q: The use of Tenoretic is not recommended in children. The safety and efficacy of Tenoretic in children has not yet been established.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to atenolol, chlortalidone (or sulphonamide-derived medicines) or excipients; bradycardia; cardiogenic shock; hypotension; metabolic acidosis; severe peripheral arterial circulatory disturbances; second- or third-degree heart block; sick sinus syndrome; untreated phaeochromocytoma; severe renal failure; uncontrolled heart failure; pregnancy; lactation.

src.q: hypersensitivity to the active substances (or to sulphonamide derived medicinal products) or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1

- bradycardia; - cardiogenic shock; - hypotension; - metabolic acidosis; - severe peripheral arterial circulatory disturbances; - second- or third-degree heart block; - sick sinus syndrome; - untreated phaeochromocytoma; - severe renal failure; - uncontrolled heart failure.
Tenoretic tablets must not be given during pregnancy or lactation.

items.t: Heart failure: may be used once signs are controlled; caution with poor cardiac reserve. Do not stop abruptly in ischaemic heart disease. First-degree heart block: caution. Prinzmetal's angina: utmost caution.

src.q: may be used in patients whose signs of heart failure have been controlled. Caution must be exercised in patients whose cardiac reserve is poor.
should not be discontinued abruptly in patients suffering from ischaemic heart disease.
caution must be exercised if it is given to patients with first-degree heart block.

items.t: Bronchospastic disease (asthma): should in general not receive beta-blockers; if used, lowest dose with utmost caution; stop if airway resistance rises.

src.q: patients with bronchospastic disease should, in general, not receive beta-blockers due to increasing in airways resistance.
If increased airways resistance does occur, Tenoretic tablets should be discontinued and bronchodilator therapy (e.g. salbutamol) administered if necessary.

items.t: May mask hypoglycaemia warning signs (tachycardia, palpitations, sweating) and thyrotoxicosis signs; impaired glucose tolerance - monitor glycaemia closely early on.

src.q: may modify warning signs of hypoglycaemia as tachycardia, palpitation and sweating.
Close monitoring of glycaemia is recommended in the initial phase of therapy

items.t: Electrolytes: hypokalaemia and hyponatraemia may occur; check electrolytes periodically, especially in the elderly, those on digitalis, on low-potassium diets or with GI complaints.

src.q: plasma electrolyte should be periodically determined in appropriate intervals to detect possible electrolyte imbalance especially hypokalaemia and hyponatraemia.

items.t: Phaeochromocytoma: give only after alpha-blockade. Anaesthesia: inform the anaesthetist. History of anaphylaxis: reactions may be more severe and less responsive to adrenaline.

src.q: in patients with phaeochromocytoma must be administered only after alfa-receptor blockade.
Such patients may be unresponsive to the usual doses of adrenaline used to treat the allergic reactions.

items.t: Impaired hepatic function or progressive liver disease: minor fluid/electrolyte changes may precipitate hepatic coma. Hyperuricaemia may occur. Choroidal effusion/acute angle-closure glaucoma: stop as rapidly as possible.

src.q: in patients with impaired hepatic function or progressive liver disease, minor alterations in fluid and electrolyte balance may precipitate hepatic coma.
The primary treatment is to discontinue drug intake as rapidly as possible.

items.t: Verapamil or diltiazem: exaggerated negative effects (severe hypotension, bradycardia, cardiac failure), especially with impaired ventricular function or conduction problems; do not give either intravenously within 48 hours of stopping the other.

src.q: This may result in severe hypotension, bradycardia and cardiac failure.
Neither the beta-blocker nor the calcium channel blocker should be administered intravenously within 48 hours of discontinuing the other.

items.t: Dihydropyridines (e.g. nifedipine): more hypotension; cardiac failure possible with latent cardiac insufficiency.

src.q: Concomitant therapy with dihydropyridines e.g. nifedipine, may increase the risk of hypotension, and cardiac failure may occur in patients with latent cardiac insufficiency.

items.t: Insulin and oral antidiabetics: blood-sugar-lowering effects may be intensified (and hypoglycaemia warning signs masked).

src.q: Concomitant use with insulin and oral antidiabetic drugs may lead to the intensification of the blood sugar lowering effects of these drugs.

items.t: NSAIDs (e.g. ibuprofen) may reduce the antihypertensive effect. Sympathomimetics (e.g. adrenaline) may counteract the beta-blocker.

src.q: Concomitant use of prostaglandin synthetase inhibiting drugs (e.g. ibuprofen, indometacin) may decrease the hypotensive effects of beta-blockers
Concomitant use of sympathomimetic agents, e.g. adrenaline (epinephrine), may counteract the effect of beta-blockers.

items.t: Lithium: renal clearance reduced (dose adjustment may be needed). Clonidine: withdraw the beta-blocker several days before stopping clonidine. Digitalis, class I antiarrhythmics and amiodarone: conduction effects.

src.q: The chlortalidone component may reduce the renal clearance of lithium leading to increased serum concentrations.
If the two drugs are co-administered, the beta-blocker should be withdrawn several days before discontinuing clonidine.

items.t: Contraindicated in severe renal failure (no CrCl/eGFR threshold given). Reduced efficacy in renal insufficiency because of the chlortalidone component.

src.q: This fixed dose combination should thus not be administrated to patients with severe renal impairment
Due to the properties of the chlortalidone component, Tenoretic tablets has reduced efficacy in the presence of renal insufficiency.

items.t: Impaired hepatic function or progressive liver disease: minor fluid and electrolyte changes may precipitate hepatic coma.

src.q: in patients with impaired hepatic function or progressive liver disease, minor alterations in fluid and electrolyte balance may precipitate hepatic coma.

items.t: SmPC: must not be given during pregnancy (section 4.3).

src.q: Pregnancy: Tenoretic tablets must not be given during pregnancy.

items.t: BUMPS (atenolol alone, not the combination): can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor; may be linked with a smaller baby. BUMPS (diuretics in general): diuretics may reduce placental blood flow, and the baby will be monitored with extra growth scans. This differs from the combination SmPC, which says must not be given.

src.q: Atenolol can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor.
Women taking atenolol may be more likely to have a smaller baby.
Diuretics may reduce blood flow to the placenta.
Your baby will be monitored with extra growth scans.

items.t: SmPC: must not be given during lactation (section 4.3).

src.q: Lactation: Tenoretic tablets must not be given during lactation.

items.t: SPS (atenolol alone): use with caution; labetalol, metoprolol or propranolol preferred. Risk of accumulation in neonates; monitor the infant for bradycardia and hypoglycaemia (drowsiness, lethargy, poor feeding).

src.q: It can be used with caution during breastfeeding, but labetalol, metoprolol, or propranolol are preferred if clinically appropriate.
Monitor infants for signs of bradycardia or hypoglycaemia including drowsiness, lethargy, and poor feeding and inadequate weight gain.

items.t: No fertility data available.

src.q: Fertility: No data on fertility available.

items.t: Common: bradycardia, cold extremities, gastrointestinal disturbance (including nausea), fatigue; and, from chlortalidone, hyperuricaemia, hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, impaired glucose tolerance.

Common Related to chlortalidone: Hyperuricaemia, hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, impaired glucose tolerance

items.t: Choroidal effusion, acute myopia and acute angle-closure glaucoma (sulfonamide-type reaction): sudden reduced vision or eye pain, usually within hours to weeks of starting. Stop the medicine as rapidly as possible; untreated angle-closure glaucoma can cause permanent vision loss.

src.q: Symptoms include acute onset of decreased visual acuity or ocular pain and typically occur within hours to weeks of drug initiation.
Untreated acute angle-closure glaucoma can lead to permanent vision loss.
The primary treatment is to discontinue drug intake as rapidly as possible.

items.t: Plasma electrolytes periodically (hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia); blood glucose closely at the start in diabetes and periodic glucosuria tests in prolonged therapy.

src.q: plasma electrolyte should be periodically determined in appropriate intervals to detect possible electrolyte imbalance especially hypokalaemia and hyponatraemia.
in prolonged therapy test for glucosuria should be carried out at regular intervals.

items.t: Stop if airway resistance increases. If slow heart rate causes symptoms, the dose may be reduced. Consider stopping if wellbeing is adversely affected by adverse reactions.

src.q: In the rare instances when a treated patient develops symptoms which may be attributable to a slow heart rate, the dose may be reduced.
Discontinuance of Tenoretic tablets should be considered if, according to clinical judgement, the well-being of the patient is adversely affected by any of the above reactions.

items.t: Oral, once daily. The score line is not for breaking the tablet.

src.q: The score line is not intended for breaking the tablet.

items.t: Do not stop suddenly (especially with heart disease). If you have ever had asthma or wheezing, check with your doctor before taking.

src.q: If you have ever had asthma or wheezing, do not take this medicine without first checking with your doctor

src.q: it should be taken into account that occasionally dizziness or fatigue may occur.

items.t: Adjunct to diet to lower total-C, LDL-C, apolipoprotein B and triglycerides in primary hypercholesterolaemia (including heterozygous familial) or mixed hyperlipidaemia, in adults and children aged 10 years or older, when diet and other measures are not enough.

src.q: in adults, adolescents and children aged 10 years or older with primary hypercholesterolaemia including familial hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous variant) or combined (mixed) hyperlipidaemia

items.t: Adults with homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, as an adjunct to other lipid-lowering treatment (e.g. LDL apheresis) or if such treatment is unavailable.

src.q: Lipitor is also indicated to reduce total-C and LDL-C in adults with homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia

items.t: Prevention of cardiovascular events in adults estimated to be at high risk of a first cardiovascular event, alongside correction of other risk factors.

src.q: Prevention of cardiovascular events in adult patients estimated to have a high risk for a first cardiovascular event

items.t: Children: use only by physicians experienced in treating paediatric hyperlipidaemia, with regular re-evaluation.

src.q: Paediatric use should only be carried out by physicians experienced in the treatment of paediatric hyperlipidaemia

items.t: General: usual starting dose 10 mg once a day; adjust at intervals of 4 weeks or more; maximum 80 mg once a day. Patient should follow a cholesterol-lowering diet.

src.q: The usual starting dose is 10 mg once a day. Adjustment of dose should be made at intervals of 4 weeks or more. The maximum dose is 80 mg once a day.

items.t: Primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed hyperlipidaemia: most patients are controlled on 10 mg once a day; maximum response usually within 4 weeks.

src.q: The majority of patients are controlled with Lipitor 10 mg once a day.

items.t: Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (adults): start 10 mg daily, adjust every 4 weeks to 40 mg daily; then either increase to a maximum of 80 mg daily or combine 40 mg once daily with a bile acid sequestrant.

src.q: Patients should be started with Lipitor 10 mg daily. Doses should be individualised and adjusted every 4 weeks to 40 mg daily.
either the dose may be increased to a maximum of 80 mg daily or a bile acid sequestrant may be combined with 40 mg atorvastatin once daily

items.t: Homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia: 10 to 80 mg daily (limited data), as an adjunct to other lipid-lowering treatment.

src.q: The dose of atorvastatin in patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia is 10 to 80 mg daily

items.t: Prevention of cardiovascular disease: 10 mg/day was used in primary prevention trials; higher doses may be needed to reach guideline cholesterol levels.

src.q: In the primary prevention trials the dose was 10 mg/day. Higher doses may be necessary in order to attain (LDL-) cholesterol levels according to current guidelines.

items.t: Maximum 20 mg/day with elbasvir/grazoprevir or letermovir; not recommended with letermovir plus ciclosporin.

src.q: the dose of atorvastatin should not exceed 20 mg/day
Use of atorvastatin is not recommended in patients taking letermovir co-administered with ciclosporin

items.t: Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, 10 years and above: start 10 mg per day; may increase to 80 mg daily by response and tolerability, adjusting at intervals of 4 weeks or more.

src.q: For patients with Heterozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia aged 10 years and above, the recommended starting dose of atorvastatin is 10 mg per day
The dose may be increased to 80 mg daily, according to the response and tolerability.

items.t: Not indicated below 10 years of age; no dose recommendation can be made (only limited data in ages 6 to 10).

src.q: Atorvastatin is not indicated in the treatment of patients below the age of 10 years.

src.q: with hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1

src.q: with active liver disease or unexplained persistent elevations of serum transaminases exceeding 3 times the upper limit of normal

src.q: during pregnancy, while breast-feeding and in women of child-bearing potential not using appropriate contraceptive measures

items.t: With the hepatitis C antivirals glecaprevir/pibrentasvir.

src.q: treated with the hepatitis C antivirals glecaprevir/pibrentasvir

items.t: Muscle effects: can cause myalgia, myositis and myopathy that may progress to rhabdomyolysis. Prescribe with caution if there are pre-disposing factors for rhabdomyolysis.

src.q: may in rare occasions affect the skeletal muscle and cause myalgia, myositis, and myopathy that may progress to rhabdomyolysis
Atorvastatin should be prescribed with caution in patients with pre-disposing factors for rhabdomyolysis.

items.t: Measure CK before starting in: renal impairment, hypothyroidism, personal/family history of hereditary muscle disorders, previous muscle toxicity with a statin or fibrate, previous liver disease and/or substantial alcohol use; consider in people over 70. Do not start if baseline CK is above 5 times ULN.

src.q: A CK level should be measured before starting statin treatment in the following situations: - Renal impairment - Hypothyroidism
If CK levels are significantly elevated (> 5 times ULN) at baseline, treatment should not be started.

items.t: Use with caution in people who drink substantial quantities of alcohol and/or have a history of liver disease.

src.q: Lipitor should be used with caution in patients who consume substantial quantities of alcohol and/or have a history of liver disease.

items.t: After recent stroke or TIA, 80 mg was linked to more haemorrhagic stroke; in people with prior haemorrhagic stroke or lacunar infarct, the benefit-risk of 80 mg is uncertain and haemorrhagic stroke risk should be carefully considered.

src.q: For patients with prior haemorrhagic stroke or lacunar infarct, the balance of risks and benefits of atorvastatin 80 mg is uncertain

items.t: Systemic fusidic acid: atorvastatin must not be given with it or within 7 days of stopping it; stop the statin during fusidic acid treatment.

src.q: Atorvastatin must not be co-administered with systemic formulations of fusidic acid or within 7 days of stopping fusidic acid treatment.

items.t: Statins can raise blood glucose; people at risk of diabetes (fasting glucose 5.6 to 6.9 mmol/L, BMI>30kg/m2, raised triglycerides, hypertension) should be monitored. This is not a reason to stop the statin.

src.q: Patients at risk (fasting glucose 5.6 to 6.9 mmol/L, BMI>30kg/m2, raised triglycerides, hypertension) should be monitored both clinically and biochemically according to national guidelines.

items.t: Myasthenia gravis: statins may cause or worsen myasthenia gravis or ocular myasthenia; stop if symptoms get worse. MHRA: advise patients with myasthenia gravis to watch for worsening symptoms.

src.q: Lipitor should be discontinued in case of aggravation of symptoms.
advise patients with pre-existing myasthenia gravis to be alert to aggravation of symptoms while taking a statin

items.t: Interstitial lung disease has been reported; stop the statin if it is suspected.

src.q: If it is suspected a patient has developed interstitial lung disease, statin therapy should be discontinued.

items.t: Contains lactose: people with rare hereditary galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take it.

src.q: Lipitor contains lactose.

items.t: Chewable tablets contain aspartame, a source of phenylalanine: may be harmful for people with phenylketonuria.

src.q: Lipitor chewable tablet contains aspartame which is a source of phenylalanine. May be harmful for people with phenylketonuria.

items.t: Potent CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. clarithromycin): avoid if possible. If unavoidable, consider lower starting and maximum atorvastatin doses with clinical monitoring.

src.q: should be avoided if possible. In cases where co-administration of these medicinal products with atorvastatin cannot be avoided lower starting and maximum doses of atorvastatin should be considered

items.t: Clarithromycin: SPS advises avoiding it with atorvastatin; consider pausing atorvastatin for the course; if both must be used, maximum atorvastatin 20 mg daily. MHRA (2008 article) also says do not exceed 20 mg atorvastatin daily with clarithromycin.

src.q: Avoid the use of clarithromycin with atorvastatin and use a non-interacting antibiotic if possible.

Clarithromycin: do not exceed 20 mg atorvastatin daily

items.t: Warfarin / coumarin anticoagulants: check prothrombin time before starting atorvastatin and often enough early on; repeat if the atorvastatin dose is changed or stopped. MHRA: monitor INR before starting and regularly, especially with dose changes.

src.q: prothrombin time should be determined before starting atorvastatin in patients taking coumarin anticoagulants
Monitor INR before starting treatment and regularly during treatment, especially with dose changes

items.t: CYP3A4 inducers such as St John's Wort can reduce atorvastatin levels.

src.q: inducers of cytochrome P450 3A (e.g. efavirenz, rifampin, St. John's Wort) can lead to variable reductions in plasma concentrations of atorvastatin

items.t: Moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. erythromycin, diltiazem, verapamil, fluconazole): consider a lower maximum dose and monitor.

src.q: a lower maximum dose of atorvastatin should be considered and appropriate clinical monitoring of the patient is recommended when concomitantly used with moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors

items.t: Amlodipine and magnesium/aluminium hydroxide antacid: small changes in atorvastatin exposure; no specific recommendation in the SmPC.

src.q: Amlodipine 10 mg, single dose 80 mg, SD 1.18 No specific recommendation.

items.t: Avoid large quantities of grapefruit juice.

src.q: Concomitant intake of large quantities of grapefruit juice and atorvastatin is not recommended.

items.t: No dose adjustment needed in renal impairment. Renal impairment is a reason to measure CK before starting.

src.q: Renal impairment No adjustment of dose is required
A CK level should be measured before starting statin treatment in the following situations: - Renal impairment

items.t: SPS (all statins): if eGFR is less than 30 mL/min/1.73m2, check the dose with a renal specialist.

src.q: If eGFR less than 30mL/min/1.73m2 check dose with renal specialist.

items.t: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; contraindicated in active liver disease.

src.q: Lipitor should be used with caution in patients with hepatic impairment
Lipitor is contraindicated in patients with active liver disease

items.t: SPS: statins are not recommended in unexplained active liver disease or unexplained ALT/AST above 3 x ULN. In stable/chronic liver disease they can be used with caution; consider a lower starting dose such as atorvastatin 20 mg daily with gradual increase.

src.q: Statins are not recommended in patients with: unexplained active liver disease or, unexplained elevations of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) or aspartate aminotransferase (AST) that are greater than 3 x the upper limit of normal (ULN).
consider a lower dose of a high-intensity statin, such as atorvastatin 20 mg daily or rosuvastatin 10 mg daily, with gradual dose escalation

items.t: Contraindicated in pregnancy; do not use in women who are pregnant, trying to become pregnant or who suspect pregnancy. Suspend for the duration of pregnancy.

src.q: Lipitor is contraindicated during pregnancy
Treatment with Lipitor should be suspended for the duration of pregnancy

items.t: BUMPS: statins are usually avoided in pregnancy; as a precaution most women are advised to stop statins three months before trying to conceive and during pregnancy.

src.q: Statins are usually avoided in pregnancy if possible as there is not enough information to say they are safe for the baby.
As a precaution, most women are advised to stop taking statins for three months before trying to conceive, and during pregnancy.

items.t: SmPC: contraindicated during breastfeeding; women taking atorvastatin should not breastfeed.

src.q: Atorvastatin is contraindicated during breast-feeding

items.t: SPS (differs from SmPC): atorvastatin is a preferred statin and can be used with caution while breastfeeding, with infant monitoring (feeding, growth, weight gain; diarrhoea, constipation, irritability). Postponing therapy until after exclusive breastfeeding is preferred if possible.

src.q: Atorvastatin can be used with caution while breastfeeding, but infant monitoring is still required.
if possible, the preferred option would be to postpone lipid-lowering therapy until after the exclusive breastfeeding period

items.t: Women of child-bearing potential should use appropriate contraception during treatment.

src.q: Women of child-bearing potential should use appropriate contraceptive measures during treatment

items.t: No effect on male or female fertility in animal studies.

src.q: In animal studies atorvastatin had no effect on male or female fertility

items.t: Common: nasopharyngitis, allergic reactions, hyperglycaemia, headache, pharyngolaryngeal pain, epistaxis, constipation, flatulence, dyspepsia, nausea, diarrhoea, myalgia, arthralgia, pain in extremity, muscle spasms, joint swelling, back pain, abnormal liver function tests, raised CK.

Common: constipation, flatulence, dyspepsia, nausea, diarrhoea.

Common: liver function test abnormal, blood creatine kinase increased.

items.t: Immune-mediated necrotising myopathy (very rare): persistent proximal weakness and raised CK despite stopping the statin.

src.q: There have been very rare reports of an immune mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) during or after treatment with some statins.

items.t: Liver injury: hepatitis (uncommon), cholestasis (rare), hepatic failure (very rare). If transaminases above 3 x ULN persist, reduce dose or stop.

src.q: Uncommon: hepatitis. Rare: cholestasis. Very rare: hepatic failure.
Should an increase in transaminases of greater than 3 times the upper limit of normal (ULN) persist, reduction of dose or withdrawal of Lipitor is recommended

items.t: Rare severe skin reactions and angioedema (angioneurotic oedema, bullous dermatitis including erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis); anaphylaxis very rare.

src.q: Rare: angioneurotic oedema, dermatitis bullous including erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis

items.t: Interstitial lung disease: stop the statin if suspected.

src.q: If it is suspected a patient has developed interstitial lung disease, statin therapy should be discontinued.

items.t: Liver function tests before starting and periodically thereafter.

src.q: Liver function tests should be performed before the initiation of treatment and periodically thereafter.

items.t: SPS before starting: ALT or AST, blood pressure, BMI, lipid profile (non-fasting), serum creatinine or eGFR, HbA1c. Consider CK if persistent muscle symptoms and TSH if thyroid symptoms.

src.q: Before starting Required Baseline ALT or AST Blood pressure Body mass index

items.t: SPS: ALT or AST and lipids between months 2 and 3; then consider annually (ALT/AST after the first year only if indicated).

src.q: Required Between months 2 and 3 ALT or AST
Annually ALT or AST · repeat after first year only if indicated

items.t: Measure CK if muscle pain, cramps or weakness occur; do not measure after strenuous exercise.

src.q: If such symptoms occur whilst a patient is receiving treatment with atorvastatin, their CK levels should be measured.

items.t: SPS: stop or do not start a statin if ALT or AST are greater than 3 times ULN, or if CK is greater than 5 times ULN.

src.q: Stop existing statin or do not initiate new statin if ALT or AST are greater than 3 times upper limit of normal (ULN).
Stop existing statin or do not initiate statin if creatine kinase (CK) greater than 5 times ULN.

items.t: Oral, once daily at any time of day, with or without food.

src.q: Each daily dose of atorvastatin is given all at once and may be given at any time of day with or without food.

items.t: Chewable tablets can be chewed or swallowed whole with water, at any time of day, with or without food.

src.q: Lipitor chewable tablets can be chewed or swallowed whole with a drink of water, and can be taken at any time of day, with or without food.

items.t: Report muscle pain, cramps or weakness promptly, especially with malaise or fever.

src.q: Patients must be asked to promptly report muscle pain, cramps, or weakness especially if accompanied by malaise or fever.

items.t: Avoid large quantities of grapefruit juice.

src.q: Concomitant intake of large quantities of grapefruit juice and atorvastatin is not recommended.

items.t: Women who could become pregnant should use contraception; stop and seek advice if pregnancy is planned or occurs.

src.q: Women of child-bearing potential should use appropriate contraceptive measures during treatment

items.t: Adults and adolescents (12 to 17 years) weighing at least 45 kg: acute streptococcal tonsillitis/pharyngitis, acute bacterial sinusitis, acute bacterial otitis media, community-acquired pneumonia, acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections, urethritis/cervicitis due to Chlamydia trachomatis, and (with another antibacterial, e.g. ceftriaxone) due to Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Adults only: acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis.
items.tag: Capsules (and suspension if unable to swallow)

src.q: Adults (18 years of age and above) and adolescents (12 - 17 years of age) weighing at least 45 kg - Acute streptococcal tonsillitis and pharyngitis - Acute bacterial sinusitis - Acute bacterial otitis media - Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP)
Acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections (ABSSSI) - Urethritis and cervicitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis
Adults (18 years of age and above) only - Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis (AECB)

items.t: Children from 6 months weighing under 45 kg: acute bacterial sinusitis, acute bacterial otitis media, community-acquired pneumonia, acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections. From 2 years: acute streptococcal tonsillitis and pharyngitis.

src.q: Paediatric patients aged 6 months and older and weighing less than 45 kg - Acute bacterial sinusitis - Acute bacterial otitis media - Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) - Acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections (ABSSSI)
Paediatric patients aged 2 years and older and weighing less than 45 kg - Acute streptococcal tonsillitis and pharyngitis

items.t: Start only after careful benefit/risk assessment considering local resistance, and when preferred regimens are not indicated (risk of resistance).

src.q: Treatment with azithromycin should only be initiated after a careful assessment of the benefit and the risks, considering the local prevalence of resistance, and when preferred treatment regimens are not indicated.

items.t: Not recommended for uncomplicated gonorrhoea or pelvic inflammatory disease unless lab results confirm susceptibility.

src.q: azithromycin is not recommended for the treatment of uncomplicated gonorrhoea and pelvic inflammatory disease unless laboratory results have confirmed susceptibility of the organism to azithromycin

items.t: Tonsillitis/pharyngitis, sinusitis, otitis media, AECB (adults only), community-acquired pneumonia, skin and skin structure infections: 500 mg/day for 3 days, or 500 mg on day 1 then 250 mg/day on days 2 to 5. Single daily dose.

src.q: 500 mg/day for 3 days or 500 mg on day 1, followed by 250 mg/day on days 2-5
Azithromycin should be administered as a single daily dose.

items.t: Urethritis/cervicitis due to Chlamydia trachomatis: 1000 mg as a single dose.

src.q: Urethritis and cervicitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis 1000 mg as a single dose

items.t: Urethritis/cervicitis due to Neisseria gonorrhoeae (with another antibacterial, e.g. ceftriaxone): 1000 mg, or 2000 mg in adults only, as a single dose.

src.q: 1000 mg or 2000 mg* as a single dose * for treatment of adults only

items.t: Missed dose: if 12 hours or less late, take it as soon as possible; if more than 12 hours, wait for the next scheduled dose.

src.q: If 12 hours or less have passed since the missed dose, the patient should be advised to take it as soon as possible
If more than 12 hours have passed since the time the dose is usually taken, the patient should be advised to wait until the next scheduled dose.

items.t: Elderly: no dose adjustment, but particular caution because of arrhythmia and torsades de pointes risk.

src.q: Since the elderly are more likely to experience proarrhythmic conditions, particular caution is recommended due to the risk of developing cardiac arrhythmia and torsades de pointes

items.t: Children 6 months and older under 45 kg, sinusitis, community-acquired pneumonia, skin and skin structure infections: 10 mg/kg/day for 3 days, or 10 mg/kg on day 1 then 5 mg/kg/day on days 2 to 5. Single daily dose.

src.q: Acute bacterial sinusitis Community-acquired pneumonia Acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections 10 mg/kg/day for 3 days or 10 mg/kg on day 1, followed by 5 mg/kg/day on days 2-5

items.t: Acute otitis media: single dose of 30 mg/kg (maximum total 1500 mg), or 10 mg/kg/day for 3 days, or 10 mg/kg on day 1 then 5 mg/kg/day on days 2 to 5.

src.q: Acute bacterial otitis media single dose of 30 mg/kg or 10 mg/kg/day for 3 days or 10 mg/kg on day 1, followed by 5 mg/kg/day on days 2-5
with exception of the 1-day treatment course (single dose) for acute bacterial otitis media for which the maximum total dose of 1500 mg should not be exceeded

items.t: Acute streptococcal tonsillitis/pharyngitis (2 years and older): 20 mg/kg/day for 3 days or 12 mg/kg/day for 5 days.

src.q: Acute streptococcal tonsillitis and pharyngitis* 20 mg/kg/day for 3 days or 12 mg/kg/day for 5 days

items.t: Daily dose must not exceed the adult 500 mg/day (except the single-dose otitis media course). Maximum total dose for any course under 45 kg is 1500 mg, except the 5-day tonsillitis/pharyngitis regimen.

src.q: The azithromycin daily dose should not exceed the adult daily dose of 500 mg
The maximum recommended total dose for any treatment for paediatric patients weighing less than 45 kg is 1500 mg, except for the 5-day regimen for acute streptococcal tonsillitis and pharyngitis.

items.t: Safety and efficacy not established under 6 months. Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis reported after use in the first 42 days of life.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of azithromycin have not been established in children under 6 months of age for any of the indications listed in section 4.1.
Cases of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis have been reported following the administration of azithromycin for the first 42 days after birth.

items.t: Capsules: for adults and adolescents weighing at least 45 kg; other forms are more suitable for children under 45 kg or those unable to swallow capsules.

src.q: Other pharmaceutical forms are available that may be more appropriate to treat patients unable to swallow capsules as well as paediatric patients weighing less than 45 kg.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to azithromycin, erythromycin, any macrolide or ketolide antibiotic, or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance, erythromycin, any macrolide or ketolide antibiotic, or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes: use with caution in ongoing proarrhythmic conditions (especially women and the elderly), e.g. congenital or documented QT prolongation, other QT-prolonging medicines, electrolyte disturbance (especially hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia), clinically relevant bradycardia, arrhythmia or severe cardiac insufficiency.

src.q: azithromycin should be used with caution in patients with ongoing proarrhythmic conditions (especially women and elderly patients) such as patients: With congenital or documented QT prolongation
With electrolyte disturbance, particularly in case of hypokalaemia and hypomagnesemia With clinically relevant bradycardia, cardiac arrhythmia or severe cardiac insufficiency

items.t: SPS (macrolides): no ECG needed when used alone without risk factors. Do not prescribe with a history of QT prolongation, ventricular arrhythmia or significant electrolyte disturbance. Monitor ECG, magnesium and potassium before and during treatment if there are non-modifiable risk factors.

src.q: Macrolides Management No ECG monitoring is required when used alone and in the absence of risk factors. Do not prescribe in people with a history of QT interval prolongation, ventricular arrhythmia, or significant electrolyte disturbance.
Monitor ECG, magnesium and potassium before and during treatment in people with non-modifiable patient and medicine risk factors.

items.t: Hepatotoxicity (fulminant hepatitis, hepatic failure, some fatal): caution in significant hepatic disease. Stop and check liver function if signs of liver dysfunction develop.

src.q: the use of azithromycin should be undertaken with caution in patients with significant hepatic disease
Patients should be advised to stop azithromycin administration and to contact their physician if signs and symptoms of liver dysfunction

items.t: Severe hypersensitivity and SCARs (SJS, TEN, DRESS, AGEP): advise patients and monitor closely; stop if an allergic reaction occurs. Symptoms may recur after symptomatic treatment stops.

src.q: If an allergic reaction occurs, azithromycin should be discontinued, and appropriate therapy should be instituted.
Physicians should be aware that reappearance of the allergic symptoms may occur when symptomatic therapy is discontinued.

items.t: Myasthenia gravis: exacerbations and new myasthenic syndrome reported.

src.q: Exacerbations of the symptoms of myasthenia gravis and new onset of myasthenia syndrome have been reported in patients receiving azithromycin therapy

items.t: C. difficile diarrhoea / pseudomembranous colitis: consider stopping; do not give medicines that inhibit peristalsis.

src.q: Medicinal products that inhibit peristalsis should not be given.

items.t: Sexually transmitted infections: exclude Mycoplasma genitalium co-infection before single-dose treatment, and exclude syphilis.

src.q: concomitant urogenital infection by Mycoplasma genitalium should be excluded due to the high risk of emergence of resistance in this organism
a concomitant infection caused by Treponema pallidum should be excluded

items.t: Ergot derivatives: should not be co-administered (theoretical ergotism).

src.q: azithromycin and ergot derivatives should not be co-administrated

items.t: Capsules contain lactose (patients with hereditary galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take them) and sulfur dioxide (may rarely cause severe hypersensitivity and bronchospasm).

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
Zithromax capsules contains sulfur dioxide which may rarely cause severe hypersensitivity reactions and bronchospasm.

items.t: Suspension contains sucrose and glucose: patients with hereditary fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take it.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take this medicinal product.

items.t: QT-prolonging medicines (e.g. class IA/III antiarrhythmics, pimozide, citalopram, fluoroquinolones such as moxifloxacin and levofloxacin, chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine): use with caution.

src.q: Azithromycin should be used with caution in patients receiving medicinal products known to prolong the QT interval
fluoroquinolones (e.g. moxifloxacin and levofloxacin), cisapride, chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine

items.t: Hydroxychloroquine: MHRA says co-administration with azithromycin in rheumatoid arthritis was linked to more cardiovascular events and cardiovascular deaths; carefully weigh benefits and risks before prescribing.

src.q: Carefully consider the benefits and risks before prescribing systemic azithromycin or other systemic macrolide antibiotics (erythromycin or clarithromycin) to patients being treated with hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine.

items.t: Statins (e.g. atorvastatin): rhabdomyolysis reported after marketing; exercise caution. SPS: statins can be continued with azithromycin; counsel patients to report unexpected side effects.

src.q: Caution should be exercised since post-marketing cases of rhabdomyolysis in patients receiving azithromycin concomitantly with statins have been reported.
Azithromycin can be given concomitantly with statins. However, counsel patients to report any unexpected side effects.

items.t: Warfarin and other coumarins: potentiated anticoagulation reported; consider more frequent prothrombin time monitoring during and after treatment.

src.q: post-marketing reports of potentiated anticoagulation of coumarin-type oral anticoagulants upon co-administration with azithromycin
A higher frequency of prothrombin time monitoring should be considered during and after treatment with azithromycin.

items.t: No clinically relevant change in studies with antacids (aluminium/magnesium hydroxide), carbamazepine, cetirizine, fluconazole, sildenafil or trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole.

src.q: No clinically relevant change in the exposure of azithromycin or the co-administered medicinal products was observed in clinical studies evaluating potential drug-drug interactions of azithromycin with oral antacids (aluminium hydroxide/magnesium hydroxide), carbamazepine, cetirizine
fluconazole, methylprednisolone, midazolam, rifabutin, sildenafil, theophylline, triazolam, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and zidovudine

items.t: P-gp substrates with a narrow therapeutic index (e.g. digoxin, colchicine, dabigatran, ciclosporin): monitor and adjust as needed during and after treatment.

src.q: For narrow therapeutic index drugs, caution and clinical and/or therapeutic drug monitoring and dose adjustment as appropriate are advised.

items.t: GFR ≥ 10 ml/min: no dose adjustment. GFR < 10 ml/min: use with caution.

src.q: No dose adjustment is necessary in patients with GFR ≥ 10 ml/min. In patients with GFR < 10 ml/min azithromycin should be administered with caution

items.t: Mild or moderate (Child-Pugh A or B): no dose adjustment. Severe (Child-Pugh C): no data; use with caution. Caution in significant hepatic disease.

src.q: No dose adjustment is required in patients with mild (Child-Pugh Class A) or moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh Class B)
No data is available in patients with severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh Class C). Therefore, azithromycin should be administered with caution in these patients

items.t: SmPC: observational data (over 7000 exposed pregnancies) mostly show no increased risk of major malformations; miscarriage evidence inconclusive. Use only if clinically needed.

src.q: Most of these studies do not suggest an increased risk of adverse foetal effects such as major congenital malformations or cardiovascular malformations.
Azithromycin should only be used during pregnancy if clinically needed.

items.t: BUMPS (UKTIS): can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor; available information does not show harm.

src.q: Azithromycin can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor.
The available information does not show that use of azithromycin in pregnancy will harm your baby.

items.t: SmPC: excreted in milk to a substantial extent; diarrhoea, fungal infection and hypersensitivity possible in the infant. Decide whether to stop breastfeeding or stop/avoid azithromycin.

src.q: Azithromycin is excreted in human milk to substantial extent.
A decision must be made whether to discontinue breast-feeding or to discontinue/abstain from azithromycin therapy

items.t: SPS: use with caution; can be used during breastfeeding with precautionary infant monitoring (GI upset, oral thrush, rash, irritability, sleep disturbance, poor feeding).

src.q: Use with caution All formulations of azithromycin, including intravenous therapy can be used during breastfeeding, with precautionary infant monitoring.
monitor for gastro-intestinal disturbances such as diarrhoea and vomiting, oral candida infection, rashes, irritability, sleep disturbances, and loss of appetite

items.t: Reduced pregnancy rates in rat fertility studies; relevance to humans unknown.

src.q: In fertility studies conducted in rat, reduced pregnancy rates were noted following administration of azithromycin. The relevance of this finding to humans is unknown.

items.t: Most commonly reported: diarrhoea, headache, vomiting, abdominal pain, nausea and abnormal laboratory values.

src.q: The most commonly reported adverse reactions during treatment include diarrhoea, headache, vomiting, abdominal pain, nausea and abnormal laboratory test values.

items.t: Anaphylaxis, torsades de pointes and arrhythmia (including ventricular tachycardia), pseudomembranous colitis, hepatic failure.

src.q: Other important adverse reactions include anaphylactic reactions, torsades de pointes , arrhythmia including ventricular tachycardia, pseudomembranous colitis and hepatic failure

items.t: SCARs (SJS, TEN, DRESS, AGEP): stop if an allergic reaction occurs.

src.q: If an allergic reaction occurs, azithromycin should be discontinued, and appropriate therapy should be instituted.

items.t: Liver dysfunction (jaundice, dark urine, bleeding tendency, encephalopathy): stop and check liver function immediately.

src.q: In such cases liver function tests/investigations should be performed immediately.

items.t: Infants: projectile vomiting or irritability with feeding (possible pyloric stenosis) after use in the first 42 days: contact a doctor.

src.q: Parents and caregivers should be asked to contact their doctor if projectile vomiting or irritability with feeding occurs.

items.t: SPS: check ECG, magnesium and potassium before and during treatment when non-modifiable risk factors are present; not needed when used alone without risk factors.

src.q: Monitor ECG, magnesium and potassium before and during treatment in people with non-modifiable patient and medicine risk factors.

items.t: On warfarin: consider more frequent prothrombin time monitoring during and after treatment. Monitor closely for skin reactions.

src.q: A higher frequency of prothrombin time monitoring should be considered during and after treatment with azithromycin.
At the time of prescription, patients should be advised of the signs and symptoms and monitored closely for skin reactions.

items.t: Stop if an allergic reaction or signs of liver dysfunction occur.

src.q: Patients should be advised to stop azithromycin administration and to contact their physician if signs and symptoms of liver dysfunction

items.t: Capsules: swallow whole, once daily, at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal.

src.q: Capsules should be swallowed whole, as a single daily dose, either at least one hour before or two hours after a meal.

items.t: Suspension: once daily with or without a meal (taking just before a meal may improve GI tolerability). Shake before each dose. Use within 5 days of reconstitution.

src.q: Powder for oral suspension should be taken as a single daily dose with or without a meal. Administration immediately before a meal may enhance the gastrointestinal tolerability.
Once reconstituted with water, Zithromax suspension has a shelf-life of 5 days.

items.t: Stop and seek advice for signs of liver problems (yellow skin/eyes, dark urine, bleeding) or allergic/skin reactions.

src.q: rapid developing asthenia associated with jaundice, dark urine, bleeding tendency or hepatic encephalopathy develop

items.t: May cause dizziness, drowsiness, convulsions, visual or hearing problems: consider before driving.

src.q: Dizziness, drowsiness and convulsions have been reported in some patients taking azithromycin and some patients experienced visual and/or auditory impairment.

items.t: Report diarrhoea during or after the course.

src.q: CDAD and pseudomembranous colitis must be considered in patients who present with diarrhoea during or subsequent to the administration of azithromycin.

items.t: Nasal spray: prevention and treatment of perennial and seasonal allergic rhinitis (including hay fever) and vasomotor rhinitis.

src.q: indicated for the prophylaxis and treatment of perennial and seasonal allergic rhinitis including hayfever, and vasomotor rhinitis

items.t: Inhaler: preventive management of mild, moderate or severe asthma.

src.q: indicated for the prophylactic management of mild, moderate, or severe asthma in adults or children

items.t: Inhaler: prescribe CFC-free beclometasone inhalers by brand; products are not interchangeable.

src.q: prescribe CFC-free beclometasone metered-dose inhalers by brand name to reduce the risk of dosing errors
Beclometasone dipropionate pressurised metered-dose inhalers are not interchangeable.

items.t: 2 sprays into each nostril twice daily (400 micrograms a day); may reduce to 1 spray each nostril twice daily once controlled. Total daily use should not normally exceed 8 sprays.
items.tag: Rhinitis, adults and children over 6 years (nasal spray)

src.q: The recommended dosage is two sprays into each nostril twice daily (400 micrograms/day).
Total daily administration should not normally exceed eight sprays.

items.t: Usually 1000 micrograms a day, may increase to 2000 micrograms a day, in 2 to 4 divided doses; reduce when stable. Use a spacer for total daily doses of 1000 micrograms or more (16 years and over).

src.q: Usually 1000 micrograms daily, which may be increased to 2000 micrograms daily.
The total daily dosage should be administered as two to four divided doses.

items.t: Nasal spray: from 6 years (adult dose); insufficient data under 6 years.

src.q: For children under six years old, there are insufficient clinical data to recommend use.

items.t: 250 micrograms inhaler: not recommended for children.

src.q: Clenil Modulite 250 is not recommended for children.

items.t: Monitor height in children on prolonged treatment; if growth slows, reduce to the lowest effective dose and consider specialist referral.

src.q: It is recommended that the height of children receiving prolonged treatment with nasal corticosteroids is regularly monitored.
It is recommended that the height of children receiving prolonged treatment with inhaled corticosteroids is regularly monitored.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to beclometasone or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.
Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Systemic steroid effects possible, mainly at high doses for long periods (adrenal suppression, growth slowing, reduced bone density, cataract, glaucoma, mood or behaviour changes). Above-recommended or prolonged high doses: consider systemic steroid cover during stress or elective surgery.

src.q: Systemic effects of nasal corticosteroids may occur, particularly at high doses prescribed for prolonged periods.
Additional systemic corticosteroid cover should be considered during periods of stress or elective surgery.

items.t: Nasal spray: treat nasal or sinus infections appropriately (not a contraindication). Contains benzalkonium chloride, which may cause bronchospasm or nasal irritation.

src.q: Infections of the nasal passages and paranasal sinuses should be appropriately treated but do not constitute a specific contra-indication
Beconase Aqueous Nasal Spray contains 0.02 mg Benzalkonium Chloride in each unit dose, which may cause bronchospasm.

items.t: Inhaler: not for acute asthma relief; do not stop abruptly. Special care in active or quiescent pulmonary tuberculosis. Moving from long-term or high-dose systemic steroids needs special care and slow oral steroid reduction.

src.q: Clenil Modulite does not provide relief of acute asthma symptoms, which require a short-acting inhaled bronchodilator.
Treatment with Clenil Modulite should not be stopped abruptly.
special care is necessary in patients with active or quiescent pulmonary tuberculosis

items.t: Blurred vision or other visual disturbance: consider referral to an ophthalmologist.

src.q: the patient should be considered for referral to an ophthalmologist for evaluation of possible causes

items.t: Beclometasone depends less on CYP3A than some other corticosteroids and interactions are generally unlikely, but systemic effects with strong CYP3A inhibitors (for example ritonavir, cobicistat) cannot be excluded: use caution and monitor.

src.q: Beclomethasone is less dependent on CYP3A metabolism than some other corticosteroids, and in general interactions are unlikely
caution and appropriate monitoring is advised with the use of such agents

items.t: MHRA: where a steroid is needed with ritonavir or cobicistat, consider beclometasone where possible (lower, but not zero, interaction risk).

src.q: use of beclomethasone should be considered where possible-particularly for long-term use

items.t: Inhaler contains a small amount of ethanol: theoretical interaction in particularly sensitive patients on disulfiram or metronidazole.

src.q: There is a theoretical potential for interaction in particularly sensitive patients taking disulfiram or metronidazole.

items.t: Inhaler: no dose adjustment needed in renal impairment. Nasal spray SmPC: not stated.

src.q: No dosage adjustment is needed in patients with hepatic or renal impairment.

items.t: Inhaler: no dose adjustment needed in hepatic impairment. Nasal spray SmPC: not stated.

src.q: No dosage adjustment is needed in patients with hepatic or renal impairment.

items.t: Nasal spray SmPC: inadequate evidence of safety; avoid in pregnancy unless thought essential by the doctor (direct nasal delivery minimises systemic exposure).

src.q: The use of beclometasone dipropionate should be avoided during pregnancy unless thought essential by the doctor.

items.t: Inhaler SmPC: should not be used in pregnancy unless the expected benefit to the mother outweighs any risk to the fetus.

src.q: It should not be used in pregnancy or lactation unless the expected benefits to the mother are thought to outweigh any potential risks to the fetus or neonate.

items.t: BUMPS: inhaled corticosteroids (including beclometasone) should be continued throughout pregnancy; no evidence of harm to the baby.

src.q: Inhaled corticosteroids should be continued throughout pregnancy to ensure that breathing problems do not occur.
There is no evidence that use of inhaled corticosteroids in pregnancy harms the baby.

items.t: SPS and BUMPS (allergic rhinitis in pregnancy): intranasal corticosteroids can be considered if non-drug measures are not enough.

src.q: intranasal corticosteroids (for example, fluticasone) can be considered if non-pharmacological management is insufficient
If this does not help, you can consider using nasal sprays containing medicines called corticosteroids

items.t: Nasal spray SmPC: low potential for significant milk levels; weigh benefits against potential hazards.

src.q: The use of beclometasone dipropionate in mothers breast feeding their babies requires that the therapeutic benefits of the drug be weighed against the potential hazards to the mother and baby.

items.t: Inhaler SmPC: should not be used in lactation unless the expected benefit outweighs any potential risk to the neonate.

src.q: It should not be used in pregnancy or lactation unless the expected benefits to the mother are thought to outweigh any potential risks to the fetus or neonate.

items.t: SPS: intranasal or inhaled beclometasone can be used during breastfeeding; no specific infant monitoring usually needed.

src.q: When applied to the skin, used intranasally, or inhaled, beclomethasone can be used during breastfeeding.
No specific infant monitoring is usually required.

reproductive.note: No fertility or contraception statement in the UK nasal spray and inhaler SmPCs checked.

items.t: Nasal spray: unpleasant taste or smell, nosebleed, nasal or throat dryness and irritation.

src.q: Unpleasant taste, unpleasant smell. Common
Epistaxis, nasal dryness, nasal irritation, throat dryness, throat irritation. Common

items.t: Inhaler: oral thrush (very common; more above 400 micrograms a day), hoarseness, throat irritation.

src.q: Oral candidiasis (of the mouth and throat) Very Common
Hoarseness, throat irritation Common

items.t: Inhaler: paradoxical bronchospasm (wheeze, breathlessness, cough straight after a dose): treat with a fast-acting bronchodilator, stop beclometasone at once, assess.

src.q: This should be treated immediately with a fast-acting inhaled bronchodilator. Clenil Modulite should be discontinued immediately

items.t: Hypersensitivity including angioedema and anaphylactic reactions (very rare).

src.q: Angioedema Very rare
Anaphylactoid/anaphylactic reactions Very rare

items.t: Nasal septum perforation; glaucoma, raised eye pressure, cataract (very rare).

src.q: Nasal septum perforation. Very rare
Glaucoma, raised intraocular pressure, cataract.

items.t: Height in children on prolonged treatment.

src.q: It is recommended that the height of children receiving prolonged treatment with nasal corticosteroids is regularly monitored.

items.t: Inhaler: severe asthma needs regular assessment including lung function; monitor adrenal function while reducing systemic steroids.

src.q: Severe asthma requires regular medical assessment, including lung-function testing
Adrenocortical function should be monitored regularly as the dose of systemic steroid is gradually reduced.

items.t: If on a strong CYP3A inhibitor: caution and appropriate monitoring.

src.q: caution and appropriate monitoring is advised with the use of such agents

items.t: Nasal spray: intranasal use only; use regularly for full benefit.

src.q: Beconase Aqueous Nasal Spray is for administration by the intranasal route only.
For full therapeutic benefit regular usage is essential.

items.t: Inhaler: inhale slowly and deeply through the mouth, press while breathing in, hold breath 5-10 seconds; wait 30 seconds before a second puff. Use a spacer if coordination is difficult. Clean at least weekly; do not put in water.

src.q: hold their breath for about 5 to 10 seconds, or as long as is comfortable, and then breathe out slowly
If another dose is required, the patient should be advised to wait 30 seconds before repeating the procedure just described.
The inhaler must not be washed or put in water.

items.t: Inhaler: rinse mouth, gargle or brush teeth after each use. Use every day even when well. Seek medical help if the reliever works less well or is needed more often.

src.q: Advise the patient to thoroughly rinse the mouth or gargle with water or brush the teeth immediately after using the inhaler.
Clenil Modulite should be used on a regular basis, even when they are asymptomatic.
Patients should be instructed to seek medical attention if short-acting relief bronchodilator treatment becomes less effective

items.t: Nasal spray: maximum relief may take more than a few doses; keep to the regular schedule.

src.q: it should be explained that maximum relief may not be obtained within the first few applications

items.t: Patients weaned off oral steroids with impaired adrenal function should carry a steroid warning card.

src.q: should carry a steroid warning card indicating that they may need supplementary systemic steroids during periods of stress

items.t: Relief of painful inflammatory conditions of the mouth and throat: pharyngitis after tonsillectomy or a nasogastric tube, pharyngitis, aphthous ulcers, oral ulceration due to radiotherapy, and after dental operations.

src.q: A locally acting analgesic and anti-inflammatory treatment for the relief of painful inflammatory conditions of the mouth and throat including:
Pharyngitis following tonsillectomy or the use of a naso-gastric tube.
Pharyngitis, aphthous ulcers and oral ulceration due to radiation therapy. Dentistry: For use after dental operations.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restrictions found in the two UK 0.15% benzydamine SmPCs (pharmacy medicines) or MHRA Drug Safety Update.

items.t: Adults and elderly: rinse or gargle with 15 mL every 1.5 to 3 hours as needed for pain; spit out after use. Do not use continuously for more than 7 days except under medical supervision.

src.q: Rinse or gargle with 15 ml (approximately 1 tablespoonful) every 1½ to 3 hours as required for pain relief.
Uninterrupted treatment should not exceed seven days, except under medical supervision.

items.t: Contraindicated (UK bisoprolol 5 mg SmPC, all patients): acute heart failure or decompensation needing IV inotropes; cardiogenic shock; sinoatrial block; second- or third-degree AV block (without pacemaker); symptomatic bradycardia (heart rate below 60 beats/min before starting); severe bronchial asthma or severe COPD; sick sinus syndrome; symptomatic hypotension (systolic blood pressure below 100 mmHg); severe peripheral arterial occlusive disease and Raynaud's syndrome; untreated phaeochromocytoma; metabolic acidosis; hypersensitivity to bisoprolol or excipients.

src.q: Bisoprolol is contraindicated in patients with:
acute heart failure or during episodes of heart failure decompensation requiring i.v. inotropic therapy
second or third degree AV block (without pacemaker).
symptomatic bradycardia (heart rate less than 60 beats/min prior to start of therapy).
severe bronchial asthma or severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
symptomatic hypotension (systolic blood pressure <100mmHg).
severe forms of peripheral arterial occlusive disease and Raynaud's syndrome.
untreated phaeochromocytoma (see section 4.4).
metabolic acidosis.
hypersensitivity to the active substance(s) or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1

src.q: Patients with psoriasis or with a history of psoriasis should only be given beta-blockers (e.g. bisoprolol) after carefully balancing the benefits against the risks.

src.q: bisoprolol may increase both the sensitivity towards allergens and the severity of anaphylactic reactions. Adrenaline treatment does not always yield the expected therapeutic effect.

Under treatment with bisoprolol the symptoms of a thyreotoxicosis may be masked.

items.t: Surgery: continue beta-blockade peri-operatively; inform the anaesthetist. If withdrawal is needed, do it gradually and complete about 48 hours before anaesthesia.

If it is thought necessary to withdraw beta-blocker therapy before surgery, this should be done gradually and completed about 48 hours before anaesthesia.

items.t: Heart failure: no experience in type 1 diabetes, severe renal or hepatic impairment, restrictive cardiomyopathy, congenital heart disease, significant valve disease, or MI within 3 months.

items.t: Verapamil (and, less so, diltiazem): not recommended; negative effect on contractility and AV conduction. IV verapamil in a patient on a beta-blocker may cause profound hypotension and AV block.

src.q: Calcium antagonists of the verapamil type and to a lesser extent of the diltiazem type: Negative influence on contractility and atrio-ventricular conduction.
Intravenous administration of verapamil in patients on β-blocker treatment may lead to profound hypotension and atrioventricular block.

items.t: Centrally acting antihypertensives (e.g. clonidine, methyldopa, moxonidine): not recommended; may worsen heart failure; abrupt withdrawal may cause rebound hypertension.

src.q: Centrally acting antihypertensive drugs such as clonidine and others (e.g. methyldopa, moxonodine, rilmenidine)
Abrupt withdrawal, particularly if prior to beta-blocker discontinuation, may increase risk of "rebound hypertension".

items.t: Dihydropyridines (e.g. amlodipine): use with caution; more risk of hypotension and possible further worsening of heart failure.

src.q: Calcium antagonists of the dihydropyridine type such as felodipine and amlodipine: Concomitant use may increase the risk of hypotension

items.t: Insulin and oral antidiabetics: increased glucose lowering; hypoglycaemia symptoms may be masked; sulfonylureas may increase the risk of severe hypoglycaemia.

src.q: Insulin and oral antidiabetic drugs: Increase of blood sugar lowering effect.
The concomitant use of beta-blockers with sulfonylureas could increase the risk of severe hypoglycaemia

items.t: NSAIDs may reduce the blood pressure lowering effect. Antihypertensives and other blood pressure lowering medicines (e.g. tricyclic antidepressants) may increase the risk of hypotension.

src.q: NSAIDs may reduce the hypotensive effect of bisoprolol.

Concomitant use with antihypertensive agents as well as with other drugs with blood pressure lowering potential (e.g. tricyclic antidepressants, barbiturates, phenothiazines) may increase the risk of hypotension.

items.t: Sympathomimetics: beta-agonists (e.g. isoprenaline) may lose effect; alpha- and beta-agonists (e.g. adrenaline) may raise blood pressure.

src.q: Sympathomimetics that activate both β- and α-adrenoceptors (e.g. noradrenaline, adrenaline): Combination with bisoprolol may unmask the α-adrenoceptor-mediated vasoconstrictor effects

items.t: MAOIs (except MAO-B inhibitors): enhanced hypotensive effect but also risk of hypertensive crisis. Digoxin and parasympathomimetics: more bradycardia/AV delay. Class I and III antiarrhythmics: AV conduction effects. Mefloquine: more bradycardia.

src.q: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (except MAO-B inhibitors): Enhanced hypotensive effect of the beta-blockers but also risk for hypertensive crisis.
Digitalis glycosides: Reduction of heart rate, increase of atrio-ventricular conduction time.

src.q: Bisoprolol can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor.
A small number of pregnant women taking bisoprolol have been studied, with no concerns raised that its use causes miscarriage or birth defects.
you may be offered additional scans at around 32 and 36 weeks
