items.t: Rare: hypersensitivity including angioedema and anaphylaxis; cardiac arrhythmias (AF, SVT, extrasystoles); hypokalaemia.

src.q: Rare Immediate and delayed hypersensitivity reactions, e.g. exanthema, urticaria, pruritus, dermatitis, angioedema and anaphylactic reaction
Rare Cardiac arrhythmias, e.g. atrial fibrillation, supraventricular tachycardia, extrasystoles

items.t: Sudden, progressive loss of asthma or COPD control is potentially life-threatening: urgent medical assessment.

src.q: Sudden and progressive deterioration in control of asthma or COPD is potentially life threatening and the patient should undergo urgent medical assessment.

items.t: Reassess regularly so use stays optimal; assess more often when starting or changing dose.

src.q: Patients should be regularly reassessed by their prescriber/health care provider so that the usage of Symbicort remains optimal.

items.t: Serum potassium in unstable or acute severe asthma; extra blood glucose checks in diabetes.

src.q: It is recommended that serum potassium levels are monitored during these circumstances.
additional blood glucose controls should be considered in diabetic patients

items.t: HPA axis function regularly in patients transferred from oral steroids; height in children on prolonged treatment.

src.q: In such circumstances HPA axis function should be monitored regularly.
It is recommended that the height of children receiving prolonged treatment with inhaled corticosteroids is regularly monitored.

items.t: Stop at once if paradoxical bronchospasm occurs.

src.q: If the patient experiences paradoxical bronchospasm Symbicort should be discontinued immediately

items.t: Breathe in forcefully and deeply through the mouthpiece; never breathe out through it; replace the cover. Rinse mouth with water after the maintenance dose to reduce thrush.

src.q: to breathe in forcefully and deeply through the mouthpiece to ensure that an optimal dose is delivered to the lungs.
never to breathe out through the mouthpiece.
to rinse their mouth out with water after inhaling the maintenance dose to minimise the risk of oropharyngeal thrush.

items.t: Keep the reliever (separate inhaler, or this inhaler if on maintenance-and-reliever) with you at all times; take maintenance doses even when well.

src.q: Patients should be advised to have their rescue inhaler available at all times
they should be reminded to take their Symbicort maintenance dose as prescribed, even when asymptomatic

items.t: Get medical help if the inhaler works less well or more inhalations than usual are needed. All asthma patients should have a written personal asthma action plan.

src.q: If patients find the treatment less effective, or need more inhalations than usual, medical attention must be sought
It is recommended that all patients with asthma are provided with a written personal asthma action plan.

items.t: Inhibition of physiological lactation soon after delivery, and suppression of established lactation (mother not breastfeeding for any reason, or after stillbirth or abortion).

src.q: Cabergoline is indicated for the inhibition of physiological lactation soon after delivery and for suppression of already established lactation

items.t: Hyperprolactinaemic disorders (amenorrhoea, oligomenorrhoea, anovulation, galactorrhoea), including prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas, idiopathic hyperprolactinaemia and empty sella syndrome.

src.q: Cabergoline is indicated for the treatment of dysfunctions associated with hyperprolactinaemia, including amenorrhoea, oligomenorrhoea, anovulation and galactorrhoea.
Cabergoline is indicated in patients with prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas (micro- and macroprolactinomas), idiopathic hyperprolactinaemia, or empty sella syndrome

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction stated in the UK SmPC or the MHRA pages accessed. MHRA fibrosis advice applies to chronic endocrine use, not to inhibition of lactation.

items.t: Inhibition of lactation: 1 mg (two 0.5 mg tablets) as a single dose on the first day after delivery.

src.q: For inhibition of lactation cabergoline should be administered during the first day post-partum. The recommended therapeutic dose is 1 mg (two 0.5 mg tablets) given as a single dose.

items.t: Suppression of established lactation: 0.25 mg every 12 hours for two days (1 mg total). Do not exceed a single dose of 0.25 mg in nursing women (postural hypotension).

src.q: For suppression of established lactation the recommended therapeutic dosage regimen is 0.25 mg (one-half 0.5 mg tablet) every 12 hours for two days (1 mg total dose).
A single dose of 0.25 mg of cabergoline should not be exceeded in nursing women treated for suppression of established lactation to avoid potential postural hypotension

items.t: Hyperprolactinaemia: start 0.5 mg per week in one or two doses; increase by 0.5 mg per week at monthly intervals to response. Usual dose 1 mg per week (range 0.25-2 mg per week). Maximum 3 mg per day. Split weekly doses above 1 mg.

src.q: The recommended initial dosage of cabergoline is 0.5 mg per week given in one or two (one-half of one 0.5 mg tablet) doses
The therapeutic dosage is usually 1 mg per week and ranges from 0.25 mg to 2 mg per week.
The maximum dose should not exceed 3mg per day.
Division of the weekly dose into multiple administrations is advised when doses higher than 1 mg per week are to be given

items.t: Valvulopathy is linked to cumulative dose: use the lowest effective dose and reassess benefit and risk at each visit.

src.q: Valvulopathy has been associated with cumulative doses, therefore, patients should be treated with the lowest effective dose.

items.t: Safety and efficacy not established under 16 years.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of cabergoline has not been established in subjects less than 16 years of age.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to cabergoline, excipients or any ergot alkaloid.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to cabergoline, any of the excipients listed in section 6.1 or any ergot alkaloid.

items.t: History of pulmonary, pericardial or retroperitoneal fibrotic disorders.

src.q: History of pulmonary, pericardial and retroperitoneal fibrotic disorders.

items.t: Hepatic insufficiency; toxaemia of pregnancy.

src.q: Cabergoline is contraindicated in patients with hepatic insufficiency and with toxaemia of pregnancy.

items.t: Do not give with antipsychotic medicines or to women with a history of puerperal psychosis.

src.q: Cabergoline should not be co-administered with anti-psychotic medications or administered to women with a history of puerperal psychosis.

items.t: Long-term treatment: evidence of cardiac valvulopathy on pre-treatment echocardiography.

src.q: For long-term treatment: Evidence of cardiac valvulopathy as determined by pre-treatment echocardiography.

items.t: Caution in severe cardiovascular disease, Raynaud's syndrome, renal insufficiency, peptic ulcer or GI bleeding, or a history of serious (especially psychotic) mental disorders. Particular care with other psychoactive medicines.

src.q: cabergoline should be given with caution to patients with severe cardiovascular disease, Raynaud's syndrome, renal insufficiency, peptic ulcer or gastrointestinal bleeding, or with a history of serious, particularly psychotic, mental disorders
Particular care should be taken when patients are taking concomitant psychoactive medication.

items.t: Fibrosis and valvulopathy (pleural, pulmonary, pericardial, valvular, retroperitoneal) after prolonged use. Before long-term treatment: echocardiogram, ESR or other inflammatory markers, lung function/chest X-ray and renal function. Stop if echo shows new or worse valve regurgitation, restriction or leaflet thickening.

src.q: All patients must undergo a cardiovascular evaluation, including echocardiogram to assess the potential presence of asymptomatic valvular disease.
Cabergoline should be discontinued if an echocardiogram reveals new or worsened valvular regurgitation, valvular restriction or valve leaflet thickening

items.t: Symptomatic and postural hypotension can occur; take care with other blood-pressure-lowering medicines.

src.q: Symptomatic hypotension can occur with cabergoline administration for any indication.
Care should be exercised when administering cabergoline concomitantly with other drugs known to lower blood pressure.

items.t: Somnolence and sudden sleep onset: warn patients; those affected must not drive or operate machines; consider dose reduction or stopping.

src.q: Patients who have experienced somnolence and/or an episode of sudden sleep onset must refrain from driving or operating machines.

items.t: Impulse control disorders (gambling, hypersexuality, compulsive spending or eating): monitor regularly; consider dose reduction or tapered withdrawal.

src.q: Patients should be regularly monitored for the development of impulse control disorders.
Dose reduction/tapered discontinuation should be considered if such symptoms develop.

items.t: Lactation inhibition: avoid in pregnancy-induced (e.g. post-partum) hypertension unless benefit outweighs risk. Hypertension, MI, seizures, stroke and psychiatric disorders have been reported post-partum; monitor blood pressure and stop if hypertension, chest pain, severe headache or CNS toxicity occurs.

src.q: cabergoline should not be used in women with pregnancy-induced hypertension, for example, post-partum hypertension, unless the potential benefit is judged to outweigh the possible risk
cabergoline should be discontinued and the patient should be evaluated promptly

items.t: Hyperprolactinaemia: full pituitary evaluation before treatment. Fertility may return before menses; pregnancy test at least every 4 weeks while amenorrhoeic.

src.q: a complete evaluation of the pituitary is indicated before treatment with cabergoline is initiated
a pregnancy test is recommended at least every four weeks during the amenorrhoeic period

items.t: Contains lactose: not for hereditary galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: Antipsychotic medicines: do not co-administer (section 4.3).

src.q: Cabergoline should not be co-administered with anti-psychotic medications

items.t: Dopamine antagonists (phenothiazines, butyrophenones, thioxanthenes, metoclopramide): should not be given together; may reduce the prolactin-lowering effect.

src.q: it should not be concurrently administered with drugs which have dopamine-antagonist activity (such as phenothiazines, butyrophenones, thioxanthenes, metoclopramide) since these might reduce the prolactin-lowering effect of cabergoline

items.t: Macrolide antibiotics (e.g. erythromycin): should not be used together; raise cabergoline exposure.

src.q: cabergoline should not be used with macrolide antibiotics (e.g. erythromycin) due to increased systemic bioavailability of cabergoline

items.t: Other ergot alkaloids during long-term treatment: not recommended.

src.q: the concomitant use of these medications during long-term treatment with cabergoline is not recommended

items.t: Other blood-pressure-lowering medicines: take care (hypotension).

src.q: Care should be exercised when administering cabergoline concomitantly with other drugs known to lower blood pressure.

items.t: Safety and efficacy not established in renal disease; give with caution in renal insufficiency. No numeric threshold given.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of cabergoline have not yet been established in patients with renal and hepatic disease.
cabergoline should be given with caution to patients with severe cardiovascular disease, Raynaud's syndrome, renal insufficiency

items.t: Section 4.3 contraindicates cabergoline in hepatic insufficiency. Section 4.4 separately advises considering lower doses in severe hepatic insufficiency (Child-Pugh C) on prolonged treatment (higher AUC).

src.q: Cabergoline is contraindicated in patients with hepatic insufficiency
Lower doses should be considered in patients with severe hepatic insufficiency who receive prolonged treatment with cabergoline.

items.t: Contraindicated in toxaemia of pregnancy. Otherwise use only if clearly indicated after benefit/risk assessment. Exclude pregnancy before starting; stop 1 month before planned conception; stop as soon as pregnancy is confirmed. Monitor pregnant women for pituitary enlargement.

src.q: Cabergoline should only be used during pregnancy if clearly indicated and after an accurate benefit/risk evaluation.
women planning to become pregnant should discontinue cabergoline one month before intended conception
If conception occurs during therapy, treatment should be discontinued as soon as pregnancy is confirmed to limit foetal exposure to the drug.

items.t: Cabergoline stops lactation: do not give to women with hyperprolactinaemia who wish to breastfeed. Advise not to breastfeed if lactation inhibition/suppression fails. Human milk excretion unknown.

src.q: Since it prevents lactation, cabergoline should not be administered to mothers with hyperprolactinemic disorders who wish to breast-feed their infants.
mothers should be advised not to breast-feed in case of failed lactation inhibition/suppression by cabergoline

items.t: Restores ovulation and fertility in hyperprolactinaemic hypogonadism. Women who want to avoid pregnancy should use mechanical contraception during treatment and after stopping until anovulation returns. After any treatment, prevent pregnancy for at least one month.

src.q: Cabergoline restores ovulation and fertility in women with hyperprolactinaemic hypogonadism.
Women who wish to avoid pregnancy should be advised to use mechanical contraception during treatment with cabergoline and after discontinuation of cabergoline until recurrence of anovulation.
after treatment pregnancy should be prevented for at least one month

items.t: Very common: valvulopathy and related disorders, headache, dizziness/vertigo, nausea, dyspepsia, gastritis, abdominal pain, asthenia, fatigue. Common: somnolence, depression, postural hypotension, hot flushes, constipation, vomiting, breast pain.

src.q: Cardiac disorders Very Common Valvulopathy (including regurgitation) and related disorders (pericarditis and pericardial effusion)
Nervous system disorders Very common Headache*, dizziness/vertigo* Common somnolence
Gastrointestinal disorders Very common Nausea*, dyspepsia, gastritis, abdominal pain* Common Constipation, vomiting**

items.t: Fibrotic reactions (pleural, pulmonary, pericardial, retroperitoneal) and cardiac valvulopathy: watch for breathlessness, persistent cough, chest pain, loin/flank pain, leg oedema or heart failure; investigate and stop if confirmed.

src.q: Pleuro-pulmonary disease such as dyspnoea, shortness of breath, persistent cough or chest pain.
cases of valvular and pericardial fibrosis have often manifested as cardiac failure

items.t: Post-partum use: hypertension, myocardial infarction, seizures, stroke or psychiatric disorders reported; stop and evaluate promptly.

src.q: Serious adverse events including hypertension, myocardial infarction, seizures, stroke or psychiatric disorders have been reported in postpartum women treated with cabergoline for inhibition of lactation.

items.t: Sudden sleep onset; impulse control disorders; psychotic disorder and hallucinations (frequency not known).

src.q: Not Known Aggression, delusions, hypersexuality, pathological gambling, psychotic disorder, hallucinations

items.t: Before long-term treatment: echocardiogram; ESR or other inflammatory markers; lung function/chest X-ray; renal function. Exclude pregnancy.

src.q: It is also appropriate to perform baseline investigations of erythrocyte sedimentation rate or other inflammatory markers, lung function/chest X-ray and renal function prior to initiation of therapy.
Before administration of cabergoline, pregnancy should be excluded.

items.t: First echocardiogram within 3-6 months of starting, then at least every 6-12 months. Serum prolactin monthly during titration.

src.q: the first echocardiogram must occur within 3-6 months
must occur at least every 6 to 12 months
Monitoring of serum prolactin levels at monthly intervals is advised

items.t: Post-partum: monitor blood pressure, especially in the first few days.

src.q: periodic monitoring of blood pressure, particularly during the first few days after cabergoline administration, is advised

items.t: Stop if echocardiogram shows new or worsened valve regurgitation, restriction or leaflet thickening; stop if pregnancy occurs.

src.q: Cabergoline should be discontinued if an echocardiogram reveals new or worsened valvular regurgitation, valvular restriction or valve leaflet thickening
Should pregnancy occur during treatment, cabergoline is to be discontinued.

items.t: MHRA: echocardiography within 3-6 months, then every 6-12 months; this fibrosis advice applies to chronic endocrine use, not to lactation inhibition.

src.q: echocardiography should be done within 3-6 months of starting treatment and subsequently at 6-12-month intervals
This new advice applies only to treatment of chronic endocrine disorders with these agents-it does not apply to the inhibition of lactation.

items.t: Oral; preferably take with meals (better tolerated).

src.q: it is recommended that cabergoline be preferably taken with meals for all the therapeutic indications

items.t: May cause drowsiness or sudden sleep; be careful driving in the first days; do not drive if sleepiness occurs.

src.q: During the first days of cabergoline administration, patients should be cautioned about re-engaging in activities requiring rapid and precise responses such as driving an automobile or operating machinery.

items.t: Tell the doctor about unusual urges (gambling, sex, spending, eating). MHRA: warn patients and carers and ask them to report unusual behaviour.

src.q: Healthcare professionals are advised to warn patients about these possible side-effects, and to inform patients to seek help from their doctor if they, their family, or their carer notice that their behaviour is unusual.

items.t: Report breathlessness, persistent cough, chest pain, loin pain or leg swelling.

src.q: Renal insufficiency or ureteral/abdominal vascular obstruction that may occur with pain in the loin/flank and lower limb oedema

items.t: Relief of symptoms of mild sunburn and other minor skin conditions.

src.q: For relief of the symptoms of mild sunburn and other minor skin conditions.

equivalent to 600mg of elemental calcium

items.t: Calcium reduces absorption of thyroxine (levothyroxine), quinolones (e.g. ciprofloxacin), tetracyclines, bisphosphonates, sodium fluoride and iron. Calcium carbonate SmPC: allow at least 4 hours before taking the calcium.

(administration should be separated by 4-5 hours)

src.q: multivalent cation-containing drugs and mineral supplements (e.g. calcium, magnesium, aluminium, iron)
ciprofloxacin should be administered either 1-2 hours before or at least 4 hours after these preparations

items.t: Hydroxychloroquine SmPC: antacids may reduce hydroxychloroquine absorption; keep a 4-hour interval.

src.q: antacids may reduce absorption of hydroxychloroquine so it is advised that a 4 hour interval be observed between hydroxychloroquine sulfate and antacid dosing

items.t: Iron: if both are needed, take at different times.

src.q: If Adcal and iron supplements are both required to be administered to the patient, they should be taken at different times

items.t: Thiazide diuretics reduce urinary calcium excretion: consider the risk of hypercalcaemia.

src.q: The risk of hypercalcaemia should be considered in patients taking thiazide diuretics since these drugs can reduce urinary calcium excretion.

items.t: Digitalis/cardiac glycosides: avoid hypercalcaemia; strict medical supervision and, if needed, ECG and calcium monitoring.

Strict medical supervision is needed and, if necessary monitoring of ECG and calcium.

The prevention and treatment of calcium deficiency/vitamin D deficiency especially in the housebound and institutionalised elderly subjects.

Hypersensitivity to any of the tablet ingredients.

src.q: Relative contra-indications are osteoporosis due to prolonged immobilisation, renal stones, severe hypercalciuria.
Relative contra-indications are osteoporosis due to prolonged immobilisation, renal stones, severe hypercalciuria.

items.t: Long-term treatment: monitor serum calcium and renal function (serum creatinine), especially in elderly patients on cardiac glycosides or diuretics and in stone formers. Reduce or stop if hypercalcaemia or impaired renal function; reduce or interrupt if urinary calcium exceeds 7.5 mmol/24 h (300 mg/24 h).

src.q: During long-term treatment, serum calcium levels should be followed and renal function should be monitored through measurements of serum creatinine.
In case of hypercalcaemia or signs of impaired renal function the dose should be reduced or the treatment discontinued.
It is advisable to reduce or interrupt treatment temporarily if urinary calcium exceeds 7.5 mmol/24 h (300 mg/24 h).

items.t: Mild to moderate renal failure or mild hypercalciuria: supervise carefully with periodic plasma calcium and urinary calcium checks. History of renal stones: measure urinary calcium to exclude hypercalciuria.

src.q: Patients with mild to moderate renal failure or mild hypercalciuria should be supervised carefully including periodic checks of plasma calcium levels and urinary calcium excretion.
In patients with a history of renal stones, urinary calcium excretion should be measured to exclude hypercalciuria.

items.t: Sarcoidosis: prescribe with caution (increased activation of vitamin D); monitor serum and urine calcium.

src.q: should be prescribed with caution to patients suffering from sarcoidosis, due to the risk of increased metabolism of vitamin D into its active form.

items.t: Immobilised patients with osteoporosis: use with caution (increased risk of hypercalcaemia).

src.q: should be used with caution in immobilised patients with osteoporosis due to increased risk of hypercalcaemia.

items.t: Allow for calcium and vitamin D from other sources. Extra calcium or vitamin D only under close medical supervision with frequent serum and urine calcium checks. Large amounts of calcium with absorbable alkali can cause milk-alkali syndrome (hypercalcaemia, alkalosis, renal impairment).

src.q: Additional doses of calcium or vitamin D should be taken under close medical supervision.
Milk-alkali syndrome (Burnett's syndrome), i.e. hypercalcaemia, alkalosis and renal impairment can develop when large amounts of calcium are ingested with absorbable alkali.

items.t: Contains sucrose: people with hereditary fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take it.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take this medicine.

items.t: Thiazides reduce urinary calcium excretion: risk of hypercalcaemia. The 600 mg / 400 IU tablet SmPC says monitor serum calcium regularly.

src.q: Due to increased risk of hypercalcaemia, serum calcium should be regularly monitored during concomitant use of thiazide diuretics.
The risk of hypercalcaemia should be considered in patients taking thiazide diuretics

items.tag: Separation times (they differ between UK sources)
items.t: 600 mg / 400 IU tablet SmPC: tetracyclines at least 2 hours before or 4-6 hours after calcium; quinolones 2 hours before or 6 hours after; iron and thyroid hormones at least 2 hours apart. 300 mg / 200 IU tablet SmPC: allow at least 4 hours before taking the calcium after thyroxine, quinolones, tetracyclines or iron.

src.q: tetracycline preparations should be administered at least two hours before or four to six hours after oral intake of calcium.
Quinolone antibiotics should be taken two hours before or six hours after intake of calcium.
the iron, zinc or strontium preparation should be taken at a distance of two hours from the calcium preparation.
It is recommended that taking Accrete D3 film-coated tablets be spaced at least 2 hours from these medicines.

Calcium salts may reduce the absorption of thyroxine, bisphosphonates, sodium fluoride, quinolone or tetracycline antibiotics, zinc, strontium ranelate and iron. It is advisable to allow a minimum period of four hours before taking calcium.

items.t: Levothyroxine SmPC: calcium salts may reduce levothyroxine absorption; separate by 4-5 hours.

src.q: Absorption of levothyroxine (thyroxine) possibly reduced by antacids, calcium salts
(administration should be separated by 4-5 hours)

items.t: Ciprofloxacin SmPC: give ciprofloxacin 1-2 hours before or at least 4 hours after calcium-containing products.

src.q: multivalent cation-containing drugs and mineral supplements (e.g. calcium, magnesium, aluminium, iron)
ciprofloxacin should be administered either 1-2 hours before or at least 4 hours after these preparations

items.t: Hypercalcaemia may increase cardiac glycoside toxicity: monitor ECG and serum calcium.

src.q: Hypercalcaemia may increase the toxicity of cardiac glycosides during treatment with calcium and vitamin D. Patients should be monitored with regard to electrocardiogram (ECG) and serum calcium levels.

items.t: Systemic corticosteroids reduce calcium absorption; the dose may need to be increased.

src.q: Systemic corticosteroids reduce calcium absorption. During concomitant use, it may be necessary to increase the dose of Accrete D3 film-coated tablets.

items.t: Bisphosphonates or sodium fluoride at least 3 hours before the calcium tablet. Rifampicin, phenytoin and barbiturates may reduce vitamin D activity. Colestyramine and paraffin oil may reduce vitamin D absorption.

src.q: these medicinal products should be administered at least three hours before the intake of Accrete D3 film-coated tablet since gastrointestinal absorption may be reduced.
Rifampicin, phenytoin or barbiturates may reduce the activity of vitamin D3, since they increase the rate of its metabolism.

items.t: Do not take within 2 hours of foods high in oxalic acid (spinach, sorrel, rhubarb) or phytic acid (whole cereals).

src.q: The patient should not take calcium products within two hours of eating foods high in oxalic acid and phytic acid.

items.t: Contraindicated in severe renal impairment and renal failure (no eGFR/CrCl threshold given). In severe renal insufficiency colecalciferol is not metabolised normally; other forms of vitamin D should be used.

src.q: Accrete D3 film-coated tablets should not be used in patients with severe renal impairment.
In patients with severe renal insufficiency, vitamin D in the form of colecalciferol is not metabolised normally and other forms of vitamin D should be used

items.t: Renal impairment: use vitamin D with caution and monitor calcium and phosphate; risk of soft tissue calcification, hyperphosphataemia, nephrolithiasis and nephrocalcinosis.

src.q: Vitamin D should be used with caution in patients with impairment of renal function and the effect on calcium and phosphate levels should be monitored.
Patients with renal impairment: potential risk of hyperphosphatemia, nephrolithiasis and nephrocalcinosis.

items.t: 600 mg / 400 IU tablet: no dose adjustment in hepatic impairment. The 300 mg / 200 IU tablet SmPC gives no hepatic advice.

src.q: Hepatic impairment No dose adjustment is required.

items.t: May be used for calcium and vitamin D deficiency. In pregnancy the daily dose should not exceed 1500 mg calcium and 600 IU vitamin D; avoid any overdose (prolonged hypercalcaemia can harm the child).

src.q: Accrete D3 film-coated tablets may be given during pregnancy in cases of calcium and vitamin D3 deficiency. During pregnancy the daily dose should not exceed 1500 mg of calcium and 600 IU of vitamin D.
In pregnant women, all calcium or vitamin D overdoses must be avoided

items.t: Use in pregnancy only under the direction of a physician; allow for calcium and vitamin D from other sources. Take iron supplements at a different time.

src.q: During pregnancy and lactation, treatment with Adcal-D3 Caplets should always be under the direction of a physician.
If the patient requires administration of both Adcal-D3 Caplets and iron supplements, they should be taken at different times

items.t: Can be used during breastfeeding. Calcium and vitamin D pass into breast milk: consider this when giving the infant extra vitamin D.

src.q: Accrete D3 film-coated tablets can be used during breast-feeding. Calcium and vitamin D pass into breast milk. This should be considered when giving additional vitamin D to the child.

items.t: Use during lactation under the direction of a physician.

src.q: During pregnancy and lactation, treatment with Adcal-D3 Caplets should always be under the direction of a physician.

items.t: No known harmful effect of normal calcium and vitamin D levels on fertility; no product data.

src.q: There is no known harmful effect of endogenous levels of calcium and vitamin D in the normal range on fertility.

items.t: No common effects listed. Uncommon: hypercalcaemia, hypercalciuria. Rare: constipation, flatulence, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhoea; pruritus, rash, urticaria.

src.q: Uncommon: Hypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria.
Rare: Constipation, flatulence, nausea, abdominal pain, and diarrhoea.

items.t: Hypersensitivity reactions (pruritus, wheezing, urticaria, oropharyngeal swelling, angioedema) have been reported.

src.q: Hypersensitivity reactions including pruritus, wheezing, urticaria, oropharyngeal swelling and angioedema have been reported in the post-marketing environment.

items.t: Overdose: hypercalcaemia (anorexia, thirst, nausea, vomiting, constipation, polyuria, confusion; severe cases arrhythmias, coma). Milk-alkali syndrome. Stop calcium and vitamin D (and thiazides, cardiac glycosides), rehydrate.

src.q: Extreme hypercalcaemia may result in coma and death.
The treatment with calcium and vitamin D must be discontinued. Treatment with thiazide diuretics, lithium, vitamin A, vitamin D and cardiac glycosides must also be discontinued.

items.t: History of renal stones: measure urinary calcium to exclude hypercalciuria.

src.q: In patients with a history of renal stones, urinary calcium excretion should be measured to exclude hypercalciuria.

items.t: Long-term treatment: serum calcium and renal function (serum creatinine); urinary calcium.

src.q: During long-term treatment, serum calcium levels should be followed and renal function should be monitored through measurements of serum creatinine.
With long-term treatment it is advisable to monitor serum and urinary calcium levels and kidney function

items.t: Reduce or stop temporarily if urinary calcium exceeds 7.5 mmol/24 hours (300 mg/24 hours); reduce or stop if hypercalcaemia or impaired renal function.

src.q: reduce or stop treatment temporarily if urinary calcium exceeds 7.5 mmol/24 hours (300 mg/24 hours)
In case of hypercalcaemia or signs of impaired renal function the dose should be reduced or the treatment discontinued.

items.t: 600 mg / 400 IU tablet: swallow with a glass of water or juice within one and a half hours of a meal, without chewing; may be broken in half to help swallowing.

src.q: It is recommended that the film-coated tablet is taken within one and a half hours of a meal with a glass of water or juice, without chewing it. The tablet can be broken in half, if needed.

items.t: Keep a gap between this tablet and levothyroxine, quinolone or tetracycline antibiotics, and iron (2-6 hours depending on the medicine and the SmPC).

src.q: Quinolone antibiotics should be taken two hours before or six hours after intake of calcium.
It is advisable to allow a minimum period of four hours before taking calcium.

items.t: Tell the prescriber about any other calcium or vitamin D products.

src.q: Allowances should be made for calcium and vitamin D supplements from other sources.

items.t: UK calcium product: prevention and treatment of calcium deficiency; adjunct in osteoporosis; rickets and osteomalacia together with vitamin D3.

src.q: Prevention and treatment of calcium deficiency
Calcium supplement as an adjunct to specific therapy in the prevention and treatment of osteoporosis
Rickets and osteomalacia, in addition to vitamin D3 therapy

restrictions.note: No prescribing restrictions in the UK calcium effervescent tablet SmPC. No UK SmPC exists for the clinic's calcium glubionate/lactobionate syrup.

items.tag: UK effervescent tablet only (not the syrup)
items.t: The UK calcium effervescent tablet SmPC gives 1000 mg calcium per day for adults and children. This is the tablet's dose. There is no UK dose for the clinic syrup: use the clinic label for the syrup dose.

src.q: Adults and children: 1000mg per day.

items.tag: UK effervescent tablet only (not the syrup)
items.t: The UK calcium effervescent tablet SmPC states the same 1000 mg calcium per day for children, with no lower age limit and no weight-based dose. It does not give a dose for the syrup: use the clinic label for the syrup dose.

src.q: Adults and children: 1000mg per day.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to the active substances or excipients.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substances or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1 of the effervescent tablet

items.t: Diseases or conditions causing hypercalcaemia and/or hypercalciuria.

src.q: Diseases and/or conditions resulting in hypercalcaemia and/or hypercalciuria

items.t: Nephrocalcinosis, nephrolithiasis.

src.q: Nephrocalcinosis, nephrolithiasis

items.t: Mild hypercalciuria (over 300 mg or 7.5 mmol/24 hours) or history of urinary stones: monitor urinary calcium; reduce or stop if needed. Stone formers should drink more fluid.

src.q: For patients with mild hypercalciuria (exceeding 300 mg/24 hours or 7.5 mmol/24 hours), or with a history of urinary calculi, monitoring of calcium excretion in the urine is required.
An increased fluid intake is recommended for patients prone to formation of calculi in the urinary tract.

items.t: Impaired renal function: take under medical supervision with monitoring of serum calcium and phosphate.

src.q: In patients with impaired renal function, calcium salts should be taken under medical supervision with monitoring of calcium and phosphate serum levels.

items.t: High doses, especially with vitamin D: risk of hypercalcaemia and kidney impairment; monitor serum calcium and renal function.

src.q: During high dose therapy and especially during concomitant treatment with vitamin D, there is a risk of hypercalcaemia with subsequent kidney function impairment.

items.t: Thiazides reduce urinary calcium excretion: monitor serum calcium regularly (risk of hypercalcaemia).

src.q: Due to increased risk of hypercalcaemia, serum calcium should be regularly monitored during concomitant use of thiazide diuretics.

items.t: Give tetracyclines at least 2 hours before or 4-6 hours after oral calcium.

src.q: tetracycline preparations should be administered at least two hours before or four to six hours after oral intake of calcium.

items.t: Levothyroxine SmPC: calcium salts may reduce levothyroxine absorption; separate by 4-5 hours.

src.q: Absorption of levothyroxine (thyroxine) possibly reduced by antacids, calcium salts
(administration should be separated by 4-5 hours)

items.t: Ciprofloxacin SmPC: give ciprofloxacin 1-2 hours before or at least 4 hours after calcium-containing products.

src.q: multivalent cation-containing drugs and mineral supplements (e.g. calcium, magnesium, aluminium, iron)
ciprofloxacin should be administered either 1-2 hours before or at least 4 hours after these preparations

items.t: Hypercalcaemia may increase cardiac glycoside toxicity: monitor ECG and serum calcium.

src.q: Cardiac glycoside toxicity may increase with hypercalcaemia resulting from treatment with calcium. Patients should be monitored with regard to electrocardiogram (ECG) and serum calcium levels.

items.t: Systemic corticosteroids reduce calcium absorption; the calcium dose may need to be increased.

src.q: Systemic corticosteroids reduce calcium absorption. During concomitant use, it may be necessary to increase the dose of Calvive 1000.

items.t: Oral bisphosphonates or sodium fluoride at least 3 hours before calcium. Do not take calcium within 2 hours of foods high in oxalic acid (spinach, rhubarb) or phytic acid (whole cereals).

src.q: this preparation should be administered at least three hours before the intake of Calvive 1000
The patient should not take calcium products within two hours of eating foods high in oxalic acid and phytic acid.

items.t: Impaired renal function: take calcium under medical supervision with serum calcium and phosphate monitoring (no eGFR/CrCl threshold given).

src.q: In patients with impaired renal function, calcium salts should be taken under medical supervision with monitoring of calcium and phosphate serum levels.

hepatic.note: No hepatic impairment advice in the UK calcium effervescent tablet SmPC. No UK SmPC exists for the clinic's calcium glubionate/lactobionate syrup.

items.t: Can be used in pregnancy for calcium deficiency. Adequate total intake is 1000-1300 mg calcium a day; in pregnancy total daily calcium intake should not exceed 1500 mg.

src.q: The adequate daily intake (including food and supplementation) for normal pregnant and lactating women is 1000-1300 mg calcium. During pregnancy, the daily intake of calcium should not exceed 1500 mg.

items.t: Can be used during lactation for calcium deficiency; calcium in milk causes no adverse effects in the neonate.

src.q: Significant amounts of calcium are secreted in milk during lactation but do not cause any adverse effects to the neonate.

reproductive.note: No fertility or contraception statements in the UK calcium effervescent tablet SmPC.

items.t: No common effects listed. Uncommon: hypercalcaemia, hypercalciuria. Rare: flatulence, constipation, diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain; rash, pruritus, urticaria.

src.q: Uncommon : Hypercalcaemia, hypercalciuria
Rare : flatulence, constipation, diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain

items.t: Very rare systemic allergic reactions (anaphylaxis, face oedema, angioneurotic oedema).

src.q: Isolated cases of systemic allergic reactions (anaphylactic reaction, face oedema, angioneurotic oedema) have been reported

items.t: Overdose: hypercalciuria and hypercalcaemia (nausea, vomiting, thirst, polyuria, dehydration, constipation). Calcium toxicity threshold: supplementation above 2000 mg a day for several months. Stop treatment and correct fluids.

src.q: The threshold for calcium intoxication is from supplementation in excess of 2000 mg per day, taken for several months.
In the case of an intoxication, treatment should be stopped immediately and the fluid deficiency should be corrected.

items.t: Mild hypercalciuria or history of stones: monitor urinary calcium. Impaired renal function: serum calcium and phosphate. High dose or with vitamin D: serum calcium and renal function.

src.q: monitoring of calcium excretion in the urine is required.
In these patients serum calcium levels should be followed and renal function should be monitored.

items.t: Reduce the dose or stop if urinary calcium is raised.

src.q: If necessary, the calcium dose should be reduced or therapy should be discontinued.

administration.note: No UK SmPC exists for the clinic syrup. The UK calcium effervescent tablet is dissolved in water, which does not apply to the syrup. Use the clinic label.

items.t: Do not take within 2 hours of spinach, rhubarb or whole cereals. Keep a gap from tetracycline antibiotics.

src.q: The patient should not take calcium products within two hours of eating foods high in oxalic acid and phytic acid.

items.t: If prone to kidney stones, drink plenty of fluids.

src.q: An increased fluid intake is recommended for patients prone to formation of calculi in the urinary tract.

items.t: Essential hypertension in adults; hypertension in children and adolescents aged 6 to under 18 years.

src.q: Treatment of essential hypertension in adults.
Treatment of hypertension in children and adolescents aged 6 to <18 years.

items.t: Adult heart failure with LVEF 40% or less, when ACE inhibitors are not tolerated, or as add-on to an ACE inhibitor when mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists are not tolerated.

src.q: Treatment of adult patients with heart failure and impaired left ventricular systolic function (left ventricular ejection fraction ≤ 40%) when Angiotensin Converting Enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are not tolerated
when mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists are not tolerated

restrictions.note: No specialist-only or shared-care restriction stated in the candesartan SmPC. Dual RAAS blockade and the ACE inhibitor + mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist + candesartan triple combination only under specialist supervision (see cautions).

items.t: Hypertension: start and usual maintenance 8 mg once daily; may increase to 16 mg, maximum 32 mg once daily. Most effect within 4 weeks.

src.q: The recommended initial dose and usual maintenance dose of Amias is 8 mg once daily.
the dose can be increased to 16 mg once daily and to a maximum of 32 mg once daily.

items.t: Possible volume depletion (risk of hypotension): consider a starting dose of 4 mg.

src.q: An initial dose of 4 mg may be considered in patients at risk for hypotension, such as patients with possible volume depletion

items.t: Heart failure: start 4 mg once daily; double the dose at intervals of at least 2 weeks up to the target of 32 mg once daily (maximum) or the highest tolerated dose.

src.q: The usual recommended initial dose of Amias is 4 mg once daily.
Up-titration to the target dose of 32 mg once daily (maximum dose) or the highest tolerated dose is done by doubling the dose at intervals of at least 2 weeks

items.t: Elderly: no initial dose adjustment needed.

src.q: No initial dose adjustment is necessary in elderly patients.

items.t: Hypertension, age 6 to under 18 years: start 4 mg once daily. Under 50 kg: maximum 8 mg once daily. 50 kg or more: may increase to 8 mg, then 16 mg once daily if needed.

src.q: Children and adolescents aged 6 to <18 years: The recommended starting dose is 4 mg once daily.
For patients weighing < 50 kg: In patients whose blood pressure is not adequately controlled, the dose can be increased to a maximum of 8 mg once daily.
the dose can be increased to 8 mg once daily and then to 16 mg once daily if needed

items.t: Contraindicated under 1 year. Safety and efficacy not established from 1 to under 6 years (no dose recommendation).

src.q: Amias is contraindicated in children aged below 1 year
The safety and efficacy in children aged 1 to <6 years of age has not been established.

items.t: Not studied in children with GFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m². Heart failure: safety and efficacy not established under 18 years.

src.q: Amias has not been studied in children with glomerular filtration rate less than 30 ml/min/1.73m2
The safety and efficacy of Amias in children aged between birth and 18 years have not been established in the treatment of heart failure.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to candesartan cilexetil or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to candesartan cilexetil or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Second and third trimesters of pregnancy.

src.q: Second and third trimesters of pregnancy

items.t: Severe hepatic impairment and/or cholestasis.

src.q: Severe hepatic impairment and/or cholestasis.

items.t: Children under 1 year.

src.q: Children aged below 1 year

items.t: With aliskiren-containing products in patients with diabetes mellitus or renal impairment (GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m²).

src.q: The concomitant use of Amias with aliskiren-containing products is contraindicated in patients with diabetes mellitus or renal impairment (GFR< 60ml/min/1.73m2)

items.t: Dual RAAS blockade (ACE inhibitor, ARB or aliskiren together) is not recommended; if absolutely necessary, only under specialist supervision with close monitoring of renal function, electrolytes and blood pressure. Do not combine an ACE inhibitor and an ARB in diabetic nephropathy.

src.q: Dual blockade of RAAS through the combined use of ACE-inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers or aliskiren is therefore not recommended

If dual blockade therapy is considered absolutely necessary, this should only occur under specialist supervision and subject to frequent close monitoring of renal function, electrolytes and blood pressure.
ACE-inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers should not be used concomitantly in patients with diabetic nephropathy.

items.t: Heart failure: adding an ACE inhibitor raises the risk of hypotension, hyperkalaemia and renal impairment. The triple combination ACE inhibitor + mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (e.g. spironolactone) + candesartan is not recommended.

src.q: may increase when Amias is used in combination with an ACE inhibitor
Triple combination of an ACE-inhibitor, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and candesartan cilexetil is also not recommended.

items.t: Hypotension: may occur in heart failure and in volume-depleted patients (e.g. high-dose diuretics). Use caution when starting and correct hypovolaemia.

src.q: It may also occur in hypertensive patients with intravascular volume depletion such as those receiving high dose diuretics.
Caution should be observed when initiating therapy and correction of hypovolemia should be attempted.

items.t: Hyperkalaemia: risk with potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements, potassium salt substitutes or heparin; monitor potassium. In heart failure, check potassium periodically.

src.q: Monitoring of potassium should be undertaken as appropriate.
In heart failure patients treated with Amias, hyperkalaemia may occur. Periodic monitoring of serum potassium is recommended.

items.t: Renal artery stenosis (bilateral or solitary kidney): urea and creatinine may rise. RAAS-dependent patients (severe heart failure, renal disease): acute hypotension, azotaemia, oliguria or rarely acute renal failure possible.

src.q: may increase blood urea and serum creatinine in patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis or stenosis of the artery to a solitary kidney
The possibility of similar effects cannot be excluded with AIIRAs.

items.t: Aortic or mitral valve stenosis, obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: special caution.

src.q: special caution is indicated in patients suffering from haemodynamically relevant aortic or mitral valve stenosis, or obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

items.t: Primary hyperaldosteronism: not recommended (will not generally respond).

src.q: Therefore, the use of Amias is not recommended in this population.

items.t: Ischaemic heart or cerebrovascular disease: an excessive fall in blood pressure could cause myocardial infarction or stroke.

src.q: excessive blood pressure decrease in patients with ischaemic cardiopathy or ischaemic cerebrovascular disease could result in a myocardial infarction or stroke

items.t: Intestinal angioedema (abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea): stop candesartan and monitor until resolved.

src.q: If intestinal angioedema is diagnosed, candesartan cilexetil should be discontinued

items.t: Anaesthesia and surgery: hypotension may occur, very rarely needing IV fluids and/or vasopressors. No experience after recent kidney transplantation.

src.q: Hypotension may occur during anaesthesia and surgery in patients treated with angiotensin II antagonists due to blockade of the renin-angiotensin system.
There is no experience regarding the administration of Amias in patients with a recent kidney transplantation.

items.t: Contains lactose: patients with galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take it.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: ACE inhibitors, other ARBs, aliskiren (dual RAAS blockade): more hypotension, hyperkalaemia and decreased renal function; not recommended.

src.q: dual blockade of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone-system (RAAS) through the combined use of ACE-inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers or aliskiren is associated with a higher frequency of adverse events
Dual blockade of RAAS through the combined use of ACE-inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers or aliskiren is therefore not recommended

items.t: Potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements, potassium salt substitutes, heparin: may raise potassium; monitor potassium as appropriate.

src.q: Concomitant use of potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements, salt substitutes containing potassium, or other medicinal products (e.g. heparin) may increase potassium levels.
Monitoring of potassium should be undertaken as appropriate (see section 4.4).

items.t: NSAIDs (including COX-2 inhibitors and aspirin above 3 g/day): reduced antihypertensive effect; risk of worsening renal function and raised potassium. Use with caution, especially in the elderly; keep hydrated; consider monitoring renal function.

src.q: acetylsalicylic acid (> 3 g/day) and non-selective NSAIDs), attenuation of the antihypertensive effect may occur
The combination should be administered with caution, especially in the elderly.
consideration should be given to monitoring renal function after initiation of concomitant therapy, and periodically thereafter

items.t: Lithium: not recommended (raised lithium levels and toxicity); if needed, monitor lithium levels carefully.

src.q: Use of candesartan with lithium is not recommended.
If the combination proves necessary, careful monitoring of serum lithium levels is recommended.

items.t: Other blood-pressure-lowering medicines may enhance the effect. No clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction found with hydrochlorothiazide, warfarin, digoxin, oral contraceptives, glibenclamide, nifedipine or enalapril.

src.q: The antihypertensive effect of candesartan may be enhanced by other medicinal products with blood pressure lowering properties
Compounds which have been investigated in clinical pharmacokinetic studies include hydrochlorothiazide, warfarin, digoxin, oral contraceptives
No clinically significant pharmacokinetic interactions with these medicinal products have been identified.

items.t: Renal impairment (including haemodialysis): start at 4 mg and titrate to response.

src.q: The starting dose is 4 mg in patients with renal impairment, including patients on haemodialysis.

items.t: Very severe or end-stage renal impairment (CrCl below 15 mL/min) and haemodialysis: limited experience; titrate carefully with thorough blood pressure monitoring.

src.q: There is limited experience in patients with very severe or end-stage renal impairment (Clcreatinine < 15 ml/min)
In these patients Amias should be carefully titrated with thorough monitoring of blood pressure.

items.t: Hypertension with renal impairment: periodic monitoring of potassium and creatinine recommended.

src.q: When Amias is used in hypertensive patients with renal impairment, periodic monitoring of serum potassium and creatinine levels is recommended.

items.t: SPS: seek specialist advice before starting if eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73 m².

src.q: Seek specialist advice prior to initiation for patients where there is: severe or unstable heart failure renovascular disease eGFR less than 30ml/min/1.73m2

items.t: Mild to moderate hepatic impairment: start 4 mg once daily and adjust to response.

src.q: An initial dose of 4 mg once daily is recommended in patients with mild to moderate hepatic impairment.

items.t: Severe hepatic impairment and/or cholestasis: contraindicated.

src.q: Amias is contraindicated in patients with severe hepatic impairment and/or cholestasis

items.t: First trimester: not recommended. Second and third trimesters: contraindicated (fetotoxicity: reduced renal function, oligohydramnios, skull ossification retardation; neonatal renal failure, hypotension, hyperkalaemia).

src.q: The use of AIIRAs is not recommended during the first trimester of pregnancy
The use of AIIRAs is contraindicated during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy
Exposure to AIIRA therapy during the second and third trimesters is known to induce human fetotoxicity

items.t: Do not start in pregnancy; stop immediately when pregnancy is diagnosed and switch if appropriate. After exposure from the second trimester: ultrasound of fetal renal function and skull; observe the infant for hypotension.

src.q: AIIRAs should not be initiated during pregnancy.
Should exposure to AIIRAs have occurred from the second trimester of pregnancy, ultrasound check of renal function and skull is recommended.
Infants whose mothers have taken AIIRAs should be closely observed for hypotension

items.t: MHRA: ACE inhibitors and ARBs should not be used at any stage of pregnancy unless absolutely necessary; stop as soon as possible on diagnosis.

src.q: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor antagonists should not be used at any stage of pregnancy unless absolutely necessary
On diagnosis of pregnancy, treatment with an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin II receptor antagonist should be stopped as soon as possible

items.t: BUMPS: early-pregnancy use is unlikely to harm the baby but the ARB should usually be stopped; use after 20 weeks can cause problems in up to 1 in 3 exposed babies, and needs extra monitoring.

src.q: Taking an ARB in early pregnancy is unlikely to harm your baby.
an ARB should usually be stopped as soon as you find out you are pregnant
Studies show that up to one in every three babies exposed in the womb to an ARB after 20 weeks of pregnancy develop some or all of these problems.
If you take an ARB after around 20 weeks you will require additional monitoring to assess amniotic fluid levels and your baby's growth and wellbeing.

items.t: SmPC: not recommended (no information); prefer alternatives, especially with a newborn or preterm infant. MHRA: not recommended for any ARB.

src.q: Because no information is available regarding the use of Amias during breastfeeding, Amias is not recommended
