src.q: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor antagonists should not be used at any stage of pregnancy unless absolutely necessary
On diagnosis of pregnancy, treatment with an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin II receptor antagonist should be stopped as soon as possible

items.t: BUMPS (ACE inhibitors, captopril named): early-pregnancy use is unlikely to harm the baby; use after about 20 weeks can cause problems in the baby and needs extra monitoring of amniotic fluid and fetal growth if continued.

src.q: Taking an ACE-I in early pregnancy is unlikely to harm your baby.
Taking an ACE-I after around 20 weeks of pregnancy can cause a number of problems in your baby
If you continue to take an ACE-I after around 20 weeks you will require additional monitoring to assess amniotic fluid levels and your baby's growth and wellbeing.

items.t: SmPC section 4.3 lists lactation as a contraindication. Section 4.6 of the same SmPC: very low milk levels; not recommended for preterm infants or in the first few weeks after delivery; with an older infant, may be considered if necessary for the mother, observing the infant for adverse effects.

src.q: Lactation (see section 4.6)
the use of captopril in breastfeeding is not recommended for pre- term infants and for the first few weeks after delivery
In the case of an older infant, the use of captopril in a breast-feeding mother may be considered if this treatment is necessary for the mother and the child is observed for any adverse effect

items.t: MHRA (2009): captopril not recommended in the first few weeks after delivery (risk of profound neonatal hypotension; preterm babies at particular risk); may be considered when the infant is older if an ACE inhibitor is needed, with careful infant follow-up for hypotension. MHRA clarification (2009): ACE inhibitors are not absolutely contraindicated in breastfeeding and may be prescribed if essential for the mother.

src.q: captopril, enalapril, or quinapril: use in breastfeeding is not recommended in the first few weeks after delivery because of the possibility of profound neonatal hypotension
use may be considered when the infant is older if an ACE inhibitor is necessary for the mother; careful follow-up of the infant for possible signs of hypotension is recommended
they are not absolutely contraindicated. Healthcare professionals may prescribe these medicines during breastfeeding if they consider that this treatment is essential for the lactating mother.

items.t: SPS (2023, no captopril-specific entry): enalapril is the preferred ACE inhibitor in breastfeeding; most ACE inhibitors can be used if clinically appropriate.

src.q: Enalapril is the preferred angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor during breastfeeding
most ACE inhibitors can be used during breastfeeding if clinically appropriate.

items.t: Planning pregnancy: switch to an antihypertensive with an established pregnancy safety profile unless continued ACE inhibitor treatment is essential.

src.q: Unless continued ACE inhibitor therapy is considered essential, patients planning pregnancy should be changed to alternative antihypertensive treatments which have an established safety profile for use in pregnancy.

items.t: Common: insomnia; taste disturbance and dizziness; dry cough and dyspnoea; nausea, vomiting, epigastric discomfort, dyspepsia, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, constipation, dry mouth; pruritus with or without rash, alopecia.

src.q: Common: insomnia
Common: dysgeusia, reversible and self-limiting taste impairment and dizziness
Common: dry, irritating (non-productive) cough (see section 4.4) and dyspnoea
Common: nausea, vomiting, epigastric discomfort, peptic ulcer, dyspepsia
Common: pruritus with or without a rash, and alopecia

items.t: Angioedema (uncommon; face, lips, tongue, glottis, larynx; also intestinal): stop the ACE inhibitor at once and do not restart. Bradykinin-mediated angioedema may not respond to adrenaline. Airway involvement needs emergency treatment and observation for at least 12-24 hours.

src.q: if angioedema is suspected in a patient taking an ACE inhibitor, discontinue the ACE inhibitor immediately and do not restart
bradykinin-mediated angioedema is unlikely to respond to standard anaphylaxis treatments including adrenaline (epinephrine)
Uncommon: angioedema (see section 4.4)
The patient should be hospitalised and observed for at least 12 to 24 hours

items.t: Very rare: neutropenia/agranulocytosis, pancytopenia, aplastic or haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia. Report sore throat or fever; stop if neutropenia.

src.q: Very rare: neutropenia/agranulocytosis (see section 4.4), pancytopenia particularly in patients with renal dysfunction
During treatment all patients should be instructed to report any sign of infection (e.g. sore throat, fever)

items.t: Insulin autoimmune syndrome (frequency not known) with severe hypoglycaemia; very rare hyperkalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia.

src.q: Not known: insulin autoimmune syndrome
Very rare: hyperkalaemia, hyponatremia, hypoglycaemia

items.t: Rare renal impairment or failure; very rare nephrotic syndrome, pancreatitis, hepatitis/cholestasis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, erythema multiforme.

src.q: Rare: renal impairment, renal failure, polyuria, oliguria, pollakiuria Very rare: nephrotic syndrome
Very rare: glossitis, pancreatitis
Steven Johnson syndrome, erythema multiforme

items.t: SmPC: renal function (potassium and creatinine) before starting and at intervals; in high-risk patients (renal impairment, collagen vascular disease, immunosuppressants, allopurinol, procainamide) white cell and differential counts before, every 2 weeks for 3 months, then periodically; urine protein in prior renal disease.

src.q: Evaluation of the patient should include assessment of renal function (monitoring of potassium and creatinine) prior to initiation of therapy and at appropriate intervals thereafter.
it is advised that white blood cell count and differential counts should be performed prior to therapy, every 2 weeks during the first 3 months of captopril therapy, and periodically thereafter.

items.t: SPS baseline: blood pressure, eGFR or serum creatinine, serum potassium, serum sodium. Starting is not normally appropriate if potassium is above 5.0 mmol/L.

src.q: Baseline Blood pressure Estimated glomerular filtration rate or Serum creatinine (for creatinine clearance) Serum potassium Serum sodium
Initiation not normally appropriate if pre-treatment potassium greater than 5.0mmol/L

items.t: SPS: after starting or a dose change, check renal function, sodium and potassium within 1-2 weeks (sooner with risk factors); once stable, every 3-6 months in heart failure and annually in hypertension. Repeat at any time if acutely unwell.

src.q: Hypertension Within 1 - 2 weeks Estimated glomerular filtration rate or Serum creatinine (for creatinine clearance) Serum sodium Serum potassium Within 1 month Blood pressure
Ongoing once stable Heart failure Every 3 - 6 months
Repeat monitoring at any time patient acutely unwell or their renal function may be compromised.
Hypertension Annually Serum sodium Serum potassium

items.t: Stop: neutrophils below 1000/mm3; angioedema; jaundice or marked liver enzyme rise; suspected insulin autoimmune syndrome. SPS: potassium 6.0 mmol/L or above in CKD - stop (after stopping other potassium-raising drugs) and seek specialist advice; sodium below 132 mmol/L - specialist advice.

src.q: should be withdrawn if neutropenia (neutrophils less than 1000/mm3) is detected or suspected.
Value 6.0 mmol/L or above in people with CKD Stop ACEI/ARB after stopping other drugs that may increase potassium and seek specialist advice.
Sodium Value is below 132mmol/L Obtain specialist advice

items.t: Oral; may be taken before, during or after meals. The score line is for ease of swallowing only, not for dividing into equal doses (one UK SmPC).

src.q: Captopril tablets may be taken before, during and after meals.
The score line is only to facilitate breaking for the ease of swallowing and not to divide into equal doses

items.t: Food reduces absorption by about 30-40%.

src.q: The presence of food in the gastrointestinal tract reduces absorption by about 30-40%.

items.t: Seek urgent help for swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, or trouble breathing or swallowing, even after long use; do not take further doses.

src.q: seek urgent medical attention if you develop swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or experience difficulty breathing or swallowing whilst taking ACE inhibitors
do not take further doses of your ACE inhibitor if angioedema is suspected and inform a healthcare professional immediately

items.t: Report any sign of infection such as sore throat or fever.

src.q: During treatment all patients should be instructed to report any sign of infection (e.g. sore throat, fever)

items.t: Planning pregnancy or pregnant: contact the doctor to switch medicine.

src.q: If you find out that you are pregnant whilst taking an ACE-I, you should contact your doctor as soon as possible so that you can be switched to another medicine.

items.t: Driving may be affected, especially at the start, after dose changes, or with alcohol.

src.q: the ability to drive and use machines may be reduced, namely at the start of the treatment, or when posology is modified, and also when used in combination with alcohol

items.t: Avoid potassium salt substitutes unless advised (risk of high potassium).

src.q: potassium supplements, or potassium-containing salt substitutes may lead to significant increase in serum potassium.

items.t: Epilepsy: generalised tonic-clonic and partial seizures (not usually effective in absences or myoclonic seizures). Paroxysmal pain of trigeminal neuralgia. Prophylaxis of manic-depressive psychosis unresponsive to lithium.

src.q: Epilepsy - generalised tonic-clonic and partial seizures.
is not usually effective in absences (petit mal) and myoclonic seizures
The paroxysmal pain of trigeminal neuralgia. For the prophylaxis of manic-depressive psychosis in patients unresponsive to lithium therapy.

items.t: Epilepsy: MHRA category 1. Maintain on a specific manufacturer's product (brand name or generic name plus manufacturer).

src.q: Ensure that the patient is maintained on a specific manufacturer's product.
Maintain on the same manufacturer's product for the following: carbamazepine phenobarbital phenytoin primidone

items.t: Han Chinese and Thai patients: screen for HLA-B*1502 whenever possible before starting; if positive, do not start unless there is no other option.

src.q: Before deciding to initiate treatment, patients of Han Chinese and Thai origin should whenever possible be screened for HLA-B*1502
If these individuals test positive, carbamazepine should not be started unless there is no other therapeutic option.

items.t: Women of childbearing potential: should not be used unless the benefit outweighs the risks after considering alternatives; highly effective contraception needed.

src.q: Carbamazepine should not be used in women of childbearing potential unless the benefit is judged to outweigh the risks following careful consideration of alternative suitable treatment options.

items.t: Start 100 to 200 mg once or twice daily; increase slowly to best response, often 800 to 1200 mg daily in divided doses (some need 1600 to 2000 mg). Target total plasma level about 4 to 12 micrograms/mL. Add to other antiepileptics gradually.

src.q: initially 100-200mg once or twice daily is recommended
This may be followed by a slow increase until the best response is obtained, often 800-1200mg daily. In some instances, 1600mg or even 2000mg daily may be necessary.
usually requires total plasma-carbamazepine concentrations of about 4 to 12 micrograms/mL (17 to 50 micromoles/litre)

items.t: Start 200 to 400 mg daily and raise slowly until pain-free (usually 200 mg 3 to 4 times daily). Maximum recommended 1200 mg/day (the same section also says some need 1600 mg). Once in remission reduce to the lowest maintenance dose and try to stop until another attack.

src.q: Slowly raise the initial dosage of 200-400mg daily until freedom from pain is achieved (normally at 200mg 3-4 times daily).
In some instances, doses of 1600mg Tegretol daily may be needed.
Maximum recommended dose is 1200mg/day. When pain relief has been obtained, attempts should be made to gradually discontinue therapy, until another attack occurs.

items.t: Elderly with trigeminal neuralgia: start 100 mg twice daily, raise slowly; maximum 1200 mg/day. All elderly: choose dose with caution (interactions, pharmacokinetics).

src.q: In elderly patients, an initial dose of 100mg twice daily is recommended.
Due to the potential for drug interactions, the dosage of Tegretol should be selected with caution in elderly patients.

items.t: Start 400 mg daily in divided doses, increase gradually until controlled or up to 1600 mg daily. Usual 400 to 600 mg daily in divided doses.

src.q: Initial starting dose of 400mg daily, in divided doses, increasing gradually until symptoms are controlled or a total of 1600mg given in divided doses is reached.
The usual dosage range is 400-600mg daily, given in divided doses.

items.t: Stopping: do not stop abruptly (may precipitate seizures); withdraw gradually.

src.q: Abrupt withdrawal of Tegretol may precipitate seizures, therefore carbamazepine withdrawal should be gradual.

items.t: Epilepsy: usually 10 to 20 mg/kg daily in several divided doses, with gradual increase. 5 to 10 years: 400 to 600 mg daily; 10 to 15 years: 600 to 1000 mg daily; over 15 years: 800 to 1200 mg daily. Maximum: up to 6 years 35 mg/kg/day; 6 to 15 years 1000 mg/day; over 15 years 1200 mg/day. Tablets not recommended for very young children.

src.q: Usual dosage 10-20mg/kg bodyweight daily taken in several divided doses.
Tegretol tablets are not recommended for very young children.
5-10 years: 400 to 600 mg daily
10-15 years: 600 to 1000mg daily
Maximum recommended dose Up to 6 years of age: 35mg/kg/day 6 to15 years of age: 1000mg/day >15 years of age: 1200mg/day.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to carbamazepine, structurally related drugs (e.g. tricyclic antidepressants) or any component.

src.q: Known hypersensitivity to carbamazepine or structurally related drugs (e.g. tricyclic antidepressants) or any other component of the formulation.

items.t: Atrioventricular block; history of bone marrow depression; history of hepatic porphyrias (acute intermittent, variegate, porphyria cutanea tarda).

src.q: Patients with atrioventricular block, a history of bone marrow depression or a history of hepatic porphyrias (e.g. acute intermittent porphyria, variegate porphyria, porphyria cutanea tarda).

items.t: MAOIs: contraindicated; stop MAOIs at least 2 weeks before starting carbamazepine.

src.q: The use of Tegretol is contraindicated in combination with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs)
before administering Tegretol MAOIs should be discontinued for a minimum of 2 weeks, or longer if the clinical situation permits

items.t: Serious skin reactions (SJS/TEN), mostly in the first months; about 10 times higher risk in some Asian countries. HLA-B*1502 (Han Chinese, Thai): screen before starting whenever possible; if positive do not start unless no other option. Consider testing other at-risk Asian groups (e.g. Philippines, Malaysia). Withdraw at once if severe skin reaction signs appear.

src.q: the risk in some Asian countries is estimated to be about 10 times higher
Whenever possible, these individuals should be screened for this allele before starting treatment with carbamazepine
testing genetically at risk populations for the presence of HLA-B*1502 may be considered
Tegretol should be withdrawn at once and alternative therapy should be considered

items.t: HLA-A*3101 (European descent, Japanese): higher risk of skin reactions including SJS, TEN, DRESS; routine screening not recommended. If known positive, use only after careful benefit-risk consideration (MHRA).

src.q: There are insufficient data supporting a recommendation for HLA-A*3101 screening before starting carbamazepine treatment.

if patients of European descent or Japanese origin are known to be positive for HLA A*3101 they should only receive carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, or eslicarbazepine after careful consideration of the benefits and risks

items.t: Hypersensitivity (including anaphylaxis, angioedema, DRESS, multi-organ reactions): stop immediately. 25 to 30% of patients hypersensitive to carbamazepine may react to oxcarbazepine; cross-hypersensitivity with phenytoin, primidone, phenobarbital possible.

src.q: In general, if signs and symptoms suggestive of hypersensitivity reactions occur, Tegretol should be withdrawn immediately.
Cross-hypersensitivity can occur between carbamazepine and aromatic antiepileptic drugs (e.g. phenytoin, primidone and phenobarbital).

items.t: Blood disorders (agranulocytosis, aplastic anaemia; low platelets or white cells): baseline and periodic full blood count. Stop if leucopenia is severe, progressive or symptomatic, or if significant bone marrow depression.

src.q: complete pre-treatment blood counts, including platelets and possibly reticulocytes and serum iron, should be obtained as a baseline, and periodically thereafter
treatment with Tegretol should be discontinued if the patient develops leucopenia which is severe, progressive or accompanied by clinical manifestations

items.t: Liver: LFTs before and periodically, especially with liver disease history and in the elderly. Withdraw immediately if liver dysfunction worsens or acute liver disease. Raised GGT/ALP from enzyme induction alone is not a reason to stop.

src.q: Liver function tests should also be performed before commencing treatment and periodically thereafter, particularly in patients with a history of liver disease and in elderly patients.
The drug should be withdrawn immediately in cases of aggravated liver dysfunction or acute liver disease.
These enhancements of hepatic metabolising capacity are not an indication for the withdrawal of carbamazepine.

items.t: History of cardiac, hepatic or renal damage, haematological reactions to other drugs, or interrupted courses: prescribe only after critical benefit-risk appraisal and under close monitoring. Baseline and periodic urinalysis and BUN recommended.

src.q: Tegretol should be prescribed only after a critical benefit-risk appraisal and under close monitoring in patients with a history of cardiac, hepatic or renal damage
Baseline and periodic complete urinalysis and BUN determinations are recommended.

items.t: Hyponatraemia: with renal conditions causing low sodium or sodium-lowering drugs (e.g. diuretics), check sodium before starting, after about 2 weeks, then monthly for 3 months. Especially in the elderly.

src.q: serum sodium levels should be measured prior to initiating carbamazepine therapy
serum sodium levels should be measured after approximately two weeks and then at monthly intervals for the first three months during therapy, or according to clinical need

items.t: Mixed seizures including absences (typical or atypical): use with caution; may worsen seizures, stop if so.

src.q: Tegretol should be used with caution in patients with mixed seizures which include absences, either typical or atypical.
In case of exacerbation of seizures, Tegretol should be discontinued.

items.t: Suicidal ideation and behaviour (antiepileptic class effect): monitor and advise patients to seek help.

src.q: patients should be monitored for signs of suicidal ideation and behaviours and appropriate treatment should be considered

items.t: Hypothyroidism: thyroid hormone levels may fall (enzyme induction); monitor thyroid function and adjust replacement.

src.q: Carbamazepine may reduce serum concentrations of thyroid hormones through enzyme induction requiring an increase in dose of thyroid replacement therapy in patients with hypothyroidism.

items.t: Mild anticholinergic activity: closely observe patients with raised intraocular pressure or urinary retention. Latent psychosis may be activated; elderly may become confused or agitated.

src.q: patients with increased intraocular pressure and urinary retention should therefore be closely observed during therapy
The possibility of activation of a latent psychosis and, in elderly patients, of confusion or agitation should be borne in mind.

items.t: Falls (ataxia, dizziness, somnolence, hypotension, confusion): reassess fall risk in long-term use. Bone: long-term use linked with reduced bone density and fractures; consider vitamin D for at-risk patients (MHRA).

src.q: complete risk assessment of fall should be considered recurrently for patients on long-term Tegretol treatment
vitamin D supplementation should be considered for at-risk patients who receive long-term treatment with primidone, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, or sodium valproate

items.t: Potent CYP3A4 inducer: lowers levels of many co-medications. Contraindicated with MAOIs.

src.q: Carbamazepine is a potent inducer of CYP3A4 and other phase I and phase II enzyme systems in the liver
The use of Tegretol is contraindicated in combination with monoamine-oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs)

items.t: Raise carbamazepine levels (adjust dose and/or monitor levels): macrolides (e.g. clarithromycin), ciprofloxacin, fluoxetine, azole antifungals (e.g. fluconazole, itraconazole), diltiazem, verapamil, possibly omeprazole, isoniazid, danazol, grapefruit juice.

src.q: the dosage of Tegretol should be adjusted accordingly and/or the plasma levels monitored when used concomitantly with the substances described below
Antibiotics: macrolide antibiotics (e.g. erythromycin, clarithromycin), ciprofloxacine. Antidepressants: fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, paroxetine, trazodone.
Antifungals: azoles (e.g. itraconazole, ketoconazole, fluconazole, voriconazole).
Cardiovascular drugs: diltiazem, verapamil. Gastrointestinal drugs: possibly cimetidine, omeprazole. Other interactions: grapefruit juice

items.t: Lower carbamazepine levels: phenytoin, phenobarbital, primidone, oxcarbazepine, rifampicin, theophylline, St John's wort. MHRA: advise patients with epilepsy not to use St John's wort.

src.q: Other interactions: herbal preparations containing St John's wort (Hypericum perforatum).
concomitant use of St John's wort and antiepileptic medicine is not recommended

items.t: Carbamazepine lowers levels of (dose may need adjusting): warfarin and DOACs (thrombosis risk), hormonal contraceptives and oestrogen/progestogen products, levothyroxine, corticosteroids (prednisolone, dexamethasone), simvastatin, atorvastatin, dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers, sertraline, tricyclics (e.g. amitriptyline), doxycycline, tramadol, paracetamol, many antiepileptics, antipsychotics and immunosuppressants.

src.q: Carbamazepine may lower the plasma level, diminish or even abolish the activity of certain drugs.
Anticoagulants: oral anticoagulants (e.g. warfarin, acenocoumarol, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, apixaban and edoxaban).
Contraceptives: hormonal contraceptives (alternative contraceptive methods should be considered).
Corticosteroids: corticosteroids (e.g. prednisolone, dexamethasone).
Thyroid agents: levothyroxine.

items.t: Paracetamol long-term with carbamazepine may be associated with hepatotoxicity.

src.q: long term administration of carbamazepine and paracetamol (acetaminophen) may be associated with hepatotoxicity

items.t: Diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide, furosemide): may cause symptomatic hyponatraemia. Lithium: enhanced neurotoxicity. Metoclopramide or major tranquillisers: more neurological side effects. Alcohol: reduced tolerance, advise abstaining.

src.q: Concomitant medication with Tegretol and some diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide, furosemide) may lead to symptomatic hyponatraemia.
The combination of lithium and carbamazepine may cause enhanced neurotoxicity in spite of lithium plasma concentrations being within the therapeutic range.
Combined use of carbamazepine with metoclopramide or major tranquillisers, e.g. haloperidol, thioridazine, may also result in an increase in neurological side-effects.
It is therefore advisable for the patient to abstain from alcohol.

items.t: Direct oral anticoagulants (rivaroxaban, dabigatran, apixaban, edoxaban): reduced levels with thrombosis risk; if needed, monitor closely for thrombosis.

src.q: if a concomitant use is necessary, closer monitoring of signs and symptoms of thrombosis is recommended

items.t: No pharmacokinetic data in renal impairment. History of renal damage: prescribe only after critical benefit-risk appraisal and under close monitoring; baseline and periodic urinalysis and BUN.

src.q: No data are available on the pharmacokinetics of carbamazepine in patients with impaired hepatic or renal function.
Tegretol should be prescribed only after a critical benefit-risk appraisal and under close monitoring in patients with a history of cardiac, hepatic or renal damage

items.t: No pharmacokinetic data in hepatic impairment. History of hepatic damage: critical benefit-risk appraisal and close monitoring; LFTs before and periodically. Withdraw immediately if liver dysfunction worsens or acute liver disease; suspend while urgently evaluating signs of liver dysfunction.

src.q: No data are available on the pharmacokinetics of carbamazepine in patients with impaired hepatic or renal function.
The drug should be withdrawn immediately in cases of aggravated liver dysfunction or acute liver disease.
The development of signs and symptoms of liver dysfunction or active liver disease should be urgently evaluated and treatment with Tegretol suspended pending the outcome of the evaluation.

items.t: SmPC: increased risk of major malformations after first-trimester exposure (about 4.93% vs 2 to 3% background: neural tube defects, cleft lip/palate, cardiac, hypospadias); neurodevelopmental risk cannot be excluded. Should not be used in pregnancy unless the benefit outweighs the risks after considering alternatives. If continued: monotherapy, lowest effective dose, monitor plasma levels; specialised antenatal surveillance.

src.q: are at an increased risk of major congenital malformations
4.93% of children of epileptic women exposed to carbamazepine monotherapy during first trimester of pregnancy suffer from congenital malformations
Carbamazepine should not be used during pregnancy unless the benefit is judged to outweigh the risks following careful consideration of alternative suitable treatment options.
monotherapy and the lowest effective dose of carbamazepine should be used and monitoring of plasma levels is recommended

items.t: Folic acid before and during pregnancy (MHRA: 5 mg/day for women planning pregnancy). Vitamin K1 to mother in the last weeks and to the neonate has been recommended. Do not stop antiepileptics suddenly. Refer pregnant women to a specialist.

src.q: Folic acid supplementation is recommended before and during pregnancy.
All women using antiepileptic drugs who are planning to become pregnant should be offered 5mg per day of folic acid before any possibility of pregnancy
Sudden discontinuation of antiepileptic drug (AED) therapy should be avoided
she should be referred to a specialist to reassess carbamazepine treatment and consider alternative treatment options

items.t: MHRA (2021): carbamazepine is associated with an increased risk of major congenital malformations; the risk is dose-dependent.

src.q: the risk of major congenital malformations with carbamazepine, phenobarbital, and topiramate is dose-dependent

items.t: BUMPS (UKTIS): can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a specialist, only when there is no safer treatment; most babies are healthy. High-dose folic acid (5 mg/day). Do not stop without advice.

src.q: Carbamazepine can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a specialist.
As a precaution, carbamazepine is only prescribed in pregnancy when there is no other safer treatment, and the benefits outweigh the possible risks.
your doctor will prescribe you a high dose folic acid supplement (5 mg/day)

items.t: SmPC: passes into milk (about 25 to 60% of plasma levels). May breastfeed if the infant is observed for adverse effects (excessive sleepiness, allergic skin reaction) and for liver/bile problems (cholestatic hepatitis reported).

src.q: Mothers taking Tegretol may breast-feed their infants, provided the infant is observed for possible adverse reactions (e.g. excessive somnolence, allergic skin reaction).
breast-fed infants of mothers treated with carbamazepine should be carefully observed for adverse hepatobiliary effects

items.t: Women of childbearing potential: consider a pregnancy test before starting; use highly effective contraception during treatment and for at least 2 weeks after stopping. Carbamazepine can make hormonal contraception fail: use at least one effective method (e.g. IUD) or two complementary methods including a barrier method. Plan any pregnancy with the doctor.

src.q: Pregnancy testing in women of childbearing potential should be considered prior to initiating treatment with carbamazepine.
Women of childbearing potential should use highly effective contraception during treatment and for at least two weeks after stopping treatment.
At least one effective method of contraception (such as an intra-uterine device) or two complementary forms of contraception including a barrier method should be used.

items.t: Hormonal contraception: alternative non-hormonal methods are recommended; breakthrough bleeding reported. If hormonal contraception is used, a preparation with not less than 50 micrograms oestrogen, or a non-hormonal method, should be considered.

src.q: Alternative non-hormonal forms of contraception are recommended when using Tegretol
Patients taking Tegretol and requiring hormonal contraception should receive a preparation containing not less than 50µg oestrogen

items.t: Men: very rare reports of impaired fertility and/or abnormal spermatogenesis.

src.q: There have been very rare reports of impaired male fertility and/or abnormal spermatogenesis.

items.t: Very common or common, especially at the start, at high initial doses or in the elderly: dizziness, headache, ataxia, drowsiness, fatigue, double vision; nausea, vomiting; allergic skin reactions. Usually settle within days or with a short dose reduction.

src.q: CNS adverse reactions (dizziness, headache, ataxia, drowsiness, fatigue, diplopia), gastrointestinal disturbances (nausea, vomiting), as well as allergic skin reactions
The dose-related adverse reactions usually abate within a few days, either spontaneously or after a transient dosage reduction.

items.t: Raised GGT from enzyme induction is very common and usually not clinically relevant.

src.q: gamma-glutamyltransferase increased (due to hepatic enzyme induction), usually not clinically relevant

items.t: Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis (mostly first months; higher risk with HLA-B*1502): withdraw at once.

src.q: Most of the SJS/TEN cases appear in the first few months of treatment with Tegretol.
Tegretol should be withdrawn at once and alternative therapy should be considered

items.t: DRESS and other hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis, angioedema, multi-organ): stop immediately.

src.q: If a patient develops these reactions after treatment with Tegretol, the drug must be discontinued, and an alternative treatment started.

items.t: Agranulocytosis, aplastic anaemia, bone marrow depression: patient should seek advice at once for fever, sore throat, rash, mouth ulcers, easy bruising or bleeding.

src.q: If reactions such as fever, sore throat, rash, ulcers in the mouth, easy bruising, petechial or purpuric haemorrhage appear, the patient should be advised to consult the physician immediately.

items.t: Hepatitis, hepatic failure, vanishing bile duct syndrome (rare/very rare).

src.q: Severe hepatic reactions to carbamazepine occur very rarely.

items.t: Hyponatraemia and water intoxication (lethargy, vomiting, headache, confusion). Cardiac conduction disorders, AV block, arrhythmia (rare).

src.q: leading in rare cases to water intoxication accompanied by lethargy, vomiting, headache, confusional state, neurological disorders
arrhythmia, atrioventricular block with syncope, bradycardia, cardiac failure congestive

items.t: Before starting: full blood count (platelets; possibly reticulocytes and serum iron), liver function tests, urinalysis and BUN; serum sodium if renal sodium loss or sodium-lowering drugs. SPS: also weight/BMI, U&Es, sodium, and HLA-B*1502 if Han Chinese or Thai origin.

src.q: complete pre-treatment blood counts, including platelets and possibly reticulocytes and serum iron, should be obtained as a baseline, and periodically thereafter
Baseline and periodic complete urinalysis and BUN determinations are recommended.
Screen for HLA-B*1502 allele genotype for individuals with Han Chinese, or Thai ancestry.

items.t: Sodium after about 2 weeks then monthly for 3 months (if at risk). Periodic full blood count, LFTs, U&Es. Thyroid function in hypothyroid patients (SPS: within 2 to 3 months). Plasma levels when needed (adherence, loss of seizure control, toxicity, interactions, pregnancy); optimum about 4 to 12 mg/litre. Watch for suicidal ideation.

src.q: serum sodium levels should be measured after approximately two weeks and then at monthly intervals for the first three months during therapy, or according to clinical need
Routine monitoring of plasma carbamazepine concentrations is not recommended.
The plasma carbamazepine concentration for optimum response 4 to 12 mg/litre (20 to 50 micromol/litre).
Hence thyroid function monitoring is suggested to adjust the dosage of thyroid replacement therapy.

items.t: Stop if leucopenia is severe, progressive or with fever/sore throat; significant bone marrow depression; aggravated liver dysfunction or acute liver disease; signs of SJS/TEN or hypersensitivity; seizure worsening in mixed/absence seizures. SPS: sodium below 120 mmol/L or symptomatic: review treatment.

src.q: Tegretol should also be discontinued if any evidence of significant bone marrow depression appears.
The drug should be withdrawn immediately in cases of aggravated liver dysfunction or acute liver disease.
Review carbamazepine treatment and correct sodium as clinically appropriate for patients with symptoms or a sodium level less than 120 mmol/L.

items.t: Oral, usually in 2 or 3 divided doses; may be taken during, after or between meals with a little liquid (e.g. a glass of water).

src.q: Tegretol is given orally, usually in two or three divided doses.
Tegretol may be taken during, after or between meals, with a little liquid e.g. a glass of water.

items.t: Seek medical advice at once for fever, sore throat, rash, mouth ulcers, easy bruising or bleeding, or signs of liver problems. Report mood changes or suicidal thoughts.

src.q: Patients and their relatives should be made aware of early toxic signs and symptoms indicative of a potential haematological problem, as well as symptoms of dermatological or hepatic reactions.
Patients (and caregivers of patients) should be advised to seek medical advice should signs of suicidal ideation or behaviour emerge.

items.t: Do not stop suddenly. Avoid alcohol. Take care driving (dizziness, drowsiness, blurred or double vision), especially at the start or after dose changes. Avoid grapefruit juice and St John's wort.

src.q: It is therefore advisable for the patient to abstain from alcohol.
Patients should therefore exercise due caution when driving a vehicle or operating machinery.
healthcare professionals should advise patients with epilepsy not to use products that contain St John's wort

items.t: Women: hormonal contraception may fail; use highly effective non-hormonal contraception and tell the doctor at once if pregnant or planning pregnancy.

src.q: Female patients of child-bearing potential should be warned that the concurrent use of Tegretol with hormonal contraceptives may render this type of contraceptive ineffective.
Women of childbearing potential should be counselled to contact the doctor immediately if they become pregnant or think they might be pregnant and are taking carbamazepine.

restrictions.note: No UK product information found.

hepatic.note: No UK product information found.

items.t: Infections due to susceptible organisms: respiratory tract infections, otitis media, skin and soft tissue infections, bone and joint infections, genito-urinary tract infections (including acute prostatitis), dental infections.

src.q: Cefalexin is indicated in the treatment of the following infections due to susceptible micro-organisms
Respiratory tract infections Otitis media Skin and soft tissue infections Bone and joint infections Genito-urinary tract infections, including acute prostatitis Dental infections

restrictions.note: No specialist-only, shared-care or brand-specific prescribing restriction found in the cefalexin capsule and suspension SmPCs.

items.t: Adults: 1 to 4 g daily in divided doses; most infections respond to 500 mg every 8 hours. If more than 4 g daily is needed, consider parenteral cephalosporins.

src.q: The adult dosage ranges from 1-4g daily in divided doses; most infections will respond to a dosage of 500 mg every 8 hours.
If daily doses of cefalexin greater than 4g are required, parenteral cephalosporins, in appropriate doses, should be considered.

items.t: Skin and soft tissue infections, streptococcal pharyngitis, mild uncomplicated UTI: usually 250 mg every 6 hours or 500 mg every 12 hours. More severe infections may need larger doses.

src.q: For skin and soft tissue infections, streptococcal pharyngitis and mild, uncomplicated urinary tract infections, the usual dosage is 250 mg every 6 hours, or 500 mg every 12 hours.

items.t: Beta-haemolytic streptococcal infections: treat for at least 10 days.

src.q: In the treatment of beta-haemolytic streptococcal infections, a therapeutic dose should be administered for at least 10 days.

items.t: Elderly and renal impairment: as for adults, but reduce the dose if renal function is markedly impaired.

src.q: The elderly and patients with impaired renal function As for adults. Reduce dosage if renal function is markedly impaired

items.t: Children: usually 25 to 50 mg/kg/day in divided doses. For skin and soft tissue infections, streptococcal pharyngitis and mild uncomplicated UTI the daily dose may be divided every 12 hours.

src.q: The usual recommended daily dosage for children is 25-50 mg/kg (10-20 mg/lb) in divided doses.
the total daily dose may be divided and administered every 12 hours

items.t: Suggested schedule for most infections: under 5 years 125 mg every 8 hours; 5 years and over 250 mg every 8 hours. In severe infections the dose may be doubled.

src.q: Children under 5 years: 125 mg every 8 hours. Children 5 years and over: 250 mg every 8 hours. In severe infections, the dosage may be doubled.

items.t: Otitis media: 75 to 100 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses.

src.q: In the therapy of otitis media, clinical studies have shown that a dosage of 75 to 100 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses is required.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to cefalexin or any excipient; known allergy to the cephalosporin group.

src.q: Cefalexin is contraindicated in patients with known allergy to the cephalosporin group of antibiotics.

items.t: Before starting, try to find out about previous hypersensitivity to cephalosporins, penicillins or other drugs. Give cautiously to penicillin-sensitive patients (partial cross-allergenicity; severe reactions including anaphylaxis to both). Stop if an allergic reaction occurs.

src.q: every effort should be made to determine whether the patient has had previous hypersensitivity reactions to the cephalosporins, penicillins or other drugs
Cefalexin should be given cautiously to penicillin-sensitive patients.
If an allergic reaction to cefalexin occurs, the drug should be discontinued

items.t: Markedly impaired renal function: use with caution; safe dose may be lower. On dialysis, the daily dose should not exceed 500 mg.

src.q: Cefalexin should be administered with caution in the presence of markedly impaired renal function.
If dialysis is required for renal failure, the daily dose of cefalexin should not exceed 500mg.

items.t: Neurotoxicity (encephalopathy, myoclonus, seizures): higher risk in the elderly, severe renal impairment or CNS disorders. Consider stopping if suspected.

src.q: Elderly patients, patients with severe renal impairment or central nervous system disorders are particularly at risk.
If cefalexin associated neurotoxicity is suspected, discontinuation of cefalexin should be considered.

items.t: Nephrotoxicity risk may increase with aminoglycosides, other cephalosporins, or furosemide and similar potent diuretics.

src.q: Concurrent administration with certain other drug substances, such as aminoglycosides, other cephalosporins, or furosemide, (frusemide) and similar potent diuretics, may increase the risk of nephrotoxicity.

items.t: AGEP: advise patients of the signs and monitor closely; withdraw immediately if it appears (mostly in the first week).

src.q: If signs and symptoms suggestive of these reactions appear, cefalexin should be withdrawn immediately and an alternative treatment considered.

items.t: Consider pseudomembranous colitis in patients with diarrhoea; it can be life-threatening. Prolonged use may cause overgrowth of non-susceptible organisms.

src.q: It is important, therefore, to consider its diagnosis in patients who develop diarrhoea in association with the use of antibiotics.
Prolonged use of cefalexin may result in the overgrowth of non-susceptible organisms.

items.t: Suspension contains sucrose: patients with hereditary fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take it. E129 may cause allergic reactions.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take this medicine.
Also contains Allura Red AC (E129), which may cause allergic reactions.

items.t: Lab tests: positive direct Coombs test (including in newborns of treated mothers); false positive urine glucose with copper-reduction tests.

src.q: Positive direct Coombs' tests have been reported during treatment with the cephalosporin antibiotics.
A false positive reaction for glucose in the urine may occur with Benedict's or Fehling's solutions or with copper sulphate test tablets.

items.t: Furosemide and similar potent diuretics, aminoglycosides, other cephalosporins: may increase the risk of nephrotoxicity.

src.q: Concurrent administration with certain other drug substances, such as aminoglycosides, other cephalosporins, or furosemide, (frusemide) and similar potent diuretics, may increase the risk of nephrotoxicity.

items.t: Metformin: single-dose study showed raised metformin levels (Cmax +34%, AUC +24%); clinical significance unclear and no lactic acidosis reported.

src.q: plasma metformin Cmax and AUC increased by an average of 34% and 24%, respectively
The clinical significance of this study is unclear

items.t: Probenecid inhibits renal excretion of cefalexin.

src.q: As with other beta-lactam drugs, renal excretion of cephalexin is inhibited by probenecid.

items.t: Markedly impaired renal function: reduce dose and use with caution; safe dose may be lower than usual. The SmPC gives no CrCl/eGFR threshold.

src.q: Reduce dosage if renal function is markedly impaired
Careful clinical and laboratory studies should be made because safe dosage may be lower than that usually recommended.

items.t: Dialysis: daily dose should not exceed 500 mg.

src.q: If dialysis is required for renal failure, the daily dose of cefalexin should not exceed 500mg.

hepatic.note: The cefalexin capsule and suspension SmPCs give no hepatic impairment advice (transient hepatitis and cholestatic jaundice are listed only as rare adverse effects).

items.t: SmPC: no evidence of teratogenicity, but exercise caution when prescribing in pregnancy.

src.q: Although laboratory and clinical studies have shown no evidence of teratogenicity, caution should be exercised when prescribing for the pregnant patient.

items.t: BUMPS (UKTIS, cephalosporins incl. cefalexin): most studies have not shown harm; no extra monitoring for major birth defects needed.

src.q: Most studies of pregnant women taking a cephalosporin have not shown that it harms the baby.
No extra monitoring for major birth defects is required following use of a cephalosporin.

items.t: SmPC: present in milk up to 8 hours after a dose. Use with caution: risk of candidiasis and CNS toxicity in the neonate, and theoretical later sensitisation.

src.q: Caution should be exercised when cefalexin is administered to a nursing woman, since the neonate is presented with the risk of candidiasis and CNS toxicity due to immaturity of the blood-brain barrier.

reproductive.note: The cefalexin capsule and suspension SmPCs give no fertility or contraception information.

items.t: Diarrhoea is the most frequent side effect (rarely severe enough to stop). Dyspepsia and abdominal pain also occur; nausea and vomiting are rare. The SmPC gives no other frequencies.

src.q: The most frequent side-effect has been diarrhoea. It was very rarely severe enough to warrant cessation of therapy.
Nausea and vomiting have been reported rarely.

items.t: Allergic rash, urticaria; genital and anal pruritus, genital candidiasis, vaginitis, dizziness, headache.

src.q: Allergic reactions have been observed in the form of rash, urticaria, angioedema
These have included genital and anal pruritus, genital candidiasis, vaginitis and vaginal discharge, dizziness, fatigue, headache

items.t: Anaphylaxis, angioedema, erythema multiforme, SJS, TEN: stop cefalexin and treat.

src.q: rarely erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis
Anaphylaxis has also been reported.

items.t: AGEP: withdraw immediately.

src.q: Acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) has been reported in association with cefalexin treatment.

items.t: Pseudomembranous colitis (mild to life-threatening), haemolytic anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, reversible interstitial nephritis, convulsions/encephalopathy (mostly with renal impairment and excessive doses).

src.q: Such colitis may range in severity from mild to life-threatening.
Eosinophilia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia and haemolytic anaemia have been reported.
Most cases occurred in patients with renal impairment who received doses that exceeded the recommended dose

items.t: Before starting: ask about previous reactions to cephalosporins, penicillins or other drugs.

src.q: every effort should be made to determine whether the patient has had previous hypersensitivity reactions to the cephalosporins, penicillins or other drugs

items.t: Markedly impaired renal function: careful clinical and laboratory monitoring. Prolonged use: observe for superinfection. Monitor closely for skin reactions.

src.q: Careful clinical and laboratory studies should be made because safe dosage may be lower than that usually recommended.
Careful observation of the patient is essential.

items.t: Stop if an allergic reaction or AGEP occurs; consider stopping if neurotoxicity is suspected.

src.q: If an allergic reaction to cefalexin occurs, the drug should be discontinued
If cefalexin associated neurotoxicity is suspected, discontinuation of cefalexin should be considered.

items.t: Oral use.

src.q: Method of administration For oral use.

items.t: Suspension: tap the bottle to loosen the granules, add 60 mL water in two portions, shaking after each. Shake well before use. Store in a refrigerator (2 to 8 °C) after reconstitution and use within 10 days.

src.q: add a total of 60 ml water in two portions, shaking after each addition until suspended
After reconstitution: to be used within 10 days
After reconstitution, the suspension should be stored in a refrigerator

items.t: Report rash, skin pustules or allergy symptoms straight away (AGEP mostly occurs in the first week).

src.q: At the time of prescription patients should be advised of the signs and symptoms and monitored closely for skin reactions.

items.t: Report diarrhoea during or after the course.

src.q: Symptoms of pseudomembranous colitis may appear either during or after antibiotic treatment.

items.t: Acute infections caused by susceptible organisms: upper respiratory tract infections (e.g. otitis media, and other URTI where the organism is known or suspected to be resistant to other common antibiotics, or where treatment failure carries significant risk); lower respiratory tract infections (e.g. bronchitis); urinary tract infections (e.g. cystitis, cystourethritis, uncomplicated pyelonephritis).

src.q: It is indicated for the treatment of the following acute infections when caused by susceptible micro-organisms

Upper Respiratory Tract Infections (URTI): e.g. otitis media; and other URTI where the causative organism is known or suspected to be resistant to other commonly used antibiotics, or where treatment failure may carry significant risk.
Lower Respiratory Tract Infection: e.g. bronchitis. Urinary Tract Infections: e.g. cystitis, cystourethritis, uncomplicated pyelonephritis.

restrictions.note: No specialist-only, shared-care or brand-specific prescribing restriction found in the UK cefixime tablet SmPC. No UK SmPC was found for the clinic's suspension or 400 mg capsule (the electronic medicines compendium and MHRA Products were searched).

items.t: UK tablet SmPC (applied to cefixime in general): adults and children over 10 years or over 50 kg: 200 to 400 mg daily by severity, as a single dose or in two divided doses. Usual course 7 days, up to 14 days if required.
items.tag: Adults and children over 10 years / over 50 kg

src.q: Adults and Children over 10 years or weighing more than 50 kg: The recommended dose is 200 - 400 mg daily according to the severity of infection, given either as a single dose or in two divided doses.
The usual course of treatment is 7 days. This may be continued for up to 14 days if required.

items.t: Elderly: same dose as adults; assess renal function and adjust the dose in severe renal impairment.

src.q: Elderly patients may be given the same dose as recommended for adults. Renal function should be assessed, and dosage should be adjusted in severe renal impairment.

items.t: The UK SmPC covers 200 mg tablets only: tablets are not recommended under 10 years. It gives no dose for younger children, and no UK suspension SmPC was found.

src.q: Suprax Tablets 200 mg are not recommended for use in children under 10 years old.

items.t: Safety and efficacy not established in children under 6 months; safety in premature or newborn infants not established.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of cefixime has not been established in children less than 6 months.
Safety of cefixime in premature or newborn infant has not been established

items.t: Hypersensitivity to cephalosporin antibiotics or to any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to cephalosporin antibiotics or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Penicillin hypersensitivity: give with caution (partial cross-allergenicity; severe reactions including anaphylaxis to both classes). Also caution with hypersensitivity to other drugs. Stop if an allergic reaction occurs.

src.q: cefixime should be given with caution to patients with a history of hypersensitivity to penicillin, as there is some evidence of partial cross-allergenicity between the penicillins and cephalosporins
Suprax should be given with caution to patients who have shown hypersensitivity to other drugs.
If an allergic effect occurs with Suprax, the drug should be discontinued

items.t: Encephalopathy (convulsions, confusion, decreased consciousness, movement disorders), particularly in the elderly, severe renal impairment, CNS disorders or overdose. Consider stopping if suspected.

src.q: Beta-lactams, including cefixime, have been associated with encephalopathy risk (which may include convulsions, confusion, decreased consciousness, movement disorders), particularly in elderly patients, in patients with severe renal impairment or central nervous system disorders
If cefixime-associated encephalopathy is suspected discontinuation should be considered.

items.t: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (TEN, SJS, DRESS, AGEP): inform patients of the signs, monitor closely, and stop at the first rash, mucosal lesion or other sign of skin hypersensitivity.

src.q: Treatment should be discontinued at the first appearance of skin rash, mucosal lesions, or any other sign of skin hypersensitivity.

items.t: Drug-induced haemolytic anaemia (including fatal cases) reported with cephalosporins; recurrence after re-exposure in patients with previous cephalosporin-associated haemolytic anaemia.

src.q: Drug-induced haemolytic anaemia, including severe cases with a fatal outcome, has been described for cephalosporins (as a class).

items.t: Acute renal failure including tubulointerstitial nephritis: stop cefixime if it occurs. Use with caution in markedly impaired renal function.

src.q: When acute renal failure occurs, cefixime should be discontinued
Suprax should be administered with caution in patients with markedly impaired renal function

items.t: Consider pseudomembranous colitis in anyone with diarrhoea during or after antibiotics. Stop if marked diarrhoea occurs.

src.q: it is therefore important to consider its diagnosis in patients who develop diarrhoea in association with the use of antibiotics
Suprax should be discontinued if marked diarrhoea occurs.

items.t: Lab tests: false positive urine glucose with copper-reduction tests (not glucose oxidase tests); false positive direct Coombs test.

src.q: A false positive reaction for glucose in the urine may occur with Benedict's or Fehling's solutions or with copper sulphate test tablets
A false positive direct Coombs test has been reported during treatment with cephalosporin antibiotics

items.t: Coumarin anticoagulants (e.g. warfarin): cefixime may enhance their effect; prolonged prothrombin time with or without bleeding. Give with caution.

src.q: Cefixime should be administered with caution to patients receiving coumarin-type anticoagulants, e.g. warfarin potassium.
Since cefixime may enhance effects of the anticoagulants, prolonged prothrombin time with or without bleeding may occur.

items.t: CrCl 20 ml/min or more: normal dose.

src.q: Normal dose and schedule may be given in patients with creatinine clearances of 20 ml/min or greater.

items.t: CrCl less than 20 ml/min, and patients on CAPD or haemodialysis: do not exceed 200 mg once daily.

src.q: In patients whose creatinine clearance is less than 20 ml/min, it is recommended that a dose of 200 mg once daily should not be exceeded.
The dose and regimen for patients who are maintained on chronic ambulatory peritoneal dialysis or haemodialysis should follow the same recommendation

hepatic.note: The UK cefixime tablet SmPC gives no hepatic impairment advice (jaundice and raised liver enzymes are listed as adverse reactions only).

items.t: SmPC: no adequate studies in pregnant women; should not be used in pregnancy unless considered essential by the physician.

src.q: Suprax should therefore not be used in pregnancy or in nursing mothers unless considered essential by the physician.

items.t: BUMPS (UKTIS, cephalosporins incl. cefixime): most studies have not shown harm to the baby; no extra monitoring for major birth defects needed.

src.q: Most studies of pregnant women taking a cephalosporin have not shown that it harms the baby.
No extra monitoring for major birth defects is required following use of a cephalosporin.

items.t: SmPC: should not be used in nursing mothers unless considered essential. No data on cefixime in human breast milk.

src.q: Suprax should therefore not be used in pregnancy or in nursing mothers unless considered essential by the physician.
No data are available on secretion of cefixime in human breast milk.

items.t: Animal studies at high doses showed no impaired fertility.

src.q: revealed no evidence of impaired fertility or harm to the fetus due to cefixime

items.t: Generally well tolerated; most reactions mild and self-limiting. Listed: diarrhoea (more common at higher doses), abdominal pain, dyspepsia, nausea, vomiting, flatulence, headache, dizziness, rash, pruritus. The SmPC gives no frequencies.

src.q: The majority of adverse reactions observed in clinical trials were mild and self-limiting in nature.
Abdominal pain Diarrhoea* Dyspepsia Nausea Vomiting Flatulence
*Diarrhoea has been more commonly associated with higher doses.

items.t: Anaphylaxis, angio-oedema, serum sickness-like reaction: stop and treat.

src.q: Anaphylactic reaction Angio-oedema Serum sickness-like reaction
If an allergic effect occurs with Suprax, the drug should be discontinued and the patient treated with appropriate agents if necessary.

items.t: Severe skin reactions (SJS, TEN, DRESS, AGEP): stop at the first sign.

src.q: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARS) including toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), and acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP)

items.t: Pseudomembranous colitis, acute renal failure with tubulointerstitial nephritis, haemolytic anaemia, agranulocytosis, convulsions/encephalopathy.

src.q: Acute renal failure with tubulointerstitial nephritis
Cases of convulsions have been reported with cephalosporins including cefixime
Agranulocytosis Leucopenia Neutropenia Granulocytopenia Haemolytic anaemia Thrombocytopenia

items.t: Elderly: assess renal function before dosing.

src.q: Renal function should be assessed, and dosage should be adjusted in severe renal impairment.

items.t: Monitor closely for skin reactions; on anticoagulants, watch prothrombin time/bleeding.

src.q: Patients should be informed about the signs and symptoms of serious skin manifestations and monitored closely.
Care should therefore be taken in patients receiving anticoagulation therapy.

items.t: Stop if allergic reaction, skin rash/mucosal lesions, acute renal failure or marked diarrhoea occurs; consider stopping if encephalopathy is suspected.

src.q: When acute renal failure occurs, cefixime should be discontinued
Suprax should be discontinued if marked diarrhoea occurs.

items.t: Oral. May be taken with or without food.

src.q: Absorption of Suprax is not significantly modified by the presence of food.
Cefixime may therefore be given without regard to meals.

items.t: Report any rash, blistering, mouth sores or allergy symptoms straight away.

src.q: Patients should be informed about the signs and symptoms of serious skin manifestations and monitored closely.

items.t: Do not drive or use machines if confusion, convulsions or other signs of encephalopathy occur.

src.q: the patient should not operate machines or drive a vehicle

items.t: Adults and children from 3 months: acute streptococcal tonsillitis and pharyngitis, acute bacterial sinusitis, acute otitis media, acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, cystitis, pyelonephritis, uncomplicated skin and soft tissue infections, early Lyme disease.

src.q: indicated for the treatment of the infections listed below in adults and children from the age of 3 months

Acute streptococcal tonsillitis and pharyngitis. Acute bacterial sinusitis. Acute otitis media. Acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis. Cystitis. Pyelonephritis. Uncomplicated skin and soft tissue infections. Treatment of early Lyme disease.

restrictions.note: No specialist-only, shared-care or brand-specific prescribing restriction found in the cefuroxime axetil tablet SmPC; it advises considering official guidance on antibacterial use.

items.t: Acute tonsillitis/pharyngitis, acute bacterial sinusitis, cystitis, pyelonephritis, uncomplicated skin and soft tissue infections: 250 mg twice daily.

src.q: Acute tonsillitis and pharyngitis, acute bacterial sinusitis 250 mg twice daily
Cystitis 250 mg twice daily Pyelonephritis 250 mg twice daily Uncomplicated skin and soft tissue infections 250 mg twice daily

items.t: Acute otitis media and acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis: 500 mg twice daily.

src.q: Acute otitis media 500 mg twice daily Acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis 500 mg twice daily

items.t: Lyme disease: 500 mg twice daily for 14 days (range 10 to 21 days).

src.q: Lyme disease 500 mg twice daily for 14 days (range of 10 to 21 days)

items.t: Usual course 7 days (range 5 to 10 days).

src.q: The usual course of therapy is seven days (may range from five to ten days).

items.t: Children < 40 kg, acute tonsillitis/pharyngitis and acute bacterial sinusitis: 10 mg/kg twice daily (maximum 125 mg twice daily).

src.q: Acute tonsillitis and pharyngitis, acute bacterial sinusitis 10 mg/kg twice daily to a maximum of 125 mg twice daily

items.t: Children < 40 kg: otitis media (aged 2 years or older) or more severe infections, cystitis, uncomplicated skin and soft tissue infections: 15 mg/kg twice daily (maximum 250 mg twice daily). Pyelonephritis: same dose for 10 to 14 days. Lyme disease: same dose for 14 days (10 to 21 days).

src.q: Children aged two years or older with otitis media or, where appropriate, with more severe infections 15 mg/kg twice daily to a maximum of 250 mg twice daily
Pyelonephritis 15 mg/kg twice daily to a maximum of 250 mg twice daily for 10 to 14 days
Lyme disease 15 mg/kg twice daily to a maximum of 250 mg twice daily for 14 days (10 to 21 days)

items.t: No experience in children under 3 months. Tablets must not be crushed; the oral suspension may be used in children.

src.q: There is no experience of using Zinnat in children under the age of 3 months.
In children Zinnat oral suspension may be used.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to cefuroxime or any excipient; known hypersensitivity to cephalosporin antibiotics.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to cefuroxime or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1. Patients with known hypersensitivity to cephalosporin antibiotics.

items.t: History of severe hypersensitivity (e.g. anaphylactic reaction) to any other beta-lactam (penicillins, monobactams, carbapenems).

src.q: History of severe hypersensitivity (e.g. anaphylactic reaction) to any other type of betalactam antibacterial agent (penicillins, monobactams and carbapenems).

items.t: After SJS, TEN or DRESS with cefuroxime, it must never be restarted.

src.q: If the patient has developed a serious reaction such as SJS, TEN or DRESS with the use of cefuroxime, treatment with cefuroxime must not be restarted in this patient at any time.

items.t: Before starting, establish any history of severe hypersensitivity to cefuroxime, other cephalosporins or other beta-lactams. Use caution with a history of non-severe hypersensitivity to other beta-lactams. Special care after allergy to penicillins or other beta-lactams (cross-sensitivity).

src.q: Before beginning treatment, it should be established whether the patient has a history of severe hypersensitivity reactions to cefuroxime, to other cephalosporins or to any other type of beta-lactam agent.
Caution should be used if cefuroxime is given to patients with a history of non-severe hypersensitivity to other beta-lactam agents.
Special care is indicated in patients who have experienced an allergic reaction to penicillins or other beta-lactam antibiotics because there is a risk of cross-sensitivity.

items.t: Severe hypersensitivity (including progression to Kounis syndrome): stop immediately and start emergency measures.

src.q: In case of severe hypersensitivity reactions, treatment with cefuroxime must be discontinued immediately and adequate emergency measures must be initiated.

items.t: SCARs (SJS, TEN, DRESS): advise patients of signs, monitor closely, withdraw immediately if they appear.

src.q: If signs and symptoms suggestive of these reactions appear, cefuroxime should be withdrawn immediately and an alternative treatment considered.

items.t: Pseudomembranous colitis: consider in diarrhoea during or after treatment; consider stopping and specific C. difficile treatment. Do not give medicines that inhibit peristalsis. Candida and other overgrowth possible.

src.q: Discontinuation of therapy with cefuroxime and the administration of specific treatment for Clostridium difficile should be considered. Medicinal products that inhibit peristalsis should not be given

items.t: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction may follow treatment of Lyme disease; common and usually self-limiting.

src.q: Patients should be reassured that this is a common and usually self-limiting consequence of antibiotic treatment of Lyme disease

items.t: Lab tests: positive Coombs test may interfere with cross-matching; use glucose oxidase or hexokinase methods for blood glucose (ferricyanide test may be falsely negative).

src.q: it is recommended that either the glucose oxidase or hexokinase methods are used to determine blood/plasma glucose levels in patients receiving cefuroxime axetil

items.t: Medicines that reduce gastric acidity (this tool applies this to PPIs and antacids): may lower cefuroxime axetil bioavailability and cancel the extra absorption seen after food.

src.q: Drugs which reduce gastric acidity may result in a lower bioavailability of cefuroxime axetil compared with that of the fasting state and tend to cancel the effect of enhanced absorption after food.

items.t: Oral anticoagulants (e.g. warfarin): increased INR may occur.

src.q: Concomitant use with oral anticoagulants may give rise to increased INR.

items.t: Combined oral contraceptives: possible reduced efficacy (lower oestrogen reabsorption).

src.q: Cefuroxime axetil may affect the gut flora, leading to lower oestrogen reabsorption and reduced efficacy of combined oral contraceptives.

items.t: Probenecid: concomitant use not recommended (raises cefuroxime levels).

src.q: Concomitant use of probenicid is not recommended.

items.t: CrCl ≥ 30 ml/min/1.73 m²: no adjustment (125 mg to 500 mg twice daily).

src.q: ≥30 ml/min/1.73 m2 1.4-2.4 no dose adjustment necessary (standard dose of 125 mg to 500 mg given twice daily)

items.t: CrCl 10 to 29 ml/min/1.73 m²: standard individual dose every 24 hours.

src.q: 10-29 ml/min/1.73 m2 4.6 standard individual dose given every 24 hours

items.t: CrCl < 10 ml/min/1.73 m²: standard individual dose every 48 hours. Haemodialysis: one extra standard dose at the end of each dialysis.

src.q: <10 ml/min/1.73 m2 16.8 standard individual dose given every 48 hours
a single additional standard individual dose should be given at the end of each dialysis

items.t: No data in hepatic impairment; hepatic dysfunction is not expected to affect cefuroxime pharmacokinetics (mainly renal elimination).

src.q: There are no data available for patients with hepatic impairment.
the presence of hepatic dysfunction is expected to have no effect on the pharmacokinetics of cefuroxime

items.t: SmPC: limited human data; animal studies show no harm. Prescribe only if the benefit outweighs the risk.

src.q: Zinnat should be prescribed to pregnant women only if the benefit outweighs the risk.
