src.q: History of jaundice/hepatic impairment due to amoxicillin/clavulanic acid

items.t: AGEP during treatment: stop and do not give amoxicillin again.

src.q: This reaction requires Augmentin discontinuation and contraindicates any subsequent administration of amoxicillin.

items.t: Hepatic events (cholestatic jaundice, hepatitis), mainly in males and elderly, may be linked to prolonged treatment; signs may appear several weeks after stopping. Can be severe, rarely fatal. Use with caution if there is evidence of hepatic impairment.

src.q: Hepatic events have been reported predominantly in males and elderly patients and may be associated with prolonged treatment.
in some cases may not become apparent until several weeks after treatment has ceased
Amoxicillin/clavulanic acid should be used with caution in patients with evidence of hepatic impairment

items.t: Ask about previous reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins or other beta-lactams. Serious, occasionally fatal reactions more likely with penicillin allergy history and atopy. Stop if an allergic reaction occurs.

src.q: careful enquiry should be made concerning previous hypersensitivity reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins or other beta-lactam agents
If an allergic reaction occurs, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid therapy must be discontinued and appropriate alternative therapy instituted.

items.t: Avoid if infectious mononucleosis is suspected (morbilliform rash).

src.q: Amoxicillin/clavulanic acid should be avoided if infectious mononucleosis is suspected

items.t: Haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)/macrophage activation syndrome: evaluate promptly if fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, high ferritin occur; stop unless another cause is found.

src.q: Patients who develop these signs and symptoms should be immediately evaluated and HLH/MAS diagnosis considered.
Amoxicillin/clavulanic acid therapy should be discontinued unless an alternative aetiology for HLH/MAS can be established.

items.t: Drug-induced enterocolitis syndrome (DIES), mainly in children: protracted vomiting 1-4 hours after a dose; severe cases can progress to shock.

src.q: Drug-induced enterocolitis syndrome (DIES) has been reported mainly in children receiving amoxicillin/clavulanic acid
There have been severe cases including progression to shock.

items.t: Convulsions may occur with impaired renal function or high doses.

src.q: Convulsions may occur in patients with impaired renal function or in those receiving high doses

items.t: Antibiotic-associated colitis: stop immediately if it occurs; anti-peristaltic medicines are contraindicated.

src.q: Should antibiotic-associated colitis occur, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid should immediately be discontinued
Anti-peristaltic medicinal products are contraindicated in this situation.

items.t: Not suitable when the likely pathogen has beta-lactam resistance not mediated by clavulanate-sensitive beta-lactamases; do not use to treat penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae.

src.q: This presentation should not be used to treat penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae .

items.t: High doses: maintain fluid intake and urine output (crystalluria risk).

src.q: During the administration of high doses of amoxicillin, it is advisable to maintain adequate fluid intake and urinary output in order to reduce the possibility of amoxicillin crystalluria.

items.t: May cause a false positive Coombs test and false positive Platelia Aspergillus EIA; use enzymatic glucose oxidase methods for urine glucose.

src.q: The presence of clavulanic acid in Augmentin may cause a non-specific binding of IgG and albumin by red cell membranes leading to a false positive Coombs test.
enzymatic glucose oxidase methods should be used whenever testing for the presence of glucose in urine

items.t: Suspensions contain aspartame (source of phenylalanine): use with caution in phenylketonuria; no data on aspartame use in infants below 12 weeks of age. They contain maltodextrin (glucose): patients with glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take them. Flavouring contains traces of benzyl alcohol (may cause allergic reactions).

src.q: This medicine should be used with caution in patients with phenylketonuria.
This medicine should be used with caution in patients with phenylketonuria.
Benzyl alcohol may cause allergic reactions.
Neither non-clinical nor clinical data are available to assess aspartame use in infants below 12 weeks of age.
Patients with rare glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: Warfarin/acenocoumarol: raised INR reported. If used together, carefully monitor prothrombin time/INR when co-amoxiclav is added or stopped; anticoagulant dose may need adjusting.

src.q: in the literature there are cases of increased international normalised ratio in patients maintained on acenocoumarol or warfarin and prescribed a course of amoxicillin
If co-administration is necessary, the prothrombin time or international normalised ratio should be carefully monitored with the addition or withdrawal of amoxicillin.

items.t: Methotrexate: penicillins may reduce methotrexate excretion (toxicity). SPS: for short penicillin courses (up to 10 days) consider using with caution and monitor for toxicity.

src.q: Penicillins may reduce the excretion of methotrexate causing a potential increase in toxicity.
If the duration of penicillin is short (up to 10 days), consider using with caution and advise to monitor for signs of toxicity.

items.t: Probenecid: concomitant use not recommended.

src.q: Probenecid Concomitant use of probenecid is not recommended.

items.t: Mycophenolate mofetil: pre-dose mycophenolic acid levels fall by about 50%; dose change not normally needed without signs of graft dysfunction, but monitor closely during and shortly after the course.

src.q: However, close clinical monitoring should be performed during the combination and shortly after antibiotic treatment.

items.t: Allopurinol: increased likelihood of allergic skin reactions.

src.q: Concomitant use of allopurinol during treatment with amoxicillin can increase the likelihood of allergic skin reactions.

items.t: No adjustment if CrCl > 30 ml/min.

src.q: No adjustment in dose is required in patients with creatinine clearance (CrCl) greater than 30 ml/min.

items.t: 500 mg/125 mg tablets (adults/children ≥ 40 kg): CrCl 10-30 ml/min 500 mg/125 mg twice daily; CrCl < 10 ml/min 500 mg/125 mg once daily; haemodialysis 500 mg/125 mg every 24 hours plus a dose during dialysis, repeated at the end of dialysis.

src.q: CrCl: 10-30 ml/min 500 mg/125 mg twice daily CrCl < 10 ml /min 500 mg/125 mg once daily
Haemodialysis 500 mg/125 mg every 24 hours, plus 500 mg/125 mg during dialysis, to be repeated at the end of dialysis

items.t: 250 mg/125 mg tablets (adults/children ≥ 40 kg): CrCl 10-30 ml/min 250 mg/125 mg twice daily; CrCl < 10 ml/min 250 mg/125 mg once daily. In children < 40 kg with CrCl less than 30 ml/min, 2:1 presentations are not recommended (no dose adjustments available).

src.q: CrCl: 10-30 ml/min 250 mg/125 mg twice daily CrCl < 10 ml /min 250 mg/125 mg once daily
the use of Augmentin presentations with an amoxicillin to clavulanic acid ratio of 2:1 is not recommended, as no dose adjustments are available

items.t: Children < 40 kg (4:1 presentations): CrCl 10-30 ml/min 15 mg/3.75 mg/kg twice daily (maximum 500 mg/125 mg twice daily); CrCl < 10 ml/min 15 mg/3.75 mg/kg once daily (maximum 500 mg/125 mg); haemodialysis 15 mg/3.75 mg/kg once daily plus a dose before and after dialysis.

src.q: Children < 40 kg CrCl: 10-30 ml/min 15 mg/3.75 mg/kg twice daily (maximum 500 mg/125 mg twice daily). CrCl < 10 ml /min 15 mg/3.75 mg/kg as a single daily dose (maximum 500 mg/125 mg).
Haemodialysis 15 mg/3.75 mg/kg per day once daily.

items.t: 7:1 presentations (875 mg/125 mg tablets, 400/57 suspension): not recommended if CrCl < 30 ml/min (no dose-adjustment recommendations available).

src.q: In patients with creatinine clearance less than 30 ml/min, the use of Co-Amoxiclav presentations with an amoxicillin to clavulanic acid ratio of 7:1 is not recommended
In patients with creatinine clearance less than 30 ml/min, the use of Augmentin presentations with an amoxicillin to clavulanic acid ratio of 7:1 is not recommended

items.t: Contraindicated if previous jaundice/hepatic impairment was caused by co-amoxiclav. Otherwise in hepatic impairment dose with caution and monitor hepatic function at regular intervals.

src.q: History of jaundice/hepatic impairment due to amoxicillin/clavulanic acid
Hepatic impairment Dose with caution and monitor hepatic function at regular intervals

items.t: SmPC: limited data do not show increased malformation risk, but one study in preterm premature rupture of membranes linked prophylactic co-amoxiclav with neonatal necrotising enterocolitis. Avoid in pregnancy unless considered essential by the physician.

src.q: prophylactic treatment with amoxicillin/clavulanic acid may be associated with an increased risk of necrotising enterocolitis in neonates
Use should be avoided during pregnancy, unless considered essential by the physician.

items.t: BUMPS (UKTIS): co-amoxiclav can be taken in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor; no concerns that penicillin use will harm the baby. (Differs in emphasis from the SmPC.)

src.q: Amoxicillin, co-amoxiclav, and penicillin V can be taken in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor.
There are no concerns that use of a penicillin antibiotic in pregnancy will harm your baby.

items.t: SmPC: both substances pass into milk (effect of clavulanic acid on the infant unknown); diarrhoea, mucosal fungal infection and sensitisation possible. Use only after benefit/risk assessment.

src.q: Both substances are excreted into breast milk (nothing is known of the effects of clavulanic acid on the breast-fed infant).
Amoxicillin/clavulanic acid should only be used during breast-feeding after benefit/risk assessment by the physician in charge.

items.t: SPS: all penicillins, including combinations such as co-amoxiclav, can be used during breastfeeding with precautionary infant monitoring (GI upset, oral thrush, rash/breathing problems, irritability, drowsiness).

src.q: All penicillin antibiotics can be used during breastfeeding with precautionary infant monitoring.
Although there is no information on how much passes into breastmilk, studies have not identified any concerns for their use in breastfeeding.

reproductive.note: No fertility, contraception or reproductive-potential statements found in section 4.6 of the co-amoxiclav SmPCs accessed.

items.t: Most common: diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting. Tablets: diarrhoea very common; nausea, vomiting, mucocutaneous candidosis common. Suspensions: diarrhoea common. Nausea is more likely with higher doses and can be reduced by taking with a meal.

src.q: The most commonly reported adverse drug reactions (ADRs) are diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting.
Gastrointestinal disorders Diarrhoea Very common Nausea2 Common Vomiting Common
Gastrointestinal disorders Diarrhoea Common Nausea2 Common Vomiting Common
Mucocutaneous candidosis Common
Nausea is more often associated with higher oral doses.

items.t: Hepatitis and cholestatic jaundice (may appear weeks after stopping; rarely fatal).

src.q: Hepatitis5 Not known Cholestatic jaundice5 Not known
Hepatic events may be severe and, in extremely rare circumstances deaths have been reported.

items.t: Anaphylaxis, angioedema, serum sickness-like syndrome, hypersensitivity vasculitis: stop and give alternative therapy.

src.q: Angioneurotic oedema Not known Anaphylaxis Not known Serum sickness-like syndrome Not known Hypersensitivity vasculitis Not known
If an allergic reaction occurs, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid therapy must be discontinued and appropriate alternative therapy instituted.

items.t: Severe skin reactions (SJS, TEN, bullous exfoliative dermatitis, AGEP, DRESS): stop treatment if any hypersensitivity dermatitis occurs.

src.q: Stevens-Johnson syndrome Not known Toxic epidermal necrolysis Not known Bullous exfoliative-dermatitis Not known Acute generalised exanthemous pustulosis (AGEP)1 Not known Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) Not known
If any hypersensitivity dermatitis reaction occurs, treatment should be discontinued

items.t: Antibiotic-associated colitis; HLH; DIES; Kounis syndrome; convulsions; interstitial nephritis; crystalluria.

src.q: Antibiotic-associated colitis3 Not known Drug-induced enterocolitis syndrome Not known
Interstitial nephritis Not known Crystalluria (including acute renal injury)7 Not known

items.t: Hepatic impairment: monitor hepatic function at regular intervals.

src.q: Dose with caution and monitor hepatic function at regular intervals

items.t: Prolonged therapy: periodic assessment of renal, hepatic and haematopoietic function is advisable. Review if treatment would go beyond 14 days.

src.q: Periodic assessment of organ system functions, including renal, hepatic and haematopoietic function is advisable during prolonged therapy.
Treatment should not be extended beyond 14 days without review

items.t: With oral anticoagulants: appropriate monitoring of prothrombin time/INR.

src.q: Appropriate monitoring should be undertaken when anticoagulants are prescribed concomitantly.

items.t: Stop for allergic reaction, hypersensitivity dermatitis, AGEP, antibiotic-associated colitis, or HLH/MAS without another cause.

src.q: If an allergic reaction occurs, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid therapy must be discontinued
Amoxicillin/clavulanic acid therapy should be discontinued unless an alternative aetiology for HLH/MAS can be established.

items.t: Take with a meal to minimise gastrointestinal intolerance (400/57 suspension: at the start of a meal, which also optimises absorption).

src.q: Augmentin should be administered with a meal to minimise potential gastrointestinal intolerance.
Administer at the start of a meal to minimise potential gastrointestinal intolerance and optimise absorption of amoxicillin/clavulanic acid.

items.t: 500 mg/125 mg tablet score line is only to help swallowing, not to divide into equal doses.

src.q: The score line is only to facilitate breaking for ease of swallowing and not to divide into equal doses.

items.t: Suspensions: reconstitute with water as directed; shake well before each dose; store reconstituted suspension at 2-8 °C (not frozen) for up to 7 days.

src.q: Shake the bottle before each dose
Reconstituted suspensions should be stored at 2°C - 8°C (but not frozen) for up to 7 days.
Reconstituted suspensions should be stored at 2°C - 8°C (but not frozen) for up to 7 days.

items.t: Take with food. Report yellowing of skin/eyes, dark urine or itching during or up to several weeks after the course (liver reaction).

src.q: If gastrointestinal reactions are evident, they may be reduced by taking amoxicillin/clavulanic acid with a meal.
in some cases may not become apparent until several weeks after treatment has ceased

items.t: Report rash, swelling, breathing problems or severe/persistent diarrhoea promptly.

src.q: it is important to consider this diagnosis in patients who present with diarrhoea during or subsequent to the administration of any antibiotics
If an allergic reaction occurs, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid therapy must be discontinued

items.t: May cause dizziness or convulsions, which can affect driving.

src.q: undesirable effects may occur (e.g. allergic reactions, dizziness, convulsions), which may influence the ability to drive and use machines

items.t: 30/500: severe pain. Codeine component: acute moderate pain not relieved by paracetamol or ibuprofen alone, in patients over 12 years.

src.q: For the relief of severe pain.

Codeine is indicated in patients older than 12 years of age for the treatment of acute moderate pain which is not considered to be relieved by other analgesics such as paracetamol or ibuprofen (alone).

items.t: 8/500: painful and febrile conditions (e.g. headache, migraine, neuralgia, toothache, dysmenorrhoea, rheumatic pain); codeine for acute moderate pain not relieved by paracetamol or ibuprofen alone, over 12 years.

src.q: This product is recommended for the relief of most painful and febrile conditions
Codeine is indicated in patients older than 12 years of age for the treatment of acute moderate pain

items.t: MHRA: codeine-containing medicines only for acute moderate pain in children over 12 years and only if paracetamol or ibuprofen alone do not work.

src.q: Codeine should only be used to relieve acute moderate pain in children older than 12 years and only if it cannot be relieved by other painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen

items.t: Adults: 2 tablets not more often than every 4-6 hours; maximum 8 tablets in 24 hours. Elderly: as adults, but a reduced dose may be needed.

src.q: Adults : Two tablets not more frequently than every 4 to 6 hours, up to a maximum of 8 tablets in any 24 hour period.
Elderly : As for adults, however a reduced dose may be required.

items.t: Adults: 2 tablets with a glass of water, not more often than every 4-6 hours; maximum 8 tablets in 24 hours.

src.q: Adults: Two tablets, to be taken with a glass of water, not more frequently than every 4 to six hours, up to a maximum of 8 tablets in any 24 hour period.

items.t: Keep treatment as short as possible; agree a treatment plan and end-of-treatment plan before starting; taper gradually when stopping.

src.q: The duration of treatment should be as short as possible
When a patient no longer requires therapy with codeine, it may be advisable to taper the dose gradually to prevent symptoms of withdrawal.

items.t: Under 12 years: should not be used (risk of opioid toxicity from variable codeine-to-morphine metabolism).

src.q: Codeine should not be used in children below the age of 12 years because of the risk of opioid toxicity due to the variable and unpredictable metabolism of codeine to morphine

items.t: 12-15 years: 1 tablet every 6 hours when necessary, maximum 4 tablets in 24 hours. 16-18 years: 1-2 tablets every 6 hours when necessary, maximum 8 tablets in 24 hours. 30/500: no more than 3 days without consulting a doctor.

src.q: Children aged 12 to 15 years: One tablet every 6 hours when necessary to a maximum of 4 tablets in 24 hours.
Children aged 16 to 18 years : One to two tablets every 6 hours when necessary up to a maximum of 8 tablets in 24 hours.
Do not take for more than 3 days without consulting your doctor.

items.t: MHRA: in 12-18 years codeine maximum 240 mg/day, intervals of no less than 6 hours, treatment limited to 3 days.

src.q: In children age 12-18 years, the maximum daily dose should not exceed 240 mg.
Duration of treatment should be limited to 3 days
up to four times a day at intervals of no less than 6 hours

items.t: Contraindicated in all under-18s having tonsillectomy and/or adenoidectomy for obstructive sleep apnoea. Not recommended in children whose breathing may be compromised.

src.q: In all paediatric patients (0-18 years of age) who undergo tonsillectomy and/or adenoidectomy for obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome
Codeine is not recommended for use in children in whom respiratory function might be compromised

items.t: Hypersensitivity to paracetamol, codeine or excipients.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to paracetamol, codeine phosphate or any of the other constituents.

In all paediatric patients (0-18 years of age) who undergo tonsillectomy and/or adenoidectomy for obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome

items.t: 30/500 also: conditions where opioids are contraindicated (acute asthma, respiratory depression, acute alcoholism, head injury, raised intracranial pressure, after biliary tract surgery) and MAOI therapy now or within 14 days.

monoamine oxidase inhibitor therapy, concurrent or within 14 days

items.t: 8/500 also: under 12 years for symptomatic treatment of colds.

src.q: In children below the age of 12 years for the symptomatic treatment of colds

items.t: Tolerance, dependence and opioid use disorder can develop with repeated use, even at therapeutic doses; risk higher with personal/family history of substance use disorder, tobacco use or mental health disorders. Agree goals and a stop plan; watch for drug-seeking behaviour.

src.q: Repeated use of Co-codamol can lead to OUD.
Patients will require monitoring for signs of drug-seeking behaviour (e.g. too early requests for refills).

items.t: Care in conditions that opioids may worsen: elderly, other CNS depressants, prostatic hypertrophy, hypothyroidism, inflammatory or obstructive bowel disorders, Addison's disease, myasthenia gravis.

src.q: those on concurrent CNS depressant drugs, those with prostatic hypertrophy, hypothyroidism and those with inflammatory or obstructive bowel disorders, Addison's disease or myasthenia gravis

items.t: CYP2D6 ultra-rapid or extensive metabolisers have a higher risk of opioid toxicity (confusion, somnolence, shallow breathing, small pupils), which can be life-threatening.

src.q: if the patient is an extensive or ultra-rapid metaboliser there is an increased risk of developing side effects of opioid toxicity even at commonly prescribed doses

items.t: Use with caution in convulsive disorders, pancreatitis and biliary tract disease (sphincter of Oddi spasm).

src.q: Use with caution in patients with convulsive disorders.
codeine/paracetamol has to be administered with caution in patients with pancreatitis and diseases of the biliary tract

items.t: Paracetamol component: care in severe renal or severe hepatic impairment; do not take other paracetamol-containing products; high anion gap metabolic acidosis risk in severe illness, malnutrition or chronic alcoholism.

src.q: Care is advised in the administration of paracetamol to patients with severe renal or severe hepatic impairment.
not take other paracetamol containing products concurrently

items.t: Sleep-related breathing disorders (central sleep apnoea): consider reducing the opioid dose.

src.q: In patients who present with CSA, consider decreasing the total opioid dosage.

items.t: Alcohol: concomitant use not recommended (sedation, respiratory depression, coma, death).

src.q: Concomitant use with alcohol is not recommended

items.t: Benzodiazepines and other sedatives: risk of sedation, respiratory depression, coma and death; co-prescribe only if no alternative, lowest dose, shortest time, monitor closely.

src.q: concomitant prescribing with these sedative medicines should be reserved for patients for whom alternative treatment options are not possible
only prescribe benzodiazepines (or benzodiazepine-like drugs) and opioids together if there is no alternative

items.t: Other opioid (narcotic) analgesics, antihypertensives, antihistamines, antipsychotics and other CNS depressants: additive CNS depression.

src.q: Patients receiving other narcotic analgesics, antitussive, antihypertensives, antihistamines, antipsychotics, antianxiety agents or other CNS depressants (including alcohol) concomitantly with this codeine containing drug may exhibit additive CNS depression.

items.t: Warfarin and other coumarins: prolonged regular paracetamol may enhance the anticoagulant effect (bleeding risk); occasional doses have no significant effect.

src.q: The anticoagulant effect of warfarin and other coumarins may be enhanced by prolonged regular use of paracetamol with increased risk of bleeding

items.t: MAOIs: do not use within two weeks of stopping an MAOI.

src.q: Co-codamol should not be used within two weeks after the discontinuation of MAOI treatment.

items.t: Gabapentin or pregabalin: respiratory depression, hypotension, profound sedation, coma or death.

src.q: Concomitant use of Co-codamol with gabapentinoids (gabapentin and pregabalin) may result in respiratory depression, hypotension, profound sedation, coma or death.

items.t: Sertraline (sertraline SmPC): serotonin syndrome / NMS risk is increased with opioids; caution and monitor for symptoms.

src.q: and with opioids. Patients should be monitored for the emergence of signs and symptoms of SS or NMS syndrome
Caution is also advised with opioids

items.t: Clopidogrel (clopidogrel SmPC): opioid agonists may delay and reduce clopidogrel absorption (clinical relevance unknown); in acute coronary syndrome consider a parenteral antiplatelet agent.

src.q: co-administration of opioid agonists has the potential to delay and reduce the absorption of clopidogrel presumably because of slowed gastric emptying. The clinical relevance is unknown.
Consider the use of a parenteral antiplatelet agent in acute coronary syndrome patients requiring co-administration of morphine or other opioid agonists.

items.t: Severe renal insufficiency: use only on medical advice; paracetamol care advised (no numeric threshold or dose stated).

src.q: Co-codamol 8/500 Tablets should be used upon medical advice in patients with: Mild-to-moderate hepatocellular insufficiency
Care is advised in the administration of paracetamol to patients with severe renal or severe hepatic impairment.

src.q: Nonetheless careful consideration should be given before prescribing the products for pregnant patients.
Regular use during pregnancy may cause drug dependence in the foetus, leading to withdrawal symptoms in the neonate.

items.t: MHRA: opioids cross the placenta; neonates may develop neonatal abstinence syndrome.

src.q: Opioids readily cross the placenta, therefore if used during pregnancy neonates may become dependent and experience neonatal abstinence syndrome at birth.

items.t: Contraindicated during breastfeeding (codeine may cause respiratory depression in the infant).

src.q: Co-codamol 30/500 Tablets are contraindicated during breast-feeding (see section 4.3), as codeine may be secreted in breast milk and may cause respiratory depression in the infant.

items.t: SPS: codeine is contra-indicated in breastfeeding, so codeine combination products should be avoided.

src.q: Codeine is contra-indicated during breastfeeding and therefore combination products containing codeine should be avoided.

src.q: Codeine can produce typical opioid effects including constipation, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, light-headedness, confusion, drowsiness and urinary retention.

items.t: Opioid toxicity / respiratory depression (especially CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolisers): confusion, somnolence, shallow breathing, small pupils; may be life-threatening.

src.q: General symptoms of opioid toxicity include confusion, somnolence, shallow breathing, small pupils, nausea, vomiting, constipation and lack of appetite.

items.t: Addiction, tolerance and drug withdrawal syndrome; taper to stop.

src.q: Regular prolonged use of codeine is known to lead to addiction and tolerance.

Not known: agranulocytosis, thrombocytopenia

items.t: After prolonged use: blood count, liver function and renal function.

src.q: Monitoring after prolonged use should include blood count, liver function and renal function.

items.t: Review benefit-risk regularly; frequent contact to assess need to continue; monitor for signs of opioid use disorder.

src.q: The risk-benefit of continued use should be assessed regularly by the prescriber.

src.q: before starting treatment with opioids, agree with the patient a treatment strategy and plan for end of treatment

src.q: Taking a painkiller for headaches too often or for too long can make them worse.

Co-Trimoxazole Paediatric Suspension is indicated in children aged 12 years and under (≥6 weeks)

src.q: As an alternative to Standard Dosage for acute uncomplicated lower urinary tract infections, short-term therapy of 1 to 3 days duration has been shown to be effective.

items.t: PJP treatment (adults and children over 12): trimethoprim 20 mg/kg + sulfamethoxazole 100 mg/kg per day in two or more divided doses for 2 weeks.

src.q: A higher dosage is recommended, using 20 mg trimethoprim and 100 mg sulfamethoxazole per kg of body weight per day in two or more divided doses for two weeks.

items.t: PJP prevention (adults and children over 12), choose one: 160 mg/800 mg DAILY 7 days a week; OR 160 mg/800 mg three times a WEEK on alternate days; OR 320 mg/1600 mg per day in two divided doses three times a WEEK on alternate days. Total daily dose must not exceed 320 mg trimethoprim / 1600 mg sulfamethoxazole.

src.q: 160 mg trimethoprim/800 mg sulfamethoxazole daily 7 days per week. 160 mg trimethoprim/800 mg sulfamethoxazole three times per week on alternate days. 320 mg trimethoprim/1600 mg sulfamethoxazole per day in two divided doses three times per week on alternate days.
The total daily dose should not exceed 320 mg trimethoprim and 1600 mg sulfamethoxazole.

items.t: Nocardiosis (adults over 18): no consensus; 6 to 8 tablets (480 mg) daily for up to 3 months have been used. Toxoplasmosis: no consensus; PJP prevention doses may suit prophylaxis.

src.q: Adult doses of 6 to 8 tablets daily for up to 3 months have been used.
For prophylaxis, however, the dosages suggested for prevention of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonitis may be appropriate.

items.t: Elderly: standard dose unless otherwise specified; take particular care (more susceptible to serious adverse effects).

src.q: Unless otherwise specified standard dosage applies.
Particular care is always advisable when treating elderly patients

items.t: Must not be given in the first 6 weeks of life (listed in SmPC 4.3 of all four co-trimoxazole SmPCs). Separately, the breastfeeding paragraph of 4.6 says co-trimoxazole should be avoided in infants younger than 8 weeks (predisposition to hyperbilirubinaemia). It sits in the breastfeeding text, so this tool applies it to breastfeeding; the paediatric suspension is still licensed from 6 weeks.

src.q: Co-trimoxazole should not be given to infants during the first 6 weeks of life.
Co-Trimoxazole Paediatric Suspension is indicated in children aged 12 years and under (≥6 weeks)
Additionally, administration of Co-Trimoxazole should be avoided in infants younger than eight weeks in view of the predisposition of young infants to hyperbilirubinaemia.

items.t: Children 12 years and under (paediatric suspension): about trimethoprim 6 mg/kg + sulfamethoxazole 30 mg/kg per day in two equal doses. By age: 6-12 years 10 ml every 12 hours; 6 months-5 years 5 ml every 12 hours; 6 weeks-5 months 2.5 ml every 12 hours.

src.q: The standard dosage for children is equivalent to approximately 6 mg trimethoprim and 30 mg sulfamethoxazole per kg body weight per day, given in two equally divided doses.
6 to 12 years 10 ml every 12 hours 6 months to 5 years 5 ml every 12 hours 6 weeks to 5 months 2.5 ml every 12 hours

items.t: PJP treatment, children 12 and under: trimethoprim 20 mg/kg + sulfamethoxazole 100 mg/kg per day in two or more divided doses for 2 weeks.

src.q: Treatment - Children aged 12 years and under: A higher dosage is recommended, using 20 mg trimethoprim and 100 mg sulfamethoxazole per kg of body weight per day in two or more divided doses for two weeks.

items.t: PJP prevention, children 12 and under: about 6 mg/kg trimethoprim per day, as the age-banded volume every 12 hours either 7 days a WEEK or 3 days a WEEK (alternate or consecutive days), or as double the volume ONCE a day on 3 consecutive days a WEEK (e.g. 6-12 years: 10 ml every 12 hours, or 20 ml once a day). Total daily dose must not exceed 320 mg trimethoprim / 1600 mg sulfamethoxazole.

src.q: 6 to 12 years 10 ml every 12 hours, seven days per week
6 to 12 years 20 ml once a day, three times per week on consecutive days
The total daily dose should not exceed 320 mg trimethoprim and 1600 mg sulfamethoxazole.

items.t: Children over 12 to under 18 (adult suspension): 10 ml every 12 hours.

src.q: >12 to <18 years old 10 ml every 12 hours

items.t: No information on renal failure dosing in children aged 12 and under.

src.q: No information is available for children aged 12 years and under with renal failure.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to sulfonamides, trimethoprim, co-trimoxazole or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance(s) sulphonamides, trimethoprim, co-trimoxazole or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Severe liver impairment (Forte tablet and adult suspension SmPCs: contra-indicated; 480 mg tablet SmPC: should not be given; all in section 4.3).

src.q: Co-Trimoxazole should not be given to patients with severe impairment of liver function.
Contra-indicated in patients with severe impairment of liver function.

items.t: Severe renal insufficiency where repeated plasma concentration measurements cannot be done.

src.q: Contra-indicated in severe renal insufficiency where repeated measurements of the plasma concentration cannot be performed.

items.t: Infants in the first 6 weeks of life.

src.q: Co-trimoxazole should not be given to infants during the first 6 weeks of life.

items.t: History of drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia with trimethoprim and/or sulfonamides.

src.q: Co-Trimoxazole should not be given to patients with a history of drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia with use of trimethoprim and/or sulphonamides.

items.t: Acute porphyria.

src.q: Co-Trimoxazole should not be given to patients with acute porphyria.

items.t: First trimester of pregnancy.

src.q: First trimester of pregnancy (see section 4.6).

items.t: Fatal reactions (very rare): SJS, TEN, fulminant hepatic necrosis, agranulocytosis, aplastic anaemia, other blood dyscrasias, respiratory hypersensitivity.

src.q: Fatalities, although very rare, have occurred due to severe reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, fulminant hepatic necrosis, agranulocytosis, aplastic anaemia, other blood dyscrasias and hypersensitivity of the respiratory tract.

items.t: SJS/TEN/DRESS: highest risk in the first weeks; stop if signs appear and never restart. AGEP at start of treatment: stop and do not re-administer.

src.q: The highest risk for occurrence of SJS or TEN is within the first weeks of treatment.
If the patient has developed SJS, TEN and DRESS with the use of Co-Trimoxazole, the treatment must not be re-started in this patient at any time.

items.t: G6PD deficiency: haemolysis may occur.

src.q: In glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G-6-PD) deficient patients haemolysis may occur.

items.t: Folate: monthly blood counts advisable for long courses, folate-deficient patients or the elderly. Folinic acid may be considered but can reduce antimicrobial efficacy.

src.q: Regular monthly blood counts are advisable when Co-Trimoxazole is given for long periods, or to folate deficient patients or to the elderly
Supplementation with folinic acid may be considered during treatment but this should be initiated with caution due to possible interference with antimicrobial efficacy

items.t: Serious haematological disorders: do not give except under careful supervision.

src.q: Except under careful supervision Co-Trimoxazole should not be given to patients with serious haematological disorders

items.t: Hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia: close potassium monitoring in at-risk patients. Metabolic acidosis reported.

src.q: Close monitoring of serum potassium is warranted in patients at risk of hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia.
Co-Trimoxazole has been associated with metabolic acidosis

items.t: Severe atopy or bronchial asthma: give with caution.

src.q: Co-Trimoxazole should be given with caution to patients with severe atopy or bronchial asthma.

items.t: Porphyria (known or suspected risk): avoid.

src.q: The administration of Co-Trimoxazole to patients known or suspected to be at risk of porphyria should be avoided.

items.t: Keep adequate urine output (crystalluria risk, higher in malnutrition).

src.q: An adequate urinary output should be maintained at all times.

items.t: Respiratory toxicity (possible ARDS) and haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH): stop if these develop.

src.q: In such circumstances, co-trimoxazole should be discontinued and appropriate treatment given.
If diagnosis of HLH is established, co-trimoxazole treatment should be discontinued.

items.t: Methotrexate: co-trimoxazole may raise free methotrexate levels; the co-trimoxazole SmPC says consider a folate supplement. SPS: avoid the combination (risk of severe bone marrow suppression, possibly delayed). One methotrexate tablet SmPC lists this combination under 4.3 Contraindications (should not be used concomitantly).

src.q: Methotrexate: co-trimoxazole may increase the free plasma levels of methotrexate.
Avoid prescribing co-trimoxazole or trimethoprim with methotrexate, due to the risk of severe bone marrow suppression.
Methotrexate tablets should not be used concomitantly with drugs with antifolate properties (e.g. co-trimoxazole)

items.t: Warfarin: anticoagulant effect potentiated; careful control of anticoagulation advised.

src.q: Careful control of the anticoagulant therapy during treatment with Co-Trimoxazole is advisable.

items.t: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics (e.g. spironolactone): caution, clinically relevant hyperkalaemia possible.

src.q: Hyperkalaemia: caution should be exercised in patients taking any other drugs that can cause hyperkalaemia, for example ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and potassium-sparing diuretics such as spironolactone.

items.t: Thiazide diuretics in elderly: increased thrombocytopenia risk.

src.q: Diuretics (thiazides): in elderly patients concurrently receiving diuretics, mainly thiazides, there appears to be an increased risk of thrombocytopenia with or without purpura.

items.t: Others not in master list: phenytoin (monitor levels), digoxin (raised levels in elderly), ciclosporin (renal deterioration), zidovudine, pyrimethamine, repaglinide (hypoglycaemia), sulfonylureas, lamivudine, azathioprine, oral contraceptives (antibiotic advice).

src.q: Close monitoring of the patient's condition and serum phenytoin levels are advisable.
Repaglinide: trimethoprim may increase the exposure of repaglinide which may result in hypoglycaemia.

items.t: Lab tests: trimethoprim may cause ~10% overestimation of serum creatinine (alkaline picrate method) and interferes with some methotrexate assays.

src.q: This may result in overestimation of serum/plasma creatinine of the order of 10%.

items.t: Adults and children over 12, by creatinine clearance (CrCl): over 30 ml/min standard dose; 15 to 30 ml/min half dose (480 mg tablets: 1 tablet every 12 hours; Forte 960 mg tablets: 1 tablet per DAY; adult suspension: 5 ml every 12 hours); under 15 ml/min not recommended. No information for children 12 and under with renal failure.

src.q: Creatinine Clearance (ml/min) Recommended Dosage >30 2 tablets every 12 hours 15 to 30 1 tablet every 12 hours <15 Not recommended
> 30 1 tablet every 12 hours 15 to 30 1 tablet per day <15 Not recommended
Creatinine Clearance (ml/min) Recommended Dosage >30 10 ml every 12 hours 15 to 30 5 ml every 12 hours <15 Not recommended
No information is available for children aged 12 years and under with renal failure.

items.t: Measure plasma sulfamethoxazole every 2 to 3 days (12 hours post-dose); interrupt if total sulfamethoxazole exceeds 150 microgram/ml until below 120 microgram/ml.

src.q: If the concentration of total sulfamethoxazole exceeds 150 microgram/ml then treatment should be interrupted until the value falls below 120 microgram/ml.

items.t: Contraindicated in severe renal insufficiency where repeated plasma measurements cannot be done.

src.q: Contra-indicated in severe renal insufficiency where repeated measurements of the plasma concentration cannot be performed.

items.t: Severe liver impairment: should not be given. No dosing data for hepatic impairment.

src.q: Co-Trimoxazole should not be given to patients with severe impairment of liver function.
Impaired hepatic function: No data are available relating to dosage in patients with impaired hepatic function.

items.t: First trimester: contraindicated (trimethoprim; miscarriage and malformations including neural tube defects, oral clefts, heart defects).

src.q: Trimethoprim is contraindicated during the first trimester of pregnancy (see section 4.3).

items.t: Second and third trimesters: avoid unless clinically necessary. Consider folate supplementation if used.

src.q: In the second and third trimesters, use should be avoided, unless clinically necessary.
Folate supplementation should be considered if Co-Trimoxazole is used in pregnancy.

items.t: Near delivery: risk of neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia and theoretical kernicterus. Avoid in late pregnancy where mother or infant has or is at particular risk of hyperbilirubinaemia.

src.q: there may be a risk of precipitating or exacerbating neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia, with an associated theoretical risk of kernicterus, when Co-Trimoxazole is administered to the mother near the time of delivery.
Administration of Co-Trimoxazole should be avoided in late pregnancy and in lactating mothers where the mother or infant has, or is at particular risk of developing, hyperbilirubinaemia.

items.t: Both components pass into breast milk. Avoid where mother or infant has, or is at particular risk of, hyperbilirubinaemia. SmPC also says avoid in infants younger than 8 weeks (young infants prone to hyperbilirubinaemia).

src.q: The components of Co-Trimoxazole (trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole) are excreted in breast milk.
administration of Co-Trimoxazole should be avoided in infants younger than eight weeks in view of the predisposition of young infants to hyperbilirubinaemia.

reproductive.note: No fertility or contraception requirement in the co-trimoxazole SmPCs (4.5 only notes antibiotic/oral contraceptive advice). No BUMPS co-trimoxazole leaflet found (URL variants returned 404).

items.t: Very common: hyperkalaemia. Common: headache, nausea, diarrhoea, rash, fungal overgrowth.

src.q: Very common Hyperkalaemia.
Common Nausea, diarrhoea.
Common Overgrowth fungal.

items.t: SJS/TEN/DRESS/AGEP: stop immediately; never restart after SJS/TEN/DRESS.

src.q: Co-Trimoxazole treatment should be discontinued (see section 4.8) and an alternative treatment considered (as appropriate).

items.t: Blood dyscrasias (agranulocytosis, aplastic anaemia, megaloblastic anaemia, thrombocytopenia), haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

src.q: Very rare Leukopenia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, agranulocytosis, anaemia megaloblastic, aplastic anaemia

items.t: Respiratory hypersensitivity (cough, dyspnoea, lung infiltrates) can be fatal; hepatic necrosis; aseptic meningitis; circulatory shock (mainly immunocompromised).

src.q: Cough, dyspnoea and lung infiltration may be early indicators of respiratory hypersensitivity which, while very rare, has been fatal
Jaundice cholestatic and hepatic necrosis may be fatal.

items.t: High PJP doses: severe hypersensitivity reactions may require stopping; rhabdomyolysis reported in HIV patients.

src.q: At the high dosages used for PJP management severe hypersensitivity reactions have been reported, necessitating cessation of therapy.

items.t: Long courses, folate-deficient or elderly patients: monthly blood counts.

src.q: Regular monthly blood counts are advisable when Co-Trimoxazole is given for long periods, or to folate deficient patients or to the elderly

items.t: Potassium in patients at risk of hyperkalaemia/hyponatraemia.

src.q: Close monitoring of serum potassium is warranted in patients at risk of hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia.

items.t: Renal impairment: plasma sulfamethoxazole every 2-3 days; interrupt above 150 microgram/ml.

src.q: Measurements of plasma concentration of sulfamethoxazole at intervals of 2 to 3 days are recommended in samples obtained 12 hours after administration of Co-Trimoxazole.

items.t: Stop for skin reactions suggesting SJS/TEN/DRESS/AGEP, HLH, or pulmonary signs suggesting ARDS.

src.q: If symptoms or signs of SJS, TEN (e.g. progressive skin rash often with blisters or mucosal lesions) or DRESS (e.g. fever, eosinophilia) are present

items.t: Oral. May be better taken with some food or drink to reduce GI upset.

src.q: It may be preferable to take Co-Trimoxazole with some food or drink to minimise the possibility of gastrointestinal disturbances.

items.t: Drink enough fluid to keep a good urine output.

src.q: An adequate urinary output should be maintained at all times.

items.t: Report any rash, blisters, mouth sores or fever at once, especially in the first weeks.

src.q: Patients should be advised of the signs and symptoms and monitored closely for skin reactions.

items.t: Women using oral contraceptives: SmPC advises temporarily adding a barrier method while on antibiotics.

src.q: Women on treatment with antibiotics should temporarily use a barrier method in addition to the oral contraceptive, or choose another method of contraception.

items.t: Acute moderate pain not relieved by paracetamol or ibuprofen alone (patients over 12 years); dry or painful cough; diarrhoea.

src.q: Codeine is indicated in patients older than 12 years of age for the treatment of acute moderate pain which is not considered to be relieved by other analgesics such as paracetamol or ibuprofen (alone).
Dry or painful cough Diarrhoea

items.t: MHRA: in children, only for acute moderate pain in those older than 12 years, and only if paracetamol or ibuprofen alone do not work.

src.q: Codeine should only be used to relieve acute moderate pain in children older than 12 years and only if it cannot be relieved by other painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen

items.t: Pain (adults): lowest effective dose for the shortest time, up to 4 times a day at intervals of not less than 6 hours; maximum 240 mg codeine per day; limit to 3 days and review if no effective relief. The SmPCs accessed give no separate adult mg-per-dose figure for pain.

src.q: Adults Codeine should be used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest period of time. The dose may be taken, up to 4 times a day at intervals of not less than 6 hours. Maximum daily dose of codeine should not exceed 240mg.
The duration of treatment should be limited to 3 days

items.t: Dry or painful cough (adults): 15-30 mg 3-4 times daily.

src.q: For dry or painful cough Adults: 15-30mg 3-4 times daily.

items.t: Diarrhoea (adults): 30 mg three to four times daily (range 15-60 mg).

src.q: Diarrhoea Adults: 30mg three to four times daily (range 15-60mg)

items.t: Elderly: reduce the dose.

src.q: Elderly Dosage should be reduced in elderly patients.

items.t: Agree a treatment plan and end-of-treatment plan before starting; taper gradually when stopping.

src.q: When a patient no longer requires therapy with codeine, it may be advisable to taper the dose gradually to prevent symptoms of withdrawal.

items.t: Under 12 years: should not be used (risk of opioid toxicity).

src.q: Codeine should not be used in children below the age of 12 years because of the risk of opioid toxicity

items.t: 12-18 years, pain: 30-60 mg every 6 hours when necessary (0.5-1 mg/kg), maximum 240 mg daily; limit to 3 days (MHRA).

src.q: The recommended codeine dose for children 12 years and older should be 30-60mg every 6 hours when necessary up to a maximum dose of codeine of 240 mg daily. The dose is based on the body weight (0.5-1mg/kg).
Duration of treatment should be limited to 3 days

items.t: Cough: contraindicated under 12 years; not recommended at 12-18 years with compromised respiratory function. Diarrhoea: not recommended in children.

src.q: Codeine is contraindicated in children below the age of 12 years for the symptomatic treatment of cough
Codeine is not recommended for use in children aged 12 years to 18 years with compromised respiratory function for the symptomatic treatment of cough

items.t: Contraindicated in all under-18s having tonsillectomy and/or adenoidectomy for obstructive sleep apnoea. Not recommended where breathing may be compromised.

src.q: In all paediatric patients (0-18 years of age) who undergo tonsillectomy and/or adenoidectomy for obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome
Codeine is not recommended for use in children in whom respiratory function might be compromised

items.t: Acute respiratory depression; hypersensitivity to codeine or other opioid analgesics; obstructive airways disease; liver disease; severe hepatic dysfunction; acute alcoholism.

src.q: Acute respiratory depression, hypersensitivity to codeine or other opioid analgesics or to any of the excipients, obstructive airways disease, liver disease, severe hepatic dysfunction, acute alcoholism.

items.t: Where inhibition of peristalsis should be avoided: risk of paralytic ileus, abdominal distension, acute ulcerative colitis, antibiotic-associated colitis, diarrhoea caused by poisoning.

src.q: Codeine is also contraindicated in conditions where inhibition of peristalsis is to be avoided, where there is a risk of paralytic ileus, where abdominal distension develops

items.t: Breastfeeding; known CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolisers; under-18s after tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy for obstructive sleep apnoea.

src.q: In women during breastfeeding (see section 4.6) In patients for whom it is known they are CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolisers

items.t: Also in section 4.3: use should be avoided in raised intracranial pressure or head injury (treated here as a contraindication); should not be given to comatose patients.

src.q: Use should be avoided in patients with raised intracranial pressure or head injury
Codeine should not be given to comatose patients.

items.t: Caution or reduced dose in asthma and decreased respiratory reserve; avoid during an acute asthma attack.

src.q: Use with caution or in reduced doses in asthma and decreased respiratory reserve, avoid use during an acute asthma attack

items.t: Caution or reduced dose: elderly or debilitated, hypotension, hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy, adrenocortical insufficiency, inflammatory or obstructive bowel disorders, urethral stricture, shock, convulsive disorders, myasthenia gravis.

src.q: in patients with hypotension, hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy, adrenocortical insufficiency, inflammatory or obstructive bowel disorders, urethral stricture, shock, convulsive disorders, myasthenia gravis

items.t: Tolerance, dependence and opioid use disorder can develop with repeated use; use with caution with a history of drug abuse; discontinue gradually.

src.q: Repeated use of codeine can lead to OUD.
Use with caution in those with a history of drug abuse.

items.t: CYP2D6 ultra-rapid or extensive metabolisers: increased risk of opioid toxicity even at usual doses.

src.q: if the patient is an extensive or ultra-rapid metaboliser there is an increased risk of developing side effects of opioid toxicity even at commonly prescribed doses

items.t: Caution in pancreatitis and biliary tract disease (sphincter of Oddi dysfunction). Another UK SmPC: opioid analgesics should be avoided in biliary tract disorders, or used with an antispasmodic.

src.q: codeine has to be administered with caution in patients with pancreatitis and diseases of the biliary tract
Opioid analgesics should be avoided in patients with biliary tract disorders or used in conjunction with an antispasmodic.

items.t: MAOIs: avoid codeine during and for 2 weeks after MAOI treatment.

src.q: the use of codeine should be avoided while the patient is taking MAOIs and for 2 weeks after MAOI discontinuation

items.t: Contains lactose (galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take).

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, the Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine as it contains lactose.

items.t: Anxiolytics and hypnotics: enhanced sedative effect. MHRA: co-prescribe benzodiazepines and opioids only if no alternative, at lowest doses for shortest time, with close monitoring.

src.q: Anxiolytics and hypnotics: enhanced sedative effect.
if a decision is made to co-prescribe, use the lowest doses possible for the shortest duration of time and carefully monitor patients for signs of respiratory depression

items.t: Alcohol, anaesthetics, sedating antihistamines, antipsychotics, sodium oxybate: increased CNS/respiratory depression and hypotension.

src.q: Alcohol: the hypotensive, sedative and respiratory depressive effects of alcohol may be enhanced.
Antipsychotics: enhanced sedative and hypotensive effect.

items.t: Gabapentin or pregabalin: respiratory depression, hypotension, profound sedation, coma or death.

src.q: The concomitant use of codeine with gabapentinoids (gabapentin and pregabalin) may result in respiratory depression, hypotension, profound sedation, coma or death

items.t: Sertraline (sertraline SmPC): serotonin syndrome / NMS risk is increased with opioids; caution and monitor for symptoms.

src.q: and with opioids. Patients should be monitored for the emergence of signs and symptoms of SS or NMS syndrome
Caution is also advised with opioids

items.t: Clopidogrel (clopidogrel SmPC): opioid agonists may delay and reduce clopidogrel absorption (clinical relevance unknown); in acute coronary syndrome consider a parenteral antiplatelet agent.

src.q: co-administration of opioid agonists has the potential to delay and reduce the absorption of clopidogrel presumably because of slowed gastric emptying. The clinical relevance is unknown.
Consider the use of a parenteral antiplatelet agent in acute coronary syndrome patients requiring co-administration of morphine or other opioid agonists.

items.t: Renal impairment: avoid or reduce the dose (no numeric threshold stated).

src.q: It should be avoided or the dose reduced in patients with renal or hepatic impairment

items.t: Liver disease and severe hepatic dysfunction are listed as contraindications; section 4.4 also says avoid or reduce the dose in hepatic impairment.

src.q: obstructive airways disease, liver disease, severe hepatic dysfunction, acute alcoholism
It should be avoided or the dose reduced in patients with renal or hepatic impairment

items.t: SmPC: caution, especially in the first trimester (possible association with respiratory and cardiac malformations). Regular use may cause neonatal withdrawal; use in labour may depress neonatal breathing.

src.q: As with all medications caution should be exercised during pregnancy, especially in the first trimester. A possible association with respiratory and cardiac malformations has been reported following first trimester exposure to codeine.
Administration during labour may depress respiration in the neonate

items.t: BUMPS: take in pregnancy only if recommended by a doctor; most studies do not show harm; use near delivery can cause neonatal withdrawal and breathing problems.

src.q: Codeine should only be taken during pregnancy if recommended by your doctor.
Codeine used around the time of delivery can affect your baby after birth.

items.t: SPS: codeine may be used where paracetamol has not been effective; most data do not suggest increased malformation risk.

src.q: The weak opioid codeine may be used where paracetamol has not been effective.

items.t: Contraindicated in breastfeeding (SmPC 4.3). Section 4.6 wording: not recommended; if opioid toxicity develops in mother or infant, stop all codeine and use non-opioid analgesics; consider naloxone in severe cases.

src.q: In women during breastfeeding (see section 4.6)
Administration to nursing women is not recommended as codeine may be secreted in breast milk and may cause respiratory depression in the infant.

items.t: MHRA: codeine should not be used by breastfeeding mothers.

src.q: Codeine should not be used by breastfeeding mothers because it can pass to the baby through breast milk and potentially cause harm

items.t: SPS: avoid. If a few doses are taken accidentally, stop codeine and monitor the infant (sedation, slow breathing/apnoea, poor feeding); get medical advice for significant effects.

src.q: Codeine should not be used during breastfeeding.
the mother should be advised to stop taking codeine and the infant monitored for side effects such as sedation, slowed breathing rate/apnoea

items.t: Sexual dysfunction, erectile dysfunction and decreased libido are listed adverse effects (frequency not stated).

src.q: Reproductive system and breast disorders: sexual dysfunction, erectile dysfunction, decreased potency. Decreased libido.

items.t: Most common: drowsiness, nausea, vomiting and confusion (tolerance develops with long-term use). Also constipation, dry mouth, dizziness, headache (frequency not tabulated).

src.q: Tolerance and some of the most common side effects - drowsiness, nausea, and vomiting, and confusion - generally develops with long term use.
Gastrointestinal disorders: nausea, vomiting, constipation, dry mouth, stomach cramps, pancreatitis.

items.t: Respiratory depression (large doses) and opioid toxicity, especially in CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolisers; may be life-threatening.

src.q: Large doses produce respiratory depression.
In severe cases this may include symptoms of circulatory and respiratory depression, which may be life-threatening and very rarely fatal.

items.t: Addiction and drug withdrawal syndrome; taper to stop.

src.q: Regular prolonged use of codeine is known to lead to addiction and tolerance.

items.t: Convulsions (especially in infants and children), pancreatitis, hypersensitivity syndrome.

src.q: convulsions (especially in infants and children)

items.t: Review benefit-risk regularly; monitor for signs of drug-seeking behaviour (e.g. early repeat requests).

src.q: The risk-benefit of continued use should be assessed regularly by the prescriber.
Patients will require monitoring for signs of drug-seeking behaviour (e.g. too early requests for refills).

items.t: Pain: if no effective relief within 3 days, seek medical review.

src.q: The duration of treatment should be limited to 3 days and if no effective pain relief is achieved the patients/carers should be advised to seek the views of a physician.

items.t: Oral.

src.q: 4.2 Posology and method of administration Oral route

items.t: Can cause drowsiness and blurred or double vision; do not drive or use machines if affected. Alcohol effects are enhanced.

src.q: Codeine produces sedation and may also cause changes in vision, including blurred or double vision. If affected, patients should not drive or operate machinery.

items.t: MHRA: explain risk of dependence and addiction even at therapeutic doses; do not stop suddenly after long-term use.

src.q: discuss with patients that prolonged use of opioids may lead to drug dependence and addiction, even at therapeutic doses

items.t: Children 12-18: parents should know the signs of morphine toxicity and stop codeine and seek help at once if they occur.

src.q: Symptoms of codeine toxicity include: reduced levels of consciousness; lack of appetite; somnolence; constipation; respiratory depression; 'pin-point' pupils; or nausea and vomiting

items.t: Prevention and treatment of vitamin D deficiency; adjunct to specific osteoporosis therapy in patients with, or at risk of, vitamin D deficiency.

src.q: The prevention and treatment of vitamin D deficiency.
As an adjunct to specific therapy for osteoporosis in patients with vitamin D deficiency or at risk of vitamin D insufficiency.

items.t: 50,000 IU capsules: treatment of vitamin D deficiency in adults only.

src.q: Treatment of Vitamin D deficiency. Target populations: Adults

items.t: 50,000 IU capsules: patients with sarcoidosis or pseudohypoparathyroidism, or taking thiazide diuretics or cardiac glycosides, must be referred to their doctor and not supplied it as a pharmacy medicine.

src.q: Patients with sarcoidosis, Pseudohypoparathyroidism and patients taking thiazide diuretics or cardiac glycosides must be referred to their doctor and not supplied this as a Pharmacy medicine.

items.tag: Treatment of deficiency (adults, 2740 IU/ml drops SmPC)
items.t: Adults and elderly: 800-4,000 IU daily for up to 12 weeks, then maintenance 800-1,600 IU daily.

src.q: Treatment vitamin D deficiency should be for up to 12 weeks dependent upon the severity of the disease
Adults and the elderly Treatment of vitamin D deficiency 12  60 drops (800  4,000 IU) daily.
Prevention of vitamin D deficiency 12  24 drops (800  1,600 IU) daily.

items.tag: Treatment of deficiency (adults, 3000 IU/ml solution SmPC)
items.t: One UK oral solution SmPC: 4000 IU daily for 10 weeks (280,000 IU in total), then maintenance 800-2000 IU daily (occasionally up to 4000 IU daily).

src.q: Treatment dose: 4000 IU daily (1.33ml) for 10 weeks (280,000 IU in total).
Maintenance dose: 800-2000 IU daily (0.27ml-0.67ml) (occasionally up to 4000 IU daily may be required).

items.t: Prevention or maintenance: 800-1,600 IU daily. Adjunct to osteoporosis therapy: 800 IU daily.

src.q: As an adjunct to specific therapy for osteoporosis 12 drops (800 IU) daily.

items.tag: Maximum daily dose (10 000 I.U./ml drops SmPC)
items.t: One UK drops SmPC: adult daily dose should not exceed 4 000 I.U.

src.q: The daily dose should not exceed 4 000 I.U. (20 drops per day).

items.t: Adults: 50,000 IU (1 capsule) once a week for 6-8 weeks, then maintenance (1400-2000 IU/day may be needed, e.g. 1 capsule per month). Re-check 25(OH)D about 3-4 months after starting maintenance.

src.q: 50,000 IU/week (1 capsule) for 6-8 weeks, followed by maintenance therapy (1400-2000 IU/day may be required, such as 1 capsule per month;
follow up 25(OH)D measurements should be made approximately three to four months after initiating maintenance therapy

items.t: Licensed from birth. Treatment of deficiency: 0-2 years 400-1,000 IU/day; 2-11 years 400-2,000 IU/day; 12-18 years 400-4,000 IU/day. Prevention/maintenance: 0-2 years 200-1,000 IU/day; 2-11 years 400-1,000 IU/day; 12-18 years 400-1,600 IU/day.

src.q: Infants aged 0 up to 2 years Treatment of vitamin D deficiency

items.tag: 10 000 I.U./ml drops SmPC: maximum daily doses
items.t: Treatment in children should not exceed 1 000 I.U./day under 1 year, 2 000 I.U./day at 1-10 years and 4 000 I.U./day over 11 years.

src.q: The daily dose should not exceed 1 000 I.U. per day for infants <1 year, 2 000 I.U. per day for children 1-10 years and 4 000 I.U. per day for adolescents >11 years.

items.tag: Do not mix into a bottle
items.t: Drops must not be mixed into a bottle of milk or a container of soft food, in case the child does not take the whole dose.

src.q: must not be mixed into a bottle of milk or container of soft foods in case the child does not consume the whole portion

items.t: One UK oral solution is licensed only over 12 years: no data under 12 years.

src.q: Children < 12 years No data are available.

items.t: Not recommended in children (lack of clinical data).

src.q: Paediatric - Due to lack of clinical data, Colecalciferol Capsule is not recommended.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to vitamin D or to any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to vitamin D or any of the excipients in the product

items.t: Hypercalcaemia and/or hypercalciuria (diseases or conditions causing them).

src.q: Diseases or conditions resulting in hypercalcaemia and/or hypercalciuria
Hypercalcaemia and/or hypercalciuria.

items.t: Hypervitaminosis D.

src.q: Hypervitaminosis D

items.t: Nephrolithiasis (kidney stones); nephrocalcinosis (oral solution and 50,000 IU capsule SmPCs). One drops SmPC limits the kidney-stone contraindication to patients with current chronic hypercalcaemia.

src.q: Nephrolithiasis
Nephrolithiasis Nephrocalcinosis
Nephrolithiasis and/or nephrocalcinosis
Kidney stones (nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis) in patients with current chronic hypercalcaemia

items.t: Severe renal impairment (one SmPC defines this as eGFR <30 ml/min/1.73m2).

src.q: Severe renal impairment
typically defined as a patient with eGFR of <30 ml/min/1.73m2

items.t: 50,000 IU capsules: also pseudohypoparathyroidism.

src.q: Pseudohypoparathyroidism as the vitamin D requirement may be reduced due to phases of normal vitamin D sensitivity, involving the risk of prolonged overdose.

items.t: Renal impairment: use with caution and monitor the effect on calcium and phosphate; consider the risk of soft tissue calcification.

src.q: Vitamin D should be used with caution in patients with impairment of renal function and the effect on calcium and phosphate levels should be monitored.

items.t: Sarcoidosis: prescribe with caution (increased conversion to the active form); monitor serum and urine calcium.

src.q: should be prescribed with caution to patients suffering from sarcoidosis because of the risk of increased metabolism of vitamin D to its active form.
These patients should be monitored with regard to the calcium content in serum and urine.

items.t: Cardiovascular disease treated with cardiac glycosides (digitalis): caution.

src.q: Caution is required in patients receiving treatment for cardiovascular disease

items.t: Allow for vitamin D from other sources. Extra calcium only under close medical supervision. Medical supervision is needed to prevent hypercalcaemia.

src.q: Allowances should be made for vitamin D supplements from other sources.
Calcium supplements should be given under close medical supervision.
Medical supervision is required whilst on treatment to prevent hypercalcaemia.

items.t: One oral solution SmPC: caution in immobilised patients with osteoporosis and in others at increased risk of hypercalcaemia (e.g. malignancy). Patients with primary hyperparathyroidism and vitamin deficiency should have serum calcium measured.

src.q: Colecalciferol should be used with caution in immobilised patients with osteoporosis due to increased risk of hypercalcaemia.
Patients with primary hyperparathyroidism and vitamin deficiency should have their serum calcium measured.

items.t: One oral solution SmPC: raised PTH or rickets - give calcium with vitamin D, because correcting vitamin D can cause hypocalcaemia ('hungry bone' syndrome).

src.q: For patients with elevated levels of parathyroid hormone (PTH) or clinical evidence of rickets, calcium should be supplemented along with vitamin D.

items.t: One oral solution SmPC contains almond oil: not suitable for someone with a nut allergy.

src.q: Almond oil (nut oil): Not suitable for someone with nut allergy.

items.t: 50,000 IU capsules: high-dose vitamin D3 (500,000 IU single annual bolus) was linked to more fractures in elderly people, mostly in the first 3 months.

src.q: Oral administration of high-dose Vitamin D3 (500,000 IU by single annual bolus) was reported to result in an increased risk of fractures in elderly subjects

items.t: Thiazides reduce urinary calcium excretion: monitor serum calcium regularly (risk of hypercalcaemia).

src.q: Due to the increased risk of hypercalcaemia, serum calcium should be regularly monitored during concomitant use of thiazide diuretics.
In cases of treatment with thiazide diuretics, which decrease urinary elimination of calcium, monitoring of serum calcium concentration is recommended.

items.t: Vitamin D may increase the risk of digitalis toxicity (arrhythmia). Strict medical supervision, with serum calcium and ECG monitoring if needed.

src.q: the administration of Vitamin D3 may increase the risk of digitalis toxicity (arrhythmia).
Strict medical supervision is needed, together with serum calcium concentration and electrocardiographic monitoring if necessary.

items.t: Glucocorticoids can decrease the effect of vitamin D; one SmPC says the colecalciferol dose may need to be increased.

src.q: Concomitant use of glucocorticoids can decrease the effect of vitamin D.
During concomitant use, it may be necessary to increase the dose of colecalciferol.

items.t: Anticonvulsants (such as phenytoin), barbiturates and possibly other enzyme-inducing drugs may reduce the effect of vitamin D.

src.q: Concomitant use of anticonvulsants (such as phenytoin) or barbiturates (and possibly other drugs that induce hepatic enzymes) may reduce the effect of vitamin D3 by metabolic inactivation.

items.t: Ion exchange resins (e.g. colestyramine), orlistat and paraffin oil may reduce vitamin D absorption.

src.q: Simultaneous treatment with ion exchange resin such as cholestyramine, colestipol hydrochloride, orlistat or laxative such as paraffin oil, may reduce the gastrointestinal absorption of vitamin D3.

items.t: Actinomycin and imidazole antifungals interfere with vitamin D activation in the kidney.

src.q: The cytotoxic agent actinomycin and imidazole antifungal agents interfere with vitamin D activity

items.t: Contraindicated in severe renal impairment. One UK SmPC defines severe as eGFR <30 ml/min/1.73m2. Colecalciferol is not metabolised normally in severe renal insufficiency: other forms of vitamin D should be used.

src.q: Colecalciferol should not be used in patients with severe renal impairment (typically defined as a patient with eGFR of <30 ml/min/1.73m2
In patients with severe renal insufficiency, vitamin D in the form of colecalciferol is not metabolised normally and other forms of vitamin D should be used

items.t: Mild or moderate renal impairment: no specific dose adjustment, but use with caution and monitor calcium and phosphate.

src.q: Patients with mild or moderate renal impairment: no specific adjustment is required
Patients with mild to moderate impairment of renal function should be supervised carefully and the effect on calcium and phosphate levels should be monitored.

items.t: 50,000 IU capsules: should not be used together with calcium in severe renal impairment.

src.q: Colecalciferol Capsule should not be used in combination with calcium in patients with severe renal impairment.

items.t: No dose adjustment required in hepatic impairment.

src.q: Dose in hepatic impairment: No dose adjustment is required.
No posology adjustment is required in patients with hepatic impairment

items.t: Recommended intake in pregnancy is 400 IU daily; deficient women may need more. The UK drops SmPCs differ on the upper treatment dose: one says up to 2 000 I.U./day, another gives 400-4,000 IU daily for treatment in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Avoid overdose: prolonged hypercalcaemia can harm the child.

src.q: The recommended daily intake for pregnant women is 400 IU, however, in women who are considered to be vitamin D deficient a higher dose may be required.
(up to 2 000 I.U. /day - 10 drops)
During pregnancy and breast-feeding Treatment of vitamin D deficiency 6  60 drops (400  4,000 IU) daily.

Overdoses of vitamin D must be avoided during pregnancy, as prolonged hypercalcaemia may lead to retardation of physical and mental development, supravalvular aortic stenosis and retinopathy in the child.

items.t: High-strength capsule not recommended in pregnancy: use a low-strength product.

src.q: In pregnancy and lactation the high strength formulation is not recommended and a low strength formulation should be used.

items.t: SPS: to treat deficiency in pregnancy consider 1000-2000 units daily (up to 4000 units daily in some severe symptomatic cases). Do not use vitamin D injections. Check adjusted calcium 1 month after starting.

src.q: Consider a daily dose between 1000 units to 2000 units to manage vitamin D deficiency during pregnancy.
It may be appropriate to consider a daily dose of up to 4000 units in some cases of severe vitamin D deficiency that is symptomatic.
Do not prescribe vitamin D injections in pregnancy.
Check adjusted plasma calcium levels 1 month after starting vitamin D in case primary hyperparathyroidism has been unmasked.

items.t: BUMPS: vitamin D is safe in pregnancy; NHS advice is a daily supplement for all pregnant women from September to March.

src.q: Vitamin D is safe during pregnancy and is needed for your health and your baby's development.

items.t: SPS: can be used. Maintenance doses up to 4000 units daily need no infant monitoring. Loading doses up to 300,000 units over 6-10 weeks can be used, but the infant must be monitored.

src.q: Vitamin D loading doses of up to 300,000 units given over 6-10 weeks can be used during breastfeeding for rapid treatment. Infant monitoring is required.
Long term maintenance doses up to 4000 units daily can also be used during breastfeeding but do not require any infant monitoring.

items.t: Vitamin D passes into breast milk. When giving extra vitamin D to a breastfed infant, consider the mother's dose.

src.q: when prescribing additional vitamin D to a breast-fed child the practitioner should consider the dose of any additional vitamin D given to the mother.

items.t: The 50,000 IU capsule SmPC says the high strength is not recommended during lactation (use a low strength), although vitamin D3 can be prescribed while breastfeeding if necessary. This is stricter than SPS.

src.q: In pregnancy and lactation the high strength formulation is not recommended and a low strength formulation should be used.
Vitamin D3 can be prescribed while the patient is breast-feeding if necessary.

items.t: No data on fertility; normal vitamin D levels are not expected to affect fertility.

src.q: However, normal endogenous levels of vitamin D are not expected to have any adverse effects on fertility.

items.t: No common effects listed. Uncommon: hypercalcaemia, hypercalciuria. Rare: pruritus, rash, urticaria.

src.q: Uncommon: Hypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria.
Rare: Pruritus, rash and urticaria.

items.t: Overdose causes hypercalcaemia (nausea, vomiting, polyuria, anorexia, weakness, thirst, constipation); chronic overdose can cause vascular and organ calcification. Stop all vitamin D and rehydrate.

src.q: The most serious consequence of acute or chronic overdose is hypercalcaemia due to vitamin D toxicity.
Treatment should consist of stopping all intake of vitamin D and rehydration.

items.t: 50,000 IU capsules: hypersensitivity reactions such as angio-oedema or laryngeal oedema (frequency not known).

src.q: Hypersensitivity reactions such as angio-oedema or laryngeal oedema.

items.t: Long-term daily doses above 1,000 IU: monitor serum calcium.

src.q: During long-term treatment with a daily dose exceeding 1,000 IU vitamin D the serum calcium values must be monitored.

items.t: One oral solution SmPC: long-term treatment - follow serum and urine calcium and serum creatinine; repeat 25(OH)D about 3-4 months after starting treatment for deficiency.

src.q: During long-term treatment, serum and urinary calcium levels should be followed and renal function should be monitored through measurements of serum creatinine.
Patients being treated specifically for vitamin D deficiency require a repeat 25(OH)D measurement approximately three to four months after initiating therapy as necessary.

items.t: Stop when serum calcium exceeds 2.65 mmol/l (10.6 mg/dl) or urine calcium exceeds 300 mg/24 hours in adults (4-6 mg/kg/day in children). One SmPC: reduce or stop if hypercalcaemia or signs of impaired renal function.

src.q: Discontinue Colecalciferol Capsule when calcaemia exceeds 10.6 mg/dl (2.65 mmol/l) or if the calciuria exceeds 300 mg/24 hours in adults or 4-6 mg/kg/day in children.
In case of hypercalcaemia or signs of impaired renal function the dose should be reduced or the treatment discontinued.

items.t: Drops: put onto a spoon, or mix with a small amount of cold or lukewarm food just before use; make sure the whole dose is taken. One SmPC advises taking with a meal.

src.q: can be dispensed onto a spoon and taken as is or to facilitate the intake it can also be mixed with a small amount of cold or lukewarm food immediately prior to use.
Patients should be advised to take THORENS preferably with a meal

items.t: Capsules: swallow whole (not chewed) with water, preferably with a meal.

src.q: The capsules should be swallowed whole (not chewed) with water. In order to enhance absorption, it is recommended to take Colecalciferol capsule with a meal.

items.t: Tell the prescriber about any other vitamin D or calcium supplements and fortified foods.

src.q: Allowances should be made for vitamin D supplements from other sources.

items.t: Report signs of too much calcium: nausea, vomiting, thirst, passing a lot of urine, constipation, weakness.

src.q: Symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, polyuria, anorexia, weakness, apathy, thirst and constipation.

items.t: 50,000 IU capsule is a weekly (not daily) dose during treatment.

src.q: 50,000 IU/week (1 capsule) for 6-8 weeks

items.t: Type 2 diabetes not controlled by diet and exercise, in adults and children aged 10 years and over: alone when metformin is not tolerated, or added to other diabetes medicines.

src.q: Forxiga is indicated in adults and children aged 10 years and above for the treatment of insufficiently controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus as an adjunct to diet and exercise
as monotherapy when metformin is considered inappropriate due to intolerance.
in addition to other medicinal products for the treatment of type 2 diabetes.

items.t: Symptomatic chronic heart failure (adults).

src.q: Forxiga is indicated in adults for the treatment of symptomatic chronic heart failure.

items.t: Chronic kidney disease (adults).

src.q: Forxiga is indicated in adults for the treatment of chronic kidney disease.

items.t: Not for type 1 diabetes. MHRA (2021): dapagliflozin is no longer authorised for type 1 diabetes; patients with type 1 diabetes should have it reviewed and stopped by, or with, a diabetes specialist.

src.q: Dapagliflozin should not be used for treatment of patients with type 1 diabetes.
dapagliflozin 5 mg is no longer authorised for the treatment of patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus
dapagliflozin should be reviewed and discontinued in patients with type 1 diabetes by or in consultation with a physician specialised in diabetes care as soon as clinically practical

items.t: 10 mg once daily.

src.q: Type 2 diabetes mellitus The recommended dose is 10 mg dapagliflozin once daily.

items.t: With insulin or an insulin secretagogue (e.g. a sulfonylurea): consider a lower dose of the insulin or secretagogue to reduce hypoglycaemia risk.
items.tag: Type 2 diabetes, add-on to insulin or sulfonylurea

src.q: When dapagliflozin is used in combination with insulin or an insulin secretagogue, such as a sulphonylurea, a lower dose of insulin or insulin secretagogue may be considered to reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia

items.t: 10 mg once daily.

src.q: Heart failure The recommended dose is 10 mg dapagliflozin once daily.

items.t: 10 mg once daily.

src.q: Chronic kidney disease The recommended dose is 10 mg dapagliflozin once daily.

items.t: Elderly (65 years and over): no dose adjustment based on age.

src.q: Elderly (≥ 65 years) No dose adjustment is recommended based on age.

items.t: Type 2 diabetes, children aged 10 years and over: no dose adjustment (10 mg once daily). No data below 10 years.

src.q: No dose adjustment is required for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus in children aged 10 years and above
No data are available for children below 10 years of age.

items.t: Heart failure and chronic kidney disease: safety and efficacy not established under 18 years; no data.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of dapagliflozin for the treatment of heart failure or for the treatment of chronic kidney disease in children < 18 years have not yet been established.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to dapagliflozin or any excipient.

src.q: 4.3 Contraindications Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Diabetic ketoacidosis (rare, can be fatal; may occur with blood glucose below 14 mmol/L).
