Assess for ketoacidosis at once if nausea, vomiting, anorexia, abdominal pain, excessive thirst, difficulty breathing, confusion, unusual fatigue or sleepiness, whatever the glucose. Stop immediately if DKA is suspected or diagnosed.

src.q: Rare cases of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), including life-threatening and fatal cases, have been reported in patients treated with sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, including dapagliflozin.
Patients should be assessed for ketoacidosis immediately if these symptoms occur, regardless of blood glucose level.
In patients where DKA is suspected or diagnosed, dapagliflozin treatment should be stopped immediately.

items.t: Interrupt treatment if hospitalised for major surgery or acute serious illness; monitor ketones (blood preferred to urine). Restart when ketones are normal and the patient is stable.

src.q: Treatment should be interrupted in patients who are hospitalised for major surgical procedures or acute serious medical illnesses. Monitoring of ketones is recommended in these patients. Measurement of blood ketone levels is preferred to urine.
Treatment with dapagliflozin may be restarted when the ketone values are normal and the patient's condition has stabilised.

items.t: Higher DKA risk (use with caution): low beta-cell reserve (e.g. low C-peptide, LADA, history of pancreatitis), restricted food intake or severe dehydration, reduced insulin doses, raised insulin needs from acute illness, surgery or alcohol abuse. Restarting after DKA on an SGLT2 inhibitor is not recommended unless another clear cause was found and resolved.

src.q: Patients who may be at higher risk of DKA include patients with a low beta-cell function reserve
SGLT2 inhibitors should be used with caution in these patients.
Restarting SGLT2 inhibitor treatment in patients experiencing a DKA while on SGLT2 inhibitor treatment is not recommended, unless another clear precipitating factor is identified and resolved.

items.t: Volume depletion and hypotension: caution where a fall in blood pressure could be a risk (e.g. on antihypertensives with a history of hypotension, elderly). In illness causing volume loss (e.g. gastrointestinal illness) monitor volume status; interrupt treatment until volume depletion is corrected.

src.q: Caution should be exercised in patients for whom a dapagliflozin-induced drop in blood pressure could pose a risk, such as patients on anti-hypertensive therapy with a history of hypotension or elderly patients.
Temporary interruption of treatment with dapagliflozin is recommended for patients who develop volume depletion until the depletion is corrected

items.t: Fournier's gangrene (necrotising fasciitis of the perineum): rare but life-threatening. If suspected, stop and start urgent treatment (antibiotics, surgical debridement).

src.q: This is a rare but serious and potentially life-threatening event that requires urgent surgical intervention and antibiotic treatment.
If Fournier's gangrene is suspected, Forxiga should be discontinued and prompt treatment (including antibiotics and surgical debridement) should be instituted.

items.t: Urinary tract infection: consider temporary interruption when treating pyelonephritis or urosepsis.

src.q: temporary interruption of dapagliflozin should be considered when treating pyelonephritis or urosepsis.

items.t: Lower limb amputation (mainly toes) increased with SGLT2 inhibitors in long-term studies; counsel on routine preventive foot care.

src.q: An increase in cases of lower limb amputation (primarily of the toe) has been observed in long-term, clinical studies in type 2 diabetes mellitus with SGLT2 inhibitors.
It is important to counsel patients with diabetes on routine preventative foot care.

items.t: Raised haematocrit: monitor and investigate pronounced rises.

src.q: Patients with pronounced elevations in haematocrit should be monitored and investigated for underlying haematological disease.

items.t: Contains lactose: patients with hereditary galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take it.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicinal product.

items.t: Urine glucose tests will be positive; 1,5-AG assay is unreliable for glycaemic control.

src.q: patients taking Forxiga will test positive for glucose in their urine.
Monitoring glycaemic control with 1,5-AG assay is not recommended

items.t: Thiazide and loop diuretics: dapagliflozin may add to the diuretic effect and increase the risk of dehydration and hypotension.

src.q: Dapagliflozin may add to the diuretic effect of thiazide and loop diuretics and may increase the risk of dehydration and hypotension

items.t: Insulin and insulin secretagogues (e.g. sulfonylureas): a lower dose of insulin or secretagogue may be needed to reduce hypoglycaemia risk.

src.q: a lower dose of insulin or an insulin secretagogue may be required to reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia when used in combination with dapagliflozin

items.t: Lithium (not in this tool's list): dapagliflozin may lower lithium levels; monitor lithium more often after starting or changing dose.

src.q: Dapagliflozin may increase renal lithium excretion and the blood lithium levels may be decreased.
Serum concentration of lithium should be monitored more frequently after dapagliflozin initiation and dose changes.

items.t: No clinically relevant effect with metformin, glimepiride, sitagliptin, hydrochlorothiazide, valsartan, simvastatin, mefenamic acid or rifampicin; dapagliflozin did not change warfarin's effect on INR.

src.q: the pharmacokinetics of dapagliflozin are not altered by metformin, pioglitazone, sitagliptin, glimepiride, voglibose, hydrochlorothiazide, bumetanide, valsartan, or simvastatin.
or the anticoagulatory effects of warfarin as measured by INR.
a 55% increase in dapagliflozin systemic exposure was seen, but with no clinically meaningful effect on 24-hour urinary glucose excretion. No dose adjustment is recommended.

items.t: No dose adjustment based on renal function.

src.q: No dose adjustment is required based on renal function.

items.t: eGFR < 15 mL/min/1.73 m²: starting treatment is not recommended (no experience; limited experience below 25).

src.q: It is not recommended to initiate treatment with dapagliflozin in patients with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) < 15 mL/min/1.73m2.

items.t: Type 2 diabetes: glucose-lowering effect is reduced when eGFR < 45 mL/min/1.73 m² and likely absent in severe renal impairment; if eGFR falls below 45, consider additional glucose-lowering treatment.

src.q: In patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus, the glucose lowering efficacy of dapagliflozin is reduced when eGFR is < 45 mL/min/1.73m2, and is likely absent in patients with severe renal impairment.
if eGFR falls below 45 mL/min/1.73m2, additional glucose lowering treatment should be considered in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus

items.t: eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m²: more reports of raised parathyroid hormone and hypotension than with placebo.

src.q: In patients with moderate renal impairment (eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73m2), a higher proportion of patients treated with dapagliflozin had adverse reactions of increase in parathyroid hormone (PTH) and hypotension, compared with placebo.

items.t: Mild or moderate hepatic impairment: no dose adjustment.

src.q: No dose adjustment is necessary for patients with mild or moderate hepatic impairment.

items.t: Severe hepatic impairment: start at 5 mg; increase to 10 mg if well tolerated (exposure is increased).

src.q: In patients with severe hepatic impairment, a starting dose of 5 mg is recommended. If well tolerated, the dose may be increased to 10 mg
Dapagliflozin exposure is increased in patients with severe hepatic impairment

items.t: SmPC: no human data. Rat studies showed toxicity to the developing kidney in the period matching the 2nd and 3rd trimesters, so use is not recommended in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters. Stop dapagliflozin when pregnancy is detected.

src.q: Therefore, the use of dapagliflozin is not recommended during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy.
When pregnancy is detected, treatment with dapagliflozin should be discontinued.

items.t: BUMPS: type 2 diabetes in pregnancy should be treated with metformin, plus insulin if needed; SGLT2 inhibitors are avoided as a precaution (very little information). With an unplanned pregnancy, keep taking the medicine until reviewed at the earliest opportunity, as uncontrolled diabetes is risky.

src.q: Type 2 diabetes during pregnancy should be treated with metformin, as well as insulin if required. Other antidiabetic drugs should not be used.
As a precaution, they are avoided in pregnancy.
you should carry on with the drug you are taking until your appointment, as uncontrolled diabetes is risky for you and your baby

items.t: SmPC: should not be used while breastfeeding (excreted in animal milk with effects in nursing offspring; risk to the infant cannot be excluded).

src.q: A risk to the newborns/infants cannot be excluded. Dapagliflozin should not be used while breast-feeding.

items.t: SPS: insulin or metformin are the preferred choices in breastfeeding; there is limited or no published information on other antidiabetic medicines.

src.q: Insulin or metformin are the preferred choices during breastfeeding.
limited or no published information on the use of other antidiabetic (blood-glucose lowering) medicines during breastfeeding.

items.t: Human fertility effect not studied; no effect on fertility in rats.

src.q: The effect of dapagliflozin on fertility in humans has not been studied. In male and female rats, dapagliflozin showed no effects on fertility at any dose tested.

items.t: Genital infections (vulvovaginitis, balanitis) are the most frequently reported reactions: 5.5% vs 0.6% with placebo, more often in women and in those with a past history.

src.q: The most frequently reported adverse reactions across the clinical studies were genital infections.
vulvovaginitis, balanitis and related genital infections were reported in 5.5% and 0.6% of subjects who received dapagliflozin 10 mg and placebo, respectively.

items.t: Hypoglycaemia when used with a sulfonylurea or insulin (higher rates in those add-on studies).

src.q: Hypoglycaemia (when used with SU or insulin)b
Studies with add-on sulphonylurea and add-on insulin therapies had higher rates of hypoglycaemia

items.t: Also listed in the SmPC table: urinary tract infection, volume depletion (dehydration, hypotension), increased urination, back pain, dizziness, rash, dysuria, raised haematocrit.

src.q: Urinary tract infection*,b,d
Volume depletionb,e
Back pain*
Polyuria*,f

items.t: Diabetic ketoacidosis (may occur with near-normal glucose): stop immediately and assess; treat urgently.

src.q: In patients where DKA is suspected or diagnosed, dapagliflozin treatment should be stopped immediately.

items.t: Fournier's gangrene: seek urgent care for pain, tenderness, redness or swelling of the genital or perineal area with fever or malaise; stop dapagliflozin and treat promptly.

src.q: Patients should be advised to seek medical attention if they experience a combination of symptoms of pain, tenderness, erythema, or swelling in the genital or perineal area, with fever or malaise.

items.t: Volume depletion (dehydration, hypotension): interrupt until corrected.

src.q: Temporary interruption of treatment with dapagliflozin is recommended for patients who develop volume depletion until the depletion is corrected

items.t: Before starting: check eGFR (do not start if eGFR < 15) and consider factors that predispose to ketoacidosis.

src.q: it is not recommended to initiate treatment with dapagliflozin in patients with eGFR < 15 mL/min/1.73m2
Before initiating dapagliflozin, factors in the patient history that may predispose to ketoacidosis should be considered.

items.t: In illness with volume loss: volume status (examination, blood pressure, haematocrit and electrolytes).

src.q: careful monitoring of volume status (e.g. physical examination, blood pressure measurements, laboratory tests including haematocrit and electrolytes) is recommended

items.t: When hospitalised for major surgery or acute serious illness: interrupt and monitor blood ketones.

src.q: interrupt sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor treatment in patients who are hospitalised for major surgical procedures or acute serious medical illnesses
monitor ketones during this period - measurement of blood ketone levels is preferred to urine

items.t: Stop immediately if DKA is suspected or diagnosed; do not restart any SGLT2 inhibitor after DKA on treatment unless another cause was found and resolved. Stop if Fournier's gangrene is suspected.

src.q: discontinue treatment with the SGLT2 inhibitor immediately if DKA is suspected or diagnosed
do not restart treatment with any SGLT2 inhibitor in patients who experienced DKA during use, unless another cause for DKA was identified and resolved
if Fournier's gangrene is suspected, stop the SGLT2 inhibitor and urgently start treatment

items.t: Once daily at any time of day, with or without food. Swallow tablets whole.

src.q: Forxiga can be taken orally once daily at any time of day with or without food. Tablets are to be swallowed whole.

items.t: SPS (off-label, swallowing difficulties in adults): the film-coated tablets can be crushed and mixed with water or given with soft food.

src.q: Dapagliflozin tablets Film-coated but can be crushed and mixed with water or given with soft food.

items.t: Know the signs of ketoacidosis (e.g. rapid weight loss, feeling or being sick, stomach pain, fast deep breathing, sleepiness, sweet-smelling breath, sweet or metallic taste) and seek medical advice at once if they occur.

src.q: inform them of the signs and symptoms of diabetic ketoacidosis ( DKA ) - see below - and advise them to seek immediate medical advice if they develop any of these

rapid weight loss, feeling sick or being sick, stomach pain, fast and deep breathing, sleepiness, a sweet smell to the breath, a sweet or metallic taste in the mouth, or a different odour to urine or sweat

items.t: Seek urgent medical attention for severe pain, tenderness, redness or swelling of the genitals or the area between the genitals and anus, with fever or feeling unwell.

src.q: advise patients to seek urgent medical attention if they experience severe pain, tenderness, erythema, or swelling in the genital or perineal area, accompanied by fever or malaise

items.t: Look after your feet (routine preventive foot care) and keep well hydrated.

src.q: advise patients receiving any sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor about the importance of routine preventive foot care and adequate hydration

items.t: With a sulfonylurea or insulin, be alert to low blood sugar, including when driving.

src.q: Patients should be alerted to the risk of hypoglycaemia when dapagliflozin is used in combination with a sulphonylurea or insulin.

items.t: Urine glucose tests will show glucose; this is expected.

src.q: patients taking Forxiga will test positive for glucose in their urine.

items.t: Type 2 diabetes in adults, with diet and exercise: when not controlled on maximally tolerated metformin alone; with other diabetes medicines when not controlled on metformin plus those medicines; or to replace separate dapagliflozin and metformin tablets.

src.q: Xigduo is indicated in adults for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus as an adjunct to diet and exercise
in patients insufficiently controlled on their maximally tolerated dose of metformin alone
in patients already being treated with the combination of dapagliflozin and metformin as separate tablets.

items.t: Not for type 1 diabetes (safety and efficacy not established; ketoacidosis was common in type 1 studies).

src.q: The safety and efficacy of Xigduo in patients with type 1 diabetes have not been established and Xigduo should not be used for treatment of patients with type 1 diabetes.

items.t: One tablet twice daily with meals. Total daily dose: dapagliflozin 10 mg plus the metformin dose already taken (or nearest suitable dose).
items.tag: Type 2 diabetes, adults (normal renal function, GFR ≥ 90 mL/min)

src.q: The recommended dose is one tablet twice daily.
should receive a total daily dose of Xigduo equivalent to dapagliflozin 10 mg, plus the total daily dose of metformin, or the nearest therapeutically appropriate dose, already being taken.

items.t: With insulin or an insulin secretagogue (e.g. a sulfonylurea): consider a lower dose of these to reduce hypoglycaemia risk.

src.q: When Xigduo is used in combination with insulin or an insulin secretagogue such as sulphonylurea, a lower dose of insulin or sulphonylurea may be considered to reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia

items.t: Switching from separate tablets: same daily doses of dapagliflozin (10 mg) and metformin, or the nearest suitable metformin dose.

src.q: Patients switching from separate tablets of dapagliflozin (10 mg total daily dose) and metformin to Xigduo should receive the same daily dose of dapagliflozin and metformin already being taken

items.t: Elderly: use with caution as age increases; monitor renal function; consider volume depletion risk.

src.q: this medicinal product should be used with caution as age increases
Monitoring of renal function is necessary to aid in prevention of metformin-associated lactic acidosis, particularly in elderly patients

items.t: Not established under 18 years; no data.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of Xigduo in children and adolescents aged 0 to < 18 years have not yet been established. No data are available.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to dapagliflozin, metformin or any excipient.

src.q: hypersensitivity to the active substances or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1

items.t: Any acute metabolic acidosis (e.g. lactic acidosis, diabetic ketoacidosis); diabetic pre-coma.

src.q: any type of acute metabolic acidosis (such as lactic acidosis, diabetic ketoacidosis); - diabetic pre-coma;

items.t: Severe renal failure (GFR < 30 mL/min).

src.q: severe renal failure (GFR < 30 mL/min)

items.t: Acute conditions that may alter renal function: dehydration, severe infection, shock.

src.q: acute conditions with the potential to alter renal function such as: - dehydration, - severe infection, - shock;

items.t: Acute or chronic disease that may cause tissue hypoxia: cardiac or respiratory failure, recent myocardial infarction, shock.

src.q: acute or chronic disease which may cause tissue hypoxia such as: - cardiac or respiratory failure, - recent myocardial infarction, - shock;

items.t: Hepatic impairment; acute alcohol intoxication, alcoholism.

src.q: hepatic impairment (see sections 4.2, 4.4 and 5.2); - acute alcohol intoxication, alcoholism

items.t: Lactic acidosis (metformin; very rare, serious): risk rises with acute worsening of renal function, cardiorespiratory illness or sepsis. Stop temporarily in dehydration (severe diarrhoea or vomiting, fever, low fluid intake). Start antihypertensives, diuretics and NSAIDs with caution.

src.q: Lactic acidosis, a very rare but serious metabolic complication, most often occurs at acute worsening of renal function or cardiorespiratory illness or sepsis.
In case of dehydration (severe diarrhoea or vomiting, fever or reduced fluid intake), Xigduo should be temporarily discontinued and contact with a healthcare professional is recommended.

Medicinal products that can acutely impair renal function (such as antihypertensives, diuretics and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs [NSAIDs]) should be initiated with caution in metformin-treated patients.

items.t: Diabetic ketoacidosis (dapagliflozin; rare, can be fatal, may occur with glucose below 14 mmol/L): assess at once if symptoms, stop immediately if suspected. Interrupt when hospitalised for major surgery or acute serious illness and monitor ketones. Restarting after DKA on an SGLT2 inhibitor is not recommended unless another clear cause was resolved. Use with caution in those at higher risk (low beta-cell reserve, pancreatitis history, restricted intake, alcohol abuse).

src.q: In patients where DKA is suspected or diagnosed, treatment with dapagliflozin should be discontinued immediately.
Treatment should be interrupted in patients who are hospitalised for major surgical procedures or acute serious medical illnesses. Monitoring of ketones is recommended in these patients.
Restarting SGLT2 inhibitor treatment in patients with previous DKA while on SGLT2 inhibitor treatment is not recommended, unless another clear precipitating factor is identified and resolved.
SGLT2 inhibitors should be used with caution in these patients.

items.t: Renal function: do not start if GFR < 60 mL/min; stop if GFR is persistently below 45 mL/min.

src.q: Xigduo should not be initiated in patients with GFR < 60 mL/min and should be discontinued at GFR persistently below 45 mL/min

items.t: Volume depletion and hypotension (dapagliflozin): caution where a fall in blood pressure is a risk (antihypertensives with a history of hypotension, elderly); interrupt if volume depletion develops until corrected.

src.q: Caution should be exercised in patients for whom a dapagliflozin-induced drop in blood pressure could pose a risk, such as patients on anti-hypertensive therapy with a history of hypotension or elderly patients.
Temporary interruption of treatment with this medicinal product is recommended for patients who develop volume depletion until the depletion is corrected

items.t: Surgery under general, spinal or epidural anaesthesia: stop at the time of surgery; restart no earlier than 48 hours after surgery or return to eating, once renal function is re-checked and stable. Iodinated contrast: stop before or at the time of imaging; restart at least 48 hours after once renal function is stable.

src.q: Xigduo must be discontinued at the time of surgery with general, spinal or epidural anaesthesia.

Xigduo should be discontinued prior to, or at the time of, the imaging procedure and not restarted until at least 48 hours after, provided that renal function has been re-evaluated and found to be stable

items.t: Fournier's gangrene: if suspected, stop and treat urgently. Consider interrupting for pyelonephritis or urosepsis.

src.q: If Fournier's gangrene is suspected, Xigduo should be discontinued and prompt treatment (including antibiotics and surgical debridement) should be instituted.
temporary interruption of treatment should be considered when treating pyelonephritis or urosepsis.

items.t: Mitochondrial disease (MELAS, MIDD): metformin is not recommended; withdraw immediately if suggestive signs appear.

src.q: metformin is not recommended due to the risk of lactic acidosis exacerbation and neurologic complications which may lead to worsening of the disease.

items.t: Vitamin B12 may fall (higher risk with dose, duration, risk factors): check levels if deficiency suspected; consider periodic checks in those at risk; continue while tolerated and treat deficiency.

src.q: In case of suspicion of vitamin B12 deficiency (such as anaemia or neuropathy), vitamin B12 serum levels should be monitored.
Periodic vitamin B12 monitoring could be necessary in patients with risk factors for vitamin B12 deficiency.

items.t: A previously stable patient who becomes unwell or has abnormal tests should be checked promptly for ketoacidosis or lactic acidosis; stop at once if acidosis occurs.

src.q: should be evaluated promptly for evidence of ketoacidosis or lactic acidosis.
If acidosis of either form occurs, treatment must be stopped immediately and other appropriate corrective measures initiated.

items.t: Lower limb amputation seen with another SGLT2 inhibitor: counsel on foot care. Raised haematocrit: investigate pronounced rises. Urine glucose tests will be positive.

src.q: Like for all diabetic patients it is important to counsel patients on routine preventative foot care.
Patients with pronounced elevations in haematocrit should be monitored and investigated for underlying haematological disease.
patients taking this medicinal product will test positive for glucose in their urine.

items.t: Thiazide and loop diuretics: may add to the diuretic effect (dehydration, hypotension).

src.q: This medicinal product may add to the diuretic effect of thiazide and loop diuretics and may increase the risk of dehydration and hypotension

items.t: Insulin and insulin secretagogues (e.g. sulfonylureas): a lower dose of these may be needed.

src.q: a lower dose of insulin or an insulin secretagogue may be required to reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia when used in combination with dapagliflozin

items.t: NSAIDs (including COX-2 inhibitors), ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor antagonists and diuretics (especially loop): may impair renal function and raise lactic acidosis risk - close monitoring of renal function is necessary.

src.q: Some medicinal products can adversely affect renal function which may increase the risk of lactic acidosis, e.g. NSAIDs, including selective cyclo-oxygenase (COX) II inhibitors, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor antagonists and diuretics, especially loop diuretics.
When starting or using such products in combination with metformin, close monitoring of renal function is necessary.

items.t: Glucocorticoids (systemic and local), beta-2 agonists and diuretics raise glucose: inform the patient, monitor glucose more often, adjust dose during and after.

src.q: Glucocorticoids (given by systemic and local routes), beta-2 agonists, and diuretics have intrinsic hyperglycaemic activity.
The patient should be informed and more frequent blood glucose monitoring performed, especially at the beginning of treatment with such medicinal products.

items.t: Alcohol: avoid alcohol and alcohol-containing medicines (lactic acidosis). Iodinated contrast: stop before imaging (see cautions). Cimetidine (not in this tool's list) raises metformin exposure.

src.q: Consumption of alcohol and medicinal products containing alcohol should be avoided.
cimetidine, administered as 400 mg twice daily, increased metformin systemic exposure (AUC) by 50% and Cmax by 81%.

items.t: Check GFR before starting and at least annually; every 3 to 6 months in the elderly or if renal function may decline (the 4.4 text says 2 to 4 times a year when GFR < 60 mL/min).

src.q: A GFR should be assessed before initiation of treatment with metformin containing medicinal products and at least annually thereafter.
For renal function with GFR levels < 60 mL/min and in elderly patients, at least 2 to 4 times per year.

items.t: GFR 60-89 mL/min: metformin max 3000 mg/day (consider reduction as function declines); dapagliflozin max 10 mg/day.

src.q: 60-89 Maximum daily dose is 3000 mg. Dose reduction may be considered in relation to declining renal function. Maximum total daily dose is 10 mg.

items.t: GFR 45-59 mL/min: do not start the combination (dapagliflozin should not be initiated). Metformin max 2000 mg/day, starting dose at most half the maximum; review lactic acidosis risk factors. If no suitable fixed-dose strength, use the single medicines.

src.q: 45-59 Maximum daily dose is 2000 mg. The starting dose is at most half of the maximum dose. Dapagliflozin should not be initiated.
If no adequate strength of Xigduo is available, individual mono-components should be used instead of the fixed dose combination.

items.t: GFR 30-44 mL/min: dapagliflozin not recommended; stop if GFR persistently below 45. Metformin max 1000 mg/day.

src.q: 30-44 Maximum daily dose is 1000 mg. The starting dose is at most half of the maximum dose. Dapagliflozin is not recommended.
If renal function falls persistently below GFR 45 mL/min, treatment should be discontinued.

items.t: GFR < 30 mL/min: contraindicated.

src.q: Metformin is contraindicated in patients with GFR of < 30 mL/min

items.t: Hepatic impairment (any): must not be used.

src.q: This medicinal product must not be used in patients with hepatic impairment

items.t: SmPC: not recommended in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters (dapagliflozin kidney toxicity in rats). When planning pregnancy and during pregnancy, do not treat diabetes with this product; use insulin.

src.q: Therefore, the use of this medicinal product is not recommended during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy.
When the patient plans to become pregnant, and during pregnancy, it is recommended that diabetes is not treated with this medicinal product, but insulin be used

items.t: BUMPS: metformin (with insulin if needed) is recommended in pregnancy; SGLT2 inhibitors are avoided as a precaution. With an unplanned pregnancy, keep taking it until reviewed promptly.

src.q: Type 2 diabetes during pregnancy should be treated with metformin, as well as insulin if required. Other antidiabetic drugs should not be used.
you should carry on with the drug you are taking until your appointment, as uncontrolled diabetes is risky for you and your baby

items.t: SmPC: should not be used while breastfeeding (dapagliflozin in animal milk with effects on offspring; metformin passes into human milk in small amounts).

src.q: Metformin is excreted in human milk in small amounts. A risk to the newborns/infants cannot be excluded. This medicinal product should not be used while breast-feeding.

items.t: SPS: insulin or metformin are preferred in breastfeeding; limited or no information on other antidiabetics (no SPS advice for the dapagliflozin component).

src.q: Insulin or metformin are the preferred choices during breastfeeding.
limited or no published information on the use of other antidiabetic (blood-glucose lowering) medicines during breastfeeding.

items.t: Human fertility not studied; no effect in rats (dapagliflozin) and no reproductive toxicity in animals (metformin).

src.q: In male and female rats, dapagliflozin showed no effects on fertility at any dose tested.

items.t: Genital infections (vulvovaginitis, balanitis): most frequently reported (5.5% vs 0.6% placebo, dapagliflozin data).

src.q: The most frequently reported adverse reactions across the clinical studies were genital infections.
vulvovaginitis, balanitis and related genital infections were reported in 5.5% and 0.6% of subjects who received dapagliflozin 10 mg and placebo, respectively.

items.t: Gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, loss of appetite), mostly when starting and usually settle.

src.q: Gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain and loss of appetite occur most frequently during initiation of therapy and resolve spontaneously in most cases.

items.t: Hypoglycaemia mainly with a sulfonylurea or insulin; also listed: urinary tract infection, vitamin B12 decrease, taste disturbance, volume depletion, increased urination.

src.q: Hypoglycaemia (when used with SU or insulin)b Vitamin B12 decrease/deficiencyj,§ Volume depletionb,e
Taste disturbance§

items.t: Lactic acidosis (acidotic breathlessness, abdominal pain, muscle cramps, weakness, low temperature, then coma): stop and seek immediate medical attention.

src.q: Lactic acidosis is characterised by acidotic dyspnoea, abdominal pain, muscle cramps, asthenia and hypothermia followed by coma.
In case of suspected symptoms, the patient should stop taking Xigduo and seek immediate medical attention.

items.t: Diabetic ketoacidosis (may occur with near-normal glucose): stop dapagliflozin immediately.

src.q: In patients where DKA is suspected or diagnosed, treatment with dapagliflozin should be discontinued immediately.

items.t: Fournier's gangrene: urgent care for genital or perineal pain, tenderness, redness or swelling with fever or malaise.

src.q: Patients should be advised to seek medical attention if they experience a combination of symptoms of pain, tenderness, erythema, or swelling in the genital or perineal area, with fever or malaise.

items.t: GFR before starting (do not start if GFR < 60 mL/min); consider ketoacidosis risk factors.

src.q: A GFR should be assessed before initiation of treatment with metformin containing medicinal products and at least annually thereafter.
Xigduo should not be initiated in patients with GFR < 60 mL/min

items.t: Renal function at least annually; 2 to 4 times a year if GFR < 60 mL/min or elderly; before and during medicines that may reduce renal function. Vitamin B12 if deficiency suspected or risk factors.

src.q: For renal function with GFR levels < 60 mL/min and in elderly patients, at least 2 to 4 times per year.
Prior to initiation of concomitant medicinal products that may reduce renal function and periodically thereafter.
Periodic vitamin B12 monitoring could be necessary in patients with risk factors for vitamin B12 deficiency.

items.t: Hospital admission for major surgery or acute serious illness: interrupt and monitor blood ketones.

src.q: monitor ketones during this period - measurement of blood ketone levels is preferred to urine

items.t: Stop if GFR persistently < 45 mL/min, if DKA or lactic acidosis is suspected, or if Fournier's gangrene is suspected. Stop temporarily in dehydration, at surgery and around iodinated contrast.

src.q: If renal function falls persistently below GFR 45 mL/min, treatment should be discontinued.
If acidosis of either form occurs, treatment must be stopped immediately and other appropriate corrective measures initiated.

items.t: Twice daily with meals (reduces metformin stomach upset).

src.q: Xigduo should be given twice daily with meals to reduce the gastrointestinal adverse reactions associated with metformin.

items.t: SPS (off-label, adults with swallowing difficulties): tablets can be crushed and mixed with water or given with soft food.

src.q: Dapagliflozin with metformin tablets Film-coated but can be crushed and mixed with water or given with soft food.

items.t: Know the signs of lactic acidosis and ketoacidosis; stop and get urgent help if they occur.

src.q: Patients and/or caregivers should be informed on the risk of lactic acidosis.
inform them of the signs and symptoms of diabetic ketoacidosis ( DKA ) - see below - and advise them to seek immediate medical advice if they develop any of these

items.t: If you have severe vomiting, diarrhoea, fever or cannot drink, stop this medicine for a while and contact a healthcare professional.

src.q: In case of dehydration (severe diarrhoea or vomiting, fever or reduced fluid intake), Xigduo should be temporarily discontinued and contact with a healthcare professional is recommended.

items.t: Avoid alcohol. Look after your feet and keep well hydrated. Seek urgent care for genital or perineal pain or swelling with fever.

src.q: Consumption of alcohol and medicinal products containing alcohol should be avoided.
advise patients receiving any sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor about the importance of routine preventive foot care and adequate hydration
advise patients to seek urgent medical attention if they experience severe pain, tenderness, erythema, or swelling in the genital or perineal area, accompanied by fever or malaise

items.t: Leprosy (all forms, as part of multi-drug therapy); dermatitis herpetiformis and other dermatoses; malaria prophylaxis with pyrimethamine; Pneumocystis (carinii) pneumonia prophylaxis in immunodeficient patients.

src.q: As part of a multi-drug regimen in the treatment of all forms of leprosy. Treatment of dermatitis herpetiformis and other dermatoses. Prophylaxis of malaria in combination with pyrimethamine.
Prophylaxis of Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia in immunodeficient subjects, especially AIDS patients.

restrictions.note: No specialist-only, shared-care or brand restrictions found in the dapsone SmPCs; no MHRA Drug Safety Update for dapsone found by keyword search; no SPS dapsone monitoring page found.

items.t: Multibacillary leprosy (3-drug regimen), adults and children over 12: 100 mg DAILY for at least 2 years.

src.q: Multibacillary leprosy (3-drug regimen): 100mg daily for at least two years.

items.t: Paucibacillary leprosy (2-drug regimen), adults and children over 12: 100 mg DAILY for at least 6 months.

src.q: Adults and children over 12 years of age:
Paucibacillary leprosy (2-drug regimen): 100mg daily for at least six months.

items.t: Dermatitis herpetiformis, adults and children over 12: start 50 mg DAILY, increase gradually to 300 mg daily if needed; once lesions subside reduce to the minimum (usually 25-50 mg daily), which may continue for years. Gluten-free diet often allows lower maintenance.

src.q: Adults and children over 12 years of age:
Dermatitis herpetiformis: Initially 50mg daily, gradually increasing to 300mg daily if required.
usually 25-50mg daily, which may be continued for a number of years

items.t: Malaria prophylaxis, adults and children over 12: 100 mg ONCE WEEKLY with pyrimethamine 12.5 mg.

src.q: Adults and children over 12 years of age:
Malaria prophylaxis: 100mg weekly with 12.5mg pyrimethamine.

items.t: Pneumocystis pneumonia (with trimethoprim), adults and children over 12: 50-100 mg DAILY, or 100 mg TWICE WEEKLY, or 200 mg ONCE WEEKLY.

src.q: Adults and children over 12 years of age:
Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia: In combination with trimethoprim, 50-100mg daily; 100mg twice weekly or 200mg once weekly.

items.t: Elderly: reduce dose where hepatic function is impaired.

src.q: Dosage should be reduced in the elderly where there is an impairment of hepatic function.

items.t: Children 6-12 years: multibacillary leprosy 50 mg daily for at least 2 years; paucibacillary leprosy 50 mg daily for at least 6 months.

src.q: Children aged 6 years to 12 years: Multibacillary leprosy (3-drug regimen): 50mg daily for at least two years. Paucibacillary leprosy (2-drug regimen): 50mg daily for at least six months.

items.t: Under 6 years: safety and efficacy not established; no data.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of Dapsone in children aged less than six years has not been established. No data are available.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to dapsone, sulfonamides, sulfones or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to dapsone, sulfonamides, sulfones, or any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Severe anaemia; porphyria; severe G6PD deficiency.

src.q: Severe anaemia. Porphyria. Severe glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency.

items.t: Cardiac or pulmonary disease: use with caution.

src.q: Dapsone should be used with caution in patients with cardiac or pulmonary disease.

items.t: Haemolysis: G6PD deficiency, methaemoglobin reductase deficiency or haemoglobin M make patients more susceptible. Subjects with G6PD deficiency are affected by doses above 50 mg daily.

src.q: Patients deficient in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, or methaemoglobin reductase, or with haemoglobin M are more susceptible to the haemolytic effects of dapsone.
subjects deficient in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase are affected by doses above 50mg daily

items.t: Anaemia: use with caution; treat severe anaemia before starting.

src.q: Dapsone should be used with caution in anaemia. Severe anaemia should be treated prior to initiation of dapsone therapy.

items.t: Sulfonamide antibiotic allergy (SPS): dapsone is a sulfone with an arylamine group; up to 20% of sulfonamide-sensitive people also react. After a serious sulfonamide reaction, avoid dapsone if possible.

src.q: Up to 20% of people sensitive to sulfonamide antibiotics also react to dapsone, but most tolerate it without issues.
Even so, people who have had a serious reaction to a sulfonamide antibiotic should avoid dapsone if possible.

items.t: Trimethoprim: increased dapsone and trimethoprim concentrations reported (AIDS patients).

src.q: Increased dapsone and trimethoprim concentrations have been reported following concurrent administration in AIDS patients.

items.t: Probenecid raises dapsone levels; rifampicin increases dapsone clearance (not in master list).

src.q: Excretion of dapsone is reduced and plasma concentrations are increased by concurrent administration of probenecid.
Rifampicin has been reported to increase the plasma clearance of dapsone.

renal.note: No renal dose adjustment or threshold in the dapsone SmPCs. No SPS renal page found.

items.t: Elderly with impaired hepatic function: reduce dose. Hepatitis, jaundice and liver test changes are uncommon adverse effects.

src.q: Dosage should be reduced in the elderly where there is an impairment of hepatic function.
Hepatic disorders Uncommon Hepatitis Jaundice Changes in liver function tests

items.t: SmPC: in leprosy, benefits are generally considered to outweigh any potential risk. Some leprologists recommend folic acid 5 mg daily in pregnancy. No BUMPS leaflet found.

src.q: It is now generally considered that the benefits of dapsone in the treatment of leprosy outweigh any potential risk to the pregnant patient.
Some leprologists recommend 5mg folic acid supplementation daily for leprosy patients receiving dapsone during pregnancy.

items.t: Passes into breast milk; haemolytic anaemia reported in a breastfed infant. Some advise against use in lactation, but leprosy therapy is generally continued.

src.q: Dapsone diffuses into breast milk and there has been a report of haemolytic anaemia in a breast fed infant.
While some feel that dapsone should not be used in lactating mothers, in general therapy for leprosy is continued in such patients.

reproductive.note: No fertility or contraception statements in the dapsone SmPCs; no BUMPS dapsone leaflet found (404).

items.t: Common: haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia (dose-related; most subjects above 200 mg daily; up to 100 mg daily does not cause significant haemolysis).

src.q: Blood disorders Common Haemolysis1 Methemoglobinaemia1
occurring in most subjects administered more than 200mg daily
doses of up to 100mg daily do not cause significant haemolysis

items.t: Agranulocytosis (rare; more often with other malaria prophylaxis medicines).

src.q: this is rare when dapsone is used alone, reports are more common when dapsone has been used with other medicines for malarial prophylaxis

items.t: Dapsone syndrome (after 3-6 weeks: rash, fever, eosinophilia): stop immediately; can progress to exfoliative dermatitis, hepatitis, psychosis; deaths recorded.

src.q: this may occur following 3-6 weeks of therapy, symptoms include rash, (always present), fever, and eosinophilia.
If dapsone is not stopped immediately; the syndrome may progress to exfoliative dermatitis, hepatitis, albuminuria and psychosis. Deaths have been recorded.

items.t: Severe skin reactions (rare): exfoliative dermatitis, TEN, SJS.

src.q: Rare Maculopapular rash Exfoliative dermatitis Toxic epidermal necrolysis Stevens-Johnson syndrome

items.t: Severe lepra reactions affecting eyes or nerves: stop or reduce dapsone.

src.q: Dapsone should be discontinued or reduced in dosage if severe lepra reactions affecting the eyes or nerve trunks occur.

items.t: Treat severe anaemia before starting.

src.q: Severe anaemia should be treated prior to initiation of dapsone therapy.

items.t: Regular blood counts during treatment (no interval stated in the SmPC).

src.q: It is recommended that regular blood counts be performed during treatment with dapsone.

items.t: Stop immediately if dapsone syndrome (rash with fever and eosinophilia) develops.

src.q: If dapsone is not stopped immediately; the syndrome may progress to exfoliative dermatitis

items.t: Oral. Note the different frequencies by indication: DAILY (leprosy, dermatitis herpetiformis), WEEKLY (malaria prophylaxis), daily or twice/once weekly (Pneumocystis).

src.q: For oral administration.
Malaria prophylaxis: 100mg weekly with 12.5mg pyrimethamine.

items.t: Report rash, fever or other new symptoms, especially 3 to 6 weeks after starting (dapsone syndrome).

src.q: this may occur following 3-6 weeks of therapy, symptoms include rash, (always present), fever, and eosinophilia.

items.t: Osteoporosis in postmenopausal women and in men at increased risk of fracture; bone loss with hormone ablation in men with prostate cancer at increased fracture risk; bone loss with long-term systemic glucocorticoid therapy in adults at increased fracture risk.

src.q: Treatment of osteoporosis in postmenopausal women and in men at increased risk of fractures.
Treatment of bone loss associated with hormone ablation in men with prostate cancer at increased risk of fractures
Treatment of bone loss associated with long-term systemic glucocorticoid therapy in adult patients at increased risk of fracture

items.t: MHRA: patients should not stop denosumab without specialist review (risk of multiple vertebral fractures after stopping or delaying).

src.q: patients should not stop denosumab without specialist review

items.t: Biological medicine: record the product name and batch number.

src.q: In order to improve the traceability of biological medicinal products, the name and the batch number of the administered product should be clearly recorded.

items.t: 60 mg by subcutaneous injection once every 6 months (thigh, abdomen or upper arm). Patients must have adequate calcium and vitamin D.

src.q: The recommended dose is 60 mg denosumab administered as a single subcutaneous injection once every 6 months into the thigh, abdomen or upper arm.
Patients must be adequately supplemented with calcium and vitamin D

items.t: Optimal treatment length not established; re-evaluate periodically, especially after 5 or more years.

src.q: The need for continued treatment should be re-evaluated periodically based on the benefits and potential risks of denosumab on an individual patient basis, particularly after 5 or more years of use

items.t: MHRA: if a dose is missed, give it as soon as possible, then schedule the next injection 6 months from that date.

src.q: In patients who have received dexamethasone for more than 3 weeks, withdrawal should not be abrupt.
Once a daily dose of approx. 1 mg dexamethasone is reached, dose reduction should be slower to allow the HPA-axis to recover.
Abrupt withdrawal of doses up to approx. 6 mg dexamethasone for 3 weeks is unlikely to lead to clinically relevant HPA-axis suppression, in the majority of patients.

items.t: Elderly, renal or hepatic impairment: no dose adjustment needed.

src.q: Elderly, renal impairment, hepatic impairment No dose adjustment is needed.

items.t: Use in children only with caution (growth retardation); dose set individually by the physician. One UK SmPC: limit to a single dose on alternate days to lessen growth retardation and adrenal suppression.

src.q: Dexamethasone should only be administered to children with caution, since glucocorticoids can induce growth retardation. The daily dose should be determined by the physician for each child individually.
Dosage should be limited to a single dose on alternate days to lessen retardation of growth and minimize suppression of hypothalamo-pituitary-adrenal axis.

items.t: Childhood croup (one UK SmPC): single dose 0.15 mg/kg; a second dose may be given after 12 hours if needed; maximum 10 mg.

src.q: Childhood Croup: A single dose of 0.15mg/kg Dexamethasone Oral Solution is recommended. A second dose may be administered after 12 hours, if considered necessary by the treating physician.
However, a maximum dose of 10mg (25ml Dexsol Oral Solution) is recommended.

items.t: COVID-19, adolescents 12 years and over (at least 40 kg): 6 mg once daily for up to 10 days.

src.q: Paediatric patients (adolescents aged 12 years and older with body weight at least 40kg) are recommended to take 6mg orally, once a day for up to 10 days.

items.t: Excipients (both UK solutions): propylene glycol (serious effects possible under 5 years with alcohol dehydrogenase substrates such as ethanol) and benzoic acid (may increase jaundice in newborns).

src.q: Co-administration with any substrate of alcohol dehydrogenase such as ethanol may induce serious adverse effects in children less than 5 years old.
Benzoic acid may increase jaundice (yellowing of the skin and eyes) in newborn babies (up to 4 weeks old).

items.t: Both UK SmPCs: hypersensitivity; gastric or duodenal ulcer; systemic fungal infection; parasitic/tropical worm infection.

src.q: Systemic fungal infections. - Stomach ulcer or duodenal ulcer - Infection with tropical worms - Parasitic infection
gastric and duodenal ulcer; acute infections: viral infections and systemic fungal infections

items.t: One UK SmPC: acute viral infections; vaccination with live vaccines. Another UK SmPC: systemic infection unless specific anti-infective therapy is given; avoid live vaccines at immunosuppressive doses; contraindications generally do not apply when glucocorticoids may be life-saving.

src.q: vaccination with live vaccines (see section 4.4. Special warnings and precautions for use)
Systemic infection unless specific anti-infective therapy is employed.
In general no contraindications apply in conditions where the use of glucocorticoids may be life saving.

items.t: Particular care and frequent monitoring in: osteoporosis, hypertension or heart failure, diabetes (or family history), tuberculosis history, glaucoma (or family history), previous steroid myopathy, liver failure, renal insufficiency, epilepsy, peptic ulceration; one UK SmPC adds myasthenia gravis, hypothyroidism, migraine, herpes simplex, ulcerative colitis/diverticulitis/fresh anastomosis. Great caution after recent myocardial infarction.

src.q: Particular care is required when considering the use of systemic glucocorticoids in patients with the following conditions and frequent patient monitoring is necessary
myasthenia gravis - non-specific ulcerative colitis, diverticulitis or fresh intestinal anastomosis - peptic ulceration - liver failure - renal insufficiency - hypothyroidism - epilepsy - migraine
corticosteroids should be used with great caution in these patients

items.t: Severe psychiatric reactions may occur, usually within days or weeks; particular care with personal or first-degree family history of severe affective disorder or steroid psychosis.

src.q: Patient/carers should be encouraged to seek medical advice if worrying psychological symptoms develop, especially if depressed mood or suicidal ideation is suspected.
These would include depressive or manic-depressive illness and previous steroid psychosis.

items.t: Infections may be masked; chickenpox and measles can be fatal in immunosuppressed patients (non-immune exposed patients need VZIG within 10 days). Rule out latent amoebiasis or strongyloidiasis in people from the tropics or with unexplained diarrhoea.

src.q: Chickenpox is a normally minor illness but may be fatal in immunosuppressed patients
It is recommended that these are ruled out before initiating corticosteroid therapy particularly in those patients who have spent time in the tropics or those with unexplained diarrhoea.

items.t: Phaeochromocytoma: crisis can be fatal; use only after risk/benefit evaluation. Tumour lysis syndrome in haematological malignancy: monitor high-risk patients.

src.q: Corticosteroids should only be administered to patients with suspected or identified pheochromocytoma after an appropriate risk/benefit evaluation
Patients at high risk of TLS such as patients with high proliferative rate, high tumour burden, and high sensitivity to cytotoxic agents, should be monitored closely

items.t: Blurred vision: consider ophthalmology referral. Hypokalaemia should be corrected before starting (one UK SmPC).

src.q: the patient should be considered for referral to an ophthalmologist for evaluation of possible causes
Hypokalemia should be corrected before corticosteroid treatment initiation.

items.t: Excipients: both UK oral solutions contain sorbitol and maltitol; people with hereditary fructose intolerance should not take them.

src.q: Patients with hereditary fructose intolerance (HFI) should not be given this medicinal product.
Patients with hereditary fructose intolerance (HFI) should not take/be given this medicinal product.

items.t: CYP3A inhibitors (including cobicistat; e.g. ketoconazole, ritonavir, erythromycin, macrolides): raise dexamethasone levels; avoid unless benefit outweighs risk, and monitor.

src.q: The combination should be avoided unless the benefit outweighs the increased risk of systemic corticosteroid side-effects, in which case patients should be monitored for systemic corticosteroid side-effects.
Macrolide antibiotics have been reported to cause a significant decrease in corticosteroid clearance

items.t: CYP3A4 inducers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, barbiturates, rifampicin, rifabutin, ephedrine): lower dexamethasone levels; dose may need increasing. Dexamethasone itself is a moderate CYP3A4 inducer and may lower levels of CYP3A4 substrates.

src.q: may lead to decreased plasma concentrations of dexamethasone and the dose may need to be increased
Dexamethasone is a moderate inducer of CYP 3A4.

items.t: NSAIDs: more peptic ulceration; monitor. Salicylates: steroids increase salicylate clearance; reduce salicylate dose as the steroid is withdrawn; caution with aspirin in hypoprothrombinaemia.

src.q: Patients taking NSAID's should be monitored since the incidence and/or severity of gastro-ulceration may increase.
The renal clearance of salicylates is increased by corticosteroids and therefore, salicylate dosage should be reduced along with steroidal withdrawal.

items.t: Oral anticoagulants (coumarins): effect may change; bleeding risk at high doses or over 10 days; monitor INR closely (one UK SmPC: check on day 8 then every 2 weeks during and after treatment).

src.q: The efficacy of coumarin anticoagulants may be altered by concurrent glucocorticoid therapy and close monitoring of the International Normalised Ratio or prothrombin time is required.
biological investigations on 8th day, then every 2 weeks during treatment and after treatment discontinuation

items.t: Insulin, sulfonylureas, metformin: blood glucose rises (sometimes ketosis); reinforce glucose self-monitoring, especially at the start.

src.q: Insulin, sulfonylureas, metformin: Increase in blood glucose, with sometimes diabetic ketosis, since corticosteroids impair carbohydrate tolerance.
blood and urine self-monitoring should be reinforced by the patient, in particular at the start of treatment

items.t: Potassium-depleting diuretics (loop, thiazide): severe hypokalaemia possible; correct hypokalaemia before starting. Antacids: take at least 2 hours apart. Methotrexate: more haematological toxicity. Antihypertensive and diuretic effects antagonised.

src.q: Concurrent use of potassium-depleting diuretics (e.g. acetazolamide, loop diuretics, thiazide diuretics or carbenoxolone) and glucocorticoids may result in severe hypokalaemia.
glucocorticoids should be taken separately from gastrointestinal topicals, antacids or charcoal, with an interval between treatment of at least two hours
Patients taking methotrexate and dexamethasone have an increased risk of haematological toxicity.

items.t: No dose adjustment needed. Renal insufficiency: particular care and frequent monitoring (fluid retention).

src.q: Elderly, renal impairment, hepatic impairment No dose adjustment is needed.
Particular care is needed when treating patients with renal impairment, hypertention and congestive heart failure.

items.t: No dose adjustment stated for hepatic impairment. Liver failure: particular care and frequent monitoring. Cirrhosis: enhanced steroid effect.

src.q: Elderly, renal impairment, hepatic impairment No dose adjustment is needed.
There is an enhanced effect of corticosteroids in patients with hypothyroidism and in those with cirrhosis.

items.t: UK SmPCs: dexamethasone crosses the placenta; for maternal indications it should not be used in pregnancy unless clearly necessary. Prolonged or repeated use increases intra-uterine growth restriction risk; neonatal adrenal suppression is expected. Monitor pre-eclampsia or fluid retention closely.

src.q: Dexamethasone should, for maternal indications, not be used during pregnancy unless clearly necessary.
Adrenal suppression in the neonate following prenatal glucocorticoid exposure is to be expected.
Patients with pre-eclampsia or fluid retention require close monitoring.

items.t: BUMPS: systemic corticosteroids can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor.

src.q: Systemic corticosteroids can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor.

items.t: One UK SmPC: no data; breastfeeding is discouraged during treatment. Another UK SmPC: decide whether to stop breastfeeding or therapy, weighing benefits.

src.q: Because corticosteroids are in general excreted into breast milk, and given the lack of experience, breast feeding is discouraged during Dexamethasone therapy.
A decision on whether to continue/discontinue breast feeding or to continue/discontinue therapy with dexamethasone should be made

items.t: SPS: can be used with caution; alternatives (e.g. prednisolone) preferred. Oral doses up to 8 mg daily unlikely to affect the infant; may reduce milk production.

src.q: Dexamethasone (including local injection) can be used with caution, although there is no published evidence for use in breastfeeding. Alternatives are preferred.

Oral doses up to 8mg daily are unlikely to cause adverse effects in the infant. There have been reports of a possible decrease in prolactin release after administration which may reduce milk production.

items.t: May cause menstrual irregularity or amenorrhoea; changes in sperm motility and number reported.

src.q: Menstrual irregularities and amenorrhoea
Increased or decreased motility and number of spermatozoa

items.t: Psychiatric reactions are common (mood change, depression, suicidal thoughts, psychosis, insomnia). Other effects (frequency not known): infections, raised glucose, fluid retention, hypokalaemia, dyspepsia, Cushingoid features, osteoporosis, myopathy, skin thinning, weight gain.

src.q: Reactions are common and may occur in both adults and children.
Sodium retention, Fluid retention, Hypokalaemia, Alkalosis hypokalaemic

items.t: Too rapid dose reduction after prolonged use can cause acute adrenal insufficiency, hypotension and death.

src.q: Too rapid a reduction of dexamethasone dosage following prolonged treatment can lead to acute adrenal insufficiency, hypotension and death.

items.t: Peptic ulcer with haemorrhage or perforation; anaphylaxis/angioedema; severe infection; severe psychiatric reactions (estimated 5-6% in adults); tumour lysis syndrome (very rare).

src.q: Gastric ulcer (haemorrhage), Duodenal ulcer (haemorrhage), dyspepsia, peptic ulcer perforation
In adults, the frequency of severe reactions has been estimated to be 5-6%.

items.t: SPS (corticosteroids): baseline blood pressure, weight, BMI, HbA1c, potassium, triglycerides, eye examination and risk factor assessment; height in children.

src.q: Before starting Required Baseline Blood pressure Weight Body mass index Bone mineral density
Serum potassium Triglycerides Risk factor assessment

items.t: SPS ongoing (long-term): HbA1c every 3 months; eye examination, potassium and triglycerides every 6-12 months; blood pressure, weight and signs of adrenal suppression periodically; children's height every 6 months.

src.q: Every 3 months HbA1c
Children and adolescents Every 6 months Height

items.t: Frequent review to titrate the dose; if no favourable response within a couple of days, continuing is undesirable (one UK SmPC).

src.q: If no favourable response is noted within a couple of days, continuation of glucocorticoid therapy is undesirable.

items.t: Oral; preferably in the morning (evening doses cause more adrenal suppression). Use an oral syringe for small doses. One UK SmPC: may be given via NG or PEG tube.

src.q: Systemic dexamethasone administered in the evening is more likely to cause clinically significant HPA suppression.
Alternatively, this product is suitable for administration via nasogastric (NG) or percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tubes.

items.t: Separate from antacids by at least 2 hours.

src.q: glucocorticoids should be taken separately from gastrointestinal topicals, antacids or charcoal, with an interval between treatment of at least two hours

items.t: Carry a steroid treatment card; do not stop suddenly after longer courses.

src.q: Patients should carry 'steroid treatment' cards

items.t: Avoid contact with chickenpox, shingles or measles if not immune; seek urgent advice if exposed. Report worrying mood changes.

src.q: Patients (or parents of children) without a definite history of chickenpox should be advised to avoid close personal contact with chickenpox or herpes zoster, and if exposed they should seek urgent medical attention.

items.t: Mood changes or visual disturbance may affect driving.

src.q: If affected, caution should be exercised in driving and operating machinery.

restrictions.note: No UK product information found.
