items.t: Tablets 50 mg (potassium): rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthrosis, low back pain, migraine attacks, acute musculoskeletal disorders and trauma, ankylosing spondylitis, acute gout, pain and inflammation after orthopaedic, dental and minor surgery, pyrophosphate arthropathy.

src.q: Rheumatoid arthritis Osteoarthrosis Low back pain Migraine attacks Acute musculo-skeletal disorders and trauma
Ankylosing spondylitis Acute gout Control of pain and inflammation in orthopaedic, dental and other minor surgery Pyrophosphate arthropathy

items.t: Gastro-resistant tablets 50 mg (sodium): pain and inflammation in rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, low back pain, acute musculoskeletal disorders and trauma, fractures, ankylosing spondylitis, acute gout, and dental, orthopaedic and other minor surgery.

src.q: Diclofenac is indicated for the relief of pain and inflammation in conditions such rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, and low back pain
The product is also indicated for the relief of pain from fractures, ankylosing spondylitis and acute gout

items.t: Prolonged-release tablets and suppositories (adults): pain and inflammation in arthritic conditions (rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute gout), acute musculoskeletal disorders, and painful conditions after trauma or minor surgery.

src.q: Relief of all grades of pain and inflammation in a wide range of conditions, including: (i) arthritic conditions: rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute gout
Relief of all grades of pain and inflammation in a wide range of conditions, including: (i) arthritic conditions: rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute gout

items.t: Gels: local relief of pain and inflammation in tendon, ligament, muscle and joint trauma (sprains, strains, bruises) and localised soft-tissue rheumatism. The 1.16% gel is also licensed for osteoarthritis of superficial joints such as the knee; the 2.32% gel for non-serious arthritic pain.

src.q: For the local symptomatic relief of pain and inflammation in: - trauma of the tendons, ligaments, muscles and joints, eg due to sprains, strains and bruises
For the treatment of osteoarthritis of superficial joints such as the knee.
For the relief of pain of non-serious arthritic conditions.

items.t: MHRA: oral diclofenac is prescription-only and must not be sold without a prescription; topical forms (gel, cream) remain available over the counter.

src.q: oral diclofenac must not be sold without prescription
topical formulations of diclofenac (eg gel and cream) remain available for sale over the counter

items.t: Tablets 50 mg (potassium): recommended only for short-term treatment.

src.q: Use of Voltarol Rapid tablets 50mg are recommended only for short term treatment.

items.t: Gels: review treatment after 14 days for soft-tissue injury and after 4 weeks for osteoarthritis (1.16%); the 2.32% gel can be used for up to 21 days under pharmacy supervision and not longer unless a doctor recommends it.

src.q: It is recommended that the treatment be reviewed after 14 days in these indications.
In the treatment of osteoarthritis, therapy should be reviewed after 4 weeks.
The gel can be used for up to 21 days under pharmacy supervision.
Do not use for more than 21 days unless recommended by a doctor.

items.t: Tablets 50 mg (potassium), adults: 100-150 mg daily in 2 or 3 divided doses; milder cases 75-100 mg daily in 2 or 3 divided doses.

src.q: The recommended daily dose is 100-150mg in two or three divided doses. For milder cases, 75-100 mg daily in two or three divided doses is usually sufficient.

items.t: Tablets 50 mg (potassium), migraine: 50 mg at the first sign of an attack; a further 50 mg after 2 hours if relief is not enough, then 50 mg every 4-6 hours if needed; no more than 200 mg in a day.

src.q: In migraine an initial dose of 50 mg should be taken at the first signs of an impending attack.
further doses of 50 mg may be taken at intervals of 4-6 hours, not exceeding a total dose of 200 mg per day

items.t: Gastro-resistant tablets 50 mg (sodium), adults: 75-150 mg daily in 2-3 divided doses; maximum 150 mg daily.

src.q: Adults 75 - 150 mg daily in 2 -3 divided doses.
The recommended maximum daily dose of diclofenac sodium is 150 mg.

items.t: Prolonged-release 100 mg, adults: one tablet once daily; can be raised to 150 mg daily by adding conventional 25 mg or 50 mg diclofenac sodium; maximum 150 mg daily.

src.q: One 100 mg diclofenac sodium prolonged-release tablet daily.
The recommended maximum daily dose of diclofenac sodium is 150mg.

items.t: Suppositories, adults: 75-150 mg daily in divided doses; the 100 mg suppository may be given once daily, usually at night. Maximum 150 mg daily, including any tablets given at the same time.

src.q: Adults: 75-150mg daily, in divided doses (25mg, 50mg and 100mg suppositories only).
The recommended maximum daily dose of Voltarol is 150mg.
100mg suppositories may also be given as a once daily treatment, usually at night.

items.t: 1.16% gel, adults and children 14 years and over: 2-4 g rubbed in 3-4 times a day, depending on the area.

src.q: 2- 4g (a circular shaped mass approximately 2.0-2.5cm in diameter) of gel should be applied 3 - 4 times a day

items.t: 2.32% gel, adults and children 14 years and over: 2-4 g twice a day (morning and evening); maximum 8 g a day.

src.q: of gel should be applied 2 times a day (preferably morning and evening). The maximum daily dose is 8g.

items.t: Elderly: use with particular caution; lowest effective dose in frail or low body-weight patients; monitor for GI bleeding.

src.q: it is recommended that the lowest effective dosage be used in frail elderly patients or those with a low body weight
the patient should be monitored for GI bleeding during NSAID therapy

items.t: Tablets 50 mg (potassium): not recommended under 14 years. Over 14 years: 75-100 mg daily in 2 or 3 divided doses. Use in migraine not established in children.

src.q: Voltarol Rapid tablets are not recommended for children under 14 years of age.
For children over 14 years of age, the recommended daily dose is 75-100 mg in two or three divided doses.

items.t: Gastro-resistant tablets 50 mg (sodium): not recommended for use in children (the SmPC gives no age limit).

src.q: Diclofenac Sodium 50 mg Gastro-resistant Tablets are not recommended for use in children.

items.t: Prolonged-release 100 mg tablets: not suitable for children (the SmPC gives no age limit).

src.q: This medicine is not suitable for children.

items.t: Suppositories: the 50 mg and 100 mg strengths are not for children. Only the 12.5 mg and 25 mg strengths are licensed in children: juvenile chronic arthritis (1-12 years) 1-3 mg/kg per day in 2 or 3 doses; post-operative pain (6-12 years) 1-2 mg/kg per day in divided doses for up to 4 days.

src.q: Voltarol 50mg and 100mg suppositories are not indicated for use in children.
Children (aged 1-12 years) with juvenile chronic arthritis: 1-3mg/kg per day divided into 2 or 3 doses (12.5mg and 25mg suppositories only).
Treatment of acute post-operative pain should be limited to 4 days treatment

items.t: 1.16% gel: contraindicated under 14 years. 2.32% gel: insufficient data under 14 years. From 14 years, see a doctor if needed for more than 7 days or if symptoms worsen.

src.q: The use in children and adolescents aged less than 14 years is contraindicated.
There are insufficient data on efficacy and safety available for the children and adolescents below 14 years of age

items.t: All forms: hypersensitivity to diclofenac; asthma, angioedema, urticaria or acute rhinitis triggered by aspirin, ibuprofen or other NSAIDs; third trimester of pregnancy.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or any of the excipients.

diclofenac is also contraindicated in patients in whom attacks of asthma, angioedema, urticaria or acute rhinitis are precipitated by ibuprofen, acetylsalicylic acid or other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
Hypersensitivity to diclofenac or any of the excipients Third trimester of pregnancy.

items.t: Tablets and suppositories: active gastric or intestinal ulcer, bleeding or perforation; history of GI bleeding or perforation related to previous NSAIDs; active or recurrent peptic ulcer/haemorrhage; hepatic failure; renal failure. The gastro-resistant tablet SmPC words this as severe hepatic, renal or cardiac failure.

src.q: Active, gastric or intestinal ulcer, bleeding or perforation.
History of gastrointestinal bleeding or perforation, relating to previous NSAID therapy
Active, or history of recurrent peptic ulcer/haemorrhage (two or more distinct episodes of proven ulceration or bleeding)
Hepatic failure Renal failure
Severe hepatic, renal or cardiac failure (see section 4.4).

items.t: Tablets and suppositories: established congestive heart failure (NYHA II-IV), ischaemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease or cerebrovascular disease. MHRA: switch such patients to another treatment at their next routine appointment.

src.q: Established congestive heart failure (NYHA II-IV), ischemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease and/or cerebrovascular disease.
Patients with these conditions should be switched to an alternative treatment at their next routine appointment.

items.t: Suppositories: also contraindicated in proctitis.

src.q: or other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Proctitis

items.t: 1.16% gel: contraindicated in children under 14 years. 2.32% gel: also lists hypersensitivity to aspirin or other NSAIDs.

src.q: The use in children and adolescents aged less than 14 years is contraindicated.
Hypersensitivity to diclofenac, acetylsalicylic acid or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

items.t: GI bleeding, ulceration or perforation can be fatal and can occur at any time; risk rises with dose, ulcer history and age. Use the lowest dose; consider a PPI or misoprostol in high-risk patients and with low-dose aspirin. Stop if GI bleeding or ulceration occurs.

src.q: If gastrointestinal bleeding or ulceration occurs in patients receiving diclofenac, the drug should be withdrawn.
Combination therapy with protective agents (e.g. misoprostol or proton pump inhibitors) should be considered for these patients

items.t: Cardiovascular: increased risk of arterial thrombotic events (MI, stroke), especially at 150 mg daily and long term. NYHA I heart failure or significant CV risk factors (hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, diabetes, smoking): use only after careful consideration; lowest dose, shortest time.

src.q: should only be treated with diclofenac after careful consideration
particularly at high dose (150mg daily) and in long term treatment
Diclofenac treatment should only be initiated after careful consideration for patients with significant risk factors for cardiovascular events

items.t: Renal: fluid retention and oedema; particular caution in impaired cardiac or renal function, hypertension, the elderly, with diuretics or other drugs affecting renal function, and in volume depletion (e.g. around major surgery). Monitor renal function in these patients.

src.q: particular caution is called for in patients with impaired cardiac or renal function, history of hypertension, the elderly
Monitoring of renal function is recommended as a precautionary measure when using diclofenac in such cases.

items.t: Hepatic: close surveillance in hepatic impairment; liver enzymes may rise and hepatitis can occur without warning. Stop if liver tests persist or worsen or liver disease develops. Hepatic porphyria: may trigger an attack.

src.q: Close medical surveillance is required when prescribing Voltarol to patients with impairment of hepatic function
Hepatitis may occur with diclofenac without prodromal symptoms.
Caution is called for when using diclofenac in patients with hepatic porphyria, since it may trigger an attack.

items.t: Asthma, seasonal allergic rhinitis, nasal polyps, COPD or chronic respiratory infection: NSAID reactions are more frequent; special precaution (readiness for emergency). Diclofenac can cause bronchospasm in asthma, including from the gels. SPS: use oral or topical NSAIDs with caution in asthma and monitor.

src.q: special precaution is recommended in such patients (readiness for emergency)
diclofenac and other NSAIDs can precipitate bronchospasm if administered to patients suffering from or with a previous history of, bronchial asthma
Use oral or topical NSAIDs with caution and monitor for symptoms such as exacerbation of asthma.

items.t: Severe skin reactions (SJS, TEN, exfoliative dermatitis, generalised bullous fixed drug eruption), mostly in the first month: stop at the first rash, mucosal lesion or other sign of hypersensitivity. Kounis syndrome (allergic MI) can occur.

src.q: Voltarol should be discontinued at the first appearance of skin rash, mucosal lesions or any other signs of hypersensitivity.
Hypersensitivity reactions can also progress to Kounis syndrome

items.t: Ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease: close surveillance and caution (may worsen). After GI surgery: caution (anastomotic leak). SLE or mixed connective tissue disease: increased risk of aseptic meningitis. Haemostasis defects: monitor carefully. May mask infection.

src.q: Close medical surveillance and caution should be exercised in patients with ulcerative colitis, or with Crohn's disease
Close medical surveillance and caution are recommended when using diclofenac after gastro-intestinal surgery.
Patients with defects of haemostasis, bleeding diathesis or haematological abnormalities should be carefully monitored.

items.t: Avoid with other systemic NSAIDs, including COX-2 inhibitors.

src.q: The concomitant use of Voltarol with systemic NSAIDs including cyclooxygenase-2 selective inhibitors should be avoided

items.t: Gels: systemic effects possible with large amounts over large areas or long use. Apply only to intact skin; not on wounds, eyes or mucous membranes; not with airtight occlusive dressings. Stop if a rash develops; avoid excessive sunlight. Isolated GI bleeding reports in patients with a significant history. Fire hazard: fabric in contact with the gel burns more easily.

src.q: Voltarol Emulgel should be applied only to intact, non-diseased skin and not to skin wounds or open injuries.
Discontinue the treatment if a skin rash develops after applying the product.
Some possibility of gastro-intestinal bleeding in those with a significant history of this condition has been reported in isolated cases.
Fabric (clothing, bedding, dressings etc) that has been in contact with this product burns more easily and is a serious fire hazard.

items.t: Tablets contain sucrose: patients with hereditary fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take them.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take this medicine.
This medicine contains sucrose.

items.t: Gastro-resistant tablets contain lactose: patients with galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take them.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, the Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: Other NSAIDs (including COX-2 inhibitors) and corticosteroids: higher risk of GI bleeding or ulceration; avoid two or more NSAIDs together. Gels: caution with systemic NSAIDs.

src.q: Co-administration of diclofenac with other systemic NSAIDs or corticosteroids may increase the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding or ulceration. Avoid concomitant use of two or more NSAIDs
Concomitant use of systemic NSAIDs should be cautioned

items.t: Anticoagulants (e.g. warfarin) and antiplatelets (e.g. aspirin): increased bleeding risk; caution and close monitoring. SSRIs: increased GI bleeding risk.

src.q: Caution is recommended since concomitant administration could increase the risk of bleeding
close monitoring of such patients is required
Concomitant administration of SSRI's may increase the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding

items.t: Diuretics and antihypertensives (e.g. beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors): reduced antihypertensive effect; give with caution, monitor blood pressure, keep hydrated and consider renal monitoring, especially with diuretics and ACE inhibitors (nephrotoxicity).

src.q: the combination should be administered with caution and patients, especially the elderly, should have their blood pressure periodically monitored
particularly for diuretics and ACE inhibitors due to the increased risk of nephrotoxicity

items.t: Potassium-sparing diuretics, trimethoprim, ciclosporin or tacrolimus: raised serum potassium; monitor potassium frequently.

src.q: Concomitant treatment with potassium-sparing diuretics, ciclosporin, tacrolimus or trimethoprim may be associated with increased serum potassium levels, which should therefore be monitored frequently

items.t: Methotrexate: serious toxicity reported when given within 24 hours of an NSAID (reduced renal clearance); caution.

src.q: Caution is recommended when NSAIDs, including diclofenac, are administered less than 24 hours before treatment with methotrexate

items.t: Antidiabetics: isolated reports of hypo- and hyperglycaemia needing dose changes; monitor blood glucose. Quinolone antibiotics: convulsions possible; caution.

src.q: monitoring of the blood glucose level is recommended as a precautionary measure during concomitant therapy
Convulsions may occur due to an interaction between quinolones and NSAIDs.

items.t: Gastro-resistant tablets: avoid two or more NSAIDs, including aspirin; potassium-sparing drugs: monitor potassium frequently.

src.q: Avoid concomitant use of two or more NSAIDs (including aspirin) as this may increase the risk of adverse effects
Concomitant treatment with potassium-sparing drugs may be associated with increased serum potassium levels, which should therefore be monitored frequently

items.t: Fluconazole: caution. The diclofenac SmPCs advise caution with potent CYP2C9 inhibitors (example: voriconazole) because diclofenac exposure can rise significantly; a UK celecoxib SmPC describes fluconazole as a potent CYP2C9 inhibitor.

src.q: Caution is recommended when co-prescribing diclofenac with potent CYP2C9 inhibitors (such as voriconazole)
fluconazole, a potent CYP2C9 inhibitor

items.t: Not in this tool's list but in the SmPC: lithium and digoxin (monitor levels), phenytoin (monitor levels), ciclosporin (use lower diclofenac dose), tacrolimus, colestipol/colestyramine (give diclofenac 1 hour before or 4-6 hours after), mifepristone (no NSAIDs for 8-12 days after), potent CYP2C9 inhibitors such as voriconazole (caution).

src.q: Monitoring of the serum lithium level is recommended.
Monitoring of the serum digoxin level is recommended.
it is recommended to administer diclofenac at least one hour before or 4 to 6 hours after administration of colestipol/ cholestyramine
NSAIDs should not be used for 8-12 days after mifepristone administration
Caution is recommended when co-prescribing diclofenac with potent CYP2C9 inhibitors (such as voriconazole)

items.t: Gels: interactions are very unlikely because systemic absorption is very low; no known interactions.

src.q: Since systemic absorption of diclofenac from a topical application is very low such interactions are very unlikely.

items.t: Tablets and suppositories: contraindicated in renal failure (no numeric threshold given). Mild to moderate renal impairment: caution; no specific dose adjustment can be recommended.

src.q: Voltarol Rapid is contraindicated in patients with renal failure
Caution is advised when administering Voltarol Rapid to patients with mild to moderate renal impairment

items.t: MHRA: patients at risk of renal impairment or failure (particularly the elderly) should avoid NSAIDs if possible; if used, monitor renal function carefully.

src.q: patients at risk of renal impairment or renal failure (particularly elderly people) should avoid NSAIDs if possible
the renal function of such patients should be carefully monitored during NSAID treatment

items.t: Tablets and suppositories: contraindicated in hepatic failure. Mild to moderate hepatic impairment: caution with close surveillance; no specific dose adjustment can be recommended.

src.q: Voltarol Rapid is contraindicated in patients with hepatic failure
Caution is advised when administering Voltarol Rapid to patients with mild to moderate hepatic impairment

items.t: All forms, including the gels: contraindicated in the third trimester (fetal ductus arteriosus closure and renal dysfunction; prolonged bleeding and delayed labour).

src.q: Consequently, Voltarol is contraindicated during the third trimester of pregnancy.
Consequently, diclofenac is contraindicated during the third trimester of pregnancy

items.t: First and second trimesters: do not give unless clearly necessary; lowest dose, shortest time. Systemic forms from week 20: oligohydramnios and ductus constriction reported; consider antenatal monitoring after several days of use and stop if found.

src.q: during the first and second trimester of pregnancy, Voltarol should not be given unless clearly necessary
Antenatal monitoring for oligohydramnios and ductus arteriosus constriction should be considered after exposure to diclofenac for several days from gestational week 20 onward.
During the first and second trimester of pregnancy, diclofenac should not be given unless clearly necessary.

items.t: MHRA (systemic NSAIDs): avoid from week 20 unless clinically required, at the lowest dose for the shortest time; contraindicated after 28 weeks. The MHRA review did not cover topical NSAIDs: follow the gel product information.

src.q: avoid prescribing systemic NSAIDs from week 20 of pregnancy unless clinically required and prescribe the lowest dose for the shortest time in these circumstances
systemic (oral and injectable) NSAIDs are contraindicated during the last trimester (after 28 weeks) of pregnancy
The review did not examine topical NSAIDs (gels and creams containing NSAIDs).

items.t: SPS: ibuprofen is the preferred NSAID in pregnancy; systemic NSAIDs from week 20 usually for no longer than 3 days. BUMPS: diclofenac is not advised unless prescribed by a doctor, especially from 20 weeks.

src.q: Ibuprofen is the preferred NSAID in pregnancy.
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration, which is usually no longer than three days.
Use of diclofenac during pregnancy is not advised unless prescribed by a doctor, especially if you are 20 or more weeks pregnant.

items.t: Tablets and suppositories SmPCs: passes into milk in small amounts; should not be given during breastfeeding.

src.q: diclofenac should not be administered during breast feeding in order to avoid undesirable effects in the infant

items.t: SPS (less restrictive): diclofenac is an NSAID of choice in breastfeeding; oral, rectal and topical forms can be used if clinically appropriate; negligible amounts in milk. Monitor the infant for vomiting and diarrhoea.

src.q: Diclofenac can be used during breastfeeding if clinically appropriate.
Oral, rectal, and parenteral diclofenac preparations can be used during breastfeeding.
Topical and ophthalmic diclofenac preparations can also be used during breastfeeding.
As a precaution, monitor infants for vomiting and diarrhoea.

items.t: Gels: use during breastfeeding only on healthcare professional advice; do not apply to the breasts or to large areas or for long periods.

src.q: the product should only be used during lactation under advice from a healthcare professional
Voltarol Emulgel should not be applied on the breasts of nursing mothers, nor elsewhere on large areas of skin or for a prolonged period of time

items.t: Systemic forms: may impair female fertility; not recommended in women trying to conceive; consider stopping in women with difficulty conceiving or under fertility investigation. Gels: no human fertility data.

src.q: the use of diclofenac may impair female fertility and is not recommended in women attempting to conceive
There are no data available on the use of topical formulations of diclofenac and its effects on fertility in humans.

items.t: Tablets and suppositories, common: headache, dizziness, vertigo, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, dyspepsia, abdominal pain, flatulence, anorexia, raised transaminases, rash.

src.q: Common Rare Very rare Unknown Headache, dizziness.
Common Rare Very rare Unknown Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, dyspepsia, abdominal pain, flatulence, anorexia.
Common Rare Very rare Transaminases increased.
Common Rare Very rare Not Known Rash.

items.t: Gels, common: rash, eczema, erythema, dermatitis (including contact dermatitis), pruritus.

src.q: Common: Rash, eczema, erythema, dermatitis (including dermatitis contact), pruritus

items.t: GI ulcer, bleeding or perforation (sometimes fatal, particularly in the elderly): stop the drug.

src.q: gastrointestinal ulcer with or without bleeding or perforation (sometimes fatal particularly in the elderly)
If gastrointestinal bleeding or ulceration occurs in patients receiving diclofenac, the drug should be withdrawn.

items.t: Arterial thrombotic events (MI, stroke): patients should see a doctor immediately if chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness or slurred speech occur.

src.q: Patients should be instructed to see a physician immediately in case of such an event.
chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness, slurring of speech

items.t: Severe skin reactions (SJS, TEN, exfoliative dermatitis): very rare; stop at first rash. Anaphylaxis and angioedema (rare/very rare).

src.q: Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), dermatitis exfoliative
Hypersensitivity, anaphylactic and anaphylactoid reactions (including hypotension and shock).

items.t: Hepatitis, fulminant hepatitis and hepatic failure (rare/very rare); acute renal failure and nephrotic syndrome (very rare); blood dyscrasias (very rare); aseptic meningitis.

src.q: Fulminant hepatitis, hepatic necrosis, hepatic failure.
Acute renal failure, haematuria, proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, interstitial nephritis, renal papillary necrosis.
Thrombocytopenia, leucopoenia, anaemia (including haemolytic and aplastic anaemia), agranulocytosis.

items.t: SPS baseline (systemic NSAIDs): blood pressure, eGFR, full blood count, serum creatinine; LFTs.

src.q: Before starting Consider Baseline Blood pressure
Estimated glomerular filtration rate Full blood count Serum creatinine Liver function tests

items.t: SPS after starting or a dose change: eGFR or serum creatinine and full blood count within 2 weeks; haemoglobin within 4 weeks.

src.q: After started or dose changed Consider Within 2 weeks Estimated glomerular filtration rate or Serum creatinine (for creatinine clearance) Full blood count
Within 4 weeks Haemoglobin

items.t: SmPC, prolonged treatment: regular liver function tests and blood counts; renal function in at-risk patients; blood pressure with antihypertensives; blood glucose with antidiabetics.

src.q: During prolonged treatment with Diclofenac, regular monitoring of hepatic function is indicated as a precautionary measure.
During prolonged treatment with diclofenac, as with other NSAIDs, monitoring of the blood count is recommended.

items.t: Stop if GI bleeding or ulceration, at the first sign of skin rash or hypersensitivity, or if abnormal liver tests persist or worsen.

src.q: If abnormal liver function tests persist or worsen, clinical signs or symptoms consistent with liver disease develop or if other manifestations occur (eosinophilia, rash), Voltarol should be discontinued.

items.t: Tablets: take with fluid, preferably with or after food. Prolonged-release tablets: swallow whole.

src.q: It is recommended that the tablets be taken with fluid, preferably with or after food.
To be taken whole with liquid, preferably with or after food.

items.t: Gastro-resistant tablets: swallow whole with water; do not crush or chew; preferably with or after food.

src.q: Swallow tablets whole with some water. Do not crush or chew. To be taken preferably with or after food.

items.t: Suppositories: rectal use only, not by mouth; insert well into the rectum, preferably after passing stools.

src.q: Not to be taken by mouth, as per rectal administration only. The suppositories should be inserted well into the rectum. It is recommended to insert the suppositories after passing stools.

items.t: Gels: for skin use only; rub gently into the affected area, then wipe and wash hands (unless treating the hands); let dry before bandaging.

src.q: The gel is applied to the affected parts of the body and gently rubbed into the skin.
Before applying a bandage, the gel should be left to dry for a few minutes on the skin.

items.t: Report unusual abdominal symptoms, especially bleeding (black stools, vomiting blood).

src.q: Patients with a history of GI toxicity, particularly when elderly, should report any unusual abdominal symptoms (especially GI bleeding).

items.t: Seek medical help at once for chest pain, breathlessness, weakness or slurred speech.

src.q: Patients should remain alert for the signs and symptoms of serious arteriothrombotic events

items.t: Do not drive or use machines if dizziness, drowsiness, vertigo or visual disturbance occur.

src.q: should refrain from driving or operating machinery

items.t: Gels: do not smoke or go near naked flames (severe burn risk); fabric that has touched the gel burns more easily. Avoid excessive sunlight.

src.q: Instruct patients not to smoke or go near naked flames - risk of severe burns.
Patients should be warned against excessive exposure to sunlight in order to reduce the incidence of photosensitivity.

items.t: Functional conditions involving smooth muscle spasm of the gastrointestinal tract.

src.q: smooth muscle antispasmodic primarily indicated for treatment of functional conditions involving smooth muscle spasm of the gastrointestinal tract

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction stated in the UK SmPCs accessed (three UK 10 mg and 20 mg tablet SmPCs).

items.t: Adults (12 years and over): 10-20 mg three times daily, before or after meals (one or two 10 mg tablets, or one 20 mg tablet, three times daily).

src.q: One to two 10 mg tablets, three times daily, before or after meals; alternatively, for those patients on a 20 mg dose, one 20 mg tablet, three times daily, before or after meals.

items.t: Another UK SmPC (20 mg tablet): adults and children over 12 years, 20 mg (1 tablet) three times a day before or after meals.

src.q: Adults and children over 12 years: 1 tablet three times a day before or after meals.

items.t: One UK SmPC: children 2-12 years, 10 mg (one 10 mg tablet) three times daily, before or after meals. Another UK SmPC (20 mg tablet) gives doses only for children over 12 years.

src.q: Children (2 years - 12 years): One 10 mg tablet, three times daily, before or after meals.
Adults and children over 12 years: 1 tablet three times a day before or after meals.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to dicycloverine or any excipient; known idiosyncrasy to dicycloverine.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1. Known idiosyncrasy to dicycloverine hydrochloride.

items.t: Glaucoma (known or suspected) or prostatic hypertrophy: use with caution.

src.q: Products containing dicycloverine hydrochloride should be used with caution in any patient with or suspected of having glaucoma or prostatic hypertrophy.

items.t: Hiatus hernia with reflux oesophagitis: use with care (anticholinergics may make it worse).

src.q: Use with care in patients with hiatus hernia associated with reflux oesophagitis because anticholinergic drugs may aggravate the condition.

items.t: Contains lactose: patients with galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take it. One 20 mg tablet also contains sucrose and glucose: not for hereditary fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, the Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take this medicine.

items.t: No interaction studies have been performed; the UK SmPCs list no interactions.

src.q: No interaction studies have been performed.
other forms of interaction None stated

renal.note: No renal impairment advice in the UK SmPCs accessed (three UK 10 mg and 20 mg tablet SmPCs).

hepatic.note: No hepatic impairment advice in the UK SmPCs accessed (three UK 10 mg and 20 mg tablet SmPCs).

items.t: SmPCs: studies (doses up to 40 mg/day) have not shown more fetal abnormalities after first-trimester use. One SmPC: use only if clearly needed; another: only if benefit outweighs risk. No BUMPS leaflet for dicycloverine found.

src.q: have not shown that dicycloverine hydrochloride increases the risk of foetal abnormalities if administered during the first trimester of pregnancy
the drug should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed
the drug should be used during pregnancy only if the benefit outweighs the risk

items.t: SmPC: not known if it passes into milk; use with caution.

src.q: It is not known whether dicycloverine is secreted in human milk.
caution should be exercised when dicycloverine is administered to a nursing mother

items.t: SPS: not recommended during breastfeeding; small amounts pass into milk and a possible case of apnoea was reported in a breastfed infant.

src.q: Dicycloverine (dicyclomine) is not recommended for use during breastfeeding.
a possible case of apnoea was reported in a breastfed infant exposed to dicycloverine, so use during breastfeeding is not recommended

items.t: Animal studies at high doses showed no impaired fertility.

src.q: have revealed no evidence of impaired fertility or harm to the foetus due to dicycloverine

items.t: No common effects listed; side effects are seldom. In susceptible people: dry mouth, thirst, dizziness. Rarely: fatigue, sedation, blurred vision, rash, constipation, anorexia, nausea and vomiting, headache, dysuria.

src.q: However, in susceptible individuals, dry mouth, thirst and dizziness may occur.
On rare occasions, fatigue, sedation, blurred vision, rash, constipation, anorexia, nausea and vomiting, headache and dysuria have also been reported.

adverseSerious.note: No serious adverse effects needing urgent action are listed in the UK tablet SmPCs accessed (three UK 10 mg and 20 mg tablet SmPCs).

monitoring.note: No monitoring requirements stated in the UK SmPCs accessed (three UK 10 mg and 20 mg tablet SmPCs); no SPS monitoring page found.

items.t: Take three times a day, before or after meals.

src.q: 1 tablet three times a day before or after meals

items.t: Rarely causes dizziness, tiredness, sleepiness or blurred vision: do not drive or use machines if affected.

src.q: In rare cases it may cause dizziness, tiredness, or sleepiness, or blurred vision, and patients should be cautioned not to drive or operate machinery if affected.

items.t: Prophylaxis and treatment of angina pectoris (60 mg tablet).

src.q: 4.1 Therapeutic indications Prophylaxis and treatment of Angina Pectoris

items.t: Other UK diltiazem products (once-daily prolonged-release capsules) are also licensed for mild to moderate hypertension.

src.q: VIAZEM XL is indicated for the management of stable angina pectoris and the treatment of mild to moderate hypertension.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction stated in the UK diltiazem 60 mg tablet SmPC.

items.t: Adults: 60 mg three times daily; may increase to 360 mg/day in divided doses. Up to 480 mg/day has been used (especially unstable angina).

src.q: The usual dose is one tablet (60 mg) three times daily.
If necessary, the divided dose may be increased to 360mg/day. Higher doses up to 480mg/day have been used with benefit in some patients especially in unstable angina.

items.t: Elderly and hepatic or renal impairment: start 60 mg twice daily; measure heart rate regularly and do not increase the dose if heart rate is below 50 beats per minute.

src.q: The recommended starting dose is one tablet (60 mg) twice daily. The heart rate should be measured regularly in these groups of patients and the dose should not be increased if the heart rate falls below 50 beats per minute.

items.t: Safety and efficacy not established; not recommended for children.

src.q: Safety and efficacy in children have not been established. Therefore, diltiazem is not recommended for use in children.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to diltiazem or excipients.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to diltiazem or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Sick sinus syndrome or second/third-degree AV block without a functioning pacemaker; severe bradycardia (below 50 beats per minute); left ventricular failure with pulmonary stasis.

src.q: Sick sinus syndrome, 2nd or 3rd degree AV block in patients without a functioning pacemaker. Severe bradycardia (less than 50 beats per minute). Left ventricular failure with pulmonary stasis.

items.t: Breastfeeding (lactation).

src.q: Left ventricular failure with pulmonary stasis. Lactation.

items.t: With dantrolene infusion, ivabradine, lomitapide or asunaprevir.

src.q: Concurrent use with dantrolene infusion (see section 4.5). Combination with ivabradine (see section 4.5). Concurrent use with lomitapide (see section 4.5). Concurrent use with asunaprevir (see section 4.5).

items.t: Close observation in reduced left ventricular function, bradycardia, first-degree AV block or prolonged PR interval (risk of complete block). Monitor closely, especially heart rate, at the start.

src.q: Close observation is necessary in patients with reduced left ventricular function, bradycardia (risk of exacerbation) or with a 1st degree AV block or prolonged PR interval detected on the electrocardiogram
close monitoring, particularly of heart rate, should be carried out at the beginning of treatment.

items.t: Elderly, renal or hepatic insufficiency: plasma levels may rise.

src.q: Increase of plasma concentrations of diltiazem may be observed in the elderly and patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency.

items.t: Acute renal failure has been reported in cardiac patients (reduced LV function, severe bradycardia or severe hypotension); monitor renal function carefully.

src.q: Cases of acute renal failure secondary to decreased renal perfusion have been reported in patients with cardiac disease
Carefully monitoring renal function is advised.

items.t: Bronchospasm, including asthma aggravation, especially with bronchial hyper-reactivity; monitor respiratory function.

src.q: The use of diltiazem may induce bronchospasm, including asthma aggravation, especially in patients with preexisting bronchial hyper-reactivity.
Patients should be monitored for signs and symptoms of respiratory impairment during diltiazem therapy.

items.t: Diabetes (latent or manifest): monitor carefully (blood glucose may rise). Intestinal obstruction risk: use with caution. Mood changes including depression: consider stopping.

src.q: Careful monitoring is necessary in patients with latent or manifest diabetes mellitus due to a possible increase in blood glucose.
it should be used with caution in patients at risk of developing an intestinal obstruction.
In such cases, drug discontinuation should be considered.

items.t: General anaesthesia: inform the anaesthetist (additive cardiac depression).

src.q: In the case of general anaesthesia, the anaesthetist must be informed that the patient is taking diltiazem.

items.t: Galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption: should not take (contains lactose).

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, the Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: Beta-blockers: risk of rhythm disturbances (marked bradycardia, sinus arrest), SA/AV conduction problems and heart failure; use only with close clinical and ECG monitoring, especially at the start. Increased risk of depression reported.

src.q: Possibility of rhythm disturbances (pronounced bradycardia, sinus arrest), sino-atrial and atrio-ventricular conduction disturbances and heart failure (synergistic effect).
Such a combination must only be used under close clinical and ECG monitoring, particularly at the beginning of treatment.

items.t: Statins metabolised by CYP3A4 (simvastatin, atorvastatin): more myopathy/rhabdomyolysis risk; statin dose may need adjusting; prefer a non-CYP3A4 statin where possible. MHRA: maximum simvastatin 20 mg daily with diltiazem.

src.q: The risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis is increased by concomitant administration of diltiazem with statins metabolised by CYP3A4 (e.g. atorvastatin, fluvastatin, and simvastatin).
An adjustment of the dose of statin may be necessary
The maximum recommended dose of simvastatin co-administered with amlodipine or diltiazem is now 20 mg per day.

items.t: Alpha-blockers: may cause or worsen hypotension; combine only with strict blood pressure monitoring.

src.q: The combination of diltiazem with an alpha antagonist should be considered only with strict monitoring of blood pressure.

items.t: Nitrates: additive vasodilatation (hypotension, faintness); increase nitrate doses gradually.

src.q: Increased hypotensive effects and faintness (additive vasodilating effects).
the prescription of nitrate derivatives should only be carried out at gradually increasing doses.

items.t: Carbamazepine: levels rise; measure carbamazepine levels and adjust dose if needed.

src.q: Increase in circulating carbamazepine levels. It is recommended that the plasma carbamazepine concentrations be assayed and that the dose should be adjusted if necessary.

items.t: QT-prolonging medicines: diltiazem may prolong QT; combine only after careful risk-benefit assessment.

src.q: Diltiazem may lead to QT prolongation, when administered with drugs with potential/ known for prolonging the QT interval.
must be based on a careful assessment of the potential risks and benefits of the treatment.

items.t: Antiplatelet drugs: possible additive effect (diltiazem inhibits platelet aggregation).

src.q: potential additive effects when used with antiplatelet drugs should be considered.

items.t: Other: ciclosporin (reduce dose, monitor levels and renal function); phenytoin and theophylline levels rise; cimetidine raises diltiazem; rifampicin lowers it; lithium neurotoxicity; colchicine not recommended; DOACs (bleeding); midazolam/triazolam and methylprednisolone levels rise; amiodarone/digoxin more bradycardia; other antiarrhythmics not recommended; grapefruit juice raises exposure.

src.q: It is recommended that the ciclosporin dose be reduced, renal function be monitored
its concomitant prescription with other antiarrhythmic agents is not recommended
Grapefruit juice should be avoided if an interaction is suspected.

items.t: Renal impairment: plasma levels may rise; start 60 mg twice daily, check heart rate regularly, do not increase if below 50 beats per minute. Monitor renal function in cardiac patients.

src.q: Elderly and patients with impaired hepatic or renal function The recommended starting dose is one tablet (60 mg) twice daily.
Carefully monitoring renal function is advised.

items.t: Hepatic impairment: plasma levels may rise; start 60 mg twice daily, check heart rate regularly, do not increase if below 50 beats per minute.

src.q: Elderly and patients with impaired hepatic or renal function The recommended starting dose is one tablet (60 mg) twice daily.

items.t: SmPC: not recommended in pregnancy or in women of child-bearing potential not using effective contraception (reproductive toxicity in animals).

src.q: Diltiazem is therefore not recommended during pregnancy, as well as in women of child-bearing potential not using effective contraception.

items.t: BUMPS (calcium-channel blockers): no clear risks; calcium-channel blockers other than nifedipine are recommended only when benefits outweigh possible risks.

src.q: There are no clear risks of taking a calcium channel blocker in pregnancy.

The other calcium channel blockers are less commonly used, and while not thought to cause problems, will only be recommended if the benefits of treating a potentially serious or lifestyle-impacting condition outweigh any possible risks.

items.t: SmPC: excreted in breast milk; breastfeeding while taking diltiazem is contraindicated.

src.q: As this drug is excreted in breast milk, breast feeding whilst taking diltiazem is contraindicated.

items.t: SPS (differs from the SmPC): negligible amounts in milk; can be used with caution, but verapamil is preferred if a rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker is needed; monitor the infant for hypotension.

src.q: Diltiazem is excreted into breast milk in negligible amounts. It can be used with caution during breastfeeding, but if a rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker is required, verapamil is preferred.

items.t: Not recommended in women of child-bearing potential not using effective contraception.

src.q: as well as in women of child-bearing potential not using effective contraception.

items.t: Dizziness and malaise are common. The SmPC table also lists headache, flushing, AV block, palpitations, constipation, dyspepsia, gastric pain, nausea and peripheral oedema (frequency columns not readable in the page text).

src.q: dizziness (common), malaise (common)
Headache, dizziness
Constipation, dyspepsia, gastric pain, nausea
Peripheral oedema Malaise

items.t: Sinoatrial block, congestive heart failure, sinus arrest, cardiac arrest (asystole); bronchospasm; hepatitis; severe skin reactions (erythema multiforme including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, AGEP, exfoliative dermatitis); angioedema.

src.q: Sinoatrial block, congestive heart failure, sinus arrest, cardiac arrest (asystole)
erythema multiforme (including Steven-Johnson's syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis), sweating, exfoliative dermatitis, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis

items.t: Overdose: marked hypotension with collapse and acute kidney injury, bradycardia, AV block, cardiac arrest; non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema may appear 24-48 hours later.

src.q: pronounced hypotension leading to collapse and acute kidney injury
Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema has rarely been reported as a consequence of diltiazem overdose that may manifest with a delayed onset (24-48 hours post-ingestion)

items.t: Heart rate at the start of treatment (and regularly in elderly, renal or hepatic impairment).

src.q: close monitoring, particularly of heart rate, should be carried out at the beginning of treatment.
The heart rate should be measured regularly in these groups of patients

items.t: Renal function in cardiac patients; blood glucose in diabetes; respiratory symptoms.

src.q: Carefully monitoring renal function is advised.
Careful monitoring is necessary in patients with latent or manifest diabetes mellitus due to a possible increase in blood glucose.

items.t: With beta-blockers: close clinical and ECG monitoring, especially at the start.

src.q: Such a combination must only be used under close clinical and ECG monitoring, particularly at the beginning of treatment.

items.t: Mood changes or depression: consider stopping.

src.q: In such cases, drug discontinuation should be considered.

administration.note: No food or swallowing instructions stated in the UK diltiazem 60 mg tablet SmPC beyond the three-times-daily schedule.

items.t: Dizziness and malaise are common and may affect driving.

src.q: dizziness (common), malaise (common), the ability to drive and use machines could be altered.

items.t: Report low mood or depression.

src.q: Treatment with diltiazem may be associated with mood changes, including depression

items.t: Avoid grapefruit juice if an interaction is suspected.

src.q: Grapefruit juice should be avoided if an interaction is suspected.

items.t: Eradication of head lice infestation.

src.q: Hedrin is indicated for the eradication of headlice infestations

restrictions.note: The UK dimeticone 4% SmPCs state no prescribing restrictions. No NICE guidance on head lice was found (CKS is geo-blocked and not used).

items.t: Apply enough lotion to cover dry hair from roots to tips so no part of the scalp is missed. Let the hair dry naturally, leave on for at least 8 hours or overnight, then wash out with normal shampoo. Repeat after 7 days (two applications 7 days apart are needed because the effect on eggs is weaker).
items.tag: Head lice (UK 4% lotion; adults and children 6 months and over)

src.q: Apply sufficient lotion to cover dry hair from the base to the tip to ensure that no part of the scalp is left uncovered.
Hedrin should be left on hair for a minimum of 8 hours or overnight.
Wash out with normal shampoo, rinsing thoroughly with water. Repeat the treatment after seven days.
It is less effective in its ovicidal activity and therefore two applications 7 days apart are required.

items.t: Licensed for adults and children aged 6 months and above. Children under 6 months should only be treated under medical supervision.

src.q: Adults and children (aged six months and above)
Children under the age of six months should only be treated under medical supervision.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to any of the ingredients.

items.t: Stop at the first sign of a skin rash or other hypersensitivity. If signs occur (rash, urticaria, generalised itching, breathing difficulty), shampoo the product off at once and get medical advice if symptoms do not settle.

src.q: Discontinue at the first appearance of a skin rash or any other signs of local or general hypersensitivity.
the product should be shampooed off immediately, and if symptoms do not resolve, medical advice sought

items.t: Fire risk: the lotion is combustible on the hair. Keep treated hair away from open flames, cigarettes and other sources of ignition. MHRA has received reports of serious burns.

src.q: Hedrin 4% cutaneous solution is combustible when on the hair and in direct contact with an open flame or other source of ignition
Eight cases of serious burns associated with Hedrin 4% cutaneous solution have been reported to the MHRA since the product was licensed in 2005.

items.t: For external use only. Avoid contact with the eyes; if it gets into the eyes, flush with water.

src.q: For external use only. Avoid contact with the eyes but if accidentally introduced into the eyes, flush with water.

items.t: One UK SmPC: consult a pharmacist if live lice are found after the second treatment or if head lice keep coming back.

src.q: Consult a pharmacist if live lice are detected after the second treatment or if head lice are a persistent or recurring problem.

items.t: Dimeticone is not known to interact with other medicines; there is little or no absorption through the skin.

src.q: Dimeticone is not known to interact with other drugs
there is little or no absorption of Hedrin through the skin

renal.note: The UK dimeticone 4% SmPCs give no renal advice.

hepatic.note: The UK dimeticone 4% SmPCs give no hepatic advice.

items.t: SmPC: no data suggest it may not be used in pregnancy.

src.q: There is no data to suggest that Hedrin may not be used in pregnancy

items.t: BUMPS: wet combing is the first option in pregnancy. If it fails or is not preferred, physical insecticides such as dimeticone can be used; they do not enter the bloodstream in amounts that could harm the baby.

src.q: Current UK guidelines recommend that pregnant women who need to treat their own or their child's head lice can use 'wet combing'.
If wet combing is not effective or is not preferred, insecticides (products that kill insects) can be used.
Physical insecticides are harmless to humans and also do not enter the bloodstream in amounts that could cause problems for the baby.

items.t: SPS: wet combing or dimeticone are the preferred choices for head lice during breastfeeding. No specific infant monitoring is needed (not absorbed through the skin). Keep hair short or tied up so the infant does not suck treated hair.

src.q: Wet combing or dimeticone are the preferred choices to treat head lice in breastfeeding.
it is not absorbed through the skin, therefore transfer into breast milk is not expected
Keep hair short or tied up to prevent infant from sucking hair during treatment.

reproductive.note: The UK dimeticone 4% SmPCs give no fertility or contraception advice.

items.t: Usually well tolerated. Minor effects: skin irritation, itchy or flaky scalp, irritation around the eyes. Single cases of hair loss reported.

src.q: Dimeticone is usually well tolerated. Minor adverse events include skin irritation, an itchy or flaky scalp and irritation around the eyes.
Single cases of hair loss have been reported.

items.t: Hypersensitivity (rash, urticaria, generalised itching, breathing difficulty): shampoo off at once; seek medical advice if symptoms do not resolve.

src.q: Signs of hypersensitivity reactions including rash, urticaria, generalised pruritus, and breathing difficulties.
the product should be shampooed off immediately, and if symptoms do not resolve, medical advice sought

items.t: Serious burns if treated hair meets a flame or other ignition source (for example lighting a cigarette).

src.q: some products for the eradication of head lice infestations are combustible/flammable when on the hair and can ignite and cause serious harm in the presence of an open flame or other source of ignition such as when lighting cigarettes

items.t: If live lice are still found after the second treatment, or lice keep returning, seek pharmacist advice (one UK SmPC).

src.q: Consult a pharmacist if live lice are detected after the second treatment or if head lice are a persistent or recurring problem.

items.t: External use on the hair and scalp only. Apply to dry hair, work in from roots to tips, let it dry naturally, leave on at least 8 hours or overnight, then wash out with normal shampoo.

src.q: For topical external use only
Work into the hair spreading the liquid evenly from roots to tips. Allow hair to dry naturally.

items.t: Spilt product can make smooth floors slippery.

src.q: Care should be taken as the product may cause a slip hazard if accidentally spilt onto smooth surfaces.

items.t: Do not smoke near treated hair and keep it away from open flames and other ignition sources, including the morning after an overnight application, until the hair is washed.

src.q: they should not smoke around treated hair and that it should be kept away from open flames or other sources of ignition, including in the morning after overnight application until hair is washed

items.t: Treat again after 7 days. Keep the product out of the eyes.

src.q: Repeat the treatment after seven days.
Avoid contact with the eyes

restrictions.note: No UK product information found.

hepatic.note: No UK product information found.

items.t: Relief of the symptoms of nausea and vomiting, in adults and adolescents 12 years and over weighing 35 kg or more (MHRA: no other indication since 2014).

src.q: Domperidone is indicated for the relief of the symptoms of nausea and vomiting.
domperidone is now authorised for the relief of symptoms of nausea and vomiting only in adults and adolescents 12 years of age or older and weighing 35 kg or more

items.t: MHRA: indication restricted to nausea and vomiting because of cardiac risk; use the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible time; maximum 30 mg in 24 hours; maximum duration usually 1 week.

src.q: Domperidone is now restricted to use in the relief of nausea and vomiting It should be used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible time
domperidone should be used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible duration and maximum treatment duration should not usually exceed 1 week

items.t: Prescription-only: must not be sold without prescription; a medical assessment is needed first because of cardiac risk.

src.q: Domperidone must not be sold without prescription
people need to have a medical assessment before taking domperidone to determine if it is suitable for them

items.t: Use beyond licensed dose or duration (e.g. Parkinson's disease treatment side effects): take the cardiac risk and interactions into account. Long-term users should be reassessed.

src.q: should be taken into account if there is a clinical need to use it at doses or durations greater than those authorised
Patients currently receiving long-term treatment with domperidone should be reassessed at a routine appointment to advise on treatment continuation, dose change, or cessation

items.t: 10 mg (tablet, or 10 mL of 1 mg/mL suspension) up to three times daily, before meals. Maximum 30 mg (30 mL) per day. Usually no longer than 1 week. Do not double a missed dose.
items.tag: Nausea and vomiting (adults and adolescents ≥ 12 years and ≥ 35 kg)

src.q: 10 ml (of oral suspension containing domperidone 1mg per ml) up to three times per day with a maximum daily dose of 30 ml per day.
One 10mg tablet up to three times per day with a maximum dose of 30 mg per day.
Usually, the maximum treatment duration should not exceed one week.
The dose should not be doubled to make up for a missed dose.

items.t: Liquid: give only with a graduated measuring device (e.g. oral syringe or measuring cup) for dose accuracy.

src.q: Oral liquid formulations of domperidone should only be given via appropriately designed, graduated measuring devices

items.t: Not licensed in children under 12 years or under 35 kg (efficacy not established; a trial in gastroenteritis showed no benefit over placebo). MHRA: consider alternative treatments in children under 12.

src.q: Domperidone is no longer licensed for use in children younger than 12 years or those weighing less than 35 kg.
consider alternative treatments to domperidone in children younger than 12 years of age who need relief of symptoms of nausea and vomiting
The efficacy of domperidone in adolescents 12 years of age and older and weighing less than 35 kg has not been established.

items.t: If a specialist judges off-label use justified in a child under 12, fully inform the patient or carer of benefits and risks.

src.q: the patient or parent/caregiver should be fully informed of the potential benefits and risks of the different options

items.t: Hypersensitivity to domperidone or any excipient.

src.q: Known hypersensitivity to domperidone or any of the excipients

items.t: Prolactin-releasing pituitary tumour (prolactinoma).

src.q: Prolactin-releasing pituitary tumour (prolactinoma).

items.t: Confirmed or suspected phaeochromocytoma (risk of severe hypertension) - new contraindication, MHRA July 2026: stop immediately and switch.

src.q: Confirmed or suspected pheochromocytoma due to the risk of severe hypertension episodes.
patients with confirmed or suspected phaeochromocytoma should stop taking domperidone immediately and be switched to an alternative treatment

items.t: When stimulating gastric motility could be harmful: GI haemorrhage, mechanical obstruction or perforation.

src.q: when stimulation of the gastric motility could be harmful, e.g .,in patients with gastro-intestinal haemorrhage, mechanical obstruction or perforation.

items.t: Moderate (Child-Pugh 7-9) or severe (Child-Pugh > 9) hepatic impairment.

src.q: Domperidone is contraindicated in moderate (Child-Pugh 7 to 9) or severe (Child-Pugh > 9) hepatic impairment

items.t: Known prolonged cardiac conduction intervals (particularly QTc), significant electrolyte disturbance (hypokalaemia, hyperkalaemia, hypomagnesaemia), bradycardia, or underlying cardiac disease such as congestive heart failure.

src.q: Domperidone is contraindicated in patients with known existing prolongation of cardiac conduction intervals, particularly QTc, in patients with significant electrolyte disturbances (hypokalaemia, hyperkalaemia, hypomagnesaemia), or bradycardia

items.t: With QT-prolonging drugs (except apomorphine under strict conditions) and with potent CYP3A4 inhibitors, regardless of their QT effect.

src.q: co-administration with QT-prolonging drugs, at the exception of apomorphine
co-administration with potent CYP3A4 inhibitors (regardless of their QT prolonging effects)

items.t: QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, serious ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death reported. Higher risk: age over 60, daily dose above 30 mg, and QT-prolonging drugs or CYP3A4 inhibitors. Use the lowest effective dose.

src.q: Epidemiological studies showed that domperidone was associated with an increased risk of serious ventricular arrhythmias or sudden cardiac death
A higher risk was observed in patients older than 60 years, patients taking daily doses greater than 30 mg, and patients concurrently taking QT-prolonging drugs or CYP3A4 inhibitors.

items.t: Stop if signs or symptoms of cardiac arrhythmia occur; patients should promptly report cardiac symptoms.

src.q: Treatment with domperidone should be stopped if signs or symptoms occur that may be associated with cardiac arrhythmia, and the patients should consult their physician.

items.t: May unmask phaeochromocytoma: if a patient has an episode of severe hypertension, consider investigating for it.

src.q: be aware that administration of domperidone can unmask phaeochromocytomas. If a patient taking domperidone has an episode of severe hypertension, consider further investigations for phaeochromocytoma

items.t: Severe renal impairment: reduce dosing frequency to once or twice daily (dose may need reducing) and review regularly.

src.q: the dosing frequency of domperidone should be reduced to once or twice daily depending on the severity of the impairment, and the dose may need to be reduced

items.t: Levodopa: plasma levodopa may rise by 30-40% (no levodopa dose change deemed necessary).

src.q: Although no dosage adjustment of levodopa is deemed necessary, an increase of plasma levodopa concentration (max 30-40%) has been observed

items.t: Suspension: contains sorbitol - patients with hereditary fructose intolerance should not take it; hydroxybenzoates may cause (possibly delayed) allergic reactions.

src.q: Patients with hereditary problems of fructose intolerance (HFI) should not take this medicine .
which may cause allergic reactions (possibly delayed)

items.t: Contraindicated with QT-prolonging medicines, e.g. class IA/III antiarrhythmics (amiodarone, sotalol), some antipsychotics (haloperidol), citalopram, escitalopram, erythromycin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, methadone (list not exhaustive).

src.q: certain anti-depressants (e.g., citalopram, escitalopram) certain antibiotics (e.g. , erythromycin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, spiramycin)
The above list of substances is representative and not exhaustive.

items.t: Contraindicated with potent CYP3A4 inhibitors: protease inhibitors, systemic azole antifungals, some macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin). Ketoconazole or erythromycin tripled domperidone levels and prolonged QTc by about 10 ms.

src.q: Potent CYP3A4 inhibitors ( regardless of their QT prolonging effects ), i.e.: protease inhibitors systemic azole antifungals some macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin, telithromycin)
Both the Cmax and AUC of domperidone at steady state were increased approximately three-fold in each of these interaction studies.

items.t: Not recommended with moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors: diltiazem, verapamil and some macrolides.

src.q: Concomitant use of the following substances is not recommended Moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors i.e. diltiazem, verapamil and some macrolides.

items.t: Caution with drugs causing bradycardia or hypokalaemia, and with azithromycin and roxithromycin.

src.q: Caution with bradycardia and hypokalaemia-inducing drugs, as well as with the following macrolides involved in QT-interval prolongation: azithromycin and roxithromycin

items.t: Suspension SmPC: do not take antacids or antisecretory drugs at the same time - take domperidone before meals and the antacid/antisecretory after meals (lower domperidone bioavailability).

src.q: Antacids or antisecretory agents should not be taken simultaneously with oral formulations of domperidone as they lower the oral bioavailability of domperidone.
Domperidone should be taken before meals and antacids or antisecretory agents after meals.

items.t: Apomorphine: contraindicated unless benefit outweighs risk and the apomorphine SmPC precautions (QT checks, ECG) are strictly followed.

src.q: apomorphine, unless the benefit of the co-administration outweighs the risks, and only if the recommended precautions for co-administration are strictly fulfilled.

items.t: Severe renal impairment (serum creatinine > 6 mg/100 mL, i.e. 0.6 mmol/L): half-life prolonged - give once or twice daily, dose may need reducing; review regularly. No eGFR/CrCl threshold is given.

src.q: Since the elimination half-life of domperidone is prolonged in severe renal impairment (serum creatinine > 6mg/100mL, i.e. 0.6 mmol/L)
Such patients with severe renal impairment should be reviewed regularly

items.t: Contraindicated in moderate (Child-Pugh 7-9) or severe (Child-Pugh > 9) hepatic impairment. Mild (Child-Pugh 5-6): no dose change.

src.q: Domperidone is contraindicated in moderate (Child-Pugh 7 to 9) or severe (Child-Pugh > 9) hepatic impairment
Dose modification in mild (Child-Pugh 5 to 6) hepatic impairment is however not needed

items.t: SmPC: limited human data; animal reproductive toxicity at maternally toxic doses. Use only when justified by the expected benefit.

src.q: There are limited post-marketing data on the use of domperidone in pregnant women.
Domperidone should only be used during pregnancy when justified by the anticipated therapeutic benefit.

items.t: BUMPS: domperidone is one of the options if an antihistamine does not help pregnancy sickness; overall these medicines are considered safe for the baby.

src.q: These include ondansetron (Zofran®), metoclopramide (Maxolon®), and domperidone.
Overall, these medicines are considered safe for your baby.

items.t: SmPC: infants receive < 0.1% of the maternal weight-adjusted dose; adverse (especially cardiac) effects cannot be excluded. Decide whether to stop breastfeeding or domperidone; caution if the infant has QTc risk factors.

src.q: Domperidone is excreted in human milk and breast-fed infants receive less than 0.1 % of the maternal weight-adjusted dose.
Caution should be exercised in case of QTc prolongation risk factors in breast-fed infants.

items.t: SPS: negligible amounts pass into milk; no serious infant effects reported - monitor for GI disturbance or dry mouth. Avoid in the mother if the infant has cardiac disease, severe liver disease or takes interacting medicines.

src.q: Very limited information shows domperidone passes into breast milk in negligible amounts (less than 0.5% of the maternal weight-adjusted dose)
As a precaution, monitor for gastro-intestinal disturbances, or signs of dry mouth , such as difficulty feeding.
If the infant has cardiac disease, severe liver disease or is receiving medicines which may be a problem, then domperidone use in the mother is best avoided.

items.t: SPS (off-licence, low milk supply): only after full assessment; 10 mg three times daily for 7 days then review; do not use higher doses.

src.q: Use 10mg three times daily, initially for 7 days then review.
Doses higher than this should not be used .

reproductive.note: No fertility or contraception statement in the UK SmPCs (1 mg/mL oral suspension, 10 mg orodispersible tablets) or the MHRA Drug Safety Updates checked.

items.t: Common: dry mouth. Uncommon: somnolence, headache, extrapyramidal disorder, diarrhoea, anxiety, agitation, loss of libido, rash, pruritus, urticaria, galactorrhoea, breast pain/tenderness, asthenia.

src.q: Dry mouth Diarrhoea
Somnolence Headache Extrapyramidal disorder
Galactorrhoea Breast pain Breast tenderness

items.t: Ventricular arrhythmias, QTc prolongation, torsade de pointes, sudden cardiac death (frequency not known): stop and seek medical help for palpitations, fainting, chest pain or irregular heartbeat.

src.q: Ventricular arrhythmias Sudden cardiac death QTc prolongation Torsade de Pointes
Seek medical attention immediately if you experience heart-related symptoms such as irregular heartbeat or fainting while taking domperidone

items.t: Anaphylactic reaction including shock; angioedema (frequency not known).

src.q: Anaphylactic reaction (including anaphylactic shock)

items.t: Severe hypertension in phaeochromocytoma.

src.q: a small number of reports have been received relating to severe episodes of hypertension in patients with phaeochromocytoma

items.t: Convulsion, oculogyric crisis, urinary retention (frequency not known).

src.q: Convulsion Restless legs syndrome*

items.t: Before prescribing, check for cardiac disease, QT prolongation, bradycardia, electrolyte disturbance, moderate/severe liver disease and interacting medicines (QT-prolonging drugs, CYP3A4 inhibitors).

src.q: Do not prescribe domperidone in people with bradycardia, congenital QT prolongation, underlying cardiac diseases or receiving other medications known to prolong QT interval or potent CYP3A4 inhibitors.

items.t: SPS: with non-modifiable patient and medicine risk factors, monitor ECG, magnesium and potassium before and during treatment.

src.q: Monitor ECG, magnesium and potassium before and during treatment in people with non-modifiable patient and medicine risk factors.

items.t: Review at 1 week (maximum usual duration); reassess any long-term use.

src.q: maximum treatment duration should not usually exceed 1 week
Patients currently receiving long-term treatment with domperidone should be reassessed at a routine appointment

items.t: Stop if arrhythmia symptoms occur, or immediately if phaeochromocytoma is confirmed or suspected.

src.q: Treatment with domperidone should be stopped if signs or symptoms occur that may be associated with cardiac arrhythmia
patients with confirmed or suspected phaeochromocytoma should stop taking domperidone immediately

items.t: Take 15-30 minutes before meals (absorption delayed if taken after meals).

src.q: It is recommended to take oral domperidone 15-30 minutes before meals. If taken after meals, absorption of the drug is somewhat delayed.

items.t: Take before meals (absorption is delayed if taken after meals). The UK SmPC used is for an orodispersible tablet; its place-on-the-tongue method does not apply to a standard tablet.

src.q: It is recommended to take Epzit 10 mg Orodispersible Tablets before meals.
If taken after meals, absorption of the drug is somewhat delayed.

items.t: Use only for short periods for nausea and vomiting. Get medical help at once for irregular heartbeat, fainting, dizziness, chest pain or palpitations.

src.q: Domperidone should only be used for short periods of time to treat nausea and vomiting
Talk to a doctor straight away if you experience dizziness; fainting; chest pain; or a rapid, fluttering, or pounding heartbeat while taking domperidone.

items.t: Seek urgent help for signs of very high blood pressure (persistent headache, blurred vision, breathlessness, chest pain).

src.q: Symptoms can include, but are not limited to: persistent headache, blurred vision, shortness of breath and chest pain.

items.t: May cause drowsiness - do not drive or use machines until you know how it affects you.

src.q: patients should be advised not to drive or use machinery or engage in other activities requiring mental alertness and coordination until they have established how domperidone affects them

items.t: Infections due to susceptible organisms: respiratory tract infections (pneumonia, Mycoplasma pneumonia, chronic bronchitis, sinusitis), urinary tract infections, sexually transmitted infections (Chlamydia, non-gonococcal urethritis; alternative for gonorrhoea and syphilis), acne vulgaris when an antibiotic is needed, ophthalmic, rickettsial and other infections (e.g. brucellosis, cholera, chloroquine-resistant falciparum malaria).

src.q: Pneumonia and other lower respiratory tract infections due to susceptible strains
Treatment of chronic bronchitis, sinusitis.
Infections due to Chlamydia trachomatis including uncomplicated urethral, endocervical or rectal infections.
Acne vulgaris , when antibiotic therapy is considered necessary.
chloroquine-resistant falciparum malaria

items.t: Prophylaxis: scrub typhus, travellers' diarrhoea (enterotoxigenic E. coli), leptospirosis and malaria (follow current guidelines).

src.q: Doxycycline capsules is indicated for prophylaxis in the following conditions: Scrub typhus, travellers' diarrhoea (enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli), leptospirosis and malaria.

restrictions.note: No specialist-only, shared-care or brand-specific prescribing restriction found in the doxycycline 100 mg capsule SmPC; it advises following official guidance on antibacterial use.

items.t: Acute infections: 200 mg on day 1 (single or divided doses), then 100 mg daily. More severe infections: 200 mg daily throughout.

src.q: is 200 mg on the first day (as a single dose or in divided doses) followed by a maintenance dose of 100 mg/day. In the management of more severe infections, 200 mg daily should be given throughout treatment.

items.t: Acne vulgaris: 50 mg daily with food or fluid for 6 to 12 weeks.

src.q: Acne vulgaris 50 mg daily with food or fluid for 6 to 12 weeks.

items.t: Uncomplicated gonococcal infections (except anorectal in men), uncomplicated chlamydial urethral/endocervical/rectal infection, non-gonococcal urethritis (Ureaplasma): 100 mg twice daily for 7 days. Epididymo-orchitis (Chlamydia or gonorrhoea): 100 mg twice daily for 10 days.

src.q: 100 mg twice daily for 7 days is recommended in the following infections
Acute epididymo-orchitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoea 100 mg twice daily for 10 days.

items.t: Primary/secondary syphilis (non-pregnant, penicillin-allergic): 200 mg twice daily for 2 weeks.

src.q: doxycycline 200 mg orally twice daily for two weeks, as an alternative to penicillin therapy

items.t: Malaria prophylaxis: 100 mg daily (adults and children over 12), starting 1 to 2 days before travel, daily during travel and for 4 weeks after leaving the malarial area.

src.q: Prophylaxis of malaria 100 mg daily in adults and children over the age of 12 years. Can begin 1-2 days before travel to malarial areas.
It should be continued daily during travel in the malarial areas and for 4 weeks after the traveller leaves the malarial area.

items.t: Chloroquine-resistant falciparum malaria: 200 mg daily for at least 7 days, always with a rapid-acting schizonticide such as quinine.

src.q: Treatment of chloroquine-resistant falciparum malaria 200 mg daily for at least 7 days.
a rapid-acting schizonticide such as quinine should always be given in conjunction with doxycycline

items.t: Other regimens: relapsing fevers 100 mg or 200 mg single dose; scrub typhus prevention 200 mg single dose; travellers' diarrhoea prevention 200 mg on day 1 then 100 mg daily; leptospirosis prevention 200 mg weekly and 200 mg at the end of the trip (prophylaxis data not available beyond 21 days); Rocky Mountain spotted fever 100 mg every 12 hours.

src.q: For the prevention of scrub typhus 200 mg as a single dose.
For the prevention of leptospirosis 200 mg once each week throughout the stay in the area and 200 mg at the completion of the trip.
Data on the use of the drug prophylactically are not available beyond 21 days.
Rocky Mountain spotted fever Adults: 100 mg every 12 hours.

items.t: Elderly: usual doses, no special precautions. Continue at least 24 to 48 hours after symptoms and fever settle; streptococcal infections 10 days.

src.q: Doxycycline may be prescribed in the elderly in the usual dosages with no special precautions.
Therapy should be continued for at least 24 to 48 hours after symptoms and fever have subsided.

items.t: Under 8 years: should not be used (risk of tooth discolouration). Use only for severe or life-threatening conditions (e.g. Rocky Mountain spotted fever) when benefits outweigh risks and there is no adequate alternative.

src.q: Doxycycline should not be used in children aged younger than 8 years due to the risk of teeth discolouration.

Use doxycycline in paediatric patients aged younger than 8 years only when the potential benefits are expected to outweigh the risks in severe or life-threatening conditions (e.g. Rocky Mountain spotted fever), only when there are no adequate alternative therapies.

items.t: 8 to < 12 years: carefully justify use (only when other drugs are unavailable, unlikely to work or contraindicated). Children 45 kg or less: 4.4 mg/kg on day 1 (single or 2 divided doses), then 2.2 mg/kg daily (single or 2 divided doses); severe infections up to 4.4 mg/kg throughout. Over 45 kg: adult dose.

src.q: The use of doxycycline for the treatment of acute infections in children aged 8 years to less than 12 years should be carefully justified in situations where other drugs are not available, are not likely to be effective or are contraindicated.
For children 45 kg or less- Initial dose: 4.4 mg/kg (in single or 2 divided doses) with maintenance dose: 2.2 mg/kg (in single or 2 divided doses).
For children, over 45 kg - Dose administered for adults should be used.

items.t: 12 to < 18 years: adult dose.

src.q: Adults and children aged 12 years to less than 18 years

items.t: Rocky Mountain spotted fever: children under 45 kg 2.2 mg/kg twice a day; 45 kg or more, adult dose (100 mg every 12 hours). Treat for at least 3 days after the fever settles; minimum course 5 to 7 days. Under 8 years only when benefits outweigh risks and no adequate alternative exists.

src.q: Children: weighing less than 45 kg: 2.2 mg/kg body weight given twice a day.
Children weighing 45 kg or more should receive the adult dose
Minimum course of treatment is 5-7 days.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to doxycycline, other tetracyclines or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or other tetracyclines, or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Pregnancy (effects on teeth and skeletal development).

src.q: Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy.

items.t: Breastfeeding (tetracyclines pass into milk).

src.q: Tetracyclines are excreted into milk and are therefore contraindicated in nursing mothers.

items.t: Tooth development (last half of pregnancy, infancy and childhood to 8 years): permanent yellow-grey-brown discolouration and enamel hypoplasia.

src.q: The use of drugs of the tetracycline class during tooth development (last half of pregnancy; infancy and childhood to the age of 8 years) may cause permanent discolouration of the teeth (yellow-grey-brown).

items.t: Hepatic impairment or other hepatotoxic medicines: give with caution.

src.q: Doxycycline should be administered with caution to patients with hepatic impairment or those receiving potentially hepatotoxic drugs.

items.t: Photosensitivity (exaggerated sunburn): warn patients exposed to sunlight or UV light; stop at the first sign of skin erythema.
