src.q: treatment should be discontinued at the first evidence of skin erythema

items.t: Benign intracranial hypertension (can cause permanent visual loss): prompt eye assessment if visual disturbance. Avoid with isotretinoin or other systemic retinoids.

src.q: If visual disturbance occurs during treatment, prompt ophthalmologic evaluation is warranted.
Concomitant use of isotretinoin or other systemic retinoids and doxycycline should be avoided

items.t: Oesophagitis and oesophageal ulceration, mostly when taken just before bed or with too little fluid.

src.q: Most of these patients took medications immediately before going to bed or with inadequate amounts of fluid.

items.t: Serious skin reactions (exfoliative dermatitis, erythema multiforme, SJS, TEN, DRESS): stop immediately.

src.q: If serious skin reactions occur, doxycycline should be discontinued immediately, and appropriate therapy should be instituted.

items.t: Myasthenia gravis: care needed (weak neuromuscular blockade). Systemic lupus erythematosus may be exacerbated. Rare porphyria reported.

src.q: Due to a potential for weak neuromuscular blockade, care should be taken in administering tetracyclines to patients with myasthenia gravis.
Tetracyclines can cause exacerbation of SLE.
There have been rare reports of porphyria in patients receiving tetracyclines.

items.t: C. difficile diarrhoea (can occur over two months after treatment) and Candida overgrowth.

src.q: CDAD must be considered in all patients who present with diarrhoea following antibiotic use.
Careful medical history is necessary since CDAD has been reported to occur over two months after the administration of antibacterial agents.

items.t: Venereal disease with suspected syphilis: dark-field examination and monthly serology for at least 4 months.

src.q: In all such cases monthly serological tests should be made for at least four months.

items.t: Antacids containing aluminium, calcium or magnesium, other medicines containing these cations, oral zinc, iron salts and bismuth: absorption of doxycycline may be impaired. Separate the doses as much as possible (the SmPC gives no specific number of hours).

src.q: The absorption of doxycycline may be impaired by concurrently administered antacids containing aluminium, calcium, magnesium or other drugs containing these cations; oral zinc, iron salts or bismuth preparations. Dosages should be maximally separated.

items.t: Penicillins: bacteriostatic drugs may interfere with penicillin's bactericidal action; advisable to avoid the combination.

src.q: Since bacteriostatic drugs may interfere with the bactericidal action of penicillin, it is advisable to avoid giving doxycycline in conjunction with penicillin.

items.t: Warfarin and other anticoagulants: prolonged prothrombin time reported; reduced anticoagulant doses may be needed.

src.q: There have been reports of prolonged prothrombin time in patients taking warfarin and doxycycline. Tetracyclines depress plasma prothrombin activity and reduced doses of concomitant anticoagulants may be necessary.

items.t: Carbamazepine (also barbiturates, phenytoin): may shorten doxycycline half-life; consider increasing the daily doxycycline dose.

src.q: The serum half-life of doxycycline may be shortened when patients are concurrently receiving barbiturates, carbamazepine or phenytoin. An increase in the daily dosage of doxycycline should be considered.

items.t: Oral contraceptives: a few cases of pregnancy or breakthrough bleeding attributed to concurrent tetracycline use.

src.q: A few cases of pregnancy or breakthrough bleeding have been attributed to the concurrent use of tetracycline antibiotics with oral contraceptives.

items.t: Hepatotoxic medicines: give doxycycline with caution.

src.q: Doxycycline should be administered with caution to patients with hepatic impairment or those receiving potentially hepatotoxic drugs.

items.t: Isotretinoin or other systemic retinoids: avoid (benign intracranial hypertension). Ciclosporin: monitor (levels may rise). Methoxyflurane: renal failure reported. Alcohol may shorten doxycycline half-life.

src.q: Doxycycline may increase the plasma concentration of ciclosporin. Co-administration should only be undertaken with appropriate monitoring.
The concurrent use of tetracyclines and methoxyflurane has been reported to result in renal failure.
Alcohol may decrease the half-life of doxycycline.

items.t: No dose adjustment in renal impairment; usual doses do not accumulate. Half-life is similar in normal and severely impaired renal function, and haemodialysis does not change it.

src.q: No dosage adjustment is necessary in the presence of renal impairment.
Haemodialysis does not alter the serum half-life of doxycycline

items.t: Give with caution in hepatic impairment; abnormal hepatic function has been reported rarely.

src.q: Doxycycline should be administered with caution to patients with hepatic impairment or those receiving potentially hepatotoxic drugs.
Abnormal hepatic function has been reported rarely

items.t: SmPC: contraindicated in pregnancy (effects on teeth and skeletal development).

src.q: Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy.
It appears that the risks associated with the use of tetracyclines during pregnancy are predominantly due to effects on teeth and skeletal development.

items.t: BUMPS (UKTIS): a tetracycline can be used in pregnancy if a doctor recommends it. Early-pregnancy use is not known to harm the baby; tetracyclines tend to be avoided after about 13 weeks (milk-teeth discolouration) unless it is the only suitable antibiotic for a serious infection. Doxycycline may be used to prevent malaria.

src.q: A tetracycline can be used in pregnancy if a doctor recommends it.
Tetracycline use in early pregnancy is not known to harm the baby. Tetracyclines tend to be avoided after about 13 weeks of pregnancy as they can affect the baby's developing milk teeth
a tetracycline may occasionally be used after 13 weeks of pregnancy if it is the only suitable antibiotic to treat a serious infection

items.t: SmPC: contraindicated in nursing mothers.

src.q: Tetracyclines are excreted into milk and are therefore contraindicated in nursing mothers.

items.t: SPS: doxycycline can be used with caution with infant monitoring (rash, vomiting/diarrhoea, thrush/nappy rash). Short courses (under 3 weeks) acceptable; long-term use generally not recommended. Tetracycline is the preferred choice.

src.q: Doxycycline can be used with caution during breastfeeding, with infant monitoring.
Short term use (a single course of less than 3 week's duration) is acceptable for most tetracyclines, with precautionary infant monitoring. Long term use is generally not recommended.

reproductive.note: The doxycycline 100 mg capsule SmPC gives no fertility information. Its interaction section notes a few cases of pregnancy or breakthrough bleeding with oral contraceptives (see Interactions).

items.t: Reported with tetracyclines including doxycycline: nausea/vomiting, dyspepsia, headache, photosensitivity reaction, rash, hypersensitivity, vaginal infection, Candida infection. The SmPC table columns could not be read, so frequencies are not given here.

src.q: The following adverse reactions have been observed in patients receiving tetracyclines, including doxycycline.
Photosensitivity reaction, rash including maculopapular and erythematous rashes

items.t: Anaphylaxis and serious hypersensitivity, DRESS, SJS, TEN, exfoliative dermatitis: stop immediately.

src.q: Hypersensitivity (including anaphylactic shock, anaphylactic reaction, anaphylactoid reaction, angioedema

Serious skin reactions, such as exfoliative dermatitis, erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) have been reported in patients receiving doxycycline
If serious skin reactions occur, doxycycline should be discontinued immediately

items.t: Benign intracranial hypertension (headache, vomiting, visual disturbance, possible permanent visual loss): stop if raised intracranial pressure is suspected.

src.q: If an increase in intracranial pressure is suspected during treatment with tetracyclines, administration should be discontinued.

items.t: Oesophageal ulcer, pseudomembranous colitis, pancreatitis, hepatic failure/hepatitis.

src.q: Pancreatitis, pseudomembranous colitis, Clostridium difficile colitis, oesophageal ulcer, oesophagitis
Hepatic failure, hepatitis, hepatotoxicity, jaundice, hepatic function abnormal

items.t: Raised intracranial pressure: prompt eye assessment if visual disturbance; monitor until stable (pressure may stay raised for weeks after stopping).

src.q: Since intracranial pressure can remain elevated for weeks after drug cessation patients should be monitored until they stabilize.

items.t: Suspected syphilis with venereal disease: monthly serology for at least 4 months.

src.q: In all such cases monthly serological tests should be made for at least four months.

items.t: Stop at the first sign of skin erythema (photosensitivity), serious skin reaction, or suspected raised intracranial pressure.

src.q: treatment should be discontinued at the first evidence of skin erythema
If serious skin reactions occur, doxycycline should be discontinued immediately

items.t: Swallow with plenty of water, sitting or standing, well before bedtime (reduces oesophageal irritation). If stomach upset, take with food or milk; food and milk do not notably reduce absorption.

src.q: The capsules should be swallowed with plenty of water in either the sitting or standing position and well before retiring at night to reduce the risk of oesophageal irritation and ulceration.
If gastric irritation occurs, it is recommended that Doxycycline capsules be given with food or milk.
Studies indicate that the absorption of doxycycline is not notably influenced by simultaneous ingestion of food or milk.

items.t: Keep doses as far apart as possible from antacids, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, iron, zinc or bismuth products.

src.q: Dosages should be maximally separated.

items.t: Take with a full glass of water while upright; do not take just before lying down.

src.q: well before retiring at night to reduce the risk of oesophageal irritation and ulceration

items.t: Avoid strong sunlight and UV light; stop and seek advice if skin reddens.

src.q: Patients likely to be exposed to direct sunlight or ultraviolet light should be advised that this reaction can occur with tetracycline drugs

items.t: Report headache with blurred or double vision.

src.q: The manifestation of clinical symptoms, including headache or visual disturbances, should suggest a possible diagnosis of intracranial hypertension.

items.t: Insufficiently controlled type 2 diabetes in patients aged 10 years and above, with diet and exercise: monotherapy when metformin is inappropriate (intolerance or contraindication), or added to other diabetes medicines.

src.q: indicated for the treatment of patients 10 years and above with insufficiently controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus as an adjunct to diet and exercise
as monotherapy when metformin is considered inappropriate due to intolerance or contraindications in addition to other medicinal products for the treatment of diabetes

items.t: SPS: prescribe and dispense by brand name (biological medicine). Only prescribe for licensed indications.

src.q: Biological medicines such as semaglutide, dulaglutide, liraglutide, and tirzepatide must be prescribed and dispensed by brand name.
Only prescribe GLP-1 RAs, or incretin mimetics, for their licensed indication and follow NHS guidance.

items.t: Monotherapy: 0.75 mg once weekly.

src.q: Monotherapy The recommended dose is 0.75 mg once weekly.

items.t: Add-on therapy: 1.5 mg once weekly. If needed, increase after at least 4 weeks to 3 mg, then after at least 4 more weeks to 4.5 mg. Maximum 4.5 mg once weekly.

src.q: Add-on therapy The recommended dose is 1.5 mg once weekly.

If needed, the 1.5 mg dose can be increased after at least 4 weeks to 3 mg once weekly. the 3 mg dose can be increased after at least 4 weeks to 4.5 mg once weekly. The maximum dose is 4.5 mg once weekly.

items.t: With metformin, pioglitazone or an SGLT2 inhibitor: continue their current dose. With a sulphonylurea or insulin: a dose reduction of these may be considered; reduce insulin stepwise with blood glucose self-monitoring.

src.q: When it is added to existing therapy of a sulphonylurea or insulin, a reduction in the dose of sulphonylurea or insulin may be considered to reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia
A stepwise approach to insulin dose reduction is recommended.

items.t: Missed dose: give as soon as possible if at least 3 days (72 hours) remain before the next dose; otherwise skip it and give the next dose on the usual day.

src.q: If a dose is missed, it should be administered as soon as possible if there are at least 3 days (72 hours) until the next scheduled dose.
If less than 3 days (72 hours) remain before the next scheduled dose, the missed dose should be skipped and the next dose should be administered on the regularly scheduled day.

items.t: Elderly and hepatic impairment: no dose adjustment.

src.q: Elderly No dose adjustment is required based on age
No dose adjustment is required in patients with hepatic impairment.

items.t: Children 10 years and above: start 0.75 mg once weekly; if needed increase to 1.5 mg once weekly after at least 4 weeks. Maximum 1.5 mg once weekly. Not established under 10 years (no data).

src.q: The starting dose for paediatric patients 10 years and above is 0.75 mg once weekly. If needed, the dose can be increased to 1.5 mg once weekly after at least 4 weeks. The maximum dose is 1.5 mg once weekly.
The safety and efficacy of dulaglutide in children aged less than 10 years have not been established and no data are available

items.t: Hypersensitivity to dulaglutide or any excipient.

src.q: Contraindications Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Should not be used in type 1 diabetes or to treat diabetic ketoacidosis; not a substitute for insulin. Diabetic ketoacidosis reported after rapid stopping or reduction of insulin.

src.q: Dulaglutide should not be used in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus or for the treatment of diabetic ketoacidosis. Dulaglutide is not a substitute for insulin.
Diabetic ketoacidosis has been reported in insulin-dependent patients after rapid discontinuation or dose reduction of insulin

items.t: Severe gastrointestinal disease, including severe gastroparesis: not studied; not recommended. Monitor and consider dose change or stopping if severe gastrointestinal symptoms develop.

src.q: Dulaglutide has not been studied in patients with severe gastrointestinal disease, including severe gastroparesis, and is therefore not recommended in these patients.
Monitor and consider dose modification or discontinuation in patients who develop severe gastrointestinal symptoms while on treatment.

items.t: General anaesthesia or deep sedation: pulmonary aspiration reported with GLP-1 receptor agonists (delayed gastric emptying); consider before procedures.

src.q: the increased risk of residual gastric content due to delayed gastric emptying (see section 4.8) should be considered prior to performing procedures with general anaesthesia or deep sedation

items.t: Dehydration, sometimes causing acute renal failure or worse renal impairment, especially at the start: warn patients and advise them to avoid fluid loss.

src.q: Dehydration, sometimes leading to acute renal failure or worsening renal impairment, has been reported in patients treated with dulaglutide, especially at the initiation of treatment.
take precautions to avoid fluid depletion

items.t: Acute pancreatitis (including necrotising and fatal cases): caution with a history of pancreatitis (not studied). Stop if suspected; do not restart if confirmed.

src.q: Dulaglutide has not been studied in patients with a history of pancreatitis, and should be used with caution in these patients.
If pancreatitis is suspected, dulaglutide should be discontinued. If the diagnosis of pancreatitis is confirmed, dulaglutide should not be restarted.

items.t: Hypoglycaemia with a sulphonylurea or insulin: may be lowered by reducing their dose.

src.q: The risk of hypoglycaemia may be lowered by a reduction in the dose of sulphonylurea or insulin

items.t: Sulphonylureas or insulin: hypoglycaemia; a dose reduction may be considered. MHRA: diabetic ketoacidosis reported when insulin was rapidly reduced or stopped; reduce insulin stepwise with glucose self-monitoring.

src.q: Patients receiving dulaglutide in combination with sulphonylurea or insulin may have an increased risk of hypoglycaemia.
if the insulin dose is to be reduced, a stepwise approach is recommended

items.t: Sitagliptin: increases dulaglutide exposure, which may enhance its blood-glucose effect.

src.q: Dulaglutide (1.5 mg) coadministration with sitagliptin increased dulaglutide exposure and Cmax by approximately 38 % and 27 %, respectively
The increased exposure may enhance the effects of dulaglutide on blood glucose levels.

items.t: Oral medicines with rapid absorption or prolonged release: delayed gastric emptying may alter exposure, particularly when starting dulaglutide. Studied medicines (paracetamol, atorvastatin, digoxin, lisinopril, metoprolol, warfarin, oral contraceptives, metformin) need no dose adjustment.

src.q: For patients receiving dulaglutide in combination with oral medicinal products with rapid gastrointestinal absorption or prolonged release, there is a potential for altered medicinal product exposure, particularly at the time of dulaglutide treatment initiation.
No dose adjustment for warfarin is necessary when given together with dulaglutide.
No dose adjustment of paracetamol is necessary when administered with dulaglutide.

items.t: SPS: use with caution with time-critical or narrow therapeutic window medicines (e.g. levodopa); extra monitoring may be needed.

src.q: Use GLP-1 RAs with caution in people who are taking medicines which are time critical, such as levodopa for Parkinson's disease.
These people may require additional monitoring.

items.t: eGFR < 90 to ≥ 15 mL/min/1.73 m²: no dose adjustment.

src.q: No dose adjustment is required in patients with mild, moderate or severe renal impairment (eGFR < 90 to ≥ 15 mL/min/1.73m2).

items.t: End-stage renal disease (eGFR < 15 mL/min/1.73 m²): very limited experience; cannot be recommended.

src.q: There is very limited experience in patients with end stage renal disease (< 15 ml/min/1.73m2), therefore Trulicity cannot be recommended in this population

items.t: Dehydration from gastrointestinal effects can cause acute renal failure or worsen renal impairment.

src.q: Many of the reported adverse renal events occurred in patients who had experienced nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, or dehydration.

items.t: No dose adjustment in hepatic impairment.

src.q: No dose adjustment is required in patients with hepatic impairment.

items.t: SmPC: no or limited human data; animal reproductive toxicity. Not recommended in pregnancy.

src.q: There are no or limited amount of data from the use of dulaglutide in pregnant women.
Therefore, the use of dulaglutide is not recommended during pregnancy.

items.t: BUMPS: GLP-1 receptor agonists should not be used in pregnancy. If used by accident in early pregnancy, available data (about 47,000 pregnancies) are reassuring; no extra monitoring for birth defects is needed.

src.q: GLP-1 receptor agonists should not be used in pregnancy.
If you accidentally used a GLP-1 receptor agonist in early pregnancy, you can be reassured that the available information suggests that it does not harm the baby.
No extra monitoring for major birth defects is required following use in early pregnancy of a GLP-1 receptor agonist.

items.t: SmPC: unknown if excreted in human milk; a risk to the infant cannot be excluded. Should not be used during breastfeeding.

src.q: A risk to newborns/infants cannot be excluded.
Dulaglutide should not be used during breast-feeding.

items.t: SPS: MHRA advise GLP-1 receptor agonists should not be taken while breastfeeding (lack of safety data). Insulin or metformin are preferred choices.

src.q: The MHRA advise GLP-1 RAs should not be taken by people who are breastfeeding due to a lack of safety data .
Insulin or metformin are the preferred choices during breastfeeding.

items.t: SPS: MHRA advise contraception throughout GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment as a precaution. Dulaglutide did not affect oral contraceptive exposure (no dose change needed).

src.q: They advise contraceptive use throughout GLP-1 RA treatment as a cautionary measure.
No dose adjustment for oral contraceptives is required when given together with dulaglutide.

items.t: Fertility: effect in humans unknown; no direct effect in rats.

src.q: The effect of dulaglutide on fertility in humans is unknown.

items.t: Most frequent: nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, usually mild or moderate and short-lived; they peak in the first 2 weeks. Up to 104 weeks at 1.5 mg: nausea 21.2%, diarrhoea 13.7%, vomiting 11.5%.

src.q: The most frequently reported adverse reactions in clinical trials were gastrointestinal, including nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea.
nausea (12.9 % and 21.2 % ) , diarrhoea (10.7 % and 13.7 %) and vomiting (6.9 % and 11.5 %)
reported to peak during the first 2 weeks of treatment

items.t: Hypoglycaemia: documented symptomatic hypoglycaemia in about 40% with a sulphonylurea plus metformin and 35.3% with insulin glargine (1.5 mg); 5.9% to 10.9% with monotherapy or metformin (with or without pioglitazone).

src.q: the incidences of documented symptomatic hypoglycaemia were 5.9 % to 10.9 %
were used in combination with a sulphonylurea and metformin were 39.0 % and 40.3 %
The incidence of documented symptomatic hypoglycaemia when dulaglutide 1.5 mg was used in combination with insulin glargine was 35.3 %

items.t: Small heart rate rise (2 to 4 beats per minute), sinus tachycardia, first-degree AV block; injection site reactions.

src.q: Small mean increases in heart rate of 2 to 4 beats per minute (bpm)
Injection site adverse events were reported in 1.9 % of patients receiving dulaglutide.

items.t: Acute pancreatitis, including necrotising and fatal cases: persistent, severe abdominal pain. Stop if suspected; do not restart if confirmed. Patients should seek urgent medical attention.

src.q: This includes post-marketing reports of necrotising pancreatitis and reports with a fatal outcome.
if pancreatitis is suspected, discontinue treatment with the GLP-1 or GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist immediately; do not restart therapy if the diagnosis of pancreatitis is confirmed

items.t: Dehydration leading to acute renal failure or worsening renal impairment.

src.q: Dehydration, sometimes leading to acute renal failure or worsening renal impairment, has been reported in patients treated with dulaglutide

items.t: Anaphylactic reaction and angioedema (post-marketing); severe gastroparesis; non-mechanical intestinal obstruction; cholelithiasis and cholecystitis.

src.q: Cases of anaphylactic reaction have been rarely reported with marketed use of dulaglutide.
Events related to impaired gastric emptying, including severe gastroparesis, have been reported.
Non-mechanical intestinal obstruction Hepatobiliary disorders Cholelithiasis, cholecystitis

items.t: Blood glucose self-monitoring is not needed for dulaglutide itself, but is needed to adjust sulphonylurea or insulin doses, especially at the start.

src.q: The use of Trulicity does not require blood glucose self-monitoring.
Blood glucose self-monitoring is necessary to adjust the dose of sulphonylurea or insulin, particularly when Trulicity therapy is started and insulin is reduced.

items.t: Watch for severe gastrointestinal symptoms; consider dose change or stopping.

src.q: Monitor and consider dose modification or discontinuation in patients who develop severe gastrointestinal symptoms while on treatment.

items.t: Stop if pancreatitis is suspected; do not restart if confirmed. Raised pancreatic enzymes alone do not predict pancreatitis.

src.q: If pancreatitis is suspected, dulaglutide should be discontinued.
elevations in pancreatic enzymes alone are not predictive of acute pancreatitis

items.t: Subcutaneous injection once weekly into the abdomen, thigh or upper arm, at any time of day, with or without meals. Never intravenous or intramuscular.

src.q: Trulicity is to be injected subcutaneously in the abdomen, thigh or upper arm. It should not be administered intravenously or intramuscularly.
The dose can be administered at any time of day, with or without meals.

items.t: The weekly injection day can be changed if the last dose was at least 3 days (72 hours) before.

src.q: The day of weekly administration can be changed if necessary, as long as the last dose was administered 3 or more days (72 hours) before.

items.t: Seek urgent medical help for severe, persistent abdominal pain that may go through to the back, with or without nausea and vomiting (possible pancreatitis).

src.q: seek urgent medical attention if you experience severe, persistent abdominal pain, that may radiate to your back and may be accompanied by nausea and vomiting

items.t: Drink plenty of fluids to avoid dehydration, especially if you have vomiting or diarrhoea.

src.q: throughout treatment stay well hydrated by drinking plenty of fluids (such as water) to avoid dehydration

items.t: Tell your healthcare team and anaesthetist before any surgery or sedation that you use this medicine; do not stop it without discussing with your doctor.

src.q: make sure you inform your healthcare team including the anaesthetist about this prior to your surgical procedure
take your prescribed medicine(s) as usual and do not stop your treatment without first discussing this with your doctor

items.t: If you also use insulin: learn the signs of diabetic ketoacidosis and get urgent help if they occur.

src.q: Inform patients of the signs and symptoms of diabetic ketoacidosis (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, excessive thirst, increased frequency of urination, difficulty breathing, confusion, unusual fatigue, or sleepiness)

items.t: With a sulphonylurea or insulin, take precautions to avoid low blood sugar while driving.

src.q: patients should be advised to take precautions to avoid hypoglycaemia while driving and using machines

items.t: Adults: major depressive disorder; diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain; generalised anxiety disorder.

src.q: Treatment of major depressive disorder. Treatment of diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain. Treatment of generalised anxiety disorder. Duloxetine is indicated in adults.
Treatment of major depressive disorder. Treatment of diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain. Treatment of generalised anxiety disorder.

items.t: Adults only. Should not be used under 18 years for major depressive disorder; safety and efficacy not established for other paediatric uses.

src.q: Duloxetine should not be used in children and adolescents under the age of 18 years for the treatment of major depressive disorder because of safety and efficacy concerns

items.t: Duloxetine is marketed under different names for several indications (including stress urinary incontinence): avoid using more than one duloxetine product at the same time.

src.q: The use of more than one of these products concomitantly should be avoided.

items.t: 60 mg once daily, with or without food (start and maintenance). Doses up to 120 mg/day studied for safety, but no evidence that non-responders benefit from increases. Response usually in 2 to 4 weeks; continue several months after response.

src.q: The starting and recommended maintenance dose is 60 mg once daily with or without food.
there is no clinical evidence suggesting that patients not responding to the initial recommended dose may benefit from dose up-titrations
Therapeutic response is usually seen after 2-4 weeks of treatment.

items.t: Start 30 mg once daily; if response is insufficient increase to 60 mg (usual maintenance). With co-morbid depression start and maintain 60 mg. 90 mg or 120 mg may be considered if response to 60 mg is insufficient.

src.q: The recommended starting dose in patients with generalised anxiety disorder is 30 mg once daily with or without food.
In patients with insufficient response, the dose should be increased to 60 mg, which is the usual maintenance dose in most patients.
In patients with insufficient response to 60 mg, escalation up to 90 mg or 120 mg may therefore be considered.

items.t: 60 mg daily, with or without food. Some may benefit from up to 120 mg/day in evenly divided doses. Assess response after 2 months; reassess benefit at least every 3 months.

src.q: Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathic Pain The starting and recommended maintenance dose is 60 mg daily with or without food.
up to a maximum dose of 120 mg per day administered in evenly divided doses
Response to treatment should be evaluated after 2 months.
The therapeutic benefit should be reassessed regularly (at least every three months)

items.t: Elderly: no dose change for age alone; caution, especially with 120 mg/day for depression or anxiety (limited data).

src.q: No dosage adjustment is recommended for elderly patients solely on the basis of age.
caution should be exercised when treating the elderly, especially with duloxetine 120 mg per day

items.t: Stopping: avoid abrupt withdrawal; reduce gradually over at least 1 to 2 weeks (4.2), no less than 2 weeks (4.4). If intolerable symptoms, resume the previous dose and taper more slowly.

src.q: When stopping treatment with duloxetine the dose should be gradually reduced over a period of at least one to two weeks in order to reduce the risk of withdrawal reactions
duloxetine should be gradually tapered when discontinuing treatment over a period of no less than 2 weeks, according to the patient's needs

items.t: Not for use under 18 years. Major depressive disorder: should not be used (safety and efficacy concerns). Generalised anxiety disorder aged 7 to 17: safety and efficacy not established. Neuropathic pain: not studied.

src.q: Duloxetine should not be used in children and adolescents under the age of 18 years for the treatment of major depressive disorder because of safety and efficacy concerns
The safety and efficacy of duloxetine for the treatment of generalised anxiety disorder in paediatric patients aged 7-17 years have not been established.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to duloxetine or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Non-selective irreversible MAOIs.

src.q: Concomitant use of duloxetine with non-selective, irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) is contraindicated

items.t: Liver disease resulting in hepatic impairment.

src.q: Liver disease resulting in hepatic impairment

items.t: Potent CYP1A2 inhibitors: fluvoxamine, ciprofloxacin, enoxacin (raised duloxetine levels).

src.q: Duloxetine should not be used in combination with fluvoxamine, ciprofloxacin or enoxacin (i.e. potent CYP1A2 inhibitors), since the combination results in elevated plasma concentrations of duloxetine

items.t: Severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance <30 mL/min).

src.q: Severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance <30 ml/min)

items.t: Starting duloxetine in uncontrolled hypertension (risk of hypertensive crisis).

src.q: The initiation of treatment with duloxetine is contraindicated in patients with uncontrolled hypertension that could expose patients to a potential risk of hypertensive crisis

items.t: Blood pressure and heart rate: rises and hypertensive crisis reported, especially with pre-existing hypertension. Monitor BP in hypertension or other cardiac disease, especially in the first month. If BP stays raised, reduce the dose or taper off.

src.q: Cases of hypertensive crisis have been reported with duloxetine, especially in patients with pre-existing hypertension.
in patients with known hypertension and/or other cardiac disease, blood pressure monitoring is recommended, especially during the first month of treatment
either dose reduction or gradual discontinuation should be considered

items.t: Serotonin syndrome / NMS, especially with other serotonergic drugs, MAOIs, antipsychotics or other dopamine antagonists: if combined use is needed, observe carefully at start and after dose increases. St John's wort: adverse reactions may be more common.

src.q: particularly with concomitant use of other serotonergic agents (including SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclic antidepressants or triptans)
careful observation of the patient is advised, particularly during treatment initiation and dose increases
Adverse reactions may be more common during concomitant use of duloxetine and herbal preparations containing St John's Wort (Hypericum perforatum).

items.t: Mania, bipolar disorder or seizures: use with caution. Raised intraocular pressure or risk of acute angle-closure glaucoma: caution (mydriasis).

src.q: Duloxetine should be used with caution in patients with a history of mania or a diagnosis of bipolar disorder, and/or seizures.
caution should be used when prescribing duloxetine to patients with increased intraocular pressure, or those at risk of acute narrow-angle glaucoma

items.t: Bleeding (ecchymoses, purpura, GI haemorrhage): caution with anticoagulants, drugs affecting platelets (e.g. NSAIDs, aspirin) and bleeding tendencies. May increase postpartum haemorrhage.

src.q: Caution is advised in patients taking anticoagulants and/or medicinal products known to affect platelet function (e.g. NSAIDs or acetylsalicylic acid (ASA)) and in patients with known bleeding tendencies.
Duloxetine may increase the risk of postpartum haemorrhage

items.t: Hyponatraemia (sometimes <110 mmol/L), often SIADH, mostly in the elderly: caution in elderly, cirrhotic or dehydrated patients and those on diuretics.

src.q: Caution is required in patients at increased risk for hyponatraemia, such as elderly, cirrhotic or dehydrated patients or patients treated with diuretics.

items.t: Suicidal thoughts and clinical worsening: monitor closely until improvement, especially early in treatment and after dose changes; higher risk under 25 years.

src.q: patients should be closely monitored until such improvement occurs
increased risk of suicidal behaviour with antidepressants compared to placebo in patients less than 25 years old

items.t: Liver injury (severe enzyme rises, hepatitis, jaundice), mostly in the first months: use with caution with other medicines associated with liver injury.

src.q: Cases of liver injury, including severe elevations of liver enzymes (>10 times upper limit of normal), hepatitis and jaundice have been reported with duloxetine
Duloxetine should be used with caution in patients treated with other medicinal products associated with hepatic injury.

items.t: Sexual dysfunction may occur and may continue after stopping. Akathisia may occur in early weeks; increasing the dose may be harmful.

src.q: There have been reports of long-lasting sexual dysfunction where the symptoms have continued despite discontinuation of SSRIs/SNRIs.
In patients who develop these symptoms, increasing the dose may be detrimental.

items.t: One UK SmPC: contains sucrose; patients with hereditary fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take it.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrose-isomaltase insufficiency should not take this medicine.

items.t: Non-selective irreversible MAOIs: contraindicated; wait 14 days after an MAOI and at least 5 days after duloxetine before an MAOI. Moclobemide: not recommended. Linezolid: should not be given.

src.q: duloxetine should not be used in combination with non-selective, irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) or within at least 14 days of discontinuing treatment with an MAOI
at least 5 days should be allowed after stopping duloxetine before starting an MAOI
The concomitant use of duloxetine with selective, reversible MAOIs, like moclobemide, is not recommended
The antibiotic linezolid is a reversible non-selective MAOI and should not be given to patients treated with duloxetine

items.t: Potent CYP1A2 inhibitors (fluvoxamine, ciprofloxacin, enoxacin): contraindicated. Fluvoxamine raised duloxetine AUC 6-fold.

src.q: duloxetine should not be administered in combination with potent inhibitors of CYP1A2 like fluvoxamine

items.t: Serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics such as amitriptyline, moclobemide, linezolid, St John's wort, triptans, tramadol, pethidine, tryptophan): caution (serotonin syndrome).

src.q: Caution is advisable if duloxetine is used concomitantly with serotonergic agents like SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclic antidepressants like clomipramine or amitriptyline
MAOIs like moclobemide or linezolid, St John's Wort (Hypericum perforatum) or triptans, tramadol, pethidine, and tryptophan

items.t: CYP2D6 substrates, especially narrow therapeutic index (e.g. flecainide, propafenone, metoprolol) and tricyclics (amitriptyline, nortriptyline, imipramine), risperidone: caution (duloxetine is a moderate CYP2D6 inhibitor).

src.q: Duloxetine is a moderate inhibitor of CYP2D6.
Caution is advised if duloxetine is co-administered with medicinal products that are predominantly metabolised by CYP2D6

items.t: Other CNS-acting drugs and alcohol (benzodiazepines, opioids, antipsychotics, phenobarbital, sedating antihistamines): caution.

src.q: caution is advised when duloxetine is taken in combination with other centrally-acting medicinal products or substances, including alcohol and sedative medicinal products
(e.g. benzodiazepines, morphinomimetics, antipsychotics, phenobarbital, sedative antihistamines)

items.t: Oral anticoagulants and antiplatelet agents: caution (bleeding). INR rises reported with warfarin.

src.q: Caution should be exercised when duloxetine is combined with oral anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents due to a potential increased risk of bleeding attributable to a pharmacodynamic interaction.
increases in INR values have been reported when duloxetine was co-administered to patients treated with warfarin

items.t: Smoking: smokers have almost 50% lower duloxetine levels. Aluminium/magnesium antacids and famotidine: no significant effect.

src.q: smokers have almost 50% lower plasma concentrations of duloxetine compared with non-smokers
Co-administration of duloxetine with aluminium- and magnesium-containing antacids, or duloxetine with famotidine, had no significant effect

items.t: Mild or moderate renal impairment (CrCl 30 to 80 mL/min): no dose change. Severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min): contraindicated.

src.q: No dosage adjustment is necessary for patients with mild or moderate renal dysfunction (creatinine clearance 30 to 80 ml/min).
Duloxetine must not be used in patients with severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance <30 ml/min; see section 4.3).

items.t: Must not be used in liver disease resulting in hepatic impairment (contraindicated).

src.q: Duloxetine must not be used in patients with liver disease resulting in hepatic impairment

items.t: SmPC: use only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. Two large observational studies do not suggest an overall increased risk of major malformations.

src.q: Duloxetine should be used in pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the foetus.
Two large observational studies do not suggest an overall increased risk of major congenital malformation

items.t: Late pregnancy: possible preterm birth (one study), postpartum haemorrhage (less than 2-fold, exposure in the month before birth), PPHN cannot be ruled out, neonatal discontinuation symptoms (hypotonia, tremor, feeding difficulty, respiratory distress, seizures). MHRA: weigh PPH risk against individual bleeding/thrombotic risk.

src.q: an increased risk (less than 2-fold) of postpartum haemorrhage following duloxetine exposure within the month prior to birth
Discontinuation symptoms seen with duloxetine may include hypotonia, tremor, jitteriness, feeding difficulty, respiratory distress and seizures.
consider the findings of the review in the context of individual patient risk factors for bleeding or thrombotic events

items.t: BUMPS (UKTIS): can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a GP or specialist; no evidence of effects on development, miscarriage, stillbirth or preterm birth. Late-pregnancy use usually means birth in hospital.

src.q: Duloxetine can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a GP or specialist.
There is no evidence that duloxetine affects your baby's development or increases the chance of miscarriage, stillbirth, or preterm birth.

items.t: SmPC: very weakly excreted into milk (about 0.14% of maternal dose), but infant safety is unknown, so use while breastfeeding is not recommended.

src.q: As the safety of duloxetine in infants is not known, the use of duloxetine while breast-feeding is not recommended.

items.t: SPS (differs from SmPC): can be used with caution and infant monitoring, but SSRIs or tricyclics are preferred. Monitor the infant for irritability, restlessness, drowsiness, GI symptoms, poor feeding and weight gain.

src.q: Duloxetine can be used with caution during breastfeeding, but SSRIs or TCAs are preferred.
Monitor infants for irritability, restlessness, drowsiness, gastrointestinal symptoms, poor feeding or not waking to feed and appropriate weight gain.

items.t: Animal studies: no effect on male fertility; effects in females only at maternally toxic doses. Women should tell their doctor if they become or plan to become pregnant.

src.q: In animal studies, duloxetine had no effect on male fertility
Women should be advised to notify their physician if they become pregnant, or intend to become pregnant, during therapy.

items.t: Most common: nausea, headache, dry mouth, somnolence, dizziness; usually mild to moderate and early in treatment.

src.q: The most commonly reported adverse reactions in patients treated with duloxetine were nausea, headache, dry mouth, somnolence and dizziness.

items.t: Withdrawal symptoms on stopping are common (about 45% on abrupt stopping in trials).

src.q: adverse events seen on abrupt treatment discontinuation occurred in approximately 45% of patients treated with duloxetine

items.t: Hypertensive crisis; sustained BP rise: reduce dose or taper off.

src.q: Cases of hypertensive crisis have been reported with duloxetine, especially in patients with pre-existing hypertension.
either dose reduction or gradual discontinuation should be considered

items.t: Serotonin syndrome or NMS (potentially life-threatening).

src.q: serotonin syndrome or neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), a potentially life-threatening condition, may occur with duloxetine treatment

items.t: Liver injury: severe enzyme rises, hepatitis, jaundice.

src.q: Cases of liver injury, including severe elevations of liver enzymes (>10 times upper limit of normal), hepatitis and jaundice have been reported with duloxetine

items.t: Severe hyponatraemia (serum sodium below 110 mmol/L reported).

src.q: Hyponatraemia has been reported when administering duloxetine, including cases with serum sodium lower than 110 mmol/l.

items.t: Suicidal thoughts and behaviour during treatment or soon after stopping: seek help immediately.

src.q: Cases of suicidal thoughts and suicidal behaviours have been reported during duloxetine therapy or early after treatment discontinuation

items.t: Before starting: check BP (do not start if hypertension is uncontrolled). Discuss the risk of suicidal thoughts and of sexual dysfunction (MHRA 2026).

src.q: The initiation of treatment with duloxetine is contraindicated in patients with uncontrolled hypertension
discuss with patients when starting or changing the dose of an antidepressant or at their next review, the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviours

items.t: BP monitoring in hypertension or cardiac disease, especially in the first month. Close supervision for suicidality early and after dose changes; monitor regularly after starting (MHRA). Neuropathic pain: review response at 2 months, then at least every 3 months.

src.q: in patients with known hypertension and/or other cardiac disease, blood pressure monitoring is recommended, especially during the first month of treatment
monitor your patients regularly after starting treatment with an antidepressant
The therapeutic benefit should be reassessed regularly (at least every three months)

items.t: Sustained BP rise: consider dose reduction or gradual stopping. Taper over at least 2 weeks when stopping.

src.q: either dose reduction or gradual discontinuation should be considered
duloxetine should be gradually tapered when discontinuing treatment over a period of no less than 2 weeks, according to the patient's needs

items.t: Oral, once daily, with or without food (neuropathic pain doses above 60 mg in evenly divided doses).

src.q: The starting and recommended maintenance dose is 60 mg once daily with or without food.
up to a maximum dose of 120 mg per day administered in evenly divided doses

items.t: May cause sedation or dizziness: if affected, avoid driving and hazardous machinery. Avoid alcohol and other sedatives unless advised.

src.q: Patients should be instructed that if they experience sedation or dizziness they should avoid potentially hazardous tasks such as driving or operating machinery.
caution is advised when duloxetine is taken in combination with other centrally-acting medicinal products or substances, including alcohol and sedative medicinal products

items.t: Do not stop suddenly (withdrawal, even after a missed dose). Seek urgent help for new or worsening suicidal thoughts. Sexual dysfunction may continue after stopping.

src.q: there have been very rare reports of such symptoms in patients who have inadvertently missed a dose
if you have new or worsening suicidal thoughts, particularly when starting or changing dose of antidepressants, seek urgent medical attention
there is the potential for you to experience sexual dysfunction with some antidepressants, which may continue even after you stop the medicine

items.t: Do not take with other duloxetine-containing products. Tell the doctor if pregnant or planning pregnancy.

src.q: The use of more than one of these products concomitantly should be avoided.
Women should be advised to notify their physician if they become pregnant, or intend to become pregnant, during therapy.

items.t: Progesterone insufficiency: dysmenorrhoea, endometriosis, irregular cycles, premenstrual syndrome. HRT: added to oestrogen in women with a uterus. Dysfunctional bleeding or secondary amenorrhoea (with an oestrogen).

src.q: Treatment of dysmenorrhoea, endometriosis, irregular menstrual cycles and pre-menstrual syndrome.
Dydrogesterone is used to supplement an estrogen treatment in non-hysterectomised women
Dysfunctional bleeding or secondary amenorrhoea: The drug may be used with an estrogen in the management of these conditions.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction stated in the UK SmPC accessed (emc 10 mg film-coated tablets).

items.t: Dysmenorrhoea: 10 mg twice daily, days 5-25. Endometriosis: 10 mg two to three times daily, days 5-25 or continuously. Irregular cycles: 10 mg twice daily, days 11-25. Premenstrual syndrome: 10 mg twice daily, days 12-26 (may be increased).

src.q: Dysmenorrhoea: 10 mg of dydrogesterone twice a day from day 5 to 25 of the cycle. Endometriosis: 10 mg of dydrogesterone two to three times daily from day 5 to 25 of the cycle, or continuously.
Irregular menstrual cycles : 10 mg of dydrogesterone twice a day from day 11 to 25 of the cycle. Pre-menstrual syndrome: 10 mg of dydrogesterone twice a day from day 12 to 26 of the cycle.

items.t: HRT with oestrogen: 10 mg daily for the last 14 days of each 28-day cycle (continuous sequential) or the last 12-14 days of oestrogen use (cyclical); may increase to 20 mg daily.

src.q: sequential supplementation of 10 mg dydrogesterone during the last 14 days of each 28-day cycle
Depending on the clinical response, the dosage may be adjusted to 20 mg dydrogesterone daily in the course of the treatment.

items.t: Dysfunctional uterine bleeding: to stop a bleed 10 mg twice daily for 5-7 days; continuing treatment 10 mg twice daily, days 11-25. Secondary amenorrhoea: 10 mg twice daily, days 11-25 (endometrium primed with oestrogen).

src.q: When treatment is started to arrest a bleeding episode 10 mg of dydrogesterone twice a day for five to seven days. For continuous treatment 10 mg of dydrogesterone twice a day from day 11 to day 25 of the cycle.
Secondary amenorrhoea: 10 mg of dydrogesterone twice a day from day 11 to 25

items.t: No relevant use before menarche. Safety and efficacy in adolescents 12-18 years not established; no dose recommendation.

src.q: There is no relevant use for dydrogesterone before menarche. The safety and efficacy of dydrogesterone in adolescents aged 12-18 years has not been established.

items.t: Hypersensitivity; known or suspected progestogen-dependent tumours; meningioma or history of meningioma; unexplained vaginal bleeding; contraindications to oestrogen when used together.

src.q: Known or suspected progestogen-dependent tumours - Meningioma or history of meningioma - Unexplained vaginal bleeding - Contraindications for the use of estrogens should be considered when used in combination with dydrogesterone

items.t: Severe acute and chronic liver disease; disorders of bilirubin metabolism (e.g. Dubin-Johnson, Rotor syndrome); previous or existing liver tumours; thrombophlebitis and thromboembolic diseases.

src.q: Severe acute and chronic liver diseases as well as disorders in the metabolism of bile pigments (e.g. Dubin-Johnson syndrome, Rotor syndrome) - Previous or existing liver tumours - Thrombophlebitis and thromboembolic diseases.

items.t: Find the cause of irregular bleeding before treating; investigate bleeding that occurs later in treatment or after it (endometrial biopsy may be needed).

src.q: If dydrogesterone is prescribed for the treatment of irregular bleeding, the etiology of this bleeding should be clarified.

items.t: Monitor closely, and consider stopping, if porphyria, depression, abnormal liver function from liver disease, or cholestatic jaundice/pruritus is present now or in the past (or worsened in pregnancy or previous hormone treatment).

src.q: discontinuation of treatment should be considered: - Porphyria - Depression - Pathological liver function values caused by acute or chronic liver disease - Cholestatic jaundice and/or pruritus

items.t: Meningioma has been reported: monitor for signs; stop if meningioma is diagnosed.

src.q: If a patient is diagnosed with meningioma, any dydrogesterone-containing treatment must be stopped

items.t: Persistent clinically significant hypertension: stop and treat. At higher doses caution with current or past cerebral apoplexy (stroke).

src.q: if persistent clinically significant hypertension develops during the use of dydrogesterone, it is advisable to discontinue dydrogesterone and to treat the hypertension
In higher doses, caution is advised with: - Cerebral apoplexy (also in the medical history)

items.t: With oestrogen as HRT: breast cancer, ovarian cancer, VTE (contraindicated in known thrombophilia), coronary disease and ischaemic stroke risks apply; review at least yearly.

src.q: Patients with known thrombophilia have an increased risk of VTE. HRT may add to this risk and is therefore contraindicated in these patients.
a careful appraisal of the risks and benefits should be undertaken at least annually

items.t: Contains lactose: people with galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take it.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: CYP enzyme inducers (e.g. carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, rifampicin, St John's wort) may increase dydrogesterone metabolism and reduce its effect.

src.q: the metabolism of dydrogesterone and DHD may be increased when used concomitantly with substances known to induce CYP enzyme activity
Clinically, increased dydrogesterone metabolism may lead to reduced effect.

items.t: Dydrogesterone does not inhibit or induce CYP enzymes at clinical concentrations (in vitro).

src.q: In vitro studies have shown that dydrogesterone and DHD at clinically relevant concentrations do not have an inhibitory or inducing effect on drug-metabolizing CYP enzyme

renal.note: No renal impairment advice in the UK SmPC accessed (emc 10 mg film-coated tablets).

items.t: Contraindicated in severe acute and chronic liver disease and liver tumours. Pathological liver function values from liver disease: monitor closely and consider stopping.

src.q: Severe acute and chronic liver diseases
Pathological liver function values caused by acute or chronic liver disease

items.t: Not authorised for use in pregnancy. No evidence of harm so far despite wide exposure; some progestogens have been linked to hypospadias but no firm conclusion can be drawn.

src.q: Nalvee 10 mg is not authorised for use in pregnancy.
So far there is no evidence of any harmful effect of dydrogesterone use during pregnancy.
The literature suggests that some progestogens are associated with an increased risk of hypospadias.

items.t: No data; progestogens pass into milk in small amounts and risk to the baby is unknown. Should not be taken while breastfeeding.

src.q: It is not known whether there is any risk to the baby. Therefore, Nalvee 10 mg should not be taken while breastfeeding.

items.t: No evidence that dydrogesterone reduces fertility at therapeutic doses.

src.q: There is no evidence that dydrogesterone decreases fertility at therapeutic doses.

items.t: Common: headache, migraine, nausea, menstrual disorders, breast pain or tenderness.

src.q: The most commonly reported adverse reactions in patients treated with dydrogesterone in clinical trials on indications without estrogen use are migraine/headache, nausea, menstrual disorders and breast pain/tension.

items.t: Mild somnolence or dizziness may occur, mainly in the first hours after a dose; take care driving or using machines.

src.q: Dydrogesterone may rarely cause mild somnolence and/or dizziness, especially during the first hours after use. Therefore, machines and vehicles should only be operated with caution.

items.t: Meningioma (growth of progestogen-dependent tumours): stop if diagnosed.

src.q: Increase in size of progestogen dependent tumours (e.g. meningioma)
If a patient is diagnosed with meningioma, any dydrogesterone-containing treatment must be stopped

items.t: Rare: abnormal liver function with jaundice, haemolytic anaemia, angioedema. Stop at once with migraine-like or unusually severe headache or sudden visual impairment.

src.q: Hepatic function abnormal (with asthenia or malaise, jaundice and abdominal pain)
migraine-like or unusually severe headache - acute vision impairment

items.t: Clarify the cause of irregular bleeding before starting; for HRT take a full personal and family history and examine as indicated.

src.q: If dydrogesterone is prescribed for the treatment of irregular bleeding, the etiology of this bleeding should be clarified.
Before starting or resuming HRT, a complete personal and family medical history should be obtained.

items.t: Monitor for meningioma signs; watch blood pressure; monitor closely with porphyria, depression, liver disease or cholestasis.

src.q: Patients should be monitored for signs and symptoms of meningiomas in accordance with clinical practice.

items.t: Stop: meningioma; persistent significant hypertension; migraine-like or unusually severe headache; acute visual impairment; VTE during HRT.

src.q: Therapy is to be discontinued immediately if there is a contraindication and if one of the following situations occurs: - migraine-like or unusually severe headache - acute vision impairment
If VTE develops after initiation of HRT, the drug must be discontinued.

items.t: Oral. Take at the same time each day; if twice daily, one in the morning and one in the evening.

src.q: When taking 2 film-coated tablets daily, it is recommended to take one in the morning and one in the evening.

items.t: Report painful leg swelling, sudden chest pain or breathlessness, severe headache or sudden vision problems at once. May cause mild drowsiness or dizziness.

src.q: especially painful swelling of a leg, sudden chest pain, dyspnoea
Dydrogesterone may rarely cause mild somnolence and/or dizziness

items.t: Type 2 diabetes not controlled by diet and exercise, in adults and children aged 10 years and over: alone when metformin is not tolerated, or added to other diabetes medicines.

src.q: Empagliflozin is indicated in adults and children aged 10 years and above for the treatment of insufficiently controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus as an adjunct to diet and exercise
as monotherapy when metformin is considered inappropriate due to intolerance

items.t: Symptomatic chronic heart failure (adults).

src.q: Empagliflozin is indicated in adults for the treatment of symptomatic chronic heart failure.

items.t: Chronic kidney disease (adults).

src.q: Empagliflozin is indicated in adults for the treatment of chronic kidney disease.

items.t: Should not be used in type 1 diabetes (ketoacidosis was more common in type 1 trials).

src.q: Empagliflozin should not be used in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus
Data from a clinical trial program in patients with type 1 diabetes showed increased ketoacidosis occurrence with common frequency

items.t: Start 10 mg once daily (alone or add-on). If tolerated, eGFR ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m² and tighter control is needed, increase to 25 mg once daily. Maximum 25 mg daily.

src.q: The recommended starting dose is 10 mg empagliflozin once daily for monotherapy and add-on combination therapy with other medicinal products for the treatment of diabetes.

In patients tolerating empagliflozin 10 mg once daily who have an eGFR ≥60 ml/min/1.73 m2 and need tighter glycaemic control, the dose can be increased to 25 mg once daily. The maximum daily dose is 25 mg

items.t: 10 mg once daily.

src.q: Heart failure The recommended dose is 10 mg empagliflozin once daily.

items.t: 10 mg once daily.

src.q: Chronic kidney disease The recommended dose is 10 mg empagliflozin once daily.

items.t: With a sulfonylurea or insulin: consider a lower dose of these to reduce hypoglycaemia risk.
items.tag: All indications, with sulfonylurea or insulin

src.q: When empagliflozin is used in combination with a sulphonylurea or with insulin, a lower dose of the sulphonylurea or insulin may be considered to reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia

items.t: Missed dose: take when remembered, but not a double dose on the same day.

src.q: If a dose is missed, it should be taken as soon as the patient remembers; however, a double dose should not be taken on the same day.

items.t: Elderly: no dose change for age; at 75 years and over consider the higher risk of volume depletion.

src.q: No dose adjustment is recommended based on age. In patients 75 years and older, an increased risk for volume depletion should be taken into account

items.t: Type 2 diabetes, children aged 10 years and over: start 10 mg once daily; if tolerated and more control is needed, increase to 25 mg once daily. No data in children with eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m² or under 10 years.

src.q: Paediatric population The recommended starting dose is 10 mg empagliflozin once daily.
No data are available for children with eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m² and children below 10 years of age.

items.t: Heart failure and chronic kidney disease: not established under 18 years.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of empagliflozin for the treatment of heart failure or for the treatment of chronic kidney disease in children under 18 years of age have not been established.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to empagliflozin or any excipient.

src.q: 4.3 Contraindications Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Ketoacidosis (rare, can be fatal; may occur with glucose below 14 mmol/L, and has occurred in people without diabetes). Assess at once if non-specific symptoms (nausea, vomiting, anorexia, abdominal pain, excessive thirst, difficulty breathing, confusion, unusual fatigue or sleepiness), whatever the glucose. Stop immediately if suspected or diagnosed.

src.q: Cases of ketoacidosis, including life-threatening and fatal cases, have been reported in patients with diabetes mellitus treated with SGLT2 inhibitors, including empagliflozin.
Although ketoacidosis is less likely to occur in patients without diabetes mellitus, cases have also been reported in these patients.
In patients where ketoacidosis is suspected or diagnosed, treatment with empagliflozin should be discontinued immediately.

items.t: Interrupt when hospitalised for major surgery or acute serious illness; monitor ketones (blood preferred). Restart when ketones are normal and the patient is stable.

src.q: Treatment should be interrupted in patients who are hospitalised for major surgical procedures or acute serious medical illnesses. Monitoring of ketones is recommended in these patients.
Treatment with empagliflozin may be restarted when the ketone values are normal and the patient's condition has stabilised.

items.t: Higher ketoacidosis risk (use with caution): low beta-cell reserve (low C-peptide, LADA, history of pancreatitis), restricted food intake or severe dehydration, reduced insulin doses, higher insulin needs from acute illness, surgery or alcohol abuse. Restarting after ketoacidosis on an SGLT2 inhibitor is not recommended unless another clear cause was found and resolved.

src.q: Patients who may be at higher risk of ketoacidosis include patients with a low beta-cell function reserve
SGLT2 inhibitors should be used with caution in these patients.

Restarting SGLT2 inhibitor treatment in patients with previous ketoacidosis while on SGLT2 inhibitor treatment is not recommended, unless another clear precipitating factor is identified and resolved.

items.t: Volume depletion: caution in known cardiovascular disease, antihypertensive users with a history of hypotension, and age 75 and over. In illness with fluid loss monitor volume status and electrolytes; consider interrupting until fluid loss is corrected.

src.q: caution should be exercised in patients for whom an empagliflozin-induced drop in blood pressure could pose a risk, such as patients with known cardiovascular disease, patients on anti-hypertensive therapy with a history of hypotension or patients aged 75 years and older
Temporary interruption of treatment with empagliflozin should be considered until the fluid loss is corrected.

items.t: Complicated urinary tract infections (pyelonephritis, urosepsis) have been reported; consider temporary interruption.

src.q: Temporary interruption of empagliflozin should be considered in patients with complicated urinary tract infections.

items.t: Fournier's gangrene: rare but life-threatening. If suspected, stop and start urgent treatment (antibiotics, surgical debridement).

src.q: If Fournier's gangrene is suspected, empagliflozin should be discontinued and prompt treatment (including antibiotics and surgical debridement) should be instituted.

items.t: Renal function: check before starting, at least yearly, and before starting any medicine that may harm renal function.

src.q: Prior to empagliflozin initiation and periodically during treatment, i.e. at least yearly
Prior to initiation of any concomitant medicinal product that may have a negative impact on renal function.

items.t: Lower limb amputation (mainly toes) seen with another SGLT2 inhibitor; counsel on preventive foot care.

src.q: Like for all diabetic patients it is important to counsel patients on routine preventative foot-care.

items.t: Hepatic injury reported in trials (causal link not established). Raised haematocrit: monitor and investigate pronounced rises.

src.q: Cases of hepatic injury have been reported with empagliflozin in clinical trials. A causal relationship between empagliflozin and hepatic injury has not been established.
Patients with pronounced elevations in haematocrit should be monitored and investigated for underlying haematological disease.

items.t: Contains lactose: patients with hereditary galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take it. Urine glucose tests will be positive; 1,5-AG assay is unreliable.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicinal product.
patients taking empagliflozin will test positive for glucose in their urine.

items.t: Thiazide and loop diuretics: may add to the diuretic effect and increase the risk of dehydration and hypotension.

src.q: Empagliflozin may add to the diuretic effect of thiazide and loop diuretics and may increase the risk of dehydration and hypotension

items.t: Insulin and insulin secretagogues (e.g. sulfonylureas): a lower dose of these may be needed to reduce hypoglycaemia risk.

src.q: a lower dose of insulin or an insulin secretagogue may be required to reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia when used in combination with empagliflozin

items.t: Age 75 and over: pay special attention to fluid intake with medicines that may cause volume depletion (e.g. diuretics, ACE inhibitors).

src.q: special attention should be given to their volume intake in case of co-administered medicinal products which may lead to volume depletion (e.g. diuretics, ACE inhibitors)

items.t: UGT enzyme inducers (e.g. rifampicin, phenytoin; not in this tool's list): co-treatment not recommended (may reduce efficacy); if needed, monitor glycaemic control.

src.q: Co-treatment with known inducers of UGT enzymes is not recommended due to a potential risk of decreased efficacy.
If an inducer of these UGT enzymes must be co-administered, monitoring of glycaemic control to assess response to empagliflozin is appropriate.

items.t: Lithium (not in this tool's list): levels may fall; monitor lithium more often after starting or dose changes.

src.q: Empagliflozin may increase renal lithium excretion and the blood lithium levels may be decreased.
Serum concentration of lithium should be monitored more frequently after empagliflozin initiation and dose changes.

items.t: No clinically relevant interaction found with metformin, glimepiride, sitagliptin, linagliptin, warfarin, verapamil, simvastatin, hydrochlorothiazide, digoxin or oral contraceptives.

src.q: the pharmacokinetics of empagliflozin were not influenced by co-administration with metformin, glimepiride, pioglitazone, sitagliptin, linagliptin, warfarin, verapamil, ramipril, simvastatin, torasemide and hydrochlorothiazide.

empagliflozin had no clinically relevant effect on the pharmacokinetics of metformin, glimepiride, pioglitazone, sitagliptin, linagliptin, simvastatin, warfarin, ramipril, digoxin, diuretics and oral contraceptives.

items.t: eGFR < 20 mL/min/1.73 m²: starting treatment is not recommended (limited experience).

src.q: Due to limited experience, it is not recommended to initiate treatment with empagliflozin in patients with an eGFR <20 ml/min/1.73 m2.

items.t: eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m²: the daily dose is 10 mg.

src.q: In patients with an eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m2 the daily dose of empagliflozin is 10 mg.

items.t: Type 2 diabetes: glucose-lowering effect reduced when eGFR < 45 and likely absent < 30 mL/min/1.73 m²; if eGFR falls below 45, consider additional glucose-lowering treatment if needed.

src.q: In patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus, the glucose lowering efficacy of empagliflozin is reduced in patients with an eGFR <45 ml/min/1.73 m2 and likely absent in patients with an eGFR <30 ml/min/1.73 m2.
if eGFR falls below 45 ml/min/1.73 m2, additional glucose lowering treatment should be considered if needed

items.t: No dose adjustment in hepatic impairment. Severe hepatic impairment: exposure increased and experience limited, so not recommended.

src.q: No dose adjustment is required for patients with hepatic impairment.
Therapeutic experience in patients with severe hepatic impairment is limited and therefore not recommended for use in this population

items.t: SmPC: no human data; animal studies showed effects on postnatal development. As a precaution, it is preferable to avoid in pregnancy.

src.q: However, animal studies have shown adverse effects on postnatal development
As a precautionary measure, it is preferable to avoid the use of empagliflozin during pregnancy.

items.t: BUMPS: treat type 2 diabetes in pregnancy with metformin, plus insulin if needed; SGLT2 inhibitors are avoided as a precaution. With an unplanned pregnancy, keep taking it until reviewed promptly.

src.q: Type 2 diabetes during pregnancy should be treated with metformin, as well as insulin if required. Other antidiabetic drugs should not be used.
you should carry on with the drug you are taking until your appointment, as uncontrolled diabetes is risky for you and your baby

items.t: SmPC: should not be used during breastfeeding (excreted in animal milk; infant risk cannot be excluded).

src.q: A risk to the newborns/infants cannot be excluded. Empagliflozin should not be used during breast-feeding.

items.t: SPS: insulin or metformin are the preferred choices; limited or no published information on other antidiabetic medicines.

src.q: Insulin or metformin are the preferred choices during breastfeeding.
limited or no published information on the use of other antidiabetic (blood-glucose lowering) medicines during breastfeeding.

items.t: No human fertility studies; animal studies show no harmful effect on fertility.

src.q: No studies on the effect on human fertility have been conducted for empagliflozin. Animal studies do not indicate direct or indirect harmful effects with respect to fertility

items.t: Hypoglycaemia when used with a sulfonylurea or insulin (the most frequent reaction in type 2 diabetes trials).

src.q: The most frequently reported adverse reaction was hypoglycaemia when used with sulphonylurea or insulin

items.t: Genital infections (vaginal thrush, vulvovaginitis, balanitis): about 4% vs 1% with placebo, more in women.

src.q: Vaginal moniliasis, vulvovaginitis, balanitis and other genital infections were reported more frequently in patients treated with empagliflozin (empagliflozin 10 mg: 4.0%, empagliflozin 25 mg: 3.9%) compared to placebo (1.0%).

items.t: Urinary tract infection (8.8% with 10 mg vs 7.2% placebo) and increased urination (about 3.5% vs 1.4%).

src.q: The overall frequency of urinary tract infection reported as adverse event was similar in patients treated with empagliflozin 25 mg and placebo (7.0% and 7.2%) and higher in empagliflozin 10 mg (8.8%).

Increased urination (including the predefined terms pollakiuria, polyuria, and nocturia) was observed at higher frequencies in patients treated with empagliflozin (empagliflozin 10 mg: 3.5%, empagliflozin 25 mg: 3.3%) compared to placebo (1.4%).

items.t: Volume depletion: the most frequent reaction in heart failure trials (11.4% vs 9.7%); more frequent at 75 years and over.

src.q: The most frequent adverse reaction of the pooled EMPEROR-Reduced and EMPEROR-Preserved studies was volume depletion (empagliflozin 10 mg: 11.4%. placebo: 9.7%).
The frequency of volume depletion events was increased in patients 75 years and older

items.t: Ketoacidosis (may occur with near-normal glucose): stop immediately and assess.

src.q: In patients where ketoacidosis is suspected or diagnosed, treatment with empagliflozin should be discontinued immediately.

items.t: Fournier's gangrene: seek care for genital or perineal pain, tenderness, redness or swelling with fever or malaise; stop and treat urgently.

src.q: Patients should be advised to seek medical attention if they experience a combination of symptoms of pain, tenderness, erythema, or swelling in the genital or perineal area, with fever or malaise.

items.t: Complicated urinary tract infection (pyelonephritis, urosepsis): consider interrupting.

src.q: Cases of complicated urinary tract infections including pyelonephritis and urosepsis have been reported in patients treated with empagliflozin

items.t: Renal function before starting; consider ketoacidosis risk factors.

src.q: Prior to empagliflozin initiation and periodically during treatment, i.e. at least yearly
Before initiating empagliflozin, factors in the patient history that may predispose to ketoacidosis should be considered.

items.t: Renal function at least yearly and before starting medicines that may harm the kidneys. Volume status and electrolytes in illness with fluid loss.

src.q: Prior to initiation of any concomitant medicinal product that may have a negative impact on renal function.
careful monitoring of volume status (e.g. physical examination, blood pressure measurements, laboratory tests including haematocrit) and electrolytes is recommended

items.t: Hospital admission for major surgery or acute serious illness: interrupt and monitor blood ketones.

src.q: monitor ketones during this period - measurement of blood ketone levels is preferred to urine

items.t: Stop immediately if ketoacidosis is suspected; do not restart any SGLT2 inhibitor after DKA on treatment unless another cause was found and resolved. Stop if Fournier's gangrene is suspected.

src.q: discontinue treatment with the SGLT2 inhibitor immediately if DKA is suspected or diagnosed
if Fournier's gangrene is suspected, stop the SGLT2 inhibitor and urgently start treatment

items.t: With or without food; swallow whole with water.

src.q: The tablets can be taken with or without food, swallowed whole with water.

items.t: SPS (off-label, adults with swallowing difficulties): tablets can be dispersed in water, or crushed and mixed with water or soft food.

src.q: Empagliflozin tablets Film-coated but can be dispersed in water, or crushed and mixed with water or given with soft food.

items.t: Know the signs of ketoacidosis (rapid weight loss, feeling or being sick, stomach pain, fast deep breathing, sleepiness, sweet-smelling breath) and seek medical advice at once.

src.q: rapid weight loss, feeling sick or being sick, stomach pain, fast and deep breathing, sleepiness, a sweet smell to the breath, a sweet or metallic taste in the mouth, or a different odour to urine or sweat

items.t: Seek urgent attention for severe pain, tenderness, redness or swelling of the genital or perineal area with fever or feeling unwell.

src.q: advise patients to seek urgent medical attention if they experience severe pain, tenderness, erythema, or swelling in the genital or perineal area, accompanied by fever or malaise

items.t: Routine foot care and good hydration are important.

src.q: advise patients receiving any sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor about the importance of routine preventive foot care and adequate hydration

items.t: With a sulfonylurea or insulin, take care to avoid low blood sugar when driving or using machines.

src.q: Patients should be advised to take precautions to avoid hypoglycaemia while driving and using machines, in particular when empagliflozin is used in combination with a sulphonylurea and/or insulin.

items.t: Type 2 diabetes in adults and children aged 10 years and over, with diet and exercise: not controlled on maximally tolerated metformin alone; with other diabetes medicines when not controlled on metformin plus those; or to replace separate empagliflozin and metformin tablets.

src.q: Synjardy is indicated in adults and children aged 10 years and above for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus as an adjunct to diet and exercise
in patients insufficiently controlled on their maximally tolerated dose of metformin alone
in patients already being treated with the combination of empagliflozin and metformin as separate tablets.

items.t: Should not be used in type 1 diabetes.

src.q: Synjardy should not be used in patients with type 1 diabetes.

items.t: One tablet twice daily with meals. Start with empagliflozin 5 mg twice daily (10 mg/day) plus the metformin dose already taken; if tolerated and more control is needed, increase to empagliflozin 12.5 mg twice daily (25 mg/day). Do not exceed the maximum metformin dose.

src.q: The recommended dose is one tablet twice daily.
the recommended starting dose of Synjardy should provide empagliflozin 5 mg twice daily (10 mg daily dose) and the dose of metformin similar to the dose already being taken.
In patients tolerating a total daily dose of empagliflozin 10 mg and who need tighter glycaemic control, the dose can be increased to a total daily dose of empagliflozin 25 mg.

items.t: With a sulfonylurea and/or insulin: a lower dose of these may be needed to reduce hypoglycaemia.

src.q: When Synjardy is used in combination with a sulphonylurea and/or insulin, a lower dose of sulphonylurea and/or insulin may be required to reduce the risk of hypoglycemia

items.t: Switching from separate tablets: same daily doses of empagliflozin (10 or 25 mg) and metformin, or nearest suitable metformin dose.

src.q: Patients switching from separate tablets of empagliflozin (10 mg or 25 mg total daily dose) and metformin to Synjardy should receive the same daily dose of empagliflozin and metformin already being taken

items.t: Missed dose: take when remembered, but not two doses at the same time; otherwise skip it.

src.q: If a dose is missed, it should be taken as soon as the patient remembers; however, a double dose should not be taken on the same time. In that case, the missed dose should be skipped.

items.t: Elderly: use with caution (renal function more often reduced); monitor renal function; at 75 and over consider volume depletion risk.

src.q: Synjardy should be used with caution in these patients.
In patients 75 years and older, an increased risk for volume depletion should be taken into account

items.t: Children 10 years and over (type 2 diabetes): keep the existing metformin dose; start empagliflozin 5 mg twice daily, increase to 12.5 mg twice daily if tolerated and needed. Maximum 25 mg empagliflozin and 2000 mg metformin daily. No data under 10 years or with eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m².

src.q: The recommended empagliflozin starting dose is 5 mg twice daily (10 mg total daily doses).
The maximum recommended daily dose of Synjardy is 25 mg of empagliflozin and 2 000 mg of metformin
No data are available for children with eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m² and children below 10 years of age.

items.t: Aged 10 to 12: particular caution (few studied). Follow growth and puberty, especially before puberty.

src.q: particular caution is recommended when prescribing to children aged between 10 and 12 years.
a careful follow-up of the effect of metformin on these parameters in metformin-treated children, especially prepubescent children, is recommended.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to empagliflozin, metformin or any excipient.
