src.q: If a rash, which is considered attributable to fluconazole, develops in a patient treated for a superficial fungal infection, further therapy with this medicinal product should be discontinued.
fluconazole discontinued if bullous lesions or erythema multiforme develop

items.t: Adrenal insufficiency has been seen with ketoconazole and could rarely apply to fluconazole.

src.q: Ketoconazole is known to cause adrenal insufficiency, and this could also although rarely seen be applicable to fluconazole.

items.t: Capsules contain lactose: people with hereditary galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take them.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, the total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: Fluconazole is a moderate CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 inhibitor and a strong CYP2C19 inhibitor. Monitor patients on narrow-therapeutic-window medicines metabolised by these enzymes. The effect lasts 4 to 5 days after stopping fluconazole.

src.q: Fluconazole is a moderate CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 inhibitor. Fluconazole is also a strong inhibitor of CYP2C19.
The enzyme inhibiting effect of fluconazole persists 4-5 days after discontinuation of fluconazole treatment

items.t: Contraindicated with QT-prolonging medicines metabolised by CYP3A4 (examples named: cisapride, astemizole, pimozide, quinidine, erythromycin). SPS: do not co-prescribe triazole antifungals with other QT-prolonging medicines; short courses or single doses only as an exception when there is no alternative.

src.q: Coadministration of fluconazole and erythromycin is contraindicated (see section 4.3).
Do not co-prescribe with other QT-prolonging medicines, particularly those that are also CYP3A4 or P-glycoprotein (P-gp) substrates.
Short courses, including single doses, may be considered as an exception. Only do so when no alternative treatment is available.

items.t: Warfarin: prothrombin time prolonged up to 2-fold with bleeding events; monitor prothrombin time carefully, warfarin dose adjustment may be needed.

src.q: During concomitant treatment with fluconazole and warfarin the prothrombin time was prolonged up to 2-fold
In patients receiving coumarin-type or indanedione anticoagulants concurrently with fluconazole the prothrombin time should be carefully monitored.

items.t: Statins metabolised by CYP3A4 (atorvastatin, simvastatin): dose-dependent rise in myopathy/rhabdomyolysis risk. If needed together, watch for muscle symptoms and monitor creatine kinase; stop the statin if CK rises markedly or myopathy is suspected.

src.q: The risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis increases (dose-dependent) when fluconazole is coadministered with HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors metabolised through CYP3A4, such as atorvastatin and simvastatin
the patient should be observed for symptoms of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis and creatine kinase should be monitored.

items.t: Sulfonylureas: longer half-life; monitor blood glucose often and reduce the sulfonylurea dose as appropriate.

src.q: Frequent monitoring of blood glucose and appropriate reduction of sulfonylurea dose is recommended during coadministration.

items.t: Celecoxib: half the celecoxib dose may be needed. Other NSAIDs metabolised by CYP2C9 (ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac): monitor for NSAID toxicity; dose adjustment may be needed.

src.q: Half of the celecoxib dose may be necessary when combined with fluconazole.
Frequent monitoring for adverse events and toxicity related to NSAIDs is recommended. Adjustment of dose of NSAIDs may be needed.

items.t: Calcium-channel blockers metabolised by CYP3A4 (nifedipine, amlodipine, verapamil): exposure may rise; monitor frequently for adverse events.

src.q: Certain calcium channel antagonists (nifedipine, isradipine, amlodipine, verapamil and felodipine) are metabolised by CYP3A4.
Frequent monitoring for adverse events is recommended.

items.t: Amitriptyline: effect increased; drug levels may be measured at the start and after one week, adjust the dose if needed. Carbamazepine: levels rise by about 30% with toxicity risk; adjust by levels/effect.

src.q: Fluconazole increases the effect of amitriptyline and nortriptyline.
There is a risk of developing carbamazepine toxicity. Dose adjustment of carbamazepine may be necessary depending on concentration measurements/effect.

items.t: Hydrochlorothiazide raised fluconazole plasma levels by 40%; the SmPC says this should not need a change in the fluconazole dose.

src.q: coadministration of multiple-dose hydrochlorothiazide to healthy volunteers receiving fluconazole increased plasma concentration of fluconazole by 40%
An effect of this magnitude should not necessitate a change in the fluconazole dose regimen in subjects receiving concomitant diuretics.

items.t: Single-dose treatment: no adjustment. Multiple doses: give a normal first dose (50 to 400 mg), then CrCl >50 mL/min 100% of the usual daily dose; CrCl ≤50 mL/min (no haemodialysis) 50%; haemodialysis: 100% after each session.

src.q: No adjustments in single dose therapy are necessary.
Creatinine clearance (ml/min) Percent of recommended dose >50 100% ≤50 (no haemodialysis) 50% Haemodialysis 100% after each haemodialysis

items.t: Limited data: use with caution in hepatic impairment.

src.q: Limited data are available in patients with hepatic impairment, therefore fluconazole should be administered with caution to patients with liver dysfunction

items.t: SmPC: increased risk of miscarriage (1st/2nd trimester) and possible small increase in musculoskeletal and cardiac malformations with first-trimester use. Standard short courses should not be used in pregnancy unless clearly necessary; high-dose or prolonged regimens only for potentially life-threatening infections.

src.q: Fluconazole in standard doses and short-term treatments should not be used in pregnancy unless clearly necessary.
Fluconazole in high dose and/or in prolonged regimens should not be used during pregnancy except for potentially life-threatening infections.

items.t: BUMPS: rarely used in pregnancy because creams and pessaries (e.g. clotrimazole) usually work; fluconazole is generally given only when these fail.

src.q: Fluconazole is not often used in pregnancy, as thrush can usually be treated with creams and pessaries instead.
Women are generally only prescribed fluconazole in pregnancy when these treatments have not worked.

items.t: Passes into milk at levels similar to plasma. Breastfeeding may continue after a single 150 mg dose; not recommended after repeated or high doses.

src.q: Breast-feeding may be maintained after a single dose of 150 mg fluconazole.
Breast-feeding is not recommended after repeated use or after high dose fluconazole.

items.t: Tell women of childbearing potential about the fetal risk. After a single dose, wait 1 week before trying to conceive; for longer courses consider contraception during treatment and for 1 week after the last dose.

src.q: After single dose treatment, a washout period of 1 week (corresponding to 5-6 half-lives) is recommended before becoming pregnant
contraception may be considered, as appropriate, in women of childbearing potential throughout the treatment period and for 1 week after the final dose.

items.t: Common: headache, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, raised ALT/AST/alkaline phosphatase, rash.

src.q: The most frequently (≥1/100 to <1/10) reported adverse reactions are headache, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, alanine aminotransferase increased, aspartate aminotransferase increased, blood alkaline phosphatase increased and rash.

items.t: Serious liver injury (hepatitis, hepatic failure): stop fluconazole immediately if asthenia, anorexia, persistent nausea, vomiting or jaundice appear.

src.q: The patient should be informed of suggestive symptoms of serious hepatic effect (important asthenia, anorexia, persistent nausea, vomiting and jaundice).

items.t: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes.

src.q: there have been very rare cases of QT prolongation and torsades de pointes in patients taking Diflucan.

items.t: SJS, TEN, DRESS, anaphylaxis: stop treatment (see cautions).

src.q: Patients have rarely developed exfoliative cutaneous reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, during treatment with fluconazole.
In rare cases anaphylaxis has been reported

items.t: If liver function tests become abnormal, monitor closely for more serious liver injury.

src.q: Patients who develop abnormal liver function tests during fluconazole therapy must be monitored closely for the development of more serious hepatic injury.

items.t: SPS (triazole antifungals): no ECG needed when used alone without other risk factors; check ECG and electrolytes before and during long courses in people with non-modifiable risk factors.

src.q: No ECG monitoring is required when used alone, and in the absence of additional patient or medicine risk factors.
Monitor ECG and electrolytes before and during long course treatment in people with non-modifiable patient and medicine risk factors.

items.t: Stop if a fluconazole-related rash appears during treatment of a superficial infection, or if signs of serious liver injury appear.

src.q: If a rash, which is considered attributable to fluconazole, develops in a patient treated for a superficial fungal infection, further therapy with this medicinal product should be discontinued.

items.t: Swallow capsules whole, with or without food. Given as a single daily dose.

src.q: The capsules should be swallowed whole and independent of food intake.
Diflucan is administered as a single daily dose.

items.t: May cause dizziness or seizures: do not drive or use machines if these occur.

src.q: should be advised not to drive or operate machines if any of these symptoms occur.

items.t: Report weakness, loss of appetite, persistent nausea, vomiting or yellow skin/eyes straight away.

src.q: The patient should be informed of suggestive symptoms of serious hepatic effect (important asthenia, anorexia, persistent nausea, vomiting and jaundice).

items.t: Interactions can persist for 4 to 5 days after the last dose: tell prescribers and pharmacists about recent fluconazole use.

src.q: The enzyme inhibiting effect of fluconazole persists 4-5 days after discontinuation of fluconazole treatment

items.t: Adults: major depressive episodes; obsessive-compulsive disorder; bulimia nervosa (with psychotherapy). Children and adolescents 8 years and over: moderate to severe major depressive episode not responding to 4 to 6 sessions of psychological therapy (given with psychological therapy).

src.q: Adults: Major depressive disorders/episodes. Obsessive-compulsive disorder. Bulimia nervosa
Moderate to severe major depressive episode, if depression is unresponsive to psychological therapy after 4-6 sessions.

items.t: Children 8 to 18 years: depression only, started and monitored under specialist supervision, with concurrent psychological therapy.

src.q: Treatment should be initiated and monitored under specialist supervision.
should only be used in children and adolescents aged 8 to 18 years for the treatment of moderate to severe major depressive episodes and it should not be used in other indications

items.t: 20 mg daily; review within 3 to 4 weeks. If response is insufficient, increase gradually up to 60 mg daily. Treat at least 6 months.

src.q: A dose of 20 mg/day is recommended. Dosage should be reviewed and adjusted if necessary, within 3 to 4 weeks of initiation of therapy
the dose may be increased gradually up to a maximum of 60mg
Patients with depression should be treated for a sufficient period of at least 6 months to ensure that they are free from symptoms.

items.t: 20 mg daily; if response is insufficient after 2 weeks, increase gradually up to 60 mg. Reconsider if no improvement within 10 weeks.

src.q: Obsessive-compulsive disorder Adults and the elderly: The recommended dose is 20mg daily.
If no improvement is observed within 10 weeks, treatment with fluoxetine should be reconsidered.

items.t: 60 mg daily.

src.q: Bulimia nervosa Adults and the elderly: A dose of 60 mg/day is recommended.

items.t: Elderly: caution when increasing; usually not more than 40 mg daily (maximum 60 mg daily).

src.q: Caution is recommended when increasing the dose, and the daily dose should generally not exceed 40mg. Maximum recommended dose is 60mg/day.

items.t: Hepatic impairment or interacting medicines: consider a lower or less frequent dose (e.g. 20 mg every second day).

src.q: A lower or less frequent dose (eg, 20mg every second day) should be considered in patients with hepatic impairment

items.t: Stopping: avoid abrupt withdrawal; reduce gradually over at least 1 to 2 weeks. The drug persists in the body for weeks after stopping.

src.q: When stopping treatment with FLUOXETINE the dose should be gradually reduced over a period of at least one to two weeks in order to reduce the risk of withdrawal reactions
When dosing is stopped, active drug substances will persist in the body for weeks.

items.t: 8 years and over (moderate to severe depression): start 10 mg/day as 2.5 ml of the liquid; after 1 to 2 weeks may increase to 20 mg/day. Lower-weight children may need lower doses. Review need after 6 months; reconsider if no benefit within 9 weeks.

src.q: The starting dose is 10mg/day given as 2.5ml of the FLUOXETINE liquid formulation.
After one to two weeks, the dose may be increased to 20mg/day.
If no clinical benefit is achieved within 9 weeks, treatment should be reconsidered.

items.t: Monitor growth and puberty (height, weight, Tanner stage) during and after treatment; monitor for mania/hypomania and suicidal symptoms.

src.q: Growth and pubertal development (height, weight, and TANNER staging) should therefore be monitored during and after treatment with fluoxetine.
regular monitoring for the occurrence of mania/hypomania is recommended

items.t: Hypersensitivity to fluoxetine or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Irreversible non-selective MAOIs (e.g. iproniazid): start fluoxetine 2 weeks after stopping one; wait at least 5 weeks after fluoxetine before starting one.

src.q: Fluoxetine is contra-indicated in combination with irreversible, non-selective monoamine oxidase inhibitors (e.g. iproniazid)
at least 5 weeks should elapse after discontinuing fluoxetine treatment before starting an irreversible, non-selective MAOI

items.t: Metoprolol used in heart failure (excess bradycardia).

src.q: Fluoxetine is contra-indicated in combination with metoprolol used in cardiac failure

items.t: Seizures: introduce cautiously if history of seizures; avoid in unstable epilepsy; monitor controlled epilepsy carefully; stop if seizures develop or increase.

src.q: fluoxetine should be introduced cautiously in patients who have a history of seizures
Fluoxetine should be avoided in patients with unstable seizure disorders/epilepsy and patients with controlled epilepsy should be carefully monitored

items.t: QT prolongation and torsade de pointes reported: use with caution in congenital long QT, family history, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, bradycardia, acute MI, uncompensated heart failure, hepatic impairment or with QT-prolonging drugs. Stable cardiac disease: consider ECG review before starting.

src.q: Fluoxetine should be used with caution in patients with conditions such as congenital long QT syndrome, a family history of QT prolongation or other clinical conditions that predispose to arrhythmias
If patients with stable cardiac disease are treated, an ECG review should be considered before treatment is started.

items.t: Bleeding: caution with oral anticoagulants, antiplatelets (aspirin), NSAIDs and in bleeding disorders. SSRIs may increase postpartum haemorrhage.

src.q: Caution is advised in patients taking SSRIs, particularly in concomitant use with oral anticoagulants, drugs known to affect platelet function
SSRIs/SNRIs may increase the risk of postpartum haemorrhage

items.t: Rash or allergic reactions with no other cause: stop fluoxetine (serious systemic reactions reported).

src.q: Upon the appearance of rash or of other allergic phenomena for which an alternative aetiology cannot be identified, fluoxetine should be discontinued.

items.t: Suicidal thoughts/behaviour: close supervision early and after dose changes, especially under 25 years.

src.q: Close supervision of patients and in particular those at high risk should accompany drug therapy especially in early treatment and following dose changes.

items.t: Mania history: use with caution; stop if manic. Diabetes: hypoglycaemia on treatment, hyperglycaemia after stopping; adjust antidiabetic doses.

src.q: Antidepressants should be used with caution in patients with a history of mania/hypomania.
Hypoglycaemia has been reported during therapy with fluoxetine and hyperglycaemia has developed following discontinuation.

items.t: Serotonin syndrome or NMS-like events (with other serotonergic or neuroleptic drugs): stop fluoxetine and give supportive care.

src.q: treatment with fluoxetine should be discontinued if such events

items.t: Raised intraocular pressure or risk of narrow-angle glaucoma: caution (mydriasis). Acute cardiac disease: caution.

src.q: caution should be used when prescribing fluoxetine in patients with raised intraocular pressure or those at risk of acute narrow-angle glaucoma
Clinical experience in acute cardiac disease is limited, therefore caution is advisable.

items.t: Akathisia in first weeks; withdrawal symptoms (common); ECT may prolong seizures; sexual dysfunction that may persist after stopping; weight loss.

src.q: There have been rare reports of prolonged seizures in patients on fluoxetine receiving ECT treatment; therefore, caution is advisable.
There have been reports of long-lasting sexual dysfunction where the symptoms have continued despite discontinuation of SSRIs/SNRI.

items.t: Long half-lives of fluoxetine and norfluoxetine: interactions may occur for weeks after stopping (e.g. when switching antidepressants).

src.q: The long elimination half-lives of both fluoxetine and norfluoxetine should be borne in mind

items.t: Contraindicated: irreversible non-selective MAOIs; metoprolol in heart failure. Not recommended: tamoxifen (avoid whenever possible), alcohol, linezolid or methylene blue (if unavoidable, close monitoring and low starting doses), mequitazine.

src.q: co-administration with potent CYP2D6 inhibitors (including fluoxetine) should whenever possible be avoided
close clinical monitoring should be undertaken and the concomitant agents should be initiated at the lower recommended doses

items.t: Serotonergic drugs (lithium, tramadol, triptans, tryptophan, selegiline, St John's wort): caution with closer, more frequent monitoring. The St John's wort herbal SPC says do not take it with SSRIs.

src.q: the concomitant use of fluoxetine with these drugs should be undertaken with caution, with closer and more frequent clinical monitoring
SSRIs e.g. Citalopram Escitalopram Fluoxetine Fluvoxamine Paroxetine Sertraline

items.t: QT-prolonging drugs (class IA/III antiarrhythmics, antipsychotics, TCAs, some antimicrobials such as moxifloxacin): use with caution.

src.q: anti-malaria treatment particularly halofantrine, certain antihistamines (astemizole, mizolastine), should be used with caution

items.t: Oral anticoagulants, antiplatelets including aspirin, NSAIDs: increased bleeding; clinical monitoring and more frequent INR checks with oral anticoagulants.

src.q: Clinical monitoring, and more frequent monitoring of INR with oral anticoagulants, should be made.

items.t: CYP2D6 substrates with narrow therapeutic index or titrated (flecainide, propafenone, nebivolol, atomoxetine, carbamazepine, TCAs, risperidone): start at or adjust to the low end of the dose range (also if fluoxetine taken in the last 5 weeks).

src.q: They should be initiated at or adjusted to the low end of their dose range. This may also apply if fluoxetine has been taken in the previous 5 weeks.

items.t: Phenytoin: level changes, sometimes toxicity; titrate conservatively and monitor. Drugs causing hyponatraemia (diuretics, desmopressin, carbamazepine) and drugs lowering the seizure threshold (TCAs, other SSRIs, tramadol, bupropion) increase risk.

src.q: Use in combination with other agents associated with hyponatremia (e.g. diuretics, desmopressin, carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine) may lead to an increased risk

Use in combination with other agents which may lower the seizure threshold (for example, TCAs, other SSRIs, phenothiazines, butyrophenones, mefloquine, chloroquine, bupropion, tramadol) may lead to an increased risk.

items.t: Severe renal failure on dialysis (GFR <10 ml/min): no difference in plasma levels at 20 mg/day for 2 months. Steady-state levels may rise with repeated dosing.

src.q: patients with severe renal failure (GFR <10ml/min) requiring dialysis showed no difference in plasma levels of fluoxetine or norfluoxetine compared to controls with normal renal function
However, after repeated administration, an increase in steady-state plateau of plasma concentrations may be observed.

items.t: Hepatic impairment: consider a lower or less frequent dose (e.g. 20 mg every second day). Half-lives longer in cirrhosis (7 and 12 days).

src.q: A lower dose, e.g., alternate day dosing, is recommended in patients with significant hepatic dysfunction
fluoxetine and norfluoxetine half-lives are increased to 7 and 12 days, respectively

items.t: SmPC: should not be used unless the woman's condition requires it and justifies the risk to the fetus. Avoid abrupt stopping in pregnancy.

src.q: Fluoxetine should not be used during pregnancy unless the clinical condition of the woman requires treatment with fluoxetine and justifies the potential risk to the foetus.
Abrupt discontinuation of therapy should be avoided during pregnancy

items.t: First trimester: possible small increased risk of cardiovascular defects (about 2/100 vs 1/100). MHRA: weigh this against the benefits of treating depression.

src.q: the risk of having an infant with a cardiovascular defect following maternal fluoxetine exposure is in the region of 2/100 compared with an expected rate for such defects of approximately 1/100
The potential increased risk should be considered in the context of the benefits of treating depression in pregnancy.

items.t: Late pregnancy: caution; neonatal irritability, tremor, hypotonia, crying, sucking or sleeping problems; PPHN about 5 per 1000; postpartum haemorrhage risk under 2-fold after use in the month before birth.

src.q: caution should be exercised, especially during late pregnancy or just prior to the onset of labour
The observed risk was approximately 5 cases per 1000 pregnancies.
Observational data indicate an increased risk (less than 2-fold) of postpartum haemorrhage following SSRI/SNRI exposure within the month prior to birth

items.t: BUMPS: SSRIs are commonly taken in pregnancy without problems; most babies have normal hearts; if well controlled it may be best to stay on fluoxetine. Do not stop without advice. Hospital delivery usually advised.

src.q: SSRIs are commonly taken during pregnancy without any problem.
If a woman's condition is well-controlled with fluoxetine, it may be best to stay on it rather than try something new and risk a relapse.
Women taking an SSRI in pregnancy will usually be advised to have a hospital delivery.

items.t: SmPC: fluoxetine and norfluoxetine pass into milk; infant adverse events reported. If treatment is needed, consider stopping breastfeeding; if breastfeeding continues, use the lowest effective dose.

src.q: Adverse events have been reported in breast-feeding infants.

If treatment with fluoxetine is considered necessary, discontinuation of breast-feeding should be considered; however, if breast-feeding is continued, the lowest effective dose of fluoxetine should be prescribed.

items.t: SPS: can be used with caution (long experience), but sertraline or paroxetine are preferred. Monitor the infant for irritability, restlessness, drowsiness, colic, GI upset, poor feeding and weight gain.

src.q: Fluoxetine can be used with caution. It has been used during breastfeeding for many years, but sertraline or paroxetine are preferred.
As a precaution, monitor for irritability, restlessness, drowsiness, colic, gastro-intestinal disturbances, poor feeding, and adequate weight-gain.

items.t: Animal data: may affect sperm quality; human SSRI reports show it is reversible. Sexual dysfunction may continue after stopping (MHRA 2026 lists fluoxetine).

src.q: Human case reports with some SSRIs have shown that an effect on sperm quality is reversible.
Citalopram, escitalopram, duloxetine, fluvoxamine, fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline, venlafaxine, amitriptyline, nortriptyline

items.t: Most common: headache, nausea, insomnia, fatigue, diarrhoea; often lessen with continued treatment.

src.q: The most commonly reported adverse reactions in patients treated with fluoxetine were headache, nausea, insomnia, fatigue and diarrhoea.
Undesirable effects may decrease in intensity and frequency with continued treatment and do not generally lead to cessation of therapy.

items.t: Withdrawal symptoms on stopping are common (dizziness, sensory disturbance, sleep problems, agitation, nausea, tremor, headache).

src.q: Discontinuation of fluoxetine commonly leads to withdrawal symptoms.

items.t: Serotonin syndrome or NMS-like events (hyperthermia, rigidity, myoclonus, confusion): potentially life-threatening; stop and treat.

src.q: As these syndromes may result in potentially life-threatening conditions, treatment with fluoxetine should be discontinued

items.t: Rash or allergic reaction (including anaphylactoid and serious systemic events): stop if no other cause.

src.q: Rash, anaphylactoid events and progressive systemic events, sometimes serious (involving skin, kidney, liver or lung) have been reported.

items.t: Signs of cardiac arrhythmia: stop and perform an ECG.

src.q: If signs of cardiac arrhythmia occur during treatment with fluoxetine, the treatment should be withdrawn and an ECG should be performed.

items.t: New or worse suicidal thoughts: seek urgent medical attention (MHRA 2026). Abnormal bleeding including GI bleeding.

src.q: if you have new or worsening suicidal thoughts, particularly when starting or changing dose of antidepressants, seek urgent medical attention
gynaecological haemorrhages, gastro-intestinal bleedings and other cutaneous or mucous bleedings

items.t: Stable cardiac disease: consider ECG review before starting. When starting or changing dose: discuss suicide risk and sexual dysfunction (MHRA 2026).

src.q: If patients with stable cardiac disease are treated, an ECG review should be considered before treatment is started.
discuss with patients when starting or changing the dose of an antidepressant or at their next review, the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviours

items.t: Monitor for suicidality early and after dose changes; INR more often with oral anticoagulants; children: growth and puberty, mania.

src.q: patients should be closely monitored until such improvement occurs
Clinical monitoring, and more frequent monitoring of INR with oral anticoagulants, should be made.
Growth and pubertal development (height, weight, and TANNER staging) should therefore be monitored during and after treatment with fluoxetine.

items.t: Stop if: seizures (or more frequent), manic phase, unexplained rash/allergy, serotonin syndrome, signs of arrhythmia.

src.q: Treatment should be discontinued in any patient who develops seizures or where there is an increase in seizure frequency.
fluoxetine should be discontinued in any patient entering a manic phase

items.t: Single or divided dose, with or between meals.

src.q: Fluoxetine may be administered as a single or divided dose, during or between meals.

items.t: Do not drive or use machines until sure performance is not affected. Avoid alcohol.

src.q: Patients should be advised to avoid driving a car or operating hazardous machinery until they are reasonably certain that their performance is not affected.
the combination of SSRI treatment and alcohol is not advisable

items.t: Seek urgent help for new or worse suicidal thoughts (NHS 111, crisis team, Samaritans 116 123). Sexual problems may continue after stopping. Do not stop without advice.

src.q: You can call NHS 111, or your local mental health crisis team, Samaritans on 116 123
do not stop taking your medicine without first speaking to your healthcare professional

items.t: Symptoms of allergic rhinitis in adults, adolescents and children 6 years and over.

src.q: Avamys is indicated in adults, adolescents and children (6 years and over)
Avamys is indicated for the treatment of the symptoms of allergic rhinitis.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restrictions stated in the UK nasal spray SmPC checked.

items.t: Start with 2 sprays in each nostril once daily (110 micrograms a day); once controlled, 1 spray each nostril once daily (55 micrograms) may be enough. Use the lowest effective dose; limit treatment to the period of allergen exposure.
items.tag: Allergic rhinitis, adults and adolescents 12 years and over

src.q: The recommended starting dose is two spray actuations (27.5 micrograms of fluticasone furoate per spray actuation) in each nostril once daily (total daily dose, 110 micrograms).
dose reduction to one spray actuation in each nostril (total daily dose 55 micrograms) may be effective for maintenance
The duration of treatment should be restricted to the period that corresponds to allergenic exposure.

items.t: 6-11 years: 1 spray in each nostril once daily (55 micrograms); may go up to 2 sprays each nostril (110 micrograms) if needed, then back to 1 spray once controlled. Not established under 6 years.

src.q: The recommended starting dose is one spray actuation (27.5 micrograms of fluticasone furoate per spray actuation) in each nostril once daily (total daily dose, 55 micrograms).
may use two spray actuations in each nostril once daily (total daily dose, 110 micrograms)
The safety and efficacy of Avamys in children under the age of 6 years has not been established.

items.t: Growth velocity fell (-0.27 cm a year) in children on 110 micrograms daily for one year: keep children on the lowest effective dose and monitor growth on prolonged treatment.

src.q: A reduction in growth velocity has been observed in children treated with fluticasone furoate 110 micrograms daily for one year
children should be maintained on the lowest possible efficacious dose which delivers adequate symptom control

items.t: Hypersensitivity to fluticasone furoate or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Systemic steroid effects possible, mainly at high doses for long periods. Above-recommended doses can cause adrenal suppression: consider systemic steroid cover during stress or elective surgery. Consider the total corticosteroid load when other steroid forms are used.

src.q: Systemic effects of nasal corticosteroid may occur, particularly at high doses prescribed for prolonged periods.
the total systemic burden of corticosteroids should be considered whenever other forms of corticosteroid treatment are prescribed concurrently

items.t: Care when transferring from systemic steroids if adrenal function may be impaired.

src.q: If there is any reason to believe that adrenal function is impaired, care must be taken when transferring patients from systemic steroid treatment to fluticasone furoate.

items.t: Blurred vision or other visual disturbance: consider referral to an ophthalmologist.

src.q: the patient should be considered for referral to an ophthalmologist for evaluation of possible causes

items.t: Ritonavir: co-administration not recommended (increased systemic exposure).

src.q: Concomitant administration with ritonavir is not recommended because of the risk of increased systemic exposure of fluticasone furoate

items.t: Potent CYP3A inhibitors, including cobicistat-containing products: caution; avoid unless the benefit outweighs the increased risk of systemic steroid effects, and if used monitor for them. Ritonavir: not recommended. Ketoconazole caused only a small rise in exposure without a significant cortisol change in a study.

src.q: Caution is recommended when co-administering fluticasone furoate with potent CYP3A inhibitors including cobicistat-containing products
Co-administration should be avoided unless the benefit outweighs the increased risk of systemic corticosteroid side effects
This small increase in exposure did not result in a statistically significant difference in 24 hour serum cortisol levels between the two groups.

items.t: Not expected to affect the CYP450 metabolism of other medicines at nasal doses.

src.q: there is no theoretical basis for anticipating metabolic interactions between fluticasone furoate and the cytochrome P450 mediated metabolism of other compounds at clinically relevant intranasal doses

items.t: No dose adjustment needed.

src.q: Renal Impairment No dose adjustment is required in this population

items.t: No dose adjustment needed in hepatic impairment.

src.q: No dose adjustment is required in patients with hepatic impairment

items.t: SmPC: no adequate human data; animal effects at high systemic exposure are unlikely to be relevant at nasal doses. Use only if the benefit to the mother outweighs the possible risk.

src.q: This is not likely to be relevant for humans given recommended nasal doses which results in minimal systemic exposure
Fluticasone furoate should be used in pregnancy only if the benefits to the mother outweigh the potential risks to the foetus or child.

items.t: SPS: intranasal corticosteroids (fluticasone given as an example) can be considered for hay fever in pregnancy if non-drug measures are not enough; they are the most effective rhinitis treatment.

src.q: intranasal corticosteroids (for example, fluticasone) can be considered if non-pharmacological management is insufficient
Intranasal corticosteroids are also the most effective treatment for allergic rhinitis.

items.t: NICE (asthma): if possible, use the same type of device for preventer and reliever when more than one inhaler is needed.

src.q: If possible, prescribe the same type of device to deliver preventer and reliever treatments where more than one inhaler is needed.

items.t: Asthma, adults and adolescents 12 years and over: one inhalation twice daily of 50/100, 50/250 or 50/500 (strength by severity). Titrate to the lowest dose that keeps control; once daily may be tried if adequate.

src.q: One inhalation of 50 micrograms salmeterol and 250 micrograms fluticasone propionate twice daily.
As an alternative, patients requiring a long-acting β2 agonist could be titrated to Seretide given once daily if, in the opinion of the prescriber, it would be adequate to maintain disease control.

items.t: COPD, adults: one inhalation of 50/500 twice daily.

src.q: One inhalation of 50 micrograms salmeterol and 500 micrograms fluticasone propionate twice daily.

items.t: Elderly and renal impairment: no dose adjustment. No data in hepatic impairment.

src.q: There is no need to adjust the dose in elderly patients or in those with renal impairment.
There are no data available for use of Seretide in patients with hepatic impairment.

items.t: Children 4 years and over: one inhalation of 50/100 twice daily only (maximum licensed fluticasone propionate 100 micrograms twice daily). The 50/250 strength is for 12 years and over. No data under 4 years.

src.q: Children 4 years and older: - One inhalation of 50 micrograms salmeterol and 100 micrograms fluticasone propionate twice daily.
The maximum licensed dose of fluticasone propionate delivered by Seretide Accuhaler in children is 100 microgram twice daily.
There are no data available for use of Seretide in children aged under 4 years.

items.t: Children and adolescents under 16 on high fluticasone doses (typically 1000 micrograms/day or more) are at particular risk of systemic effects; monitor height on prolonged treatment.

src.q: Children and adolescents <16 years taking high doses of fluticasone propionate (typically ≥ 1000 micrograms/day) may be at particular risk.
It is recommended that the height of children receiving prolonged treatment with inhaled corticosteroid is regularly monitored.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to fluticasone propionate, salmeterol or the excipient (lactose, which contains milk proteins).

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substances or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.
Excipient: Lactose monohydrate (which contains milk proteins).

items.t: Not for acute symptoms (use a fast-acting reliever); do not start during an exacerbation or acutely deteriorating asthma; do not stop abruptly in asthma (down-titrate under supervision).

src.q: Seretide Accuhaler should not be used to treat acute asthma symptoms for which a fast- and short- acting bronchodilator is required.
Treatment with Seretide should not be stopped abruptly in patients with asthma due to risk of exacerbation.

items.t: Use with caution in severe cardiovascular disorders or heart rhythm abnormalities, diabetes, thyrotoxicosis, uncorrected hypokalaemia or predisposition to low potassium.

src.q: Seretide should be used with caution in patients with severe cardiovascular disorders or heart rhythm abnormalities and in patients with diabetes mellitus, thyrotoxicosis, uncorrected hypokalaemia or patients predisposed to low levels of serum potassium.

items.t: Adrenal suppression and acute adrenal crisis with prolonged high doses (rarely at 500 to under 1000 micrograms fluticasone); consider extra systemic steroid cover in stress or elective surgery.

src.q: Prolonged treatment of patients with high doses of inhaled corticosteroids may result in adrenal suppression and acute adrenal crisis.
Additional systemic corticosteroid cover should be considered during periods of stress or elective surgery.

items.t: Caution in active or quiescent pulmonary tuberculosis and fungal, viral or other airway infections.

src.q: Seretide should be administered with caution in patients with active or quiescent pulmonary tuberculosis and fungal, viral or other infections of the airway.

items.t: COPD: increased pneumonia incidence with inhaled corticosteroids; stay vigilant.

src.q: An increase in the incidence of pneumonia, including pneumonia requiring hospitalisation, has been observed in patients with COPD receiving inhaled corticosteroids.

items.t: Refer to an ophthalmologist if blurred vision or other visual disturbance.

src.q: If a patient presents with symptoms such as blurred vision or other visual disturbances, the patient should be considered for referral to an ophthalmologist

items.t: Beta-blockers (selective and non-selective): avoid unless there are compelling reasons.

src.q: Both non-selective and selective β blockers should be avoided unless there are compelling reasons for their use.

items.t: CYP3A inhibitors: ritonavir, ketoconazole, itraconazole, cobicistat (potent) and erythromycin (moderate) raise fluticasone exposure (Cushing's syndrome, adrenal suppression reported); ketoconazole raises salmeterol exposure (QTc, palpitations). Avoid unless benefit outweighs risk; if used, monitor for systemic corticosteroid effects.

src.q: Co-treatment with other potent CYP3A inhibitors, such as itraconazole and cobicistat-containing products, and moderate CYP3A inhibitors, such as erythromycin, is also expected to increase the systemic fluticasone propionate exposure

Combinations should be avoided unless the benefit outweighs the potential increased risk of systemic corticosteroid side-effects, in which case patients should be monitored for systemic corticosteroid side-effects.
The concomitant administration of ketoconazole should be avoided, unless the benefits outweigh the potentially increased risk of systemic side effects of salmeterol treatment.

items.t: Xanthines, steroids and diuretics may potentiate hypokalaemia: particular caution in acute severe asthma.

src.q: Particular caution is advised in acute severe asthma as this effect may be potentiated by concomitant treatment with xanthine derivatives, steroids and diuretics.

items.t: No dose adjustment in renal impairment.

src.q: There is no need to adjust the dose in elderly patients or in those with renal impairment.

items.t: No data in hepatic impairment; no dose advice stated.

src.q: There are no data available for use of Seretide in patients with hepatic impairment.

items.t: SmPC: over 1000 pregnancy outcomes show no malformative or feto/neonatal toxicity. Consider only if benefit to the mother outweighs any risk to the fetus; use the lowest effective fluticasone dose.

src.q: A large amount of data on pregnant women (more than 1000 pregnancy outcomes) indicates no malformative or feto/neonatal toxicity related to Seretide.
Administration of Seretide to pregnant women should only be considered if the expected benefit to the mother is greater than any possible risk to the fetus.

items.t: BUMPS: inhaled corticosteroids should be continued in pregnancy; no evidence they harm the baby.

src.q: Inhaled corticosteroids should be continued throughout pregnancy to ensure that breathing problems do not occur.
There is no evidence that use of inhaled corticosteroids in pregnancy harms the baby.

items.t: SmPC: unknown whether excreted in human milk; risk to the infant cannot be excluded. Decide whether to stop breastfeeding or stop therapy.

src.q: A risk to breastfed newborns/infants cannot be excluded. A decision must be made whether to discontinue breastfeeding or to discontinue Seretide therapy

items.t: SPS: inhaled fluticasone can be used during breastfeeding (salmeterol not covered on this page).

src.q: When applied to the skin, inhaled or used intranasally, fluticasone can be used during breastfeeding.

items.t: No human fertility data; animal studies showed no effect on fertility.

src.q: There are no data in humans. However, animal studies showed no effects of salmeterol or fluticasone propionate on fertility.

items.t: Very common: headache, nasopharyngitis (both also common or very common with placebo). Common: mouth and throat candidiasis, pneumonia and bronchitis (COPD), hypokalaemia, throat irritation, hoarseness/dysphonia, sinusitis, bruising, muscle cramps, fractures, joint and muscle pain. Tremor, palpitations and headache tend to be transient.

src.q: Nervous System Disorders Headache Tremor Very Common1 Uncommon
Respiratory, Thoracic & Mediastinal Disorders Nasopharyngitis Throat irritation Hoarseness/dysphonia Sinusitis Paradoxical bronchospasm Very Common2, 3 Common Common Common1, 3 Rare4
Infections & Infestations Candidiasis of the mouth and throat Pneumonia (in COPD patients) Bronchitis Oesophageal candidiasis Common Common1, 3, 5 Common1, 3 Rare
Metabolism & Nutrition Disorders Hypokalaemia Hyperglycaemia Common3 Uncommon4
Musculoskeletal & Connective Tissue Disorders Muscle cramps Traumatic fractures Arthralgia Myalgia Common Common1, 3 Common Common

items.t: Paradoxical bronchospasm: treat straight away with a rapid-acting bronchodilator; stop this inhaler and assess.

src.q: Paradoxical bronchospasm responds to a rapid-acting bronchodilator and should be treated straightaway. Seretide Accuhaler should be discontinued immediately, the patient assessed and alternative therapy instituted if necessary.

items.t: Rare: anaphylactic reactions including shock, angioedema, bronchospasm; cardiac arrhythmias.

src.q: Anaphylactic reactions including anaphylactic shock
Rarely, Seretide may cause cardiac arrhythmias e.g. supraventricular tachycardia, extrasystoles and atrial fibrillation

items.t: Sudden, progressive loss of asthma control is potentially life-threatening: urgent medical assessment.

src.q: Sudden and progressive deterioration in control of asthma is potentially life-threatening and the patient should undergo urgent medical assessment.

items.t: Regular review so the strength stays optimal; reduce to the lowest effective dose.

src.q: Patients should be regularly reassessed by a doctor, so that the strength of Seretide they are receiving remains optimal and is only changed on medical advice.

items.t: Regularly monitor adrenocortical function after transfer from oral steroids; monitor height in children on prolonged treatment.

src.q: Therefore these patients should be treated with special care and adrenocortical function regularly monitored.
It is recommended that the height of children receiving prolonged treatment with inhaled corticosteroid is regularly monitored.

items.t: Stop at once if paradoxical bronchospasm occurs.

src.q: Seretide Accuhaler should be discontinued immediately, the patient assessed and alternative therapy instituted if necessary.

items.t: Open and prime by sliding the lever, close lips round the mouthpiece, inhale, then close the device. Rinsing the mouth or brushing teeth after use can reduce hoarseness and thrush.

src.q: The device is opened and primed by sliding the lever. The mouthpiece is then placed in the mouth and the lips closed round it. The dose can then be inhaled and the device closed.
may be relieved by rinsing the mouth with water and/or brushing the teeth after using the product

items.t: Use every day, even when well. Keep a reliever inhaler for acute attacks available at all times.

src.q: Patients should be made aware that Seretide Accuhaler must be used daily for optimum benefit, even when asymptomatic.
Patients should be advised to have their inhaler to be used for relief in an acute asthma attack available at all times.

items.t: See a doctor if more reliever is needed, the reliever works less well, or symptoms worsen after starting.

src.q: Increased requirements for use of reliever medication (short-acting bronchodilators), or decreased response to reliever medication indicate deterioration of control and patients should be reviewed by a physician.

items.t: Folate-deficient megaloblastic anaemia (malnutrition, malabsorption, increased need as in pregnancy). Not to be used alone in undiagnosed megaloblastic anaemia, pernicious anaemia or macrocytic anaemia of unknown cause unless given with enough hydroxocobalamin.

src.q: For the treatment of folate-deficient megaloblastic anaemia due to malnutrition, malabsorption syndromes (such as coeliac disease or sprue) and increased utilisation as in pregnancy.

It should not be used alone in undiagnosed megaloblastic anaemia including in infancy, pernicious anaemia or macrocytic anaemia of unknown aetiology, unless administered with adequate amounts of hydroxocobalamin.

items.t: Prophylaxis of drug-induced folate deficiency (e.g. phenytoin, phenobarbital, primidone); prophylaxis in chronic haemolytic states or renal dialysis.

src.q: For the prophylaxis of drug induced folate deficiency e.g. caused by administration of phenytoin, phenobarbital and primidone.
For the prophylaxis against folate deficiency in chronic haemolytic states or in renal dialysis.

items.t: Prevention of neural tube defects in women planning pregnancy who are known to be at risk.

src.q: For the prevention of neural tube defects for woman planning a pregnancy and known to be at risk.

items.t: The 5 mg tablet is not intended for healthy pregnant women (lower doses are recommended); it is for folate deficiency or women at risk of neural tube defect recurrence.

src.q: This product is not intended for healthy pregnant women where lower doses are recommended, but for pregnant women with folic acid deficiency or women at risk for the reoccurrence of neural tube defect.

items.t: Adults: 5 mg daily for 4 months; up to 15 mg daily may be needed in malabsorption.

src.q: In folate deficient megaloblastic anaemia : 5mg daily for 4 months; up to 15mg daily may be necessary for malabsorption states.

items.t: Adults: 5 mg daily for 4 months; up to 15 mg daily in malabsorption.

src.q: In drug induced folate deficiency : 5mg daily for 4 months; up to 15mg daily may be necessary for malabsorption states.

items.t: 5 mg every 1-7 days depending on the underlying disease.

src.q: For prophylaxis in chronic haemolytic states or in renal dialysis : 5mg every 1- 7 days depending on underlying disease.

items.tag: Prevention of neural tube defects (women at risk)
items.t: 5 mg daily, started before conception and continued through the first trimester.

src.q: Prevention of neural tube defects in women known to be at risk : 5mg daily started before conception and continued throughout the first trimester.

items.t: 5 mg daily continued to term.

src.q: Pregnancy: In established folate deficiency: 5mg daily continued to term.

items.t: SPS: folic acid 5 mg once weekly on a different day from methotrexate is the most commonly recommended regimen to reduce methotrexate adverse effects (off-label use).

src.q: Folic acid 5mg weekly, on a different day to the methotrexate dose, is the most commonly recommended regimen from clinical studies and national guidance.
Use of folic acid to reduce adverse effects is off-label.

items.t: Child 1-18 years: 5 mg daily for 4 months; maintenance 5 mg every 1-7 days. For young children use a more suitable dosage form.

src.q: In folate deficient megaloblastic anaemia: Child 1-18 years 5mg daily for 4 months; maintenance 5mg every 1-7 days.
For young children a more suitable dosage form should be used.

items.t: Child 1-12 years: 2.5-5 mg once daily. Child 12-18 years: 5-10 mg once daily.

src.q: In haemolytic anaemia; metabolic disorders: Child 1-12 years 2.5mg-5mg once daily. Child 12-18 years 5-10mg once daily.

items.t: Child 1-12 years: 250 micrograms/kg (max 10 mg) once daily. Child 12-18 years: 5-10 mg once daily.

src.q: Prophylaxis of folate deficiency in renal dialysis: Child 1-12 years 250 microgram/kg (max 10mg) once daily. Children 12-18 years 5-10mg once daily.

items.t: Long-term folate in untreated cobalamin (vitamin B12) deficiency, including untreated pernicious anaemia and lifelong vegetarians: it can precipitate cobalamin neuropathy and subacute combined degeneration of the cord. Never give folic acid alone for Addisonian pernicious anaemia or other B12 deficiency.

src.q: Long-term folate therapy is contraindicated in any patient with untreated cobalamin deficiency.

Folic acid should never be given alone in the treatment of Addisonian pernicious anaemia and other vitamin B12 deficiency states because it may precipitate the onset of subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord.

items.t: Malignant disease, unless megaloblastic anaemia due to folate deficiency is an important complication.

src.q: Folic acid should not be used in malignant disease unless megaloblastic anaemia owing to folate deficiency is an important complication.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to folic acid or any excipient.

src.q: Known hypersensitivity to folic acid or any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Vitamin B12 deficiency must not be treated with folic acid unless enough hydroxocobalamin is also given: folic acid can mask it while nerve damage continues.

src.q: Patients with vitamin B12 deficiency should not be treated with folic acid unless administered with adequate amounts of hydroxocobalamin, as it can mask the condition but the subacute irreversible damage to the nervous system will continue.

items.t: Caution in patients who may have folate-dependent tumours.

src.q: Caution should be exercised when administering folic acid to patients who may have folate dependent tumours.

items.t: Contains lactose and sucrose: not for people with hereditary galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency, glucose-galactose malabsorption, fructose intolerance or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take this medicine.

items.t: Correcting folate deficiency lowers plasma phenytoin, with possible loss of seizure control. A similar but weaker effect occurs with other anticonvulsants, including carbamazepine, valproate and barbiturates.

src.q: Correction of the folate deficiency reduces plasma phenytoin with potential loss of seizure control.
Similar but less marked relationship exist with all anti-convulsant treatments including sodium valproate, carbamazepine and the barbiturates

items.t: Folic acid may interfere with the toxic and therapeutic effects of methotrexate. Folate deficiency caused by methotrexate or trimethoprim cannot be treated with folic acid: use folinic acid. SPS: folic acid is routinely given with methotrexate in rheumatoid arthritis to reduce adverse effects, usually not on the methotrexate day.

src.q: Folic acid may interfere with the toxic and therapeutic effects of methotrexate.
Methotrexate and trimethoprim are specific anti-folates and the folate deficiency caused by their prolonged use cannot be treated by Folic Acid Tablets BP. Folinic acid should be used.
Folic acid supplements are usually avoided on the day of oral or subcutaneous methotrexate.

items.t: Co-trimoxazole and chloramphenicol may interfere with folate metabolism.

src.q: Antibacterials - chloramphenicol and co-trimoxazole, may interfere with folate metabolism.

items.t: Sulfasalazine and triamterene inhibit folate absorption. Folate enhances lithium efficacy. Nitrous oxide may cause acute folate deficiency. Ethanol and aspirin increase folate elimination.

src.q: Sulphasalazine and triamterene also inhibit absorption.
Folate supplements enhance the efficacy of lithium therapy.
Both ethanol and aspirin increase folic elimination.

items.t: No renal dose adjustment stated. Used for folate prophylaxis in renal dialysis (5 mg every 1-7 days). Folic acid is removed by haemodialysis.

src.q: For prophylaxis in chronic haemolytic states or in renal dialysis : 5mg every 1- 7 days depending on underlying disease.
Folic acid is removed by haemodialysis.

hepatic.note: No hepatic impairment advice in the UK folic acid 5 mg tablet SmPC.

items.t: No known hazards in pregnancy; folic acid supplements are often beneficial. Folate deficiency is linked to neural tube and other birth defects.

src.q: There are no known hazards to the use of folic acid in pregnancy, supplements of folic acid are often beneficial.

items.t: BUMPS: most women need about 400 micrograms daily before conception and for the first 12 weeks; a higher 5 mg dose is prescribed for some (e.g. some medicines such as for epilepsy, diabetes, or a family history of neural tube defect).

src.q: Most women are advised to take a supplement containing a daily dose of around 400 micrograms (mcg) of folic acid.

If you are taking certain medicines (for example, to treat epilepsy), have a health condition like diabetes, or have a close family member with a neural tube defect, your doctor will prescribe you a higher daily dose of 5 milligrams (mg) folic acid.

items.t: Folic acid passes into breast milk; no adverse effects seen in breastfed infants.

src.q: No adverse effects have been observed in breast fed infants whose mothers were receiving folic acid.

items.t: Women planning pregnancy who are at risk of neural tube defects: 5 mg daily from before conception through the first trimester.

src.q: Prevention of neural tube defects in women known to be at risk : 5mg daily started before conception and continued throughout the first trimester.

items.t: No common effects listed. Rare: anorexia, nausea, abdominal distension, flatulence.

src.q: Anorexia, nausea, abdominal distension and flatulence

items.t: Rare allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis (shock).

src.q: Allergic reactions, comprising erythema, rash, pruritus, urticaria, dyspnoea and Anaphylactic reaction (including shock)

items.t: In untreated B12 deficiency, folate for 3 months or longer has precipitated cobalamin neuropathy.

src.q: Folate given to such patients for 3 months or longer has precipitated cobalamin neuropathy.

items.t: Exclude untreated vitamin B12 deficiency before long-term folate. In elderly people do a cobalamin absorption test before long-term therapy.

src.q: In elderly people, a cobalamin absorption test should be done before long-term folate therapy.

items.t: For oral use.

src.q: Method of administration For oral administration.

items.t: If taken with weekly methotrexate, take folic acid on a different day from the methotrexate (SPS).

src.q: Folic acid supplements are usually avoided on the day of oral or subcutaneous methotrexate.

items.t: Oedema with congestive heart failure, liver cirrhosis or renal disease (including nephrotic syndrome); peripheral oedema due to mild to moderate hypertension.

src.q: The treatment of oedema associated with congestive heart failure, cirrhosis of the liver, renal disease including nephrotic syndrome.
The treatment of peripheral oedema due to mild to moderate hypertension

items.t: One UK SmPC also lists oliguria due to acute or chronic renal insufficiency.

src.q: Management of oliguria due to acute or chronic renal insufficiency.

items.t: Another UK SmPC also lists pulmonary oedema and peripheral oedema due to mechanical obstruction or venous insufficiency.

src.q: renal disease including nephrotic syndrome and pulmonary oedema.
The treatment of peripheral oedema due to mechanical obstruction, venous insufficiency, mild to moderate hypertension.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restrictions stated in the UK SmPCs.

items.t: Adults and children over 12: initially 40 mg in the morning; maintenance 20 mg daily or 40 mg on alternate days; up to 80 mg daily in resistant oedema.

src.q: Initially 40mg daily in the morning
Maintenance dose is 20mg daily or 40mg on alternate days, increased in resistant oedema to 80mg daily.

items.t: 20-40 mg twice daily. If 40 mg twice daily is not enough, add another antihypertensive rather than increasing the dose.

src.q: Hypertension: 20-40mg twice daily; if 40mg twice daily does not lead to a clinically satisfactory response, the addition of other antihypertensive agents, rather than an increase in the dose of furosemide should be considered.

items.t: One UK SmPC (chronic renal insufficiency): 250 mg daily initially, increased in 250 mg steps every 4-6 hours to a maximum of 1,500 mg in 24 hours (exceptionally 2,000 mg). This conflicts with the same SmPC's contraindication when creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min per 1.73 m²; the SmPC does not resolve this.

src.q: In patients with chronic renal insufficiency, an initial daily dose of 250mg is employed.
up to a maximum daily dose of 1,500mg in 24 hours. In exceptional cases up to 2,000mg in 24 hours may be given.
Anuria and impaired renal function (creatinine clearance below 30mL/min per 1.73 m2 body surface area)

items.t: Elderly: eliminated more slowly; titrate to response. Dose changes may be needed in hypoproteinaemia or liver congestion/dysfunction.

src.q: Elderly: Generally eliminated more slowly. Dosage should be titrated until the required response is achieved.
Dosage adjustment may be necessary in patients with Hypoproteinaemia Liver congestion/dysfunction

items.t: Children over 12 years: adult doses.

src.q: Adults and children over 12 years:

items.t: Children under 12: one UK SmPC gives 1-3 mg/kg daily, maximum 40 mg per day; another UK SmPC says a more suitable dosage form should be used.

src.q: Children under 12 years: From 1-3mg/kg body weight daily, up to a maximum total dose of 40mg per day.
Children under 12 years : A more suitable dosage form should be used in this age group.

items.t: Premature infants: risk of nephrocalcinosis/nephrolithiasis (renal function must be monitored and renal ultrasound performed) and of persistent patent ductus arteriosus.

src.q: In premature infants there is a risk of development of nephrocalcinosis/nephrolithiasis.
In premature infants with respiratory distress syndrome, administration of furosemide tablets in the initial weeks after birth entails an increased risk of a persistent patent ductus arteriosus.
Renal function must be monitored and renal ultrasonography performed

items.t: Hypersensitivity to furosemide, excipients, sulphonamides, sulphonamide derivatives or amiloride; anuria; CrCl below 30 mL/min per 1.73 m²; renal failure from nephrotoxic or hepatotoxic poisoning.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to furosemide, any of the excipients, sulphonamides, sulphonamide derivatives/amiloride
Anuria and impaired renal function (creatinine clearance below 30mL/min per 1.73 m2 body surface area) and renal failure resulting from poisoning by nephrotoxic and/or hepatotoxic agents

items.t: Severe hypokalaemia, severe hyponatraemia, hypovolaemia, dehydration and/or hypotension; concomitant potassium supplements or potassium-sparing diuretics; pre-coma/coma with cirrhosis or encephalopathy; Addison's disease; digitalis intoxication; breastfeeding.

src.q: Electrolyte disturbances (severe hypokalaemia, severe hyponatraemia, hypovolaemia), dehydration and/or hypotension

Concomitant potassium supplements or potassium-sparing diuretics (see section 4.5) Pre-coma/coma associated with hepatic cirrhosis or encephalopathy Addison's disease Digitalis intoxication (see section 4.5) Breast-feeding women

items.t: Correct hypotension, hypovolaemia and acid-base disturbance before starting. Symptomatic hypotension (dizziness, fainting) is more likely in the elderly and with other blood-pressure-lowering medicines.

src.q: These and any acid-base disturbance should be corrected before furosemide is started.
Symptomatic hypotension leading to dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness can occur in patients treated with furosemide, particularly in the elderly

items.t: Caution in impaired hepatic or renal function, hepatorenal syndrome, diabetes (latent diabetes may appear; insulin needs may rise), the elderly, urinary outflow obstruction including prostatic hypertrophy (acute retention), gout, and those at risk from marked falls in blood pressure. Stop before a glucose tolerance test.

src.q: Diabetes mellitus (latent diabetes may become overt: insulin requirements in established diabetes may increase)
Difficulty with micturition/potential obstruction in the urinary tract including prostatic hypertrophy (increased risk of acute retention) Gout (increased risk of hyperuricaemia)
Impaired renal function and hepato-renal syndrome
Impaired hepatic function (see sections 4.2 and 4.3 and below - monitoring required)
Elderly patients
Patients at risk of pronounced falls in blood pressure
Furosemide should be discontinued before a glucose tolerance test

items.t: Hypoproteinaemia (e.g. nephrotic syndrome): careful dose titration (reduced effect, more ototoxicity).

src.q: Patients with hypoproteinaemia (such as that associated with the nephrotic syndrome) require careful dose titration (reduced furosemide effect: increased risk of ototoxicity)

items.t: Lactose: patients with galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: Sulfonamide allergy (SPS): loop diuretics are non-antibiotic sulfonamides; cross-reactivity with sulfonamide antibiotics is not expected, but the SmPC lists sulphonamide hypersensitivity as a contraindication.

src.q: Classes where all members have a sulfonamide group include: carbonic anhydrase inhibitors loop diuretics
Cross-reactivity between antibiotic and non-antibiotic sulfonamides is not expected, including in people who had a life-threatening reaction to a sulfonamide.

items.t: ACE inhibitors: marked fall in blood pressure and worse renal function. Reduce the furosemide dose for at least 3 days, or stop it, before starting or increasing an ACE inhibitor.

src.q: A marked fall in blood pressure and deterioration in renal function may be seen when ACE inhibitors are added to furosemide therapy.
The dose of furosemide should be reduced for at least three days, or the drug stopped, before initiating the ACE inhibitor or increasing the dose of an ACE inhibitor.
Furosemide should be stopped or the dose reduced before starting an ACE-inhibitor.

items.t: Potassium supplements and potassium-sparing diuretics: contraindicated in section 4.3 (one SmPC notes increased hyperkalaemia risk with potassium salts).

src.q: Concomitant potassium supplements or potassium-sparing diuretics
Potassium salts: There is an increased risk of hyperkalaemia when given with potassium salts.

items.t: Aminoglycosides, polymyxins, vancomycin: more ototoxicity (may be irreversible); use only if there are compelling medical reasons. Aminoglycosides and some high-dose cephalosporins: more nephrotoxicity.

src.q: There is an increased risk of ototoxicity when loop diuretics are given with aminoglycosides, polymyxins or vancomycin. Since this may lead to irreversible damage, these drugs must only be used with furosemide if there are compelling medical reasons.
Impairment of renal function may develop in patients receiving concurrent treatment with furosemide and high doses of certain cephalosporins.

items.t: NSAIDs: more nephrotoxicity and reduced diuretic effect; acute renal insufficiency if dehydrated. Salicylate toxicity may be increased.

src.q: NSAIDs - increased risk of nephrotoxicity (especially if there is hypovolaemia).
In patients with dehydration or hypovolaemia, NSAIDs may cause acute renal insufficiency.
Salicylic toxicity may be increased by furosemide.

items.t: Lithium: reduced lithium excretion and toxicity risk; avoid unless plasma lithium levels are monitored (one SmPC); monitor lithium levels carefully and adjust the lithium dose where necessary (another SmPC).

src.q: Avoid concomitant administration unless plasma levels are monitored.
Lithium: Loop diuretics reduce the excretion of lithium
it is recommended that lithium levels are carefully monitored and where necessary the lithium dosage is adjusted

items.t: Hypokalaemia (and hypomagnesaemia) increases cardiac toxicity with QT-prolonging drugs, antiarrhythmics and cardiac glycosides; avoid with pimozide. Extra hypokalaemia with thiazides, corticosteroids and high-dose beta2 agonists (e.g. salbutamol).

src.q: Drugs associated with QT prolongation - cardiac toxicity may be increased by furosemide-induced hypokalaemia and/or hypomagnesaemia.
There is an increased risk of hypokalaemia when loop diuretics are given with thiazides and related diuretics.
There is an increased risk of hypokalaemia when loop diuretics are given with corticosteroids.
Anti-arrhythmics (including amiodarone, disopyramide, flecainide and sotalol) - risk of cardiac toxicity (because of furosemide-induced hypokalaemia).
Cardiac glycosides - hypokalaemia and electrolyte disturbances (including magnesium) increases the risk of cardiac toxicity.
Avoid concurrent use with pimozide.
Sympathomimetics - increased risk of hypokalaemia with high doses of beta2 sympathomimetics

items.t: Other: enhanced hypotension with other antihypertensives, nitrates, alpha-blockers (first-dose effect), tricyclics (postural); antidiabetic effect antagonised; carbamazepine (hyponatraemia); oestrogens and progestogens antagonise the diuretic effect; laxative abuse adds to potassium loss; one SmPC says antihistamines add hypokalaemia-related cardiac toxicity; sucralfate and bile acid sequestrants reduce absorption (separate doses); methotrexate and probenecid (mutual renal-secretion effects); warfarin (albumin binding in low albumin).

src.q: Antidiabetics - hypoglycaemic effects antagonised by furosemide.
Furosemide and sucralfate must not be taken within 2 hours of each other
Conversely, furosemide may decrease renal elimination of these drugs.
