src.q: Fucidin H cream can be used during breastfeeding but it is recommended to avoid applying Fucidin H cream on the breast.

items.t: SPS: topical hydrocortisone can be used during breastfeeding, with no extra risk from combination products containing antimicrobials; fusidic acid can also be used.

src.q: There are no additional risks when combination topical preparations containing antimicrobials or urea are used.
Fusidic acid can be used during breastfeeding.

items.t: No clinical studies on fertility.

src.q: There are no clinical studies with Fucidin H cream regarding fertility.

items.t: Application-site reactions (itching, burning, irritation).

src.q: Application site reaction (incl. pruritus, burning and irritation)

items.t: Hypersensitivity (uncommon).

src.q: Immune system disorders Uncommon (≥1/1,000 and <1/100) Hypersensitivity

items.t: Adrenal suppression, especially with prolonged use; raised intra-ocular pressure and glaucoma if used near the eyes. Large amounts for more than 3 weeks can cause Cushing's syndrome and adrenocortical insufficiency.

src.q: include adrenal suppression especially during prolonged topical administration
Raised intra-ocular pressure and glaucoma may also occur after topical use of corticosteroids near the eyes
Cushing's syndrome and adrenocortical insufficiency may develop following topical application of corticosteroids in large amounts and for more than three weeks.

items.t: Topical steroid withdrawal reactions after stopping: spreading redness, burning or stinging, itch, peeling, oozing pustules.

src.q: Withdrawal reactions - redness of the skin which may extend to areas beyond the initial affected area, burning or stinging sensation, itch, skin peeling, oozing pustules

items.t: Review if there is no clinical improvement after 7 days; switch to systemic therapy if infection is not controlled.

src.q: Steroid antibiotic combinations should not be continued for more than 7 days in the absence of any clinical improvement.
It is advised to switch to systemic therapy if infection cannot be controlled with topical treatment

items.t: Be vigilant for topical steroid withdrawal reactions.

src.q: be vigilant for the signs and symptoms of topical steroid withdrawal reactions

items.t: For use on the skin only. Apply a small quantity to the affected area; keep away from the eyes, open wounds and mucous membranes.

src.q: Cream for topical administration
Contact with open wounds and mucous membranes should be avoided.

items.t: Use only for the course prescribed (normally no more than 2 weeks); return if no better after 7 days.

src.q: A single treatment course should not normally exceed 2 weeks.
Steroid antibiotic combinations should not be continued for more than 7 days in the absence of any clinical improvement.

items.t: If the skin worsens within 2 weeks of stopping, do not restart without consulting the doctor (unless already advised).

src.q: if your skin worsens within 2 weeks of stopping a topical corticosteroid, do not start treatment again without consulting your doctor

items.t: Do not smoke or go near naked flames: clothing, bedding and dressings with cream on them burn more easily.

src.q: Fabric (clothing, bedding, dressings etc) that has been in contact with this product burns more easily and is a serious fire hazard.

items.t: Bacterial infections of the external eye and its adnexa: conjunctivitis, keratitis, keratoconjunctivitis, corneal ulcers, blepharitis, blepharoconjunctivitis, acute meibomianitis, episcleritis and dacryocystitis.

src.q: Treatment of infections of the external structures of the eye and its adnexa caused by susceptible bacteria.
Such infections include conjunctivitis, keratitis, kerato-conjunctivitis, corneal ulcers, blepharitis and blepharo-conjunctivitis, acute meibomianitis, episcleritis and dacryocystitis.

items.t: Prevention of eye infection after foreign-body removal, burns or lacerations of the conjunctiva, chemical or physical damage, and eye surgery.

src.q: It may be used for the prevention of ocular infection after: removal of a foreign body, burns or lacerations of the conjunctiva; damage from chemical or physical agents and after ocular surgery.

items.t: Otitis externa; superficial ear infections caused by gentamicin-sensitive organisms; prevention of infection after ear trauma.

src.q: Also indicated for the treatment of otitis externa.
For the treatment of superficial eye and ear infections caused by organisms sensitive to gentamicin.
For prophylaxis against infection in trauma of the eye or ear.

items.t: Prescription-only medicine in the UK.

src.q: Prescription only medicine

items.t: Eye: 1 to 2 drops into the affected eye up to six times a day, or more often if needed. Severe infection: 1 to 2 drops every 15 to 20 minutes at first, then reduce gradually as the infection is controlled.

src.q: Instill 1-2 drops into the affected eye up to six times a day, or more frequently if required.
severe infections may require 1 or 2 drops every fifteen to twenty minutes initially, reducing the frequency of instillation gradually as the infection is controlled

items.t: Ear: clean the area, then 2 to 3 drops into the affected ear 3 to 4 times a day and at night, or more often if needed.

src.q: The area should be cleansed and 2-3 drops instilled in the affected ear 3-4 times a day and at night or more frequently if required.

items.t: Eye ointment: no UK SmPC dose is available for the ointment.

src.q: Method of administration Auricular and ocular use.

items.t: Children use the same dose as adults. Children's eyes may react more strongly to irritation, which can affect adherence.

src.q: Adults, the elderly and the paediatric population
Generally, however, eyes in children show a stronger reaction for a given stimulus than the adult eye.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to gentamicin or any excipient; known allergy to gentamicin or other aminoglycosides.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to active substance, Gentamicin or to any of the excipient listed in section 6.1.
Should not be administered to patients with a known allergy to gentamicin and other aminoglycosides.

items.t: Myasthenia gravis and related conditions (gentamicin may cause neuromuscular blockade).

src.q: gentamicin may cause neuromuscular blockade and is therefore contra-indicated in myasthenia gravis and related conditions
Myasthenia gravis

items.t: Perforated eardrum, known or suspected.

src.q: Perforated tympanic membrane.
Known or suspected perforation of the ear drum.

items.t: Ear use: always check the eardrum before prescribing; do not use if eardrum integrity cannot be guaranteed. Direct contact with the middle and inner ear can cause irreversible toxicity. Weigh this against the risk of the infection itself causing hearing loss.

src.q: The condition of the ear drum must always be checked before this medicinal product is prescribed.
The medicinal product must not be used if the integrity of the ear drum cannot be guaranteed.
Irreversible toxic effects may result from direct contact of gentamicin with the middle and inner ear.

items.t: Avoid prolonged use: it may cause skin sensitisation and resistant organisms. Cross-sensitivity with other aminoglycosides may occur.

src.q: Avoid prolonged use. Prolonged use may lead to skin sensitisation and the emergence of resistant organisms.
Cross-sensitivity with other aminoglycoside antibiotics may occur.

items.t: Ototoxicity (vestibular damage, irreversible deafness) can occur when gentamicin is given systemically or put on open wounds or damaged skin. This is dose-related, worse with renal or hepatic impairment and more likely in the elderly.

src.q: Gentamicin may cause ototoxicity (vestibular damage; irreversible partial or total deafness) when given systemically or when applied topically to open wounds or damaged skin.
This effect is dose-related and is enhanced by renal and/or hepatic impairment and is more likely in the elderly.

items.t: Mitochondrial DNA variants (especially m.1555A>G): increased risk of aminoglycoside ototoxicity, sometimes with a maternal history of deafness. MHRA: consider the need for aminoglycoside treatment versus alternatives in patients with these variants.

src.q: There have been observed cases of an increased risk of ototoxicity with aminoglycosides administered to patients with mitochondrial mutations, particularly the m.1555A>G mutation
consider the need for aminoglycoside treatment versus alternative options available to minimise the risks of adverse events, including ototoxicity

items.t: Severe infections: add a suitable systemic antibiotic.

src.q: In severe infections, topical use of gentamicin should be supplemented with appropriate systemic antibiotic treatment.

items.t: Benzalkonium chloride (drops): can irritate the eye and cause dry-eye symptoms; use with caution in dry eye or a compromised cornea, and monitor with prolonged use.

src.q: Should be used with caution in dry eye patients and in patients where the cornea may be compromised.
Patients should be monitored in case of prolonged use.

items.t: Contact lenses: one UK SmPC says do not use the drops while wearing soft lenses (remove before use, wait at least 15 minutes before reinserting); another says remove contact lenses during treatment of eye infections.

src.q: Gentamicin should not be used while wearing these lenses.
The lenses should be removed before instillation of the drops and not reinserted earlier than 15 minutes after use.
Contact lenses should be removed during the period of treatment of ocular infections.

items.t: Caution if the patient is also on systemic aminoglycosides (systemic gentamicin has caused neurotoxicity, ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity; not reported after ear use).

src.q: Although these effects have not been reported following topical otic use of gentamicin, caution is advised when used concomitantly with systemic aminoglycosides.

items.t: Potent diuretics such as furosemide may increase the risk of ototoxicity. Avoid using with other potentially ototoxic or nephrotoxic drugs unless the doctor considers it essential. This is the SmPC's general gentamicin interaction text; the systemic toxicities have not been reported after ear use of the drops.

src.q: Potent diuretics such as ethacrynic acid and furosemide are believed to enhance any risk of ototoxicity
Concurrent use with other potentially nephrotoxic or ototoxic drugs should be avoided unless considered essential by the physician.
Although these effects have not been reported following topical otic use of gentamicin

items.t: Amphotericin B, cisplatin, ciclosporin and cephalosporins may increase the risk of nephrotoxicity.

src.q: amphotericin B, cisplatin and cyclosporine and cephalosporins are potential enhancers of nephrotoxicity

items.t: Curare-type muscle relaxants: neuromuscular blockade and respiratory paralysis have been reported with aminoglycosides.

src.q: Neuromuscular blockade and respiratory paralysis have been reported in patients from the administration of aminoglycosides to patients who have received curare-type muscle relaxants during anaesthesia.

items.t: Systemic absorption after topical use is likely too low to carry a risk comparable to systemic gentamicin (SmPC comment on nephrotoxicity).

src.q: it is likely that systemic absorption following topical administration does not constitute a comparable risk

items.t: No dose advice for the drops. Ototoxicity from gentamicin is enhanced by renal impairment (stated for systemic use or use on open wounds or damaged skin). One SmPC: care is needed in anuria because elimination is much slower.

src.q: This effect is dose-related and is enhanced by renal and/or hepatic impairment and is more likely in the elderly.
*Therefore in those with anuria care must be exercised.

items.t: No dose advice for the drops. Ototoxicity from gentamicin is enhanced by hepatic impairment (stated for systemic use or use on open wounds or damaged skin).

src.q: This effect is dose-related and is enhanced by renal and/or hepatic impairment and is more likely in the elderly.

items.t: SmPC: safety in pregnancy not established; use only when the doctor considers it essential after weighing risks and benefits.

src.q: Safety for use in pregnancy has not been established.
Gentamicin should only be used in pregnancy when considered essential by the physician, after careful assessment of the potential risks and benefits.

items.t: BUMPS: aminoglycoside eye or ear drops do not enter the bloodstream in amounts that could harm the baby.

src.q: when used in the form of eye or ear drops, do not enter the bloodstream in amounts that could harm the baby

items.t: SmPC: safety in breastfeeding not established; milk intake is unlikely to give significant infant blood levels (no gut inflammation). Use only when the doctor considers it essential.

src.q: In the absence of gastrointestinal inflammation the amount of gentamicin ingested from the milk is unlikely to result in significant blood levels in breast-fed infants.
Gentamicin should only be used in lactation when considered essential by the physician, after careful assessment of the potential risks and benefits.

items.t: SPS (chloramphenicol breastfeeding page): gentamicin (or fusidic acid) eye and ear preparations are preferred over chloramphenicol during breastfeeding, if clinically appropriate.

src.q: Fusidic acid or gentamicin preparations would be preferred, if clinically appropriate.

items.t: No fertility data.

src.q: Fertility No data available.

items.t: Frequencies are not known. Eye: local sensitivity, blurred vision, irritation, burning, stinging, itching. Skin: burning, stinging, itching, dermatitis.

src.q: all the undesirable effects listed are classed as "frequency unknown"
Local sensitivity; blurred vision, eye irritation, burning sensation, stinging sensation, itching (eye pruritus)

items.t: Ear: ototoxicity, vestibular disorder and hearing loss (frequency not known).

src.q: Local sensitivity; ototoxicity; vestibular disorder; hearing loss

items.t: Stop treatment if irritation, sensitivity or superinfection occurs, and start suitable therapy.

src.q: In the event of irritation, sensitivity or super-infection, treatment should be discontinued and appropriate therapy instituted.

items.t: Before ear use: check the eardrum is intact.

src.q: The condition of the ear drum must always be checked before this medicinal product is prescribed.

items.t: Monitor patients on prolonged use (benzalkonium chloride effects on the eye surface).

src.q: Patients should be monitored in case of prolonged use.

items.t: Stop if irritation, sensitivity or superinfection develops.

src.q: In the event of irritation, sensitivity or super-infection, treatment should be discontinued and appropriate therapy instituted.

items.t: Ear: clean the ear area before putting in the drops.

src.q: The area should be cleaned and 2 - 3 drops instilled in the affected ear three to four times a day and at night

items.t: Soft contact lenses: remove before using the drops and wait 15 minutes before putting them back.

src.q: Contact lenses should be removed before using this medicine and put back 15 minutes afterwards.

items.t: Eye use may blur vision for a short time; do not drive or use machines until vision is clear.

src.q: If affected, patients should not drive or operate machinery until vision has cleared.

items.t: Do not wear contact lenses while treating an eye infection.

src.q: Contact lenses should be removed during the period of treatment of ocular infections.

restrictions.note: No UK product information found.

hepatic.note: No UK product information found.

items.t: Type 2 diabetes in adults when diet, exercise and weight loss alone do not control blood glucose.

src.q: Non insulin-dependent diabetes (type 2) in adults when dietary measures, physical exercise and weight loss alone are not sufficient to control blood glucose.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restrictions in the two UK 60 mg modified-release gliclazide SmPCs checked.

items.t: 30 mg to 120 mg once daily at breakfast. Start 30 mg daily; if not controlled, increase in steps to 60, 90 or 120 mg, at least 1 month apart (or after 2 weeks if glucose has not fallen). Maximum 120 mg daily.

src.q: The daily dose may vary from 30 mg to 120 mg per day, taken orally in a single intake at breakfast time.
The recommended starting dose is 30 mg daily.

If blood glucose is not adequately controlled, the dose may be increased to 60, 90 or 120 mg daily, in successive steps. The interval between each dose increment should be at least 1 month except in patients whose blood glucose has not reduced after two weeks of treatment.
The maximum recommended daily dose is 120 mg.

items.t: Switching from another oral antidiabetic: start at 30 mg and titrate. From a sulfonylurea with a long half-life, a treatment-free period of a few days may be needed to avoid additive hypoglycaemia.

src.q: A starting dose of 30 mg should be used and this should be adjusted to suit the patient's blood glucose response

When switching from a hypoglycaemic sulfonylurea with a prolonged half-life , a treatment free period of a few days may be necessary to avoid an additive effect of the two products, which might cause hypoglycaemia.

items.t: Can be combined with biguanides, alpha-glucosidase inhibitors or insulin; start insulin only under close medical supervision.

src.q: can be given in combination with biguanides, alpha glucosidase inhibitors or insulin.
concomitant insulin therapy can be initiated under close medical supervision.

items.t: Elderly: same regimen as under 65 years.

src.q: should be prescribed using the same dosing regimen recommended for patients under 65 years of age.

items.t: At risk of hypoglycaemia (undernourished, severe or poorly compensated endocrine disorders such as hypopituitarism, hypothyroidism or adrenocorticotrophic insufficiency, withdrawal of long or high-dose corticosteroids, severe vascular disease): use the minimum starting dose of 30 mg.

src.q: Patients at risk of hypoglycaemia: - Undernourished or malnourished - Severe or poorly compensated endocrine disorders (hypopituitarism, hypothyroidism, adrenocorticotrophic insufficiency)
It is recommended that the minimum daily starting dose of 30 mg is used.

items.t: Missed dose: do not increase the next day's dose.

src.q: If a dose is forgotten, there must be no increase in the dose taken the next day.

items.t: Not established in children and adolescents; no data in children.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of Xywin 60 mg Prolonged-Release Tablets in children and adolescents have not been established. No data are available in children.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to gliclazide, other sulfonylureas, sulfonamides or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to gliclazide or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1, other sulfonylureas, sulfonamides

items.t: Type 1 diabetes; diabetic pre-coma and coma; diabetic ketoacidosis.

src.q: Type 1 diabetes, Diabetic pre-coma and coma, diabetic keto-acidosis

items.t: Severe renal or hepatic insufficiency (insulin is recommended).

src.q: Severe renal or hepatic insufficiency: in these cases the use of insulin is recommended

items.t: Treatment with miconazole (systemic or oromucosal gel).

src.q: Treatment with miconazole (see section 4.5)
Miconazole (systemic route, oromucosal gel): increases the hypoglycaemic effect with possible onset of hypoglycaemic symptoms, or even coma.

items.t: Breastfeeding.

src.q: Lactation (see section 4.6).

items.t: Hypoglycaemia, sometimes severe and prolonged (may need hospital care and glucose for several days). Prescribe only if the patient is likely to eat regularly, including breakfast. Risk factors: irregular or skipped meals, fasting, low-calorie diet, strenuous exercise, alcohol, renal or severe hepatic insufficiency, thyroid disorders, hypopituitarism, adrenal insufficiency, other interacting medicines.

src.q: This treatment should be prescribed only if the patient is likely to have a regular food intake (including breakfast).
Some cases may be severe and prolonged. Hospitalisation may be necessary and glucose administration may need to be continued for several days.
Hypoglycaemia is more likely to occur during low-calorie diets, following prolonged or strenuous exercise, alcohol intake or if a combination of hypoglycaemic agents is being used.

items.t: Renal or hepatic insufficiency: hypoglycaemic episodes may be prolonged; manage appropriately.

src.q: A hypoglycaemic episode occurring in these patients may be prolonged, so appropriate management should be initiated.

items.t: G6PD deficiency: sulfonylureas can cause haemolytic anaemia; use with caution and consider a non-sulfonylurea alternative.

src.q: caution should be used in patients with G6PD-deficiency and a non-sulfonylurea alternative should be considered.

items.t: Loss of glucose control with fever, trauma, infection, surgery or St John's wort; insulin may be needed.

src.q: St. John's Wort ( Hypericum perforatum) preparations (see section 4.5) , fever, trauma, infection or surgical intervention. In some cases, it may be necessary to administer insulin.

items.t: Fluoroquinolones: hypo- and hyperglycaemia reported, especially in the elderly; careful glucose monitoring recommended.

src.q: careful monitoring of blood glucose is recommended in all patients receiving at the same time Xywin 60mg Prolonged-Release Tablets and a fluoroquinolone.

items.t: Acute porphyria: cases described with some other sulfonylureas in patients with porphyria.

src.q: Cases of acute porphyria have been described with some other sulfonylurea drugs, in patients who have porphyria.

items.t: Contains lactose: should not be given to patients with hereditary galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption.

src.q: should not be administered to patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, the Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption.

items.t: Secondary failure: effect may weaken over time; check dose and diet adherence first.

src.q: Adequate dose adjustment and dietary compliance should be considered before classifying the patient as secondary failure.

items.t: Miconazole (systemic or oromucosal gel): contraindicated - increased hypoglycaemic effect, possibly coma.

src.q: Contra-indicated combination Miconazole (systemic route, oromucosal gel): increases the hypoglycaemic effect with possible onset of hypoglycaemic symptoms, or even coma.

items.t: Alcohol: not recommended - increases hypoglycaemia, can lead to hypoglycaemic coma. Avoid alcohol and alcohol-containing medicines. Phenylbutazone (not in this tool's list): not recommended.

src.q: Alcohol : increases the hypoglycaemic reaction (by inhibiting compensatory reactions) that can lead to the onset of hypoglycaemic coma. Avoid alcohol or medicines containing alcohol.
Phenylbutazone (systemic route): increases the hypoglycaemic effect of sulfonylureas

items.t: Precautions (risk of hypoglycaemia): other antidiabetics (insulin, metformin, DPP-4 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, acarbose, thiazolidinediones), beta-blockers, fluconazole, ACE inhibitors, H2-receptor antagonists, MAOIs, sulfonamides, clarithromycin, NSAIDs.

src.q: Other anti-diabetic agents (insulins, acarbose, metformin), thiazolidinediones, dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists), beta-blockers, fluconazole

angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors (captopril, enalapril), H2-receptor antagonists, monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs), sulfonamides, clarithromycin and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents.

items.t: Raise blood glucose: glucocorticoids (systemic and local, including intra-articular, skin and rectal), high-dose chlorpromazine, IV salbutamol/terbutaline, danazol (not recommended). Warn the patient, monitor glucose, adjust dose during and after.

src.q: Glucocorticoids (systemic and local route: intra-articular, cutaneous and rectal preparations) and tetracosactrin: increase blood glucose levels with possible ketosis

Warn the patient and emphasise the importance of blood glucose monitoring, particularly at the start of treatment. It may be necessary to adjust the dose of the anti-diabetic active substance during and after treatment with glucocorticoids.
Ritodrine, salbutamol and terbutaline (I.V. ): Increased blood glucose levels due to beta-2 agonist effects.

items.t: St John's wort: lowers gliclazide exposure - monitor blood glucose.

src.q: Gliclazide exposure is decreased by Saint John's Wort- Hypericum perforatum . Emphasise the importance of blood glucose levels monitoring.

items.t: Fluoroquinolones: dysglycaemia - warn the patient and monitor blood glucose.

src.q: the patient should be warned of the risk of dysglycaemia, and the importance of blood glucose monitoring should be emphasised.

items.t: Warfarin: sulfonylureas may potentiate anticoagulation; anticoagulant dose adjustment may be needed.

src.q: Sulfonylureas may lead to potentiation of anticoagulation during concurrent treatment. Adjustment of the anticoagulant may be necessary.

items.t: Mild to moderate renal insufficiency: usual dose with careful monitoring.

src.q: In patients with mild to moderate renal insufficiency the same dosing regimen can be used as in patients with normal renal function with careful patient monitoring.

items.t: Severe renal insufficiency: contraindicated (insulin recommended). The SmPC gives no numeric threshold.

src.q: Severe renal or hepatic insufficiency: in these cases the use of insulin is recommended

items.t: Severe hepatic insufficiency: contraindicated (insulin recommended).

src.q: Severe renal or hepatic insufficiency: in these cases the use of insulin is recommended

items.t: Hepatic insufficiency: pharmacokinetics may be altered and hypoglycaemia may be prolonged.

src.q: The pharmacokinetics and/or pharmacodynamics of gliclazide may be altered in patients with hepatic insufficiency or severe renal failure.

items.t: SmPC: limited data; as a precaution preferably avoid. Insulin is the drug of first choice in pregnancy; change to insulin before trying to conceive or as soon as pregnancy is found.

src.q: As a precautionary measure, it is preferable to avoid the use of Gliclazide during pregnancy.

insulin is the drug of first choice for treatment of diabetes during pregnancy. It is recommended that oral hypoglycaemic therapy is changed to insulin before a pregnancy is attempted, or as soon as pregnancy is discovered.

items.t: BUMPS: treat type 2 diabetes in pregnancy with metformin, plus insulin if needed; sulfonylureas are avoided as a precaution. With an unplanned pregnancy, keep taking it until reviewed promptly.

src.q: Type 2 diabetes during pregnancy should be treated with metformin, as well as insulin if required. Other antidiabetic drugs should not be used.
you should carry on with the drug you are taking until your appointment, as uncontrolled diabetes is risky for you and your baby

items.t: SmPC: contraindicated in breastfeeding (risk of neonatal hypoglycaemia).

src.q: Given the risk of neonatal hypoglycaemia, the product is contra-indicated in breast-feeding mothers.

items.t: SPS: insulin or metformin are the preferred choices; limited or no published information on other antidiabetic medicines.

src.q: Insulin or metformin are the preferred choices during breastfeeding.
limited or no published information on the use of other antidiabetic (blood-glucose lowering) medicines during breastfeeding.

items.t: No effect on fertility in rats.

src.q: No effect on fertility or reproductive performance was noted in male and female rats

items.t: Hypoglycaemia is the most frequent adverse reaction, especially with irregular or skipped meals.

src.q: The most frequent adverse reaction with gliclazide is hypoglycaemia.
if meal times are irregular and, in particular, if meals are skipped.

items.t: Gastrointestinal upset (abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, dyspepsia, diarrhoea, constipation); taking it with breakfast can reduce this. The SmPC gives no frequencies.

src.q: These can be avoided or minimised if gliclazide is taken with breakfast.

items.t: Transient visual disturbances, mainly when starting, from changes in blood glucose.

src.q: Transient visual disturbances may occur especially on initiation of treatment, due to changes in blood glucose levels.

items.t: Severe or prolonged hypoglycaemia (confusion, convulsions, loss of consciousness, coma): needs immediate medical treatment or hospital admission even if sugar helps at first; it can recur.

src.q: Experience with other sulfonylureas shows that hypoglycaemia can recur even when measures prove effective initially.
If a hypoglycaemic episode is severe or prolonged, and even if it is temporarily controlled by intake of sugar, immediate medical treatment or even hospitalisation are required.

items.t: Severe skin reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS) and angioedema reported.

src.q: bullous reactions (such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis and autoimmune bullous disorders) and exceptionally, drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS).

items.t: Cholestatic jaundice: stop treatment. Hepatitis and raised liver enzymes reported.

src.q: Discontinue treatment if cholestatic jaundice appears.

items.t: Blood disorders (anaemia, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia, granulocytopenia) are rare and usually reversible on stopping.

src.q: Changes in haematology are rare. They may include anaemia, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia, granulocytopenia. These are in general reversible upon discontinuation of medication.

items.t: HbA1c (or fasting venous plasma glucose) to assess control; blood glucose self-monitoring may help.

src.q: Measurement of glycated haemoglobin levels (or fasting venous plasma glucose) is recommended in assessing blood glucose control. Blood glucose self-monitoring may also be useful.

items.t: Adjust dose to metabolic response (blood glucose, HbA1c).

src.q: the dose should be adjusted according to the individual patient's metabolic response (blood glucose, HbAlc).

items.t: Stop if cholestatic jaundice appears.

src.q: Discontinue treatment if cholestatic jaundice appears.

items.t: Once daily at breakfast; swallow tablet(s) whole.

src.q: taken orally in a single intake at breakfast time. It is recommended that the tablet(s) be swallowed whole.

items.t: Explain hypoglycaemia (symptoms, treatment and triggers) to the patient and family; follow dietary advice, exercise regularly and monitor blood glucose.

src.q: The risks of hypoglycaemia, together with its symptoms (see section 4.8), treatment and conditions that predispose to its development, should be explained to the patient and to family members.
The patient should be informed of the importance of following dietary advice, of taking regular exercise, and of regular monitoring of blood glucose levels.

items.t: Eat regular meals, including breakfast; low blood sugar is more likely if meals are late, small or low in carbohydrate.

src.q: It is important to have a regular carbohydrate intake due to the increased risk of hypoglycaemia if a meal is taken late, if an inadequate amount of food is consumed or if the food is low in carbohydrate.

items.t: Avoid alcohol and alcohol-containing medicines.

src.q: Avoid alcohol or medicines containing alcohol.

items.t: Sugar treats low blood sugar; artificial sweeteners do not.

src.q: Usually, symptoms disappear after intake of carbohydrates (sugar). However, artificial sweeteners have no effect.

items.t: Know hypoglycaemia symptoms and take care when driving or using machines, especially at the start.

src.q: patients should be made aware of the symptoms of hypoglycaemia and should be careful if driving or operating machinery, especially at the beginning of treatment.

items.t: Type 2 diabetes when diet, exercise and weight reduction alone are not adequate.

src.q: Glimepiride is indicated for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus, when diet, physical exercise and weight reduction alone are not adequate.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restrictions in the UK glimepiride 2 mg and 3 mg SmPCs checked.

items.t: Start 1 mg once daily. If needed, increase stepwise about every 1 to 2 weeks to 2, 3 or 4 mg daily. More than 4 mg helps only in exceptional cases. Maximum 6 mg daily.

src.q: The starting dose is 1 mg glimepiride per day.

in a stepwise manner with an interval of about 1 to 2 weeks between each step, to 2, 3 or 4 mg glimepiride per day. A dose of more than 4 mg glimepiride per day gives better results only in exceptional cases.
The maximum recommended dose is 6 mg glimepiride per day.

items.t: Added to maximum-dose metformin, or with insulin added to maximum-dose glimepiride: start the new medicine low and titrate under close medical supervision.

src.q: In patients not adequately controlled with the maximum daily dose of metformin, concomitant glimepiride therapy can be initiated if necessary.
The combination therapy should be initiated under close medical supervision.

items.t: Requirements may fall as control improves: consider timely dose reduction or stopping to avoid hypoglycaemia. Hypoglycaemia on 1 mg daily suggests diet alone may be enough.

src.q: To avoid hypoglycaemia timely dose reduction or cessation of therapy must therefore be considered.
If a patient has a hypoglycaemic reaction on 1 mg glimepiride daily, this indicates that they can be controlled by diet alone.

items.t: Switching from another oral hypoglycaemic: start at 1 mg; after long half-life agents a washout of a few days may be advisable.

src.q: In some cases, especially in antidiabetic medicines with a long half life (e.g. chlorpropamide), a wash out period of a few days is advisable

items.t: Missed dose: do not correct by increasing the next dose.

src.q: If a dose is forgotten, this should not be corrected by increasing the next dose.

items.t: Not recommended in children: no data under 8 years and insufficient data at 8 to 17 years.

src.q: There are no data available on the use of glimepiride in patients under 8 years of age.
The available data on safety and efficacy are insufficient in the paediatric population and therefore such use is not recommended.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to glimepiride, other sulfonylureas, sulfonamides or any excipient.

src.q: hypersensitivity to glimepiride, other sulfonylureas or sulfonamides or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1

items.t: Type 1 diabetes; diabetic coma; ketoacidosis.

src.q: diabetes mellitus type 1, - diabetic coma, - ketoacidosis,

items.t: Severe renal or hepatic function disorders (change to insulin).

src.q: severe renal or hepatic function disorders. In case of severe renal or hepatic function disorders, a changeover to insulin is required.

items.t: Hypoglycaemia: take shortly before or with a meal; irregular or skipped meals can cause hypoglycaemia. Severe or prolonged episodes need immediate medical treatment and sometimes hospital care; it may recur. Severe attacks can look like a stroke.

src.q: When meals are taken at irregular hours or skipped altogether, treatment with Glimepiride may lead to hypoglycaemia.
The clinical picture of a severe hypoglycaemic attack may resemble that of a stroke.
Severe hypoglycaemia or prolonged hypoglycaemia, only temporarily controlled by the usual amounts of sugar, require immediate medical treatment and occasionally hospitalisation.

items.t: Risk factors for hypoglycaemia: poor co-operation (more often elderly), poor nutrition or missed meals, diet changes, exercise without enough carbohydrate, alcohol, impaired renal function, serious liver dysfunction, some thyroid, pituitary or adrenal disorders, and interacting medicines.

src.q: unwillingness or (more commonly in elderly patients) incapacity of the patient to cooperate
consumption of alcohol, especially in combination with skipped meals, - impaired renal function, - serious liver dysfunction

items.t: Stress (accidents, acute operations, febrile infections): a temporary switch to insulin may be indicated.

src.q: In stress-situations (e.g. accidents, acute operations, infections with fever, etc.) a temporary switch to insulin may be indicated.

items.t: No experience in severe liver impairment or in dialysis patients.

src.q: No experience has been gained concerning the use of Glimepiride in patients with severe impairment of liver function or dialysis patients.

items.t: G6PD deficiency: risk of haemolytic anaemia; use with caution and consider a non-sulfonylurea alternative.

src.q: caution should be used in patients with G6PD-deficiency and a non-sulfonylurea alternative should be considered.

items.t: Contains lactose: patients with hereditary galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take it.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: Glimepiride is metabolised by CYP2C9: inducers (e.g. rifampicin) and inhibitors (e.g. fluconazole) change its effect; fluconazole roughly doubles glimepiride exposure. Other medicines should only be taken with the doctor's knowledge.

src.q: Glimepiride is metabolized by cytochrome P450 2C9 (CYP2C9).
glimepiride AUC is increased approximately 2-fold by fluconazole
other medicinal products should only be taken with the knowledge (or at the prescription) of the doctor.

items.t: May increase glucose lowering (hypoglycaemia): insulin and other oral antidiabetics (e.g. metformin), salicylates, some long-acting sulfonamides, tetracyclines, quinolones, clarithromycin, coumarin anticoagulants, fibrates, ACE inhibitors, fluoxetine, MAOIs, allopurinol, miconazole, fluconazole, and others.

src.q: insulin and oral antidiabetic products, such as metformin, - salicylates and p-amino-salicylic acid
chloramphenicol, certain long acting sulfonamides, tetracyclines, quinolone antibiotics and clarithromycin, - coumarin anticoagulants
fibrates, - ACE inhibitors, - fluoxetine, MAO-inhibitors, - allopurinol, probenecid, sulfinpyrazone
miconazole, fluconazole

items.t: May weaken glucose lowering (raised glucose): oestrogens and progestogens, thiazide diuretics, glucocorticoids, thyroid-stimulating agents, phenothiazines, adrenaline and sympathomimetics, long-term laxatives, phenytoin, rifampicin, acetazolamide, and others.

src.q: oestrogens and progestogens, - saluretics, thiazide diuretics, - thyroid stimulating agents, glucocorticoids
adrenaline and sympathicomimetics
laxatives (long term use)

items.t: Beta-blockers (and clonidine, reserpine, H2 antagonists): may increase or weaken the effect; beta-blockers may reduce or abolish the warning signs of hypoglycaemia.

src.q: H2 antagonists, beta blockers, clonidine and reserpine may lead to either potentiation or weakening of the blood glucose lowering effect.
the signs of adrenergic counterregulation to hypoglycaemia may be reduced or absent.

items.t: Alcohol: may increase or weaken the effect unpredictably. Coumarin anticoagulants: glimepiride may increase or weaken their effect.

src.q: Alcohol intake may potentiate or weaken the hypoglycaemic action of glimepiride in an unpredictable fashion.
Glimepiride may either potentiate or weaken the effects of coumarin derivatives.

items.t: Colesevelam (not in this tool's list): give glimepiride at least 4 hours before.

src.q: glimepiride should be administered at least 4 hours prior to colesevelam.

items.t: Severe renal function disorders: contraindicated; change to insulin. The SmPC gives no numeric threshold. Impaired renal function increases hypoglycaemia risk.

src.q: severe renal or hepatic function disorders. In case of severe renal or hepatic function disorders, a changeover to insulin is required.
impaired renal function

items.t: No experience in dialysis patients.

src.q: No experience has been gained concerning the use of Glimepiride in patients with severe impairment of liver function or dialysis patients.

items.t: Severe hepatic function disorders: contraindicated; change to insulin. Serious liver dysfunction increases hypoglycaemia risk.

src.q: severe renal or hepatic function disorders. In case of severe renal or hepatic function disorders, a changeover to insulin is required.
serious liver dysfunction

items.t: SmPC: should not be used at any stage of pregnancy (animal reproductive toxicity). If planning pregnancy or pregnant, switch to insulin as soon as possible.

src.q: Consequently, glimepiride should not be used during the whole pregnancy.
In case of treatment by glimepiride, if the patient plans to become pregnant or if a pregnancy is discovered, the treatment should be switched as soon as possible to insulin therapy.

items.t: BUMPS: treat type 2 diabetes in pregnancy with metformin, plus insulin if needed; sulfonylureas are avoided as a precaution. With an unplanned pregnancy, keep taking it until reviewed promptly.

src.q: Type 2 diabetes during pregnancy should be treated with metformin, as well as insulin if required. Other antidiabetic drugs should not be used.
you should carry on with the drug you are taking until your appointment, as uncontrolled diabetes is risky for you and your baby

items.t: SmPC: breastfeeding is advised against (other sulfonylureas pass into milk; risk of hypoglycaemia in the infant).

src.q: As other sulfonylureas are excreted in human milk and because there is a risk of hypoglycaemia in nursing infants, breast-feeding is advised against during treatment with glimepiride.

items.t: SPS: insulin or metformin are the preferred choices; limited or no published information on other antidiabetic medicines.

src.q: Insulin or metformin are the preferred choices during breastfeeding.
limited or no published information on the use of other antidiabetic (blood-glucose lowering) medicines during breastfeeding.

items.t: No fertility data. Patients considering pregnancy should tell their doctor.

src.q: No data on fertility is available.
Patients who consider pregnancy should inform their physician.

items.t: The SmPC lists no very common or common reactions. Listed as rare: hypoglycaemia (may be severe and hard to correct), taste disturbance, alopecia, weight gain, and blood count changes.

src.q: Rare: hypoglycaemia. These hypoglycaemic reactions mostly occur immediately, may be severe and are not always easy to correct.
Rare: dysgeusia.
Rare: alopecia.
Rare: weight gain.

items.t: Transient visual disturbances, especially when starting, from changes in blood glucose (frequency not known).

src.q: Not known: visual disturbances, transient, may occur especially on initiation of treatment, due to changes in blood glucose levels.

items.t: Severe or prolonged hypoglycaemia: needs immediate medical treatment, sometimes in hospital; may recur.

src.q: Severe hypoglycaemia or prolonged hypoglycaemia, only temporarily controlled by the usual amounts of sugar, require immediate medical treatment and occasionally hospitalisation.

items.t: Blood disorders (rare: thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, agranulocytosis, haemolytic anaemia, pancytopenia; not known: severe thrombocytopenia with purpura).

src.q: Rare: thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, granulocytopenia, agranulocytosis, erythropenia, haemolytic anaemia and pancytopenia, which are in general reversible upon discontinuation of medication.
Not known: severe thrombocytopenia with platelet count less than 10,000/μl and thrombocytopenic purpura.

items.t: Very rare: hypersensitivity that may progress to breathlessness, low blood pressure and shock; hepatitis and hepatic failure; low sodium.

src.q: Very rare: leukocytoclaslic vasculitis, mild hypersensitivity reactions that may develop into serious reactions with dyspnoea, fall in blood pressure and sometimes shock.
Very rare: hepatic function abnormal (e.g. with cholestasis and jaundice), hepatitis and hepatic failure.

items.t: Blood and urine glucose regularly; HbA1c recommended.

src.q: Treatment with Glimepiride requires regular monitoring of glucose levels in blood and urine. In addition determination of the proportion of glycosylated haemoglobin is recommended.

items.t: Liver function and blood counts (especially white cells and platelets) regularly.

src.q: Regular hepatic and haematological monitoring (especially leucocytes and thrombocytes) are required during treatment with Glimepiride.

items.t: Review dose as control improves; reduce or stop if hypoglycaemia occurs.

src.q: To avoid hypoglycaemia timely dose reduction or cessation of therapy must therefore be considered.

items.t: Once daily shortly before or during a substantial breakfast (or the first main meal). Swallow with some liquid.

src.q: It is recommended that this dose be taken shortly before or during a substantial breakfast or - if none is taken - shortly before or during the first main meal.
Tablets should be swallowed whole with some liquid.

items.t: Take shortly before or with a meal and do not skip meals; know the signs of low blood sugar. Sugar treats it; artificial sweeteners do not.

src.q: Glimepiride must be taken shortly before or during a meal.
Symptoms can almost always be promptly controlled by immediate intake carbohydrates (sugar). Artificial sweeteners have no effect.

items.t: Take precautions to avoid low blood sugar when driving, especially with reduced awareness of warning signs or frequent episodes.

src.q: Patients should be advised to take precautions to avoid hypoglycaemia whilst driving.

items.t: Take other medicines only with your doctor's knowledge.

src.q: other medicinal products should only be taken with the knowledge (or at the prescription) of the doctor.

items.t: Short-acting vasodilator: relief of angina pectoris, prophylaxis of angina pectoris, and relief of acute spontaneous coronary artery spasm.

src.q: As a short-acting vasodilator Relief of angina pectoris Prophylaxis of angina pectoris Relief of acute spontaneous coronary artery spasm

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction or brand-specific prescribing statement in the two UK SPCs used (MHRA products); no MHRA Drug Safety Update or SPS advice found for glyceryl trinitrate tablets. No GTN sublingual tablet SmPC is listed on emc.

items.t: Acute attack: one tablet (0.5 mg) under the tongue when angina starts; may repeat every 5 minutes up to a total of three doses. If symptoms persist after three doses, seek prompt medical attention. Rest sitting down (risk of postural hypotension).

src.q: When angina starts, 0.5 mg glyceryl trinitrate (one tablet) should be taken and if symptoms do not resolve, may be repeated at five minute intervals for a total of three doses.
If symptoms have not resolved after a total of three doses, the patient should seek prompt medical attention.
The patient should preferably rest in the sitting position because of the risk of symptomatic postural hypotension.

items.t: Prophylaxis: one tablet (0.5 mg) before activity likely to bring on angina.

src.q: Glyceryl trinitrate, 0.5 mg (one tablet), may be used prior to activity which is likely to precipitate angina pectoris.

items.t: Elderly: hypotension and syncope are a particular problem; advise sitting down when taking it.

src.q: Hypotension and syncope can be a particular problem with use of nitrates in the elderly.
Patients should be advised to sit down whenever possible when taking sublingual glyceryl trinitrate.

items.t: No data on use in children; no child dose given.

src.q: Children No data are available on the use of glyceryl trinitrate in children.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to glyceryl trinitrate, other nitro compounds or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance, to other nitro compounds or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Patients taking PDE5 inhibitors (e.g. sildenafil, vardenafil, tadalafil).

src.q: Glyceryl trinitrate is contraindicated in patients taking phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors (e.g. sildenafil, vardenafil, tadalafil)

items.t: Angina caused by hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (may worsen outflow obstruction); possible raised intracranial pressure (e.g. cerebral haemorrhage, head trauma); marked anaemia; closed-angle glaucoma.

src.q: Glyceryl trinitrate is contraindicated in angina caused by hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy as it may exaggerate outflow obstruction.
Glyceryl trinitrate should not be used in patients with possible increased intracranial pressure (e.g. cerebral haemorrhage or head trauma). - Marked anaemia - Closed angle glaucoma

items.t: Use with caution where adequate preload is needed for cardiac output: acute circulatory shock (hypovolaemic, or cardiogenic with inadequate filling pressure), severe mitral stenosis, pericardial tamponade, constrictive pericarditis, orthostatic dysfunction.

src.q: Glyceryl trinitrate should be used with caution in patients in whom adequate preload is important for maintaining cardiac output (e.g. acute circulatory shock including hypovolemic shock or cardiogenic shock with inadequate diastolic filling pressures, severe mitral stenosis

items.t: Use with caution in severe hypotension (systolic below 90 mmHg) and in cerebrovascular disease (hypotension may precipitate symptoms).

src.q: Glyceryl trinitrate should be used with caution in patients with severe hypotension (systolic blood pressure below 90 mm Hg)
Glyceryl trinitrate should be used with caution in patients with cerebrovascular disease since symptoms may be precipitated by hypotension.

items.t: May worsen hypoxaemia in lung disease or cor pulmonale. Hypotension with bradycardia may occur after myocardial infarction. Be cautious in angina with moderate to severe valvular aortic stenosis.

src.q: Glyceryl trinitrate may worsen hypoxaemia in patients with lung disease or cor pulmonale.
Arterial hypotension with bradycardia may occur in patients with myocardial infarction
it seems prudent to be cautious in treating ambulant patients with the combination of angina and moderate to severe valvular aortic stenosis

items.t: Caution in severe hepatic or renal impairment, hypothyroidism, hypoxaemia, hypothermia, recent myocardial infarction and malnutrition.

src.q: Caution is necessary in patients with severe hepatic or renal impairment, hypothyroidism, hypoxaemia, hypothermia or a recent history of myocardial infaraction and malnutrition.

items.t: Contains lactose: patients with hereditary galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take it.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, the Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose- galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, vardenafil, tadalafil): potentiate the hypotensive effect. Contraindicated.

src.q: have been shown to potentiate the hypotensive effects of nitrates, and coadministration with glyceryl trinitrate is therefore contraindicated

items.t: Other hypotensive agents (vasodilators, antihypertensives, beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, neuroleptics, tricyclic antidepressants, sapropterin) may increase the hypotensive effect; alcohol may increase hypotension and syncope.

src.q: Treatment with other agents with hypotensive effects (e.g. vasodilators, antihypertensives, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers and neuroleptics, tricyclic antidepressants and sapropterin) may potentiate the hypotensive effect of glyceryl trinitrate.
the risk of hypotension and syncope with use of glyceryl trinitrate may be enhanced by alcohol

items.t: Medicines that cause dry mouth (anticholinergics, antimuscarinics, tricyclic antidepressants) may reduce the effect of sublingual nitrates.

src.q: There is a potential for drugs that cause dry mouth (eg anticholinergic, antimuscarinics, tricyclic antidepressants) to reduce the effectiveness of sublingual nitrates.

items.t: Long-acting nitrates: consider the possibility of tolerance to glyceryl trinitrate.

src.q: The possibility of tolerance to the effects of glyceryl trinitrate should be considered when used in conjunction with long-acting nitrate preparations.

items.t: Heparin: systemic nitrates may interfere with its anticoagulant effect; monitor anticoagulation early and often. Also: N-acetylcysteine (more vasodilatation), sublingual apomorphine (more hypotension), ergot alkaloids (oppose effect; higher dihydroergotamine exposure).

src.q: Early and frequent monitoring of anticoagulation is recommended when systemic nitrates and heparin are used in combination.
N-acetylcysteine may potentiate the vasodilator effects of glyceryl trinitrate.
An enhanced hypotensive effect with sublingual apomorphine may occur
Ergot alkaloids may oppose the coronary vasodilatation of nitrates.

items.t: Caution in severe renal impairment. No numeric threshold or dose adjustment given.

src.q: Caution is necessary in patients with severe hepatic or renal impairment

items.t: Caution in severe hepatic impairment. No dose adjustment given.

src.q: Caution is necessary in patients with severe hepatic or renal impairment

items.t: Animal studies show no harm, but human relevance is unknown. Consider use only if the expected benefit to the mother is greater than any possible risk to the fetus. No BUMPS leaflet for nitrates was found.

src.q: The administration of glyceryl trinitrate during pregnancy should only be considered if the expected benefit to the mother is greater than any possible risk to the foetus.

items.t: Not known whether it passes into milk; a risk to the infant cannot be excluded. Decide whether to stop breastfeeding or stop treatment, weighing benefits. No SPS breastfeeding page for oral nitrates was found.

src.q: It is unknown if glyceryl trinitrate or its metabolites are excreted in human milk. A risk to the suckling child cannot be excluded.
A decision must be made whether to discontinue/abstain from breast-feeding or to discontinue/abstain from glyceryl trinitrate therapy

items.t: Animal studies showed no harmful effects on fertility; relevance to humans unknown.

src.q: Fertility Animal studies did not indicate harmful effects with respect to fertility.

items.t: Headache and dizziness (can persist after the pain has gone; removing the tablet before it fully dissolves can reduce this); postural hypotension, especially at the start of treatment or after a dose increase; local burning or tingling under the tongue. The frequency table in the SPC PDF text could not be read reliably, so frequencies are not given here.

src.q: Particularly upon initiation of therapy and following an increase in dose.
because of the risk of symptomatic postural hypotension
Headache and dizziness, persisting after relief of angina may be minimised by removing the glyceryl trinitrate tablet before it has completely dissolved.
A local burning or tingling sensation may occur.

items.t: Hypotension from glyceryl trinitrate may cause cerebral ischaemia; circulatory collapse and syncope are listed.

src.q: Glyceryl trinitrate-induced hypotension may cause cerebral ischaemia.

items.t: Large doses may cause vomiting, cyanosis, restlessness, methaemoglobinaemia and impaired breathing. If angina is not relieved after three doses, seek prompt medical attention.

src.q: Large dose of glyceryl trinitrate may cause vomiting, cyanosis, restlessness, methaemoglobinaemia and impairment of respiration.
If angina symptoms have not resolved after a total of three doses, the patient should be instructed to seek prompt medical attention

monitoring.note: No laboratory or routine monitoring stated in the two UK SPCs used; no SPS monitoring page found for nitrates.

items.t: Place under the tongue and keep in the mouth until dissolved or discarded. A local burning or tingling sensation may occur.

src.q: Glyceryl trinitrate must be placed under the tongue (administered sublingually) and retained in the mouth until dissolved or discarded.

items.t: Keep in the original glass bottle with the cap tightly closed, below 25°C and protected from light; do not add cotton wool or other tablets. Discard 8 weeks after first opening.

src.q: Keep them in this. After use reclose the bottle cap tightly. Do not put cotton wool, other drugs, or anything else in the bottle with the tablets.
If you do not use the tablets within 8 weeks of first opening the bottle, obtain a fresh supply and return the old tablets to your pharmacist.

items.t: Sit down when taking a tablet. Take one tablet at the start of an attack; repeat every 5 minutes up to three tablets. If pain is not relieved after three tablets, get urgent medical help.

src.q: If symptoms have not resolved after a total of three doses, the patient should seek prompt medical attention.
Patients should be advised to sit down whenever possible when taking sublingual glyceryl trinitrate.

items.t: Never take sildenafil, tadalafil or vardenafil (erectile dysfunction medicines) with this medicine.

src.q: Glyceryl trinitrate is contraindicated in patients taking phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors (e.g. sildenafil, vardenafil, tadalafil)

items.t: A fresh tablet should give a slight burning feeling under the tongue; if not, get a new supply. Carry tablets in a bag or wallet, not close to the body.

src.q: A fresh tablet should produce a slight burning sensation when placed under the tongue; if this does not occur, obtain a fresh supply
If you need to carry them with you DO NOT carry them close to your body, rather in a purse, wallet or handbag.

items.t: Dizziness can occur; check you are not affected before driving. Alcohol makes this worse.

src.q: As Glyceryl trinitrate can cause dizziness, patients should make sure they are not affected before driving or operating machinery. This effect appears to be accentuated by alcohol.

restrictions.note: No UK product information found.

hepatic.note: No UK product information found.

items.t: Diabetes mellitus in patients who need insulin to maintain glucose homeostasis.

src.q: For the treatment of patients with diabetes mellitus who require insulin for the maintenance of glucose homeostasis.
For the treatment of patients with diabetes mellitus who require insulin for the maintenance of glucose homeostasis.
Actrapid is indicated for treatment of diabetes mellitus.
Insulatard is indicated for treatment of diabetes mellitus.

items.t: Prescribe by brand name and device; where a brand has several strengths or devices, also state strength and device (SPS). Any switch between brands or formulations should be under strict supervision; a dose change may be needed.

src.q: NICE guidance recommends insulins are prescribed by brand name.
It is important to ensure patients receive an administration device they have been trained to use.
Where a single insulin brand is available in multiple strengths or delivery devices, using only a brand name is insufficient.
Manufacturers advise any switch between brands or formulation of insulin should be done under strict supervision; a change in dose may be required.

items.t: Transfer to another type or brand of insulin only under strict medical supervision; changes in strength, brand, type (soluble, isophane, mixture), species or manufacture may need a dose change.

src.q: Transferring a patient to another type or brand of insulin should be done under strict medical supervision.
Transferring a patient to another type or brand of insulin should be done under strict medical supervision.

items.t: Dose is individual and set by the physician; usual total requirement 0.3 to 1.0 IU/kg/day (one UK SmPC). Soluble insulin: before a meal or snack, alone or with intermediate/long-acting insulin; follow each injection with a carbohydrate meal or snack within 30 minutes.

src.q: The dosage should be determined by the physician, according to the requirement of the patient.
The individual insulin requirement is usually between 0.3 and 1.0 international unit/kg/day.
It can be used alone or in combination with intermediate-acting or long-acting insulin before a meal or a snack.
An injection should be followed within 30 minutes by a meal or snack containing carbohydrates.

items.t: Isophane: once or several times daily as decided by the physician; alone, mixed with fast-acting insulin, or as basal insulin (evening and/or morning) with fast-acting insulin at meals. Usual total requirement 0.3 to 1.0 IU/kg/day.

src.q: The physician determines whether one or several daily injections are necessary. Insulatard may be used alone or mixed with fast-acting insulin.
In intensive insulin therapy the suspension may be used as basal insulin (evening and/or morning injection) with fast-acting insulin given at meals.
The individual insulin requirement is usually between 0.3 and 1.0 international unit/kg/day.

items.t: Biphasic 30/70: ready-made mixture so patients do not need to mix insulins; regimen based on individual metabolic needs, dose set by the physician.

src.q: Humulin Mixture formulation is a ready-made defined mixture of soluble and isophane insulin designed to avoid the need for the patient to mix insulin preparations.
A patient's treatment regimen should be based on their individual metabolic requirements.

items.t: Elderly: intensify glucose monitoring and adjust the dose individually.

src.q: In elderly patients, glucose monitoring should be intensified and the insulin dose adjusted on an individual basis.
In elderly patients, glucose monitoring should be intensified and the insulin dose adjusted on an individual basis.

items.t: UK SmPCs differ: one manufacturer's soluble and isophane SmPCs say they can be used in children and adolescents; another manufacturer's SmPCs (soluble, isophane and 30/70) state no paediatric data are available.

src.q: Actrapid can be used in children and adolescents.
Insulatard can be used in children and adolescents.
Paediatric population No data are available
Paediatric population No data are available

items.t: Hypoglycaemia (one manufacturer's SmPCs, section 4.3). The other manufacturer's SmPCs: must not be injected during hypoglycaemia or suspected hypoglycaemia (section 4.4).

src.q: Hypoglycaemia. Hypersensitivity to the active substance
Hypoglycaemia. Hypersensitivity to the active substance
In case of hypoglycaemia or if hypoglycaemia is suspected, Actrapid must not be injected.
In case of hypoglycaemia or if hypoglycaemia is suspected, Insulatard must not be injected.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to human insulin or any excipient (one manufacturer's SmPCs: unless as part of a desensitisation programme).

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1, unless used as part of a desensitisation programme.
Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Isophane and biphasic suspensions must never be given intravenously; only soluble insulin may be given IV.

src.q: Under no circumstances should any Humulin formulation other than Humulin S (Soluble) be given intravenously.
Insulin suspensions are never to be administered intravenously.

items.t: Hypoglycaemia warning symptoms may be less pronounced or different with much improved control, long-standing diabetes, diabetic neuropathy, after a change of insulin, or with medicines such as beta-blockers. Uncorrected hypo- or hyperglycaemia can cause loss of consciousness, coma or death.

src.q: Other conditions which may make the early warning symptoms of hypoglycaemia different or less pronounced include long duration of diabetes, diabetic nerve disease, or medications such as beta blockers.
Uncorrected hypoglycaemic and hyperglycaemic reactions can cause loss of consciousness, coma or death.

items.t: Inadequate doses or stopping treatment (especially insulin-dependent diabetes) can cause hyperglycaemia and potentially lethal diabetic ketoacidosis.

src.q: may lead to hyperglycaemia and diabetic ketoacidosis; conditions which are potentially lethal
Inadequate dosing or discontinuation of treatment, especially in type 1 diabetes, may lead to hyperglycaemia and diabetic ketoacidosis.

items.t: Insulin needs may change markedly with adrenal, pituitary or thyroid disease and with renal or hepatic impairment; they rise with illness (especially infection and fever) or emotional upset; change with exercise or diet.

src.q: Insulin requirements may change significantly in diseases of the adrenal, pituitary or thyroid glands and in the presence of renal or hepatic impairment.
Concomitant illness, especially infections and feverish conditions, usually increases the patient's insulin requirement.

items.t: Rotate injection sites (lipodystrophy, cutaneous amyloidosis); monitor blood glucose after a site change.

src.q: Patients must be instructed to perform continuous rotation of the injection site to reduce the risk of developing lipodystrophy and cutaneous amyloidosis.
A sudden change in the injection site to an unaffected area has been reported to result in hypoglycaemia.

items.t: With pioglitazone: watch for heart failure, weight gain and oedema; stop pioglitazone if cardiac symptoms worsen.

src.q: patients should be observed for signs and symptoms of heart failure, weight gain and oedema. Pioglitazone should be discontinued, if any deterioration in cardiac symptoms occurs.

items.t: Soluble insulin should not be used in pumps (one SmPC: risk of precipitation in pump catheters); suspensions are not for pumps.

src.q: Due to the risk of precipitation in pump catheters, Actrapid should not be used in insulin pumps for continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion.
Insulin suspensions are not to be used in insulin infusion pumps.

items.t: Check the insulin label before each injection. Seek advice before travel across time zones.

src.q: Patients must be instructed to always check the insulin label before each injection to avoid accidental mix-ups between Actrapid and other insulin products.
Before travelling between different time zones, the patient should seek the doctor's advice

items.t: May lower insulin requirement (hypoglycaemia): oral hypoglycaemics, salicylates (e.g. aspirin), MAOIs, captopril and enalapril, angiotensin II receptor blockers, non-selective beta-blockers, alcohol (one SmPC); oral antidiabetics, MAOIs, beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, salicylates, anabolic steroids, sulfonamides (other SmPC). One SmPC says the physician should be consulted and take interactions into account.

src.q: Insulin requirements may be reduced in the presence of substances with hypoglycaemic activity, such as oral hypoglycaemics (OHA), salicylates (for example, acetylsalicylic acid), certain antidepressants (monoamine oxidase inhibitors)
certain angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors (captopril, enalapril), angiotensin II receptor blockers, non-selective beta-blocking agents and alcohol
Oral antidiabetic medicinal products, monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOI), beta-blockers, angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, salicylates, anabolic steroids and sulfonamides.
The physician must therefore take possible interactions into account

items.t: May raise insulin requirement: glucocorticoids, thyroid hormones, growth hormone, danazol, beta2 sympathomimetics (e.g. salbutamol, terbutaline), thiazides; the other SmPC also lists oral contraceptives and sympathomimetics.

src.q: Insulin requirements may be increased by substances with hyperglycaemic activity, such as glucocorticoids, thyroid hormones, growth hormone, danazol, beta2- sympatomimetics (such as ritodrine, salbutamol, terbutaline), thiazides.
Oral contraceptives, thiazides, glucocorticoids, thyroid hormones, sympathomimetics, growth hormone and danazol.

items.t: Beta-blockers may mask hypoglycaemia symptoms. Octreotide/lanreotide may raise or lower requirement. Alcohol may intensify or reduce the effect.

src.q: Beta-blockers may mask the symptoms of hypoglycaemia.
Somatostatin analogues (octreotide, lanreotide) may both decrease or increase insulin dose requirements.
Alcohol may intensify or reduce the hypoglycaemic effect of insulin.

items.t: GLP-1 receptor agonists (MHRA): when one is added to insulin, an insulin dose reduction may be considered to lower hypoglycaemia risk, but reduce insulin stepwise with blood glucose self-monitoring; abrupt reduction or stopping of insulin has led to diabetic ketoacidosis. src.q: blood glucose self-monitoring is necessary when adjusting the dose of insulin, particularly when GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy is initiated and insulin is reduced

GLP-1 receptor agonists are not substitutes for insulin.

items.t: Renal impairment may reduce insulin requirement: intensify glucose monitoring and adjust the dose individually. No eGFR/CrCl thresholds given.

src.q: Renal or hepatic impairment may reduce the patient's insulin requirements. In patients with renal or hepatic impairment, glucose monitoring should be intensified and the human insulin dose adjusted on an individual basis.
in the presence of renal or hepatic impairment

items.t: Hepatic impairment may reduce insulin requirement: intensify glucose monitoring and adjust the dose individually.

src.q: In patients with renal or hepatic impairment, glucose monitoring should be intensified and the human insulin dose adjusted on an individual basis.

items.t: No restriction on insulin in pregnancy (insulin does not cross the placenta); poorly controlled diabetes (hypo- or hyperglycaemia) raises the risk of malformation and death in utero. Keep good control and monitor glucose and general health closely; requirements usually fall in the first trimester, rise in the second and third, and fall quickly after delivery.

src.q: There are no restrictions on treatment of diabetes with insulin during pregnancy, as insulin does not pass the placental barrier.
increase the risk of malformations and death in utero
Careful monitoring of glucose control, as well as general health, is essential in pregnant patients with diabetes.
Insulin requirements usually fall during the first trimester and increase during the second and third trimesters.

items.t: UKTIS/BUMPS: insulin can be used in pregnancy to treat diabetes; there are no known risks to the baby. Insulin around delivery can cause short-lived low blood glucose in the newborn, which is checked after birth.

src.q: Insulin can be used in pregnancy to treat diabetes.
There are no known risks to your baby from using insulin in pregnancy.
Insulin use around the time of delivery can lead to your baby having low blood sugar for a short period after birth.

items.t: No restriction during breastfeeding; insulin presents no risk to the baby. Dose and/or diet may need adjusting.

src.q: There is no restriction on treatment with Actrapid during breast-feeding. Insulin treatment of the nursing mother presents no risk to the baby.

items.t: No adverse effects on fertility in animal studies.

items.t: Hypoglycaemia: the most frequent adverse effect (very common in one SmPC).

src.q: Hypoglycaemia is the most frequent undesirable effect of insulin therapy
Very common - Hypoglycaemia

items.t: Local injection-site allergy (redness, swelling, itching) is common and usually settles in days to weeks.

items.t: Uncommon: lipodystrophy, injection-site reactions, oedema, urticaria/rash, refraction disorders, painful peripheral neuropathy. Not known: cutaneous amyloidosis.

Uncommon - Injection site reactions Uncommon - Oedema

items.t: Severe hypoglycaemia can cause loss of consciousness, convulsions or death. Mild: oral glucose or sugar. Moderately severe: glucagon IM/SC then oral carbohydrate. No response to glucagon (or not available): IV glucose. Give a meal on recovery; observe, as hypoglycaemia may recur.

src.q: Severe hypoglycaemia may lead to loss of consciousness, and in extreme cases, death.

Patients who fail to respond to glucagon must be given glucose solution intravenously.

items.t: Systemic allergy is very rare but may be life-threatening (whole-body rash, breathlessness, wheeze, low blood pressure, fast pulse, sweating); treat immediately; a change of insulin or desensitisation may be needed.

src.q: Systemic allergy, which is very rare (< 1/10,000) but potentially more serious, is a generalised allergy to insulin.
In the rare event of a severe allergy to Humulin, treatment is required immediately. A change of insulin or desensitisation may be required.

items.t: Blood glucose monitoring to achieve good control; close monitoring when transferring from another insulin and in the first weeks after.

src.q: Blood glucose monitoring is recommended to achieve optimal glycaemic control.
Close glucose monitoring is recommended during the transfer and in the initial weeks thereafter

items.t: Intravenous soluble insulin: blood glucose monitoring is necessary during the infusion.

src.q: Monitoring of blood glucose is necessary during the insulin infusion.

items.t: MHRA (high-strength, combination and biosimilar insulins): monitor glucose closely after starting a new insulin product and in the following weeks; doses and timing of other insulins and antidiabetic treatment may need adjusting.

src.q: Monitor glucose levels closely after starting a new treatment and in the following weeks.
You may need to adjust doses and timing of concurrent rapid acting or short acting insulin products and other antidiabetic treatments.

items.t: Subcutaneous injection (upper arm, thigh, buttock or abdomen); intramuscular is possible but not recommended. Rotate sites; do not massage. Use insulin syringes with the matching unit scale.

src.q: should be given by subcutaneous injection but may, although not recommended, also be given by intramuscular injection
Subcutaneous administration should be in the upper arms, thighs, buttocks or abdomen.
Actrapid vials are for use with insulin syringes with a corresponding unit scale.

items.t: Soluble insulin may be given intravenously by healthcare professionals: 0.05 to 1.0 IU/mL in sodium chloride 0.9%, glucose 5% or glucose 10% with 40 mmol/L potassium chloride (polypropylene bags), stable 24 hours at room temperature.

src.q: It may also be administered intravenously.

infusion systems with Actrapid at concentrations from 0.05 international unit/ml to 1.0 international unit/ml human insulin

items.t: Isophane may be mixed with soluble insulin in the syringe; always mix in the same order. Thigh injection gives slower, less variable absorption of isophane.

src.q: Humulin I (Isophane) may be administered in combination with Humulin S (Soluble).
When two types of insulin are mixed always mix the insulin medicinal products in the same sequence.
Subcutaneous injection into the thigh results in a slower and less variable absorption compared to the other injection sites.

items.t: Storage: unopened vials in a refrigerator (2 to 8°C), not frozen. In use: 28 days below 30°C (one manufacturer) or up to 6 weeks below 25°C, not refrigerated (other manufacturer).

src.q: Unopened vials Store in a refrigerator
After first use 28 days.

src.q: An injection should be followed within 30 minutes by a meal or snack containing carbohydrates.

src.q: Patients should be advised to take precautions to avoid hypoglycaemia whilst driving

items.t: MHRA: cutaneous amyloidosis can occur at insulin injection sites and affect glycaemic control. Remind patients to rotate sites within the same body region; consider amyloidosis when a patient has lumps at injection sites; advise patients to contact their doctor before moving away from a lumpy area (a sudden change may cause hypoglycaemia) and to monitor blood glucose after a change of site.

src.q: remind patients to rotate injection sites within the same body region to reduce or prevent the risk of cutaneous amyloidosis and other skin reactions
consider cutaneous amyloidosis as a differential diagnosis to lipodystrophy when a patient presents with subcutaneous lumps at an insulin injection site
before changing injection site since a sudden change may result in hypoglycaemia
to monitor carefully blood glucose after a change in injection site

items.t: Adults: oedema of cardiac or renal origin; oedema of hepatic origin (usually with a potassium-sparing diuretic); arterial hypertension.

src.q: Oedemas of cardiac or renal origin. Oedemas of hepatic origin, usually in combination with a potassium-sparing diuretic. Arterial hypertension.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restrictions stated in the UK SPC.

items.t: 12.5 or 25 mg daily (single dose or two divided doses, with or without food). Full effect in 3-4 weeks. If 25 mg/day is not enough, add another antihypertensive rather than increasing the dose.
