If blood pressure is not sufficiently lowered with a dose of 25 mg/day, combined treatment with another antihypertensive drug is recommended.
For a given dose, the maximum effect is achieved within 3 to 4 weeks.
The daily dose of Hydrochlorothiazide can be given as a single dose or divided over two doses, with or without food.

items.t: Start 50-100 mg/day (possibly 200 mg/day); titrate to the lowest effective dose for limited periods. Maintenance 25-50 mg daily or on alternate days.

src.q: The starting dose is 50 to 100 mg/day, possibly 200 mg/day.
The maintenance dose is 25 mg to 50 mg/day or every other day.
The lowest effective dose should be identified by titration and only administered for limited periods.

items.t: Correct sodium and/or volume depletion before combining with an ACE inhibitor, angiotensin II antagonist or direct renin inhibitor; otherwise start under close medical supervision. After long-term use, withdraw gradually.

src.q: Sodium depletion and / or volume must be corrected before using hydrochlorothiazide in combination with an ACE inhibitor, an antagonist of angiotensin II or a direct renin inhibitor.
After long-term treatment, therapy with hydrochlorothiazide should be discontinued gradually.
Otherwise, treatment should be initiated under close medical supervision.

items.t: Elderly: take possible reduced renal function into account.

src.q: In the treatment of elderly patients, attention should be paid to possible restrictions to renal function.

items.t: No experience in children and adolescents; should not be used.

src.q: There is no experience in children and adolescents. Therefore, hydrochlorothiazide should not be used in children and adolescents.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to hydrochlorothiazide or any excipient; anuria; severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance less than 30 ml/min).

src.q: Hypersensitivity to hydrochlorothiazide or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1. Anuria. Severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance less than 30 ml/min).

items.t: Generally not recommended with bilateral renal artery stenosis, a single functioning kidney, or hypokalaemia.

src.q: Hydrochlorothiazide is generally not recommended in patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis or a single functioning kidney or with hypokalaemia.

items.t: Non-melanoma skin cancer (basal and squamous cell): risk rises with cumulative dose. Tell patients the risk, advise regular skin checks and sun/UV protection; examine suspicious lesions; reconsider use after previous skin cancer (SPC and MHRA).

src.q: An increased risk of non-melanoma skin cancer (NMSC) [basal cell carcinoma (BCC) and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)] with increasing cumulative dose of hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) exposure has been observed
reconsider the use of hydrochlorothiazide in patients who have had previous skin cancer
Suspicious skin lesions should be promptly examined

items.t: Electrolytes: hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia (major arrhythmia risk with long QT, heart disease, digitalis). Start only after correcting hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia, and after normalising sodium/volume depletion.

src.q: Treatment with thiazide diuretics should only be started after correction of hypokalaemia and concurrently occurring existing hypomagnesemia.
Thiazides should be only used after normalization of any existing sodium and / or volume depletion.

items.t: Hypercalcaemia: use with caution and only after correction; stop if hypercalcaemia develops. Stop before parathyroid function tests.

src.q: Hydrochlorothiazide should be used with caution in patients with hypercalcemia and should be administered only after correction of any pre- existing hypercalcemia.
Hydrochlorothiazide should be discontinued if hypercalcemia occurs during treatment.
Thiazides should be discontinued before carrying out parathyroid function tests.

items.t: Severe liver damage: use with caution (electrolyte imbalance, hepatic encephalopathy, hepatorenal syndrome in cirrhotic ascites).

src.q: Thiazides, like other diuretics may induce electrolyte imbalance, hepatic encephalopathy or hepatorenal syndrome when used to treat cirrhotic ascites.
Hydrochlorothiazide should be used with caution particularly in patients with severe liver damage.

items.t: Uric acid may rise and trigger gout; glucose tolerance may fall and lipids rise (antidiabetic dose changes may be needed).

src.q: This can trigger attacks of gout in susceptible patients.
In diabetic patient dosage adjustments of insulin or oral hypoglycaemic agents may be required.

items.t: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (very rare): withdraw if suspected; do not give again to anyone who had ARDS after hydrochlorothiazide.

src.q: If diagnosis of ARDS is suspected, Hydrochlorothiazide should be withdrawn and appropriate treatment given.
Hydrochlorothiazide should not be administered to patients who previously experienced ARDS following hydrochlorothiazide intake.

items.t: Choroidal effusion, acute myopia and acute angle-closure glaucoma: stop as soon as possible. Risk factors include sulphonamide or penicillin allergy.

src.q: The primary treatment is to discontinue hydrochlorothiazide as soon as possible.
Risk factors for developing acute angle-closure glaucoma include a history of sulphonamide or penicillin allergy.

items.t: Systemic lupus erythematosus may be exacerbated or activated. Photosensitivity: stop treatment if it occurs.

src.q: exacerbation or activation of systemic lupus erythematosus has been reported with thiazide diuretics, including hydrochlorothiazide.
If a photosensitivity reaction occurs treatment should be discontinued.

items.t: Sulfonamide: cross-reactivity with sulfonamide antibacterials is theoretical and not clinically confirmed (SPC); SPS also states it is not expected.

src.q: The possibility of cross-reactivity especially with other antibacterials including sulfonamides is theoretical and not clinically confirmed.
Cross-reactivity between antibiotic and non-antibiotic sulfonamides is not expected, including in people who had a life-threatening reaction to a sulfonamide.

items.t: Lactose: patients with galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, the Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption syndrome should not take this medicine.

items.t: Lithium: not recommended (raised lithium, toxicity). If essential, monitor lithium closely and adjust its dose.

src.q: Concomitant use not recommended: Lithium: Increased serum lithium levels with signs of lithium overdose
If this combination proves essential, serum lithium levels should be closely monitored and the lithium dose should be adjusted.

items.t: Medicines that may cause torsades de pointes (e.g. amiodarone, sotalol, citalopram, escitalopram, domperidone, erythromycin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, haloperidol, methadone): correct hypokalaemia first; clinical, electrolyte and ECG monitoring.

src.q: Increased risk of ventricular arrhythmias, especially torsades de pointes. Correct any hypokalaemia before administering the medicine and perform clinical, electrolyte and electrocardiographic monitoring.

items.t: NSAIDs, and aspirin at analgesic/antipyretic doses (500 mg or more per dose) or anti-inflammatory doses (1 g or more per dose and/or 3 g or more daily): acute renal failure in at-risk (elderly/dehydrated) patients and reduced antihypertensive effect. Hydrate and monitor renal function at the start.

src.q: Acute renal failure in at risk patients (elderly and / or dehydrated)
For anti-inflammatory doses of acetylsalicylic acid (≥1 g per dose and / or ≥3 g daily) or for analgesic or antipyretic doses (≥500 mg per dose and / or <3 g per day)
Hydrate the patient and monitor renal function at start of treatment.

items.t: Hyponatraemia risk adds up with other diuretics, desmopressin, SSRIs, carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine. Carbamazepine: monitor; if possible use another class of diuretic.

src.q: These are diuretics, desmopressin, serotonin reuptake inhibiting antidepressants, carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine. The combination of these drugs increase the risk of hyponatremia.
Carbamazepine Risk of symptomatic hyponatraemia. Clinical and biological monitoring. If possible, use another class of diuretic.

items.t: ACE inhibitors / angiotensin II antagonists: sudden hypotension and/or acute renal failure if sodium-depleted. Stop the diuretic first or start at a low dose; monitor creatinine in the first weeks.

src.q: Risk of sudden hypotension and / or acute renal failure when starting or increasing the dose of an ACE inhibitor or an angiotensin II antagonist when there is pre-existing sodium depletion.
renal function (serum creatinine) should be monitored during the first weeks of treatment with ACE inhibitors or angiotensin II antagonists.

items.t: Other potassium-lowering medicines (loop diuretics, stimulant laxatives, glucocorticoids): more hypokalaemia; monitor and correct potassium. Potassium-sparing diuretics: hypo- or hyperkalaemia possible; monitor potassium.

src.q: These are potassium lowering diuretics, alone or combined; stimulant laxatives; glucocorticoids
Monitor serum potassium, possibly ECG and, if necessary, reconsider the treatment.

items.t: Other antihypertensives: reducing the dose is advised when combined, at least initially. Orthostatic hypotension: alpha-blockers (including tamsulosin), nitrates, PDE5 inhibitors, tricyclic antidepressants. Calcium: hypercalcaemia risk. Digitalis: hypokalaemia increases its toxicity (correct potassium; clinical, electrolyte and ECG monitoring). Iodinated contrast: rehydrate first. Ciclosporin: creatinine may rise. Chelating resins: separate doses by more than 2 hours if possible.

src.q: Alpha-blockers for urological problems (alfuzosin, doxazosin, prazosin, silodosin, tamsulosin, terazosin) Hypotensive effect increased.
Especially nitrates, phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors, alpha blockers for urological problems, of tricyclic antidepressants and phenothiazines
Calcium Risk of hypercalcaemia due to reduced urinary calcium excretion.

Risk of increased creatinine without changes in ciclosporin blood levels
with an interval of more than 2 hours, if possible

src.q: The use of hydrochlorothiazide during breast-feeding is not recommended. If hydrochlorothiazide is indicated, the doses should be as low as possible.

src.q: There are no human fertility data for hydrochlorothiazide.

can be given as a single dose or divided over two doses, with or without food.

items.t: Pharmacy-sale SmPC: should not be used in pregnancy without medical advice.

src.q: This product should not be used in pregnancy without medical advice.

items.t: BUMPS: topical corticosteroids (hydrocortisone is named) can be used in pregnancy; no known risks.

src.q: Topical corticosteroids can be used in pregnancy.
There are no known risks.

items.t: Pharmacy-sale SmPC: should not be used while breastfeeding unless recommended by a healthcare professional; a risk to the infant cannot be excluded.

src.q: This product should not be used whilst breast-feeding unless recommended by a health care professional.
A risk to new-borns/infants cannot be excluded.

items.t: SPS: hydrocortisone applied to the skin can be used during breastfeeding (low potency). Avoid infant contact with treated skin; if applied to the breast, wipe off with warm water before feeds. Large areas for long periods may need infant monitoring of feeding, growth and weight.

src.q: When applied to the skin, used rectally or for use in the ear, hydrocortisone can be used during breastfeeding.
This should be removed with warm water before breastfeeding, and be reapplied after feeding.

items.t: Fertility: no known effects (pharmacy-sale SmPC).

src.q: Fertility No known effects.

items.t: No common or very common effects are listed. Reported effects (frequency not known) include skin atrophy, telangiectasia, striae, acne, rosacea, pigmentation changes and hypertrichosis. Blurred vision is uncommon in the pharmacy-sale SmPC (frequency not known in the prescription SmPC).

src.q: Skin atrophy, telangiectasia, skin striae, acne, rosacea, pigmentation disorder, hypertrichosis
Eye Disorders Uncommon Vision, blurred
Eye disorders Not known (cannot be estimated from the available data): Vision, blurred

items.t: Hypersensitivity (including allergic contact dermatitis) or worsening of the condition: stop treatment immediately.

src.q: If any signs of hypersensitivity, including allergic contact dermatitis or worsening of the original condition appear, treatment should be immediately discontinued.

items.t: Topical steroid withdrawal reactions after stopping: redness spreading beyond the treated area, burning or stinging, itch, peeling, oozing pustules.

src.q: Withdrawal reactions - redness of the skin which may extend to areas beyond the initial affected area, burning or stinging sensation, itch, skin peeling, oozing pustules.

items.t: Systemic absorption from skin folds or the nappy area can cause hypercorticism and HPA-axis suppression with prolonged use, more likely in infants and children and under occlusion. MHRA: adrenal suppression (low blood pressure, dizziness, fainting) is life-threatening and needs urgent treatment; stopping suddenly is dangerous.

src.q: Sufficient systemic absorption may also occur in such sites to produce the features of hypercorticism and suppression of the HPA axis after prolonged treatment.
This is a serious, life-threatening condition that needs urgent treatment.
Stopping the topical steroid suddenly is dangerous if there is adrenal suppression

items.t: If the condition does not improve, the patient should see a doctor.

src.q: If the condition does not improve consult your doctor.

items.t: Be vigilant for topical steroid withdrawal reactions; for long-term users consider reducing potency or frequency (or both).

src.q: for patients currently on long-term topical corticosteroid treatment, consider reducing potency or frequency of application (or both)
be vigilant for the signs and symptoms of topical steroid withdrawal reactions

items.t: Stop if hypersensitivity or worsening occurs; withdraw the steroid if infection spreads.

src.q: treatment should be immediately discontinued
Any spread of infection requires withdrawal of topical corticosteroid therapy

items.t: For use on the skin only. Apply sparingly to the affected area and massage in gently, after gently cleansing the area.

src.q: Massage gently into the skin.
after gently cleansing the area

items.t: The cream often suits moist or weeping skin; an ointment often suits dry, lichenified or scaly lesions.

src.q: Hydrocortisone cream is often appropriate for moist or weeping surfaces, and Hydrocortisone ointment for dry-lichenified or scaly lesions

items.t: Explain how much to apply, how often, where, and when to stop; get advice before using on a new body area.

src.q: when prescribing or dispensing topical steroids, advise on the amount of product to apply, how often, where to apply it and when to stop treatment
seek medical advice before using a topical corticosteroid on a new body area

items.t: If the skin worsens within 2 weeks of stopping, do not restart without consulting the doctor (unless already advised).

src.q: if your skin worsens within 2 weeks of stopping a topical corticosteroid, do not start treatment again without consulting your doctor

items.t: Do not smoke or go near naked flames: clothing, bedding and dressings with cream on them burn more easily; washing reduces but does not remove build-up.

src.q: Instruct patients not to smoke or go near naked flames - risk of severe burns.
Washing clothing and bedding may reduce product build-up but not totally remove it.

items.t: Adults: rheumatoid arthritis, discoid and systemic lupus erythematosus, and skin conditions caused or aggravated by sunlight.

src.q: Treatment of rheumatoid arthritis, discoid and systemic lupus erythematosus, and dermatological conditions caused or aggravated by sunlight.

items.t: Children: juvenile idiopathic arthritis (with other therapies), discoid and systemic lupus erythematosus.

src.q: Treatment of juvenile idiopathic arthritis (in combination with other therapies), discoid and systemic lupus erythematosus.

items.t: Prescriber is responsible for referring patients for retinal monitoring and acting on results (SPS, RCOphth).

src.q: It is the prescriber's responsibility to refer patients for monitoring.
It is the prescribing doctor's responsibility to ensure their patients are adequately monitored and to act on the results of monitoring.

items.t: Adults (including elderly): lowest effective dose; NOT more than 6.5 mg/kg/day by IDEAL (not actual) body weight; this will be 200 mg or 400 mg per day.

src.q: This dose should not exceed 6.5 mg/kg/day (calculated from ideal body weight and not actual body weight) and will be either 200 mg or 400 mg per day.

items.t: If 400 mg daily is suitable: start 400 mg daily in divided doses; reduce to 200 mg when no further improvement; increase maintenance back to 400 mg daily if response lessens.

src.q: In patients able to receive 400 mg daily: Initially 400 mg daily in divided doses. The dose can be reduced to 200 mg when no further improvement is evident. The maintenance dose should be increased to 400 mg daily if the response lessens.

items.t: Rheumatic disease: stop if no improvement by 6 months. Light-sensitive diseases: give only during periods of maximum light exposure.

src.q: For rheumatic disease treatment should be discontinued if there is no improvement by 6 months.
In light-sensitive diseases, treatment should only be given during periods of maximum exposure to light.

items.t: RCOphth retinopathy guidance (differs from SmPC): ideally keep the dose below 5 mg/kg/day ("5 x 5 rule"), calculated by ABSOLUTE (actual) body weight - the SmPC maximum of 6.5 mg/kg/day uses IDEAL body weight. SPS also uses actual body weight for its over 5 mg/kg/day risk factor.

src.q: A useful aide memoir for these guidelines for hydroxychloroquine is the 5 x 5 rule (ideally keep dosage < 5mg/kg/day and monitor after five years of drug use).
ensuring safe drug dosing according to absolute body weight
Whilst patients taking >5mg/kg of absolute body weight were shown by this data to be in the highest risk group

items.t: Lowest effective dose, not more than 6.5 mg/kg/day by ideal body weight. The 200 mg tablet is not suitable for children with ideal body weight under 31 kg.

src.q: The minimum effective dose should be employed and should not exceed 6.5 mg/kg/day based on ideal body weight. The 200 mg tablet is therefore not suitable for use in children with an ideal body weight of less than 31 kg.

items.t: Small children are particularly sensitive to 4-aminoquinoline toxicity: keep tablets out of reach of children.

src.q: Small children are particularly sensitive to the toxic effects of 4-aminoquinolines; therefore patients should be warned to keep hydroxychloroquine sulfate out of the reach of children.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to 4-aminoquinoline compounds or any excipient.

src.q: Known hypersensitivity to 4-aminoquinoline compounds or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Pre-existing maculopathy of the eye.

src.q: Pre-existing maculopathy of the eye.

items.t: Retinopathy: risk rises above the recommended maximum dose. Stop immediately for pigmentary abnormality, visual field defect or other unexplained abnormality.

src.q: The administration of doses in excess of the recommended maximum is likely to increase the risk of retinopathy, and accelerate its onset.

Hydroxychloroquine sulfate should be discontinued immediately in any patient who develops a pigmentary abnormality, visual field defect, or any other abnormality not explainable by difficulty in accommodation or presence of corneal opacities.

items.t: QT prolongation: use with caution in congenital/acquired QT prolongation or risk factors (heart failure, MI, bradycardia under 50 bpm, ventricular dysrhythmias, uncorrected hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia, QT-prolonging drugs). Do not exceed the recommended dose.

src.q: Hydroxychloroquine should be used with caution in patients with congenital or documented acquired QT prolongation and/or known risk factors for prolongation of the QT interval
uncorrected hypokalemia and/or hypomagnesemia

items.t: Hypoglycaemia: severe hypoglycaemia (including loss of consciousness) reported with or without antidiabetic medicines. Warn patients; check blood glucose and review treatment if symptoms.

src.q: Hydroxychloroquine has been shown to cause severe hypoglycaemia including loss of consciousness that could be life threatening in patients treated with and without antidiabetic medications.
Patients presenting with clinical symptoms suggestive of hypoglycaemia during treatment with hydroxychloroquine should have their blood glucose level checked and treatment reviewed as necessary.

items.t: Psychiatric reactions and suicidal behaviour: typically in the first month, also in people with no psychiatric history. MHRA: be vigilant, especially in the first month.

src.q: Psychiatric side effects typically occur within the first month after the start of treatment with hydroxychloroquine and have been reported also in patients with no prior history of psychiatric disorders.
be vigilant for psychiatric reactions associated with hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine, especially in the first month of treatment

items.t: Cardiomyopathy (sometimes fatal): monitor for signs; stop if it develops.

src.q: Clinical monitoring for signs and symptoms of cardiomyopathy is advised and hydroxychloroquine sulfate should be discontinued if cardiomyopathy develops.

items.t: Other cautions: G6PD deficiency, quinine sensitivity, porphyria cutanea tarda (may be exacerbated), psoriasis (more skin reactions), hepatic or renal disease, severe GI, neurological or blood disorders.

src.q: Caution should also be applied when it is used in the following: patients with a sensitivity to quinine, those with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, those with porphyria cutanea tarda which can be exacerbated by hydroxychloroquine and in patients with psoriasis
patients with severe gastrointestinal, neurological or blood disorders.

items.t: Liver injury (including fulminant failure) reported; check LFTs if symptoms. Hepatitis B reactivation with other immunosuppressants.

src.q: Prompt clinical evaluation and measurement of liver function tests should be performed in patients who report symptoms that may indicate liver injury.

items.t: Severe skin reactions (DRESS, AGEP, SJS, TEN): stop at once.

src.q: If signs and symptoms suggestive of severe skin reactions appear, hydroxychloroquine should be withdrawn at once and alternative therapy should be considered.

items.t: Contains lactose.

src.q: Hydroxychloroquine sulfate contains lactose monohydrate.

items.t: Macrolides (azithromycin, clarithromycin, erythromycin): increased cardiovascular events and mortality seen with azithromycin; carefully weigh benefit and risk; caution in cardiac risk factors (MHRA).

src.q: Similar careful consideration of the balance of benefits and risks should also be undertaken before prescribing hydroxychloroquine for any patients taking other macrolide antibiotics, such as clarithromycin or erythromycin
if there is a clinical need to prescribe systemic macrolide antibiotics with hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine, use caution in patients with risk factors for cardiac events

items.t: Other QT-prolonging medicines: use with caution (ventricular arrhythmia risk).

src.q: Hydroxychloroquine should be used with caution in patients receiving drugs known to prolong the QT interval

items.t: Insulin and antidiabetic medicines: effect may be enhanced; dose reduction may be needed.

src.q: As hydroxychloroquine may enhance the effects of a hypoglycaemic treatment, a decrease in doses of insulin or anti-diabetic drugs may be required.

items.t: Antacids: may reduce absorption; separate doses by 4 hours.

src.q: antacids may reduce absorption of hydroxychloroquine so it is advised that a 4 hour interval be observed between hydroxychloroquine sulfate and antacid dosing.

items.t: Tamoxifen (retinal toxicity): not recommended. Digoxin: monitor levels. Halofantrine: do not give together. Mefloquine/antiepileptics: convulsion threshold. Ciclosporin levels may rise.

src.q: Concomitant use of drugs known to induce retinal toxicity, e.g. tamoxifen and hydroxychloroquine sulfate, is not recommended (see section 4.4).
Halofantrine should not be administered with hydroxychloroquine.

items.t: SmPC: caution in renal disease; in severely compromised renal function measure plasma levels and adjust dose (no threshold given).

src.q: Estimation of plasma hydroxychloroquine levels should be undertaken in patients with severely compromised renal or hepatic function and dosage adjusted accordingly.

items.t: RCOphth/SPS: eGFR under 60 ml/min/1.73m2 is a retinopathy risk factor; retinal monitoring can start after 1 year instead of 5.

src.q: Impaired renal function (eGFR <60ml/min/1.73m2)
renal insufficiency (eGFR less than 60ml/min/1.73m2)

items.t: Caution in hepatic disease; in severely compromised hepatic function measure plasma levels and adjust dose. Serious drug-induced liver injury reported.

src.q: patients with hepatic or renal disease, and in those taking drugs known to affect those organs.
Estimation of plasma hydroxychloroquine levels should be undertaken in patients with severely compromised renal or hepatic function and dosage adjusted accordingly.

items.t: SmPC: avoid unless the physician judges benefit outweighs hazard; use the lowest effective dose. Small increase in malformation risk at 400 mg/day or more in the first trimester (RR 1.33).

src.q: Hydroxychloroquine sulfate should be avoided in pregnancy except when, in the judgement of the physician, the individual potential benefits outweigh the potential hazards.
For a daily dose of ≥ 400 mg the RR was 1.33 (95% CI, 1.08 - 1.65).

items.t: BUMPS (UKTIS): can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a specialist; no concerns that it harms the baby; often the safest option to keep autoimmune disease controlled. (More permissive than the SmPC.)

src.q: Hydroxychloroquine can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a specialist.
There are no concerns that taking hydroxychloroquine in pregnancy can harm your baby.

items.t: Passes into breast milk (under 2% of maternal dose); very limited long-term infant data. Prescriber should weigh risks and benefits by indication and duration. No SPS breastfeeding page found.

src.q: Hydroxychloroquine is excreted in breast milk (less than 2% of the maternal dose after bodyweight correction).
the prescriber should assess the potential risks and benefits of use during breastfeeding, according to indication and duration of treatment.

items.t: No human fertility data; chloroquine impaired male fertility in animals. BUMPS: no evidence that use by the father harms the baby.

src.q: Animal studies showed an impairment of male fertility for chloroquine (see section 5.3). There are no data in humans.
There is currently no evidence that hydroxychloroquine used by the father can harm your baby through effects on the sperm.

items.t: Very common: abdominal pain, nausea. Common: diarrhoea, vomiting, anorexia, affect lability, headache, blurred vision (accommodation; dose-dependent, reversible), rash, pruritus.

src.q: Very common: abdominal pain, nausea Common: diarrhoea, vomiting
Common: blurring of vision due to a disturbance of accommodation which is dose dependent and reversible
Common: skin rash, pruritus

items.t: Retinopathy/maculopathy (may be irreversible): stop and refer.

src.q: cases of maculopathies and macular degeneration have been reported (the onset ranging from 3 months to several years of exposure to hydroxychloroquine) and may be irreversible.

items.t: QT prolongation and arrhythmia (torsade de pointes); cardiomyopathy with heart failure. MHRA: tell patients to seek urgent help for palpitations, fainting, chest pain or unexplained breathlessness.

src.q: QT interval prolongation in patients with specific risk factors, which may lead to arrhythmia (torsade de pointes, ventricular tachycardia)
seek urgent medical help if you have any signs of problems with your heart (for example, palpitations, fainting, chest pain, or unexplained breathlessness)

items.t: Suicidal behaviour, psychosis, depression; severe hypoglycaemia; bone marrow depression; DILI; SCARs; myopathy/neuromyopathy (stop if weakness).

src.q: Not known: suicidal behaviour, psychosis, depression, hallucinations, anxiety, agitation, confusion, delusions, mania and sleep disorders.
If weakness occurs, the drug should be withdrawn (see section 4.8).

items.t: SPS baseline: albumin, ALT or AST, blood pressure, FBC, height, weight, serum creatinine/CrCl or calculated GFR, vaccination status. Hepatitis B/C and HIV if at risk.

src.q: Before starting Required Baseline Albumin ALT or AST Blood pressure Full blood count Height Serum creatinine (for creatinine clearance) or Calculated glomerular filtration rate Weight Vaccination status

items.t: Eye baseline - SOURCES DIFFER: SmPC says eye examination before starting and at least every 12 months; SPS and RCOphth say baseline eye testing is no longer recommended.

src.q: All patients should have an ophthalmological examination before initiating treatment with hydroxychloroquine sulfate. Thereafter, ophthalmological examinations must be repeated at least every 12 months.
Before starting hydroxychloroquine, ophthalmological examination is not currently recommended .
Baseline testing for new initiators of hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine is no longer recommended.

items.t: Retinal monitoring (RCOphth): annual from 5 years of use; annual from 1 year if risk factors (tamoxifen, eGFR under 60, dose over 5 mg/kg/day). SD-OCT plus fundus autofluorescence.

src.q: All individuals who have taken hydroxychloroquine for greater than five years should receive annual monitoring for retinopathy.

Concomitant tamoxifen use - Impaired renal function (eGFR <60ml/min/1.73m2) - Dose of hydroxychloroquine greater than 5mg per kg per day - Chloroquine use Monitoring begins after 1 year of drug therapy

items.t: SmPC: eye examinations should be more frequent and adapted to the patient if the daily dose exceeds 6.5 mg/kg lean body weight, renal insufficiency, visual acuity below 6/8, age above 65 years, cumulative dose more than 200 g, or tamoxifen use.

src.q: This examination should be more frequent and adapted to the patient in the following situations
visual acuity below 6/8
age above 65 years
cumulative dose more than 200 g

items.t: SPS: risk-factor dose threshold is over 5 mg/kg/day by ACTUAL body weight (SmPC maximum uses IDEAL body weight).

src.q: very high dose of drug therapy (hydroxychloroquine dose over 5mg per kg per day- based on actual body weight)

items.t: Long-term: periodic FBC; periodic skeletal muscle function and tendon reflexes (SmPC). SPS: periodically albumin, ALT/AST, eGFR, weight.

src.q: Patients on long-term therapy should have periodic full blood counts, and hydroxychloroquine should be discontinued if abnormalities develop (see section 4.8).
All patients on long-term therapy should undergo periodic examination of skeletal muscle function and tendon reflexes.

items.t: Stop for: retinal pigmentary change or field defect; blood count abnormalities; muscle weakness; cardiomyopathy; severe skin reaction. Drivers with definite retinal toxicity: advise not to drive until reviewed; inform DVLA (SPS).

src.q: Hydroxychloroquine sulfate should be discontinued if abnormalities develop.
Patients who are drivers with definite toxicity should be advised not to drive until reviewed by an ophthalmologist.

items.t: Take each dose with a meal or a glass of milk. Effect builds up over several weeks.

src.q: Each dose should be taken with a meal or glass of milk.
Hydroxychloroquine is cumulative in action and will require several weeks to exert its beneficial effects

items.t: Separate from antacids by 4 hours.

src.q: it is advised that a 4 hour interval be observed between hydroxychloroquine sulfate and antacid dosing.

items.t: Stop and contact the prescriber for any change in vision, including colour vision.

src.q: Patients should be advised to stop taking the drug immediately and seek the advice of their prescribing doctor if any disturbances of vision are noted, including abnormal colour vision.

items.t: Seek medical advice promptly for new or worse mental health symptoms (family/carers too).

src.q: speak to your doctor as soon as possible if you or your family members or caregivers notice any new or worsening mental health symptoms

items.t: Know the signs of low blood sugar.

src.q: Patients treated with hydroxychloroquine should be warned about the risk of hypoglycaemia and the associated clinical signs and symptoms.

items.t: Blurred vision early in treatment may affect driving.

src.q: Impaired visual accommodation soon after the start of treatment has been reported and patients should be warned regarding driving or operating machinery.

items.t: Keep out of reach of children (toxic to small children).

src.q: patients should be warned to keep hydroxychloroquine sulfate out of the reach of children.

items.t: Relief of spasm of the genito-urinary or gastro-intestinal tract, and symptomatic relief of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).

src.q: indicated for the relief of spasm of the genito- urinary tract or gastro- intestinal tract and for the symptomatic relief of Irritable Bowel Syndrome

items.t: One UK SmPC (IBS-only tablet) is licensed only for gastro-intestinal spasm in medically confirmed IBS.

src.q: indicated for the relief of gastro-intestinal tract spasm associated with medically confirmed Irritable Bowel Syndrome

items.t: IBS-only tablet: to be taken only for IBS diagnosed by a doctor; see a doctor first if red-flag features are present (age 40 or over with a change in symptoms, rectal bleeding, severe constipation, nausea or vomiting, weight loss, difficulty or pain passing urine, fever, recent travel abroad).

src.q: Only take Buscopan IBS Relief 10 mg Coated Tablets if your doctor has diagnosed Irritable Bowel Syndrome.

if you are 40 years or over and it is some time since your last attack of IBS or the symptoms are different this time if you have recently passed blood from the bowel if you suffer from severe constipation
if you are feeling sick or vomiting if you have lost your appetite or lost weight if you have difficulty or pain passing urine if you have a fever if you have recently travelled abroad

items.t: Adults: 20 mg (2 x 10 mg tablets) four times daily.

src.q: Adults: 2 tablets four times daily.

items.t: IBS: start 10 mg (1 tablet) three times daily; may increase to 20 mg (2 tablets) four times daily if necessary.

src.q: the recommended starting dose is 1 tablet three times daily, this can be increased up to 2 tablets four times daily if necessary

items.t: Do not take continuously every day or for long periods without investigating the cause of the abdominal pain.

src.q: should not be taken on a continuous daily basis or for extended periods without investigating the cause of abdominal pain

items.t: Children 6-12 years: 10 mg (1 tablet) three times daily (general 10 mg tablet SmPCs).

src.q: Children 6 - 12 years: 1 tablet three times daily.

items.t: The IBS-only tablet SmPC: 12 years and over same as adults; under 12 years not recommended.

src.q: Adults and Children 12 years or over: The recommended starting dose is 1 tablet three times daily
Children under 12 years: Not recommended.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to hyoscine butylbromide or any other component.

src.q: patients who have demonstrated prior hypersensitivity to hyoscine butylbromide or any other component of the product

items.t: Myasthenia gravis.

src.q: contraindicated in: - patients who have demonstrated prior hypersensitivity to hyoscine butylbromide or any other component of the product - myasthenia gravis - mechanical stenosis in the gastrointestinal tract

items.t: Mechanical stenosis of the gastrointestinal tract; paralytic or obstructive ileus; megacolon.

src.q: contraindicated in: - patients who have demonstrated prior hypersensitivity to hyoscine butylbromide or any other component of the product - myasthenia gravis - mechanical stenosis in the gastrointestinal tract
paralytical or obstructive ileus - megacolon - narrow angle glaucoma

items.t: Narrow-angle glaucoma.

src.q: paralytical or obstructive ileus - megacolon - narrow angle glaucoma

items.t: Severe unexplained abdominal pain that persists or worsens, or comes with fever, nausea, vomiting, change in bowel habit, tenderness, low blood pressure, fainting or blood in stool: seek medical advice immediately.

src.q: In case severe, unexplained abdominal pain persists or worsens, or occurs together with symptoms like fever, nausea, vomiting, changes in bowel movements, abdominal tenderness, decreased blood pressure, fainting, or blood in stool, medical advice should immediately be sought.

items.t: Conditions with tachycardia (thyrotoxicosis, cardiac insufficiency or failure) and cardiac surgery: use with caution; it may further increase heart rate.

src.q: should be used with caution in conditions characterised by tachycardia such as thyrotoxicosis, cardiac insufficiency or failure and in cardiac surgery where it may further accelerate the heart rate

items.t: Patients susceptible to intestinal or urinary outlet obstruction: use with caution (anticholinergic complications).

src.q: Due to the risk of anticholinergic complications, caution should be used in patients susceptible to intestinal or urinary outlet obstructions.

items.t: Pyrexia: give with caution (may reduce sweating).

src.q: Because of the possibility that anticholinergics may reduce sweating, Buscopan should be administered with caution to patients with pyrexia.

items.t: Undiagnosed narrow-angle glaucoma: intraocular pressure may rise. A painful red eye with loss of vision needs urgent eye assessment.

src.q: patients should seek urgent ophthalmological advice in case they should develop a painful, red eye with loss of vision whilst or after taking Buscopan

items.t: Tablet coating contains sucrose: patients with hereditary fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take the tablets.

src.q: patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take Buscopan Cramps

items.t: Anticholinergic effect of tri- and tetracyclic antidepressants, antihistamines, quinidine, amantadine, antipsychotics, disopyramide and other anticholinergics (e.g. tiotropium, ipratropium) may be intensified.

src.q: The anticholinergic effect of drugs such as tri- and tetracyclic antidepressants, antihistamines, quinidine, amantadine, antipsychotics (e.g. butyrophenones, phenothiazines), disopyramide and other anticholinergics (e.g. tiotropium, ipratropium, atropine-like compounds) may be intensified

items.t: Dopamine antagonists such as metoclopramide: the effects of both drugs on the gastrointestinal tract may be reduced.

src.q: Concomitant treatment with dopamine antagonists such as metoclopramide may result in diminution of the effects of both drugs on the gastrointestinal tract.

items.t: Beta-adrenergic agents: tachycardic effects may be enhanced.

src.q: The tachycardic effects of beta-adrenergic agents may be enhanced by Buscopan.

renal.note: No renal impairment advice in the UK SmPCs accessed (three UK 10 mg tablet SmPCs).

hepatic.note: No hepatic impairment advice in the UK SmPCs accessed (three UK 10 mg tablet SmPCs).

items.t: SmPC: limited human data; as a precaution not recommended in pregnancy.

src.q: There are limited data from the use of hyoscine butylbromide in pregnant women.
As a precautionary measure Buscopan is not recommended during pregnancy.

items.t: BUMPS: only recommended in pregnancy if there is no alternative treatment; available information does not suggest harm, but data are very limited.

src.q: hyoscine is only recommended in pregnancy if there are no alternative treatments as there is very little information about how it might affect the unborn baby
Although the available information does not suggest it harms the baby in the womb

items.t: SmPC: risk to the breastfed child cannot be excluded; use is not recommended.

src.q: A risk to the breastfeeding child cannot be excluded. Use of Buscopan during breastfeeding is not recommended.

items.t: SPS: a preferred antispasmodic in breastfeeding; low levels in milk expected. As a precaution monitor the infant for drowsiness, poor feeding, weight gain, irritability, constipation and urinary retention.

src.q: Hyoscine butylbromide can be used during breastfeeding.
monitor infants for drowsiness, not waking to feed or poor feeding, adequate weight gain, irritability, constipation and urinary retention (decrease in wet nappies)

items.t: SPS: theoretical risk of reduced milk supply with antimuscarinics; monitor feeding and weight gain, especially with long-term use.

src.q: There is a theoretical risk that suppression of breast milk production could occur with antimuscarinic drugs (atropine, hyoscine butylbromide, propantheline).

items.t: No human fertility studies.

src.q: No studies on the effects on human fertility have been conducted.

items.t: No common or very common effects listed. Uncommon: tachycardia, dry mouth, skin reactions (urticaria, pruritus), abnormal sweating.

src.q: Uncommon: tachycardia
Uncommon: dry mouth
Uncommon: skin reactions (e.g. urticaria, pruritus), abnormal sweating

items.t: Anaphylactic shock and anaphylactic or other hypersensitivity reactions, including dyspnoea (frequency not known).

src.q: anaphylactic shock, anaphylactic reactions, dyspnoea, other hypersensitivity

items.t: Urinary retention (rare).

src.q: Rare: urinary retention

items.t: Painful red eye with loss of vision (possible raised intraocular pressure): urgent eye assessment.

src.q: patients should seek urgent ophthalmological advice in case they should develop a painful, red eye with loss of vision whilst or after taking Buscopan

monitoring.note: No monitoring requirements stated in the UK SmPCs accessed (three UK 10 mg tablet SmPCs); no SPS monitoring page found.

items.t: Swallow tablets whole with enough water.

src.q: should be swallowed whole with adequate water

items.t: May blur vision (accommodation): do not drive or use machines if affected.

src.q: Because of possible visual accommodation disturbances patients should not drive or operate machinery if affected.

items.t: IBS: see a doctor if new symptoms appear, symptoms worsen, or there is no improvement after two weeks.

src.q: Consult your doctor if you develop new symptoms, or if your symptoms worsen or have not improved over two weeks.

items.t: Rheumatoid arthritis (including juvenile), ankylosing spondylitis, osteoarthritis and other arthropathies; soft-tissue and periarticular conditions (e.g. frozen shoulder, bursitis, tendonitis, low back pain, sprains); mild to moderate pain such as dysmenorrhoea, dental and post-operative pain, headache and migraine.

src.q: Brufen is indicated for its analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis (including juvenile rheumatoid arthritis or Still's disease), ankylosing spondylitis, osteoarthritis

Brufen is also indicated for its analgesic effect in the relief of mild to moderate pain such as dysmenorrhoea, dental and post-operative pain and for the symptomatic relief of headache including migraine headache.

items.t: Suspension: mild to moderate pain, post-immunisation pyrexia, fever and cold/flu symptoms; on prescription also rheumatic and inflammatory conditions including juvenile rheumatoid arthritis.

src.q: is used as an analgesic for relief of mild to moderate muscular pain, post-immunisation pyrexia
rheumatoid arthritis (including juvenile rheumatoid arthritis or Still's disease)

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction stated in the SmPCs or the MHRA pages accessed (suspension SmPC splits indications into OTC and prescription-only).

items.t: Adults and children over 12 (tablets): 1200-1800 mg daily in divided doses; some patients can be maintained on 600-1200 mg daily. In severe or acute conditions may increase, but total must not exceed 2400 mg/day in divided doses. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time.

src.q: The recommended dosage of Brufen is 1200-1800 mg daily in divided doses. Some patients can be maintained on 600-1200 mg daily.
provided that the total daily dose does not exceed 2400 mg in divided doses

items.t: Suspension, adults and children over 12: 200-400 mg (10-20 ml) up to three times a day; at least 4 hours apart; maximum 1200 mg (60 ml) in 24 hours. See a doctor if needed for more than 10 days.

src.q: The recommended dose is 200 mg-400 mg (10-20 ml), up to three times a day as required. Leave at least four hours between doses and do not take more than 1200 mg (60 ml) in any 24 hour period.
or if the product is required for more than 10 days

items.t: Elderly: higher risk of serious adverse effects; lowest effective dose for the shortest time; monitor regularly for GI bleeding.

src.q: The elderly are at increased risk of serious consequences of adverse reactions.
The patient should be monitored regularly for GI bleeding during NSAID therapy.

items.t: MHRA: avoid high-dose ibuprofen (2400 mg/day or more) in established ischaemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease, cerebrovascular disease, congestive heart failure (NYHA II-III) or uncontrolled hypertension. No increased cardiovascular risk seen up to 1200 mg/day.

src.q: avoid use of high-dose ibuprofen (≥2400 mg per day) in patients with established: ischaemic heart disease peripheral arterial disease cerebrovascular disease congestive heart failure
consider that no increase in cardiovascular risk is seen with ibuprofen at doses up to 1200 mg per day

items.t: Tablets, children: 20 mg/kg/day in divided doses; juvenile rheumatoid arthritis up to 40 mg/kg/day in divided doses. Not recommended under 7 kg; more suitable formulations exist for young children.

src.q: Children: The daily dosage of Brufen is 20 mg/kg of body weight in divided doses. For young children, more suitable formulations are available.
In Juvenile Rheumatoid Arthritis, up to 40 mg/kg of body weight daily in divided doses may be taken. Not recommended for children weighing less than 7 kg.

items.t: Suspension, pain and fever: 20 mg/kg/day in divided doses. By age: 3-6 months (over 5 kg) 2.5 ml up to 3 times in 24 hours, no longer than 24 hours; 6 months-1 year 2.5 ml 3-4 times a day; 1-4 years 5 ml three times a day; 4-7 years 7.5 ml three times a day; 7-12 years 10 ml three times a day.

src.q: For pain and fever - 20 mg/kg/day in divided doses (including OTC use).
Infants 3-6 months weighing more than 5 kg: One 2.5 ml dose may be taken 3 times in 24 hours. Do not use for more than 24 hours
Infants 6 months-1 year: 2.5 ml three to four times a day. Children 1-4 years: 5 ml three times a day. Children 4-7 years: 7.5 ml three times a day. Children 7-12 years: 10 ml three times a day.

items.t: Post-immunisation fever: 2.5 ml (50 mg), then one more 2.5 ml six hours later if needed; no more than 2 doses in 24 hours.

src.q: Post-immunisation fever: 2.5 ml (50 mg) followed by one further dose of 2.5 ml (50 mg) six hours later if necessary. No more than 2 doses in 24 hours.

items.t: Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (prescription only, suspension): up to 30-40 mg/kg/day in 3 or 4 divided doses.

src.q: For Juvenile Rheumatoid Arthritis (prescription only use): Doses up to 30-40mg/kg/day may be taken in three or four divided doses.

items.t: Do not give under 3 months. Infants 3-5 months: seek advice if symptoms worsen or persist beyond 24 hours; from 6 months seek advice if needed for more than 3 days.

src.q: Do not give to children under 3 months of age.
If in children aged from 6 months and in adolescents this medicinal product is required for more than 3 days, or if symptoms worsen a doctor should be consulted.

items.t: Risk of renal impairment in dehydrated children and adolescents.

src.q: There is a risk of renal impairment in dehydrated children and adolescents.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to ibuprofen; previous hypersensitivity (asthma, urticaria, angioedema, rhinitis) to ibuprofen, aspirin or other NSAIDs.

src.q: Patients who have previously shown hypersensitivity reactions (e.g. asthma, rhinitis, angioedema or urticaria) after taking ibuprofen, aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).

items.t: History of GI bleeding or perforation related to previous NSAIDs; active or history of recurrent peptic ulcer/haemorrhage; conditions with increased bleeding tendency.

src.q: History of gastrointestinal bleeding or perforation, related to previous NSAID therapy. Active or history of recurrent peptic ulcer/gastrointestinal haemorrhage (two or more distinct episodes of proven ulceration or bleeding). Patients with conditions involving an increased tendency to bleeding.

items.t: Severe heart failure (NYHA IV), hepatic failure, renal failure; last trimester of pregnancy.

src.q: Brufen is contraindicated in patients with severe heart failure (NYHA Class IV), hepatic failure and renal failure
Brufen is contraindicated during the last trimester of pregnancy

items.t: GI bleeding, ulceration or perforation can occur at any time and can be fatal; risk rises with dose, ulcer history and age. Start at the lowest dose; consider misoprostol or a PPI in these patients and with low-dose aspirin or other drugs raising GI risk. Stop if GI bleeding or ulceration occurs.

src.q: Combination therapy with protective agents (e.g. misoprostol or proton pump inhibitors) should be considered for these patients
When GI bleeding or ulceration occurs in patients receiving Brufen, the treatment should be withdrawn.

items.t: Cardiovascular: high dose (2400 mg/day) may slightly increase arterial thrombotic risk; low dose (1200 mg/day or less) not shown to. Uncontrolled hypertension, heart failure NYHA II-III, ischaemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease or cerebrovascular disease: only after careful consideration and avoid 2400 mg/day.

src.q: Patients with uncontrolled hypertension, congestive heart failure (NYHA II-III), established ischaemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease, and/or cerebrovascular disease should only be treated with ibuprofen after careful consideration and high doses (2400mg/day) should be avoided.

items.t: Renal: may precipitate renal failure; highest risk with renal, cardiac or liver impairment, diuretics, ACE inhibitors and in the elderly. Use lowest dose, shortest time and monitor renal function. Caution in significant dehydration.

src.q: For these patients, use the lowest effective dose, for the shortest possible duration and monitor renal function especially in long-term treated patients
Caution should be used when initiating treatment with ibuprofen in patients with considerable dehydration.

items.t: Asthma, chronic rhinitis or allergic disease: caution (bronchospasm, urticaria, angioedema).

src.q: Caution is required if Brufen is administered to patients suffering from, or with a previous history of, bronchial asthma, chronic rhinitis or allergic diseases

items.t: Ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease: give with care (may be exacerbated). SLE / mixed connective tissue disease: increased risk of aseptic meningitis.

src.q: NSAIDs should be given with care to patients with a history of ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease as these conditions may be exacerbated
In patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and mixed connective tissue disorders there may be an increased risk of aseptic meningitis

items.t: Severe skin reactions (SJS, TEN, DRESS, AGEP): stop immediately at first signs. Avoid in chickenpox. May mask signs of infection.

src.q: If signs and symptoms suggestive of these reactions appear ibuprofen should be withdrawn immediately
Thus, it is advisable to avoid use of Ibuprofen in case of varicella.

items.t: Avoid with other NSAIDs including COX-2 inhibitors.

src.q: The use of Brufen with concomitant NSAIDs, including cyclooxygenase-2 selective inhibitors, should be avoided due to the increased risk of ulceration or bleeding

items.t: Renal tubular acidosis and hypokalaemia with long-term high doses (usually over 4 weeks) or overdose.

src.q: Renal tubular acidosis and hypokalaemia may occur following acute overdose and in patients taking ibuprofen products over long periods at high doses (typically greater than 4 weeks)

items.t: Anticoagulants (e.g. warfarin): NSAIDs may enhance their effect. Antiplatelets and SSRIs: increased GI bleeding risk. Corticosteroids: increased GI ulceration or bleeding.

src.q: Anticoagulants: NSAIDs may enhance the effects of anticoagulants, such as warfarin
Anti-platelet agents and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs): Increased risk of gastrointestinal bleeding with NSAIDs
Corticosteroids: Increased risk of gastrointestinal ulceration or bleeding with NSAIDs

items.t: ACE inhibitors, angiotensin-II receptor antagonists, beta-blockers, diuretics: reduced antihypertensive effect; diuretics increase nephrotoxicity risk.

src.q: NSAIDs may reduce the effect of anti-hypertensives, such as ACE inhibitors, angiotensin-II receptor antagonists, beta-blockers and diuretics. Diuretics can also increase the risk of nephrotoxicity of NSAIDs.

items.t: Methotrexate: NSAIDs may reduce methotrexate clearance. Tablets SmPC: take care. Suspension SmPC lists methotrexate under combinations to avoid.

src.q: Methotrexate: NSAIDs may inhibit the tubular secretion of methotrexate and reduce clearance of methotrexate.
Ibuprofen should be avoided in combination with:

items.t: Quinolone antibiotics: possible increased risk of convulsions.

src.q: Patients taking NSAIDs and quinolones may have an increased risk of developing convulsions.

items.t: Aspirin: not generally recommended together; regular ibuprofen may reduce the cardioprotective effect of low-dose aspirin. Other NSAIDs: avoid.

src.q: the possibility that regular, long-term use of ibuprofen may reduce the cardioprotective effect of low-dose acetylsalicylic acid cannot be excluded
Avoid concomitant use of two or more NSAIDs, including Cox-2 inhibitors

items.t: Others: lithium (reduced elimination), ciclosporin and tacrolimus (nephrotoxicity), sulfonylureas (hypoglycaemia, rare), CYP2C9 inhibitors such as fluconazole/voriconazole (consider ibuprofen dose reduction), zidovudine, cardiac glycosides.

src.q: Lithium: Decreased elimination of lithium.
Reduction of the ibuprofen dose should be considered when potent CYP2C9 inhibitors are administered concomitantly

items.t: Warfarin (warfarin SmPC): NSAIDs should be avoided if possible, or given with caution and increased clinical and laboratory monitoring.

src.q: The following examples should be avoided, or administered with caution with increased clinical and laboratory monitoring

items.t: Spironolactone (spironolactone SmPC): use with NSAIDs may lead to severe hyperkalaemia. ACE inhibitors (lisinopril SmPC): worsening renal function and raised serum potassium; caution, keep hydrated, monitor renal function.

src.q: may lead to severe hyperkalaemia
The combination should be administered with caution, especially in the elderly.

items.t: Metformin (metformin SmPC): close monitoring of renal function is necessary when an NSAID is started or used with metformin.

src.q: When starting or using such products in combination with metformin, close monitoring of renal function is necessary.

items.t: Methotrexate (SPS, methotrexate SmPC): increased risk of methotrexate toxicity; use with caution on specialist advice; not recommended if renal impairment (even mild) is present.

src.q: Use NSAIDs in combination with methotrexate with caution on the advice of the specialist (for example, rheumatologist).
If risk factors such as renal function disorders, including mild renal impairment, are present, combined administration with NSAIDs is not recommended.

items.t: Renal failure / severe renal insufficiency: contraindicated (no numeric threshold given).

src.q: patients with severe renal insufficiency (see section 4.3 - Contraindications)
Brufen is contraindicated in patients with severe heart failure (NYHA Class IV), hepatic failure and renal failure

items.t: Mild to moderate renal impairment: lowest effective dose, shortest duration, monitor renal function; dose assessed individually.

src.q: If renal or hepatic function is impaired, dosage should be assessed individually.
use the lowest effective dose, for the shortest possible duration and monitor renal function

items.t: MHRA: patients at risk of renal impairment or failure (particularly elderly) should avoid NSAIDs if possible; if essential, lowest dose for shortest time with careful renal monitoring.

src.q: patients at risk of renal impairment or renal failure (particularly elderly people) should avoid NSAIDs if possible
the renal function of such patients should be carefully monitored during NSAID treatment

items.t: Hepatic failure / severe hepatic dysfunction: contraindicated. Mild to moderate impairment: caution; dose assessed individually.

src.q: For patients with mild to moderate hepatic impairment (see section 4.4 Special warnings and precautions for use) and patients with severe hepatic dysfunction (see section 4.3-Contraindications).

items.t: Third trimester: contraindicated (ductus arteriosus closure, fetal renal dysfunction, prolonged bleeding, delayed labour).

src.q: Consequently, Brufen is contraindicated during the third trimester of pregnancy.

items.t: First and second trimesters: do not give unless clearly necessary; lowest dose and shortest time. From week 20: oligohydramnios and ductus arteriosus constriction reported; consider antenatal monitoring after several days of use; stop if found.

src.q: Therefore, during the first and second trimester of pregnancy, Brufen should not be given unless clearly necessary.
Antenatal monitoring for oligohydramnios and ductus arteriosus constriction should be considered after exposure to ibuprofen for several days from gestational week 20 onward.

items.t: MHRA: avoid systemic NSAIDs from week 20 unless clinically required; contraindicated after 28 weeks. Patients should not swap paracetamol for ibuprofen in pregnancy.

src.q: avoid prescribing systemic NSAIDs from week 20 of pregnancy unless clinically required and prescribe the lowest dose for the shortest time in these circumstances
patients should not swap to alternatives such as ibuprofen

items.t: SPS: ibuprofen is the preferred NSAID in pregnancy; may be used if needed in the first trimester; usually no longer than 3 days from week 20. BUMPS: not advised unless prescribed by a doctor, especially from 20 weeks.

src.q: Ibuprofen is the preferred NSAID in pregnancy.
Use of ibuprofen during pregnancy is not advised unless prescribed by a doctor, especially if you are 20 or more weeks pregnant.

items.t: SmPCs: NSAIDs appear in milk in very low concentrations; avoid if possible when breastfeeding.

src.q: NSAIDs should, if possible, be avoided when breastfeeding.

items.t: SPS (less restrictive): ibuprofen is the NSAID of choice in breastfeeding; negligible amounts in milk; monitor infant for vomiting and diarrhoea.

src.q: Ibuprofen is the NSAID of choice for treating mild to moderate pain during breastfeeding.
As a precaution, monitor infants for vomiting and diarrhoea.

items.t: May impair female fertility; not recommended in women attempting to conceive; consider stopping in women with difficulty conceiving or under investigation.

src.q: The use of Brufen may impair female fertility and is not recommended in women attempting to conceive.

items.t: Common: headache, dizziness, dyspepsia, diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, flatulence, constipation, melaena, haematemesis, GI haemorrhage, rash, fatigue.

src.q: Nervous system disorders Common Headache, dizziness
Gastrointestinal disorders Common Dyspepsia, diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, flatulence, constipation, melaena, haematemesis, gastrointestinal haemorrhage
Skin and subcutaneous tissue disorders Common Rash

items.t: Peptic ulcer, perforation or GI bleeding (sometimes fatal, especially elderly): stop treatment.

src.q: Peptic ulcers, perforation or GI bleeding, sometimes fatal, particularly in the elderly, may occur

items.t: Severe skin reactions (SJS/TEN very rare; DRESS, AGEP not known): withdraw immediately.

src.q: Very rare Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs) (including Erythema multiforme, exfoliative dermatitis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis)

items.t: Anaphylaxis (rare), bronchospasm/asthma (uncommon), angioedema (uncommon).

src.q: Rare Anaphylactic reaction
Uncommon Asthma, bronchospasm, dyspnoea

items.t: Nephrotoxicity including renal failure (uncommon); cardiac failure and myocardial infarction (very rare); hepatic failure (very rare); aseptic meningitis and blood dyscrasias (rare).

src.q: Uncommon Nephrotoxity in various forms e.g.Tubulointerstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome and renal failure
Cardiac disorders Very rare Cardiac failure, myocardial infarction

items.t: SPS baseline: blood pressure, eGFR, full blood count, serum creatinine; LFTs if hepatic impairment.

src.q: Estimated glomerular filtration rate Full blood count Serum creatinine Liver function tests
Before starting Consider Baseline Blood pressure

items.t: SPS after starting or dose change: eGFR or serum creatinine and FBC within 2 weeks; blood pressure within 4 weeks; haemoglobin within 4 weeks if high GI risk.

src.q: After started or dose changed Consider Within 2 weeks Estimated glomerular filtration rate or Serum creatinine (for creatinine clearance) Full blood count
Within 4 weeks Haemoglobin

items.t: SmPC: monitor renal function in at-risk and long-term patients; monitor elderly regularly for GI bleeding; monitoring and advice in hypertension or heart failure (fluid retention).

src.q: Appropriate monitoring and advice are required for patients with a history of hypertension and/or mild to moderate congestive heart failure as fluid retention and oedema have been reported in association with NSAID therapy.

items.t: Stop if GI bleeding or ulceration, or at first signs of severe skin reaction.

src.q: When GI bleeding or ulceration occurs in patients receiving Brufen, the treatment should be withdrawn.

items.t: Tablets: preferably with or after food with plenty of fluid; swallow whole, do not chew, break, crush or suck.

src.q: To be taken preferably with or after food, with plenty of fluid. Brufen tablets should be swallowed whole and not chewed, broken, crushed or sucked on

items.t: Report any unusual abdominal symptoms, especially bleeding (black stools, vomiting blood), particularly early in treatment.

src.q: should report any unusual abdominal symptoms (especially gastrointestinal bleeding) particularly in the initial stages of treatment

items.t: Pregnant patients: avoid non-prescription NSAIDs from week 20 unless advised by a healthcare professional (MHRA).

src.q: please advise patients who are pregnant to avoid use of NSAIDs available without prescription from week 20 of pregnancy onwards unless advised by their healthcare professional

items.t: May cause dizziness, drowsiness, fatigue or visual disturbance; do not drive if affected.

src.q: If affected, patients should not drive or operate machinery.

items.t: Chronic eczema.

src.q: For the treatment of chronic eczema.

restrictions.note: The UK ichthammol SPC states no prescribing restrictions. No NICE or SPS advice on ichthammol was found.

items.t: Apply to the skin 1 to 3 times daily.

src.q: To be applied topically 1-3 times daily.

items.t: The SPC gives the same dose (1 to 3 times daily) for adults, the elderly and children under 12 years. No lower age limit is stated.

src.q: Adults, the elderly and children under 12 years To be applied topically 1-3 times daily.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to ichthammol or to any excipient (glycerol in the UK product).

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.
6.1. List of Excipients Glycerol.

items.t: Do not apply to broken skin. For external use only.

src.q: Do not apply to broken skin. For external use only.

items.t: Keep out of the reach of children.

src.q: Keep out of the reach of children.

items.t: No significant interactions have been reported. Ichthammol is probably not absorbed through intact skin.

src.q: No significant interactions have been reported.
it is probably not absorbed through intact skin

renal.note: The UK ichthammol SPC gives no renal advice.

hepatic.note: The UK ichthammol SPC gives no hepatic advice.

items.t: No significant problems reported in pregnancy, but use (especially in the first 3 months) only when the benefits outweigh any risks.

src.q: No significant problems have been reported either with pregnant women or with nursing mothers who are breast feeding
its use especially in the first 3 months of pregnancy, is recommended only when the benefits outweigh any risks

items.t: No significant problems have been reported in breastfeeding mothers.

src.q: No significant problems have been reported either with pregnant women or with nursing mothers who are breast feeding

reproductive.note: The UK ichthammol SPC gives no fertility or contraception advice.

items.t: Skin irritation (frequency not stated).

src.q: Skin irritation has been reported.

adverseSerious.note: The UK ichthammol SPC lists only skin irritation; no serious adverse effects are stated.

monitoring.note: The UK ichthammol SPC states no monitoring.

items.t: Apply to the skin only (topical, external use). Do not apply to broken skin.

src.q: Route of administration Topical.
Do not apply to broken skin. For external use only.

items.t: Use on unbroken skin only; stop and seek advice if the skin becomes irritated.

src.q: Do not apply to broken skin.
Skin irritation has been reported.

items.t: Essential hypertension in adults.

src.q: is indicated in essential hypertension in adults.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restrictions stated in the UK SmPC.

items.t: One 1.5 mg tablet every 24 hours, preferably in the morning. Higher doses do not add antihypertensive effect but increase the saluretic (diuretic) effect; do not increase the dose if treatment is ineffective.

src.q: One tablet per 24 hours, preferably in the morning
At higher doses the antihypertensive action of indapamide is not enhanced but the saluretic effect is increased.
The dose should not be increased if treatment is ineffective.

items.t: Elderly: can be treated when renal function is normal or only minimally impaired; interpret plasma creatinine in relation to age, weight and gender.

src.q: Elderly patients can be treated with Natrilix SR when renal function is normal or only minimally impaired.
In the elderly, the plasma creatinine must be adjusted in relation to age, weight and gender.

items.t: Safety and efficacy in children and adolescents have not been established; no data are available.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of Natrilix SR in children and adolescents have not been established. No data are available.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to indapamide, to other sulfonamides or to any excipient; severe renal failure; hepatic encephalopathy or severe impairment of liver function; hypokalaemia.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance, to other sulfonamides or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.
- Severe renal failure. - Hepatic encephalopathy or severe impairment of liver function. - Hypokalaemia.

items.t: Severe renal failure is defined in section 4.2 as creatinine clearance below 30 ml/min.

src.q: In severe renal failure (creatinine clearance below 30 ml/min), treatment is contraindicated.

items.t: Impaired liver function: thiazide-related diuretics may cause hepatic encephalopathy (especially with electrolyte imbalance), which can progress to hepatic coma. Stop immediately if this occurs.

src.q: When liver function is impaired, thiazide-related diuretics may cause, particularly in case of electrolyte imbalance, hepatic encephalopathy which can progress to hepatic coma.
Administration of the diuretic must be stopped immediately if this occurs.

items.t: Hyponatraemia (sometimes with very serious consequences): measure sodium before starting and regularly after; more often in the elderly and in cirrhosis.

src.q: This must be measured before starting treatment, then at regular intervals subsequently.
Any diuretic treatment may cause hyponatraemia, sometimes with very serious consequences.

items.t: Hypokalaemia is the major risk: prevent potassium below 3.4 mmol/l in high-risk groups (elderly, malnourished or on many medicines, cirrhosis with oedema/ascites, coronary disease, heart failure, long QT). Hypokalaemia and bradycardia predispose to torsades de pointes.

src.q: Potassium depletion with hypokalaemia is the major risk of thiazide and related diuretics.
The risk of onset of hypokalaemia (< 3.4 mmol/l) must be prevented in certain high risk populations
Individuals with a long QT interval are also at risk, whether the origin is congenital or iatrogenic.

items.t: Calcium may rise slightly; marked hypercalcaemia may reveal hyperparathyroidism (stop before testing parathyroid function). Hypomagnesaemia can occur.

src.q: Frank hypercalcaemia may be due to previously unrecognised hyperparathyroidism.
Treatment should be withdrawn before the investigation of parathyroid function.
which may result in hypomagnesaemia

items.t: Diabetes: monitoring of blood glucose is important, especially with hypokalaemia. Gout: attacks may be more likely in hyperuricaemia.

src.q: Monitoring of blood glucose is important in diabetics, in particular in the presence of hypokalaemia.
Tendency to gout attacks may be increased in hyperuricaemic patients.

items.t: Choroidal effusion, acute myopia and secondary acute angle-closure glaucoma can occur within hours to weeks; stop the drug as rapidly as possible. History of sulfonamide or penicillin allergy may be a risk factor.

src.q: The primary treatment is to discontinue drug intake as rapidly as possible.
Risk factors for developing acute angle-closure glaucoma may include a history of sulfonamide or penicillin allergy.

items.t: Photosensitivity: stop treatment if it occurs; if re-treatment is needed, protect skin from sun and artificial UVA.

src.q: If photosensitivity reaction occurs during treatment, it is recommended to stop the treatment.
it is recommended to protect exposed areas to the sun or to artificial UVA

items.t: Lactose: patients with galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: Sulfonamide allergy (SPS): cross-reactivity between sulfonamide antibiotics and non-antibiotic sulfonamides (which include thiazides and thiazide-like diuretics) is not expected, but product information often contraindicates them. This SmPC lists hypersensitivity to other sulfonamides as a contraindication.

src.q: thiazides and thiazide-like diuretics
Cross-reactivity between antibiotic and non-antibiotic sulfonamides is not expected, including in people who had a life-threatening reaction to a sulfonamide.

items.t: Lithium: combination not recommended (raised lithium, toxicity). If a diuretic is needed, monitor plasma lithium carefully and adjust the dose.

src.q: Combinations that are not recommended: Lithium: Increased plasma lithium with signs of overdosage
careful monitoring of plasma lithium and dose adjustment are required.

items.t: Medicines that can cause torsades de pointes (e.g. class Ia and III antiarrhythmics, some antipsychotics, moxifloxacin, methadone): higher risk of ventricular arrhythmia, as hypokalaemia is a risk factor. Correct hypokalaemia first; monitor clinically, electrolytes and ECG.

src.q: Increased risk of ventricular arrhythmias, particularly torsades de pointes (hypokalaemia is a risk factor).
Monitor for hypokalaemia and correct, if required, before introducing this combination. Clinical, plasma electrolytes and ECG monitoring.

items.t: NSAIDs (systemic, including COX-2 inhibitors) and high-dose aspirin (3 g/day or more): may reduce the antihypertensive effect; risk of acute renal failure if dehydrated. Hydrate the patient and monitor renal function at the start.

src.q: N.S.A.I.Ds. (systemic route) including COX-2 selective inhibitors, high dose acetylsalicylic acid (≥ 3 g/day)
Risk of acute renal failure in dehydrated patients (decreased glomerular filtration). Hydrate the patient; monitor renal function at the start of treatment.

items.t: ACE inhibitors: risk of sudden hypotension and/or acute renal failure when started with pre-existing sodium depletion. Either stop the diuretic 3 days before, or start the ACE inhibitor at a low dose; monitor creatinine in the first weeks.

src.q: Risk of sudden hypotension and/or acute renal failure
either to stop the diuretic 3 days before starting treatment with the A.C.E. inhibitor
monitor renal function (plasma creatinine) during the first weeks of treatment

items.t: Other potassium-lowering medicines (systemic corticosteroids, stimulant laxatives, IV amphotericin B, tetracosactide): additive hypokalaemia; monitor and correct potassium; use non-stimulant laxatives. Systemic corticosteroids also reduce the antihypertensive effect.

src.q: gluco- and mineralo-corticoids (systemic route), tetracosactide, stimulant laxatives: Increased risk of hypokalaemia (additive effect).
Use non-stimulant laxatives.
Decreased antihypertensive effect (water/sodium retention due to corticosteroids).

items.t: Potassium-sparing diuretics (amiloride, spironolactone): hypokalaemia or hyperkalaemia can still occur, especially in renal failure or diabetes; monitor potassium and ECG.

src.q: hypokalaemia or hyperkalaemia (particularly in patients with renal failure or diabetes) may still occur. Plasma potassium and ECG should be monitored

items.t: Metformin: higher risk of lactic acidosis from diuretic-related renal impairment. Do not use metformin when plasma creatinine exceeds 135 µmol/l (men) or 110 µmol/l (women).

src.q: Increased risk of metformin induced lactic acidosis
Do not use metformin when plasma creatinine exceeds 15 mg/l (135 µmol/l) in men and 12 mg/l (110 µmol/l) in women.

items.t: Allopurinol: more hypersensitivity reactions to allopurinol. Tricyclic (imipramine-like) antidepressants and neuroleptics: additive orthostatic hypotension. Calcium salts: risk of hypercalcaemia. Digitalis: hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia increase toxicity (monitor potassium, magnesium and ECG). Iodinated contrast: rehydrate first. Baclofen: increased antihypertensive effect. Ciclosporin, tacrolimus: plasma creatinine may rise.

src.q: Concomitant treatment with indapamide may increase the incidence of hypersensitivity reactions to allopurinol.
Imipramine-like antidepressants, neuroleptics: Antihypertensive effect and increased risk of orthostatic hypotension (additive effect).
Calcium (salts): Risk of hypercalcaemia resulting from decreased urinary elimination of calcium.
Hypokalaemia and/or hypomagnesaemia predispose to the toxic effects of digitalis.
Rehydration before administration of the iodinated compound.
Baclofen: Increased antihypertensive effect.
Ciclosporin, tacrolimus: Risk of increased plasma creatinine

items.t: Contraindicated in severe renal failure (creatinine clearance below 30 ml/min). Thiazide-related diuretics are fully effective only when renal function is normal or minimally impaired (plasma creatinine below about 220 µmol/l in an adult).

src.q: In severe renal failure (creatinine clearance below 30 ml/min), treatment is contraindicated.
plasma creatinine below levels of the order of 25 mg/l, i.e . 220 µmol/l in an adult

items.t: Early hypovolaemia can reduce glomerular filtration and worsen existing renal insufficiency.

src.q: This transitory functional renal insufficiency is of no consequence in individuals with normal renal function but may worsen preexisting renal insufficiency.

items.t: Contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment or hepatic encephalopathy. In any liver impairment, risk of hepatic encephalopathy; stop immediately if it occurs.

src.q: In severe hepatic impairment, treatment is contraindicated.
Hepatic encephalopathy or severe impairment of liver function.

items.t: SmPC: limited data. Prolonged third-trimester thiazide exposure can reduce maternal plasma volume and uteroplacental blood flow (fetoplacental ischaemia, growth retardation). Preferably avoid in pregnancy as a precaution.

src.q: Prolonged exposure to thiazide during the third trimester of pregnancy can reduce maternal plasma volume as well as uteroplacental blood flow
As a precautionary measure, it is preferable to avoid the use of Indapamide during pregnancy.

items.t: BUMPS (diuretics): can be used in pregnancy if prescribed by a doctor but rarely needed; may reduce blood flow to the placenta, so extra growth scans are offered. For hypertension a different medicine is usually offered.

src.q: A diuretic can be used in pregnancy if prescribed by a doctor.
Diuretics may reduce blood flow to the placenta.
If you take a diuretic to treat high blood pressure, you will usually be offered a different medicine that is known to be safe during pregnancy.

items.t: Not recommended. Insufficient information on excretion in milk; risk of sulfonamide hypersensitivity and hypokalaemia in the infant cannot be excluded; thiazides can reduce or suppress milk production.

src.q: Indapamide is not recommended during breast-feeding.
A risk to the newborns/infants cannot be excluded.
decrease or even suppression of milk lactation

items.t: No effect on fertility in rat studies; no effects on human fertility are anticipated.

src.q: No effects on human fertility are anticipated.

items.t: Common: hypokalaemia, hypersensitivity reactions (mainly skin, in people prone to allergy/asthma), maculopapular rash. At 1.5 mg, potassium below 3.4 mmol/l was seen in 10% of patients after 4-6 weeks.

src.q: The most commonly reported adverse reactions are hypokalaemia, hypersensitivity reactions, mainly dermatological, in subjects with a predisposition to allergic and asthmatic reactions and maculopapular rashes.
Indapamide 1.5mg: Plasma potassium <3.4 mmol/l was seen in 10 % of patients

items.t: Uncommon: hyponatraemia, vomiting, purpura, erectile dysfunction.

src.q: Hyponatraemia (see section 4.4) Uncommon
Erectile dysfunction Uncommon

items.t: Torsade de pointes (potentially fatal) and QT prolongation (frequency not known), linked to hypokalaemia.

src.q: Torsade de pointes (potentially fatal)

items.t: Acute angle-closure glaucoma / choroidal effusion (not known): sudden reduced vision or eye pain - stop the drug as rapidly as possible.
