items.t: With aliskiren-containing products in patients with diabetes or renal impairment (GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m²).

src.q: The concomitant use of Zestoretic with aliskiren-containing products is contraindicated in patients with diabetes mellitus or renal impairment (GFR < 60 ml/min/1.73 m2)

items.t: Non-melanoma skin cancer (basal and squamous cell): risk rises with cumulative hydrochlorothiazide dose. Inform patients, advise regular skin checks and sun protection, examine suspicious lesions, and reconsider use after previous skin cancer.

src.q: Patients taking HCTZ should be informed of the risk of NMSC and advised to regularly check their skin for any new lesions and promptly report any suspicious skin lesions.
The use of HCTZ may also need to be reconsidered in patients who have experienced previous NMSC
reconsider the use of hydrochlorothiazide in patients who have had previous skin cancer

items.t: Symptomatic hypotension: more likely with volume depletion (diuretics, salt restriction, dialysis, diarrhoea, vomiting) or severe renin-dependent hypertension. Check electrolytes regularly; start and change doses under close supervision in those at risk, including ischaemic heart or cerebrovascular disease.

src.q: is more likely to occur if the patient has been volume-depleted, e.g. by diuretic therapy, dietary salt restriction, dialysis, diarrhoea or vomiting, or has severe renin-dependant hypertension
In patients at increased risk of symptomatic hypotension, initiation of therapy and dose adjustment should be monitored under close medical supervision.

Particular consideration applies to patients with ischaemic heart or cerebrovascular disease, because an excessive fall in blood pressure could result in a myocardial infarction or cerebrovascular accident.
Regular determination of serum electrolytes should be performed at appropriate intervals in such patients.

items.t: Mitral stenosis, aortic stenosis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: give lisinopril with caution.

src.q: lisinopril should be given with caution to patients with mitral valve stenosis and obstruction in the outflow of the left ventricle such as aortic stenosis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

items.t: Renal impairment: thiazides are ineffective at CrCl 30 mL/min or below. With CrCl 80 mL/min or below, do not give the combination until titration of the separate components shows these doses are needed. Renal artery stenosis: start under close supervision with low doses; monitor renal function in the first few weeks.

src.q: are ineffective at creatinine clearance values of 30 ml/min or below (corresponds to moderate or severe renal insufficiency).

Lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide should not be administered to patients with renal insufficiency (creatinine clearance less than or equal to 80 ml/min) until titration of the individual components has shown the need for the doses present in the combination tablet.
renal function should be monitored during the first few weeks of lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide therapy.

items.t: Hepatic: use thiazides with caution in impaired liver function or progressive liver disease (small fluid/electrolyte changes may precipitate hepatic coma). Stop if jaundice or marked liver enzyme rise.

src.q: Thiazides should be used with caution in patients with impaired hepatic function or progressive liver disease, since minor alterations of fluid and electrolyte balance may precipitate hepatic coma
Patients receiving lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide who develop jaundice or marked elevations of hepatic enzymes should discontinue lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide

items.t: Electrolytes: thiazides can cause hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypochloraemic alkalosis and hypomagnesaemia, and can raise serum calcium; ACE inhibitors can cause hyperkalaemia (renal impairment, diabetes, potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics, trimethoprim, ARBs). Check serum electrolytes periodically.

src.q: periodic determination of serum electrolytes should be performed at appropriate intervals.
can cause fluid or electrolyte imbalance (hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, and hypochloremic alkalosis).
Thiazides have been shown to increase the urinary excretions of magnesium, which may result in hypomagnesaemia.
Thiazides may decrease urinary calcium excretion and may cause intermittent and slight elevation of serum calcium.
other drugs associated with increase in serum potassium (e.g. heparin, trimethoprim or co-trimoxazole also known as trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole)
Potassium-sparing diuretics and angiotensin-receptor blockers should be used with caution in patients receiving ACE inhibitors, serum potassium and renal function should be monitored

items.t: Metabolic: may impair glucose tolerance; antidiabetic (including insulin) doses may need adjustment; monitor glycaemia closely in the first month. Thiazides may unmask latent diabetes, raise lipids and precipitate hyperuricaemia or gout.

src.q: ACE inhibitor and thiazide therapy may impair glucose tolerance. Dosage adjustment of antidiabetic agents, including insulin, may be required.
In diabetic patients treated with oral antidiabetic agents or insulin, glycaemia levels should be closely monitored during the first month of treatment with an ACE inhibitor.
Latent diabetes mellitus may become manifest during thiazide therapy.
Increases in cholesterol and triglyceride levels may be associated with thiazide diuretic therapy.
Thiazide therapy may precipitate hyperuricaemia and/or gout in certain patients.

items.t: Angioedema can occur at any time; stop promptly. Airway involvement needs emergency treatment. Higher rate in black patients. History of angioedema not caused by an ACE inhibitor may raise risk. Caution when starting racecadotril, mTOR inhibitors or vildagliptin.

src.q: This may occur at any time during therapy. In such cases, lisinopril should be discontinued promptly
In such cases emergency therapy should be administered promptly.
ACE inhibitors cause a higher rate of angioedema in black patients than in non-black patients.
Patients with a history of angioedema unrelated to ACE inhibitor therapy may be at increased risk of angioedema while receiving an ACE inhibitor
Caution should be used when starting racecadotril, mTOR inhibitors (e.g. sirolimus, everolimus, temsirolimus) and vildagliptin in a patient already taking an ACE inhibitor.

items.t: Dual RAAS blockade (ACE inhibitor with ARB or aliskiren) not recommended; do not combine an ACE inhibitor and ARB in diabetic nephropathy.

src.q: Dual blockade of RAAS through the combined use of ACE-inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers or aliskiren is therefore not recommended
ACE-inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers should not be used concomitantly in patients with diabetic nephropathy.

items.t: Neutropenia/agranulocytosis: extreme caution in collagen vascular disease, immunosuppressant therapy, allopurinol or procainamide, especially with renal impairment; check white cell counts periodically. Thiazides can exacerbate or activate SLE.

src.q: Lisinopril should be used with extreme caution in patients with collagen vascular disease, immunosuppressant therapy, treatment with allopurinol or procainamide
periodic monitoring of white blood cell counts is advised and patients should be instructed to report any sign of infection.
Exacerbation or activation of systemic lupus erythematosus has been reported with the use of thiazides.

items.t: Choroidal effusion, acute myopia and secondary angle-closure glaucoma (sulfonamide reaction), usually within hours to weeks: stop as rapidly as possible. Sulfonamide or penicillin allergy may be a risk factor.

src.q: Sulfonamide or sulfonamide derivative drugs can cause an idiosyncratic reaction resulting in choroidal effusion with visual field defect, transient myopia and acute angle-closure glaucoma.
The primary treatment is to discontinue drug intake as rapidly as possible.
Risk factors for developing acute angle-closure glaucoma may include a history of sulfonamide or penicillin allergy.

items.t: Acute respiratory toxicity (ARDS) very rarely, within minutes to hours of a dose: withdraw. Do not give hydrochlorothiazide to anyone who previously had ARDS after it.

src.q: If diagnosis of ARDS is suspected, Zestoretic should be withdrawn and appropriate treatment given.
Hydrochlorothiazide should not be administered to patients who previously experienced ARDS following hydrochlorothiazide intake.

items.t: Recent kidney transplant: should not be used. Not indicated in patients needing dialysis for renal failure. Anaphylactoid reactions with high-flux membranes and LDL apheresis with dextran sulphate: consider a different membrane or antihypertensive class; for apheresis, withholding the ACE inhibitor before each session avoided reactions. Anaphylactoid reactions also reported during desensitisation (e.g. hymenoptera venom).

src.q: Should not be used, since there is no experience with patients recently transplanted with a kidney.
The use of lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide is not indicated in patients requiring dialysis for renal failure.

Anaphylactoid reactions have been reported in patients, undergoing certain haemodialysis procedures (e.g. with the high-flux membranes AN 69 and during low-density lipoproteins (LDL) apheresis with dextran sulphate) and treated concomitantly with an ACE inhibitor.
In these patients consideration should be given to using a different type of dialysis membrane or a different class of antihypertensive agent.
These symptoms could be avoided by temporary discontinuation of the treatment with ACE inhibitors before each apheresis.
Patients receiving ACE inhibitors during desensitisation treatment (e.g. hymenoptera venom) have sustained anaphylactoid reactions.

items.t: Persistent dry cough can occur and resolves after stopping. Lisinopril may be less effective in black patients. Major surgery/anaesthesia: hypotension can be corrected by volume expansion. Hydrochlorothiazide may give a positive anti-doping test. Stop thiazides before parathyroid function tests.

src.q: Characteristically, the cough is non-productive, persistent and resolves after discontinuation of therapy.
lisinopril may be less effective in lowering blood pressure in black patients than in non-black patients
If hypotension occurs and is considered to be due to this mechanism, it can be corrected by volume expansion.
The hydrochlorothiazide contained in this medication could produce a positive analytic result in an anti-doping test.
Thiazides should be discontinued before carrying out tests for parathyroid function.

items.t: Potassium-sparing diuretics (e.g. spironolactone, amiloride), potassium supplements, potassium salt substitutes, trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole: significant rise in potassium, especially with renal impairment or diabetes. Combination not recommended; if needed, use with caution and monitor potassium frequently.

src.q: Use of potassium sparing diuretics (e.g. spironolactone, triamterene or amiloride), potassium supplements or potassium-containing salt substitutes, particularly in patients with impaired renal function or diabetes mellitus, may lead to a significant increase in serum potassium.
such as trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole
Therefore, the combination of Zestoretic with the above-mentioned drugs is not recommended.
they should be used with caution and with frequent monitoring of serum potassium

items.t: ARBs or aliskiren (dual RAAS blockade): more hypotension, hyperkalaemia and reduced renal function; not recommended. Aliskiren should be avoided (contraindicated with diabetes or GFR below 60).

src.q: is associated with a higher frequency of adverse events such as hypotension, hyperkalaemia and decreased renal function (including acute renal failure)
The combination of lisinopril with aliskiren-containing medicines should be avoided
Combination use of medicines from two classes of RAS blocking agents (ACE-inhibitors, ARBs, or aliskiren) is not recommended.

items.t: NSAIDs (including COX-2 inhibitors and aspirin above 3 g/day): reduced antihypertensive and diuretic effect; additive rise in potassium and worsening renal function, rarely acute renal failure (especially elderly or dehydrated).

src.q: Chronic administration of NSAID (selective cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors, acetylsalicylic acid >3 g/day and non-selective NSAIDs) may reduce the antihypertensive and diuretic effect of ACE inhibitors and thiazide diuretics.
NSAID and ACE inhibitors may exert an additive effect on the increase in serum potassium and may result in a deterioration of renal function.
Rarely, acute renal failure may occur, especially in patients with compromised renal function such as the elderly or dehydrated.

items.t: Torsades de pointes-inducing medicines (some antiarrhythmics, antipsychotics, others): use with caution because of hydrochlorothiazide-induced hypokalaemia.

src.q: Because of the risk of hypokalaemia the concomitant administration of hydrochlorothiazide and medicinal products that induce torsades de pointes
other drugs known to induce torsades de pointes, should be used with caution.

items.t: Potassium-losing medicines (corticosteroids, ACTH, stimulant laxatives, other kaliuretic diuretics such as loop diuretics, salicylic acid derivatives, amphotericin): greater potassium loss.

src.q: The potassium depleting effect of hydrochlorothiazide could be expected to be potentiated by drugs associated with potassium loss and hypokalaemia (e.g. other kaliuretic diuretics, laxatives, amphotericin, carbenoxolone, salicylic acid derivatives).
Hypokalemia may develop during concomitant use of steroids or adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH).

items.t: Antidiabetics including insulin: glucose tolerance may be impaired, mostly in the first weeks and in renal impairment; requirements may change. Monitor glycaemia closely in the first month.

src.q: Treatment with a thiazide diuretic may impair glucose tolerance.
Other antidiabetic drugs including insulin requirements in diabetic patients may be increased, decreased, or unchanged.
glycaemia levels should be closely monitored during the first month of treatment with an ACE inhibitor.

items.t: Other antihypertensives, nitrates and vasodilators: additive fall in blood pressure. Tricyclic antidepressants, antipsychotics and some anaesthetics: further BP lowering. Alcohol, barbiturates or anaesthetics: worse postural hypotension. Diuretics: stop 2-3 days before starting if possible.

src.q: When combined with other antihypertensive agents, additive falls in blood pressure may occur.
Concomitant use of certain anaesthetic medicinal products, tricyclic antidepressants and antipsychotics with ACE inhibitors may result in further lowering of blood pressure
Postural hypotension may become aggravated by simultaneous intake of alcohol, barbiturates or anaesthetics.
The diuretic therapy should be discontinued for 2-3 days prior to initiation of therapy with Zestoretic.

items.t: Calcium salts or vitamin D: thiazides can raise serum calcium; monitor calcium and adjust the dose.

src.q: Thiazide diuretics may increase serum calcium levels due to decreased excretion.
If calcium supplements or Vitamin D must be prescribed, serum calcium levels should be monitored and the dose adjusted accordingly.

items.t: Allopurinol: higher risk of renal damage and leucopenia. Methotrexate and other cytotoxics: thiazides may reduce their renal excretion and increase myelosuppression.

src.q: Concomitant administration of ACE inhibitors and allopurinol increases the risk of renal damage and can lead to an increased risk of leucopoenia.
Thiazides may reduce the renal excretion of cytotoxic medicinal products (e.g. cyclophosphamide, methotrexate) and potentiate their myelosuppressive effects

items.t: Sacubitril/valsartan: contraindicated. Racecadotril, vildagliptin, mTOR inhibitors and tissue plasminogen activator: higher angioedema risk.

src.q: Concomitant use of ACE inhibitors with sacubitril/valsartan is contraindicated as this increases the risk of angioedema
Concomitant use of ACE inhibitors with racecadotril, mTOR inhibitors (e.g. sirolimus, everolimus, temsirolimus,) and vildagliptin may lead to an increase in the risk of angioedema
Concomitant treatment with tissue plasminogen activators may increase the risk of angioedema.

items.t: Sympathomimetics can reduce the antihypertensive effect.

src.q: Sympathomimetics can reduce the antihypertensive effect of ACE inhibitors.

items.t: Lithium: high risk of lithium toxicity; not recommended; if necessary, monitor lithium levels carefully. Colestyramine/colestipol: take the thiazide at least 1 hour before or 4-6 hours after. Digoxin: hypokalaemia increases toxicity. Sotalol: hypokalaemia increases arrhythmia risk. Ciclosporin, heparin: monitor potassium. Lovastatin: higher hyperkalaemia risk. Injectable gold: nitritoid reactions. Amantadine: more adverse effects. Diazoxide: hyperglycaemic effect enhanced. Non-depolarising muscle relaxants: response may increase.

src.q: The combination of lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide with lithium is therefore not recommended and careful monitoring of serum lithium levels should be performed if the combination proves necessary
Therefore sulphonamide diuretics should be taken at least 1 hour before or 4-6 hours after intake of these agents.
Hypokalemia can sensitise or exaggerate the response of the heart to the toxic effects of digitalis
Thiazide induced hypokalaemia can increase the risk of sotalol induced arrhythmia.
Concomitant administration of ACE inhibitors and ciclosporin increases the risk of renal damage and hyperkalaemia. Monitoring of serum potassium is recommended.
Hyperkalaemia may occur during concomitant use of ACE inhibitors with heparin. Monitoring of serum potassium is recommended.
Concomitant administration of ACE inhibitors and lovastatin increases the risk of hyperkalaemia.
Nitritoid reactions (symptoms of vasodilatation including flushing, nausea, dizziness and hypotension, which can be very severe) following injectable gold
Thiazides may increase the risk of adverse effects caused by amantadine.
The hyperglycaemic effect of diazoxide may be enhanced by thiazides.
Thiazides may increase the responsiveness to non-depolarising skeletal muscle relaxants

items.t: CrCl below 30 mL/min: contraindicated. Thiazides are ineffective at CrCl 30 mL/min or below.

src.q: Severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance < 30 ml/min).
are ineffective at creatinine clearance values of 30 ml/min or below (i.e. moderate or severe renal insufficiency).

items.t: CrCl above 30 and below 80 mL/min: may be used, but only after titration of the separate components; never as initial therapy. Lisinopril alone in mild renal insufficiency: 5-10 mg.

src.q: In patients with creatinine clearance of >30 and <80 ml/min, Zestoretic may be used, but only after titration of the individual components.
Zestoretic is not to be used as initial therapy in any patient with renal insufficiency.
The recommended dose of lisinopril, when used alone, in mild renal insufficiency, is 5 to 10 mg.

items.t: SPS: seek specialist advice before starting an ACE inhibitor if eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73 m². A creatinine rise under 50% (if below 266 micromol/L) or eGFR fall under 10% (if eGFR over 25) can be acceptable.

src.q: Seek specialist advice prior to initiation for patients where there is: severe or unstable heart failure renovascular disease eGFR less than 30ml/min/1.73m2

An increase in serum creatinine of less than 50% above baseline, as long as it is less than 266 micromol/L, or a decrease in eGFR of less than 10% from baseline, as long as eGFR is over 25 mL/min/1.73 m2, can be considered as acceptable.

items.t: Severe hepatic impairment: contraindicated.

src.q: Anuria. Severe hepatic impairment.

items.t: Impaired liver function or progressive liver disease: use thiazides with caution (risk of hepatic coma). Stop if jaundice or marked liver enzyme rise.

src.q: Thiazides should be used with caution in patients with impaired hepatic function or progressive liver disease
Patients receiving lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide who develop jaundice or marked elevations of hepatic enzymes should discontinue lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide

items.t: SmPC (ACE inhibitor): not recommended in the first trimester; contraindicated in the second and third trimesters. Stop as soon as pregnancy is diagnosed and switch if appropriate. If exposed from the second trimester, ultrasound check of fetal kidneys and skull; observe the newborn for hypotension.

src.q: The use of ACE inhibitors is not recommended during the first trimester of pregnancy
The use of ACE inhibitors is contra-indicated during the second and third trimester of pregnancy
When pregnancy is diagnosed, treatment with ACE inhibitors should be stopped immediately, and, if appropriate, alternative therapy should be started.
Should exposure to ACE inhibitors have occurred from the second trimester of pregnancy, ultrasound check of renal function and skull is recommended.
Infants whose mothers have taken ACE inhibitors should be closely observed for hypotension

items.t: SmPC (hydrochlorothiazide): may reduce placental perfusion and cause fetal/neonatal jaundice, electrolyte disturbance and thrombocytopenia. Should not be used for gestational oedema, gestational hypertension or pre-eclampsia, nor for primary hypertension in pregnancy except in rare situations with no alternative.

src.q: may compromise foeto-placental perfusion and may cause foetal and neonatal effects like icterus, disturbance of electrolyte balance and thrombocytopenia.
Hydrochlorothiazide should not be used for gestational oedema, gestational hypertension or preeclampsia
Hydrochlorothiazide should not be used for primary hypertension in pregnant women except in rare situations where no other treatment could be used.

items.t: MHRA: ACE inhibitors should not be used at any stage of pregnancy unless absolutely necessary; stop as soon as possible on diagnosis.

src.q: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor antagonists should not be used at any stage of pregnancy unless absolutely necessary
On diagnosis of pregnancy, treatment with an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin II receptor antagonist should be stopped as soon as possible

items.t: BUMPS: ACE inhibitor use in early pregnancy is unlikely to harm the baby, but use after about 20 weeks can cause problems in the baby and needs extra monitoring. Diuretics can be used in pregnancy if prescribed, but may reduce placental blood flow; for high blood pressure a different medicine is usually offered.

src.q: Taking an ACE-I in early pregnancy is unlikely to harm your baby.
Taking an ACE-I after around 20 weeks of pregnancy can cause a number of problems in your baby
as your baby will need extra monitoring
Diuretics may reduce blood flow to the placenta.
If you take a diuretic to treat high blood pressure, you will usually be offered a different medicine that is known to be safe during pregnancy.

items.t: SmPC: not recommended. No information for the combination; hydrochlorothiazide passes into milk in small amounts and high thiazide doses can suppress milk production. If used, keep doses as low as possible; alternatives preferred, especially with a newborn or preterm infant.

src.q: The use of lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide during breast feeding is not recommended. If lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide is used during breast feeding, doses should be kept as low as possible.
alternative treatments with better established safety profiles during breast-feeding are preferable, especially while nursing a newborn or preterm infant.
Hydrochlorothiazide is excreted in human milk in small amounts.
Thiazides in high doses causing intense diuresis can inhibit the milk production.

items.t: MHRA (2009): lisinopril not recommended in breastfeeding; clarification: not absolutely contraindicated and may be prescribed if essential for the mother.

src.q: ramipril, lisinopril, fosinopril, trandolapril, moexipril, or perindopril: use in breastfeeding is not recommended
they are not absolutely contraindicated. Healthcare professionals may prescribe these medicines during breastfeeding if they consider that this treatment is essential for the lactating mother.

items.t: SPS (lisinopril component only): can be used with caution, enalapril preferred; monitor the infant for hypotension and, in younger infants, wet nappies. The SPS page does not cover hydrochlorothiazide.

src.q: Lisinopril can be used with caution during breastfeeding, but enalapril is preferred.
As a precaution, monitor the infant for hypotension which may manifest as drowsiness, lethargy, pallor, poor feeding and inadequate weight gain.
In younger infants, monitor for normal urine production (wet nappies).

items.t: Planning pregnancy: switch to an antihypertensive with an established pregnancy safety profile unless continued ACE inhibitor treatment is essential.

src.q: Unless continued ACE inhibitor therapy is considered essential, patients planning pregnancy should be changed to alternative anti-hypertensive treatments which have an established safety profile for use in pregnancy.

items.t: Most common: cough, dizziness, hypotension and headache (1-10%). Common with lisinopril: dizziness, headache, syncope, orthostatic hypotension, cough, diarrhoea, vomiting, renal dysfunction. Hydrochlorothiazide (frequency not known): electrolyte imbalance, hyperglycaemia, hyperuricaemia/gout, raised lipids, photosensitivity.

src.q: The most commonly reported ADRs are cough, dizziness, hypotension, and headache which may occur in 1 to 10% of treated patients.
Common Dizziness, headache, syncope.
Common Orthostatic effects (including orthostatic hypotension).
Common Diarrhoea, vomiting.
Common Renal dysfunction.
Anorexia, hyperglycaemia, glycosuria, hyperuricaemia
electrolyte imbalance (including hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, hypochloremic alkalosis and hypomagnesaemia), increases in cholesterol and triglycerides, gout.
Photosensitivity reactions, rash, systemic lupus erythematosus

items.t: Angioedema (face, lips, tongue, glottis, larynx; also intestinal): can occur at any time. Stop the ACE inhibitor at once and do not restart. Bradykinin-mediated angioedema may not respond to adrenaline. Airway involvement needs emergency treatment.

src.q: if angioedema is suspected in a patient taking an ACE inhibitor, discontinue the ACE inhibitor immediately and do not restart
bradykinin-mediated angioedema is unlikely to respond to standard anaphylaxis treatments including adrenaline (epinephrine)
This may occur at any time during therapy.
Very rare Pancreatitis, intestinal angioedema.
Patients with involvement of the tongue, glottis or larynx, are likely to experience airway obstruction
In such cases emergency therapy should be administered promptly.

items.t: Sudden reduced vision or eye pain (choroidal effusion, acute myopia, acute angle-closure glaucoma): stop as rapidly as possible; untreated it can cause permanent vision loss.

src.q: Symptoms include acute onset of decreased visual acuity or ocular pain and typically occur within hours to weeks of drug initiation.
The primary treatment is to discontinue drug intake as rapidly as possible.
Untreated acute angle-closure glaucoma can lead to permanent vision loss.

items.t: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (very rare): dyspnoea, fever, pulmonary deterioration and hypotension within minutes to hours; withdraw and treat.

src.q: At the onset, symptoms include dyspnoea, fever, pulmonary deterioration and hypotension.
If diagnosis of ARDS is suspected, Zestoretic should be withdrawn and appropriate treatment given.

items.t: Hyperkalaemia (uncommon); acute renal failure (rare); hyponatraemia (rare); SIADH (rare).

src.q: Uncommon Increases in blood urea, increases in serum creatinine, hyperkalaemia. Rare Hyponatraemia.
Rare Uraemia, acute renal failure.
Rare Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH).

items.t: Very rare: bone marrow depression, agranulocytosis; pancreatitis; hepatitis, jaundice, hepatic failure (stop if jaundice or marked enzyme rise); Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis. Non-melanoma skin cancer with hydrochlorothiazide.

src.q: Very rare Bone marrow depression, anaemia, thrombocytopenia, leucopenia, neutropenia, agranulocytosis
Very rare Pancreatitis, intestinal angioedema.
Very rare Hepatitis - either hepatocellular or cholestatic, jaundice and hepatic failure
Patients receiving lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide who develop jaundice or marked elevations of hepatic enzymes should discontinue lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide
toxic epidermal necrolysis, Stevens-Johnson Syndrome
Not Known Non-melanoma skin cancer (Basal cell carcinoma and Squamous cell carcinoma).

items.t: SPS baseline (ACE inhibitor): blood pressure, eGFR or serum creatinine, serum potassium, serum sodium. Starting is not normally appropriate if potassium is above 5.0 mmol/L.

src.q: Baseline Blood pressure Estimated glomerular filtration rate or Serum creatinine (for creatinine clearance) Serum potassium Serum sodium
Initiation not normally appropriate if pre-treatment potassium greater than 5.0mmol/L

items.t: SmPC: check serum electrolytes periodically; monitor renal function during the first few weeks; monitor glycaemia closely in the first month in diabetes; periodic white cell counts in collagen vascular disease or immunosuppression.

src.q: periodic determination of serum electrolytes should be performed at appropriate intervals.
renal function should be monitored during the first few weeks of lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide therapy.
In diabetic patients treated with oral antidiabetic agents or insulin, glycaemia levels should be closely monitored during the first month of treatment with an ACE inhibitor.
If lisinopril is used in such patients, periodic monitoring of white blood cell counts is advised

items.t: SPS (hypertension): renal function, sodium and potassium within 1-2 weeks of starting or a dose change (7 days with risk factors), BP within 1 month; once stable, annually. Repeat any time the patient is acutely unwell.

src.q: Hypertension Within 1 - 2 weeks Estimated glomerular filtration rate or Serum creatinine (for creatinine clearance) Serum sodium Serum potassium Within 1 month Blood pressure
Hypertension Annually Serum sodium Serum potassium
Repeat monitoring at any time patient acutely unwell or their renal function may be compromised.

items.t: Skin: advise regular checks for new or changed lesions; examine suspicious lesions (biopsy if needed).

src.q: advise them to regularly check for and report any new or changed skin lesions or moles
examine all suspicious moles or skin lesions (potentially including histological examination of biopsies)

items.t: SPS abnormal results: potassium 6.0 mmol/L or above in CKD - stop the ACE inhibitor (after other potassium-raising drugs) and seek specialist advice; sodium below 132 mmol/L - specialist advice. Stop if angioedema, jaundice/marked liver enzyme rise, ARDS or acute eye symptoms.

src.q: Value 6.0 mmol/L or above in people with CKD Stop ACEI/ARB after stopping other drugs that may increase potassium and seek specialist advice.
Sodium Value is below 132mmol/L Obtain specialist advice
if angioedema is suspected in a patient taking an ACE inhibitor, discontinue the ACE inhibitor immediately and do not restart
Patients receiving lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide who develop jaundice or marked elevations of hepatic enzymes should discontinue lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide
If diagnosis of ARDS is suspected, Zestoretic should be withdrawn and appropriate treatment given.
The primary treatment is to discontinue drug intake as rapidly as possible.

items.t: Once daily at about the same time each day. Lisinopril absorption is not affected by food.

src.q: should be taken at approximately the same time each day.
absorption is not affected by the presence of food.

items.t: If taking colestyramine or colestipol: take this medicine at least 1 hour before or 4-6 hours after.

src.q: sulphonamide diuretics should be taken at least 1 hour before or 4-6 hours after intake of these agents.

items.t: Seek urgent help for swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, or trouble breathing or swallowing, even after long use; do not take further doses.

src.q: even if you have been taking it for a long period without problems
seek urgent medical attention if you develop swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or experience difficulty breathing or swallowing whilst taking ACE inhibitors
do not take further doses of your ACE inhibitor if angioedema is suspected and inform a healthcare professional immediately

items.t: Skin cancer risk with long-term use: check skin regularly and report new or changed lesions or moles; limit sun and UV exposure and use sun protection.

src.q: advise them to regularly check for and report any new or changed skin lesions or moles
advise patients to limit their exposure to sunlight and UV rays and use adequate protection when exposed to sunlight and UV rays to minimise the risk of skin cancer

items.t: Report sudden blurred vision or eye pain at once.

src.q: Symptoms include acute onset of decreased visual acuity or ocular pain

items.t: Planning pregnancy or pregnant: contact the doctor to switch medicine.

src.q: If you are taking an ACE-I and planning a pregnancy you should speak to your GP or specialist to discuss switching to a different medicine before trying to conceive.
If you find out that you are pregnant whilst taking an ACE-I, you should contact your doctor as soon as possible so that you can be switched to another medicine.

items.t: Dizziness or tiredness can affect driving, especially at the start, after dose changes and with alcohol. Potassium-containing salt substitutes are not recommended with this medicine.

src.q: When driving vehicles or operating machines it should be taken into account that occasionally dizziness or tiredness may occur.
Especially at the start of the treatment or when the dose is modified, and also when used in combination with alcohol
potassium-containing salt substitutes
Therefore, the combination of Zestoretic with the above-mentioned drugs is not recommended.

items.t: Symptomatic treatment of acute diarrhoea (12 years and over); acute episodes of diarrhoea with irritable bowel syndrome in adults 18 and over after initial diagnosis by a doctor.

src.q: For the symptomatic treatment of acute diarrhoea in adults and children aged 12 years and over.
For the symptomatic treatment of acute episodes of diarrhoea associated with Irritable Bowel Syndrome in adults aged 18 years and over following initial diagnosis by a doctor.

items.t: Symptomatic treatment of acute diarrhoea (including acute exacerbations of chronic diarrhoea) for up to 5 days in adults and children over 9 years; chronic diarrhoea in adults.

src.q: For the symptomatic treatment of acute diarrhoea of any aetiology including acute exacerbations of chronic diarrhoea for periods of up to 5 days in adults and children over 9 years.
For the symptomatic treatment of chronic diarrhoea in adults.

items.t: MHRA: on general sale the maximum daily dose is 12 mg; from pharmacists 16 mg.

src.q: is available on general sale (maximum daily dose 12 mg) and from pharmacists (maximum daily dose 16 mg).

items.t: IBS use: only after IBS has been diagnosed by a doctor.

src.q: Only take this medicine to treat acute episodes of diarrhoea associated with Irritable Bowel Syndrome if your doctor has previously diagnosed IBS.

items.t: Adults and children over 12: 4 mg initially, then 2 mg after each loose stool. Maximum 12 mg (6 capsules) a day.

src.q: Adults and children over 12: 2 capsules (4 mg) initially followed by 1 capsule (2 mg) after every loose stool.
The maximum daily dose should not exceed 6 capsules (12 mg).

items.t: Adults 18 and over: 4 mg initially, then 2 mg after each loose stool. Maximum 12 mg a day.

src.q: Two capsules (4 mg) to be taken initially, followed by 1 capsule (2 mg) after every loose stool, or as previously advised by your doctor.

items.t: Adults and children over 12: 4 mg initially, then 2 mg after each loose stool; usual 6-8 mg a day. Maximum 16 mg (8 capsules) a day.

src.q: Adults and children over 12 years: Two capsules (4 mg) initially, followed by one capsule (2 mg) after each loose stool.
The usual dose is 3-4 capsules (6 mg - 8 mg) a day. The total daily dose should not exceed 8 capsules (16 mg).

items.t: Adults: start 4-8 mg a day in divided doses; adjust up to a maximum of 16 mg (8 capsules) a day. Maintenance can be given twice daily.

items.t: When inhibition of peristalsis must be avoided (risk of ileus, megacolon, toxic megacolon). Stop promptly if ileus, constipation or abdominal distension develop.

Imodium must be discontinued promptly when ileus, constipation or abdominal distension develop.

items.t: Overdose: cardiac events including QT and QRS prolongation and torsades de pointes, some fatal; overdose can unmask Brugada syndrome. Do not exceed the recommended dose or duration.

Patients should not exceed the recommended dose and/or the recommended duration of treatment.

items.t: MHRA: serious cardiac events (QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, cardiac arrest), including deaths, with high doses taken as a drug of abuse or to self-treat opioid withdrawal.

src.q: There have been reports of cardiac events including QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, and cardiac arrest in patients who have taken high or very high doses of loperamide as a drug of abuse or for self-treatment of opioid withdrawal.

items.t: History of drug abuse: caution. Loperamide is an opioid; abuse and misuse are described.

src.q: Caution is needed in patients with a history of drug abuse. Abuse and misuse of loperamide, has been described
Loperamide is an opioid with low bioavailability and limited potential to penetrate the blood brain barrier at therapeutic doses.

items.t: Hepatic impairment: use with caution (reduced first-pass metabolism; relative overdose may cause CNS toxicity).

src.q: this medicine should be used with caution in such patients because of reduced first pass metabolism, as it may result in a relative overdose leading to CNS toxicity.

items.t: Acute diarrhoea: no improvement within 48 hours - stop and see a doctor. Persistent diarrhoea needs investigation; replace fluid and electrolytes.

src.q: In acute diarrhoea, if clinical improvement is not observed within 48 hours, the administration of Imodium should be discontinued and patients should be advised to consult their doctor.
Use of this medicine does not preclude the administration of appropriate fluid and electrolyte replacement therapy.

items.t: AIDS: stop at the earliest signs of abdominal distension (toxic megacolon reported with infectious colitis).

src.q: Patients with AIDS treated with this medicine for diarrhoea should have therapy stopped at the earliest signs of abdominal distension.

items.t: Galactose intolerance, lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption: should not take (contains lactose).

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, the Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine because it contains lactose.

items.t: P-glycoprotein inhibitors (quinidine, ritonavir): 2-3-fold higher loperamide levels; clinical relevance at usual doses unknown.

src.q: Concomitant administration of loperamide (16 mg single dose) with quinidine, or ritonavir, which are both P-glycoprotein inhibitors, resulted in a 2 to 3-fold increase in loperamide plasma levels.

items.t: Itraconazole (3-4-fold), ketoconazole (5-fold) and gemfibrozil (about 2-fold) raise loperamide levels; itraconazole plus gemfibrozil gave a 13-fold rise in exposure. No CNS effects were seen in these studies.

src.q: resulted in a 3 to 4-fold increase in loperamide plasma concentrations
The combination of itraconazole and gemfibrozil resulted in a 4-fold increase in peak plasma levels of loperamide and a 13-fold increase in total plasma exposure.

items.t: Oral desmopressin: plasma levels rose 3-fold (slower gut motility).

src.q: Concomitant treatment with oral desmopressin resulted in a 3-fold increase of desmopressin plasma concentrations, presumably due to slower gastrointestinal motility.

items.t: Drugs with similar pharmacology may potentiate loperamide; drugs that speed GI transit may reduce its effect.

src.q: It is expected that drugs with similar pharmacological properties may potentiate loperamide's effect and that drugs that accelerate gastrointestinal transit may decrease its effect.

src.q: loperamide is only recommended during pregnancy if there is no suitable alternative, as there is not enough information to say it is safe for the baby.
It is unclear if there is any risk.

items.t: Small amounts may pass into breast milk: not recommended during breastfeeding.

src.q: Small amounts of loperamide may appear in human breast milk. Therefore, this medicine is not recommended during breast-feeding.

items.t: Severe symptomatic hypomagnesaemia: give IV magnesium first to restore levels, before oral magnesium glycerophosphate.

src.q: Patients with severe, symptomatic hypomagnesaemia should receive intravenous magnesium repletion for acute recovery of magnesium levels prior to receiving Neomag.

items.t: Adults (over 18 years): start 4-8 mmol (1-2 tablets) three times a day (12-24 mmol/day in divided doses); adjust to serum total magnesium. Elderly: no dose adjustment.

src.q: Starting doses for adult patients are recommended as 4-8 mmol (1-2 tablets) administered 3 times a day.
This equates to a total dose of 12 to 24 mmol per day taken in divided doses.
Elderly: No dose adjustment is necessary.

items.t: SPS (mild hypomagnesaemia, 0.5-0.7 mmol/L): total daily oral dose 10-24 mmol magnesium in divided doses. Commonly given for up to 7 days, then recheck serum magnesium; continue 1-2 days after levels normalise.
items.tag: SPS: mild acute hypomagnesaemia in adults

src.q: Give a total daily oral dose of 10 to 24mmol of magnesium in divided doses.
It is common practice to prescribe oral magnesium replacement for up to 7 days and then repeat the serum magnesium level.
Continue treatment for 1 to 2 days after magnesium levels normalise.

items.t: Start low (e.g. 1 tablet per dose) and increase gradually to the maximum tolerated dose.

src.q: Start with a low dose, such as 1 tablet per dose, and gradually increase to a maximum tolerated dose.

items.t: Under 4 years: not recommended (insufficient information).

src.q: Children: below 4 years : Not recommended as there is insufficient information regarding the use of Neomag tablets in this age group.

items.t: 4 to 12 years: start 4 mmol (1 tablet) twice a day (8 mmol/day); adjust to serum total magnesium.

src.q: A starting dose for children 4 to 12 years is recommended as 4 mmol (1 tablet) administered 2 times a day.
This equates to a total dose of 8 mmol per day taken in divided doses.

items.t: 12 to 18 years: start 4 mmol (1 tablet) three times a day (12 mmol/day); adjust to serum total magnesium.

src.q: A starting dose for children 12 to 18 years is recommended as 4 mmol (1 tablet) administered 3 times a day.
This equates to a total dose of 12 mmol per day taken in divided doses.

items.t: Use only under supervision of physicians experienced in childhood hypomagnesaemia; monitor serum magnesium regularly.

src.q: under the supervision of physicians experienced in the management of children with hypomagnesaemia

items.t: Hypersensitivity to magnesium glycerophosphate or any excipient.

src.q: Do not administer Neomag tablets if there is evidence of hypersensitivity to the active substance

items.t: Severe renal impairment (glomerular filtration rate < 30 ml/min).

src.q: Neomag is contraindicated in patients with severe renal impairment (glomerularfiltration rate < 30 ml/min).

items.t: Should not be given in phenylketonuria (contains aspartame) or hyperphosphataemia (contains phosphate). Both are listed in SmPC 4.3.

src.q: Neomag should not be administered to patients with phenylketonuria as Neomag tablets contain Aspartame.
Neomag should not be administered to patients with hyperphosphataemia as Neomag tablets contain phosphate.

items.t: Absorption may be reduced after extensive bowel resection.

src.q: in patients who have undergone extensive bowel resection the absorption of magnesium may be reduced

items.t: Look for and correct hypocalcaemia and hypokalaemia, which often occur with magnesium deficiency.

src.q: concomitant hypocalcaemia and hypokalaemia should be suspected and corrected if confirmed

items.t: Hypermagnesaemia is possible with higher doses and impaired renal function.

src.q: Hypermagnesaemia is possible with higher doses and with impaired renal function.

items.t: Magnesium and other medicines can affect each other's absorption: generally keep 2 to 3 hours apart where possible.

src.q: As magnesium and other medicinal products may mutually influence each other's absorption, a time interval of 2 to 3 hours should generally be respected if possible.

items.t: Iron, aminoquinolines (e.g. hydroxychloroquine), quinidine, nitrofurantoin, penicillamine, bisphosphonates, eltrombopag, nitroxoline: take magnesium 3 to 4 hours before or after these.

src.q: Aminoquinolines, quinidine and quinidine derivatives, nitrofurantoin, penicillamine, iron, bisphosphonates (such as alendronate and risedronate), eltrombopag, nitroxoline
magnesium preparations should be taken 3 to 4 hours before or after the administration of those drugs

items.t: Ciprofloxacin SmPC: give ciprofloxacin 1-2 hours before or at least 4 hours after magnesium-containing products.

src.q: multivalent cation-containing drugs and mineral supplements (e.g. calcium, magnesium, aluminium, iron)
ciprofloxacin should be administered either 1-2 hours before or at least 4 hours after these preparations

items.t: Proton pump inhibitors (e.g. omeprazole), thiazide and loop diuretics, aminoglycosides, cisplatin, ciclosporin and others increase magnesium loss: the magnesium dose may need adjusting.

src.q: Because of increased magnesium losses, a dose adjustment of magnesium may be necessary when taking the following substances
proton pump inhibitors (such as omeprazole and pantoprazole)

items.t: Tetracyclines and fluorides: separate doses by 2 to 3 hours or more.

src.q: Fluorides and tetracycline : if they must be used, the doses must be separated by 2 to 3 hours or more

items.t: Digoxin: magnesium deficiency may enhance digoxin toxicity.

src.q: Magnesium deficiency may enhance digoxin toxicity.

items.t: SmPC: contraindicated if glomerular filtration rate < 30 ml/min. No dose adjustment in mild to moderate renal impairment.

src.q: Neomag is contraindicated in patients with severe renal impairment (glomerularfiltration rate < 30 ml/min).
There is no dose adjustment necessary in patients with mild to moderate renal impairment.

items.t: SPS: seek specialist advice before magnesium replacement in severe kidney disease (CKD 4 or 5), acute kidney injury, dialysis or kidney transplant. No oral dose adjustment needed in CKD 1 to 3.

src.q: Seek specialist advice before prescribing magnesium replacement to patients with the following: severe kidney disease (CKD 4 or 5) acute kidney injury receiving dialysis a kidney transplant
No dose adjustments are needed for oral magnesium replacement.

items.t: SPS (general, all routes): lower doses may be required in renal impairment because of the risk of hypermagnesaemia.

src.q: Lower doses may be required in renal impairment due to the risk of hypermagnesaemia.

items.t: Monitor serum magnesium regularly, especially in renal impairment.

src.q: particularly in children and in patients with renal impairment

hepatic.note: No hepatic impairment advice in the magnesium glycerophosphate SmPC or the SPS hypomagnesaemia page.

items.t: Safety not established in pregnancy: use only if benefits outweigh risks. Long-term data from pre-eclampsia treatment do not suggest malformative or fetal/neonatal toxicity of magnesium.

src.q: Neomag tablets should only be used in pregnancy if the benefits of the treatment outweigh any potential risks.
long-term data available from treatment of pre-eclampsia do not indicate malformative or feto/neonatal toxicity of magnesium

items.t: Can be used during breastfeeding; passes into milk but no effects on the infant are expected at therapeutic doses.

src.q: Neomag can be used during breast-feeding.
at therapeutic doses of Neomag no effects on the breastfed newborns/infants are anticipated

items.t: No effects on male or female fertility are expected.

src.q: no effects of magnesium on male and female fertility are anticipated

items.t: Diarrhoea, usually dose dependent: reduce the daily dose, then increase gradually if needed. Frequency not stated.

src.q: Neomag may cause diarrhoea, which is usually dose dependent.
If diarrhoea occurs, the daily dose should be reduced and gradually increased later if needed.

items.t: Hypermagnesaemia (flushing, thirst, low blood pressure, drowsiness, confusion, loss of tendon reflexes, muscle weakness, respiratory depression, arrhythmias): stop magnesium; IV calcium gluconate in severe toxicity.

src.q: Hypermagnesaemia characterised by flushing, thirst, hypotension, drowsiness, nausea, vomiting, confusion, loss of tendon reflexes due to neuromuscular blockade, muscle weakness, respiratory depression, cardiac arrhythmias, coma and cardiac arrest.
When hypermagnesaemia is found, magnesium therapy should be withdrawn

items.t: Persistent diarrhoea or symptoms: IV replacement may be needed (SPS).

src.q: If diarrhoea persists or the patient becomes symptomatic, IV magnesium replacement may be necessary.

items.t: Before and during treatment: adjust the dose to the serum total magnesium level; look for and correct hypocalcaemia and hypokalaemia.

src.q: The dosage regimen should be adjusted according to the serum total magnesium level of the individual patient.
concomitant hypocalcaemia and hypokalaemia should be suspected and corrected if confirmed

items.t: SmPC: monitor serum magnesium at regular intervals (e.g. every 3-6 months), especially in children and renal impairment.

src.q: It is recommended that serum magnesium levels should be monitored at regular intervals (e.g. every 3-6 months)

items.t: SPS: repeat serum magnesium 7 days after starting oral therapy and again after 1 to 3 months; also monitor serum calcium, potassium and renal function.

src.q: Repeat the serum magnesium level 7 days after starting oral therapy and again after 1 to 3 months
serum calcium and potassium renal function

items.t: If hypermagnesaemia develops, withdraw magnesium.

src.q: When hypermagnesaemia is found, magnesium therapy should be withdrawn

items.t: Tablets may be broken into quarters and chewed or swallowed with water.

src.q: The tablet may be broken into quarters and chewed or swallowed with water.

items.t: SPS: take with meals and in divided doses.

src.q: Advise patients to take oral magnesium with meals and in divided doses.

items.t: May cause diarrhoea; tell the prescriber if it happens (dose can be reduced).

src.q: If diarrhoea occurs, the daily dose should be reduced and gradually increased later if needed.

items.t: Contains aspartame (a source of phenylalanine): not for people with phenylketonuria.

src.q: Neomag should not be administered to patients with phenylketonuria as Neomag tablets contain Aspartame.

items.t: Keep 3 to 4 hours apart from iron tablets and some other medicines.

src.q: magnesium preparations should be taken 3 to 4 hours before or after the administration of those drugs

items.t: Gastrointestinal worm infections, single or mixed: threadworm/pinworm (Enterobius), whipworm (Trichuris), roundworm (Ascaris), hookworms (Ancylostoma, Necator). Not shown to work for cysticercosis.

src.q: For the treatment of Trichuris trichuria (whipworm), Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm or threadworm), Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm), Ancylostoma duodenale (common hookworm), Necator americanus (American hookworm) in single or mixed gastrointestinal infestations.
There is no evidence that Vermox Tablets are effective in the treatment of cysticercosis.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction (specialist-only, shared care or brand prescribing) in the UK tablet and suspension SmPCs checked.

items.t: Threadworm (enterobiasis): 100 mg (one tablet or 5 ml) as a single dose; a second dose after 2 weeks is highly recommended if re-infection is suspected.

src.q: For the control of enterobiasis a single tablet is administered. It is highly recommended that a second tablet is taken after two weeks, if re-infection is suspected.
Enterobiasis: 1 x 5 ml (1 dosing cup).

items.t: Whipworm, roundworm, hookworm and mixed infections: 100 mg (one tablet or 5 ml) twice daily for 3 days.

src.q: For the control of trichuriasis, ascariasis and hookworm infections, one tablet twice a day for three consecutive days.
Ascariasis, trichuriasis, ancylostomiasis, necatoriasis and mixed infections: 1 x 5 ml (1 dosing cup) bd for three days.

items.t: Over 2 years: adult dose. Under 2 years: not recommended (section 4.4); not well studied and no dose recommendation can be made. Children 1 to 2 years: use only if the potential benefit justifies the risk and the worms significantly affect nutrition or development. Under 1 year: should not be used. Convulsions have been reported very rarely in children, including infants under 1 year.

src.q: Not recommended in the treatment of children under 2 years
Because of the lack of sufficient safety data, Vermox should not be used in children below the age of 1 year
Therefore, Vermox should be used in children aged 1-2 years only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk.
Convulsions in children, including in infants below 1 year of age, have been reported very rarely during post-marketing experience

items.t: Young children who cannot swallow tablets: consider the suspension. Tablets can be crushed for a young child; always supervise.

src.q: Crush the tablet before giving it to a young child. Always supervise a child while they are taking this medicine.

items.t: Pregnancy; hypersensitivity to mebendazole or any component.

src.q: Vermox is contraindicated in pregnancy and in patients who have shown hypersensitivity to the product or any components.

items.t: Metronidazole: avoid using together (a possible link with Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN in one outbreak).

src.q: Although there are no additional data on this potential interaction, concomitant use of mebendazole and metronidazole should be avoided.

items.t: Rare reversible liver function disturbances, hepatitis and neutropenia at usual doses; agranulocytosis and glomerulonephritis in high-dose echinococcosis treatment.

src.q: There have been rare reports of reversible liver function disturbances, hepatitis and neutropenia described in patients who were treated with mebendazole at recommended dosages for indicated conditions

items.t: Children under 2 years: not recommended (see paediatric).

src.q: Not recommended in the treatment of children under 2 years

items.t: Suspension: contains sucrose; hereditary fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take it.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take this medicine.

items.t: Impaired liver function, metabolism or biliary elimination may raise mebendazole levels.

src.q: Impaired hepatic function, impaired metabolism, or impaired biliary elimination may lead to higher plasma levels of mebendazole.

items.t: Metronidazole: avoid the combination (possible Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN).

src.q: Concomitant use of mebendazole and metronidazole should be avoided (see section 4.4).

items.t: Cimetidine may inhibit mebendazole metabolism and raise its levels.

src.q: Concomitant treatment with cimetidine may inhibit the metabolism of mebendazole in the liver, resulting in increased plasma concentrations of the drug.

renal.note: The UK tablet and suspension SmPCs give no renal dosing advice.

items.t: No dose advice. Mainly metabolised by the liver; impaired hepatic function or biliary elimination may raise mebendazole levels. Rare reversible liver function disturbances and hepatitis reported.

src.q: Impaired hepatic function, impaired metabolism, or impaired biliary elimination may lead to higher plasma levels of mebendazole.

items.t: SmPC: contraindicated in pregnancy; anyone who is or may be pregnant should not take it (animal studies showed developmental harm).

src.q: Since Vermox is contraindicated in pregnancy, patients who think they are, or may be, pregnant should not take this preparation.

items.t: BUMPS (UKTIS): threadworms do not harm the baby. Strict hygiene measures may clear them; if not, or if medicine is preferred, mebendazole can be used: no evidence of harm and little is absorbed. Some may prefer hygiene measures first and delay mebendazole until after about 12 weeks.

src.q: If hygiene measures do not clear up threadworms, or medicine use is preferred, mebendazole (Vermox®, Ovex®) can be used.
There is no evidence that mebendazole harms the baby, and it is only absorbed into the body in small amounts.
some women may prefer to try hygiene measures first and delay mebendazole treatment until the baby is fully developed at around 12 weeks of pregnancy

items.t: A small amount passes into breast milk: use with caution.

src.q: Therefore, caution should be exercised when Vermox is administered to breast-feeding women.

items.t: No effect on fetuses and offspring when given to male and female rats before conception. BUMPS: no increased risk expected if the father used mebendazole around conception.

src.q: had no effect upon fetuses and offspring
We would not expect any increased risk to your baby if the father had threadworms or used mebendazole before or around the time your baby was conceived.

items.t: Common: abdominal pain. Uncommon: abdominal discomfort, diarrhoea, flatulence, nausea, vomiting.

src.q: Gastrointestinal Disorders Abdominal paina Abdominal discomforta; Diarrhoeaa; Flatulencea Nauseaa, Vomitinga

items.t: Rare: hypersensitivity including anaphylaxis, convulsions, hepatitis, neutropenia/agranulocytosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, angioedema, glomerulonephritis.

src.q: Hypersensitivity including anaphylactic reaction and anaphylactoid reactionb
Toxic epidermal necrolysisb; Stevens-Johnson syndromeb

monitoring.note: The UK tablet and suspension SmPCs give no routine monitoring advice for standard short courses.

items.t: Tablets may be chewed or swallowed whole; crush for a young child and supervise. Suspension: use the 5 ml dosing cup; consider it for young children who cannot swallow tablets.

src.q: Tablets may be chewed or swallowed whole.
Vermox oral suspension should be considered for patients such as young children who are unable to swallow the tablet.

items.t: Threadworm: take a second dose after 2 weeks if re-infection is suspected.

src.q: It is highly recommended that a second tablet is taken after two weeks, if re-infection is suspected.

items.t: Do not take if you are or may be pregnant (SmPC).

src.q: patients who think they are, or may be, pregnant should not take this preparation

items.t: Symptomatic relief of irritable bowel syndrome.

src.q: For the symptomatic relief of irritable bowel syndrome.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction stated in the UK SmPC accessed (UK 200 mg modified-release capsule SmPC).

items.t: Adults: 200 mg (one capsule) twice daily, one in the morning and one in the evening. Duration of use is not limited.

src.q: One capsule of 200 mg twice daily, to be given one in the morning and one in the evening.
Duration of use is not limited.

items.t: Elderly, renal or hepatic impairment: no dose adjustment considered necessary (no dedicated studies).

src.q: No dosage adjustment is deemed necessary in elderly, renal and/or hepatic impaired patients.

items.t: Not recommended under 18 years (insufficient safety and efficacy data).

src.q: not recommended for use in children and adolescents below 18, due to insufficient data on safety and efficacy

items.t: Hypersensitivity to mebeverine or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Contains sucrose: patients with hereditary fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take it.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrose-isomaltese insufficiency should not take this medicine.

items.t: No interaction studies except with alcohol; animal studies showed no interaction with ethanol.

src.q: No interaction studies have been performed, except with alcohol.
demonstrated the absence of any interaction between mebeverine hydrochloride and ethanol

items.t: No dose adjustment considered necessary in renal impairment (no posology studies; no specific risk seen post-marketing).

src.q: No posology studies in elderly, renal and/or hepatic impaired patients have been performed.
No dosage adjustment is deemed necessary in elderly, renal and/or hepatic impaired patients.

items.t: No dose adjustment considered necessary in hepatic impairment (no posology studies; no specific risk seen post-marketing).

src.q: No posology studies in elderly, renal and/or hepatic impaired patients have been performed.
No dosage adjustment is deemed necessary in elderly, renal and/or hepatic impaired patients.

items.t: SmPC: no or limited human data; not recommended in pregnancy.

src.q: There are no or limited amounts of data from the use of mebeverine in pregnant women.
Mebeverine is not recommended during pregnancy.

items.t: BUMPS: antispasmodics are occasionally used in pregnancy when needed to control IBS or diverticular disease; very little information, so safety for the baby is unclear.

src.q: Antispasmodics are occasionally used in pregnancy if they are needed to control diverticular disease or IBS.
There is very little information on women taking antispasmodics in pregnancy so it unclear if they are safe for the baby.

items.t: SmPC: not known if it passes into milk; should not be used during breastfeeding.

src.q: It is unknown whether mebeverine or its metabolites are excreted in human milk.
Mebeverine should not be used during breast-feeding.

items.t: SPS: can be used with caution; low milk levels expected; monitor the infant for allergic reactions or unusual behaviour.

src.q: Mebeverine can be used during breastfeeding, but infant monitoring is required.
monitor infants for allergic reactions or any other signs of unusual behaviour

items.t: No clinical fertility data; animal studies show no harmful effect.

src.q: There are no clinical data on male or female fertility; however, animal studies do not indicate harmful effects of mebeverine

adverseCommon.note: The UK 200 mg modified-release capsule SmPC lists only post-marketing reactions with no frequency (see serious adverse effects).

items.t: Hypersensitivity including anaphylactic reactions; urticaria, angioedema, face oedema, exanthema (frequency not known).

src.q: Hypersensitivity (anaphylactic reactions)
Urticaria, angioedema, face oedema, exanthema.

monitoring.note: No monitoring requirements stated in the UK SmPC accessed (UK 200 mg modified-release capsule SmPC); no SPS monitoring page found.

items.t: Swallow capsules with plenty of water (at least 100 mL); do not chew (modified-release coating).

src.q: The capsules should be swallowed with a sufficient amount of water (at least 100 ml water). They should not be chewed because the coating is intended to ensure a prolonged release mechanism

items.t: Missed dose: carry on with the next dose; do not take extra to make up.

src.q: the missed dose(s) should not be taken in addition to the regular dose

items.t: Not expected to affect driving or using machines.

src.q: do not indicate any harmful effect of mebeverine on the ability to drive or to use machines

items.t: Anti-inflammatory analgesic for rheumatoid arthritis (including Still's disease), osteoarthritis, and muscular, traumatic, dental, headache, post-operative and postpartum pain; pyrexia in children.

src.q: As an anti-inflammatory analgesic for the symptomatic relief of rheumatoid arthritis (including Still's Disease), osteoarthritis, and pain including muscular, traumatic and dental pain
headaches of most aetiology, post-operative and postpartum pain; pyrexia in children.

items.t: Primary dysmenorrhoea; menorrhagia due to dysfunctional causes or an IUD once other pelvic pathology is ruled out.

src.q: Primary dysmenorrhoea.
Menorrhagia due to dysfunctional causes and presence of an IUD when other pelvic pathology has been ruled out.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction stated in the UK SmPCs (two UK 250 mg capsule SmPCs) or the MHRA/SPS pages accessed.

items.t: Adults: 500 mg (2 capsules) three times daily. Do not exceed the stated dose; lowest effective dose for the shortest time.

src.q: Adults 2 capsules (500 mg) three times daily.
Do not exceed the stated dose.
Undesirable effects may be minimised by using the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration necessary to control symptoms

items.t: Menorrhagia: start on the first day of excessive bleeding. Dysmenorrhoea: start at the onset of menstrual pain. Continue as the physician judges.

src.q: In menorrhagia to be administered on the first day of excessive bleeding and continued according to the judgment of the physician.
In dysmenorrhoea to be administered at the onset of menstrual pain and continued according to the judgment of the physician.

items.t: Elderly (over 65): adult dose, but higher risk of serious adverse effects; lowest dose for the shortest time, monitor regularly for GI bleeding; caution with dehydration and renal disease.

src.q: Elderly (over 65 years) As for adults.
The patient should be monitored regularly for GI bleeding during NSAID therapy
should be used with caution in elderly patients suffering from dehydration and renal disease.

items.t: Under 12 years: one UK SmPC recommends the 50 mg/5 ml suspension instead of capsules; another UK capsule SmPC says not recommended under 12.

src.q: It is recommended that children under 12 years of age should be given Mefenamic Acid Suspension (50 mg / 5 ml).
Children (under 12 years): Not recommended.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to mefenamic acid or excipients; previous hypersensitivity (asthma, bronchospasm, rhinitis, angioedema, urticaria) to aspirin, ibuprofen or other NSAIDs.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.
mefenamic acid must not be given to patients who have previously shown hypersensitivity reaction (e.g. asthma, bronchospasm, rhinitis, angioedema or urticaria) to these medicines.

items.t: Inflammatory bowel disease; history of GI bleeding or perforation related to previous NSAIDs; active or history of recurrent peptic ulcer/haemorrhage.

src.q: Inflammatory bowel disease.
History of gastrointestinal bleeding or perforation, related to previous NSAIDs therapy.
Active, or history of recurrent peptic ulcer/haemorrhage (two or more distinct episodes of proven ulceration or bleeding).

items.t: Severe heart failure, hepatic failure, renal failure; last trimester of pregnancy; pain after coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery.

src.q: Severe heart failure, hepatic failure and renal failure (see section 4.4).
During the last trimester of pregnancy (see section 4.6).
Treatment of pain after coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery.

items.t: The generic capsule SmPC also lists intestinal ulceration and use with other NSAIDs (including COX-2 inhibitors) in section 4.3; the originator SmPC lists other NSAIDs under warnings and interactions only.

src.q: intestinal ulceration and history of upper gastrointestinal bleeding or perforation
Use with concomitant NSAIDs including cyclo oxygenase 2 specific inhibitors (See section 4.5 Interactions).

items.t: GI bleeding, ulceration or perforation can occur at any time and can be fatal; risk rises with dose, ulcer history and age; smoking and alcohol add risk. Consider gastroprotection (misoprostol or a PPI) in those at risk. Withdraw if GI bleeding or ulceration occurs.

src.q: GI bleeding, ulceration or perforation, which can be fatal, has been reported with all NSAIDs at any time during treatment
Smoking and alcohol use are added risk factors.
Combination therapy with protective agents (e.g. misoprostol or proton pump inhibitors) should be considered for patients at risk of GI bleeding
When GI bleeding or ulceration occurs in patients receiving mefenamic acid the treatment should be withdrawn.

items.t: Cardiovascular: uncontrolled hypertension, congestive heart failure, ischaemic heart disease, peripheral arterial or cerebrovascular disease only after careful consideration; a thrombotic risk cannot be excluded. Hypertension or mild to moderate heart failure needs monitoring and advice (fluid retention, oedema).

src.q: Patients with uncontrolled hypertension, congestive heart failure, established ischaemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease, and/or cerebrovascular disease should only be treated with mefenamic acid after careful consideration.
There are insufficient data to exclude such a risk for mefenamic acid.
Appropriate monitoring and advice are required for patients with a history of hypertension and/or mild to moderate congestive heart failure

items.t: Renal: may precipitate renal failure; highest risk with renal, cardiac or liver impairment, diuretics and in the elderly; monitor renal function. Take precautions in dehydration and renal disease.

src.q: precipitate renal failure
Patients at greatest risk of this reaction are those with impaired renal function, cardiac impairment, liver dysfunction, those taking diuretics and the elderly.
Renal function should be monitored in these patients
Precaution should be taken in patients suffering from dehydration and renal disease, particularly the elderly.

items.t: Asthma (current or past): caution, bronchospasm possible. Intracranial haemorrhage or bleeding diathesis: use with caution (platelet effects). Epilepsy: caution.

src.q: Caution is required if administered to patients suffering from, or with a previous history of, bronchial asthma
they should be used in caution in patients with intracranial haemorrhage and bleeding diathesis
Caution should be exercised when treating patients suffering from epilepsy.

items.t: Diarrhoea: withdraw immediately and do not give mefenamic acid again (associated with proctocolitis). Prolonged therapy: watch for liver dysfunction, rash, blood dyscrasias or diarrhoea, and stop immediately if they appear.

src.q: If diarrhoea does develop the drug should be withdrawn immediately and this patient should not receive mefenamic acid again.
Patients on prolonged therapy should be kept under regular surveillance with particular attention to liver dysfunction, rash, blood dyscrasias or development of diarrhoea.
Appearance of any of these symptoms should be regarded as an indication to stop therapy immediately

items.t: Serious skin reactions (exfoliative dermatitis, SJS, TEN), mostly in the first month: stop at the first rash, mucosal lesion or sign of hypersensitivity.

src.q: Mefenamic acid should be stopped at the first appearance of skin rash, mucosal lesions or any other sign of hypersensitivity.

items.t: SLE / mixed connective tissue disease: possible increased risk of aseptic meningitis. Known or suspected poor CYP2C9 metabolisers: use with caution (raised plasma levels).

src.q: In patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and mixed connective tissue disorders there may be an increased risk of aseptic meningitis
In patients who are known or suspected to be poor CYP2C9 metabolisers based on previous history/experience with other CYP2C9 substrates, mefenamic acid should be administered with caution

items.t: Medication-overuse headache with prolonged use for headaches: stop treatment. Lactose: hereditary galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine. Lack of response in dysmenorrhoea or menorrhagia: look for other causes.

src.q: Prolonged use of any type of painkiller for headaches can make them worse.
Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
In dysmenorrhoea and menorrhagia lack of response should alert the physician to investigate other causes.

items.t: Anticoagulants such as warfarin: NSAIDs may enhance the effect; oral anticoagulants need careful prothrombin time monitoring; NSAIDs with warfarin or heparin are considered unsafe unless under direct medical supervision.

src.q: NSAIDs may enhance the effects of anti-coagulants, such as warfarin
Concurrent administration of mefenamic acid with oral anti-coagulant drugs requires careful prothrombin time monitoring.
It is considered unsafe to take NSAIDs in combination with warfarin or heparin unless under direct medical supervision.

items.t: Other NSAIDs, including aspirin and COX-2 inhibitors: avoid two or more together. Antiplatelets, SSRIs, corticosteroids: increased GI bleeding/ulceration risk; use with caution.

src.q: Avoid concomitant use of two or more NSAIDs (including aspirin) as this may increase the risk of adverse effects

Caution should be advised in patients receiving concomitant medications which could increase the risk of gastrotoxicity or bleeding such as corticosteroids, anticoagulants such as warfarin, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors or anti-platelet agents such as aspirin

items.t: Low-dose aspirin: experimental data suggest mefenamic acid may interfere with its antiplatelet effect; no firm conclusion for regular use.

src.q: Experimental data implies that mefenamic acid interferes with the anti-platelet effect of low-dose aspirin when given concomitantly
no firm conclusions can be made for regular mefenamic acid use

items.t: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin-II receptor antagonists: reduced antihypertensive effect and risk of renal impairment (especially elderly); keep hydrated and assess renal function at the start and during use. Diuretics and antihypertensives: reduced effect; diuretics increase nephrotoxicity.

src.q: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin-II-receptor antagonists: A reduction in antihypertensive effect and an increased risk of renal impairment especially in elderly patients.
Patients should be adequately hydrated, and the renal function assessed in the beginning and during concomitant therapy.
Antihypertensives and diuretics: A reduction in antihypertensive and diuretic effect has been observed.
Diuretics can increase the nephrotoxicity of NSAIDs.

items.t: Sulfonylureas: inhibited metabolism, longer half-life, increased hypoglycaemia risk. Methotrexate: reduced elimination, higher levels. Quinolone antibiotics: possible increased convulsion risk. Aminoglycosides: reduced renal function and higher aminoglycoside levels.

src.q: Oral hypoglycaemic agents : Inhibition of metabolism of sulfonylurea drugs, prolonged half-life and increased risk of hypoglycaemia.
Methotrexate: Elimination of the drug can be reduced, resulting in increased plasma levels.
Patients taking NSAIDs and quinolones may have an increased risk of developing convulsions.
Aminoglycosides : Reduction in renal function in susceptible individuals, decreased elimination of aminoglycoside and increased plasma concentrations.

items.t: Others: lithium (raised levels; watch for toxicity), cardiac glycosides (raised levels, worse heart failure), ciclosporin and tacrolimus (nephrotoxicity), zidovudine (haematological toxicity), probenecid (reduced NSAID elimination), mifepristone (no NSAIDs for 8-12 days after), other plasma-protein-bound drugs (dose change may be needed).

src.q: Patients should be observed carefully for signs of lithium toxicity.
NSAIDs may exacerbate cardiac failure, reduce GFR and increase plasma cardiac glycoside levels.
The risk of nephrotoxicity of ciclosporin may be increased with NSAIDs.
Zidovudine: Increased risk of haematological toxicity when NSAIDs are given with zidovudine.
NSAIDs should not be taken for 8-12 days after mifepristone administration
Concurrent therapy with other plasma protein binding drugs may necessitate a modification in dosage.

items.t: Warfarin (warfarin SmPC): NSAIDs should be avoided, or given with caution and increased clinical and laboratory monitoring.

src.q: The following examples should be avoided, or administered with caution with increased clinical and laboratory monitoring
NSAIDs (including aspirin and cox-2 specific NSAIDS)

items.t: Spironolactone (spironolactone SmPC): NSAIDs such as mefenamic acid may reduce its diuretic effect; NSAIDs with spironolactone may lead to severe hyperkalaemia. ACE inhibitors (lisinopril SmPC): worsening renal function and raised potassium; caution, especially in the elderly. Metformin (metformin SmPC): close renal monitoring.

src.q: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as aspirin, indomethacin, and mefenamic acid may attenuate the natriuretic efficacy of diuretics
may lead to severe hyperkalaemia
The combination should be administered with caution, especially in the elderly.
When starting or using such products in combination with metformin, close monitoring of renal function is necessary.

items.t: Methotrexate (SPS, methotrexate SmPC): increased toxicity risk; use with caution on specialist advice; not recommended with any renal impairment.

src.q: Use NSAIDs in combination with methotrexate with caution on the advice of the specialist (for example, rheumatologist).
If risk factors such as renal function disorders, including mild renal impairment, are present, combined administration with NSAIDs is not recommended.

items.t: Renal failure: contraindicated (no numeric threshold given).

src.q: Severe heart failure, hepatic failure and renal failure (see section 4.4).

items.t: Renal impairment, dehydration or renal disease (especially elderly): take precautions and monitor renal function. Non-oliguric renal failure has occurred mainly in elderly patients who did not stop after diarrhoea.

src.q: Renal function should be monitored in these patients
Precaution should be taken in patients suffering from dehydration and renal disease, particularly the elderly.
Non-oliguric renal failure and proctocolitis have been reported mainly in elderly patients who have not discontinued mefenamic acid after the development of diarrhoea.

items.t: MHRA: patients at risk of renal impairment or failure (particularly elderly) should avoid NSAIDs if possible; if used, monitor renal function carefully.

src.q: patients at risk of renal impairment or renal failure (particularly elderly people) should avoid NSAIDs if possible
the renal function of such patients should be carefully monitored during NSAID treatment

items.t: Hepatic failure: contraindicated. Liver dysfunction: higher risk of NSAID renal failure; monitor renal function. Stop if symptoms of liver dysfunction appear in prolonged therapy.
