the use of the drug in women who are, or may become pregnant requires that anticipated benefits be weighed against possible risks.

items.t: BUMPS: can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor; no concern that it harms the baby. Switch to a different medicine within a few days of delivery (risk of low mood/depression after birth).

src.q: Methyldopa can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor.
If you take methyldopa at the end of pregnancy, your doctor will advise that you switch to a different medicine within a few days of delivery.

items.t: Appears in breast milk; weigh anticipated benefits against possible risks.

src.q: Methyldopa appears in breast milk. The use of the drug in breast-feeding mothers requires that anticipated benefits be weighed against possible risks.

items.t: BUMPS: after birth methyldopa can increase the chance of low mood and depression; a switch is usually advised within a few days of delivery.

src.q: This is because taking methyldopa after the baby's birth can increase your chance of low mood and depression.

items.t: BUMPS: no increased risk to the baby is expected if the father takes methyldopa. The SmPC gives no fertility or contraception information.

src.q: We do not expect any increased risk to your baby if the father takes methyldopa.

items.t: Frequencies not known. Sedation (usually transient, at start or after dose increases), headache, weakness, dizziness, light-headedness, dry mouth, nasal congestion, orthostatic hypotension (reduce dose), oedema/weight gain.

src.q: Many patients experience sedation for two or three days when therapy with methyldopa is started or when the dose is increased.
Orthostatic hypotension (decrease daily dosage)

items.t: Haemolytic anaemia, bone-marrow failure, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia; hepatitis/jaundice (stop; do not re-use); myocarditis, pericarditis, AV block, bradycardia; depression, psychosis; toxic epidermal necrolysis, angioedema; pancreatitis; lupus-like syndrome.

src.q: Haemolytic anaemia, bone-marrow failure, leucopenia, granulocytopenia, thrombocytopenia, eosinophilia
Rare cases of fatal hepatic necrosis have been reported.

items.t: Stop if oedema progresses or signs of heart failure appear.

src.q: (Discontinue methyldopa if oedema progresses or signs of heart failure appear.)

items.t: Liver function tests and total and differential white cell count before therapy.

src.q: Liver-function tests and a total and differential white bloodcell count are advisable before therapy and at intervals during the first six weeks to twelve weeks of therapy, or whenever an unexplained fever occurs.

items.t: Repeat liver tests and white cell count at intervals in the first 6-12 weeks and whenever unexplained fever occurs; haemoglobin/haematocrit if anaemia is suspected.

src.q: at intervals during the first six weeks to twelve weeks of therapy, or whenever an unexplained fever occurs.
should symptoms suggest anaemia, haemoglobin and/or haematocrit determinations should be made.

items.t: Stop if haemolytic anaemia, fever, abnormal liver function, jaundice or choreoathetotic movements occur.

src.q: Should fever, abnormality in liver function, or jaundice occur, therapy should be withdrawn.
If haemolytic anaemia is present, Methyldopa tablets should be discontinued.

items.t: Oral. When increasing the dose, increase the evening dose first to limit daytime sedation.

src.q: When increasing the dosage, therefore, it may be desirable to increase the evening dose first.

items.t: Drowsiness, dizziness and light-headedness can occur, especially at the start or after a dose increase; do not drive or operate machinery if affected.

src.q: If affected, patients should not attempt to drive, or operate machinery.

items.t: Report unexplained fever, yellow skin/eyes or symptoms of anaemia promptly. Urine may darken on standing (harmless).

src.q: Rarely, when urine is exposed to air after voiding, it may darken because of breakdown of methyldopa or its metabolites.

items.t: Adults: prevention of delayed chemotherapy-induced and radiotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting; symptomatic treatment of nausea and vomiting, including acute migraine (may also improve absorption of oral analgesics). Also diagnostic use (barium meal, duodenal intubation).

src.q: Prevention of delayed chemotherapy induced nausea and vomiting (CINV) - Prevention of radiotherapy induced nausea and vomiting (RINV). - Symptomatic treatment of nausea and vomiting, including acute migraine induced nausea and vomiting.
Metoclopramide can be used in combination with oral analgesics to improve the absorption of analgesics in acute migraine.

items.t: Children 1-18 years: second-line option for prevention of delayed chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting only.

src.q: Maxolon is indicated in children (aged 1-18 years) for: - Prevention of delayed chemotherapy induced nausea and vomiting (CINV) as a second line option

items.t: MHRA (2013, neurological risk): short-term use only (up to 5 days); adult maximum 30 mg (or 0.5 mg/kg) in 24 hours; in children only as a second-line option; contraindicated under 1 year.

src.q: metoclopramide should only be prescribed for short-term use (up to 5 days)
for adults, the maximum dose in 24 hours is 30 mg (or 0.5 mg per kg bodyweight)
use of metoclopramide is contraindicated in children younger than 1 year

items.t: MHRA: risks of extrapyramidal disorders and tardive dyskinesia outweigh benefits in long-term or high-dose treatment; acute neurological risk is higher in children.

src.q: The conclusion of the review was that these risks outweigh the benefits in long-term or high-dose treatment.
The risk of acute neurological effects is higher in children than in adults.

items.t: 10 mg up to three times daily. Maximum 30 mg or 0.5 mg/kg per day. Maximum duration 5 days. Keep at least 6 hours between doses, even if a dose is vomited.

src.q: The recommended single dose is 10 mg, repeated up to three times daily. The maximum recommended daily dose is 30 mg or 0.5mg/kg body weight. The maximum recommended treatment duration is 5 days.
A minimal interval of 6 hours between two administrations is to be respected, even in case of vomiting or rejection of the dose

items.t: Elderly: consider a dose reduction based on renal and hepatic function and frailty.

src.q: In elderly patients a dose reduction should be considered, based on renal and hepatic function and overall frailty.

items.t: Diagnostic use: a single dose 5-10 minutes before the examination (adjust for body weight).

src.q: may be given 5-10 minutes before the examination, subject to body weight consideration

items.t: Delayed CINV only (1-18 years, second line): 0.1 to 0.15 mg/kg up to three times daily; maximum 0.5 mg/kg in 24 hours; maximum 5 days. Tablets only for children over 60 kg (15-18 years: 10 mg up to three times daily); use another form for lighter children.

src.q: The recommended dose is 0.1 to 0.15 mg/kg body weight, repeated up to three times daily by oral route. The maximum dose in 24 hours is 0.5mg/kg body weight.
15-18 years Over 60kg 10 mg Up to 3 times daily
Tablets are not suitable for use in children weighing less than 61 kg.

items.t: Contraindicated under 1 year (increased risk of extrapyramidal disorders).

src.q: Use in children less than 1 year of age due to an increased risk of extrapyramidal disorders

items.t: Hypersensitivity to metoclopramide or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1

items.t: GI haemorrhage, mechanical obstruction or perforation where stimulating motility is a risk; the first 3-4 days after pyloroplasty or gut anastomosis.

src.q: Gastrointestinal haemorrhage, mechanical obstruction or gastro-intestinal perforation for which the stimulation of gastrointestinal motility constitutes a risk
should not be used during the first three to four days following operations such as pyloroplasty or gut anastomosis

items.t: Confirmed or suspected phaeochromocytoma (risk of severe hypertension).

src.q: Confirmed or suspected pheochromocytoma, due to the risk of severe hypertension episodes

items.t: History of neuroleptic- or metoclopramide-induced tardive dyskinesia; epilepsy; Parkinson's disease.

src.q: History of neuroleptic or metoclopramide-induced tardive dyskinesia - Epilepsy (increased crises frequency and intensity) - Parkinson's disease

items.t: Combination with levodopa or dopaminergic agonists.

src.q: Combination with levodopa or dopaminergic agonists

items.t: History of methaemoglobinaemia with metoclopramide or NADH cytochrome-b5 deficiency.

src.q: Known history of methaemoglobinaemia with metoclopramide or of NADH cytochrome-b5 deficiency.

items.t: Children under 1 year.

src.q: Use in children less than 1 year of age due to an increased risk of extrapyramidal disorders

items.t: Extrapyramidal disorders (especially children, young adults, high doses), even after one dose: stop immediately. Respect the 6-hour minimum interval.

src.q: Extrapyramidal disorders may occur, particularly in children and young adults, and/or when high doses are used.
Metoclopramide should be discontinued immediately in the event of extrapyramidal symptoms.

items.t: Tardive dyskinesia (possibly irreversible, especially in the elderly): treatment should not exceed 3 months; stop if signs appear.

src.q: Treatment should not exceed 3 months because of the risk of tardive dyskinesia (see section 4.8). Treatment must be discontinued if clinical signs of tardive dyskinesia appear.

items.t: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: stop immediately and treat.

src.q: Metoclopramide should be discontinued immediately in the event of symptoms of neuroleptic malignant syndrome and appropriate treatment should be initiated.

items.t: Special care in underlying neurological conditions and with other centrally acting drugs; may worsen Parkinson's symptoms.

src.q: Special care should be exercised in patients with underlying neurological conditions and in patients being treated with other centrally-acting drugs

items.t: Methaemoglobinaemia: stop immediately and permanently and treat (e.g. methylene blue).

src.q: In such cases, metoclopramide should be immediately, and permanently discontinued and appropriate measures initiated (such as treatment with methylene blue).

items.t: Cardiac effects (circulatory collapse, severe bradycardia, cardiac arrest, QT prolongation), mainly with injection. Special care in the elderly, cardiac conduction disturbance (including QT prolongation), uncorrected electrolyte imbalance, bradycardia, and with other QT-prolonging drugs.

src.q: There have been reports of serious cardiovascular undesirable effects including cases of circulatory collapse, severe bradycardia, cardiac arrest and QT prolongation following administration of metoclopramide by injection
to patients with cardiac conduction disturbances (including QT prolongation), patients with uncorrected electrolyte imbalance, bradycardia and those taking other drugs known to prolong QT interval

items.t: Care in atopy (including asthma) or porphyria. If vomiting persists, reassess for an underlying disorder.

src.q: Care should be exercised when using Maxolon in patients with a history of atopy (including asthma) or porphyria.
If vomiting persists the patient should be reassessed to exclude the possibility of an underlying disorder e.g. cerebral irritation.

items.t: Contains lactose: hereditary galactose intolerance, lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take it. May raise prolactin.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency of glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
Metoclopramide may cause elevation of serum prolactin levels.

items.t: Contraindicated with levodopa or dopaminergic agonists (e.g. cabergoline) - mutual antagonism.

src.q: Levodopa or dopaminergic agonists and metoclopramide have a mutual antagonism
it should not be concurrently administered with drugs which have dopamine-antagonist activity (such as phenothiazines, butyrophenones, thioxanthenes, metoclopramide)

items.t: Alcohol: avoid (increases sedation). CNS depressants (opioids, anxiolytics, sedating antihistamines, sedating antidepressants, barbiturates, clonidine): sedation potentiated.

src.q: Combination to be avoided Alcohol potentiates the sedative effect of metoclopramide.
Sedative effects of Central Nervous System depressants and metoclopramide are potentiated.

items.t: Anticholinergics and opioids (morphine derivatives) may antagonise metoclopramide's effect on gut motility.

src.q: Anticholinergics and morphine derivatives may have both a mutual antagonism with metoclopramide on the digestive tract motility.

items.t: Serotonergic drugs such as SSRIs: may increase the risk of serotonin syndrome.

src.q: The use of metoclopramide with serotonergic drugs such as SSRIs may increase the risk of serotonin syndrome.

items.t: Strong CYP2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine) raise metoclopramide exposure - monitor for adverse reactions.

src.q: Metoclopramide exposure levels are increased when co-administered with strong CYP2D6 inhibitors such as fluoxetine and paroxetine. Although the clinical significance is uncertain, patients should be monitored for adverse reactions.

items.t: Other: neuroleptics (additive extrapyramidal effects); digoxin (bioavailability may fall - monitor levels); ciclosporin (levels rise - monitor); atovaquone (levels may fall). Absorption of some drugs may change because of faster gastric emptying.

src.q: Metoclopramide may have an additive effect with other neuroleptics on the occurrence of extrapyramidal disorders.
Metoclopramide may decrease digoxin bioavailability. Careful monitoring of digoxin plasma concentration is required.
Due to the prokinetic effect of metoclopramide, the absorption of certain drugs may be modified.

items.t: CrCl ≤ 15 mL/min (end-stage renal disease): reduce the daily dose by 75%. CrCl 15-60 mL/min (moderate to severe): reduce the dose by 50%.

src.q: In patients with end stage renal disease (Creatinine clearance ≤ 15 ml/min), the daily dose should be reduced by 75%. In patients with moderate to severe renal impairment (Creatinine clearance 15-60 ml/min), the dose should be reduced by 50%

items.t: Severe hepatic impairment: reduce the dose by 50%.

src.q: In patients with severe hepatic impairment, the dose should be reduced by 50%

items.t: SmPC: > 1000 pregnancy outcomes show no malformative or feto/neonatal toxicity; can be used if clinically needed. Avoid at the end of pregnancy (risk of extrapyramidal syndrome in the newborn); if used, monitor the neonate.

src.q: Metoclopramide can be used during pregnancy if clinically needed.
Metoclopramide should be avoided at the end of pregnancy. If metoclopramide is used, neonatal monitoring should be undertaken.

items.t: BUMPS: metoclopramide is an option for pregnancy sickness if an antihistamine does not help; overall these medicines are considered safe for the baby.

src.q: These include ondansetron (Zofran®), metoclopramide (Maxolon®), and domperidone.
Overall, these medicines are considered safe for your baby.

items.t: SmPC: excreted in milk at low level; infant adverse reactions cannot be excluded - not recommended; consider stopping metoclopramide.

src.q: Adverse reactions in the breast-fed baby cannot be excluded. Therefore, metoclopramide is not recommended during breastfeeding.

items.t: SPS (differs from SmPC): can be used with caution short term for nausea, with infant monitoring (sedation, GI upset, poor feeding, irritability, extrapyramidal symptoms). Do not exceed 30 mg daily for up to 5 days; avoid in people with a history of depression.

src.q: Metoclopramide, for short-term use, can be used with caution during breastfeeding for nausea, but monitoring is required.
The dose should not exceed 30mg daily for a maximum of five days. Avoid in people with a history of depression.

items.t: Fertility: no data available. Long-term use may cause hyperprolactinaemia (amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, gynaecomastia).

src.q: Fertility No data available.
Endocrine disorders during prolonged treatment in relation with hyperprolactinaemia (amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, gynaecomastia).

items.t: Very common: somnolence. Common: extrapyramidal disorders, parkinsonism, akathisia, depression, diarrhoea, asthenia, hypotension (mainly with injection).

src.q: Nervous system disorders Very common Somnolence Common Extrapyramidal disorders
Psychiatric disorders Common Depression
Gastrointestinal disorders Common Diarrhoea General disorders and administration site conditions Common Asthenia

items.t: Uncommon: dystonia (including oculogyric crisis), dyskinesia, hallucination, amenorrhoea, hyperprolactinaemia, bradycardia, hypersensitivity.

src.q: Uncommon Dystonia (including visual disturbances and oculogyric crisis), Dyskinesia, Depressed level of consciousness

items.t: Tardive dyskinesia (may be persistent, especially in the elderly) and neuroleptic malignant syndrome: stop at once.

src.q: Tardive dyskinesia which may be persistent, during or after prolonged treatment, particularly in elderly patients (see section 4.4), Neuroleptic malignant syndrome

items.t: Acute dystonia/oculogyric crisis, even after a single dose (especially children and young adults): stop; treat symptomatically.

src.q: These reactions occur usually at the beginning of the treatment and can occur after a single administration.

items.t: Methaemoglobinaemia (especially neonates); convulsions (rare, mainly in epilepsy); QT prolongation, torsade de pointes, AV block.

src.q: Methaemoglobinaemia, which could be related to NADH cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency, particularly in neonates
Rare Convulsion especially in epileptic patients
Electrocardiogram QT prolonged; Torsade de Pointes;

items.t: Anaphylactic reaction including shock; acute hypertension in phaeochromocytoma.

src.q: Acute hypertension in patients with phaeochromocytoma

items.t: Check for contraindications: epilepsy, Parkinson's disease, previous tardive dyskinesia, phaeochromocytoma, levodopa/dopamine agonists, GI obstruction or bleeding.

src.q: History of neuroleptic or metoclopramide-induced tardive dyskinesia - Epilepsy (increased crises frequency and intensity) - Parkinson's disease

items.t: Watch for extrapyramidal symptoms (SPS: monitor for them); with strong CYP2D6 inhibitors, monitor for adverse reactions.

src.q: Monitor the person for extrapyramidal side effects.
Although the clinical significance is uncertain, patients should be monitored for adverse reactions.

items.t: Stop after 5 days (licensed maximum); stop at once for extrapyramidal symptoms, tardive dyskinesia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome or methaemoglobinaemia.

src.q: The maximum recommended treatment duration is 5 days.
Treatment must be discontinued if clinical signs of tardive dyskinesia appear.

items.t: Oral use only. Leave at least 6 hours between doses, even if vomited.

src.q: Method of administration For oral use only
A minimal interval of 6 hours between two administrations is to be respected, even in case of vomiting or rejection of the dose

items.t: Stop and seek advice for abnormal movements (spasms of face, neck, eyes or tongue, restlessness, tremor). Do not take more than prescribed or for longer than 5 days.

src.q: Metoclopramide should be discontinued immediately in the event of extrapyramidal symptoms.
The maximum recommended treatment duration is 5 days.

items.t: May cause drowsiness, dizziness or movement disorders - do not drive or use machines if affected; avoid alcohol.

src.q: Metoclopramide may cause drowsiness, dizziness, dyskinesia and dystonias which could affect the vision and also interfere with the ability to drive and operate machinery.
Combination to be avoided Alcohol potentiates the sedative effect of metoclopramide.

items.t: Prophylaxis and treatment of infections where anaerobic bacteria are identified or suspected: prevention of post-operative anaerobic infection; septicaemia, bacteraemia, peritonitis, brain abscess, necrotising pneumonia, osteomyelitis, puerperal sepsis, pelvic abscess or cellulitis and post-operative wound infections with anaerobes.

src.q: Metronidazole is indicated in the prophylaxis and treatment of infections in which anaerobic bacteria have been identified or are suspected to be the cause.

The treatment of septicaemia, bacteraemia, peritonitis, brain abscess, necrotising pneumonia, osteomyelitis, puerperal sepsis, pelvic abscess, pelvic cellulitis, and post-operative wound infections from which pathogenic anaerobes have been isolated.

items.t: Urogenital trichomoniasis (women and men), bacterial vaginosis, all forms of amoebiasis, giardiasis, acute ulcerative gingivitis, anaerobically infected leg ulcers and pressure sores, acute dental infections.

src.q: Urogenital trichomoniasis in the female

All forms of amoebiasis (intestinal and extra-intestinal disease and that of symptomless cyst passers). 6. Giardiasis. 7. Acute ulcerative gingivitis. 8. Anaerobically-infected leg ulcers and pressure sores. 9. Acute dental infections

items.t: Suspension SmPC: bacterial vaginosis, acute dental infections and leg ulcers/pressure sores are licensed only for adults and children over 10 years; Helicobacter pylori eradication is listed for children.

src.q: Adults and children over 10 years only for: Bacterial vaginosis
Children for Eradication of Helicobacter pylori

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction (specialist-only, shared care or brand prescribing) in the four UK SmPCs checked (two 200 mg tablet SmPCs, one 500 mg tablet SmPC, one oral suspension SmPC); they only say to consider official guidance on antibacterial use.

items.t: Surgical prophylaxis (mainly colorectal and gynaecological surgery): 400 mg every 8 hours during the 24 hours before the operation, then intravenous or rectal metronidazole until tablets can be taken.

src.q: 400 mg 8 hourly during 24 hours immediately preceding operation followed by post-operative intravenous or rectal administration until the patient is able to take tablets.

items.t: Established anaerobic infection: 800 mg, then 400 mg every 8 hours. A course is usually about 7 days, depending on clinical and bacteriological assessment.

src.q: Adults : 800 mg followed by 400 mg 8 hourly.
The duration of a course of metronidazole treatment is about 7 days

items.t: Urogenital trichomoniasis: 2000 mg as a single dose, or 200 mg three times daily for 7 days, or 400 mg twice daily for 5 to 7 days. Where re-infection is likely, treat the partner at the same time.

src.q: 2000 mg as a single dose Or 200 mg three times daily or 400 mg twice daily
in adults the consort should receive a similar course of treatment concurrently

items.t: Bacterial vaginosis: 400 mg twice daily for 5 to 7 days, or 2000 mg as a single dose.

src.q: Bacterial vaginosis 5 - 7 Or 1 400 mg twice daily Or 2000 mg as a single dose

items.t: Amoebiasis: invasive intestinal disease 800 mg three times daily for 5 days; less susceptible intestinal disease or chronic amoebic hepatitis 400 mg three times daily for 5 to 10 days; symptomless cyst passers 400 to 800 mg three times daily for 5 to 10 days. Alternatively 35 to 50 mg/kg daily in 3 divided doses for 5 to 10 days, not more than 2400 mg/day.

src.q: Invasive intestinal disease in susceptible subjects 5 800 mg three times daily
Intestinal disease in less susceptible subjects and chronic amoebic hepatitis 5 - 10 400 mg three times daily
35 to 50 mg/kg daily in 3 divided doses for 5 to 10 days, not to exceed 2400 mg/day

items.t: Giardiasis: 2000 mg once daily for 3 days, or 400 mg three times daily for 5 days, or 500 mg twice daily for 7 to 10 days.

src.q: Giardiasis 3 Or 5 Or 7 - 10 2000 mg once daily Or 400 mg three times daily Or 500 mg twice daily

items.t: Acute ulcerative gingivitis: 200 mg three times daily for 3 days. Acute dental infections: 200 mg three times daily for 3 to 7 days. Leg ulcers and pressure sores: 400 mg three times daily for 7 days.

src.q: Acute ulcerative gingivitis 3 200 mg three times daily
Acute dental infections 3 - 7 200 mg three times daily
Leg ulcers and pressure sores 7 400 mg three times daily

items.t: Elderly: well tolerated, but use high-dose regimens with caution.

src.q: a pharmacokinetic study suggests cautious use of high dosage regimens in this age group

items.t: Surgical prophylaxis: children under 12 years 20 to 30 mg/kg as a single dose 1 to 2 hours before surgery; newborns with gestation age under 40 weeks 10 mg/kg as a single dose before the operation.

src.q: Children < 12 years : 20-30mg/kg as a single dose given 1-2 hours before surgery
Newborns with a gestation age < 40 weeks: 10 mg/kg body weight as a single dose before operation.

items.t: Anaerobic infection, over 8 weeks to 12 years: 20 to 30 mg/kg/day as a single dose or 7.5 mg/kg every 8 hours; may be increased to 40 mg/kg/day; usually 7 days. Under 8 weeks: 15 mg/kg once daily or 7.5 mg/kg every 12 hours. Newborns under 40 weeks gestation can accumulate metronidazole in the first week; monitor serum levels after a few days.

src.q: The usual daily dose is 20-30 mg/kg/day as a single dose or divided into 7.5 mg/kg every 8 hours. The daily dose may be increased to 40 mg/kg, depending on the severity of the infection.
Children < 8 weeks of age : 15 mg/kg as a single dose daily or divided into 7.5 mg/kg every 12 hours.
accumulation of metronidazole can occur during the first week of life

items.t: Trichomoniasis (children): 40 mg/kg as a single dose, or 15 to 30 mg/kg/day in 2 to 3 divided doses, not more than 2000 mg per dose (suspension SmPC; the tablet SmPC table prints this limit as "2000 mg/kg dose"). Giardiasis for 3 days: 7 to 10 years 1000 mg once daily, 3 to 7 years 600 to 800 mg once daily, 1 to 3 years 500 mg once daily (or 15 to 40 mg/kg/day in 2 to 3 doses). Amoebiasis and gingivitis doses are banded by age in the SmPC table.

src.q: 40 mg/kg orally as a single dose Or 15 - 30 mg/kg/day divided in 2 - 3 doses
1000 mg once daily 600 - 800 mg once daily 500 mg once daily
15 - 40 mg/kg/day divided in 2 - 3 doses
15 - 30mg/kg/day divided in 2 - 3 doses not to exceed 2000mg/dose

items.t: Helicobacter pylori eradication (part of combination therapy): 20 mg/kg/day, not more than 500 mg twice daily, for 7 to 14 days; consult official guidelines first.

src.q: 20 mg/kg/day not to exceed 500 mg twice daily for 7 - 14 days

items.t: Children and infants under 10 kg: give proportionally smaller doses.

src.q: Children and infants weighing less than 10 kg should receive proportionally smaller dosages.

items.t: Known hypersensitivity to nitroimidazoles, metronidazole or any excipient. The suspension also lists hydroxybenzoates (parabens).

src.q: Known hypersensitivity to nitroimidazoles, metronidazole or any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.
Known hypersensitivity to metronidazole, nitroimidazoles and/or hydroxybenzoates or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Tablets: one UK SmPC (500 mg tablets) also lists in section 4.3: first trimester of pregnancy when treating trichomoniasis or bacterial vaginosis; breastfeeding must stop for 12 to 24 hours after single high-dose (e.g. 2 g) therapy; Cockayne syndrome. The two 200 mg tablet SmPCs and the suspension SmPC do not list these in 4.3.

src.q: Pregnancy - metronidazole should not be used in the first trimester in patients with trichomoniasis or bacterial vaginosis
Breast feeding should be discontinued for 12-24 hours when single high dose (e.g. 2g) therapy is used
Patients with Cockayne syndrome (see section 4.8)

items.t: Cockayne syndrome: severe and fatal hepatotoxicity with very rapid onset reported. Do not use unless benefit outweighs risk and there is no alternative. Check liver function just before, during and after treatment; stop if tests become markedly raised. (The suspension SmPC words this as use only after careful benefit-risk assessment and if no alternative.)

src.q: In this population, metronidazole should not be used unless the benefit is considered to outweigh the risk and if no alternative treatment is available.
Liver function tests must be performed just prior to the start of therapy, throughout and after end of treatment
metronidazole should therefore be used after careful benefit-risk assessment and only if no alternative treatment is available

items.t: Treatment for more than 10 days: regular clinical and laboratory monitoring (especially leucocyte count) and watch for peripheral or central neuropathy (paraesthesia, ataxia, dizziness, vertigo, seizures). Longer courses than usual should be carefully considered (mutagenicity data inadequate).

src.q: Regular clinical and laboratory monitoring (especially leucocyte count) are advised if administration of metronidazole for more than 10 days is considered to be necessary
the use of metronidazole for longer treatment than usually required should be carefully considered

items.t: Active or chronic severe peripheral or central nervous system disease: use with caution (risk of neurological worsening).

src.q: Metronidazole should be used with caution in patients with active or chronic severe peripheral and central nervous system disease due to the risk of neurological aggravation.

items.t: One UK SmPC (500 mg tablets): caution in epilepsy or previous seizures, as high doses can induce seizures.

src.q: Caution in patients with epilepsy or those who have had seizures as high doses of Metronidazole can induce seizures.

items.t: Hepatic encephalopathy: use with caution; metronidazole can accumulate and worsen encephalopathy. Reduce the daily dose to one third, which may be given once daily (see hepatic).

src.q: Metronidazole Tablets should therefore, be administered with caution to patients with hepatic encephalopathy. The daily dosage should be reduced to one third and may be administered once daily.

items.t: Severe bullous skin reactions (SJS, TEN, AGEP): stop metronidazole immediately if signs appear.

src.q: If symptoms or signs of SJS, TEN or AGEP are present, metronidazole treatment must be immediately discontinued.

items.t: Gonococcal infection may persist after Trichomonas is cleared. Metronidazole may give falsely low results for ALT, AST, LDH, triglycerides and glucose in some assays.

src.q: There is a possibility that after Trichomonas vaginalis has been eliminated a gonococcal infection might persist.
which may lead to false negative or an abnormally low result

items.t: Suspension excipients: hereditary fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take it (sorbitol, sucrose). Contains propylene glycol (medical monitoring in renal or hepatic impairment) and methyl parahydroxybenzoate (possible delayed allergy).

src.q: Patients with hereditary fructose intolerance (HFI) should not take/be given this medicinal product.
Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take this medicine.
Medical monitoring is required in patients with impaired renal or hepatic functions

items.t: Alcohol: advise no alcohol during treatment and for at least 48 hours afterwards (disulfiram-like reaction).

src.q: Patients should be advised not to take alcohol during metronidazole therapy and for at least 48 hours afterwards because of the possibility of a disulfiram-like (antabuse effect) reaction.

items.t: Warfarin-type oral anticoagulants: anticoagulant effect may be increased; the anticoagulant dose may need reducing; monitor prothrombin time. No interaction with heparin.

src.q: Some potentiation of anti-coagulant therapy has been reported when metronidazole has been used with the warfarin type oral anticoagulants. Dosage of the latter may require reducing. Prothrombin times should be monitored.

items.t: Carbamazepine (suspension SmPC): raised carbamazepine levels and toxicity reported.

src.q: Increased serum carbamazepine levels and toxicity have been seen in patients given concomitant metronidazole.

items.t: QT-prolonging drugs (tablet SmPCs): QT prolongation has been reported, mainly when metronidazole was given with drugs that can prolong the QT interval.

src.q: QT prolongation has been reported, particularly when metronidazole was administered with drugs with the potential for prolonging the QT interval.

items.t: Mebendazole: the mebendazole SmPC says avoid the combination (possible link with Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN).

src.q: concomitant use of mebendazole and metronidazole should be avoided

items.t: Lithium: taper or stop lithium before metronidazole; if both are used, monitor lithium, creatinine and electrolytes. Disulfiram: psychotic reactions. Ciclosporin (and tacrolimus, suspension SmPC): monitor levels and creatinine closely. Also raises 5-fluorouracil and busulfan toxicity. Phenytoin and phenobarbital speed up metronidazole metabolism.
items.tag: Other medicines (not in the checker list)

src.q: Lithium treatment should be tapered or withdrawn before administering metronidazole.
Psychotic reactions have been reported in patients who were using metronidazole and disulfiram concurrently.
Serum ciclosporin / tacrolimus and serum creatinine should be closely monitored when coadministration is necessary.
Plasma levels of busulfan may be increased by metronidazole which may lead to severe busulfan toxicity.

items.t: Renal failure: half-life unchanged, so no dose reduction is needed (metabolites are retained; significance unknown).

src.q: The elimination half-life of metronidazole remains unchanged in the presence of renal failure. The dosage of metronidazole therefore needs no reduction.

items.t: Haemodialysis removes metronidazole: give the dose again immediately after haemodialysis. No routine adjustment on intermittent peritoneal dialysis or CAPD.

src.q: Metronidazole should therefore be re-administered immediately after haemodialysis.
No routine adjustment in the dosage of Metronidazole need be made in patients with renal failure undergoing intermittent peritoneal dialysis (IPD) or continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD).

items.t: Mainly metabolised by the liver; clearance may be substantially reduced in advanced hepatic insufficiency. In hepatic encephalopathy use with caution and reduce the daily dose to one third, which may be given once daily (one tablet SmPC says 'should', the suspension SmPC says 'may').

src.q: Substantial impairment of metronidazole clearance may occur in the presence of advanced hepatic insufficiency.
The daily dosage should be reduced to one third and may be administered once daily.
The daily dosage may be reduced to one third and may be administered once daily.

items.t: SmPCs: safety evidence in pregnancy is inadequate (though widely used without apparent harm). Do not give in pregnancy unless the physician considers it essential; if used, short high-dose regimens are not recommended.

src.q: should not be given during pregnancy or during lactation unless the physician considers it essential; in these circumstances the short, high-dosage regimens are not recommended

items.t: One UK SmPC (500 mg tablets): contraindicated in the first trimester when treating trichomoniasis or bacterial vaginosis; use with caution in the second and third trimesters for these; for other indications use only if benefit outweighs risk or no alternative, especially in the first trimester.

src.q: Metronidazole is contraindicated in the first trimester (see section 4.3) and should be used with caution in the second and third trimester when used to treat trichomoniasis or bacterial vaginosis
For all other indications Metronidazole should only be used if the benefits outweigh the risks or no other alternative is available especially in the first trimester.

items.t: BUMPS (UKTIS): metronidazole is well studied in pregnancy and not known to cause birth defects, stillbirth, low birth weight or preterm delivery; it may be recommended where benefits outweigh possible risks. Some studies suggest more miscarriage with early use, but the infection itself may be the cause.

src.q: Metronidazole use in pregnancy has been well studied and is not known to cause birth defects, stillbirth, low birth weight, or preterm delivery.
Metronidazole may be recommended for some types of infection where the benefits of treatment are thought to outweigh the possible risks.

items.t: SmPCs: do not give during breastfeeding unless the physician considers it essential. Suspension SmPC: a significant amount passes into milk; avoid breastfeeding after a large dose (milk may taste bitter).

src.q: should not be given during pregnancy or during lactation unless the physician considers it essential
A significant amount of metronidazole is found in breast milk and breast feeding should be avoided after a large dose.

items.t: One UK SmPC (500 mg tablets): stop breastfeeding for 12 to 24 hours after single high-dose (e.g. 2 g) therapy (section 4.3), and it is advisable to stop until 12 to 24 hours after treatment ends.

src.q: Breast feeding should be discontinued for 12-24 hours when single high dose (e.g. 2g) therapy is used
It is advisable to stop breast feeding until 12 - 24 hours after Metronidazole therapy has been discontinued

items.t: SPS: short courses of oral metronidazole are compatible with breastfeeding with infant monitoring; no interruption is needed, even after 2 g doses (single or daily for 3 days). Monitor the infant for poor feeding, weight gain, vomiting/diarrhoea, oral thrush, irritability and rash. Seek specialist advice for use longer than a few weeks.

src.q: Short courses of oral, intravenous or rectal metronidazole are considered to be compatible with breastfeeding, but infant monitoring is recommended.
No interruption of breastfeeding is required, even after 2g oral doses (as a single dose, or daily for a three-day course).
If use is required for longer than a few weeks, contact our specialist service for further advice.

items.t: The UK SmPCs checked give no fertility or contraception advice. BUMPS: no evidence that use by the father harms the baby through effects on sperm.

src.q: There is no evidence that metronidazole used by the father can harm the baby through effects on the sperm.

items.t: The SmPCs list no adverse effect as common. Gastrointestinal effects (taste disturbance, oral mucositis, furred tongue, nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, diarrhoea) and darkening of urine are listed (frequency not known or very rare).

src.q: Not known: taste disorders, oral mucositis, furred tongue, nausea, vomiting, gastro-intestinal disturbances such as epigastric pain and diarrhoea
Very rare: darkening of urine (due to metronidazole metabolite).

items.t: Peripheral sensory neuropathy or epileptiform seizures (mainly intensive or prolonged treatment), encephalopathy and cerebellar syndrome: usually resolve when stopped or dose reduced. Weigh benefit against neuropathy risk before long-term use.

src.q: during intensive and/or prolonged metronidazole therapy, peripheral sensory neuropathy or transient epileptiform seizures have been reported
consider the possible therapeutic benefit against the risk of peripheral neuropathy

items.t: Stevens-Johnson syndrome, TEN, AGEP: stop immediately.

src.q: If symptoms or signs of SJS, TEN or AGEP are present, metronidazole treatment must be immediately discontinued.

items.t: Hepatitis, jaundice and pancreatitis (reversible on withdrawal); liver failure needing transplant reported with metronidazole plus other antibiotics; fatal acute liver failure in Cockayne syndrome.

src.q: cholestatic or mixed hepatitis and hepatocellular liver injury, jaundice and pancreatitis which is reversible on drug withdrawal
cases of liver failure requiring liver transplant have been reported in patients treated with metronidazole in combination with other antibiotic drugs

items.t: Agranulocytosis, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, pancytopenia (very rare); anaphylaxis (rare); optic neuropathy, hearing loss and aseptic meningitis (frequency not known).

src.q: Very rare: agranulocytosis, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, pancytopenia
Rare: anaphylaxis
Not known: optic neuropathy/neuritis

items.t: Cockayne syndrome: liver function tests just before starting, during and after treatment until normal or back to baseline; stop if markedly raised.

src.q: Liver function tests must be performed just prior to the start of therapy, throughout and after end of treatment until liver function is within normal ranges, or until the baseline values are reached.

items.t: Treatment longer than 10 days: regular clinical and laboratory monitoring, especially leucocyte count, and watch for neuropathy.

src.q: Regular clinical and laboratory monitoring (especially leucocyte count) are advised if administration of metronidazole for more than 10 days is considered to be necessary

items.t: On warfarin: monitor prothrombin time. On lithium: monitor lithium, creatinine and electrolytes.

src.q: Prothrombin times should be monitored.
Plasma concentrations of lithium, creatinine and electrolytes should be monitored in patients under treatment with lithium while they receive metronidazole.

items.t: Stop if SJS/TEN/AGEP signs appear, or (Cockayne syndrome) if liver tests become markedly raised.

src.q: If the liver function tests become markedly elevated during treatment, the drug should be discontinued.

items.t: Tablets: swallow with water, do not chew; take during or after a meal.

src.q: Metronidazole tablets should be swallowed with water (not chewed). It is recommended that the tablets be taken during or after a meal.

items.t: Suspension: shake the bottle well; use an oral dosing device for doses under 5 ml. Discard 14 days after opening.

src.q: Shake the bottle well before use. If a dose of under 5ml is required, the suspension should be administered using an oral dosing device.
After opening discard any unused suspension after 14 days.

items.t: Do not drink alcohol during the course and for at least 48 hours after the last dose.

src.q: Patients should be advised not to take alcohol during metronidazole therapy and for at least 48 hours afterwards

items.t: Urine may turn dark.

src.q: Patients should be warned that metronidazole may darken urine.

items.t: Do not drive or use machines if drowsiness, dizziness, vertigo, confusion, hallucinations, fits or visual problems occur.

src.q: advised not to drive or operate machinery if these symptoms occur

items.t: Cockayne syndrome: stop taking it and report any sign of liver injury to the doctor at once.

src.q: Patients with Cockayne Syndrome should be advised to immediately report any symptoms of potential liver injury to their physician and stop taking metronidazole

items.t: Oral gel: candidosis of the oropharynx in adults, children and infants 4 months and older.

src.q: Oral treatment of candidosis of the oropharynx.
Miconazole gel is for use in adults, children and infants 4 months and older.

items.t: Cream: fungal infections of the skin and nails, and superinfections due to Gram-positive bacteria.

src.q: For the treatment of mycotic infections of the skin and nails and superinfections due to Gram-positive bacteria.

items.t: Vaginal (UK vaginal cream): local treatment of vulvovaginal candidosis and Gram-positive superinfections.

src.q: For the local treatment of vulvovaginal candidosis and superinfections due to gram- positive bacteria.

items.t: MHRA: patients taking warfarin should not use over-the-counter miconazole oral gel; prescribe the oral gel to a warfarin patient only with close monitoring.

src.q: patients taking warfarin should not use over-the-counter miconazole oral gel available from pharmacies
If you plan to prescribe miconazole oral gel in a patient on warfarin, you should closely monitor them

items.t: Oral gel, adults and children 2 years and over: 2.5 mL four times a day after meals; keep in the mouth as long as possible before swallowing. Continue for at least a week after symptoms have gone.

src.q: Adults and children 2 years of age and older: 2.5 mL (1/2 measuring spoon) of gel, applied four times a day after meals.
The treatment should be continued for at least a week after the symptoms have disappeared.

items.t: Cream: apply to lesions twice daily for 2 to 6 weeks, continuing for at least a week after all signs have gone. Nails: once or twice daily, continuing 10 days after lesions have gone.

src.q: Apply some cream to the lesions two times daily.
The duration of therapy varies from 2 to 6 weeks depending on the localisation and the severity of the lesion.
Treatment should be prolonged for 10 days after all lesions have disappeared to prevent relapse.

items.t: UK vaginal cream (adults 18 and over): one applicator (about 5 g) deep into the vagina at bedtime for 7 days. No UK dosing found for the 400 mg pessary.

src.q: Administer the contents of one applicator (about 5g of cream) once daily before bedtime deeply into vagina for 7 days.

items.t: Oral gel, infants 4 to 24 months: 1.25 mL four times a day after meals, divided into small portions and applied with a clean finger, not to the back of the throat. Not under 4 months; in pre-term or slowly developing infants raise the lower age limit to 5 to 6 months.

src.q: Infants: 4-24 months: 1.25 ml (1/4 measuring spoon) of gel, applied four times a day after meals.
The lower age limit should be increased to 5-6 months of age for infants who are pre-term, or infants exhibiting slow neuromuscular development.

items.t: Cream: same dose for all ages.

src.q: Recommended dosage: For all ages:

items.t: Vaginal cream: not studied under 18 years.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of Gyno-Daktarin vaginal cream in children and adolescents has not been studied.

items.t: All forms: hypersensitivity to miconazole, other imidazoles or any excipient.

src.q: Known hypersensitivity to miconazole, other imidazole derivatives or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.
Hypersensitivity to the active substance, other imidazole derivatives or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Oral gel: infants under 4 months or with an immature swallowing reflex; liver dysfunction.

src.q: In infants less than 4 months of age or in those whose swallowing reflex is not yet sufficiently developed
In patients with liver dysfunction.

items.t: Oral gel: medicines metabolised by CYP3A4 that prolong the QT interval (e.g. cisapride, pimozide, quinidine, terfenadine), ergot alkaloids, statins such as simvastatin and lovastatin, triazolam and oral midazolam.

src.q: Coadministration of the following drugs that are subject to metabolism by CYP3A4
Substrates known to prolong the QT-interval e.g. astemizole, cisapride, dofetilide, mizolastine, pimozide, quinidine, sertindole and terfenadine
HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors such as simvastatin and lovastatin

items.t: Oral gel, sugar-free 2% gel SmPC only: warfarin is also listed as a contraindication (the prescription-only gel SmPC lists it as a caution).

src.q: Triazolam and oral midazolam - Warfarin
WARNING: Do not use if you are taking warfarin

items.t: Oral gel and warfarin: the gel is absorbed and inhibits CYP2C9 and CYP3A4. Bleeding, some fatal, has been reported. If use with warfarin is planned, monitor and titrate the anticoagulant effect carefully; tell the patient to stop the gel and seek advice at any sign of bleeding.

src.q: Bleeding events, some with fatal outcomes, have been reported with concurrent use of miconazole oral gel and warfarin
caution should be exercised and the anticoagulant effect must be carefully monitored and titrated

items.t: Oral gel, choking risk in infants and young children (4 months to 2 years): divide each dose, apply with a clean finger, not to the back of the throat; observe for choking. Do not apply to a breastfeeding mother's nipple.

src.q: Particularly in infants and young children (aged 4 months - 2 years), caution is required, to ensure that the gel does not obstruct the throat.
the gel must not be applied to the nipple of a breastfeeding woman for administration to an infant.

items.t: Oral gel and sulfonylureas: enhanced effect with hypoglycaemia may occur; take appropriate measures. Monitor phenytoin and miconazole levels if used together.

src.q: In patients using certain oral hypoglycaemics such as sulphonylureas, an enhanced therapeutic effect leading to hypoglycaemia may occur

items.t: Cream: absorption is limited, but use with warfarin or other vitamin K antagonists with caution and monitor/titrate the anticoagulant effect. Keep away from the eyes.

items.t: All forms: severe hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis, angioedema) reported; stop if hypersensitivity or irritation occurs. Oral gel: stop at the first sign of skin rash (SJS/TEN reported).

use of miconazole be discontinued at the first appearance of skin rash.

items.t: Oral gel: not known if it passes into milk; use with caution. Do not apply gel to the nipple to treat the infant (choking).

items.t: Oral gel (adults): nausea, abnormal taste, oral discomfort, dry mouth, vomiting. Children: nausea and vomiting very common, regurgitation common.

src.q: common adverse reactions reported included nausea (4.5%), product taste abnormal (4.5%), oral discomfort (3.4%), dry mouth (2.3%), dysgeusia (1.1%), and vomiting (1.1%).
the frequency of nausea (13.0%) and vomiting (13.0%) was very common, and regurgitation (8.7%) was common.

Common Rash

to stop treatment with miconazole and seek medical advice.

Serious skin reactions (e.g. Toxic epidermal necrolysis and Stevens-Johnson syndrome) have been reported in patients receiving miconazole

However, in patients on warfarin or other vitamin K antagonists, caution should be exercised and anticoagulant effect should be monitored.

src.q: It is advisable to monitor miconazole and phenytoin levels, if these two drugs are used concomitantly.

items.t: Stop if hypersensitivity, irritation or skin rash appears.

items.t: Oral gel: apply after meals, keep in the mouth as long as possible before swallowing. Infants: small portions with a clean finger, never to the back of the throat. Dentures: remove at night and brush with the gel.

src.q: The gel should not be swallowed immediately, but kept in the mouth as long as possible.
For oral candidosis, dental prostheses should be removed at night and brushed with the gel.

items.t: Cream: rub into the lesions until absorbed.

src.q: Rub the cream into the skin with your finger until it has fully penetrated.

items.t: Vaginal cream: insert deeply at bedtime; continue even if itching stops or menstruation starts.

src.q: Continue the course of treatment even after pruritus and leukorrhoea have disappeared or menstruation begins.

items.t: Tell your doctor or pharmacist if you take warfarin before using any miconazole product; seek advice for unexplained bruising, nosebleeds or blood in the urine.

src.q: Patients should be advised to tell their doctor or pharmacist if they are receiving warfarin before using products that contain miconazole

items.t: Oral gel in infants: watch for choking.

src.q: Observe the patient for possible choking.

items.t: If symptoms persist, worsen or new symptoms occur, stop and see a doctor.

src.q: If symptoms persist or get worse, or if new symptoms occur, stop use and consult a doctor.

src.q: Athlete's foot and candidal intertrigo where there are co-existing symptoms of inflammation.
indicate it particularly for the initial stages of treatment

items.t: Elderly: skin is naturally thinner, so use sparingly and for short periods.

src.q: Tubercular or viral infections of the skin or those caused by Gram-negative bacteria.

similarly application to the face should be avoided
Long term continuous topical corticosteroid therapy should be avoided. Adrenal suppression can occur even without occlusion.

items.t: Blurred vision or other visual disturbance: consider referral to an ophthalmologist.

src.q: the patient should be considered for referral to an ophthalmologist for evaluation of possible causes

it is recommended to wear cotton underwear if this clothing comes into contact with the affected area

src.q: long-term continuous or inappropriate use of topical corticosteroids, particularly those of moderate to high potency, can result in the development of rebound flares after stopping treatment

items.t: Warfarin and other vitamin K antagonists: miconazole (CYP2C9 inhibition) can increase the anticoagulant effect, even from topical products. Use with caution, monitor INR and reduce the warfarin dose if needed; the patient should stop the cream and seek advice if bleeding signs occur.

if miconazole and warfarin are used concurrently, the anticoagulant effect should be carefully monitored and, if necessary, the dose of warfarin reduced
Patients should be advised of the symptoms of bleeding events and to immediately stop treatment with miconazole and seek medical advice should they occur

src.q: Serum concentrations of hydrocortisone may be higher with the use of Daktacort Hydrocortisone Cream compared with topical preparations containing hydrocortisone alone.

src.q: As a precautionary measure, it is preferable to avoid the use of Daktacort Hydrocortisone during pregnancy.
Treatment of large surfaces and the application under occlusive dressing should be avoided during that time.

src.q: Topical corticosteroids can be used in pregnancy.

A risk to the newborn child cannot be excluded.

items.t: SPS: topical hydrocortisone can be used during breastfeeding, with no extra risk from combination products containing antimicrobials. No SPS page for topical miconazole was found.

src.q: When applied to the skin, used rectally or for use in the ear, hydrocortisone can be used during breastfeeding.
There are no additional risks when combination topical preparations containing antimicrobials or urea are used.

reproductive.note: The UK SmPC has no fertility statement. Latex contraceptives may be damaged (see cautions).

Patients should be advised of the symptoms of bleeding events and to immediately stop treatment with miconazole and seek medical advice should they occur

items.t: Adults: episodes of major depression.

src.q: Mirtazapine is indicated in adults for the treatment of episodes of major depression.

items.t: Not for children and adolescents under 18 (efficacy not shown; safety concerns).

src.q: Mirtazapine should not be used in children and adolescents under the age of 18 years as efficacy was not demonstrated in two short-term clinical trials

items.t: Start 15 mg or 30 mg daily; usual effective dose 15 mg to 45 mg daily. Effect usually after 1 to 2 weeks; response expected within 2 to 4 weeks. If response is poor, increase up to the maximum; if still no response after a further 2 to 4 weeks, stop. Treat at least 6 months.

src.q: The effective daily dose is usually between 15 and 45 mg; the starting dose is 15 or 30 mg.
Treatment with an adequate dose should result in a positive response within 2-4 weeks.
If there is no response within a further 2-4 weeks, then treatment should be stopped.
Patients with depression should be treated for a sufficient period of at least 6 months to ensure that they are free from symptoms.

items.t: Elderly: same dose as adults; increase only under close supervision.

src.q: In elderly patients an increase in dosing should be done under close supervision to elicit a satisfactory and safe response.

items.t: Stopping: discontinue gradually to avoid withdrawal symptoms.

src.q: It is recommended to discontinue treatment with mirtazapine gradually to avoid withdrawal symptoms

items.t: With carbamazepine or other enzyme inducers the dose may need increasing (and reducing when the inducer is stopped). With potent CYP3A4 inhibitors, azole antifungals, erythromycin, HIV protease inhibitors or cimetidine the dose may need reducing.

src.q: When carbamazepine or any other inducer of hepatic metabolism (such as rifampicin) is added to mirtazapine therapy, the mirtazapine dose may have to be increased.

Caution should be exercised and the dose may have to be decreased when co-administering mirtazapine with potent CYP3A4 inhibitors, HIV protease inhibitors, azole antifungals, erythromycin, cimetidine or nefazodone.

items.t: Should not be used under 18 years. Paediatric trials did not show efficacy; suicidal behaviour and hostility were more frequent with antidepressants; marked weight gain, urticaria and raised triglycerides seen.

src.q: Mirtazapine should not be used in the treatment of children and adolescents under the age of 18 years.
The following adverse events were observed commonly in clinical trials in children: weight gain, urticaria and hypertriglyceridaemia

items.t: Hypersensitivity to mirtazapine or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1 .

items.t: Use with MAO inhibitors (and within 2 weeks of stopping one; about 2 weeks should pass after mirtazapine before starting one).

src.q: Concomitant use of mirtazapine with monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitors
Mirtazapine should not be administered concomitantly with MAO inhibitors or within two weeks after discontinuation of MAO inhibitor therapy.

items.t: Bone marrow depression (granulocytopenia, agranulocytosis), occasionally fatal, mostly over 65 years: stop and check blood count if fever, sore throat, stomatitis or other signs of infection.

src.q: Bone marrow depression, usually presenting as granulocytopenia or agranulocytosis, has been reported during treatment with Mirtazapine.
when such symptoms occur, treatment should be stopped and blood counts taken

items.t: Careful dosing and regular close monitoring needed in: epilepsy or organic brain syndrome, hepatic or renal impairment, cardiac disease (conduction disturbance, angina, recent MI), low blood pressure, diabetes (close monitoring; antidiabetic dose may need adjustment).

src.q: Careful dosing as well as regular and close monitoring is necessary in patients with:
cardiac diseases like conduction disturbances, angina pectoris and recent myocardial infarction, where normal precautions should be taken and concomitant medicines carefully administered
Insulin and/or oral hypoglycaemic dosage may need to be adjusted and close monitoring is recommended.

items.t: Epilepsy: introduce cautiously; stop if seizures develop or become more frequent.

src.q: Mirtazapine should be introduced cautiously in patients who have a history of seizures.
Treatment should be discontinued in any patient who develops seizures, or where there is an increase in seizure frequency.

items.t: QT prolongation, torsade de pointes and sudden death reported post-marketing (mostly overdose or other risk factors): caution with cardiovascular disease, family history of QT prolongation or other QT-prolonging drugs.

src.q: Cases of QT prolongation, Torsades de Pointes, ventricular tachycardia, and sudden death, have been reported during the post-marketing use of mirtazapine.
Caution should be exercised when Mirtazapine is prescribed in patients with known cardiovascular disease or family history of QT prolongation

items.t: Schizophrenia/psychosis: symptoms may worsen. Bipolar: may switch to mania; monitor closely, stop if manic. Prostate hypertrophy, micturition problems, narrow-angle glaucoma or raised eye pressure: take care.

src.q: Worsening of psychotic symptoms can occur when antidepressants are administered to patients with schizophrenia or other psychotic disturbances
Patients with a history of mania/hypomania should be closely monitored. Mirtazapine should be discontinued in any patient entering a manic phase.
Care should be taken in patients with micturition disturbances like prostate hypertrophy and in patients with acute narrow-angle glaucoma and increased intra-ocular pressure

items.t: Suicidal thoughts/behaviour: close supervision early and after dose changes; give the smallest quantity consistent with good care (overdose risk).

src.q: Close supervision of patients and in particular those at high risk should accompany therapy with antidepressants especially in early treatment and following dose changes.
onlythe smallest amount of Mirtazapine film-coated tablets should be given to the patient consistent with good patient management, in order to reduce the risk of overdose

items.t: Severe skin reactions (SJS, TEN, DRESS, bullous dermatitis, erythema multiforme): stop at once; never restart after such a reaction.

src.q: If signs and symptoms suggestive of these reactions appear, Mirtazapine should be withdrawn immediately.

items.t: Hyponatraemia (SIADH), very rare: caution in elderly or with medicines that cause hyponatraemia. Serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic drugs: caution and closer monitoring; stop if it occurs.

src.q: Caution should be exercised in patients at risk, such as elderly patients or patients concomitantly treated with medications known to cause hyponatraemia.
Treatment with mirtazapine should be discontinued if such events occur and supportive symptomatic treatment initiated.

items.t: Akathisia usually in first weeks (increasing the dose may be harmful). Withdrawal symptoms after abrupt stop. Jaundice: stop treatment. Lactose: not for hereditary galactose intolerance.

src.q: In patients who develop these symptoms, increasing the dose may be detrimental.
Treatment should be discontinued if jaundice occurs.
Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: Contraindicated: MAO inhibitors (and within 2 weeks).

src.q: Mirtazapine should not be administered concomitantly with MAO inhibitors or within two weeks after discontinuation of MAO inhibitor therapy.

items.t: Serotonergic drugs (L-tryptophan, triptans, tramadol, linezolid, methylene blue, SSRIs, venlafaxine, lithium, St John's wort): serotonin syndrome risk; caution and closer clinical monitoring.

src.q: co-administration with other serotonergic active substances (L-tryptophan, triptans, tramadol, linezolid, methylene blue, SSRIs, venlafaxine, lithium and St. John's Wort - Hypericum perforatum - preparations)
Caution should be advised and a closer clinical monitoring is required when these active substances are combined with mirtazapine.

items.t: Benzodiazepines and other sedatives (most antipsychotics, H1 antihistamines, opioids): more sedation, caution. Alcohol: avoid.

src.q: Mirtazapine may increase the sedating properties of benzodiazepines and other sedatives (notably most antipsychotics, antihistamine H1 antagonists, opioids).
Patients should therefore be advised to avoid alcoholic beverages while taking mirtazapine.

items.t: Warfarin: small rise in INR at 30 mg; monitor INR.

src.q: it is advisable to monitor the INR in case of concomitant treatment of warfarin with mirtazapine

items.t: QT-prolonging drugs (some antipsychotics and antibiotics): higher risk of QT prolongation/torsade de pointes.

src.q: The risk of QT prolongation and/or ventricular arrhythmias (e.g. Torsades de Pointes) may be increased with concomitant use of medicines which prolong the QTc interval

items.t: Carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampicin (inducers): mirtazapine levels fall 45% to 60%; dose may need increasing. Ketoconazole, cimetidine and other potent CYP3A4 inhibitors raise levels; dose may need decreasing.

src.q: Carbamazepine and phenytoin, CYP3A4 inducers, increased mirtazapine clearance about twofold
Co-administration of the potent CYP3A4 inhibitor ketoconazole increased the peak plasma levels and the AUC of mirtazapine by approximately 40 % and 50 % respectively.

items.t: No relevant pharmacokinetic interaction with paroxetine, amitriptyline, risperidone or lithium.

src.q: Interaction studies did not indicate any relevant pharmacokinetic effects on concurrent treatment of mirtazapine with paroxetine, amitriptyline, risperidone or lithium.

items.t: Moderate to severe renal impairment (CrCl <40 ml/min): clearance may be reduced (about 30% at CrCl <40, 50% at CrCl ≤10 ml/min); take this into account when prescribing. Mild impairment (CrCl <80 ml/min): no significant difference.

src.q: The clearance of mirtazapine may be decreased in patients with moderate to severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance <40 ml/min). This should be taken into account when prescribing Mirtazapine to this category of patients
No significant differences were found in patients with mild renal impairment (creatinine clearance <80 ml/min) as compared to the control group.

items.t: Clearance may be reduced (about 35% in mild to moderate impairment); take into account when prescribing, particularly in severe impairment (not studied).

src.q: This should be taken into account when prescribing Mirtazapine to this category of patients, particularly with severe hepatic impairment, as patients with severe hepatic impairment have not been investigated
the clearance of mirtazapine was approximately 35 % decreased in mild to moderate hepatically impaired patients

items.t: SmPC: limited data do not suggest a raised malformation risk. Possible risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn cannot be ruled out. Use with caution; if used until or near birth, monitor the newborn.

src.q: Limited data of the use of mirtazapine in pregnant women do not indicate an increased risk for congenital malformations.
Caution should be exercised when prescribing to pregnant women.
If Mirtazapine is used until, or shortly before birth, postnatal monitoring of the newborn is recommended to account for possible discontinuation effects.

items.t: BUMPS: can be used if recommended by a GP or specialist; no evidence of harm to development or of miscarriage/stillbirth. Later pregnancy use: hospital delivery usually advised (neonatal withdrawal; rarely PPHN with similar drugs).

src.q: Mirtazapine can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a GP or specialist.
There is no evidence that mirtazapine affects the baby's development or increases the chance of miscarriage or stillbirth.
If you take mirtazapine in later pregnancy, you will usually be advised to have a hospital delivery.

items.t: SmPC: very small amounts in milk; decide on breastfeeding versus therapy, weighing benefits.

src.q: Animal studies and limited human data have shown excretion of mirtazapine in breast milk only in very small amounts.
A decision on whether to continue/discontinue breast-feeding or to continue/discontinue therapy with Mirtazapine should be made

items.t: SPS: can be used with caution, but SSRIs or TCAs are preferred. Monitor the infant for irritability, drowsiness, GI symptoms, feeding changes and weight gain. No need to switch if used successfully in pregnancy (term, healthy infant).

src.q: Mirtazapine can be used with caution during breastfeeding, but SSRIs or TCAs are preferred.
Monitor infants for irritability, drowsiness, gastrointestinal symptoms, changes in feeding or not waking to feed, and appropriate weight gain.
there is no need to switch to a preferred choice in breastfeeding, as long as the infant has been born full term and healthy

items.t: Fertility: no effect in animal studies. Priapism reported (frequency not known).

src.q: Non-clinical reproductive toxicity studies in animals did not show any effect on fertility.
Reproductive system and breast disorders Priapism

items.t: Most common (over 5% in trials): somnolence, sedation, dry mouth, weight gain, increased appetite, dizziness, fatigue. Lowering the dose usually does not reduce sleepiness.

items.t: Aortic aneurysm/dissection and heart valve regurgitation: use only after careful benefit-risk assessment and considering other options if there is a family history of aneurysm, congenital or existing valve disease, existing aneurysm/dissection, or predisposing conditions (Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos, Turner, Behcet's, hypertension, rheumatoid arthritis, Takayasu or giant cell arteritis, atherosclerosis, Sjögren's, infective endocarditis).

src.q: fluoroquinolones should only be used after careful benefit-risk assessment and after consideration of other therapeutic options in patients with positive family history of aneurysm disease or congenital heart valve disease

fluoroquinolones should only be used after careful benefit-risk assessment and after consideration of other therapeutic options in the following patients at risk

items.t: Fulminant hepatitis, sometimes fatal: patients should contact the doctor before continuing if jaundice, dark urine, bleeding tendency or rapid weakness develop; test liver function if liver dysfunction is suspected.

Liver function tests/investigations should be performed in cases where indications of liver dysfunction occur.

items.t: Seizures: use with caution in CNS disorders or other seizure risk factors; stop if seizures occur.

src.q: Use should be with caution in patients with CNS disorders or in the presence of other risk factors which may predispose to seizures or lower the seizure threshold.

items.t: Psychiatric reactions, rarely leading to suicidal thoughts or attempts, can occur after the first dose: stop if they occur; caution in psychotic patients or a history of psychiatric disease.

note that fluoroquinolones can exacerbate existing psychiatric symptoms

items.t: Dysglycaemia (mainly elderly diabetics on oral hypoglycaemics or insulin), including hypoglycaemic coma: monitor blood glucose carefully.

src.q: Cases of hypoglycaemic coma have been reported. In diabetic patients, careful monitoring of blood glucose is recommended.

items.t: Myasthenia gravis: use with caution (symptoms can worsen). G6PD deficiency (or family history): use with caution (haemolysis).

src.q: Moxifloxacin should be used with caution in patients with myasthenia gravis because the symptoms can be exacerbated.
Therefore, moxifloxacin should be used with caution in these patients.

items.t: Severe skin reactions (SJS, TEN, AGEP, DRESS): stop at once and never restart. Peripheral neuropathy: patients should report pain, burning, tingling, numbness or weakness before continuing.

src.q: treatment with moxifloxacin must not be restarted in this patient at any time

items.t: Elderly with renal disorders who cannot keep up fluid intake: use with caution (dehydration may increase renal failure risk). Avoid UV and strong sunlight. antipsychotics (e.g. phenothiazines, pimozide, sertindole, haloperidol, sultopride) - tricyclic antidepressive agents

avoid coadministration of a corticosteroid with a fluoroquinolone since this could exacerbate fluoroquinolone-induced tendinitis and tendon rupture

ranitidine, probenecid, oral contraceptives, calcium supplements

severe tiredness, depressed mood, anxiety, problems with your memory or severe problems sleeping changes in your vision, taste, smell or hearing

a rapid onset of shortness of breath, especially when lying down flat in bed swelling of the ankles, feet, or abdomen new-onset heart palpitations
