src.q: Rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis and ankylosing spondylitis 500mg to 1g taken in 2 doses at 12-hour intervals or alternatively, as a single administration.
a loading dose of 750mg or 1g per day for the acute phase is recommended

items.t: Acute gout (tablets): 750 mg at once, then 250 mg every 8 hours until the attack has passed.

src.q: Acute gout 750mg at once then 250mg every 8 hours until the attack has passed.

items.t: Acute musculoskeletal disorders and dysmenorrhoea: 500 mg initially, then 250 mg every 6-8 hours as needed; maximum 1250 mg/day after the first day.

src.q: Acute musculoskeletal disorders and dysmenorrhoea 500mg initially followed by 250mg at 6 - 8 hour intervals as needed, with a maximum daily dose after the first day of 1250mg.

items.t: Older people: lowest effective dose for the shortest time; monitor regularly for GI bleeding. Gastro-resistant: start at the lowest recommended dose, especially in older people.

src.q: The patient should be monitored regularly for GI bleeding during NSAID therapy.
Therapy should be started at the lowest recommended dose, especially in older people.

items.t: Review treatment at regular intervals; stop if no benefit or intolerance.

src.q: Treatment should be reviewed at regular intervals and discontinued if no benefit is seen or intolerance occurs.

items.t: Tablets, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (over 5 years): 10 mg/kg/day in 2 doses 12 hours apart. Not recommended for any other indication under 16 years.

src.q: Paediatric population (over 5 years) For juvenile rheumatoid arthritis: 10mg/kg/day taken in 2 doses at 12-hour intervals. Naprosyn is not recommended for use in any other indication in children under 16 years of age.

items.t: Gastro-resistant tablets: not recommended under 16 years.

src.q: Naproxen is not recommended for use in children under 16 years of age.

items.t: Active or history of peptic ulceration or active GI bleeding; history of GI bleeding or perforation related to previous NSAIDs.

src.q: Active or history of peptic ulceration or active gastrointestinal bleeding (two or more distinct episodes of proven ulceration or bleeding). History of gastrointestinal bleeding or perforation, related to previous NSAIDs therapy.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to naproxen or naproxen sodium. Should not be given if aspirin or other NSAIDs induce asthma, rhinitis, nasal polyps or urticaria (potentially fatal).

src.q: Hypersensitivity to naproxen, naproxen sodium, or any of the excipients.
Naprosyn should not be given to patients in whom aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory/analgesic drugs induce the syndrome of asthma, rhinitis, nasal polyps or urticaria.

items.t: Severe renal, hepatic or heart failure; baseline creatinine clearance less than 30 ml/minute; last trimester of pregnancy.

src.q: Severe renal, hepatic or heart failure
Naprosyn is contraindicated in patients with baseline creatinine clearance less than 30 ml/minute
Naproxen is contraindicated during the last trimester of pregnancy

items.t: GI bleeding, ulceration or perforation can occur at any time and can be fatal; risk rises with dose, ulcer history and age. Start at the lowest dose; consider misoprostol or a PPI in at-risk patients and with low-dose aspirin. Withdraw if GI bleeding or ulceration occurs.

src.q: Combination therapy with protective agents (e.g. misoprostol or proton pump inhibitors) should be considered for these patients
When GI bleeding or ulceration occurs in patients receiving Naprosyn, the treatment should be withdrawn.

items.t: Cardiovascular: naproxen 1000 mg daily may carry a lower thrombotic risk but some risk cannot be excluded. Uncontrolled hypertension, congestive heart failure, ischaemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease or cerebrovascular disease: only after careful consideration.

src.q: Although data suggest that the use of naproxen (1000mg daily) may be associated with a lower risk, some risk cannot be excluded.

Patients with uncontrolled hypertension, congestive heart failure, established ischaemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease, and/or cerebrovascular disease should only be treated with naproxen after careful consideration.

items.t: Renal: use with great caution in impaired renal function; monitor serum creatinine and/or creatinine clearance and keep hydrated. Assess renal function before and during treatment when renal blood flow is compromised (volume depletion, cirrhosis, sodium restriction, heart failure, renal disease, diuretics, older people).

src.q: it should be used with great caution in patients with impaired renal function and the monitoring of serum creatinine and/or creatinine clearance is advised and patients should be adequately hydrated
should have renal function assessed before and during Naprosyn therapy

items.t: Coagulation disorders or drugs affecting haemostasis: observe carefully; naproxen prolongs bleeding time.

src.q: Patients who have coagulation disorders or are receiving drug therapy that interferes with haemostasis should be carefully observed if naproxen- containing products are administered.

items.t: Asthma or allergic disease: bronchospasm may be precipitated. Ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease: give with care. SLE / mixed connective tissue disease: aseptic meningitis risk.

src.q: Bronchospasm may be precipitated in patients suffering from, or with a history of, bronchial asthma or allergic disease.
NSAIDs should be given with care to patients with a history of gastrointestinal disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease)

items.t: Liver: LFT elevations and severe hepatic reactions (including fatal hepatitis) reported. Visual disturbance: ophthalmological examination.

src.q: Severe hepatic reactions, including jaundice and hepatitis (some cases of hepatitis have been fatal) have been reported
patients who develop visual disturbances during treatment with naproxen-containing products should have an ophthalmological examination

items.t: Serious skin reactions (SJS, TEN, DRESS): stop at the first rash, mucosal lesion or sign of hypersensitivity; never restart after SJS/TEN/DRESS.

src.q: Naprosyn should be discontinued at the first appearance of skin rash, mucosal lesions, or any other sign of hypersensitivity.
treatment with Naprosyn must not be restarted and should be permanently discontinued

items.t: Long-term use: regular medical supervision; prolonged use in older or debilitated patients is not recommended.

src.q: Patients treated with NSAIDs long-term should undergo regular medical supervision to monitor for adverse events.
Prolonged use of NSAIDs in these patients is not recommended.

items.t: If steroids are reduced or stopped during therapy, taper slowly and watch for adrenal insufficiency.

src.q: If steroid dosage is reduced or eliminated during therapy, the steroid dosage should be reduced slowly

items.t: Anticoagulants (e.g. warfarin, heparin): considered unsafe unless under direct medical supervision (NSAIDs may enhance anticoagulant effects).

src.q: It is considered unsafe to take NSAIDs in combination with anti-coagulants such as warfarin or heparin unless under direct medical supervision

items.t: Other NSAIDs including aspirin and COX-2 inhibitors: avoid. Regular naproxen for more than one day may inhibit the antiplatelet effect of low-dose aspirin.

src.q: Avoid concomitant use of two or more NSAIDs (including aspirin) as this may increase the risk of adverse effects
concomitant naproxen usage for more than one day consecutively may inhibit the effect of low-dose acetylsalicylic acid on platelet activity

items.t: Antiplatelets and SSRIs: increased GI bleeding risk. Corticosteroids: increased GI ulceration or bleeding (caution).

src.q: There is an increased risk of gastrointestinal bleeding (see Section 4.4) when anti-platelet agents and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are combined with NSAIDs.
caution should be taken when co-administering with cortico-steroids because of the increased risk of gastrointestinal ulceration or bleeding

items.t: Diuretics: decreased diuretic effect and higher nephrotoxicity risk (caution). Antihypertensives: reduced effect. ACE inhibitors / ARBs: increased risk of renal impairment, especially with poor renal function.

src.q: Caution is advised when Naprosyn is co-administered with diuretics as there can be a decreased diuretic effect.
Concomitant use of NSAIDs with ACE inhibitors or angiotensin-II receptor antagonists may increase the risk of renal impairment, especially in patients with pre-existing poor renal function

items.t: Methotrexate: caution (possible enhanced toxicity from reduced tubular secretion).

src.q: Caution is advised where methotrexate is given concurrently because of possible enhancement of its toxicity

items.t: Highly protein-bound drugs (hydantoins, sulfonamides, sulfonylureas, anticoagulants): observe for overdosage; adjust dose if needed. Quinolones: possible increased convulsion risk. Lithium, ciclosporin, tacrolimus, cardiac glycosides, probenecid, mifepristone, zidovudine also interact.

src.q: Patients simultaneously receiving Naprosyn and a hydantoin, sulfonamide or sulfonylurea should be observed for adjustment of dose if required.
Patients taking quinolones may have an increased risk of developing convulsions.

items.t: Antacids or colestyramine may delay (not reduce) absorption.

src.q: Concomitant administration of antacid or colestyramine can delay the absorption of naproxen but does not affect its extent.

items.t: Warfarin (warfarin SmPC): NSAIDs should be avoided if possible, or given with caution and increased clinical and laboratory monitoring.

src.q: The following examples should be avoided, or administered with caution with increased clinical and laboratory monitoring

items.t: Spironolactone (spironolactone SmPC): use with NSAIDs may lead to severe hyperkalaemia. ACE inhibitors (lisinopril SmPC): worsening renal function and raised serum potassium; caution, keep hydrated, monitor renal function.

src.q: may lead to severe hyperkalaemia
The combination should be administered with caution, especially in the elderly.

items.t: Metformin (metformin SmPC): close monitoring of renal function is necessary when an NSAID is started or used with metformin.

src.q: When starting or using such products in combination with metformin, close monitoring of renal function is necessary.

items.t: Methotrexate (SPS, methotrexate SmPC): increased risk of methotrexate toxicity; use with caution on specialist advice; not recommended if renal impairment (even mild) is present.

src.q: Use NSAIDs in combination with methotrexate with caution on the advice of the specialist (for example, rheumatologist).
If risk factors such as renal function disorders, including mild renal impairment, are present, combined administration with NSAIDs is not recommended.

items.t: Contraindicated if baseline creatinine clearance (CrCl) is less than 30 ml/minute (metabolites accumulate; haemodialysis does not lower naproxen levels).

src.q: Naprosyn is contraindicated in patients with baseline creatinine clearance less than 30 ml/minute because accumulation of naproxen metabolites has been seen in patients with severe renal failure or those on dialysis
Haemodialysis does not decrease the plasma concentration of naproxen because of the high degree of protein binding.

items.t: Renal impairment (CrCl 30 ml/minute or more): consider a lower dose; use with great caution; monitor serum creatinine and/or creatinine clearance.

src.q: A lower dose should be considered in patients with renal or hepatic impairment.
it should be used with great caution in patients with impaired renal function

items.t: MHRA: patients at risk of renal impairment or failure (particularly elderly) should avoid NSAIDs if possible.

src.q: patients at risk of renal impairment or renal failure (particularly elderly people) should avoid NSAIDs if possible

items.t: Severe hepatic failure: contraindicated. Other hepatic impairment or cirrhosis: consider a lower dose; use the lowest effective dose (unbound naproxen increased).

src.q: Severe renal, hepatic or heart failure
The implication of this finding for Naprosyn dosing is unknown but it is prudent to use the lowest effective dose.

items.t: Last trimester: contraindicated (SmPC 4.3).

src.q: Naproxen is contraindicated during the last trimester of pregnancy
Use of Naproxen in the last trimester of pregnancy is contraindicated

items.t: First and second trimesters: do not give unless clearly necessary; lowest dose, shortest time. From week 20: oligohydramnios and ductus arteriosus constriction reported; consider antenatal monitoring after several days of use; stop if found.

src.q: Therefore, during the first and second trimester of pregnancy, naproxen should not be given unless clearly necessary.
Antenatal monitoring for oligohydramnios and ductus arteriosus constriction should be considered after exposure to naproxen for several days from gestational week 20 onward.

items.t: Note: the 500 mg tablet SmPC section 4.6 ends with 'contraindicated during pregnancy' (whole pregnancy), which conflicts with its own section 4.3 (last trimester only) and with the gastro-resistant SmPC (third trimester).

src.q: Consequently, Naproxen is contraindicated during pregnancy.
Consequently, Naproxen is contraindicated during the third trimester of pregnancy

items.t: MHRA: avoid systemic NSAIDs from week 20 unless clinically required; contraindicated after 28 weeks. BUMPS: not advised unless prescribed by a doctor, especially from 20 weeks; paracetamol usually recommended instead.

src.q: avoid prescribing systemic NSAIDs from week 20 of pregnancy unless clinically required and prescribe the lowest dose for the shortest time in these circumstances
Use of naproxen during pregnancy is not advised unless prescribed by a doctor, especially if you are 20 or more weeks pregnant.

items.t: SmPC: found in breast milk; avoid in breastfeeding.

src.q: Naproxen has been found in the milk of lactating women. The use of Naprosyn should be avoided in patients who are breast-feeding.

items.t: SPS: short-term use only, with caution, because its long half-life risks accumulation; monitor infant for vomiting, diarrhoea, drowsiness, bruising or bleeding. Ibuprofen or diclofenac are preferred.

src.q: Naproxen can be used during breastfeeding for short-term use only, due to the risk of accumulation in breastfed infants. Infant monitoring is required.
Monitor infants for vomiting and diarrhoea, drowsiness, or signs of bruising or bleeding.

items.t: May impair fertility; not recommended in women attempting to conceive; consider stopping if difficulty conceiving or under investigation.

src.q: may impair fertility and is not recommended in women attempting to conceive

items.t: Most common are gastrointestinal: heartburn, nausea, vomiting, constipation, diarrhoea, flatulence, dyspepsia, abdominal discomfort (SmPC gives no frequency table).

src.q: The most commonly observed adverse events are gastrointestinal in nature. Heartburn, nausea, vomiting, constipation, diarrhoea, flatulence, dyspepsia, abdominal discomfort and epigastric distress.

items.t: GI bleeding (sometimes fatal, especially older people), ulceration, perforation: stop treatment.

src.q: More serious reactions which may occur are gastro-intestinal bleeding, which is sometimes fatal, particularly in older people

items.t: Anaphylactic/anaphylactoid reactions (may be fatal); serious skin reactions including SJS, TEN, DRESS.

src.q: Anaphylactoid reactions, like anaphylaxis, may have a fatal outcome.

items.t: Renal failure, interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome; hyperkalaemia; heart failure; fatal hepatitis; blood dyscrasias (agranulocytosis, aplastic and haemolytic anaemia); aseptic meningitis.

src.q: glomerular nephritis, interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome, haematuria, raised serum creatinine, renal papillary necrosis and renal failure
Metabolic and nutrition disorders: hyperkalaemia.

items.t: SPS baseline: blood pressure, eGFR, full blood count, serum creatinine; LFTs if hepatic impairment. SmPC: assess renal function before treatment if renal blood flow compromised.

src.q: Estimated glomerular filtration rate Full blood count Serum creatinine Liver function tests
should have renal function assessed before and during Naprosyn therapy

items.t: SPS after starting or dose change: eGFR or serum creatinine and FBC within 2 weeks; blood pressure within 4 weeks; then periodically.

src.q: After started or dose changed Consider Within 2 weeks Estimated glomerular filtration rate or Serum creatinine (for creatinine clearance) Full blood count

items.t: SmPC: monitor serum creatinine and/or creatinine clearance in renal impairment; regular supervision for long-term use; monitor older people for GI bleeding.

src.q: the monitoring of serum creatinine and/or creatinine clearance is advised

items.t: Stop if GI bleeding or ulceration, at the first skin rash or sign of hypersensitivity, or if no benefit.

src.q: When GI bleeding or ulceration occurs in patients receiving Naprosyn, the treatment should be withdrawn.

items.t: Take preferably with or after food.

src.q: To be taken preferably with or after food.

items.t: Gastro-resistant tablets: swallow whole; do not break or crush.

src.q: Naproxen Gastro-Resistant tablets should be swallowed whole and not broken or crushed.

items.t: Report any unusual abdominal symptoms, especially bleeding, particularly early in treatment.

src.q: should report any unusual abdominal symptoms (especially GI bleeding) particularly in the initial stages of treatment

items.t: May cause drowsiness, dizziness, vertigo, visual disturbance; do not drive if affected.

src.q: If patients experience these or similar undesirable effects, they should not drive or operate machinery.

items.t: Short-term treatment of steroid-responsive eye conditions when preventive antibiotic cover is also needed, after fungal and viral disease have been excluded.

src.q: indicated for the short-term treatment of steroid responsive conditions of the eye when prophylactic antibiotic treatment is also required, after excluding the presence of fungal and viral disease

items.t: Prescription-only medicine in the UK. Short-term use only.

src.q: Prescription only medicine
indicated for the short-term treatment of steroid responsive conditions of the eye

items.t: Eye drops: 1 to 2 drops into each affected eye up to six times daily, or more often if needed.

src.q: Apply one or two drops to each affected eye up to six times daily or, more frequently if required.

items.t: Eye ointment: a small amount into the conjunctival sac(s) up to 3 to 4 times daily, or at bedtime alongside the drops.

src.q: Apply a small amount into the conjunctival sac(s) up to three to four times daily or, may be used adjunctively with drops at bedtime.

items.t: Same dose as adults. Children may have a greater and earlier risk of steroid-induced raised eye pressure; check intraocular pressure with prolonged use. Children are among those predisposed to Cushing's syndrome or adrenal suppression with intensive or long-term use.

src.q: Children and Adults (including the Elderly)
the risk of corticosteroid-induced ocular hypertension may be greater in children and may occur earlier than in adults
may occur after intensive or long-term continuous therapy in predisposed patients, including children

items.t: Hypersensitivity to neomycin, polymyxin B, dexamethasone or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substances or to any of the excipients.

items.t: Herpes simplex keratitis; vaccinia, varicella and other viral infections of the cornea or conjunctiva.

src.q: Herpes simplex keratitis. Vaccinia, varicella, and other viral infection of cornea or conjunctiva.

items.t: Fungal disease of the eye; untreated parasitic eye infection; mycobacterial eye infection.

src.q: Fungal diseases of ocular structures or untreated parasitic eye infections. Mycobacterial ocular infections.

items.t: Prolonged eye steroid use can cause raised intraocular pressure or glaucoma (optic nerve damage, loss of vision or visual field) and posterior subcapsular cataract. Check intraocular pressure routinely and often with prolonged use. Risk is higher in predisposed patients (e.g. diabetes).

src.q: Prolonged use of ophthalmic corticosteroids may result in ocular hypertension and/or glaucoma, with damage to the optic nerve, reduced visual acuity and visual field defects, and posterior subcapsular cataract formation.
In patients receiving prolonged ophthalmic corticosteroid therapy, intraocular pressure should be checked routinely and frequently.
The risk of corticosteroid-induced raised intraocular pressure and/or cataract formation is increased in predisposed patients (e.g. diabetes).

items.t: Steroids may lower resistance to infection and mask signs of infection. Suspect fungal infection if a corneal ulcer persists; stop the steroid if fungal infection occurs. Frequent slit-lamp examination is essential to avoid worsening herpetic corneal disease.

src.q: Corticosteroids may reduce resistance to and aid in the establishment of nonsusceptible bacterial, fungal, parasitic or viral infections and mask the clinical signs of infection
corticosteroid therapy should be discontinued if fungal infection occurs
To avoid the risk of enhancement of herpetic corneal disease, frequent slit lamp examination is essential.

items.t: Diseases that thin the cornea or sclera: perforation has occurred with topical steroids. Topical eye steroids may slow corneal healing.

src.q: In those diseases causing thinning of the cornea or sclera, perforations have been known to occur with the use of topical corticosteroids.
Topical ophthalmic corticosteroids may slow corneal wound healing.

items.t: Neomycin sensitivity can occur, with possible cross-sensitivity to other aminoglycosides; reactions range from local to anaphylaxis. Stop if serious or hypersensitivity reactions occur.

src.q: Sensitivity to topically applied aminoglycosides may occur in some patients. Cross-sensitivity to other aminoglycosides may also occur.
If signs of serious reactions or hypersensitivity occur, discontinue the use of this product.

items.t: Cushing's syndrome or adrenal suppression can occur after intensive or long-term use in predisposed patients, including children and patients on CYP3A4 inhibitors; withdraw gradually in these cases.

src.q: Cushing's syndrome and/or adrenal suppression associated with systemic absorption of ocular dexamethasone may occur after intensive or long-term continuous therapy in predisposed patients
In these cases, treatment should be progressively discontinued.

items.t: Personal or family history of diabetes: use with caution (possible reduced glucose tolerance).

src.q: caution is recommended when administering MAXITROL to patients with a personal or family history of diabetes

items.t: Blurred vision or other visual disturbance: consider referral to an ophthalmologist (cataract, glaucoma, central serous chorioretinopathy).

src.q: the patient should be considered for referral to an ophthalmologist for evaluation of possible causes which may include cataract, glaucoma or rare diseases such as central serous chorioretinopathy (CSCR)

items.t: Contact lenses are discouraged during treatment of an eye infection. Drops contain benzalkonium chloride: if lenses are allowed, remove them before use and wait 15 minutes. Use with caution in dry eye or a compromised cornea.

src.q: patients should be advised not to wear contact lenses during treatment
must be instructed to remove contact lenses prior to application of MAXITROL eye drops, suspension and wait 15 minutes after instillation of the dose before reinsertion
Should be used with caution in dry eye patients and in patients where the cornea may be compromised.

items.t: Systemic neomycin and polymyxin B can be nephrotoxic, neurotoxic and ototoxic (not reported after eye use); caution with systemic aminoglycoside or polymyxin B therapy.

src.q: Although these effects have not been reported following topical ocular use of this product, caution is advised when used concomitantly with systemic aminoglycoside or polymyxin B therapy.

items.t: CYP3A4 inhibitors (including ritonavir and cobicistat) may reduce dexamethasone clearance, causing adrenal suppression or Cushing's syndrome. Avoid unless the benefit outweighs the risk; if used, monitor for systemic steroid effects.

src.q: CYP3A4 inhibitors (including ritonavir and cobicistat): may decrease dexamethasone clearance resulting in increased effects and adrenal suppression/Cushing's syndrome.

The combination should be avoided unless the benefit outweighs the increased risk of systemic corticosteroid side-effects, in which case patients should be monitored for systemic corticosteroid effects.

items.t: Other drugs with neurotoxic, ototoxic or nephrotoxic effects (systemic, oral or topical), given at the same time or one after another: additive toxicity with neomycin; avoid whenever possible.

src.q: Concomitant and/or sequential use of an aminoglycoside (neomycin) and other systemic, oral, or topical drugs that have neurotoxic, ototoxic, or nephrotoxic effects may result in additive toxicity and should be avoided, whenever possible.

items.t: Antidiabetic medicines: a higher dose may be needed because the steroid may reduce their glucose-lowering effect.

src.q: The possibility of a higher need for hypoglycaemic medicinal products must be taken into consideration when administering MAXITROL to diabetic patients

items.t: Topical (eye) NSAIDs with topical steroids may increase corneal healing problems.

src.q: Concomitant use of topical steroids and topical NSAIDs may increase the potential for corneal healing problems.

items.t: Other eye medicines: give at least 5 minutes apart; use eye ointments last.

src.q: If more than one ophthalmic medicinal product is being used, the medicines must be administered at least 5 minutes apart. Eye ointments should be administered last.

items.t: Not studied in renal impairment; no dose adjustment needed because systemic absorption is low.

src.q: However, due to low systemic absorption of the active substances after topical administration of this product, dose adjustment is not necessary.

items.t: Not studied in hepatic impairment; no dose adjustment needed because systemic absorption is low.

src.q: However, due to low systemic absorption of the active substances after topical administration of this product, dose adjustment is not necessary.

items.t: SmPC: not recommended in pregnancy. Prolonged or repeated corticosteroid use has been linked to intrauterine growth restriction; observe newborns of mothers given substantial steroid doses for hypoadrenalism. Neomycin at this low eye dose is not expected to cause fetal ototoxicity or nephrotoxicity.

src.q: MAXITROL eye drops, suspension is not recommended during pregnancy.
Prolonged or repeated corticoid use during pregnancy has been associated with an increased risk of intra-uterine growth retardation.
At the low dose administered via this topical product, neomycin is not expected to cause ototoxicity or nephrotoxicity from in utero exposure.

items.t: BUMPS: most eye drops can be used in pregnancy because very little reaches the baby; aminoglycoside eye or ear drops do not enter the bloodstream in amounts that could harm the baby.

src.q: Most types of eye drops can be used during pregnancy.
when used in the form of eye or ear drops, do not enter the bloodstream in amounts that could harm the baby

items.t: SmPC: unknown whether excreted in milk; a risk to the infant cannot be excluded. Decide whether to stop breastfeeding or stop treatment, weighing the benefits.

src.q: Because systemic corticosteroids and aminoglycosides may be distributed into milk, a risk to the suckling child cannot be excluded.
A decision must be made whether to discontinue/abstain from breast-feeding or to discontinue therapy

items.t: SPS: dexamethasone for eye use can be used during breastfeeding with no monitoring needed; combination products containing antibiotics add no extra risk.

src.q: Dexamethasone for ophthalmic use or use in the ear can be used during breastfeeding.
There are no additional risks when combination topical preparations containing antibiotics are used.

items.t: No data on effects on male or female fertility.

src.q: There are no available data on the use of this medicine affecting male or female fertility.

items.t: No common or very common effects listed. Most frequent in trials (0.7% to 0.9%): eye discomfort, keratitis, eye irritation. Uncommon: raised intraocular pressure, eye itching.

src.q: the most common adverse reactions were ocular discomfort, keratitis, and eye irritation, occurring in 0.7% to 0.9% of patients
Uncommon: keratitis, intraocular pressure increased, eye pruritus, ocular discomfort, , eye irritation

items.t: Raised intraocular pressure with optic nerve damage, posterior subcapsular cataract, corneal thinning or perforation (especially after long treatment). Check intraocular pressure with prolonged use.

src.q: in diseases causing thinning of the cornea or sclera there is a higher risk for perforation especially after long treatments
Topical ophthalmic steroid use may result in increased intraocular pressure with damage to the optic nerve, reduced visual acuity and visual field defects.

items.t: Hypersensitivity (local to anaphylaxis), Stevens-Johnson syndrome, Cushing's syndrome or adrenal suppression (frequency not known). Stop if serious reactions or hypersensitivity occur.

src.q: Not known: Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Not known: Cushing's syndrome, adrenal suppression
If signs of serious reactions or hypersensitivity occur, discontinue the use of this product.

items.t: Prolonged use: check intraocular pressure routinely and often (especially in children).

src.q: In patients receiving prolonged ophthalmic corticosteroid therapy, intraocular pressure should be checked routinely and frequently.
This is especially important in paediatric patients

items.t: Frequent slit-lamp examination to avoid worsening herpetic corneal disease.

src.q: To avoid the risk of enhancement of herpetic corneal disease, frequent slit lamp examination is essential.

items.t: With CYP3A4 inhibitors: monitor for systemic corticosteroid effects.

src.q: in which case patients should be monitored for systemic corticosteroid effects

items.t: Stop the steroid if fungal infection occurs; stop the product if serious or hypersensitivity reactions occur.

src.q: corticosteroid therapy should be discontinued if fungal infection occurs
If signs of serious reactions or hypersensitivity occur, discontinue the use of this product.

items.t: Drops: shake the bottle well. Do not let the dropper tip touch the eyelids or any surface.

src.q: Shake the bottle well before use.
caution should be exercised to ensure that the dropper tip does not touch the eyelids, the surroundings of the eye, or any other surface

items.t: Press on the inner corner of the eye (nasolacrimal occlusion) or close the eyelid gently after use to reduce systemic absorption.

src.q: Nasolacrimal occlusion or gently closing the eyelid after administration is recommended.

items.t: Ointment: do not touch the tube tip to any surface.

src.q: Do not touch the top of the tube to any surface as this may contaminate the contents.

items.t: Vision may blur for a short time after use; wait until it clears before driving or using machines.

src.q: If transient blurred vision occurs upon instillation, the patient must wait until the vision clears before driving or using machinery.

items.t: See a doctor if eye pain, redness, swelling or irritation gets worse or does not settle.

src.q: Patients using ophthalmic preparations containing neomycin sulphate should be advised to consult a physician if ocular pain, redness, swelling, or irritation worsens or persists.

items.t: Do not wear contact lenses during treatment.

src.q: patients should be advised not to wear contact lenses during treatment with MAXITROL eye ointment

restrictions.note: No UK product information found.

hepatic.note: No UK product information found.

items.t: All grades of hypertension; prophylaxis of chronic stable angina (alone or with a beta-blocker).

src.q: For the treatment of all grades of hypertension. For the prophylaxis of chronic stable angina pectoris either as monotherapy or in combination with a beta-blocker.

items.t: Not for acute angina attacks, not for secondary prevention of MI; safety in malignant hypertension not established.

src.q: should not be used for the treatment of acute attacks of angina.
should not be used for secondary prevention of myocardial infarction.
The safety of Adalat LA in malignant hypertension has not been established.

items.t: Hypertension: mild to moderate start 20 mg once daily; severe start 30 mg once daily; up to a maximum of 90 mg once daily.

src.q: In mild to moderate hypertension, the recommended initial dose is one 20 mg tablet once-daily. In severe hypertension, the recommended initial dose is one 30 mg tablet once-daily.
up to a maximum of 90 mg once-daily.

items.t: Angina prophylaxis: start 30 mg once daily; up to a maximum of 90 mg once daily. When switching from another calcium-channel blocker, start at 30 mg once daily.

src.q: For the prophylaxis of angina pectoris, the recommended initial dose is one 30 mg tablet once-daily.
Patients switched from other calcium antagonists should initiate therapy at the recommended initial dose of 30 mg Adalat LA once-daily.

items.t: Different UK product (twice-daily retard 20 mg tablets): 20 mg every 12 hours, up to 40 mg every 12 hours. Shown only because the clinic product is labelled retard; the once-daily doses above do not apply to a twice-daily retard tablet.

src.q: The recommended dose is one tablet (20 mg) every 12 hours.
The dosage may be increased up to 40 mg every 12 hours to achieve the desired effect.

items.t: Elderly over 65 years and renal impairment: no dose adjustment needed.

src.q: Based on pharmacokinetic data for Adalat LA no dose adaptation in elderly people above 65 years is necessary.
no dosage adjustment is required in patients with renal impairment

items.t: Safety and efficacy below 18 years not established.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of Adalat LA in children below 18 years has not been established.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to nifedipine, other dihydropyridines (theoretical cross-reactivity) or excipients.

src.q: should not be administered to patients with known hypersensitivity to the active substance, or to other dihydropyridines because of the theoretical risk of cross-reactivity

items.t: Cardiogenic shock; clinically significant aortic stenosis; unstable angina; during or within one month of a myocardial infarction.

src.q: Adalat LA should not be used in cases of cardiogenic shock, clinically significant aortic stenosis, unstable angina, or during or within one month of a myocardial infarction.

items.t: Hepatic impairment (long duration of action of this formulation).

src.q: Owing to the duration of action of the formulation, Adalat LA should not be administered to patients with hepatic impairment.

items.t: History of gastrointestinal or oesophageal obstruction or any narrowing of the GI tract; Kock pouch; inflammatory bowel disease or Crohn's disease.

src.q: should not be administered to patients with a history of gastro-intestinal obstruction, oesophageal obstruction, or any degree of decreased lumen diameter of the gastro-intestinal tract.
Adalat LA must not be used in patients with a Kock pouch (ileostomy after proctocolectomy).
Adalat LA is contra-indicated in patients with inflammatory bowel disease or Crohn's disease.

items.t: With rifampicin (nifedipine levels too low).

src.q: Adalat LA should not be administered concomitantly with rifampicin since effective plasma levels of nifedipine may not be achieved owing to enzyme induction

items.t: Hypotension: caution; care if systolic BP below 90 mmHg.

src.q: Caution should be exercised in patients with hypotension as there is a risk of further reduction in blood pressure and care must be exercised in patients with very low blood pressure (severe hypotension with systolic blood pressure less than 90 mm Hg).

items.t: Poor cardiac reserve: use with caution; heart failure has occasionally worsened.

src.q: Adalat LA should be used with caution in patients whose cardiac reserve is poor. Deterioration of heart failure has occasionally been observed with nifedipine.

items.t: Non-digestible tablet shell: may appear in stools; obstructive symptoms and, very rarely, bezoars can occur.

src.q: Bezoars can occur in very rare cases and may require surgical intervention.

items.t: Diabetes: control may need adjusting. Dialysis with malignant hypertension and hypovolaemia: marked fall in blood pressure possible.

src.q: Diabetic patients taking Adalat LA may require adjustment of their control.
In dialysis patients with malignant hypertension and hypovolaemia, a marked decrease in blood pressure can occur.

items.t: With beta-blockers or other antihypertensives: additive effect may cause postural hypotension. Does not prevent rebound after stopping other antihypertensives.

src.q: the possibility of an additive effect resulting in postural hypotension should be borne in mind.
Adalat LA will not prevent possible rebound effects after cessation of other antihypertensive therapy.

items.t: CYP3A4 inhibitors (macrolides e.g. erythromycin, azole antifungals e.g. ketoconazole, HIV protease inhibitors, fluoxetine, nefazodone, valproic acid, cimetidine, diltiazem): raise nifedipine levels; monitor blood pressure and consider a lower nifedipine dose.

src.q: Drugs increasing nifedipine exposure: - macrolide antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin) - anti-HIV protease inhibitors (e.g., ritonavir) - azole anti-mycotics (e.g., ketoconazole) - fluoxetine
valproic acid - cimetidine - diltiazem
Upon co-administration of known inhibitors of the cytochrome P450 3A4 system, the blood pressure should be monitored and, if necessary, a reduction in the nifedipine dose considered

items.t: CYP3A4 inducers (rifampicin - contraindicated; phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital): lower nifedipine levels; monitor response and consider a dose increase (and reduce again when the inducer stops).

src.q: Drugs decreasing nifedipine exposure: - rifampicin (see above) - phenytoin - carbamazepine - phenobarbital
Upon co-administration of inducers of the cytochrome P450 3A4 system, the clinical response to nifedipine should be monitored and, if necessary, an increase in the nifedipine dose considered.

items.t: Beta-blockers: monitor carefully (heart failure may worsen in isolated cases). Other antihypertensives: increased blood pressure lowering.

src.q: When nifedipine is administered simultaneously with ß-receptor blockers the patient should be carefully monitored, since deterioration of heart failure is also known to develop in isolated cases.
Nifedipine may increase the blood pressure lowering effect of concomitant applied antihypertensives.

items.t: Grapefruit or grapefruit juice: avoid (raised levels, effect may last 3 days).

src.q: Ingestion of grapefruit/grapefruit juice is therefore to be avoided while taking nifedipine

items.t: Digoxin (check for digoxin toxicity), quinidine (monitor levels), tacrolimus (monitor levels, consider lower dose). IV magnesium sulfate in pregnancy: monitor blood pressure carefully.

src.q: The patient should therefore be subjected to precautionary checks for symptoms of digoxin overdosage
Careful monitoring of blood pressure must be exercised when administering nifedipine with I.V. magnesium sulfate

items.t: No dose adjustment needed in renal impairment.

src.q: Based on pharmacokinetic data, no dosage adjustment is required in patients with renal impairment

items.t: Prolonged-release tablets should not be given in hepatic impairment (4.3). Section 4.4 also says impaired liver function needs careful monitoring and, in severe cases, possibly a dose reduction.

src.q: Owing to the duration of action of the formulation, Adalat LA should not be administered to patients with hepatic impairment.
In patients with impaired liver function careful monitoring and, in severe cases, a dose reduction may be necessary.

items.t: SmPC: should not be used in pregnancy unless the woman needs nifedipine; reserve for severe hypertension unresponsive to standard therapy; very careful individual risk-benefit assessment.

src.q: Adalat LA should not be used during pregnancy unless the clinical condition of the woman requires treatment with nifedipine.
Adalat LA should be reserved for women with severe hypertension who are unresponsive to standard therapy
any use in pregnancy requires a very careful individual risk benefit assessment

items.t: BUMPS (calcium-channel blockers): nifedipine is commonly used in pregnancy and unlikely to cause harm; no extra monitoring for major birth defects.

src.q: Nifedipine is commonly used in pregnancy and is unlikely to cause harm.
No extra monitoring for major birth defects is required following use of a calcium channel blocker.

items.t: SmPC: excreted in milk in small amounts; no specific safety concerns from limited data; advise watching for low blood pressure in the infant; weigh benefit of breastfeeding against benefit of therapy.

src.q: Limited clinical evidence suggests no specific safety concerns, but patients should be advised of signs of low blood pressure in the infant
Decisions on whether to breastfeed during treatment or to abstain from nifedipine therapy should take into account the benefit of breastfeeding for the child and the benefit of therapy for the woman.

items.t: SPS: the dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker of choice (very small amounts in milk); as a precaution monitor the infant for hypotension. Applies to any formulation, including modified-release.

src.q: This is a preferred choice due to very small amounts in breast milk and extensive experience of use during breastfeeding.
Recommendations apply to any indication the medicine is being used for and to any formulation, including modified-release preparations.

items.t: Male fertility: reversible sperm changes reported in IVF; consider nifedipine as a cause in men with repeated unsuccessful IVF.

src.q: calcium antagonists like nifedipine should be considered as possible causes.

items.t: Common: oedema (9.9%, including peripheral oedema), headache (3.9%), vasodilatation, constipation, feeling unwell (others below 3%).

src.q: ADRs listed under "common" were observed with a frequency below 3% with the exception of oedema (9.9%) and headache (3.9%).
Oedema (incl. peripheral oedema) Vasodilatation

items.t: Allergic oedema/angioedema including larynx oedema (may be life-threatening); anaphylactic reactions; agranulocytosis; toxic epidermal necrolysis; jaundice; bezoar and intestinal obstruction.

src.q: Allergic oedema/angioedema (incl. larynx oedema*)
* = may result in life-threatening outcome
Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis

items.t: Chest pain (angina) may occur. Pulmonary oedema reported when used as a tocolytic in pregnancy.

src.q: Chest pain (Angina pectoris)
**cases have been reported when used as tocolytic during pregnancy

items.t: Overdose: reduced consciousness to coma, hypotension, tachy- or bradycardia, hyperglycaemia, metabolic acidosis, cardiogenic shock with pulmonary oedema; observe at least 12 hours after a sustained-release overdose.

src.q: Disturbances of consciousness to the point of coma, a drop in blood pressure, tachycardia, bradycardia, hyperglycaemia, metabolic acidosis, hypoxia, cardiogenic shock with pulmonary oedema.
for 12 hours if a sustained release preparation has been taken.

items.t: Blood pressure when starting a CYP3A4 inhibitor; clinical response with a CYP3A4 inducer.

src.q: Upon co-administration of known inhibitors of the cytochrome P450 3A4 system, the blood pressure should be monitored and, if necessary, a reduction in the nifedipine dose considered
Upon co-administration of inducers of the cytochrome P450 3A4 system, the clinical response to nifedipine should be monitored and, if necessary, an increase in the nifedipine dose considered.

items.t: With beta-blockers: monitor carefully for worsening heart failure.

src.q: When nifedipine is administered simultaneously with ß-receptor blockers the patient should be carefully monitored

items.t: Swallow whole with water, with or without food; never bite, chew or break. Take at about the same time each day, preferably in the morning.

src.q: The tablets should be swallowed whole with a glass of water, either with or without food.
under no circumstances should they be bitten, chewed or broken up.
The tablets should be taken at approximately 24-hour intervals, i.e. at the same time each day, preferably during the morning.

items.t: The empty tablet shell may be seen in the stools; this is expected.

src.q: As the outer membrane of the Adalat LA tablet is not digested, what appears to be the complete tablet may be seen in the toilet or associated with the patient's stools.

items.t: Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice.

src.q: Ingestion of grapefruit/grapefruit juice is therefore to be avoided while taking nifedipine

items.t: Driving may be affected, especially at the start, on changes, or with alcohol.

src.q: This applies particularly at the start of treatment, on changing the medication and in combination with alcohol.

items.t: One UK SmPC: treatment of and prophylaxis against acute or recurrent uncomplicated lower UTI or pyelitis, spontaneous or after surgery; adults, children and infants over 3 months.

src.q: For the treatment of and prophylaxis against acute or recurrent, uncomplicated lower urinary tract infections or pyelitis either spontaneous or following surgical procedures. It is indicated in adults, children and infants over 3 months old.

items.t: Another UK SmPC: acute uncomplicated lower UTI; short-term prophylaxis after urological procedures and catheterisation; long-term treatment of UTI up to 6 months (longer only if benefits clearly outweigh risks, and only if no suitable alternative).

src.q: In acute uncomplicated lower urinary tract infections; For short-term prophylaxis after surgical procedures, transurethral interventions, catheterization, cystoscopy and indwelling catheter
For long-term treatment of urinary tract infections up to 6 months; longer than 6 months only if the benefits clearly outweigh the potential risks.
In view of the side effects, long-term therapy should only be used if no suitable alternative is available

items.t: MHRA: do not use to treat sepsis secondary to UTI or suspected upper UTI. Consult official guidance on antibiotic use.

src.q: Nitrofurantoin should not be used to treat sepsis syndrome secondary to urinary tract infection or suspected upper urinary tract infections

items.t: One UK SmPC: prolonged use is not recommended; long-term therapy only if no suitable alternative.

src.q: Prolonged use of Nitrofurantoin is not recommended.

items.t: Acute uncomplicated UTI: 50 mg four times daily for 7 days (one UK SmPC); 50 mg four times a day for 5 to 7 days or at least 3 days after the urine is clear (another UK SmPC, adults and children from 12 years).

src.q: Acute Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infections (UTIs): 50 mg four times daily for seven days.
Adults and children aged from 12 years: one 50 mg capsule 4 times a day. General use: 5 to 7 days or at least 3 days after no infection is detectable in the urine.

items.t: Severe chronic recurrence: 100 mg four times daily for 7 days (one UK SmPC).

src.q: Severe chronic recurrence (UTIs): 100 mg four times daily for seven days.

items.t: Long-term suppression / long-term treatment: 50 to 100 mg once a day (usually in the evening).

src.q: Long term suppression: 50-100 mg once a day.
Adults and children from 12 years: 50 to 100 mg once a day, usually in the evening before sleep.

items.t: Surgical prophylaxis: 50 mg four times daily for the procedure (or day of surgery) and 3 days after.

src.q: Prophylaxis: 50 mg four times daily for the duration of procedure and for three days thereafter.

items.t: MHRA: treatment courses for infections last 3 to 7 days.

src.q: Treatment courses for infections are indicated to last between 3 and 7 days.

items.t: Elderly: normal adult dose provided there is no significant renal impairment (where it is contraindicated).

src.q: Provided there is no significant renal impairment, in which Nitrofurantoin is contraindicated, the dosage should be that for any normal adult.

items.t: One UK SmPC (children and infants over 3 months): acute UTI 3 mg/kg/day in four divided doses for 7 days; suppressive 1 mg/kg once a day. Under 25 kg, consider the suspension.

src.q: Acute Urinary Tract Infections: 3mg/kg day in four divided doses for seven days. Suppressive - 1mg/kg, once a day.
For children under 25 kg body weight consideration should be given to the use of Nitrofurantoin Suspension.

items.t: Another UK SmPC: girls aged 5 to 12 years usually 3 to 6 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses for 7 days (or 3 days after urine clear); capsules may not be suitable at this age. From 12 years: adult dose.

src.q: In girls aged 5 to 12 years: the usual dose is 3 to 6 mg/kg body weight per day divided into 4 doses
This pharmaceutical form (capsules) may not be suitable for use in children in this age group.

items.t: Contraindicated in infants under 3 months (risk of haemolytic anaemia).

src.q: In infants under three months of age as well as pregnant patients at term (during labour and delivery)

items.t: Hypersensitivity to nitrofurantoin, other nitrofurans or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance, other nitrofurans or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Renal impairment with eGFR below 45 (both UK SmPCs print the unit as ml/min; MHRA gives ml/min/1.73 m²). One UK SmPC also lists increased serum creatinine. MHRA: a short course may be used with caution in certain patients with eGFR 30 to 44 (see Renal).

src.q: Patients suffering from renal dysfunction with an eGFR below 45 ml/minute.
for patients with renal impairment (eGFR below 45 ml/min) or with an increased serum creatinine
Nitrofurantoin is contraindicated in patients with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of less than 45 ml/min/1.73m2.

items.t: G6PD deficiency; acute porphyria.

src.q: G6PD deficiency (see also Section 4.6) Acute porphyria.

items.t: Infants under 3 months and pregnant women at term (labour and delivery): theoretical haemolytic anaemia in the fetus or newborn.

src.q: In infants under three months of age as well as pregnant patients at term (during labour and delivery) because of the theoretical possibility of haemolytic anaemia in the foetus or in the newborn infant

items.t: One UK SmPC: previous lung or liver reaction (other than peripheral neuropathy) to nitrofurantoin or other nitrofurans.

src.q: for patients who have previously had a lung or liver reaction other than a peripheral neuropathy after use of nitrofurantoin or other nitrofurans

items.t: Pulmonary reactions (acute, subacute, chronic; fibrosis, interstitial pneumonitis) can occur with short- or long-term use. Be especially vigilant in the first week; monitor closely on long-term therapy, especially in the elderly. Stop immediately if they occur.

src.q: pulmonary reactions may occur with short- or long-term use of nitrofurantoin, and increased vigilance for acute pulmonary reactions is required in the first week of treatment
Close monitoring of the lung disease of patients receiving long-term therapy is indicated (especially in the elderly).
If these reactions occur, nitrofurantoin should be discontinued immediately.

items.t: Hepatotoxicity (hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, cholestatic jaundice, chronic active hepatitis, hepatic necrosis; some fatal): monitor periodically; withdraw immediately if hepatitis occurs.

src.q: patients should be monitored periodically for changes in biochemical tests that would indicate liver injury. If hepatitis occurs, the drug should be withdrawn immediately

items.t: Use with caution in pulmonary disease, hepatic dysfunction, neurological disorders and allergic diathesis (these can mask adverse reactions).

src.q: Nitrofurantoin should be used with caution in patients with pulmonary disease, hepatic dysfunction, neurological disorders, and allergic diathesis.

items.t: Peripheral neuropathy (may be severe or irreversible): stop at the first signs (paraesthesia). Use with caution with anaemia, diabetes, electrolyte imbalance, debilitating conditions or vitamin B (especially folate) deficiency; one SmPC also names renal insufficiency and alcoholism as risk factors.

src.q: Therefore, treatment should be stopped at the first signs of neural involvement (paraesthesia).
Nitrofurantoin should be used in caution with patients with anaemia, diabetes mellitus, electrolyte imbalance, debilitating conditions and vitamin B (particularly folate) deficiency.

Conditions such as renal insufficiency, anaemia, diabetes mellitus, alcoholism, electrolyte disorder, vitamin B deficiency (especially folate deficiency) and exhaustive conditions increase the risk of developing peripheral neuropathy.

items.t: Stop at any sign of haemolysis in suspected G6PD deficiency.

src.q: Nitrofurantoin should be discontinued at any sign of haemolysis in those with suspected glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency.

items.t: Stop if otherwise unexplained pulmonary, hepatic, haematological or neurological syndromes occur.

src.q: Discontinue treatment with Nitrofurantoin if otherwise unexplained pulmonary, hepatic, haematological or neurological syndromes occur.

items.t: Not effective for parenchymal infection of a unilaterally non-functioning kidney; exclude a surgical cause in recurrent or severe cases.

src.q: Nitrofurantoin is not effective for the treatment of parenchymal infections of unilaterally non-functioning kidney. A surgical cause for infection should be excluded in recurrent or severe cases.

items.t: Capsules contain lactose: patients with hereditary galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take them. Urine may turn yellow or brown; false positive urine glucose with reducing-substance tests.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
Urine may be coloured yellow or brown after taking Nitrofurantoin.

items.t: Quinolones (e.g. ciprofloxacin): antibacterial antagonism; one UK SmPC says simultaneous use is not recommended.

src.q: There may be an antagonism between quinolones and nitrofurantoin: simultaneous application is not recommended.
Anti-bacterial antagonism by quinolone anti-infectives.

items.t: Urinary alkalinisers (e.g. potassium citrate) and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors: reduce the antibacterial activity of nitrofurantoin.

src.q: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and alkalising agents can reduce the antibacterial activity of nitrofurantoin.
Decreased anti-bacterial activity by carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and urine alkalisation.

items.t: Magnesium trisilicate reduces absorption. Probenecid and sulfinpyrazone reduce renal excretion. Food and medicines that delay gastric emptying increase absorption. Oral typhoid vaccine is inactivated by antibacterials.

src.q: Decreased absorption with magnesium trisilicate.
Decreased renal excretion of Nitrofurantoin by probenecid and sulfinpyrazone.
Antibacterials inactivate oral typhoid vaccine.

items.t: eGFR below 45: contraindicated. Both UK SmPCs print the unit as ml/min (ml/minute); MHRA gives eGFR less than 45 ml/min/1.73 m². One SmPC also contraindicates use with raised serum creatinine, and another says it is contraindicated in renal dysfunction.

src.q: Nitrofurantoin is contraindicated in patients with renal dysfunction and in patients with an eGFR of less than 45 ml/minute
for patients with renal impairment (eGFR below 45 ml/min) or with an increased serum creatinine
Nitrofurantoin is contraindicated in patients with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of less than 45 ml/min/1.73m2.

items.t: eGFR 30 to 44: MHRA and one UK SmPC allow a short course (3 to 7 days, MHRA) with caution, only for uncomplicated lower UTI with suspected or proven multidrug-resistant pathogens when benefits outweigh risks.

src.q: A short course (3 to 7 days) may be used with caution in certain patients with an eGFR of 30 to 44 ml/min/1.73m2.

Only prescribe to such patients to treat lower urinary tract infection with suspected or proven multidrug resistant pathogens when the benefits of nitrofurantoin are considered to outweigh the risks of side effects.

Nitrofurantoin may be used with caution as short-course therapy only for the treatment of uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection in individual cases with an eGFR between 30-44 ml/min to treat resistant pathogens

items.t: MHRA: reduced renal secretion lowers efficacy and raises side-effect risk. Consider checking renal function before treating, especially in the elderly.

src.q: Consider checking renal function when choosing to treat with nitrofurantoin, especially in the elderly.

items.t: Use with caution in hepatic dysfunction (may mask adverse reactions); hepatic reactions can be fatal. MHRA: use caution in hepatic dysfunction.

src.q: Nitrofurantoin should be used with caution in patients with pulmonary disease, hepatic dysfunction, neurological disorders, and allergic diathesis.
use caution when prescribing nitrofurantoin in patients with pulmonary disease or hepatic dysfunction, which may mask the signs and symptoms of adverse reactions

items.t: One UK SmPC: contraindicated at term (labour and delivery). Otherwise use the lowest appropriate dose only after careful assessment.

src.q: Nitrofurantoin is however contraindicated in infants under three months of age and in pregnant women during labour and delivery
The drug should be used at the lowest dose as appropriate for a specific indication, only after careful assessment.

items.t: Another UK SmPC: can be used in pregnancy if prescribed by a doctor (large data set shows no teratogenicity), but best not given just before and during delivery.

src.q: If prescribed by a doctor, nitrofurantoin can be used during pregnancy.
it is best not to be administered just before and during the delivery

items.t: BUMPS (UKTIS): commonly used in the first and second trimesters and not known to affect the baby; tends to be avoided in the third trimester (small chance of lowering the baby's red cells) unless tests show it is the best antibiotic.

src.q: Nitrofurantoin is commonly used during the first and second trimesters and is not known to affect the baby.
Nitrofurantoin tends to be avoided during the third trimester as there is a small possibility that it could lower the baby's red blood cell levels.

items.t: One UK SmPC: temporarily avoid breastfeeding an infant known or suspected to have an erythrocyte enzyme deficiency (including G6PD deficiency); trace amounts in milk.

src.q: Breast feeding an infant known or suspected to have an erythrocyte enzyme deficiency (including G6PD deficiency), must be temporarily avoided

items.t: Another UK SmPC: can be used during breastfeeding (amounts in milk very small).

src.q: Nitrofurantoin can be used during breastfeeding.

items.t: SPS: can be used with caution, including long-term prophylaxis; monitor the infant for GI upset and oral thrush. Avoid if the infant has known G6PD deficiency, hyperbilirubinaemia or jaundice.

src.q: Nitrofurantoin can be used with caution during breastfeeding. This includes modified release preparations and when used for longer term prophylaxis.
Avoid using nitrofurantoin if the infant has known glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, hyperbilirubinaemia, or jaundice due to the risk of haemolytic anaemia and kernicterus.

items.t: One UK SmPC: temporary stop in sperm production and reduced sperm counts at supratherapeutic doses; clinical doses are not linked to male infertility.

src.q: Clinical doses are not associated with male infertility.

items.t: The UK SmPCs give no reliable frequencies for common effects (one lists nearly all effects as frequency not known). Reported: nausea, vomiting, anorexia, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, headache, dizziness, drowsiness, rash, pruritus, transient alopecia, and yellow or brown urine.

src.q: Sialadenitis, pancreatitis, , anorexia, emesis, abdominal pain, diarrhoea and nausea.
nystagmus, vertigo, dizziness, headache and drowsiness
urticaria, rash, pruritus and transient alopecia

items.t: Acute pulmonary reactions (fever, chills, cough, chest pain, breathlessness, infiltrates/effusion, eosinophilia), usually in the first week; chronic reactions (pulmonary fibrosis) with 6 months or more of therapy, more in the elderly. Stop immediately.

src.q: Acute pulmonary reactions are commonly manifested by fever, chills, cough, chest pain, dyspnoea, pulmonary infiltration with consolidation or pleural effusion on chest x-ray, and eosinophilia.
immediately discontinue nitrofurantoin if new or worsening symptoms of pulmonary damage occur

items.t: Hepatic reactions (chronic active hepatitis with fatalities, hepatic necrosis, autoimmune hepatitis, cholestatic jaundice): withdraw immediately.

src.q: Chronic active hepatitis (fatalities have been reported), hepatic necrosis, autoimmune hepatitis, cholestatic jaundice

items.t: Peripheral neuropathy including optic neuritis; benign intracranial hypertension; haemolytic anaemia, agranulocytosis, aplastic anaemia; anaphylaxis, DRESS, SJS.

src.q: Benign intracranial hypertension, peripheral neuropathy including optic neuritis (sensory as well as motor involvement)
Drug Rash With Eosinophilia And Systemic Symptoms (DRESS syndrome)

items.t: MHRA: consider checking renal function (eGFR) before treating, especially in the elderly.

src.q: Consider checking renal function when choosing to treat with nitrofurantoin, especially in the elderly.

items.t: MHRA: monitor periodically for signs of hepatitis and liver test changes (any duration, especially long-term). Long-term therapy: closely monitor for new or worsening respiratory symptoms, especially in the elderly.

src.q: monitor patients periodically for signs of hepatitis and for changes in biochemical tests that would indicate hepatitis or liver injury
patients receiving long-term therapy, for example for recurrent urinary tract infections, should be closely monitored for new or worsening respiratory symptoms, especially if elderly

items.t: MHRA: closely monitor for pulmonary, hepatic, neurological, haematological and GI side effects during treatment.

src.q: Closely monitor for signs of pulmonary, hepatic, neurological, haematological, and gastrointestinal side effects during treatment

items.t: Stop immediately for pulmonary symptoms, hepatitis, first signs of neuropathy (paraesthesia), or haemolysis in suspected G6PD deficiency.

src.q: immediately discontinue nitrofurantoin if new or worsening symptoms of pulmonary damage occur
Therefore, treatment should be stopped at the first signs of neural involvement (paraesthesia).

items.t: Always take with food or milk: this improves absorption and is important for efficacy.

src.q: This medicine should always be taken with food or milk.
Taking Nitrofurantoin with a meal improves absorption and is important for optimal efficacy.

items.t: Seek medical advice for breathing trouble, shortness of breath, lingering cough, coughing up blood or mucus, or painful breathing.

src.q: seek medical advice if you experience trouble breathing, shortness of breath, a lingering cough, coughing up blood or mucus, or pain or discomfort when breathing

items.t: Seek advice promptly for yellow skin or eyes, upper right abdominal pain, dark urine, pale stools, itching or joint pain and swelling.

src.q: talk to your doctor or another healthcare professional promptly if you develop yellowing of the skin or eyes, upper right abdominal pain, dark urine and pale or grey-coloured stools, itching or joint pain and swelling

items.t: Urine may turn yellow or brown. May cause dizziness or drowsiness: do not drive if affected.

src.q: Urine may be coloured yellow or brown after taking Nitrofurantoin.
Nitrofurantoin may cause dizziness and drowsiness and the patient should not drive or operate machinery if affected this way.

items.t: Low dose: dysfunctional uterine bleeding, polymenorrhoea, menorrhagia, metropathia haemorrhagica, premenstrual syndrome, postponement of menstruation (one UK SmPC also endometriosis and dysmenorrhoea). High dose (generic 5 mg SmPC only): disseminated breast carcinoma.

src.q: At low dose: Dysfuntional uterine bleeding Polymenorrhoea Menorrhagia Metropathia Haemorrhagia Pre-menstrual syndrome Postponement of menstruation At high dose: Disseminated carcinoma of the breast.
Metropathia haemorrhagica. Premenstrual syndrome. Postponement of menstruation. Endometriosis. Menorrhagia. Dysmenorrhoea.

items.t: SPS: norethisterone is the only progestogen licensed in the UK to delay periods.

src.q: Norethisterone is the only progestogen licensed in the UK to delay periods.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction stated in the UK SmPCs or SPS page accessed.

items.t: Dysfunctional uterine bleeding, polymenorrhoea, menorrhagia, metropathia haemorrhagica: 5 mg three times daily for 10 days; to prevent recurrence, 5 mg twice daily on days 19-26 of the next two cycles.

src.q: 1 tablet three times daily for 10 days; bleeding usually stops within 48 hours.
One tablet twice daily, from days 19 to 26 of the two subsequent cycles, should be given to prevent recurrence of the condition.

items.t: Postponement of menstruation: 5 mg three times daily, starting 3 days before the expected period. One UK SmPC: continue for no longer than 10-14 days. SPS: can be taken for up to 3 to 4 weeks if necessary.

src.q: Postponement of menstruation: 1 tablet three times daily, starting three days before the expected onset of menstruation.
continuing for not longer than 10 to 14 days
Norethisterone can be taken for up to 3 to 4 weeks if necessary.

items.t: Endometriosis: generic SmPC 5 mg three times daily for at least 6 months (increase to 20-25 mg daily if spotting); another UK SmPC starts 5 mg twice daily from day 1-5 of the cycle for 4-6 months.

src.q: Endometriosis: 1 tablet three times daily for a minimum treatment period of six months. The dosage should be increased to 4 or 5 tablets a day if spotting occurs.
Treatment should begin between the first and 5th day of the cycle with 1 of tablet Primolut N twice daily.

items.t: Premenstrual syndrome: generic SmPC 5 mg daily on days 16-25; another UK SmPC 5-15 mg daily on days 19-26, repeated for several cycles.

src.q: Pre-menstrual syndrome: 1 tablet daily from days 16 to 25 of the menstrual cycle.
may be relieved by the administration of 1-3 tablets daily from the 19th to the 26th day of the cycle

items.t: Disseminated breast carcinoma (generic SmPC): start 40 mg daily, increasing to 60 mg daily if no regression.

src.q: For disseminated breast carcinoma the starting dose is 8 tablets (40mg) per day increasing to 12 tablets (60mg) if no regression is noted.

items.t: One UK SmPC: not intended for use in children.

src.q: Not intended for use in children.

items.t: Both UK SmPCs: hypersensitivity; pregnancy; previous idiopathic or current venous thromboembolism; active or recent arterial thromboembolic disease (e.g. angina, myocardial infarction); history in pregnancy of idiopathic jaundice or severe pruritus; undiagnosed genital/vaginal bleeding.

src.q: Previous idiopathic or current venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism) Active or recent arterial thromboembolic disease (e.g. angina, myocardial infarction)
History during pregnancy of idiopathic jaundice Severe pruritus or pemphigoid gestationis Undiagnosed irregular vaginal bleeding Porphyria

items.t: Generic 5 mg SmPC also: disturbance of liver function; porphyria.

src.q: Disturbance of liver function

items.t: Another UK SmPC also: breastfeeding; prodromi of thrombosis (e.g. TIA, angina); high risk of venous or arterial thrombosis; migraine with focal neurological symptoms; diabetes with vascular involvement; severe hepatic disease until liver values are normal; previous or existing liver tumours; known, past or suspected sex-hormone-dependent malignancy; untreated endometrial hyperplasia.

src.q: 3. Lactation.

src.q: Special care should be taken when prescribing norethisterone in patients with conditions which might be aggravated by this factor: - Epilepsy - Migraine - Asthma - Cardiac dysfunction - Renal dysfunction

items.t: VTE: personal or strong family history of thromboembolism should be investigated for thrombophilia; until evaluated or anticoagulated, treat progestogens as contraindicated. Consider stopping 4-6 weeks before elective surgery with expected prolonged immobilisation; stop if VTE develops.

src.q: Until a thorough evaluation of thrombophillic factors has been made or anticoagulant treatment initiated, use of progestogens in these patients should be viewed as contraindicated.
consideration should be given to stopping progestogen therapy 4-6 weeks pre-operatively
If VTE develops after initiating therapy the drug should be withdrawn.

items.t: Sudden visual impairment, proptosis, diplopia or migraine: ophthalmological assessment before continuing. Very rarely, hepatic adenoma.

src.q: Any patient who develops an acute impairment of vision, proptosis, diplopia or migraine headache should be carefully evaluated ophthalmologically
In very rare cases, hepatic adenomas may be associated with progesterone-only pill (POP) use.

items.t: Enzyme inducers (e.g. carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, rifampicin, St John's wort; generic SmPC also lists tetracyclines, ampicillin and co-trimoxazole) may increase progestogen metabolism and reduce levels.

src.q: These compounds include anticonvulsants (e.g., phenobarbital, phenytoin, carbamazepine) and anti-infectives (e.g., rifampicin, rifabutin, nevirapine, efavirenz, tetracyclines, ampicillin, oxacillin and cotrimoxazole)
Herbal preparations containing St John's wort ( Hypericum perforatum ) may induce the metabolism of progestogens. Progestogen levels may therefore be reduced.

items.t: Special care with other drugs that cause fluid retention, such as NSAIDs and vasodilators.

src.q: Special care should be taken when progestogens are administered with other drugs which also cause fluid retention, such as NSAIDs and vasodilators.

items.t: Already on anticoagulants: weigh risks and benefits of progestogen therapy carefully.

src.q: Where a patient is already taking anticoagulants, the risks and benefits of progestogen therapy should be carefully considered.

items.t: One UK SmPC: CYP3A4 inhibitors such as azole antifungals (e.g. fluconazole), verapamil, macrolides (e.g. clarithromycin) and diltiazem can increase progestin levels; clinical relevance unknown. Ciclosporin levels may rise; lamotrigine levels may fall.

src.q: Strong and moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors such as azole antifungals (e.g. itraconazole, voriconazole, fluconazole), verapamil, macrolides (e.g. clarithromycin, erythromycin), diltiazem and grapefruit juice can increase plasma concentrations of the estrogen or the progestin or both.
The clinical relevance of potential interactions with enzyme inhibitors remains unknown.

items.t: Progestogens can affect some laboratory tests (liver function, thyroid function, coagulation).

src.q: Progestogens can influence certain laboratory tests (e.g., tests for hepatic function, thyroid function and coagulation).

items.t: No dose advice. Renal dysfunction: special care because of fluid retention.

items.t: Not a contraceptive: use another method of contraception to avoid pregnancy when delaying periods (SPS).

src.q: The individual should be advised that norethisterone is not a contraceptive and so another form of contraceptive should be used to avoid pregnancy.

items.t: At 5-10 mg norethisterone suppresses ovulation.

src.q: Norethisterone given at intermediate doses (5-10mg) suppresses ovulation via its effect on the pituitary.

items.t: Frequencies are not given in the UK SmPCs checked. Reported effects include breakthrough bleeding, spotting, amenorrhoea, breast tenderness, headache, nausea, fluid retention and weight gain.

items.t: Thromboembolic disorders, cerebral and myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, retinal thrombosis: if VTE develops, stop. Patients should contact a doctor at once with leg swelling, sudden chest pain or breathlessness.

src.q: thrombo-embolic disorders, cerebral and myocardial infarction, congestive heart failure, increased blood pressure, palpitations, pulmonary embolism, retinal thrombosis
Patients should be advised to contact their doctor immediately if they become aware of a potential thromboembolic symptom (e.g., painful swelling in the leg, sudden pain in the chest, dyspnoea).

Jaundice or deterioration in liver function

src.q: the possibility of pregnancy must be excluded before a further course is given
Personal or strong family history of thromboembolism or recurrent spontaneous abortion should be investigated in order to exclude a thrombophillic predisposition.

items.t: Stop if jaundice or worsening liver function, significant blood pressure rise, new migraine-type headache, or VTE.

items.t: Oral. Swallow tablets whole with some liquid (one UK SmPC). For period delay start at least 3 days before the expected period.

src.q: The tablets are to be swallowed whole with some liquid.
To be effective, norethisterone should be started at least 3 days before the expected period.

items.t: Not a contraceptive. Periods usually return within about 3 days of stopping.

norethisterone is not a contraceptive

items.t: Oral suspension: prevention and treatment of candidal infections of the mouth, oesophagus and intestinal tract; prophylaxis of oral candidosis in babies born to mothers with vaginal candidosis.

src.q: The prevention and treatment of candidal infections of the oral cavity, oesophagus and intestinal tract.
The suspension provides effective prophylaxis against oral candidosis in those born of mothers with vaginal candidosis.

items.t: Oral preparations should not be used to treat systemic fungal infections.

src.q: Nystatin oral preparations should not be used for treatment of systemic mycoses.

items.t: Adults (denture sores, oral candida): 1 mL dropped into the mouth four times daily, kept in contact with the affected areas as long as possible. Continue for at least 48 hours after symptoms resolve; re-evaluate if not better after 14 days.

src.q: 1 ml of the suspension should be dropped into the mouth four times daily; it should be kept in contact with the affected areas as long as possible.
should be continued for at least 48 hours after symptoms have disappeared.
If signs and symptoms worsen or persist (beyond 14 days of treatment), the patient should be reevaluated, and alternate therapy considered.

items.t: Older people: no specific dose changes.

src.q: No specific dosage recommendations or precautions.

items.t: Infants and children (oral and intestinal thrush): 1 mL into the mouth four times a day. Newborn prophylaxis: 1 mL once daily.

src.q: In intestinal and oral candidosis (thrush) in infants and children, 1 ml should be dropped into the mouth four times a day.
For prophylaxis in the newborn the suggested dose is 1 ml once daily.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to nystatin or any excipient.

items.t: No animal reproduction studies; GI absorption negligible. Prescribe in pregnancy only if the benefit outweighs the potential risk.

src.q: Nystatin should be prescribed during pregnancy only if the potential benefits to be derived outweigh the potential risk to the foetus.

items.t: Not known if excreted in milk; absorption insignificant. Use with caution.

src.q: Although gastrointestinal absorption is insignificant, caution should be exercised when nystatin is prescribed for a nursing woman.

reproductive.note: UK SmPCs state only that effects on reproductive capacity are not known; no specific advice.

src.q: Nausea has been reported occasionally during therapy.
Large oral doses of Nystatin have occasionally produced diarrhoea, gastrointestinal distress, nausea and vomiting.

items.t: Hypersensitivity and angioedema (including facial swelling); very rarely Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Stop if irritation or sensitisation develops.

src.q: Hypersensitivity and angioedema, including facial oedema have been reported.
Steven-Johnson Syndrome has been reported very rarely.
