items.t: Endogenous hypertriglyceridaemia, as a supplement to diet when diet alone is not enough: type IV alone; type IIb/III with a statin when triglycerides are not controlled. Not for exogenous hypertriglyceridaemia (type 1 hyperchylomicronaemia).

src.q: Endogenous hypertriglyceridaemia as a supplement to diet when dietary measures alone are insufficient to produce an adequate response
type IIb/III in combination with statins, when control of triglycerides is insufficient
Omacor is not indicated in exogenous hypertriglyceridaemia (type 1 hyperchylomicronaemia).

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction or brand-specific prescribing statement in the three UK SmPCs used; the MHRA Drug Safety Update (January 2024) covers atrial fibrillation risk only. No SPS advice found.

items.t: Start with 2 capsules (2 g) daily; if response is not adequate, increase to 4 capsules (4 g) daily.

src.q: Initial treatment two capsules daily. If adequate response is not obtained, the dose may be increased to four capsules daily.

items.t: Limited data in people over 70 years and in renal impairment; no information in hepatic impairment.

src.q: There is limited clinical data regarding the use of Omacor in elderly patients over 70 years of age and patients with renal impairment

items.t: Not recommended in children (no efficacy or safety data).

src.q: In the absence of efficacy and safety data, use of this medication in children is not recommended.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or any excipient. Two UK SmPCs also list soya; one says do not use if allergic to peanut or soya (contains soya oil).

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance, to soya or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.
If you are allergic to peanut or soya, do not use this medicinal product.

items.t: Dose-dependent increased risk of atrial fibrillation in patients with cardiovascular disease or risk factors, highest at 4 g/day. If atrial fibrillation develops, stop permanently.

src.q: The observed risk is highest with a dose of 4 g/daily (see section 4.8). If atrial fibrillation develops, treatment should be permanently discontinued.
if a patient develops atrial fibrillation whilst taking these medicines for the treatment of hypertriglyceridaemia then the medicine should be discontinued permanently

items.t: Bleeding time rises moderately at 4 capsules daily: monitor patients on anticoagulants and adjust the anticoagulant dose if needed; allow for this in patients at high bleeding risk (severe trauma, surgery).

src.q: patients receiving anticoagulant therapy must be monitored and the dosage of anticoagulant adjusted if necessary
Make allowance for the increased bleeding time in patients at high risk of haemorrhage (because of severe trauma, surgery, etc).

items.t: Use with caution in known fish sensitivity or allergy.

src.q: Omacor should be used with caution in patients with known sensitivity or allergy to fish.

items.t: Monitor ALT and AST if there are signs of liver damage (especially at 4 capsules daily). No experience with fibrates; limited experience in secondary hypertriglyceridaemia (e.g. uncontrolled diabetes).

src.q: ALAT and ASAT levels should be monitored in patients with any signs of liver damage (in particular with the high dosage, i.e. 4 capsules).
There is no experience regarding hypertriglyceridaemia in combination with fibrates.

items.t: Warfarin / oral anticoagulants: given together without bleeding complications, but prothrombin time must be checked when combined and when omega-3 is stopped; at 4 capsules daily monitor and adjust the anticoagulant dose if needed.

src.q: the prothrombin time must be checked when Omacor is combined with warfarin or when treatment with Omacor is stopped
patients receiving anticoagulant therapy must be monitored and the dosage of anticoagulant adjusted if necessary

items.t: Only limited information in renal impairment; no threshold or dose adjustment given.

src.q: Only limited information regarding the use in patients with renal impairment is available.

items.t: No information in hepatic impairment; no data showing increased risk. Monitor ALT/AST if there are signs of liver damage.

src.q: there are no data indicating an increased risk for patients with hepatic impairment
ALAT and ASAT levels should be monitored in patients with any signs of liver damage

items.t: No adequate human data; animal studies show no reproductive toxicity. Should not be used in pregnancy unless clearly necessary. No BUMPS leaflet found.

src.q: Omacor should not be used during pregnancy unless clearly necessary

items.t: No data on passage into milk. Should not be used during breastfeeding. No SPS breastfeeding page for omega-3 medicines was found.

src.q: Omacor should not be used during lactation.

items.t: No adequate data on fertility.

src.q: There are no adequate data on the effect of Omacor on fertility.

items.t: Common: atrial fibrillation; gastrointestinal disorders (abdominal distension or pain, constipation, diarrhoea, dyspepsia, flatulence, belching, reflux, nausea or vomiting). Uncommon: dizziness, taste change, headache, hypotension, nosebleed, rash, raised blood glucose, gout.

Gastrointestinal disorders: Common: gastrointestinal disorders (including abdominal distension, abdominal pain, constipation, diarrhoea, dyspepsia, flatulence, eructation, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, nausea or vomiting)
Nervous system disorders: Uncommon: dizziness, dysgeusia, headache

items.t: Atrial fibrillation (common): advise patients to seek medical attention for palpitations, dizziness, breathlessness or tiredness; stop permanently if it develops.

src.q: advise patients taking omega-3-acid ethyl ester medicines for the treatment of hypertriglyceridaemia to seek medical attention if they develop symptoms of atrial fibrillation
talk to your doctor if you experience palpitations, dizziness, shortness of breath and tiredness

Rare: liver disorders (including transaminases increased

items.t: Tell the doctor about any heart problems before starting. Report palpitations, dizziness, breathlessness or tiredness (possible atrial fibrillation). Do not stop treatment without talking to the doctor.

do not stop your hypertriglyceridaemia treatment without first discussing this with your doctor

items.t: Tell the doctor about any fish, soya or peanut allergy.

src.q: If you are allergic to peanut or soya, do not use this medicinal product.
Omacor should be used with caution in patients with known sensitivity or allergy to fish.

items.t: Adults: duodenal and gastric ulcer (treatment and prevention of relapse); H. pylori eradication with antibiotics; treatment and prevention of NSAID-associated ulcers; reflux oesophagitis (treatment and long-term management); symptomatic GORD; Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

items.t: 20 mg once daily for 2 weeks (a further 2 weeks if not healed). Poorly responsive: 40 mg once daily, usually healed within 4 weeks.

src.q: The recommended dose in patients with an active duodenal ulcer is Losec 20 mg once daily. In most patients healing occurs within two weeks.
In patients with poorly responsive duodenal ulcer Losec 40 mg once daily is recommended and healing is usually achieved within four weeks.

items.t: Prevention of duodenal ulcer relapse (H. pylori negative or eradication not possible): 20 mg once daily (10 mg may suffice; up to 40 mg if needed).

src.q: the recommended dose is Losec 20 mg once daily. In some patients a daily dose of 10 mg may be sufficient. In case of therapy failure, the dose can be increased to 40 mg.

items.t: 20 mg once daily for 4 weeks (a further 4 weeks if not healed). Poorly responsive: 40 mg once daily, usually healed within 8 weeks. Relapse prevention: 20 mg once daily, up to 40 mg.

src.q: Treatment of gastric ulcers The recommended dose is Losec 20 mg once daily. In most patients healing occurs within four weeks.
In patients with poorly responsive gastric ulcer Losec 40 mg once daily is recommended and healing is usually achieved within eight weeks.

items.t: H. pylori eradication (one week, choose antibiotics by local guidance): omeprazole 20 mg + clarithromycin 500 mg + amoxicillin 1 g, each twice daily; or omeprazole 20 mg + clarithromycin 250-500 mg + metronidazole 400-500 mg (or tinidazole 500 mg), each twice daily; or omeprazole 40 mg once daily + amoxicillin 500 mg and metronidazole 400 mg three times daily.

src.q: Losec 20 mg + clarithromycin 500 mg + amoxicillin 1 000 mg, each twice daily for one week

items.t: NSAID-associated ulcers: treatment 20 mg once daily for 4 weeks (further 4 weeks if needed). Prevention in at-risk patients (age > 60, previous ulcer or upper GI bleed): 20 mg once daily.

src.q: For the treatment of NSAID - associated gastric and duodenal ulcers, the recommended dose is Losec 20 mg once daily.
(age > 60, previous history of gastric and duodenal ulcers, previous history of upper GI bleeding) the recommended dose is Losec 20 mg once daily

items.t: Reflux oesophagitis: 20 mg once daily for 4 weeks (further 4 weeks if needed); severe oesophagitis 40 mg once daily for 8 weeks. Long-term management of healed oesophagitis: 10 mg once daily, up to 20-40 mg.

src.q: In patients with severe oesophagitis Losec 40 mg once daily is recommended and healing is usually achieved within eight weeks.
For the long-term management of patients with healed reflux oesophagitis the recommended dose is Losec 10 mg once daily. If needed, the dose can be increased to Losec 20 mg to 40 mg once daily.

items.t: Symptomatic GORD: 20 mg daily (10 mg may be enough). If no control after 4 weeks, investigate further.

src.q: Treatment of symptomatic gastro-oesophageal reflux disease The recommended dose is Losec 20 mg daily.
If symptom control has not been achieved after four weeks treatment with Losec 20 mg daily, further investigation is recommended.

items.t: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome: start 60 mg daily, adjust individually (20 to 120 mg daily). Doses above 80 mg daily: divide and give twice daily.

src.q: The recommended initial dose is Losec 60 mg daily.
When dose exceed Losec 80 mg daily, the dose should be divided and given twice daily.

items.t: Elderly: no dose adjustment needed.

src.q: Elderly Dose adjustment is not needed in the elderly

items.t: Reflux oesophagitis / GORD symptoms: ≥ 1 year and 10-20 kg: 10 mg once daily (up to 20 mg). ≥ 2 years and > 20 kg: 20 mg once daily (up to 40 mg). Duration: oesophagitis 4 to 8 weeks; GORD symptoms 2 to 4 weeks (investigate if not controlled).

src.q: ≥ 1 year of age 10 to 20 kg 10 mg once daily. The dose can be increased to 20 mg once daily if needed ≥ 2 years of age > 20 kg 20 mg once daily. The dose can be increased to 40 mg once daily if needed
Reflux oesophagitis : The treatment time is 4 to 8 weeks.

items.t: H. pylori duodenal ulcer, over 4 years (specialist supervised, one week, all twice daily): 15-30 kg: omeprazole 10 mg + amoxicillin 25 mg/kg + clarithromycin 7.5 mg/kg; 31-40 kg: omeprazole 20 mg + amoxicillin 750 mg + clarithromycin 7.5 mg/kg; > 40 kg: omeprazole 20 mg + amoxicillin 1 g + clarithromycin 500 mg.

src.q: 15 to 30 kg Combination with two antibiotics: Losec 10 mg, amoxicillin 25 mg/kg body weight and clarithromycin 7.5 mg/kg body weight are all administered together two times daily for one week.

items.t: Not licensed under 1 year (capsule and dispersible tablet SmPCs). Long-term treatment in children is not recommended, although some with chronic illness may need it.

src.q: Children over 1 year of age and ≥ 10 kg
Some children with chronic illnesses may require long-term treatment although it is not recommended.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to omeprazole, substituted benzimidazoles or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance, substituted benzimidazoles or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Must not be used with nelfinavir.

src.q: Omeprazole like other proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) must not be used concomitantly with nelfinavir

items.t: Alarm symptoms (unintended weight loss, recurrent vomiting, dysphagia, haematemesis, melaena) or suspected gastric ulcer: exclude malignancy first - treatment may mask symptoms.

src.q: In the presence of any alarm symptom (e.g. significant unintentional weight loss, recurrent vomiting, dysphagia, haematemesis or melena) and when gastric ulcer is suspected or present, malignancy should be excluded

items.t: Hypomagnesaemia (severe; usually after ≥ 3 months, mostly after 1 year): fatigue, tetany, delirium, convulsions, dizziness, ventricular arrhythmia. Consider measuring magnesium before and during prolonged treatment, especially with digoxin or diuretics.

src.q: Severe hypomagnesaemia has been reported in patients treated with proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) like omeprazole for at least three months, and in most cases for a year.

consider measurement of magnesium levels before starting PPI treatment and periodically during prolonged treatment, especially in those who will take a PPI concomitantly with digoxin or drugs that may cause hypomagnesaemia (eg, diuretics)

items.t: Fractures: high doses and long use (> 1 year) may modestly increase hip, wrist and spine fracture risk (10-40%), mainly in the elderly. Patients at risk of osteoporosis need guideline care with adequate vitamin D and calcium.

src.q: Proton pump inhibitors, especially if used in high doses and over long durations (> 1 year), may modestly increase the risk of hip, wrist and spine fracture, predominantly in the elderly or in presence of other recognised risk factors.
treat patients at risk of osteoporosis according to current clinical guidelines and ensure they have an adequate intake of vitamin D and calcium

items.t: Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE): if lesions (especially sun-exposed) with arthralgia, seek help promptly and consider stopping. SCLE with one PPI may raise risk with others.

src.q: If lesions occur, especially in sun-exposed areas of the skin, and if accompanied by arthralgia, the patient should seek medical help promptly and the health care professional should consider stopping Losec.
a patient who develops SCLE with a particular PPI may be at risk of the same reaction with another

items.t: GI infections: slightly increased risk of Salmonella and Campylobacter, and possibly Clostridioides difficile in hospital.

src.q: Treatment with proton pump inhibitors may lead to slightly increased risk of gastrointestinal infections such as Salmonella and Campylobacter and, in hospitalised patients, possibly also Clostridioides difficile

items.t: Vitamin B12: absorption may fall on long-term therapy - consider in those with low stores or risk factors.

src.q: This should be considered in patients with reduced body stores or risk factors for reduced vitamin B12 absorption on long-term therapy.

items.t: Acute tubulointerstitial nephritis can occur at any time and may progress to renal failure: stop omeprazole if suspected.

src.q: Omeprazole should be discontinued in case of suspected TIN, and appropriate treatment should be promptly initiated.

items.t: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SJS, TEN, DRESS, AGEP) reported rarely/very rarely.

src.q: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs) including Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) and acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP), which can be life-threatening or fatal

items.t: Chromogranin A tests: stop omeprazole at least 5 days before CgA measurement.

src.q: omeprazole treatment should be stopped for at least 5 days before CgA measurements

items.t: Long-term use (especially > 1 year): keep patients under regular surveillance.

src.q: As in all long-term treatments, especially when exceeding a treatment period of 1 year, patients should be kept under regular surveillance.

items.t: Excipients: capsules contain lactose; dispersible tablets contain sucrose.

src.q: Each capsule contains 8 mg lactose.
Losec gastro-resistant tablets contain sucrose.

items.t: Clopidogrel: omeprazole reduces exposure to clopidogrel's active metabolite. SmPC and MHRA: concomitant use should be discouraged (MHRA: unless considered essential). SPS: avoid this combination; other PPIs are considered safe with clopidogrel.

src.q: As a precaution, concomitant use of omeprazole and clopidogrel should be discouraged
Concomitant use of clopidogrel and omeprazole or esomeprazole is to be discouraged unless considered essential.
Avoid the combined use of clopidogrel with omeprazole or esomeprazole due to a significant interaction. Other PPIs are considered safe with clopidogrel.

items.t: Nelfinavir: contraindicated. Atazanavir: not recommended (if unavoidable, monitor closely, raise atazanavir dose, do not exceed omeprazole 20 mg). Posaconazole, erlotinib: avoid. Ketoconazole/itraconazole absorption reduced.

src.q: Concomitant administration of omeprazole with nelfinavir is contraindicated
Concomitant administration of omeprazole with atazanavir is not recommended
For posaconazole and erlotinib concomitant use should be avoided.

items.t: CYP2C19 substrates: omeprazole (moderate CYP2C19 inhibitor) may raise levels of R-warfarin and other vitamin K antagonists, cilostazol, diazepam and phenytoin (monitor phenytoin for the first 2 weeks).

src.q: Examples of such drugs are R-warfarin and other vitamin K antagonists, cilostazol, diazepam and phenytoin.
Monitoring phenytoin plasma concentration is recommended during the first two weeks after initiating omeprazole treatment

items.t: Methotrexate: levels may rise with PPIs; with high-dose methotrexate consider temporarily stopping omeprazole.

src.q: In high-dose methotrexate administration a temporary withdrawal of omeprazole may need to be considered.

items.t: Digoxin: bioavailability increased ~10%; caution with high omeprazole doses in the elderly - reinforce digoxin monitoring. Tacrolimus: levels may rise - monitor.

src.q: caution should be exercised when omeprazole is given at high doses in elderly patients. Therapeutic drug monitoring of digoxin should then be reinforced.

items.t: CYP2C19/CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. clarithromycin, voriconazole) raise omeprazole levels - dose change not usually needed (consider in severe hepatic impairment with long-term use). Inducers (rifampicin, St John's wort) lower omeprazole levels.

src.q: active substances known to inhibit CYP2C19 or CYP3A4 (such as clarithromycin and voriconazole) may lead to increased omeprazole serum levels
Active substances known to induce CYP2C19 or CYP3A4 or both (such as rifampicin and St John's wort) may lead to decreased omeprazole serum levels

items.t: Diuretics (and digoxin): consider magnesium monitoring with long-term PPI use (hypomagnesaemia).

src.q: For patients expected to be on prolonged treatment or who take PPIs with digoxin or drugs that may cause hypomagnesaemia (e.g. diuretics), healthcare professionals should consider measuring magnesium levels before starting PPI treatment and periodically during treatment.

items.t: No dose adjustment needed in renal impairment. Acute tubulointerstitial nephritis can occur - stop if suspected.

src.q: Dose adjustment is not needed in patients with impaired renal function
Acute tubulointerstitial nephritis can progress to renal failure.

items.t: Hepatic impairment: a daily dose of 10 mg to 20 mg may be sufficient. Very rarely, encephalopathy in pre-existing liver disease.

src.q: In patients with impaired hepatic function a daily dose of 10 mg to 20 mg may be sufficient
Very rare: Hepatic failure, encephalopathy in patients with pre-existing liver disease

items.t: SmPC: omeprazole can be used in pregnancy (> 1000 exposed outcomes, no adverse effects on pregnancy or fetus/newborn).

src.q: indicate no adverse effects of omeprazole on pregnancy or on the health of the foetus/newborn child
Omeprazole can be used during pregnancy.

items.t: BUMPS: omeprazole is the preferred PPI in pregnancy (most safety information); no good evidence linking PPIs to miscarriage, birth defects, stillbirth, preterm delivery or low birth weight.

src.q: Omeprazole is the PPI that is preferred for use in pregnancy as there is more information about its safety.
There is no good evidence that omeprazole or other PPIs are linked to miscarriage, birth defects, stillbirth, preterm delivery, or low infant birth weight.

items.t: Excreted in breast milk but not likely to affect the child at therapeutic doses.

src.q: Omeprazole is excreted in breast milk but is not likely to influence the child when therapeutic doses are used.

items.t: SPS: omeprazole can be used in breastfeeding and is a PPI of choice (with pantoprazole). As a precaution monitor the infant for constipation, diarrhoea, sickness, poor sleeping, irritability or rash.

src.q: Any PPI can be used during breastfeeding, however omeprazole and pantoprazole are the PPIs of choice
Omeprazole can be used during breastfeeding.
As a precaution monitor for constipation, diarrhoea, sickness, poor sleeping, irritability or rash.

items.t: Fertility: animal studies show no effect.

src.q: Animal studies with the racemic mixture omeprazole, given by oral administration do not indicate effects with respect to fertility.

items.t: Common (1 to 10%): headache, abdominal pain, constipation, diarrhoea, flatulence, nausea/vomiting, benign fundic gland polyps.

src.q: The most common side effects (1 to 10% of patients) are headache, abdominal pain, constipation, diarrhoea, flatulence and nausea/vomiting.
Common: Abdominal pain, constipation, diarrhoea, flatulence, nausea/vomiting, fundic gland polyps (benign)

items.t: Uncommon: hip, wrist or spine fracture; dizziness; rash; raised liver enzymes.

src.q: Uncommon: Fracture of the hip, wrist or spine

items.t: Hypersensitivity reactions (rare): fever, angioedema, anaphylactic reaction/shock.

src.q: Rare: Hypersensitivity reactions e.g. fever, angioedema and anaphylactic reaction/shock

items.t: Severe skin reactions - SJS/TEN (very rare), DRESS/AGEP (rare): can be life-threatening.

src.q: Very rare: Erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN)

items.t: Tubulointerstitial nephritis (rare, may progress to renal failure): stop omeprazole.

src.q: Rare: Tubulointerstitial nephritis (with possible progression to renal failure)

items.t: Severe hypomagnesaemia (frequency not known; may cause hypocalcaemia and hypokalaemia).

src.q: Not known: Hypomagnesaemia; severe hypomagnesaemia may result in hypocalcaemia. Hypomagnesaemia may also be associated with hypokalaemia.

items.t: Blood disorders: rare leucopenia, thrombocytopenia; very rare agranulocytosis, pancytopenia. Hepatitis (rare), hepatic failure (very rare). Rare hyponatraemia.

src.q: Rare: Leukopenia, thrombocytopenia Very rare: Agranulocytosis, pancytopenia
Rare: Hepatitis with or without jaundice

items.t: Consider serum magnesium before starting if prolonged treatment is expected or with digoxin/diuretics.

src.q: consider measurement of magnesium levels before starting PPI treatment and periodically during prolonged treatment

items.t: Periodic magnesium during prolonged treatment; regular surveillance beyond 1 year; consider vitamin B12 in those at risk.

src.q: healthcare professionals should consider measuring magnesium levels before starting PPI treatment and periodically during treatment
As in all long-term treatments, especially when exceeding a treatment period of 1 year, patients should be kept under regular surveillance.

items.t: Stop if tubulointerstitial nephritis is suspected; consider stopping if SCLE develops.

src.q: Omeprazole should be discontinued in case of suspected TIN
consider stopping use of the PPI unless it is imperative for a serious acid-related condition

items.t: OTC use: do not use non-prescription PPIs for more than 4 weeks without consulting a doctor; see a doctor if no relief within 2 weeks.

src.q: PPIs obtained without prescription over-the-counter should not be used for more than 4 weeks without consulting a doctor.

items.t: Take in the morning, swallowed whole with half a glass of water; do not chew or crush.

src.q: It is recommended to take Losec capsules in the morning, swallowed whole with half a glass of water. The capsules must not be chewed or crushed.

items.t: Capsules, swallowing difficulty or children: open and swallow the pellets with water, or mix into slightly acidic fluid (e.g. fruit juice, applesauce) or non-carbonated water; take within 30 minutes; do not chew the pellets.

src.q: Patients can open the capsule and swallow the contents with half a glass of water or after mixing the contents in a slightly acidic fluid e.g. fruit juice or applesauce, or in non-carbonated water.
The enteric-coated pellets must not be chewed.

items.t: Dispersible tablets, swallowing difficulty or children: break and disperse in a spoonful of non-carbonated water (juice or applesauce may be added); take within 30 minutes; do not use milk or carbonated water.

src.q: Patients can break the tablet and disperse it in a spoonful of non-carbonated water and if so wished, mix with some fruit juices or applesauce.
DO NOT USE milk or carbonated water.

items.t: Report rash on sun-exposed skin with joint pain (possible SCLE); avoid sun exposure if it occurs.

src.q: advise them to avoid exposing the skin to sunlight

items.t: If buying omeprazole without prescription, tell the pharmacist if you take clopidogrel.

src.q: Doctors should check whether patients who are taking clopidogrel are also buying over-the-counter omeprazole

items.t: Make sure you get enough vitamin D and calcium on long-term use.

src.q: consult your doctor to make sure you are taking enough vitamin D and calcium

items.t: Dizziness or visual disturbance may occur - do not drive if affected.

src.q: If affected, patients should not drive or operate machinery.

items.t: Adults: nausea and vomiting from cytotoxic chemotherapy and radiotherapy; prevention of post-operative nausea and vomiting (PONV). Established PONV: injection recommended.

src.q: Ondansetron is indicated for the management of nausea and vomiting induced by cytotoxic chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Ondansetron is indicated for the prevention of post-operative nausea and vomiting (PONV).
For treatment of established PONV, administration by injection is recommended.

items.t: Children aged 6 months and over: chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. Oral ondansetron has not been studied for PONV in children (IV recommended).

src.q: Ondansetron is indicated for the management of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV) in children aged ≥6 months.
No studies have been conducted on the use of orally administered ondansetron in the prevention and treatment of PONV in children aged ≥1 month

items.t: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy is outside the licensed indications (MHRA: second-line use in hyperemesis gravidarum only after full discussion of benefits and risks).

src.q: Outside of its authorised indications, ondansetron is also used second line for treating women with hyperemesis gravidarum
this decision should be made in consultation with the patient after she has been fully informed of the potential benefits and risks of the different treatment options

items.t: 8 mg 1-2 hours before chemotherapy or radiotherapy, then 8 mg every 12 hours for up to 5 days. Highly emetogenic chemotherapy: a single dose of up to 24 mg with dexamethasone 12 mg orally, 1-2 hours before.

src.q: The recommended oral dose is 8mg taken 1 to 2 hours before chemotherapy or radiation treatment, followed by 8 mg every 12 hours for a maximum of 5 days
For highly emetogenic chemotherapy a single dose of up to 24 mg ondansetron taken with 12 mg oral dexamethasone sodium phosphate, 1 to 2 hours before chemotherapy, may be used.

items.t: 16 mg one hour before anaesthesia.

src.q: The recommended oral dose is 16 mg taken one hour prior to anaesthesia.

items.t: Elderly and renal impairment: no change to oral dose. Moderate or severe hepatic impairment: maximum 8 mg per day.

src.q: Elderly No alteration of oral dose or frequency of administration is required.
In such patients a total daily dose of 8 mg should not be exceeded.

items.t: CINV, 6 months to 17 years: IV dose first (by BSA or weight), then oral dosing from 12 hours later for up to 5 days - BSA > 0.6 to ≤ 1.2 m²: 4 mg every 12 hours; > 1.2 m²: 8 mg every 12 hours; weight > 10 kg: 4 mg every 12 hours. Total daily dose must not exceed the adult dose of 32 mg.

src.q: Oral dosing can commence 12 hours later and may be continued for up to 5 days (Table 1). The total dose over 24 hours (given as divided doses) must not exceed adult dose of 32 mg.
> 1.2 m2 5 mg/m2 or 8 mg IV plus 8 mg syrup or tablet after 12 hours 8 mg syrup or tablet every 12 hours
> 10 kg Up to 3 doses of 0.15 mg/kg IV every 4 hours 4 mg syrup or tablet every 12 hours

items.t: Not licensed for CINV under 6 months; oral use for PONV in children not studied (IV recommended). Children on hepatotoxic chemotherapy: monitor liver function closely.

src.q: Ondansetron is indicated for the management of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV) in children aged ≥6 months.
Paediatric patients receiving ondansetron with hepatotoxic chemotherapeutic agents should be monitored closely for impaired hepatic function.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to ondansetron or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the ondansetron or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: With apomorphine (profound hypotension and loss of consciousness reported).

src.q: Concomitant use with apomorphine is contraindicated
Based on reports of profound hypotension and loss of consciousness when ondansetron was administered with apomorphine hydrochloride

items.t: Dose-dependent QT prolongation; torsade de pointes reported. Avoid in congenital long QT syndrome. Caution if QTc is or may become prolonged: electrolyte abnormalities, congestive heart failure, bradyarrhythmias, or other QT-prolonging drugs. Correct hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia first.

src.q: Ondansetron prolongs the QT interval in a dose-dependent manner
Avoid ondansetron in patients with congenital long QT syndrome.
Ondansetron should be administered with caution to patients who have or may develop prolongation of QTc, including patients with electrolyte abnormalities, congestive heart failure, bradyarrhythmias
Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia should be corrected prior to ondansetron administration.

items.t: Serotonin syndrome reported with other serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs): if the combination is needed, observe the patient.

src.q: If concomitant treatment with ondansetron and other serotonergic drugs is clinically warranted, appropriate observation of the patient is advised.

items.t: Myocardial ischaemia reported (mostly with IV use): alert patients to the signs and symptoms.

src.q: Cases of myocardial ischemia have been reported in patients treated with ondansetron.
Patients should be alerted to the signs and symptoms of myocardial ischemia.

items.t: Increases large bowel transit time: monitor patients with signs of subacute intestinal obstruction.

src.q: As ondansetron is known to increase large bowel transit time, patients with signs of subacute intestinal obstruction should be monitored following administration.

items.t: Adenotonsillar surgery: may mask occult bleeding - follow carefully.

src.q: In patients with adenotonsillar surgery prevention of nausea and vomiting with ondansetron may mask occult bleeding. Therefore, such patients should be followed carefully after ondansetron.

items.t: Hypersensitivity has occurred in patients sensitive to other 5-HT3 antagonists.

src.q: Hypersensitivity reactions have been reported in patients who have exhibited hypersensitivity to other selective 5-HT3 receptor antagonists.

items.t: Contains lactose: hereditary galactose intolerance, lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take it.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: QT-prolonging drugs or drugs causing electrolyte disturbance: caution - additional QT prolongation. Cardiotoxic drugs (anthracyclines, trastuzumab), erythromycin, ketoconazole, amiodarone and beta-blockers (e.g. atenolol) may increase the risk of arrhythmias.

src.q: Caution should be exercised when ondansetron is coadministered with drugs that prolong the QT interval and/or cause electrolyte abnormalities.
antiarrhythmics (such as amiodarone) and beta blockers (such as atenolol or timolol) may increase the risk of arrhythmias

items.t: Serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs): serotonin syndrome reported; observe the patient if combined.

src.q: There have been post-marketing reports describing patients with serotonin syndrome (including altered mental status, autonomic instability and neuromuscular abnormalities) following the concomitant use of ondansetron and other serotonergic drugs (including SSRIs and SNRIs).

items.t: Apomorphine: contraindicated (profound hypotension, loss of consciousness).

src.q: concomitant use with apomorphine is contraindicated

items.t: Tramadol: ondansetron may reduce its analgesic effect.

src.q: Data from small studies indicate that ondansetron may reduce the analgesic effect of tramadol.

items.t: Potent CYP3A4 inducers (phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampicin) lower ondansetron levels. No interaction with alcohol, temazepam, furosemide, morphine or tramadol pharmacokinetics in studies.

src.q: In patients treated with potent inducers of CYP3A4 (i.e. phenytoin, carbamazepine, and rifampicin), the oral clearance of ondansetron was increased and ondansetron blood concentrations were decreased.
Specific studies have shown that there are no interactions when ondansetron is administered with alcohol, temazepam, furosemide, alfentanil, tramadol, morphine, lidocaine, propofol and thiopental.

items.t: No change in dose, frequency or route.

src.q: Patients with Renal Impairment No alteration of daily dosage or frequency of dosing, or route of administration are required.

items.t: Moderate or severe hepatic impairment: clearance much reduced and half-life prolonged - do not exceed 8 mg per day.

src.q: Clearance of ondansetron is significantly reduced and serum half-life significantly prolonged in subjects with moderate or severe impairment of hepatic function.
In such patients a total daily dose of 8 mg should not be exceeded.

items.t: SmPC: suspected to cause orofacial malformations with first-trimester use (about 3 extra oral clefts per 10,000 women treated); cardiac malformation data conflict. Should not be used in the first trimester.

src.q: ondansetron is suspected to cause orofacial malformations when administered during the first trimester of pregnancy
Ondansetron should not be used during the first trimester of pregnancy.

items.t: MHRA: small increased risk of cleft lip/palate after first-trimester use. If ondansetron is considered for severe pregnancy sickness, counsel the woman on benefits and risks and decide jointly.

src.q: use of ondansetron during the first trimester of pregnancy is associated with a small increased risk of the baby having a cleft lip and/or cleft palate
women must be counselled on the potential benefits and risks of use, both to her and to her unborn baby and the final decision should be made jointly

items.t: BUMPS (differs in emphasis): can be used for pregnancy sickness that stops normal life; birth-defect risks are very low; no concern about miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth or low birth weight.

src.q: Ondansetron can be used to treat pregnancy sickness that is stopping you from living your normal life.
It is clear that these risks are very low, and most babies exposed in the womb to ondansetron do not have these birth defects.

items.t: SmPC: passes into animal milk - mothers taking ondansetron should not breastfeed.

src.q: It is therefore recommended that mothers receiving ondansetron should not breast-feed their babies.

items.t: SPS (differs from SmPC): can be used with caution; monitor the infant for sedation, irritability, diarrhoea, constipation and urinary retention. Unlikely to pass into milk in significant amounts.

src.q: Ondansetron can be used with caution during breastfeeding, but monitoring is required.
As a precaution, monitor for sedation, irritability, diarrhoea, or constipation and urinary retention.

items.t: Women of childbearing potential should consider contraception. No human fertility data.

src.q: Women of childbearing potential should consider the use of contraception.
There is no information on the effects of ondansetron on human fertility.

items.t: Very common: headache. Common: warmth or flushing, constipation.

src.q: Very common: Headache.
Common: Sensation of warmth or flushing.
Common: Constipation .

items.t: Uncommon: seizures, movement disorders (extrapyramidal reactions), arrhythmias, chest pain, bradycardia, hypotension, hiccups, raised liver function tests.

src.q: Uncommon: Arrhythmias, chest pain with or without ST segment depression, bradycardia.

items.t: QTc prolongation including torsade de pointes (rare); myocardial ischaemia (frequency not known).

src.q: Rare: QTc prolongation (including Torsade de Pointes)
Not known: Myocardial ischemia*

items.t: Immediate hypersensitivity, sometimes severe, including anaphylaxis (rare).

src.q: Rare : Immediate hypersensitivity reactions sometimes severe, including anaphylaxis.

items.t: Serotonin syndrome (altered mental state, autonomic instability, neuromuscular abnormalities) with other serotonergic drugs.

src.q: serotonin syndrome (including altered mental status, autonomic instability and neuromuscular abnormalities)

items.t: Seizures and extrapyramidal reactions (oculogyric crisis, dystonia) - uncommon.

src.q: Uncommon: Seizures, movement disorders (including extrapyramidal reactions (such as oculogyric crisis, dystonic reactions and dyskinesia)

items.t: Correct hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia before treatment.

src.q: Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia should be corrected prior to ondansetron administration.

items.t: SPS: no monitoring needed for oral use without risk factors; with non-modifiable risk factors, monitor ECG, magnesium and potassium before and during IV or prolonged treatment.

src.q: No monitoring is required in the absence of risk factors or in oral use.
Monitor ECG, magnesium and potassium before and during intravenous or prolonged treatment in people with non-modifiable patient and medicine risk factors.

items.t: Observe for serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic drugs; monitor for subacute intestinal obstruction; children on hepatotoxic chemotherapy: liver function.

src.q: appropriate observation of the patient is advised
patients with signs of subacute intestinal obstruction should be monitored following administration

items.t: Swallow tablets whole with liquid.

src.q: The tablets should be swallowed whole with liquid.

items.t: Seek urgent help for chest pain or pressure (possible myocardial ischaemia), palpitations or fainting.

src.q: Patients should be alerted to the signs and symptoms of myocardial ischemia.

items.t: Tell the prescriber if pregnant or planning pregnancy; consider contraception if of childbearing potential.

src.q: Women of childbearing potential should consider the use of contraception.

items.t: Can cause constipation.

src.q: Ondansetron is known to increase the large bowel transit time and may cause constipation in some patients.

items.t: Oral correction of fluid and electrolyte loss in infants, children and adults; watery diarrhoea of any cause, including gastroenteritis, in all age groups.

src.q: Oral correction of fluid and electrolyte loss in infants, children and adults.
Treatment of watery diarrhoea of various aetiologies including gastro-enteritis, in all age groups.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restrictions in the UK sachet SmPC (self-treatment limits are listed under cautions).

items.t: 1-2 sachets (each in 200 ml water) after every loose motion; more may be needed at first for full volume repletion.

src.q: Adults (including the elderly): One or two sachets after every loose motion.
More may be required initially to ensure early and full volume repletion.

items.t: Daily intake may be based on 20-40 ml/kg for adults and children (150 ml/kg for infants up to 2 years), adapted to age, weight, stage and severity.

src.q: Daily intake may be based on a volume of 150ml/kg body weight for infants up to the age of 2 and 20-40ml/kg body weight for adults and children.

items.t: Severe dehydration may first need parenteral fluids, then oral maintenance.

src.q: Severe dehydration may need to be corrected by parenteral fluids initially, followed by oral maintenance if indicated.

items.t: Infants under 2 years: use only under medical supervision and see a doctor as soon as possible; volume about 1 to 1.5 times the usual 24-hour feed volume (150 ml/kg/day).

src.q: Dioralyte shall not be used for treatment in infants below the age of 24 months without medical supervision.
Infants under the age of 2 years with diarrhoea should be seen by a physician as soon as possible.
Infants up to the age of 2: One to one and a half times the usual 24 hour feed volume.

items.t: Children: one sachet in 200 ml water after every loose motion.

src.q: Children: One sachet dissolved in 200ml of water after every loose motion.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to the active substances or any excipient. No other known contraindications, but treatment may be inappropriate, e.g. intestinal obstruction needing surgery.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substances or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.
There are no known contraindications to Dioralyte.
intestinal obstruction requiring surgical intervention

items.t: Not for self-treatment (physician supervision needed) in chronic or persistent diarrhoea, liver or kidney disease, diabetes, low-potassium or low-sodium diets, or intestinal obstruction.

src.q: Dioralyte should not be used for self-treatment by patients: with chronic or persistent diarrhea. with liver or kidney disease. with diabetes. on low potassium or sodium diets. with an intestinal obstruction.
The use of Dioralyte in patients with these conditions should be supervised by a physician.

items.t: Reconstitute only with water, one sachet in 200 ml: a weaker solution is not optimal; a stronger one may cause electrolyte imbalance.

src.q: Dioralyte should not be reconstituted in diluents other than water.
a stronger solution than recommended may give rise to electrolyte imbalance

items.t: Diarrhoea lasting more than 24-48 hours: patient should see a doctor.

src.q: If diarrhoea persists for longer than 24-48 hours the patient should be seen by a physician.

items.t: Sodium: about 300 mg per sachet (15% of the WHO adult maximum daily intake of 2 g).

src.q: This medicinal product contains approximately 300 mg sodium per sachet, equivalent to 15% of the WHO recommended maximum daily intake of 2 g sodium for an adult.

interactions.note: The UK sachet SmPC section 4.5 says 'None stated'. The aluminium hydroxide/magnesium hydroxide SmPC states that aluminium hydroxide with citrates may raise aluminium levels (recorded under that medicine).

items.t: Kidney disease: not for self-treatment; use under physician supervision. After significant overdose, checking electrolytes is particularly important in severe renal failure.

src.q: Dioralyte should not be used for self-treatment by patients: with chronic or persistent diarrhea. with liver or kidney disease. with diabetes. on low potassium or sodium diets. with an intestinal obstruction.
The use of Dioralyte in patients with these conditions should be supervised by a physician.
This is particularly important in the very young and in cases of severe hepatic of renal failure.

items.t: With normal kidney function it is difficult to over-hydrate by mouth.

src.q: Where the kidneys are functioning normally, it is difficult to over-hydrate by mouth

items.t: Liver disease: not for self-treatment; use under physician supervision.

src.q: Dioralyte should not be used for self-treatment by patients: with chronic or persistent diarrhea. with liver or kidney disease. with diabetes. on low potassium or sodium diets. with an intestinal obstruction.
The use of Dioralyte in patients with these conditions should be supervised by a physician.

items.t: Not contraindicated in pregnancy; medical supervision is recommended.

src.q: Dioralyte is not contra-indicated in pregnancy or lactation.
Medical supervision is recommended for use during pregnancy and lactation.

items.t: Not contraindicated during breastfeeding; medical supervision is recommended.

src.q: Dioralyte is not contra-indicated in pregnancy or lactation.
Medical supervision is recommended for use during pregnancy and lactation.

items.t: For a breastfed infant with diarrhoea, breast milk need not be withheld.

src.q: However breast milk need not be withheld.

reproductive.note: No fertility or contraception statements in the UK sachet SmPC.

adverseCommon.note: The UK sachet SmPC section 4.8 says 'None stated'.

adverseSerious.note: The UK sachet SmPC lists no adverse effects ('None stated'); a too-strong solution may cause electrolyte imbalance (see cautions).

items.t: No improvement within 24-48 hours: the patient should be seen by a doctor.

src.q: If no improvement is seen within 24-48 hours it is recommended that the patient be seen by a physician.

items.t: Significant overdose: check serum electrolytes as soon as possible and monitor until normal.

src.q: In the event of significant overdose, serum electrolytes should be evaluated as soon as possible

items.t: Dissolve one sachet in 200 ml drinking water (freshly boiled and cooled for infants). Make up just before use; keep up to 24 hours in a fridge, otherwise discard after 1 hour. Do not boil the solution.

src.q: The contents of each sachet should be dissolved in 200ml (approx. 7fl oz) of drinking water.
For infants, and where drinking water is unavailable, the water should be freshly boiled and cooled.
may be stored for up 24 hours in a refrigerator, otherwise any solution remaining an hour after reconstitution should be discarded
The solution itself must not be boiled.

items.t: With vomiting, give small amounts frequently, but give the whole required volume.

src.q: When vomiting is present with the diarrhoea it is advisable that small amounts of Dioralyte be taken frequently.

items.t: At first stop all foods including cow's or formula milk (breast milk can continue); restart the normal diet gradually after 24-48 hours when symptoms settle.

src.q: In the initial stages of treatment of diarrhoea all foods, including cow's or artificial milk, should be stopped.
After 24 - 48 hours, when symptoms have subsided, the normal diet should be resumed but this should be gradual to avoid exacerbation of the condition.

items.t: If unsure of the amount, give more rather than less (when kidneys work normally).

src.q: where there is doubt about the dosage, more rather than less should be taken

restrictions.note: No UK product information found.

hepatic.note: No UK product information found.

items.t: Treatment of influenza in adults and children including full-term neonates with typical symptoms when influenza is circulating; efficacy shown when started within 2 days of symptom onset.

src.q: Tamiflu is indicated in adults and children including full term neonates who present with symptoms typical of influenza, when influenza virus is circulating in the community.
Efficacy has been demonstrated when treatment is initiated within two days of first onset of symptoms.

items.t: Post-exposure prevention from 1 year of age (under 1 year only during a pandemic); seasonal prevention only in exceptional situations. Not a substitute for vaccination.

src.q: Post-exposure prevention in individuals 1 year of age or older following contact with a clinically diagnosed influenza case when influenza virus is circulating in the community.
Tamiflu is not a substitute for influenza vaccination .

items.t: NICE (treatment, outside a pandemic): recommended only when national surveillance shows influenza A or B circulating, the person is in an at-risk group, and treatment can start within 48 hours of symptom onset.

src.q: Oseltamivir and zanamivir are recommended, within their marketing authorisations, for the treatment of influenza in adults and children if all the following circumstances apply
the person is in an 'at-risk' group as defined in 1.2

items.t: NICE at-risk groups: chronic respiratory, heart, renal, liver or neurological disease, diabetes, age 65 or over, or possible immunosuppression.

src.q: chronic heart disease chronic renal disease chronic liver disease chronic neurological conditions diabetes mellitus.
People who are aged 65 years or older and people who might be immunosuppressed are also defined as 'at-risk' for the purpose of this guidance.

items.t: NICE (post-exposure prophylaxis): recommended when influenza is circulating and conditions are met, including starting within 48 hours of contact and the person not effectively protected by vaccination.

src.q: Oseltamivir and zanamivir are recommended, within their marketing authorisations, for the post-exposure prophylaxis of influenza if all of the following circumstances apply.
The person has not been effectively protected by vaccination

items.t: SmPC: use only when reliable data show influenza is circulating, and take current susceptibility patterns into account.

src.q: Tamiflu should be used for the treatment and prevention of influenza only when reliable epidemiological data indicate that influenza virus is circulating in the community.

items.t: Treatment, adults and adolescents 13 years and over: 75 mg twice daily for 5 days (10 days if immunocompromised). Start as soon as possible, within 2 days of symptom onset.

src.q: The recommended oral dose is 75 mg oseltamivir twice daily for 5 days for adolescents (13 to 17 years of age) and adults.
The recommended treatment duration in immunocompromised adults and adolescents is 10 days.

items.t: Post-exposure prevention, adults and adolescents 13 years and over: 75 mg once daily for 10 days, starting within 2 days of exposure.

src.q: The recommended dose for prevention of influenza following close contact with an infected individual is 75 mg oseltamivir once daily for 10 days
Therapy should begin as soon as possible within two days of exposure to an infected individual.

items.t: Prevention during a community epidemic: 75 mg once daily for up to 6 weeks (up to 12 weeks if immunocompromised).

src.q: The recommended dose for prevention of influenza during a community outbreak is 75 mg oseltamivir once daily for up to 6 weeks

items.t: Elderly: no adjustment unless moderate or severe renal impairment.

src.q: No dose adjustment is required, unless there is evidence of moderate or severe renal impairment.

items.t: 1 to 12 years, treatment (twice daily for 5 days): 10 to 15 kg 30 mg; >15 to 23 kg 45 mg; >23 to 40 kg 60 mg; >40 kg 75 mg. Post-exposure prevention: same doses once daily for 10 days.

src.q: 10 kg to 15 kg 30 mg twice daily 30 mg twice daily > 15 kg to 23 kg 45 mg twice daily 45 mg twice daily > 23 kg to 40 kg 60 mg twice daily 60 mg twice daily > 40 kg 75 mg twice daily 75 mg twice daily
10 kg to 15 kg 30 mg once daily 30 mg once daily > 15 kg to 23 kg 45 mg once daily 45 mg once daily

items.t: Infants 0 to 12 months, treatment: 3 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days (10 days if immunocompromised). Pandemic post-exposure prevention: 3 mg/kg once daily for 10 days. Not for premature infants (<36 weeks post-conceptual age).

src.q: The recommended treatment dose for infants 0 - 12 months of age is 3 mg/kg twice daily.
This dosing recommendation is not intended for premature infants, i.e. those with a post-conceptual age less than 36 weeks.

items.t: Seasonal (epidemic) prevention not studied under 12 years. No dosing advice for children 12 years and under with renal impairment.

src.q: Prevention during an influenza epidemic has not been studied in children below 12 years of age.
There is insufficient clinical data available in infants and children (12 years of age and younger) with renal impairment to be able to make any dosing recommendation.

items.t: The oral suspension is preferred for children and adults who cannot swallow capsules or need lower doses.

src.q: Commercially manufactured Tamiflu powder for oral suspension (6 mg/ml) is the preferred product for paediatric and adult patients who have difficulties swallowing capsules or where lower doses are needed.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to oseltamivir or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Neuropsychiatric events (especially children and adolescents): monitor closely for behavioural changes and weigh continuing treatment.

src.q: Patients should be closely monitored for behavioural changes, and the benefits and risks of continuing treatment should be carefully evaluated for each patient

items.t: Effective only against influenza; protection lasts only while taking it; not a substitute for vaccination.

src.q: Oseltamivir is effective only against illness caused by influenza viruses.
The protection against influenza lasts only as long as Tamiflu is administered.

items.t: Severe renal impairment: dose adjustment needed in adults and adolescents.

src.q: Dose adjustment is recommended for both treatment and prevention in adolescents (13 to 17 years of age) and adults with severe renal impairment.

items.t: Suspension contains sorbitol (not for hereditary fructose intolerance) and sodium benzoate (may increase jaundice in newborns).

src.q: Patients with hereditary fructose intolerance (HFI) should not take thismedicinal product.
Sodium benzoate (E211) may increase jaundice in newborn babies (up to 4 weeks old).

items.t: Clinically significant interactions are unlikely (no CYP450 metabolism, low protein binding).

src.q: suggest that clinically significant drug interactions via these mechanisms are unlikely.

items.t: Take care with co-excreted medicines with a narrow therapeutic margin (e.g. methotrexate, chlorpropamide).

src.q: care should be taken when prescribing oseltamivir in subjects when taking co-excreted agents with a narrow therapeutic margin (e.g. chlorpropamide, methotrexate, phenylbutazone).

items.t: No pharmacokinetic interaction with paracetamol, aspirin, antacids, amoxicillin or warfarin (stable patients without influenza).

src.q: No pharmacokinetic interactions between oseltamivir or its major metabolite have been observed when co-administering oseltamivir with paracetamol, acetylsalicylic acid,
rimantadine or warfarin (in subjects stable on warfarin and without influenza).

items.t: Treatment (adults and adolescents 13+): CrCl >60 mL/min 75 mg twice daily; >30 to 60 mL/min 30 mg twice daily; >10 to 30 mL/min 30 mg once daily; ≤10 mL/min not recommended; haemodialysis 30 mg after each session; peritoneal dialysis 30 mg single dose.

src.q: > 30 to 60 (ml/min) 30 mg (suspension or capsules) twice daily > 10 to 30 (ml/min) 30 mg (suspension or capsules) once daily ≤ 10 (ml/min) Not recommended (no data available)
Haemodialysis patients 30 mg after each haemodialysis session

items.t: Prevention: CrCl >60 mL/min 75 mg once daily; >30 to 60 mL/min 30 mg once daily; >10 to 30 mL/min 30 mg every second day; ≤10 mL/min not recommended; haemodialysis 30 mg after every second session; peritoneal dialysis 30 mg once weekly.

src.q: > 30 to 60 (ml/min) 30 mg (suspension or capsules) once daily > 10 to 30 (ml/min) 30 mg (suspension or capsules) every second day
Haemodialysis patients 30 mg after every second haemodialysis session

items.t: Children 12 years and under with renal impairment: insufficient data for a dose recommendation.

src.q: There is insufficient clinical data available in infants and children (12 years of age and younger) with renal impairment to be able to make any dosing recommendation.

items.t: No dose adjustment for treatment or prevention. Not studied in children with liver disease.

src.q: No dose adjustment is required either for treatment or for prevention in patients with hepatic dysfunction.

items.t: SmPC: large data (over 1000 first-trimester outcomes) show no malformative or fetal/neonatal toxicity, although one study was not conclusive for major congenital heart defects; may be considered if necessary after weighing safety, benefit and virus pathogenicity.

src.q: indicate no malformative nor feto/neonatal toxicity by oseltamivir.
the results for major congenital heart defects diagnosed within 12 months of birth were not conclusive.
The use of Tamiflu may be considered during pregnancy if necessary and after considering the available safety and benefit information

items.t: SmPC: low levels in milk (subtherapeutic for the infant); may be considered where there are clear benefits.

src.q: administration of oseltamivir may be considered, where there are clear potential benefits to breastfeeding mothers.

items.t: SPS: preferred antiviral in breastfeeding; monitor the infant for vomiting, diarrhoea, irritability and changes in sleep.

src.q: Oseltamivir is the preferred choice during breastfeeding. Infant monitoring is still required.
As a precaution, infants should be monitored for vomiting, diarrhoea, irritability, and changes in sleep.

items.t: No evidence of an effect on male or female fertility (preclinical data).

src.q: Based on preclinical data, there is no evidence that Tamiflu has an effect on male or female fertility

items.t: Adults: nausea and vomiting most common (usually on day 1 or 2, settle within 1 to 2 days); also headache. Children: vomiting most common.

src.q: the most commonly reported adverse reactions (ARs) were nausea and vomiting in the treatment studies, and nausea in the prevention studies.
In children, the most commonly reported adverse reaction was vomiting.

items.t: Rare: anaphylaxis, fulminant hepatitis/hepatic failure, angioedema, SJS/TEN, GI bleeding and neuropsychiatric events (convulsions, delirium, self-injury).

src.q: Anaphylactic and anaphylactoid reactions, hepatic disorders (fulminant hepatitis, hepatic function disorder and jaundice), angioneurotic oedema, Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, gastrointestinal bleeding and neuropsychiatric disorders.

items.t: Watch closely for behavioural changes, especially in children and adolescents.

src.q: Patients should be closely monitored for behavioural changes

items.t: Check renal function (CrCl) to set the dose in adults and adolescents.

src.q: Dose adjustment is recommended for adults and adolescents (13 to 17 years of age) with moderate or severe renal impairment.

items.t: Oral. Capsules and suspension are bioequivalent; patients who cannot swallow capsules can take the suspension. The suspension is best made up by a pharmacist; oral dispensers (3 mL and 10 mL) are supplied.

src.q: Tamiflu hard capsules and Tamiflu suspension are bioequivalent formulations.
It is recommended that Tamiflu powder for oral suspension be constituted by a pharmacist prior to dispensing to the patient

items.t: Start as soon as possible (within 2 days of symptoms or exposure). It does not replace the flu vaccine.

src.q: Treatment should be initiated as soon as possible within the first two days of onset of symptoms of influenza.
Use of Tamiflu must not affect the evaluation of individuals for annual influenza vaccination.

items.t: Report unusual behaviour, confusion or hallucinations promptly, especially in children.

src.q: Neuropsychiatric events have been reported during administration of Tamiflu in patients with influenza, especially in children and adolescents.

restrictions.note: No UK product information found.

hepatic.note: No UK product information found.

items.t: Adults and adolescents 12 years and over: reflux oesophagitis. Adults only: H. pylori eradication (with antibiotics) in H. pylori-associated ulcers; gastric and duodenal ulcer; Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and other hypersecretory conditions.

src.q: Pantoprazole is indicated for use in adults and adolescents 12 years of age and above for: - Reflux oesophagitis.
Gastric and duodenal ulcer. - Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome and other pathological hypersecretory conditions.

restrictions.note: No specialist-only, shared-care or brand restriction stated in the UK SmPC (40 mg gastro-resistant tablets), MHRA Drug Safety Updates on PPIs or SPS pages checked.

items.t: 40 mg once daily, usually for 4 weeks (a further 4 weeks if not healed). May be doubled to 80 mg daily in individual cases, especially if no response to other treatment.

src.q: In individual cases the dose may be doubled (increase to 2 tablets Pantoprazole daily) especially when there has been no response to other treatment.
A 4-week period is usually required for the treatment of reflux oesophagitis. If this is not sufficient, healing will usually be achieved within a further 4 weeks.

items.t: 40 mg twice daily with two antibiotics (e.g. amoxicillin 1000 mg + clarithromycin 500 mg, each twice daily), usually for 7 days (up to 14 days). Take the second dose 1 hour before the evening meal.

src.q: Twice daily one tablet Pantoprazole + twice daily 1000 mg amoxicillin + twice daily 500 mg clarithromycin
The combination therapy is implemented for 7 days in general and can be prolonged for a further 7 days to a total duration of up to two weeks.
the second Pantoprazole tablet should be taken 1 hour before the evening meal

items.t: Gastric ulcer: 40 mg once daily for 4 weeks (a further 4 weeks if needed). Duodenal ulcer: 40 mg once daily, usually heals in 2 weeks (a further 2 weeks if needed). Dose may be doubled in individual cases.

src.q: A 4-week period is usually required for the treatment of gastric ulcers.
A duodenal ulcer generally heals within 2 weeks. If a 2-week period of treatment is not sufficient, healing will be achieved in almost all cases within a further 2 weeks.

items.t: Start 80 mg daily, then titrate by gastric acid measurements. Doses above 80 mg daily: divide and give twice daily. A temporary increase above 160 mg is possible but only as long as needed.

src.q: patients should start their treatment with a daily dose of 80 mg (2 tablets of Pantoprazole 40 mg)
With doses above 80 mg daily, the dose should be divided and given twice daily.

items.t: Elderly and renal impairment: no dose adjustment.

src.q: Elderly No dose adjustment is necessary in the elderly

items.t: Not recommended under 12 years (limited safety and efficacy data). From 12 years: reflux oesophagitis only, at the adult dose.

src.q: Pantoprazole is not recommended for use in children below 12 years of age because of limited data on safety and efficacy in this age group

items.t: Hypersensitivity to pantoprazole, substituted benzimidazoles or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance, substituted benzimidazoles, any of the other excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Must not be used in H. pylori combination therapy in moderate to severe hepatic dysfunction or in impaired renal function (no data).

src.q: Pantoprazole must not be used in combination treatment for eradication of H. pylori in patients with moderate to severe hepatic dysfunction
Pantoprazole must not be used in combination treatment for eradication of H. pylori in patients with impaired renal function

items.t: Alarm symptoms (weight loss, recurrent vomiting, dysphagia, haematemesis, anaemia, melaena) or suspected gastric ulcer: exclude malignancy first - treatment may mask symptoms.

src.q: In the presence of any alarm symptom (e.g. significant unintentional weight loss, recurrent vomiting, dysphagia, haematemesis, anaemia or melaena) and when gastric ulcer is suspected or present, malignancy should be excluded.

items.t: Severe hepatic impairment: monitor liver enzymes regularly (especially long term); stop if enzymes rise.

src.q: In patients with severe liver impairment, the liver enzymes should be monitored regularly during treatment with pantoprazole, particularly on long-term use. In the case of a rise of the liver enzymes, the treatment should be discontinued

items.t: Hypomagnesaemia (rare, severe; usually after ≥ 3 months, mostly after 1 year). Consider magnesium before and during prolonged treatment, especially with digoxin or diuretics.

src.q: Severe hypomagnesaemia has been rarely reported in patients treated with proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) like pantoprazole for at least three months, and in most cases for a year.

consider measurement of magnesium levels before starting PPI treatment and periodically during prolonged treatment, especially in those who will take a PPI concomitantly with digoxin or drugs that may cause hypomagnesaemia (eg, diuretics)

items.t: Fractures: high doses and long use (> 1 year) may modestly increase hip, wrist and spine fracture risk, mainly in the elderly. Patients at risk of osteoporosis need guideline care with adequate vitamin D and calcium.

src.q: Proton pump inhibitors, especially if used in high doses and over long durations (>1year), may modestly increase the risk of hip, wrist and spine fracture
Patients at risk of osteoporosis should receive care according to current clinical guidelines and they should have an adequate intake of vitamin D and calcium.

items.t: Severe skin reactions (erythema multiforme, SJS, TEN, DRESS) can be life-threatening: warn patients of the signs; stop pantoprazole immediately if they appear.

src.q: If signs and symptoms suggestive of these reactions appear, pantoprazole should be withdrawn immediately and an alternative treatment considered.

items.t: Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE): if lesions (especially sun-exposed) with arthralgia, seek help promptly and consider stopping. SCLE with one PPI may raise risk with others.

src.q: the patient should seek medical help promptly and the healthcare professional should consider stopping pantoprazole
SCLE after previous treatment with a proton pump inhibitor may increase the risk of SCLE with other proton pump inhibitors.

items.t: GI infections: slightly increased risk of Salmonella, Campylobacter or C. difficile.

src.q: Treatment with Pantoprazole may lead to a slightly increased risk of gastrointestinal infections caused by bacteria such as Salmonella and Campylobacter or C. difficile .

items.t: Vitamin B12 absorption may fall on long-term therapy: consider in those with low stores or risk factors. Long-term use (> 1 year): keep under regular surveillance.

src.q: This should be considered in patients with reduced body stores or risk factors for reduced vitamin B12 absorption on long-term therapy
In long-term treatment, especially when exceeding a treatment period of 1 year, patients should be kept under regular surveillance.

items.t: Chromogranin A tests: stop pantoprazole at least 5 days before CgA measurement. False-positive urine THC screens reported - confirm by another method.

src.q: Pantoprazole treatment should be stopped for at least 5 days before CgA measurements
There have been reports of false-positive results in some urine screening tests for tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) in patients receiving pantoprazole.

items.t: Contains lactose: patients with hereditary galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take it.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: Warfarin (coumarins): no pharmacokinetic effect in studies, but raised INR/prothrombin time reported with PPIs, which may cause abnormal bleeding or death. Monitor INR and prothrombin time.

src.q: there have been reports of increased INR and prothrombin time in patients receiving PPIs and warfarin or phenprocoumon concomitantly
Patients treated with pantoprazole and warfarin or phenprocoumon may need to be monitored for increase in INR and prothrombin time.

items.t: Methotrexate (high dose, e.g. 300 mg): levels may rise; consider temporarily stopping pantoprazole.

src.q: in settings where high-dose methotrexate is used, for example cancer and psoriasis, a temporary withdrawal of pantoprazole may need to be considered

items.t: HIV protease inhibitors that need acid pH (e.g. atazanavir): not recommended. If unavoidable, monitor closely (e.g. viral load) and do not exceed pantoprazole 20 mg daily.

src.q: Co-administration of pantoprazole is not recommended with HIV protease inhibitors for which absorption is dependent on acidic intragastric pH such as atazanavir
A pantoprazole dose of 20 mg per day should not be exceeded.

items.t: Drugs needing gastric acid for absorption (e.g. ketoconazole, itraconazole, posaconazole, erlotinib): absorption may be reduced.

src.q: e.g. some azole antifungals such as ketoconazole, itraconazole, posaconazole and other medicines such as erlotinib

items.t: Enzyme inducers (rifampicin, St John's wort) may lower pantoprazole levels; CYP2C19 inhibitors (e.g. fluvoxamine) may raise them.

src.q: Enzyme inducers affecting CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 such as rifampicin and St John's wort ( Hypericum perforatum ) may reduce the plasma concentrations of PPIs
Inhibitors of CYP2C19 such as fluvoxamine could increase the systemic exposure of pantoprazole.

items.t: Diuretics (and digoxin): consider magnesium checks before and during prolonged PPI treatment.

src.q: For patients expected to be on prolonged treatment or who take PPIs with digoxin or medicinal products that may cause hypomagnesaemia (e.g. diuretics), health care professionals should consider measuring magnesium levels before starting PPI treatment and periodically during treatment.

items.t: Clopidogrel: SPS advises avoiding clopidogrel only with omeprazole or esomeprazole; other PPIs are considered safe with clopidogrel. No clinically relevant interaction found with clarithromycin, metronidazole, amoxicillin, diclofenac, naproxen, nifedipine or antacids.

src.q: Other PPIs are considered safe with clopidogrel.

Interaction studies have also been performed by concomitantly administering pantoprazole with the respective antibiotics (clarithromycin, metronidazole, amoxicillin). No clinically relevant interactions were found.

items.t: No dose adjustment needed (including dialysis). Must not be used in H. pylori combination therapy in impaired renal function. Tubulointerstitial nephritis reported (frequency not known).

src.q: Patients with renal impairment No dose adjustment is necessary in patients with impaired renal function.
Pantoprazole must not be used in combination treatment for eradication of H. pylori in patients with impaired renal function
Tubulointerstitial nephritis (TIN) (with possible progression to renal failure)

items.t: Severe hepatic impairment: do not exceed 20 mg daily; monitor liver enzymes regularly and stop if they rise.

src.q: A daily dose of 20 mg Pantoprazole (1 tablet of 20 mg Pantoprazole) should not be exceeded in patients with severe liver impairment.
In the case of a rise of the liver enzymes, the treatment should be discontinued

items.t: Moderate to severe hepatic dysfunction: must not be used in H. pylori combination therapy.

src.q: Pantoprazole must not be used in combination treatment for eradication of H. pylori in patients with moderate to severe hepatic dysfunction

items.t: SmPC: 300-1000 pregnancy outcomes show no malformative or feto/neonatal toxicity, but as a precaution it is preferable to avoid pantoprazole in pregnancy.

src.q: A moderate amount of data on pregnant women (between 300-1000 pregnancy outcomes) indicate no malformative or feto/ neonatal toxicity of pantoprazole.
As a precautionary measure, it is preferable to avoid the use of pantoprazole during pregnancy.

items.t: BUMPS: omeprazole is the preferred PPI in pregnancy, but other PPIs can be used if advised by a doctor; no good evidence linking PPIs to miscarriage, birth defects, stillbirth, preterm delivery or low birth weight.

src.q: However, other PPIs can also be used if advised by a doctor.
There is no good evidence that omeprazole or other PPIs are linked to miscarriage, birth defects, stillbirth, preterm delivery, or low infant birth weight.

items.t: SmPC: excretion into human milk reported; risk to the infant cannot be excluded - decide whether to stop breastfeeding or pantoprazole.

src.q: There is insufficient information on the excretion of pantoprazole in human milk but excretion into human milk has been reported. A risk to the newborns/infants cannot be excluded.

items.t: SPS: any PPI can be used in breastfeeding; omeprazole and pantoprazole are the PPIs of choice.

src.q: Any PPI can be used during breastfeeding, however omeprazole and pantoprazole are the PPIs of choice

items.t: Fertility: no impairment in animal studies.

src.q: There was no evidence of impaired fertility following the administration of pantoprazole in animal studies

items.t: About 5% of patients have adverse reactions. Common: benign fundic gland polyps. Uncommon: headache, dizziness, diarrhoea, nausea/vomiting, bloating, constipation, dry mouth, abdominal pain, raised liver enzymes, rash, pruritus, sleep disorders, fracture, asthenia.

src.q: Approximately 5 % of patients can be expected to experience adverse drug reactions (ADRs).
Fundic gland polyps (benign) Diarrhoea; Nausea / vomiting; Abdominal distension and bloating; Constipation; Dry mouth; Abdominal pain and discomfort

items.t: Severe skin reactions (SJS, TEN, erythema multiforme, DRESS): stop immediately.

src.q: Stevens-Johnson syndrome; Lyell syndrome (TEN); Erythema multiforme

items.t: Hypersensitivity including anaphylactic reactions and shock (rare).

src.q: Hypersensitivity (including anaphylactic reactions and anaphylactic shock)

items.t: Hepatocellular injury, jaundice, hepatocellular failure (frequency not known).

src.q: Hepatocellular injury; Jaundice; Hepatocellular failure

items.t: Tubulointerstitial nephritis (may progress to renal failure); hypomagnesaemia (may cause hypocalcaemia, hypokalaemia); hyponatraemia.

src.q: Tubulointerstitial nephritis (TIN) (with possible progression to renal failure)
Hyponatraemia; Hypomagnesaemia (see section 4.4)

items.t: Blood disorders: agranulocytosis (rare); thrombocytopenia, leucopenia, pancytopenia (very rare).

src.q: Agranulocytosis Thrombocytopenia; Leukopenia; Pancytopenia

src.q: consider measurement of magnesium levels before starting PPI treatment and periodically during prolonged treatment
