src.q: health care professionals should consider measuring magnesium levels before starting PPI treatment and periodically during treatment
In patients with severe liver impairment, the liver enzymes should be monitored regularly during treatment with pantoprazole, particularly on long-term use.

items.t: Stop if liver enzymes rise (severe hepatic impairment) or if severe skin reaction signs appear; consider stopping if SCLE develops.

src.q: In the case of a rise of the liver enzymes, the treatment should be discontinued
consider stopping use of the PPI unless it is imperative for a serious acid-related condition

items.t: Swallow whole with some water 1 hour before a meal; do not chew or crush.

src.q: The tablets should not be chewed or crushed, and should be swallowed whole 1 hour before a meal with some water.

items.t: Report rash, blistering or peeling skin promptly; report rash on sun-exposed skin with joint pain (possible SCLE).

src.q: At the time of prescription, patients should be advised of the signs and symptoms and monitored closely for skin reactions.
advise them to avoid exposing the skin to sunlight

items.t: Dizziness or visual disturbance may occur - do not drive or operate machines if affected.

src.q: If affected, patients should not drive or operate machines.

items.t: On long-term use, make sure you get enough vitamin D and calcium.

src.q: consult your doctor to make sure you are taking enough vitamin D and calcium

items.t: Mild to moderate pain and fever (e.g. headache, migraine, toothache, neuralgia, colds and influenza, sore throat, backache, rheumatic pain, dysmenorrhoea).

src.q: Paracetamol is a mild analgesic and antipyretic, and is recommended for the treatment of most painful and febrile conditions

items.t: Infant suspension: mild to moderate pain and fever, including teething and post-immunisation fever.

src.q: is indicated for the treatment of mild to moderate pain and as an antipyretic
teething, sore throat, colds & influenza, aches and pains and post-immunisation fever

items.t: 250 mg/5 mL suspension: mild to moderate pain and fever; adjunct for symptoms of cold and flu.

src.q: For the treatment of mild to moderate pain
For the reduction of fever and to be used as an adjunctive treatment to relieve symptoms of cold and flu.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction stated in the SmPCs or MHRA pages accessed.

items.t: Adults (including elderly) and children over 16 years: 1 g (two 500 mg tablets) every 4 hours as required. Maximum 8 tablets (4 g) in 24 hours; no more than 4 doses in 24 hours. Do not take for more than 3 days without consulting a doctor.

src.q: Adults, Elderly and Children over 16 years: Two tablets every four hours as required. Not more than eight tablets in 24 hours
nor should more than four doses be given in any 24 hour period
Do not take for more than 3 days without consulting your doctor.

items.t: 250 mg/5 mL suspension, adults and children over 16 years: 10-20 mL (500 mg-1 g) up to 4 times a day.

src.q: Adults and children over 16 years: Two - four 5mL spoonfuls (large end) up to 4 times a day.

items.t: Elderly: absorption is normal but half-life is longer and clearance lower than in young adults (no specific dose change stated).

src.q: In the elderly, the rate and extent of paracetamol absorption is normal but plasma half-life is longer and paracetamol clearance is lower than in young adults.

items.t: Low body weight or hepatic risk factors: no reduced maximum daily dose is stated in the oral SmPCs used (BNF not accessed); this is a gap in these sources, not evidence that no reduction is needed. Overdose thresholds stated: liver damage is possible after 10 g or more in adults (500 mg tablet SmPC) or 7.5 g or more in adults and adolescents aged 12 years and over (suspension SmPCs), and after 5 g or more with risk factors (long-term liver enzyme inducers, regular excess alcohol, glutathione depletion e.g. eating disorders, cystic fibrosis, HIV, starvation, cachexia).

src.q: Liver damage is possible in adults who have taken 10g or more of paracetamol. Ingestion of 5g or more of paracetamol may lead to liver damage if the patient has risk factors
Liver damage is possible in adults and adolescents (≥12 years of age) who have taken 7.5g or more of paracetamol.
is likely to be glutathione deplete e.g. eating disorders, cystic fibrosis, HIV infection, starvation, cachexia

items.t: Tablets: not recommended under 10 years. Children 10-15 years: one 500 mg tablet every 4-6 hours when necessary, maximum 4 doses in 24 hours; no more than 3 days without a doctor.

src.q: Children under 10 years: Not recommended for children under 10 years of age.
Children aged 10 to 15 years: One tablet every four to six hours when necessary to a maximum of four doses in 24 hours.

items.t: 120 mg/5 ml, fever after vaccination at 2, 3 and 4 months: 2.5 ml, up to 4 times a day starting at the time of vaccination, at least 4 hours apart; see a doctor or pharmacist if still needed 2 days after the vaccine.

src.q: For the relief of fever after vaccinations at 2, 3 and 4 months 2.5ml. This dose may be given up to 4 times a day starting at the time of vaccination.
If your baby still needs this medicine two days after receiving the vaccine talk to your doctor or pharmacist.

items.t: MHRA 2011 table (older): post-vaccination fever at 2-3 months 2.5 mL, then a second 2.5 mL after 4-6 hours if necessary; no more than 2 doses. This differs from the current 120 mg/5 ml suspension SmPC (up to 4 doses a day).

src.q: Post-vaccination fever 2.5 mL If necessary, after 4-6 hours, give a second 2.5 mL dose

src.q: 6 - 8 years One 5 mL spoonful (large end) 4 times 8 - 10 years One 5.0 mL spoonful (large end) and one 2.5 mL spoonful (small end) 4 times 10 - 12 years Two 5 mL spoonfuls (large end) 4 times

items.t: Care in severe renal or severe hepatic impairment. Overdose risk is greater in non-cirrhotic alcoholic liver disease.

src.q: Care is advised in the administration of paracetamol to patients with severe renal or severe hepatic impairment. The hazard of overdose is greater in those with non-cirrhotic alcoholic liver disease.

items.t: Do not exceed the dose and do not take with other paracetamol-containing products.

src.q: Do not exceed the recommended dose.
Do not take with any other paracetamol-containing products.

items.t: High anion gap metabolic acidosis (pyroglutamic acidosis) reported with prolonged therapeutic use in severe illness (e.g. severe renal impairment, sepsis), malnutrition or chronic alcoholism, or with flucloxacillin. If suspected, stop paracetamol promptly and monitor closely.

src.q: Cases of high anion gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA) due to pyroglutamic acidosis have been reported in patients with severe illness such as severe renal impairment and sepsis
If HAGMA due to pyroglutamic acidosis is suspected, prompt discontinuation of paracetamol and close monitoring is recommended.

items.t: Suspensions: chronic alcohol users should consult a doctor before use.

src.q: Chronic alcohol users should consult a doctor before use.

items.t: Warfarin and other coumarins: prolonged regular daily use of paracetamol may enhance the anticoagulant effect and increase bleeding risk; occasional doses have no significant effect.

src.q: The anticoagulant effect of warfarin and other coumarins may be enhanced by prolonged regular daily use of paracetamol with increased risk of bleeding; occasional doses have no significant effect.

items.t: Long-term St John's Wort or other liver enzyme inducers are listed as overdose risk factors (liver damage possible from 5 g or more).

src.q: rifampicin, St. John's Wort or other drugs that induce liver enzymes

items.t: Absorption may be speeded by metoclopramide or domperidone and reduced by colestyramine.

src.q: The speed of absorption of paracetamol may be increased by metoclopramide or domperidone and absorption reduced by cholestyramine.

items.t: Severe renal impairment: care advised (no numeric threshold or dose change stated).

src.q: Care is advised in the administration of paracetamol to patients with severe renal or severe hepatic impairment.

items.t: 250 mg/5 mL suspension (contains propylene glycol): medical monitoring is required in impaired renal function.

src.q: Medical monitoring is required in patients with impaired renal or hepatic functions because various adverse events attributed to propylene glycol have been reported
such as renal dysfunction (acute tubular necrosis), acute renal failure and liver dysfunction

items.t: Severe hepatic impairment: care advised (tablets, 120 mg/5 ml suspension).

src.q: Care is advised in the administration of paracetamol to patients with severe renal or severe hepatic impairment.

items.t: Severe hepatic dysfunction: contraindicated (250 mg/5 mL suspension SmPC).

src.q: Patients with severe hepatic dysfunction.

items.t: 250 mg/5 mL suspension (contains propylene glycol): medical monitoring is required in impaired hepatic function.

src.q: Medical monitoring is required in patients with impaired renal or hepatic functions because various adverse events attributed to propylene glycol have been reported
such as renal dysfunction (acute tubular necrosis), acute renal failure and liver dysfunction

items.t: Can be used in pregnancy if clinically needed, at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time and lowest frequency. Large amount of data shows no malformative or feto/neonatal toxicity.

src.q: A large amount of data on pregnant women indicate neither malformative, nor feto/neonatal toxicity.
it should be used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible time and at the lowest possible frequency

items.t: MHRA (2025): paracetamol is the first-choice pain reliever in pregnancy; no evidence it causes autism. Patients should not swap to ibuprofen (NSAIDs generally not recommended in pregnancy).

src.q: paracetamol is recommended as the first-choice pain reliever for pregnant women, used at the lowest dose and for the shortest duration
there is no evidence that taking paracetamol during pregnancy causes autism in children
patients should not swap to alternatives such as ibuprofen
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen, are generally not recommended during pregnancy

items.t: BUMPS: can be used throughout pregnancy for pain and fever; no extra monitoring needed.

src.q: Paracetamol can be used throughout pregnancy to treat pain and high temperature (fever).
No extra monitoring for birth defects is required following paracetamol use in pregnancy.

items.t: SPS: analgesic of choice for mild to moderate pain in pregnancy.

src.q: Paracetamol is the analgesia of choice for mild to moderate pain in pregnancy.

items.t: Compatible: excreted in breast milk but not in clinically significant amounts.

src.q: Paracetamol is excreted in breast milk but not in a clinically significant amount. Available published data do not contraindicate breast feeding.

items.t: SPS: analgesic of choice for mild to moderate pain during breastfeeding; as a precaution monitor the infant for diarrhoea and vomiting.

src.q: Paracetamol is the analgesic of choice for treating mild to moderate pain during breastfeeding.
As a precaution, monitor infants for diarrhoea and vomiting.

reproductive.note: Suspension SmPCs state there is no information on fertility; no fertility or contraception advice in the sources accessed.

adverseCommon.note: The paracetamol SmPCs accessed list no common or very common adverse reactions; listed reactions are 'not known' or very rare.

items.t: Hypersensitivity: anaphylactic shock and angioedema (frequency not known). Stop at the first sign of skin rash or other hypersensitivity; very rare serious skin reactions.

src.q: Not known: anaphylactic shock; angioedema
use of the drug should be discontinued at the first appearance of skin rash or any other sign of hypersensitivity

items.t: Blood dyscrasias including thrombocytopenia and agranulocytosis (frequency not known).

src.q: Not known: blood dyscrasias including thrombocytopenia and agranulocytosis

items.t: Overdose: risk of delayed, serious liver damage even if the patient feels well; refer to hospital urgently.

src.q: Immediate medical advice should be sought in the event of an overdose, even if you feel well, because of the risk of delayed, serious liver damage.
patients should be referred to hospital urgently for immediate medical attention

items.t: High anion gap metabolic acidosis (frequency not known) in patients with risk factors.

src.q: Not known: high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

items.t: If HAGMA (pyroglutamic acidosis) is suspected: stop paracetamol and monitor closely; urinary 5-oxoproline may help confirm.

src.q: The measurement of urinary 5-oxoproline may be useful to identify pyroglutamic acidosis
prompt discontinuation of paracetamol and close monitoring is recommended

items.t: Leave at least 4 hours between doses.

src.q: These doses should not be repeated more frequently than every four hours

items.t: Suspensions: shake the bottle for at least 10 seconds before use; use the syringe or spoon supplied.

src.q: It is important to shake the bottle for at least 10 seconds before use.
Always use the syringe supplied with the pack.

items.t: Do not take anything else containing paracetamol at the same time.

src.q: Do not give anything else containing paracetamol while giving this medicine.

items.t: Get medical help at once after taking too much, even if feeling well.

src.q: Talk to a doctor at once if your child takes too much of this medicine, even if they seem well.

items.t: Children: do not give for more than 3 days without speaking to a doctor or pharmacist.

src.q: Do not give this medicine to your child for more than 3 days without speaking to your doctor or pharmacist

items.t: Hypertension; symptomatic heart failure; stable coronary artery disease (to reduce the risk of cardiac events after myocardial infarction and/or revascularisation).

src.q: Hypertension: Treatment of hypertension. Heart failure: Treatment of symptomatic heart failure.
Stable coronary artery disease: Reduction of risk of cardiac events in patients with a history of myocardial infarction and/or revascularisation.

restrictions.note: No specialist-only or shared-care restriction stated in the perindopril arginine SmPC. Dual RAAS blockade, if absolutely necessary, only under specialist supervision (see cautions).

items.t: Start 5 mg once daily in the morning; may increase to 10 mg once daily after one month. Strongly activated renin-angiotensin system (renovascular hypertension, salt/volume depletion, cardiac decompensation, severe hypertension): start 2.5 mg under medical supervision.

src.q: The recommended starting dose is 5 mg given once daily in the morning.
A starting dose of 2.5 mg is recommended in such patients and the initiation of treatment should take place under medical supervision.
The dose may be increased to 10 mg once daily after one month of treatment.

items.t: Already on a diuretic: stop the diuretic 2-3 days before if possible; if it cannot be stopped, start at 2.5 mg and monitor renal function and serum potassium.

src.q: If possible, the diuretic should be discontinued 2 to 3 days before beginning therapy with Coversyl Arginine
In hypertensive patients in whom the diuretic cannot be discontinued, therapy with Coversyl Arginine should be initiated with a 2.5 mg dose. Renal function and serum potassium should be monitored.

items.t: Start 2.5 mg in the morning under close medical supervision; may increase after 2 weeks to 5 mg once daily if tolerated. Monitor blood pressure, renal function and potassium closely before and during treatment.

src.q: be introduced under close medical supervision with a recommended starting dose of 2.5 mg taken in the morning. This dose may be increased after 2 weeks to 5 mg once daily if tolerated.
Blood pressure, renal function and serum potassium should be monitored closely, both before and during treatment with Coversyl Arginine

items.t: 5 mg once daily for two weeks, then 10 mg once daily if the 5 mg dose is well tolerated, depending on renal function.

src.q: Coversyl Arginine should be introduced at a dose of 5 mg once daily for two weeks, then increased to 10 mg once daily, depending on renal function and provided that the 5 mg dose is well tolerated.

items.t: Elderly: hypertension - start 2.5 mg, increase to 5 mg after one month, then 10 mg if needed depending on renal function. Stable coronary artery disease - 2.5 mg once daily for one week, then 5 mg the next week, then up to 10 mg depending on renal function.

src.q: In elderly patients, treatment should be initiated at a dose of 2.5 mg which may be progressively increased to 5 mg after one month then to 10 mg if necessary depending on renal function
Elderly patients should receive 2.5 mg once daily for one week, then 5 mg once daily the next week, before increasing the dose up to 10 mg once daily depending on renal function

items.t: Safety and efficacy below 18 years not established; no posology recommendation. Use in children and adolescents is not recommended.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of perindopril in children and adolescents aged below 18 years have not been established.
Therefore, use in children and adolescents is not recommended.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to perindopril, any excipient or any other ACE inhibitor.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance, to any of the excipients or to any other ACE inhibitor

items.t: History of angioedema with previous ACE inhibitor therapy; hereditary or idiopathic angioedema.

src.q: History of angioedema associated with previous ACE inhibitor therapy
Hereditary or idiopathic angioedema

items.t: Second and third trimesters of pregnancy.

src.q: Second and third trimesters of pregnancy (see sections 4.4 and 4.6)

items.t: With aliskiren-containing products in patients with diabetes or renal impairment (GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m²).

src.q: Concomitant use of Coversyl Arginine with aliskiren-containing products in patients with diabetes mellitus or renal impairment (GFR < 60 ml/min/1.73 m2)

items.t: With sacubitril/valsartan; do not start perindopril within 36 hours of the last sacubitril/valsartan dose.

src.q: Concomitant use with sacubitril/valsartan therapy, Coversyl Arginine must not be initiated earlier than 36 hours after the last dose of sacubitril/valsartan

items.t: Extracorporeal treatments where blood contacts negatively charged surfaces (e.g. certain high-flux dialysis/haemofiltration membranes, LDL apheresis with dextran sulfate).

src.q: Extracorporeal treatments leading to contact of blood with negatively charged surfaces (see section 4.5)

items.t: Significant bilateral renal artery stenosis or stenosis of the artery to a single functioning kidney.

src.q: Significant bilateral renal artery stenosis or stenosis of the artery to a single functioning kidney

items.t: Symptomatic hypotension: more likely with volume depletion (diuretics, salt restriction, dialysis, diarrhoea, vomiting), severe renin-dependent hypertension or more severe heart failure. Monitor starting and dose changes closely in those at risk, including ischaemic heart or cerebrovascular disease.

src.q: more likely to occur in patients who have been volume-depleted e.g. by diuretic therapy, dietary salt restriction, dialysis, diarrhoea or vomiting, or who have severe renin-dependent hypertension
In patients at increased risk of symptomatic hypotension, initiation of therapy and dose adjustment should be closely monitored

items.t: Stable coronary artery disease: if unstable angina occurs in the first month, carefully reassess benefit and risk before continuing.

src.q: If an episode of unstable angina pectoris (major or not) occurs during the first month of perindopril treatment, a careful appraisal of the benefit/risk should be performed before treatment continuation.

items.t: Mitral stenosis, aortic stenosis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: give with caution.

src.q: should be given with caution to patients with mitral valve stenosis and obstruction in the outflow of the left ventricle such as aortic stenosis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

items.t: Renal impairment (CrCl below 60 mL/min): adjust the starting dose to creatinine clearance; monitor potassium and creatinine. Renal artery stenosis: urea and creatinine may rise; start under close supervision with low doses and careful titration.

src.q: In cases of renal impairment (creatinine clearance < 60 ml/min) the initial perindopril dosage should be adjusted according to the patient's creatinine clearance
In these patients, treatment should be started under close medical supervision with low doses and careful dose titration.

items.t: Angioedema (face, lips, tongue, glottis, larynx; also intestinal angioedema presenting as abdominal pain) can occur at any time. Stop promptly and monitor until resolved; airway involvement needs emergency treatment. Higher rate in black patients.

src.q: This may occur at any time during therapy . In such cases, Coversyl Arginine should promptly be discontinued and appropriate monitoring should be initiated and continued until complete resolution of symptoms has occurred.
Where there is involvement of the tongue, glottis or larynx, likely to cause airway obstruction, emergency therapy should be administered promptly.
Intestinal angioedema should be included in the differential diagnosis of patients on ACE inhibitors presenting with abdominal pain.
ACE inhibitors cause a higher rate of angioedema in black patients than in non-black patients.

items.t: History of angioedema not caused by an ACE inhibitor: may be at higher risk of angioedema on an ACE inhibitor.

src.q: Patients with a history of angioedema unrelated to ACE inhibitor therapy may be at increased risk of angioedema while receiving an ACE inhibitor

items.t: Neutropenia/agranulocytosis: extreme caution in collagen vascular disease, immunosuppressant therapy, allopurinol or procainamide, especially with renal impairment; check white cell counts periodically.

src.q: Perindopril should be used with extreme caution in patients with collagen vascular disease, immunosuppressant therapy, treatment with allopurinol or procainamide
periodic monitoring of white blood cell counts is advised

items.t: Hyperkalaemia risk with renal impairment, age over 70, diabetes, dehydration, acute cardiac decompensation, metabolic acidosis, potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements or salt substitutes, heparin, co-trimoxazole, aldosterone antagonists or ARBs. Use such combinations with caution and monitor potassium and renal function.

src.q: Risk factors for the development of hyperkalaemia include those with renal insufficiency, worsening of renal function, age (> 70 years), diabetes mellitus
in particular dehydration, acute cardiac decompensation, metabolic acidosis

or those patients taking other drugs associated with increases in serum potassium (e.g. heparin, co-trimoxazole also known as trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole) and especially aldosterone antagonists or angiotensin-receptor blockers
Potassium-sparing diuretics and angiotensin-receptor blockers should be used with caution in patients receiving ACE inhibitors, and serum potassium and renal function should be monitored.

items.t: Dual RAAS blockade (ACE inhibitor with ARB or aliskiren) not recommended; if absolutely necessary only under specialist supervision with close monitoring. Do not combine an ACE inhibitor and ARB in diabetic nephropathy.

src.q: Dual blockade of RAAS through the combined use of ACE-inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers or aliskiren is therefore not recommended
ACE-inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers should not be used concomitantly in patients with diabetic nephropathy.

items.t: Diabetes on insulin or oral antidiabetics: monitor glycaemic control closely in the first month.

src.q: glycaemic control should be closely monitored during the first month of treatment with an ACE inhibitor

items.t: Hepatic failure (rare): stop if jaundice or marked rise in liver enzymes.

src.q: Patients receiving ACE inhibitors who develop jaundice or marked elevations of hepatic enzymes should discontinue the ACE inhibitor and receive appropriate medical follow-up

items.t: Major surgery or anaesthesia: stop perindopril one day before surgery; correct hypotension with volume expansion.

src.q: The treatment should be discontinued one day prior to the surgery.
If hypotension occurs and is considered to be due to this mechanism, it can be corrected by volume expansion.

items.t: Primary hyperaldosteronism: generally will not respond; not recommended.

src.q: Patients with primary hyperaldosteronism generally will not respond to anti-hypertensive drugs acting through inhibition of the renin-angiotensin system. Therefore, the use of this product is not recommended.

items.t: Lithium and potassium-raising combinations generally not recommended (see interactions).

src.q: The combination of lithium and perindopril is generally not recommended
The combination of perindopril and potassium-sparing drugs, potassium supplements or potassium-containing salt substitutes is generally not recommended

items.t: Persistent dry cough can occur and resolves after stopping.

src.q: Characteristically, the cough is non-productive, persistent and resolves after discontinuation of therapy.

items.t: Anaphylactoid reactions with high-flux dialysis membranes, LDL apheresis with dextran sulfate, and desensitisation (e.g. hymenoptera venom); withhold the ACE inhibitor before each apheresis or desensitisation.

src.q: Anaphylactoid reactions have been reported in patients dialysed with high flux membranes, and treated concomitantly with an ACE inhibitor.
These reactions were avoided by temporarily withholding ACE inhibitor therapy prior to each apheresis.

items.t: Recent kidney transplant: no experience.

src.q: There is no experience regarding the administration of Coversyl Arginine in patients with a recent kidney transplantation.

items.t: Contains lactose: patients with rare hereditary galactose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or total lactase deficiency should not take it.

src.q: Due to the presence of lactose, patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption, or total lactase deficiency should not take this medicinal product.

items.t: Aliskiren, potassium salts, potassium-sparing diuretics (e.g. spironolactone, amiloride), other ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs, heparins, ciclosporin, tacrolimus, trimethoprim, co-trimoxazole: increased risk of hyperkalaemia. Combination not recommended; if needed, use with caution and monitor potassium frequently.

src.q: Some drugs or therapeutic classes may increase the occurrence of hyperkalaemia: aliskiren, potassium salts, potassium-sparing diuretics

potassium-sparing diuretics (e.g. spironolactone, triamterene or amiloride), ACE inhibitors, angiotensin-II receptors antagonists, NSAIDs, heparins, immunosuppressant agents such as ciclosporin or tacrolimus, trimethoprim and cotrimoxazole (trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole)

Therefore, the combination of Coversyl Arginine with the above-mentioned drugs is not recommended. If concomitant use is indicated, they should be used with caution and with frequent monitoring of serum potassium.

items.t: Spironolactone or eplerenone in heart failure (12.5-50 mg/day with low-dose ACE inhibitor): risk of potentially lethal hyperkalaemia. Check for hyperkalaemia and renal impairment before starting; monitor potassium and creatinine weekly in the first month, then monthly. MHRA: use with caution, lowest effective doses, regular potassium and renal monitoring.

src.q: Before initiating the combination, check the absence of hyperkalaemia and renal impairment. A close monitoring of the kalaemia and creatininaemia is recommended in the first month of the treatment once a week at the beginning and, monthly thereafter.
concomitant use of spironolactone with ACEi or ARB increases the risk of severe hyperkalaemia, particularly in patients with marked renal impairment, and should be used with caution
With eplerenone or spironolactone at doses between 12.5 mg to 50 mg by day and with low doses of ACE inhibitors
use the lowest effective doses of spironolactone and ACEi or ARB if coadministration is considered essential

items.t: NSAIDs (including aspirin at anti-inflammatory doses of 3 g/day or more, COX-2 inhibitors): reduced antihypertensive effect; risk of worsening renal function (possible acute renal failure) and raised potassium. Use with caution, especially in the elderly; keep hydrated and consider monitoring renal function.

src.q: Concomitant use of ACE-inhibitors and NSAIDs may lead to an increased risk of worsening of renal function, including possible acute renal failure, and an increase in serum potassium

The combination should be administered with caution, especially in the elderly. Patients should be adequately hydrated and consideration should be given to monitoring renal function after initiation of concomitant therapy, and periodically thereafter.
acetylsalicylic acid at anti-inflammatory dosage regimens, COX-2 inhibitors and non-selective NSAIDs

items.t: ARBs or aliskiren (dual RAAS blockade): more hypotension, hyperkalaemia and renal failure. Not recommended (aliskiren is contraindicated with diabetes or renal impairment: see contraindications).

src.q: is associated with a higher frequency of adverse events such as hypotension, hyperkalaemia and decreased renal function (including acute renal failure) compared to the use of a single RAAS-acting agent
Combination use of medicines from two classes of RAS blocking agents (ACE-inhibitors, ARBs, or aliskiren) is not recommended.

items.t: Sacubitril/valsartan: contraindicated (angioedema); 36-hour gap either way. Racecadotril, mTOR inhibitors and gliptins (e.g. linagliptin, sitagliptin, vildagliptin): higher angioedema risk; take care when starting them in a patient already on an ACE inhibitor.

src.q: Concomitant use of ACE inhibitors with sacubitril/valsartan is contraindicated as this increases the risk of angioedema

Concomitant use of ACE inhibitors with racecadotril, mTOR inhibitors (e.g. sirolimus, everolimus, temsirolimus) and gliptins (e.g. linagliptin, saxagliptin, sitagliptin, vildagliptin) may lead to an increased risk for angioedema

items.t: Antidiabetic medicines (insulins, oral agents): greater glucose lowering with risk of hypoglycaemia, mostly in the first weeks and in renal impairment.

src.q: may cause an increased blood-glucose lowering effect with risk of hypoglycaemia

items.t: Non-potassium-sparing diuretics: excessive fall in blood pressure when perindopril is started; stop the diuretic or start low; monitor creatinine in the first weeks.

src.q: Patients on diuretics, and especially those who are volume and/or salt depleted, may experience excessive reduction in blood pressure after initiation of therapy with an ACE inhibitor.

The possibility of hypotensive effects can be reduced by discontinuation of the diuretic, by increasing volume or salt intake prior to initiating therapy with low and progressive doses of perindopril.
In all cases, renal function (creatinine levels) must be monitored during the first few weeks of ACE inhibitor therapy.

items.t: Other antihypertensives, nitrates and vasodilators, tricyclic antidepressants, antipsychotics, some anaesthetics: further fall in blood pressure. Sympathomimetics may reduce the antihypertensive effect.

src.q: Concomitant use with nitroglycerin and other nitrates, or other vasodilators, may further reduce blood pressure.
Concomitant use of certain anaesthetic medicinal products, tricyclic antidepressants and antipsychotics with ACE inhibitors may result in further reduction of blood pressure
Sympathomimetics may reduce the antihypertensive effects of ACE inhibitors.

items.t: Lithium: not recommended; if needed, monitor lithium levels carefully. Baclofen: increased antihypertensive effect, monitor blood pressure. Estramustine: more angioedema. Injectable gold: rare nitritoid reactions.

src.q: Use of perindopril with lithium is not recommended, but if the combination proves necessary, careful monitoring of serum lithium levels should be performed
Baclofen: Increased antihypertensive effect. Monitor blood pressure and adapt antihypertensive dosage if necessary.
Estramustine: Risk of increased adverse effects such as angioneurotic oedema (angioedema).
Nitritoid reactions (symptoms include facial flushing, nausea, vomiting and hypotension) have been reported rarely in patients on therapy with injectable gold (sodium aurothiomalate)

items.t: Dose by creatinine clearance: 60 mL/min or more - 5 mg daily; above 30 and below 60 mL/min - 2.5 mg daily; above 15 and below 30 mL/min - 2.5 mg every other day; below 15 mL/min on haemodialysis - 2.5 mg on the day of dialysis, taken after dialysis.

src.q: Dosage in patients with renal impairment should be based on creatinine clearance as outlined in table 1 below
ClCR ≥ 60 5 mg per day 30 < ClCR < 60 2.5 mg per day 15 < ClCR < 30 2.5 mg every other day Haemodialysed patients * ClCR < 15 2.5 mg on the day of dialysis
For patients on haemodialysis, the dose should be taken after dialysis.

items.t: SPS: seek specialist advice before starting if eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73 m².

src.q: eGFR less than 30ml/min/1.73m2
Seek specialist advice prior to initiation for patients where there is:

items.t: SPS: some rise in creatinine is expected; a transient fall in renal function should not prompt stopping. Acceptable: creatinine rise under 50% above baseline (if below 266 micromol/L) or eGFR fall under 10% (if eGFR over 25 mL/min/1.73 m²). In CKD: eGFR fall under 25% or creatinine rise under 30% - do not change the dose; eGFR fall over 25% or creatinine rise over 30% - look for other causes (e.g. volume depletion, NSAIDs) and, if none, stop or reduce to the previously tolerated dose.

src.q: A transient decrease in renal function should not prompt stopping ACEI/ARB

An increase in serum creatinine of less than 50% above baseline, as long as it is less than 266 micromol/L, or a decrease in eGFR of less than 10% from baseline, as long as eGFR is over 25 mL/min/1.73 m2, can be considered as acceptable.
Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease eGFR decrease less than 25% or creatinine increase less than 30% from baseline Do not change dose
eGFR decrease more than 25%; creatinine increase more than 30% Investigate other causes of deteriorating renal function, such as volume depletion or concurrent medication such as, NSAIDs.
If no alternative cause is identified: Stop ACEI/ARB or reduce to previously tolerated dose

items.t: No dose adjustment needed in hepatic impairment (in cirrhosis, parent-drug clearance halves but perindoprilat formation is not reduced).

src.q: No dosage adjustment is necessary in patients with hepatic impairment
However, the quantity of perindoprilat formed is not reduced and therefore no dosage adjustment is required

items.t: Rarely ACE inhibitors cause cholestatic jaundice progressing to fulminant hepatic necrosis; stop if jaundice or marked liver enzyme rise.

src.q: Rarely, ACE inhibitors have been associated with a syndrome that starts with cholestatic jaundice and progresses to fulminant hepatic necrosis and (sometimes) death.

items.t: SmPC: not recommended in the first trimester; contraindicated in the second and third trimesters. Do not start in pregnancy; stop as soon as pregnancy is diagnosed and switch if appropriate. If exposed from the second trimester, ultrasound check of fetal renal function and skull; watch the newborn for hypotension.

src.q: The use of ACE inhibitors is not recommended during the first trimester of pregnancy
The use of ACE inhibitors is contra-indicated during the 2nd and 3rd trimester of pregnancy
ACE inhibitors should not be initiated during pregnancy.
When pregnancy is diagnosed, treatment with ACE inhibitors should be stopped immediately, and, if appropriate, alternative therapy should be started.
Should exposure to ACE inhibitor have occurred from the second trimester of pregnancy, ultrasound check of renal function and skull is recommended.

items.t: MHRA: ACE inhibitors should not be used at any stage of pregnancy unless absolutely necessary. On diagnosis of pregnancy, stop as soon as possible.

src.q: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor antagonists should not be used at any stage of pregnancy unless absolutely necessary
On diagnosis of pregnancy, treatment with an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin II receptor antagonist should be stopped as soon as possible

items.t: BUMPS: early-pregnancy use is unlikely to harm the baby; use after about 20 weeks can cause problems in the baby. Extra monitoring of amniotic fluid and fetal growth is needed if continued after about 20 weeks.

src.q: Taking an ACE-I in early pregnancy is unlikely to harm your baby.
Taking an ACE-I after around 20 weeks of pregnancy can cause a number of problems in your baby
If you continue to take an ACE-I after around 20 weeks you will require additional monitoring to assess amniotic fluid levels and your baby's growth and wellbeing.

items.t: SmPC: no information; not recommended. Alternatives with better established safety are preferable, especially with a newborn or preterm infant.

src.q: is not recommended and alternative treatments with better established safety profiles during breast-feeding are preferable, especially while nursing a newborn or preterm infant.

items.t: MHRA (2009): perindopril not recommended in breastfeeding; prefer alternatives, especially with a newborn or preterm baby. Clarification: not absolutely contraindicated; may be prescribed if essential for the mother.

src.q: ramipril, lisinopril, fosinopril, trandolapril, moexipril, or perindopril: use in breastfeeding is not recommended
they are not absolutely contraindicated. Healthcare professionals may prescribe these medicines during breastfeeding if they consider that this treatment is essential for the lactating mother.

items.t: SPS (2023): perindopril can be used with caution; enalapril is preferred. Very long half-life raises the risk of accumulation in the infant (not shown to date). Watch the infant for hypotension (drowsiness, lethargy, pallor, poor feeding, poor weight gain) and, in younger infants, for normal wet nappies.

src.q: Perindopril can be used with caution during breastfeeding, but enalapril is preferred.
Perindopril has a very long half life (30 hours for perindopril and 120 hours for perindoprilat), which increases the risk of drug accumulation in the infant and side-effects.
monitor the infant for hypotension which may manifest as drowsiness, lethargy, pallor, poor feeding and inadequate weight gain
In younger infants, monitor for normal urine production (wet nappies).

items.t: Planning pregnancy: switch to an antihypertensive with an established pregnancy safety profile unless continued ACE inhibitor treatment is essential. No effect on fertility reported.

src.q: Unless continued ACE inhibitor therapy is considered essential, patients planning pregnancy should be changed to alternative antihypertensive treatments which have an established safety profile for use in pregnancy.
Fertility: There was no effect on reproductive performance or fertility.

items.t: Common: dizziness, headache, paraesthesia, vertigo, visual disturbances, tinnitus, hypotension, cough, dyspnoea, abdominal pain, constipation, diarrhoea, taste disturbance, dyspepsia, nausea, vomiting, itching, rash, muscle cramps, asthenia.

src.q: The most frequent adverse events reported in clinical trials and observed with perindopril are: dizziness, headache, paraesthesia, vertigo, visual disturbances, tinnitus, hypotension, cough, dyspnoea
abdominal pain, constipation, diarrhoea, dysgeusia, dyspepsia, nausea, vomiting, pruritus, rash, muscle cramps, and asthenia.

items.t: Angioedema (face, lips, tongue, glottis, larynx; also intestinal): can occur at any time. Stop the ACE inhibitor at once and do not restart. Bradykinin-mediated angioedema may not respond to adrenaline. Airway involvement needs emergency treatment.

src.q: if angioedema is suspected in a patient taking an ACE inhibitor, discontinue the ACE inhibitor immediately and do not restart
bradykinin-mediated angioedema is unlikely to respond to standard anaphylaxis treatments including adrenaline (epinephrine)
Angioedema associated with laryngeal oedema may be fatal.

items.t: Uncommon: hyperkalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, renal insufficiency. Rare: acute renal failure, anuria/oliguria, SIADH.

Renal insufficiency Uncommon Acute renal failure Rare* Anuria/Oliguria Rare*

items.t: Very rare: agranulocytosis or pancytopenia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia; haemolytic anaemia in G6PD deficiency; pancreatitis; hepatitis; erythema multiforme; myocardial infarction or stroke possibly from excessive hypotension in high-risk patients.

Leucopenia/neutropenia Very rare

items.t: SPS baseline: blood pressure, eGFR or serum creatinine, serum potassium, serum sodium. Starting is not normally appropriate if potassium is above 5.0 mmol/L.

Initiation not normally appropriate if pre-treatment potassium greater than 5.0mmol/L

items.t: SPS: seek specialist advice before starting in severe or unstable heart failure, renovascular disease, eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m², sodium below 130 mmol/L, hypovolaemia, systolic BP below 90 mmHg, multiple or high-dose diuretics (equivalent to furosemide 80 mg daily or more), high-dose vasodilator, or haemodynamically significant valve disease.

src.q: Seek specialist advice prior to initiation for patients where there is: severe or unstable heart failure renovascular disease eGFR less than 30ml/min/1.73m2 hyponatraemia (sodium less than 130mmol/L) hypovolaemia hypotension (systolic blood pressure less than 90mmHg)
concomitant multiple or high-dose diuretics (equivalent to 80mg furosemide daily or more) concomitant high-dose vasodilator haemodynamically significant valve disease

items.t: SPS after starting or a dose change: heart failure - renal function, sodium and potassium within 1-2 weeks (5-7 days with other risk factors); hypertension - renal function, sodium, potassium within 1-2 weeks, BP within 1 month.

src.q: Heart failure with other risk factors Within 5 - 7 days
Hypertension Within 1 - 2 weeks Estimated glomerular filtration rate or Serum creatinine (for creatinine clearance) Serum sodium Serum potassium Within 1 month Blood pressure

items.t: SPS once stable: heart failure every 3-6 months; hypertension annually. Repeat at any time if acutely unwell.

src.q: Ongoing once stable Heart failure Every 3 - 6 months
Hypertension Annually Serum sodium Serum potassium
Repeat monitoring at any time patient acutely unwell or their renal function may be compromised.

items.t: SPS abnormal results: potassium 6.0 mmol/L or above in CKD - stop the ACE inhibitor (after stopping other potassium-raising drugs) and seek specialist advice; sodium below 132 mmol/L - specialist advice.

src.q: Value 6.0 mmol/L or above in people with CKD Stop ACEI/ARB after stopping other drugs that may increase potassium and seek specialist advice.
Sodium Value is below 132mmol/L Obtain specialist advice

items.t: Stop if angioedema, jaundice or marked rise in liver enzymes.

src.q: Coversyl Arginine should promptly be discontinued
Patients receiving ACE inhibitors who develop jaundice or marked elevations of hepatic enzymes should discontinue the ACE inhibitor

items.t: Once daily in the morning before a meal (food reduces conversion to the active metabolite).

src.q: Coversyl Arginine is recommended to be taken once daily in the morning before a meal.
As ingestion of food decreases conversion to perindoprilat, hence bioavailability

items.t: Seek urgent help for swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, or trouble breathing or swallowing, even after long use; do not take further doses.

src.q: seek urgent medical attention if you develop swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or experience difficulty breathing or swallowing whilst taking ACE inhibitors
do not take further doses of your ACE inhibitor if angioedema is suspected and inform a healthcare professional immediately

items.t: Planning pregnancy or pregnant: contact the doctor to switch medicine.

src.q: If you find out that you are pregnant whilst taking an ACE-I, you should contact your doctor as soon as possible so that you can be switched to another medicine.

items.t: Low blood pressure reactions (especially at the start) can affect driving or using machines.

src.q: As a result the ability to drive or operate machinery may be impaired.

items.t: Report any sign of infection (e.g. sore throat, fever).

src.q: patients should be instructed to report any sign of infection (e.g. sore throat, fever)

items.t: Avoid potassium salt substitutes unless advised (risk of high potassium).

src.q: The use of potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics, or potassium-containing salt substitutes particularly in patients with impaired renal function may lead to a significant increase in serum potassium.

items.t: Substitution therapy for essential hypertension and/or stable coronary artery disease in patients already controlled on perindopril and amlodipine given together at the same doses.

src.q: Perindopril/Amlodipine is indicated as substitution therapy for treatment of essential hypertension and/or stable coronary artery disease, in patients already controlled with perindopril and amlodipine given concurrently at the same dose level.

items.t: Licensed only as substitution therapy; the fixed-dose combination is not suitable for starting treatment. Dose changes are made by titrating the separate components.

src.q: The fixed dose combination is not suitable for initial therapy.
If the change of the dosage is needed, it should be carried out by individual titration of the free combination's ingredients.

items.t: One tablet once daily, at the strength matching the separate perindopril and amlodipine doses that already control the patient. Not for initial therapy; titrate with the separate components if a dose change is needed. Perindopril strengths depend on the salt: 5 mg and 10 mg arginine (clinic product) match 4 mg and 8 mg tert-butylamine (UK SmPC).
items.tag: Hypertension and/or stable coronary artery disease

src.q: One tablet per day as a single dose, preferably to be taken in the morning and before a meal.
in patients already controlled with perindopril and amlodipine given concurrently at the same dose level.
The fixed dose combination is not suitable for initial therapy.
8 mg perindopril tert-butylamine (equivalent to 10 mg perindopril arginine)

One film-coated tablet contains 3.395 mg perindopril corresponding to 5 mg perindopril arginine.

items.t: Elderly: elimination of perindoprilat is reduced; follow-up includes frequent monitoring of creatinine and potassium. Increase the dose with care.

src.q: Elimination of perindoprilat is decreased in the elderly and in patients with renal failure. Therefore, the usual medical follow-up will include frequent monitoring of creatinine and potassium.
In the elderly increase of the dosage should take place with care

items.t: Should not be used in children and adolescents: efficacy and tolerability not established.

src.q: Perindopril/Amlodipine should not be used in children and adolescents as the efficacy and tolerability of perindopril alone or in combination with amlodipine, have not been established in children and adolescents.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to perindopril or any other ACE inhibitor; history of angioedema with previous ACE inhibitor therapy; hereditary or idiopathic angioedema.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to perindopril or to any other ACE inhibitor.
History of angioedema associated with previous ACE inhibitor therapy.
Hereditary or idiopathic angioedema.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to amlodipine or any other dihydropyridine, or to any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to amlodipine or to any other dihydropyridines
Hypersensitivity to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Second and third trimesters of pregnancy.

src.q: Second and third trimesters of pregnancy (see sections 4.4 and 4.6).

items.t: With sacubitril/valsartan; do not start within 36 hours of the last sacubitril/valsartan dose. With aliskiren-containing products in diabetes or renal impairment (GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m²).

src.q: Concomitant use with sacubitril/valsartan therapy.
must not be initiated earlier than 36 hours after the last dose of sacubitril/valsartan
The concomitant use of Perindopril/Amlodipine with aliskiren-containing products is contraindicated in patients with diabetes mellitus or renal impairment (GFR < 60 ml/min/1.73 m2)

items.t: Extracorporeal treatments bringing blood into contact with negatively charged surfaces (e.g. some high-flux dialysis membranes, LDL apheresis with dextran sulphate).

src.q: Extracorporeal treatments leading to contact of blood with negatively charged surfaces (see section 4.5).

items.t: Significant bilateral renal artery stenosis or stenosis of the artery to a single functioning kidney.

src.q: Significant bilateral renal artery stenosis or stenosis of the artery to a single functioning kidney (see section 4.4).

items.t: Severe hypotension; shock, including cardiogenic shock; left ventricular outflow obstruction (e.g. high-grade aortic stenosis); haemodynamically unstable heart failure after acute myocardial infarction.

src.q: Severe hypotension, - Hypersensitivity to amlodipine

Shock, including cardiogenic shock, - Obstruction of the outflow-tract of the left ventricle (e.g. high grade aortic stenosis), - Haemodynamically unstable heart failure after acute myocardial infarction.

items.t: Angioedema (face, lips, tongue, glottis, larynx; also intestinal) can occur at any time. Stop promptly and monitor until full resolution; airway involvement needs emergency treatment. Higher rate in black patients.

src.q: This may occur at any time during therapy
Perindopril/Amlodipine should promptly be discontinued and appropriate monitoring should be initiated and continued until complete resolution of symptoms has occurred.
Where there is involvement of the tongue, glottis or larynx, likely to cause airway obstruction, emergency therapy should be administered promptly.
ACE inhibitors cause a higher rate of angioedema in black patients than in non-black patients.

items.t: History of angioedema not caused by an ACE inhibitor: may be at higher risk on an ACE inhibitor.

src.q: Patients with a history of angioedema unrelated to ACE inhibitor therapy may be at increased risk of angioedema while receiving an ACE inhibitor

items.t: Symptomatic hypotension more likely with volume depletion (diuretics, salt restriction, dialysis, diarrhoea, vomiting) or severe renin-dependent hypertension; monitor BP, renal function and potassium closely in those at risk, including ischaemic heart or cerebrovascular disease.

src.q: is more likely to occur in patients who have been volume-depleted e.g. by diuretic therapy, dietary salt restriction, dialysis, diarrhoea or vomiting, or who have severe renin-dependent hypertension
In patients at high risk of symptomatic hypotension, blood pressure, renal function and serum potassium should be monitored closely during treatment with Perindopril/Amlodipine.

Similar considerations apply to patients with ischaemic heart or cerebrovascular disease in whom an excessive fall in blood pressure could result in a myocardial infarction or cerebrovascular accident.

items.t: Mitral stenosis, aortic stenosis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: give with caution.

src.q: perindopril should be given with caution to patients with mitral valve stenosis and obstruction in the outflow of the left ventricle such as aortic stenosis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

items.t: Heart failure: treat with caution; calcium channel blockers may increase the risk of future cardiovascular events and mortality in congestive heart failure.

src.q: Patients with heart failure should be treated with caution.
Calcium channel blockers, including amlodipine, should be used with caution in patients with congestive heart failure, as they may increase the risk of future cardiovascular events and mortality.

items.t: Hyperkalaemia risk with renal impairment, age over 70, diabetes, dehydration, acute cardiac decompensation, metabolic acidosis, potassium supplements or salt substitutes, potassium-sparing diuretics, heparin, trimethoprim/co-trimoxazole, aldosterone antagonists or ARBs. Use potassium-sparing diuretics and ARBs with caution and monitor potassium and renal function.

src.q: Hyperkalaemia can cause serious, sometimes fatal arrhythmias.
Potassium-sparing diuretics and angiotensin-receptor blockers should be used with caution in patients receiving ACE inhibitors, and serum potassium and renal function should be monitored

items.t: Dual RAAS blockade (ACE inhibitor with ARB or aliskiren) not recommended; if absolutely necessary, only under specialist supervision with frequent monitoring. Do not combine an ACE inhibitor and ARB in diabetic nephropathy.

src.q: Dual blockade of RAAS through the combined use of ACEinhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers or aliskiren is therefore not recommended

If dual blockade therapy is considered absolutely necessary, this should only occur under specialist supervision and subject to frequent close monitoring of renal function, electrolytes and blood pressure.
ACE-inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers should not be used concomitantly in patients with diabetic nephropathy.

items.t: Neutropenia/agranulocytosis: extreme caution in collagen vascular disease, immunosuppressant therapy, allopurinol or procainamide, especially with renal impairment; check white cell counts periodically.

src.q: Perindopril should be used with extreme caution in patients with collagen vascular disease, immunosuppressant therapy, treatment with allopurinol or procainamide
periodic monitoring of white blood cell counts is advised and patients should be instructed to report any sign of infection (e.g. sore throat, fever).

items.t: Diabetes on insulin or oral antidiabetics: monitor glycaemic control closely in the first month.

src.q: In diabetic patients treated with oral antidiabetic agents or insulin, glycaemic control should be closely monitored during the first month of treatment with an ACE inhibitor

items.t: Hepatic impairment: amlodipine half-life and exposure rise; no dose recommendation, so use with caution. Hepatic failure linked to ACE inhibitors (rare): stop if jaundice or marked liver enzyme rise.

src.q: The half life of amlodipine is prolonged and AUC values are higher in patients with impaired liver function; dosage recommendations have not been established.
Patients receiving ACE inhibitors who develop jaundice or marked elevations of hepatic enzymes should discontinue the ACE inhibitor and receive appropriate medical follow-up

items.t: Primary hyperaldosteronism: generally no response; use not recommended.

src.q: Patients with primary hyperaldosteronism generally will not respond to anti-hypertensive drugs acting through inhibition of the renin-angiotensin system. Therefore, the use of this product is not recommended.

items.t: Major surgery or anaesthesia: stop treatment one day before surgery; correct any hypotension with volume expansion.

src.q: The treatment should be discontinued one day prior to the surgery.
If hypotension occurs and is considered to be due to this mechanism, it can be corrected by volume expansion.

items.t: Anaphylactoid reactions during LDL apheresis with dextran sulphate or desensitisation (e.g. hymenoptera venom); avoided by temporarily withholding the ACE inhibitor.

src.q: These reactions were avoided by temporarily withholding ACE inhibitor therapy prior to each apheresis.
Patients receiving ACE inhibitors during desensitisation treatment (e.g. hymenoptera venom) have experienced anaphylactoid reactions.

items.t: Persistent dry cough can occur and resolves after stopping.

src.q: Characteristically, the cough is nonproductive, persistent and resolves after discontinuation of therapy.

items.t: Safety and efficacy of amlodipine in hypertensive crisis not established.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of amlodipine in hypertensive crisis has not been established.

items.t: Potassium-sparing diuretics (e.g. spironolactone, amiloride), potassium supplements, potassium salt substitutes, trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole: risk of significant (potentially lethal) hyperkalaemia. Combination not recommended; if needed, use with caution and monitor potassium frequently.

src.q: Potassium sparing diuretics (e.g. spironolactone, triamterene, or amiloride), potassium supplements, or potassium-containing salt substitutes may lead to significant increases in serum potassium.

Therefore, the combination of perindopril with the above-mentioned drugs is not recommended. If concomitant use is indicated, they should be used with caution and with frequent monitoring of serum potassium.

items.t: Spironolactone (12.5-50 mg/day) in heart failure with low-dose ACE inhibitor: potentially lethal hyperkalaemia. Check no hyperkalaemia or renal impairment first; monitor potassium and creatinine weekly in the first month, then monthly.

src.q: Before initiating the combination, check the absence of hyperkalaemia and renal impairment.
A close monitoring of the kalaemia and creatinemia is recommended in the first month of the treatment once a week at the beginning and, monthly thereafter.

items.t: ARBs or aliskiren (dual RAAS blockade): more hypotension, hyperkalaemia and renal failure. Not recommended; aliskiren contraindicated in diabetes or renal impairment.

src.q: Dual blockade of RAAS through the combined use of ACEinhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers or aliskiren is therefore not recommended
Combination use of medicines from two classes of RAS blocking agents (ACE-inhibitors, ARBs, or aliskiren) is not recommended.

items.t: NSAIDs (including COX-2 inhibitors and aspirin at anti-inflammatory doses of 3 g/day or more): reduced antihypertensive effect; risk of worsening renal function including acute renal failure, and raised potassium. Use with caution (especially elderly), keep hydrated, consider monitoring renal function.

src.q: Concomitant use of ACE-inhibitors and NSAIDs may lead to an increased risk of worsening of renal function, including possible acute renal failure, and an increase in serum potassium
The combination should be administered with caution, especially in the elderly.

items.t: Strong or moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors (protease inhibitors, azole antifungals, erythromycin, clarithromycin, verapamil, diltiazem): amlodipine exposure may rise significantly, with hypotension risk (more so in the elderly); clinical monitoring and dose adjustment may be needed. CYP3A4 inducers (e.g. rifampicin, St John's wort): monitor blood pressure and consider dose adjustment during and after use.

src.q: Concomitant use of amlodipine with strong or moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors (protease inhibitors, azole antifungals, macrolides like erythromycin or clarithromycin, verapamil or diltiazem) may give rise to significant increase in amlodipine exposure resulting in an increased risk of hypotension.
The clinical translation of these PK variations may be more pronounced in the elderly.
Clinical monitoring and dose adjustment may thus be required.
blood pressure should be monitored and dose regulation considered both during and after concomitant medication particularly with strong CYP3A4 inducers (e.g. rifampicin, hypericum perforatum).

items.t: Simvastatin: limit simvastatin to 20 mg daily with amlodipine.

src.q: Limit the dose of simvastatin in patients on amlodipine to 20 mg daily.

items.t: Antidiabetic medicines (insulin, oral agents): greater glucose lowering with risk of hypoglycaemia, mostly in the first weeks and in renal impairment.

src.q: may cause an increased blood-glucose lowering effect with risk of hypoglycaemia

items.t: Racecadotril and gliptins (linagliptin, sitagliptin, vildagliptin): higher angioedema risk; take care when starting them in a patient on an ACE inhibitor. Sacubitril/valsartan: contraindicated.

src.q: This risk may be elevated when used concomitantly with racecadotril
Increased risk of angio-oedema, due to dipeptidyl peptidase IV (DPP-IV) decreased activity by the gliptine, in patients co-treated with an ACE inhibitor.

items.t: Diuretics: excessive BP fall when starting, especially if volume/salt depleted; stop the diuretic first or start low, and monitor creatinine in the first weeks. Nitrates, other antihypertensives, alpha-blockers, tricyclic antidepressants: additive hypotension; corticosteroids and sympathomimetics: reduced antihypertensive effect.

src.q: In all cases, renal function (creatinine levels) must be monitored during the first few weeks of ACE inhibitor therapy.
Concomitant use with nitroglycerine and other nitrates or other vasodilators, may further reduce blood pressure and therefore should be considered with caution.
Sympathomimetics may reduce the antihypertensive effects of ACE inhibitors.

items.t: Lithium: not recommended; if needed, monitor lithium levels. Ciclosporin, heparin: monitor potassium. Tacrolimus: monitor levels. Dantrolene infusion: avoid. Grapefruit juice: not recommended.

src.q: The combination of perindopril with lithium is not recommended.
Administration of amlodipine with grapefruit or grapefruit juice is not recommended

items.t: Can be used if CrCl is 60 mL/min or more; not suitable if CrCl is below 60 mL/min (titrate the separate components instead). Monitor creatinine and potassium frequently.

src.q: Perindopril/Amlodipine can be administered in patients with Clcr ≥ 60 ml/min, and is not suitable for patients with Clcr < 60 ml/min. In these patients, an individual dose titration with the monocomponents is recommended.
Therefore, the usual medical follow-up will include frequent monitoring of creatinine and potassium.

items.t: Amlodipine plasma levels are not related to the degree of renal impairment; amlodipine is not dialysable.

src.q: Changes in amlodipine plasma concentrations are not correlated with degree of renal impairment.
Amlodipine is not dialysable.

items.t: SPS (ACE inhibitors): seek specialist advice before starting if eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73 m². Some creatinine rise is expected; if eGFR falls over 25% or creatinine rises over 30% in CKD with no other cause, stop or reduce to the previously tolerated dose.

src.q: Seek specialist advice prior to initiation for patients where there is: severe or unstable heart failure renovascular disease eGFR less than 30ml/min/1.73m2
Some increase in serum creatinine and potassium levels is expected after starting or increasing the dose of an ACEI or ARB.
eGFR decrease more than 25%; creatinine increase more than 30%
If no alternative cause is identified: Stop ACEI/ARB or reduce to previously tolerated dose

items.t: No dose regimen established; use with caution. Find the dose by titrating the separate perindopril and amlodipine components. Severe hepatic impairment: start amlodipine at the lowest dose and titrate slowly.

src.q: A dosage regimen for patients with hepatic impairment has not been established. Therefore, Perindopril/Amlodipine should be administered with caution.
the patients should be individually titrated using the free combination of amlodipine and perindopril.
Amlodipine should be initiated at the lowest dose and titrated slowly in patients with severe hepatic impairment.

items.t: Cirrhosis: hepatic clearance of perindopril halves but perindoprilat formation is not reduced (no perindopril adjustment needed). Amlodipine exposure rises about 40-60%.

src.q: However, the quantity of perindoprilat formed is not reduced and therefore no dosage adjustment is required
Patients with hepatic insufficiency have decreased clearance of amlodipine resulting in a longer half-life and an increase in AUC of approximately 40-60%.

items.t: SmPC: not recommended in the first trimester; contraindicated in the second and third trimesters. Stop as soon as pregnancy is diagnosed and switch if appropriate. If exposed from the second trimester, ultrasound check of fetal renal function and skull; watch the newborn for hypotension.

src.q: Perindopril/Amlodipine is not recommended during the first trimester of pregnancy. Perindopril/Amlodipine is contraindicated during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy.
When pregnancy is diagnosed, treatment with ACE inhibitors should be stopped immediately, and, if appropriate, alternative therapy should be started.
Should exposure to ACE inhibitor have occurred from the second trimester of pregnancy, ultrasound check of renal function and skull is recommended.

items.t: MHRA: ACE inhibitors should not be used at any stage of pregnancy unless absolutely necessary; on diagnosis of pregnancy, stop as soon as possible.

src.q: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor antagonists should not be used at any stage of pregnancy unless absolutely necessary
On diagnosis of pregnancy, treatment with an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin II receptor antagonist should be stopped as soon as possible

items.t: BUMPS (ACE inhibitors): early-pregnancy use is unlikely to harm the baby; use after about 20 weeks can cause several problems in the baby, and continued use needs extra monitoring of amniotic fluid and growth.

src.q: Taking an ACE-I in early pregnancy is unlikely to harm your baby.
Taking an ACE-I after around 20 weeks of pregnancy can cause a number of problems in your baby
If you continue to take an ACE-I after around 20 weeks you will require additional monitoring to assess amniotic fluid levels and your baby's growth and wellbeing.

items.t: Amlodipine component: safety in pregnancy not established; possible prolonged delivery. BUMPS: no clear risks from calcium channel blockers in pregnancy.

src.q: The safety of amlodipine in human pregnancy has not been established.
However, there may be a risk of prolonged delivery.
There are no clear risks of taking a calcium channel blocker in pregnancy.

items.t: SmPC: not recommended during breastfeeding; decide whether to stop breastfeeding or stop treatment. Alternatives with better established safety are preferable, especially with a newborn or preterm infant. Amlodipine passes into milk (infant dose estimated 3-7%, maximum 15%).

src.q: Perindopril/Amlodipine is not recommended during lactation.
alternative treatments with better established safety profiles during breast-feeding are preferable, especially while nursing a newborn or preterm infant.
The proportion of the maternal dose received by the infant has been estimated with an interquartile range of 3-7%, with a maximum of 15%.

items.t: MHRA (2009): perindopril not recommended in breastfeeding. Clarification: not absolutely contraindicated; may be prescribed if essential for the mother.

src.q: ramipril, lisinopril, fosinopril, trandolapril, moexipril, or perindopril: use in breastfeeding is not recommended
they are not absolutely contraindicated. Healthcare professionals may prescribe these medicines during breastfeeding if they consider that this treatment is essential for the lactating mother.

items.t: SPS: perindopril and amlodipine can each be used with caution (enalapril is the preferred ACE inhibitor; nifedipine the preferred dihydropyridine). Watch the infant for hypotension (drowsiness, lethargy, pallor, poor feeding, poor weight gain). Advice applies to full-term healthy infants.

src.q: Perindopril can be used with caution during breastfeeding, but enalapril is preferred.
Amlodipine is excreted into breast milk usually in very small amounts. It can be used with caution during breastfeeding, but nifedipine is the preferred dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker.
As a precaution, monitor the infant for hypotension which may manifest as drowsiness, lethargy, looking pale , poor feeding and inadequate weight gain.
Recommendations apply to full term and healthy infants only.

items.t: Planning pregnancy: switch to an antihypertensive with an established pregnancy safety profile unless continued ACE inhibitor treatment is essential.

src.q: Unless continued ACE inhibitor therapy is considered essential, patients planning pregnancy should be changed to alternative antihypertensive treatments which have an established safety profile for use in pregnancy.

items.t: Calcium channel blockers have caused reversible biochemical changes in sperm heads; clinical data on amlodipine and fertility are insufficient. No effect of perindopril on fertility.

src.q: Reversible biochemical changes in the head of spermatozoa have been reported in some patients treated by calcium channel blockers.
There was no effect on reproductive performance or fertility.

items.t: Very common: oedema (amlodipine). Common: somnolence, dizziness, headache, dysgeusia, paraesthesia, visual impairment, tinnitus, vertigo, palpitations, flushing, hypotension, dyspnoea, cough, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, dyspepsia, diarrhoea, constipation, pruritus, rash, ankle swelling, muscle cramps, fatigue, asthenia.

src.q: Oedema Very common

The most commonly reported adverse reactions with perindopril and amlodipine given separately are: oedema, somnolence, dizziness, headache (especially at the beginning of the treatment), dysgeusia, paraesthesia, visual impairment (including diplopia), tinnitus, vertigo, palpitations, flushing

hypotension (and effects related to hypotension), dyspnoea, cough, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, dyspepsia, change of bowel habit, diarrheoa, constipation, prurit, rash, exanthema, joint swelling (ankle swelling), muscle spasms, fatigue, asthenia.

items.t: Angioedema (face, lips, tongue, glottis, larynx; also intestinal): can occur at any time. Stop the ACE inhibitor at once and do not restart. Bradykinin-mediated angioedema may not respond to adrenaline. Airway involvement needs emergency treatment.

src.q: if angioedema is suspected in a patient taking an ACE inhibitor, discontinue the ACE inhibitor immediately and do not restart
bradykinin-mediated angioedema is unlikely to respond to standard anaphylaxis treatments including adrenaline (epinephrine)
Angioedema associated with laryngeal oedema may be fatal.

items.t: Hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia (uncommon); acute renal failure (rare); SIADH (rare).

Renal failure acute - Rare

items.t: Very rare: agranulocytosis/pancytopenia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia; myocardial infarction or stroke possibly from excessive hypotension; pancreatitis; hepatitis; Stevens-Johnson syndrome; toxic epidermal necrolysis (not known).

src.q: Agranulocytosis or pancytopenia (see section 4.4) - Very rare
Pancreatitis Very rare Very rare

Toxic epidermal necrolysis Not known

items.t: SmPC: frequent monitoring of creatinine and potassium (perindoprilat elimination is reduced in the elderly and in renal failure). In those at high risk of hypotension, monitor blood pressure, renal function and potassium closely.

src.q: Therefore, the usual medical follow-up will include frequent monitoring of creatinine and potassium.
In patients at high risk of symptomatic hypotension, blood pressure, renal function and serum potassium should be monitored closely during treatment with Perindopril/Amlodipine.
