In patients with hypertension, it should be remembered that correction of hypokalaemia may lower blood pressure.

items.t: Excipients: the effervescent tablets (sucrose) and the oral solution (sorbitol) should not be taken in hereditary fructose intolerance; the oral solution contains E122 and parabens (may cause allergic reactions).

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take this medicine.
Patients with hereditary fructose intolerance (HFI) should not take/be given this medicine.

items.t: ACE inhibitors (e.g. lisinopril): risk of hyperkalaemia; use with caution. Lisinopril SmPC: combination with potassium supplements is not recommended; if needed, use with caution and frequent serum potassium monitoring.

src.q: If co-administered with potassium-sparing diuretics and ACE-inhibitors, the risk of hyperkalaemia must be considered.
Therefore, the combination of Lisinopril tablet with the above-mentioned drugs is not recommended.
If concomitant use is indicated, they should be used with caution and with frequent monitoring of serum potassium.

items.t: Potassium-sparing diuretics and aldosterone antagonists (e.g. spironolactone): risk of hyperkalaemia. Spironolactone SmPC: potassium supplements should not be given routinely with spironolactone.

src.q: Hyperkalaemia can result from the concurrent use of potassium supplements with ACE inhibitors, aldosterone antagonists, angiotensin II receptor antagonists, ciclosporin, potassium sparing diuretics and tacrolimus.
potassium supplements should not be given routinely with Aldactone as hyperkalaemia may be induced

items.t: Trimethoprim SmPC: potassium supplements with trimethoprim may significantly raise serum potassium; monitor potassium as appropriate.

src.q: Concomitant use of drugs that may increase serum potassium levels may lead to a significant increase in serum potassium.
Monitoring of potassium should be undertaken as appropriate

items.t: Co-trimoxazole SmPC: co-trimoxazole may cause clinically relevant hyperkalaemia; use caution with other drugs that can cause hyperkalaemia. Oral solution SmPC: use potassium supplements with caution with medicines that may raise plasma potassium.

src.q: Hyperkalaemia: caution should be exercised in patients taking any other drugs that can cause hyperkalaemia
Concomitant use of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole) may result in clinically relevant hyperkalaemia.
Potassium supplements should be used with caution in patients who are receiving medications that may increase plasma potassium levels.

items.t: The effervescent tablets contain potassium bicarbonate. Ferrous sulfate SmPCs say bicarbonate-containing compounds may reduce iron absorption: separate by at least 2 hours.

src.q: Each tablet contains 600 mg potassium chloride and 400 mg potassium bicarbonate.
Administration of iron preparations with such compounds should be separated by at least 2 hours.

items.t: Other drugs that raise potassium (angiotensin II receptor antagonists, ciclosporin, tacrolimus, digoxin overdose) increase hyperkalaemia risk; renal impairment increases it further.

src.q: Potassium supplements should be used with caution in patients who are receiving medications that may increase plasma potassium levels.
The incidence of hyperkalaemia is increased by renal impairment.

items.t: Contraindicated in severe renal impairment with oliguria (effervescent tablet SmPC) / advanced severe renal failure or impaired renal function with oliguria (oral solution SmPC). No eGFR/CrCl thresholds given.

src.q: Severe renal impairment with oliguria
Advanced, severe renal failure or impaired renal function with oliguria

items.t: Other renal impairment: avoid excess dosing (effervescent tablet SmPC); extreme caution (oral solution SmPC); lower doses may be needed (SPS).

src.q: Care should be taken to avoid dosage in excess of requirements for patients with impaired renal function.
Potassium salts should only be administered with extreme caution to patients with renal dysfunction or hepatic disease
Lower doses may be required in renal impairment due to the risk of hyperkalaemia.

items.t: Oral solution SmPC: give only with extreme caution in hepatic disease (hyperkalaemia risk). Potassium depletion may persist in hepatic ascites.

src.q: Potassium salts should only be administered with extreme caution to patients with renal dysfunction or hepatic disease because of the risk of hyperkalaemia.
Some patients may develop potassium depletion despite the use of potassium supplements particularly in digitalised patients, or those with hepatic ascites.

items.t: Effervescent tablet SmPC: no clinical problems reported; weigh benefit against risk before use in pregnancy.

src.q: No clinical problems have been encountered during pregnancy and lactation.
the benefit of treatment should be considered in relation to the risks before this medicinal product is given to pregnant or nursing women

items.t: Oral solution SmPC: should not be used in pregnancy unless considered essential by the physician.

src.q: should not be used during pregnancy or by nursing women unless considered essential by the physician

items.t: Effervescent tablet SmPC: weigh benefit against risk before giving to nursing women.

src.q: the benefit of treatment should be considered in relation to the risks before this medicinal product is given to pregnant or nursing women

items.t: Oral solution SmPC: should not be used by nursing women unless considered essential. No SPS breastfeeding page for potassium chloride was found.

src.q: should not be used during pregnancy or by nursing women unless considered essential by the physician

reproductive.note: No fertility or contraception statements in the effervescent tablet or oral solution SmPCs.

items.t: Abdominal discomfort, diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting may occur (frequency not stated). Give with or after food if there is gastric irritation.

src.q: Abdominal discomfort, diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting may occur.

items.t: Oral solution SmPC: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and abdominal cramps occur rarely.

src.q: In rare cases, oral potassium may invoke nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and abdominal cramps.

items.t: GI ulceration or obstruction: symptoms or signs are a reason to stop treatment.

src.q: Symptoms or signs suggesting ulceration or obstruction should be regarded as reasons to discontinue medication.

items.t: Hyperkalaemia (may be silent; paraesthesia, weakness, confusion, paralysis, hypotension, arrhythmias, heart block, cardiac arrest). ECG changes start with tall peaked T waves.

src.q: Hyperkalaemic symptoms include paraesthesia of the extremities, listlessness, mental confusion, weakness, paralysis, hypotension, cardiac arrhythmias, heart block and cardiac arrest.
Hyperkalaemia is often asymptomatic.

items.t: During replacement: periodic clinical review, serum electrolytes and ECG, especially with cardiac disease or digitalis.

src.q: Periodic evaluation of the patient's clinical status, serum electrolytes and the ECG should be carried out when replacement therapy is undertaken.

items.t: Serum potassium monitoring is particularly needed with renal or cardiac disease, especially in the elderly (oral solution SmPC).

src.q: Monitoring of serum potassium is particularly necessary in patients with renal or cardiac diseases, especially the elderly.

items.t: SPS: monitor serum potassium, serum magnesium and renal function during replacement.

src.q: The monitoring parameters during potassium replacement should include: serum potassium serum magnesium renal function

items.t: Stop if symptoms or signs of GI ulceration or obstruction appear.

src.q: Symptoms or signs suggesting ulceration or obstruction should be regarded as reasons to discontinue medication.

items.t: Dissolve the effervescent tablet in water before taking; may be taken with food. Give with or after food if there is gastric irritation.

src.q: Oral administration, after dissolution of the tablet in water. May be taken with food if preferred.
should be given with or after food

items.t: Take the syrup after food, in divided amounts; use a graduated dropper for children.

src.q: in divided amounts after food
The dose should be administered using a graduated dropper.

items.t: SPS: give oral potassium with or after food; large doses are limited by nausea and vomiting.

src.q: Oral potassium should be given with or after food.
large doses are limited by nausea and vomiting

items.t: Take with or after food; dissolve effervescent tablets fully in water.

src.q: Oral administration, after dissolution of the tablet in water.
Oral potassium should be given with or after food.

items.t: Report difficulty swallowing, chest or stomach pain, black stools or vomiting blood (possible GI ulceration).

src.q: may induce ulceration, haemorrhage or stricture formation in the gastrointestinal tract

items.t: Do not use potassium-containing salt substitutes without advice when taking ACE inhibitors or potassium-sparing diuretics (named in the lisinopril SmPC).

src.q: Use of potassium sparing diuretics (e.g. spironolactone, triamterene or amiloride), potassium supplements or potassium-containing salt substitutes, particularly in patients with impaired renal function, may lead to a significant increase in serum potassium.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction stated in the two UK SPCs (5% cream, 2.5% cutaneous spray powder) accessed; no MHRA Drug Safety Update, SPS or BUMPS page on topical povidone-iodine was found.

items.t: Cream (UK): clean and dry the wound; apply a small pea-sized amount once or twice daily for up to 7 consecutive days. The daily application must not cover more than 1% of total body surface area. Adult maximum: 8 to 9 pea-sized amounts twice a day.

src.q: Apply a small pea sized amount to the affected area (once or twice daily) up to a maximum of 7 consecutive days.
The maximum daily application should not exceed over 1% of the total body surface area.
Adults 8-9 small pea sized amount twice a day

items.t: Spray powder: adults and children over 2 years: clean the wound, spray evenly for 3 seconds from 15 cm, once or twice a day for up to 7 consecutive days.

src.q: Spray evenly onto the wound area for three (3) seconds from a distance of 15 cm (6 inches).
Apply the spray once or twice a day for up to 7 consecutive days.

items.t: Contraindicated in children under 1 year.

src.q: Children below the age of 1.
Children below the age of 1 year.

In infants and children 1-2 years of age, Betadine Cutaneous spray, powder should only be used after evaluation of risks and benefits by healthcare professional.

items.t: Cream maximum amounts by age: 2 to 6 years 1 to 2 pea-sized amounts a day; 7 to 8 years 2 twice a day; 9 to 12 years 3 twice a day; 13 to 18 years 5 twice a day.

Children 7-8 years 2 small pea sized amount twice a day

src.q: Hypersensitivity to iodine or povidone or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.
Hypersensitivity to iodine or povidone or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

src.q: Thyroid dysfunction.
Thyroid dysfunction.

items.t: During radioiodine scans or radioiodine treatment; allow at least 4 weeks before or after these.

src.q: During radioiodine scintigraphy or radioiodine treatment.
An interval of at least 4 weeks is required prior to or after radioiodine investigations/treatments

items.t: Do not use with mercury-containing products (a substance that damages the skin can form).

src.q: Products containing mercury should not be used concomitantly due to formation of a substance which can damage the skin.

Children below the age of 1 year.

items.t: Large amounts absorbed (e.g. treating burns) may cause electrolyte imbalance, metabolic acidosis, abnormal blood osmolarity and acute renal failure.

src.q: May occur following uptake of large amounts of povidone iodine (e.g. in the treatment of burns)
Electrolyte imbalance ** Metabolic acidosis **

items.t: Thyroid: hyperthyroidism may follow notable iodine uptake in people with past thyroid disease; hypothyroidism may follow prolonged or extensive use.

src.q: In patients with a history of thyroid disease
Hypothyroidism following prolonged or extensive use of povidone iodine

items.t: Fire risk: fabric that has been in contact with the cream burns more easily (no smoking or naked flames); the spray propellant is flammable, and electrocautery should wait until the spray mist has gone.

src.q: Do not smoke or go near naked flames - risk of severe burns.
that has been in contact with this product burns more easily and is a serious fire hazard
The propellant gases are flammable, keep away from heat, hot surfaces, sparks, open flames.
Electrocautery should only be used after spray mist has completely vanished.

items.t: Silver-containing products (such as silver sulfadiazine), hydrogen peroxide and taurolidine: mutual reduction of effect; the SPCs say povidone-iodine should not be used together with silver salts.

src.q: Products containing mercury, silver, hydrogen peroxide, and taurolidine may interact with povidone-iodine and cause mutual reduction of effects.
Povidone-iodine should not be used together with alkali, hydrogen peroxide, taurolidine, tannic acid, and silver and mercury salts.
Povidone-Iodine should not be used together with alkali, hydrogen peroxide, taurolidine, tannic acid, and silver and mercury salts.

items.t: Lithium: avoid prolonged use, especially on large areas, as more iodine may be absorbed (spray SPC). Lithium is not in this checker's medicine list.

src.q: Prolonged use, especially on extensive surfaces, should be avoided in patients undergoing lithium therapy as larger amounts of iodine may be absorbed.

items.t: Thyroid tests and radioiodine: iodine absorption can lower thyroid radioiodine uptake and interfere with thyroid scans, protein-bound iodine tests and radioiodine therapy. Allow 4 weeks after treatment before a new scan.

src.q: Absorption of iodine from povidone iodine cream may lower the radioiodine uptake of the thyroid.
After the end of the treatment, 4 weeks should be allowed before a new scintigram is carried out

items.t: Enzymatic wound preparations: both are weakened. Octenidine before or after: transient dark skin discoloration. Lab tests (toluidine, guaiac for blood or glucose in stool or urine) may give false positives.

src.q: The concomitant use of wound-treatment preparations containing enzymatic components leads to a weakening effect of both substances.
Povidone-iodine products when used before or after application of octenidine may lead to transient dark discolorations at the application sites.
various diagnostic agents can show false-positive lab results

items.t: No renal dose advice in the UK SPCs. Acute renal failure may occur after uptake of large amounts (e.g. treating burns).

src.q: May occur following uptake of large amounts of povidone iodine (e.g. in the treatment of burns)
Acute renal failure**, Blood osmolarity abnormal **

hepatic.note: No hepatic impairment statement in the two UK SPCs (5% cream, 2.5% cutaneous spray powder) accessed.

items.t: Insufficient data. Absorbed iodine crosses the placenta. Use only if the clinical condition requires it and only if clearly necessary, after a benefit/risk assessment.

src.q: There is insufficient data on the use of povidone iodine during pregnancy.
Absorbed iodine has been shown to cross the placental barrier
should only be used if the clinical condition of the woman requires treatment with povidone iodine
povidone-iodine should only be administered if clearly necessary

items.t: Should not be used during breastfeeding: iodine concentrates in breast milk and may cause transient hypothyroidism with raised TSH in the newborn; the baby's thyroid function may need checking.

src.q: Betadine Cream should not be used during breastfeeding.
Absorbed iodine is excreted in breast milk to such an extent that effects on breastfed newborns are likely.
may induce transient hypothyroidism with elevation of TSH (thyroid stimulating hormone) in the newborn
a check of the child's thyroid function may be necessary

items.t: The same SPCs (section 4.4) also allow use when breastfeeding only if clearly necessary after a benefit/risk assessment, on a doctor's advice.

src.q: if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, unless advised to do so by your doctor
Special caution is needed in pregnant and breast-feeding women.

items.t: No data on fertility.

src.q: There are no data on the effects of povidone iodine on fertility.

items.t: No common or very common effects listed. Rare: hypersensitivity and contact dermatitis (redness, small blisters, itching). Skin discoloration at the site (frequency not known).

src.q: Rare Contact dermatitis (with symptoms such as erythema, small blisters and pruritus)
Povidone-iodine use could lead to transient skin discolouration at the application site

items.t: Very rare anaphylaxis and angioedema.

Very rare Angioedema

items.t: Very rare hyperthyroidism (fast heart rate, restlessness) in people with past thyroid disease; hypothyroidism after prolonged or extensive use.

Hypothyroidism following prolonged or extensive use of povidone iodine

items.t: After large amounts (e.g. burns): electrolyte imbalance, metabolic acidosis, acute renal failure.

Acute renal failure**, Blood osmolarity abnormal **

src.q: Clean and dry the wound area before application.
If required, a dressing or bandage can be applied.
For external use only.

items.t: Spray: shake the inverted can for 5 seconds; use in a well-ventilated area; do not inhale or spray into or around the eyes; clean the nozzle after use.

src.q: Shake the can well in inverted orientation for 5 seconds before each use.
Spray in a well-ventilated area.
do not inhale the spray and do not spray into the eyes or on areas around the eyes

src.q: Povidone-iodine use could lead to transient skin discolouration at the application site

items.t: Do not use if pregnant or breastfeeding, or in children under 2 years, unless a doctor advises it.

src.q: Do not use in Children less than 2 years old, or if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, unless advised to do so by your doctor.

items.t: Conditions likely to benefit from short- or long-term glucocorticoid therapy, e.g. severe allergy and asthma, collagen and rheumatic disorders, severe skin disease, inflammatory bowel disease, sarcoidosis, blood disorders, leukaemia/lymphoma, nephrotic syndrome.

src.q: Prednisolone is indicated in the management of all conditions deemed likely to benefit from short- or long-term glucocorticoid therapy.
Some of the principal indications are: bronchial asthma, severe hypersensitivity reactions, anaphylaxis; rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction stated in the UK SmPCs (5 mg tablets, 20 mg tablets, 10 mg/mL oral solution) or SPS pages accessed.

items.t: Adults: lowest effective dose for the shortest time. Initial dose 5-60 mg daily depending on the condition (divided doses usually used); reduce gradually to the lowest maintenance dose.

src.q: The lowest effective dose should be used for the minimum period in order to minimise side effects.
The initial dosage of Prednisolone Tablets may vary from 5mg to 60mg or more depending on the disorder being treated.

items.t: Guide doses: allergic and skin disorders 5-15 mg daily; collagenosis 20-30 mg daily; rheumatoid arthritis 10-15 mg daily initially (oral solution SmPC: 7.5-10 mg daily); blood disorders and lymphoma 15-60 mg daily.

src.q: Allergic and skin disorders : Initial doses of 5-15 mg daily are commonly adequate. Collagenosis : Initial doses of 20-30 mg daily are frequently effective.
Rheumatoid arthritis : The usual initial dose is 10-15 mg daily.
Blood disorders and lymphoma : An initial daily dose of 15-60 mg is often necessary
Rheumatoid arthritis: 7.5mg (0.75ml) to 10mg (1ml) daily.

items.t: Oral solution SmPC, short-term treatment: 20-30 mg daily for the first few days, then reduce by 2.5-5 mg every 2-5 days. Most other conditions: 10-100 mg daily for 1-3 weeks, then reduce to the minimum effective dose.

src.q: Short-term treatment: 20mg (2ml) to 30mg (3ml) daily for the first few days, subsequently reducing the daily dosage by 2.5mg (0.25ml) or 5mg (0.5ml) every two to five days
Most other conditions: 10mg (1ml) to 100mg (10ml) daily for one to three weeks, then reducing to the minimum effective dosage.

items.t: Withdrawal: after more than about 7.5 mg daily for over 3 weeks, do not stop abruptly. Courses of up to 40 mg daily for up to 3 weeks can usually be stopped abruptly if relapse is unlikely, except in at-risk groups (repeated courses, recent long-term therapy, other causes of adrenal insufficiency, more than 40 mg daily, evening doses).

src.q: In patients who have received more than physiological dose for systemic corticosteroids (approximately 7.5mg prednisolone or equivalent) for greater than 3 weeks, withdrawal should not be abrupt.
Abrupt withdrawal of doses of up to 40mg daily of prednisolone, or equivalent for 3 weeks is unlikely to lead to clinically relevant HPA-axis suppression, in the majority of patients.

items.t: During prolonged therapy, intercurrent illness, trauma or surgery need a temporary dose increase.

src.q: During prolonged therapy any intercurrent illness, trauma or surgical procedure will require a temporary increase in dosage

items.t: Use only when specifically indicated, at the minimum dose for the shortest time; alternate-day dosing preferred. Fractions of the adult dose may be used (e.g. 75% at 12 years, 50% at 7 years, 25% at 1 year).

src.q: Prednisolone should be used only when specifically indicated, in a minimum dosage and for the shortest possible time.
Fractions of the adult dosage may be used (e.g. 75% at 12 years, 50% at 7 years and 25% at 1 year)

items.t: Acute asthma (oral solution SmPC): over 5 years 30-40 mg; 2-5 years 20 mg; under 2 years (hospital) 10 mg, for up to 3 days; no taper needed.

src.q: For children over 5 years use a dose of 30-40mg (3-4ml) prednisolone. For children aged 2-5 years use a dose of 20mg (2ml) prednisolone.
at a dose of 10mg (1ml) for up to three days
There is no need to taper the dose at the end of treatment.

items.t: Acute asthma in children already on maintenance steroid tablets: 2 mg/kg, maximum 60 mg.

src.q: Those already receiving maintenance steroid tablets should receive 2mg/kg prednisolone up to a maximum dose of 60mg (6ml).

items.t: Steroids cause growth retardation, which may be irreversible: avoid long-term pharmacological doses; monitor growth.

src.q: Corticosteroids cause growth retardation in infancy, childhood and adolescence, which may be irreversible and therefore long-term administration of pharmacological doses should be avoided.

items.t: All UK SmPCs: hypersensitivity to prednisolone or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1. Systemic infections unless specific anti-infective therapy is employed.

items.t: 5 mg tablet and oral solution SmPCs: systemic infection unless specific anti-infective treatment is given. 5 mg tablet SmPC: ocular herpes simplex (risk of perforation).

src.q: Patients with ocular herpes simplex due to the possibility of perforation.
Systemic infections, unless specific anti-infective therapy is employed. Live virus immunisation.

items.t: Oral solution SmPC: live virus immunisation. 20 mg tablet SPC: systemic fungal infection; live vaccines in patients on immunosuppressive doses. The 20 mg SPC adds that in life-saving situations the contraindications generally do not apply.

src.q: Systemic fungal infection. Administration of live vaccines is contraindicated in patients receiving corticosteroids in immunosuppressive doses.
In those conditions when treatment with prednisolone can save lives, none of the contraindications generally apply.

items.t: Caution and frequent monitoring in: diabetes (or family history), glaucoma (or family history), hypertension or heart failure, liver failure, epilepsy, osteoporosis, severe affective disorder or previous steroid psychosis, peptic ulcer, previous steroid myopathy, thromboembolic disorders, renal insufficiency, tuberculosis history, recent myocardial infarction.

src.q: Caution is necessary when corticosteroids, including prednisolone, are prescribed to patients with the following conditions and frequent patient monitoring is necessary: Diabetes mellitus or in those with a family history of diabetes.
Peptic ulceration. Previous steroid myopathy.
Renal insufficiency. Tuberculosis: Those with a history of, or X-ray changes characteristic of tuberculosis.

items.t: Psychiatric reactions (mood change, depression, suicidal thoughts, psychosis) are common and usually start within days or weeks; patients/carers should seek advice if worrying symptoms occur. Particular care with a personal or first-degree family history of severe affective disorder.

src.q: Patients/carers should be encouraged to seek medical advice if worrying psychological symptoms develop, especially if depressed mood or suicidal ideation is suspected.

Particular care is required when considering the use of systemic corticosteroids in patients with existing or previous history of severe affective disorders in themselves or in their first degree relatives.

items.t: Infections may be masked. Chickenpox and measles can be severe or fatal: non-immune exposed patients need urgent advice (VZIG within 10 days for chickenpox exposure). Do not stop steroids if chickenpox develops.

src.q: Chickenpox is of particular concern since this normally minor illness may be fatal in immunosuppressed patients.
this should be given within 10 days of exposure to chickenpox
Corticosteroids should not be stopped and the dose may need to be increased.

items.t: Systemic sclerosis: increased risk of scleroderma renal crisis at 15 mg/day or more; check blood pressure and serum creatinine routinely.

src.q: Caution is required in patients with systemic sclerosis because of an increased incidence of (possibly fatal) scleroderma renal crisis with hypertension and decreased urinary output observed with a daily dose of 15 mg or more prednisolone.

items.t: Myasthenia gravis on anticholinesterases: use cautiously. Hypothyroidism or chronic liver disease: effect may be enhanced. Phaeochromocytoma (20 mg SPC): only after risk/benefit evaluation.

src.q: Glucocorticoids should be used cautiously in patients with myasthenia gravis receiving anticholinesterase therapy.
The effect of corticosteroids may be enhanced in patients with hypothyroidism in those with chronic liver disease with impaired hepatic function.
Corticosteroids should only be administered to patients with suspected or identified pheochromocytoma following consideration of individual risk/benefit.

items.t: Blurred vision or visual disturbance: consider ophthalmology referral (cataract, glaucoma, central serous chorioretinopathy). Elderly: closer supervision.

src.q: If a patient presents with symptoms such as blurred vision or other visual disturbances, the patient should be considered for referral to an ophthalmologist
Close clinical supervision is required to avoid life threatening reactions.

items.t: Tablets contain lactose: not for galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: CYP3A inhibitors (including cobicistat): avoid unless benefit outweighs the increased risk of systemic steroid effects; if used, monitor.

src.q: The combination should be avoided unless the benefit outweighs the increased risk of systemic corticosteroid side-effects, in which case patients should be monitored for systemic corticosteroid side-effects.

items.t: Enzyme inducers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, primidone, rifampicin, rifabutin) reduce prednisolone effect; dose may need increasing.

src.q: Lack of expected response may be observed and dosage of prednisolone tablets may need to be increased.

items.t: NSAIDs and aspirin: higher risk of GI ulceration and bleeding. Use salicylates with caution; steroid withdrawal may cause salicylate toxicity.

src.q: Concomitant use of aspirin and Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs) with corticosteroids increases the risk of gastro-intestinal bleeding and ulceration.
Salicylates and corticosteroids should be used concurrently with caution.

items.t: Anticoagulants (warfarin): effect may be reduced or enhanced; monitor INR closely.

src.q: Response to anticoagulants may be reduced or less often, enhanced by corticosteroids. Close monitoring of the INR or prothrombin time is required to avoid spontaneous bleeding.

items.t: Antidiabetic medicines (including insulin): steroids raise blood glucose; antidiabetic dose may need adjusting.

src.q: Patients with diabetes mellitus receiving concurrent insulin and/or oral hypoglycemic agents may require dosage adjustments of such therapy.

items.t: Potassium-lowering drugs (thiazides, loop diuretics, beta2-agonists at high doses, theophylline, amphotericin): more hypokalaemia; 20 mg SPC: monitor serum potassium closely.

src.q: Serum potassium should be closely monitored in patients receiving glucocorticoids and potassium reducing agents.
Increased risk of hypokalaemia if high doses of corticosteroids given with high doses of bambuterol, fenoteral, formoteral, ritodrine, salbutamol, salmeterol and terbutaline.

items.t: Antihypertensives and diuretics: their effects are antagonised. Methotrexate: increased risk of haematological toxicity. Ciclosporin raises prednisolone levels. Live vaccines: see contraindications.

src.q: The desired effects of hypoglycaemic agents (including insulin), antihypertensives and diuretics are antagonised by corticosteroids
Cytotoxics: Increased risk of haematological toxicity with methotrexate.

items.t: No dose adjustment stated. Use with caution in renal insufficiency (fluid retention); monitor frequently.

src.q: Because of the possibility of fluid retention, care must be taken when corticosteroids are administered to patients with renal insufficiency or hypertension or congestive heart failure.
Corticosteroids should be used with caution in patients with renal insufficiency.

items.t: Liver failure: blood levels may rise; caution and frequent monitoring. Chronic liver disease or cirrhosis: effect enhanced.

src.q: In patients with liver failure, blood levels of corticosteroid may be increased, as with other drugs which are metabolised in the liver. Frequent patient monitoring is therefore necessary.
Patients with hypothyroidism or liver cirrhosis will have an enhanced effect of corticosteroids.

items.t: SmPC: prescribe only when benefits outweigh risks; 88% of prednisolone is inactivated crossing the placenta. Prolonged or repeated use may increase the risk of intra-uterine growth restriction. Monitor pre-eclampsia or fluid retention closely.

src.q: As with all drugs, corticosteroids should only be prescribed when the benefits to the mother and child outweigh the risks.
88% of prednisolone is inactivated as it crosses the placenta
Patients with pre-eclampsia or fluid retention require close monitoring.

items.t: BUMPS: systemic corticosteroids can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor; usually among the safest options for rheumatic and autoimmune disease. Some studies link early use with cleft lip/palate.

src.q: Systemic corticosteroids can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor.
Corticosteroid use in early pregnancy has been linked in some (but not all) studies to a higher chance of having a baby with a cleft lip and/or palate.

items.t: SmPC: up to 40 mg daily unlikely to affect the infant; at 40 mg or more monitor the infant for adrenal suppression. SPS: prednisolone is a preferred corticosteroid in breastfeeding; use lowest dose and duration.

src.q: Cyclogest should not be used during pregnancy except as indicated during the first trimester of pregnancy for use as part of an assisted reproduction (ART) treatment
There is limited and inconclusive data on the risk of congenital anomalies

src.q: Use rectally if barrier methods of contraception are used.

src.q: Use rectally if patients suffer from vaginal infection (especially moniliasis) or recurrent cystitis or have recently given birth. Use vaginally if patients suffer from colitis or faecal incontinence.
400 mg administered vaginally twice a day starting at oocyte retrieval.

items.t: Hypertension; angina; long-term prevention of re-infarction after MI; most cardiac dysrhythmias; migraine prophylaxis; essential tremor; situational and generalised anxiety (somatic symptoms); prophylaxis of upper GI bleeding in portal hypertension with oesophageal varices; adjunct in thyrotoxicosis; hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy; peri-operative phaeochromocytoma (with an alpha-blocker).

src.q: a) the control of hypertension; b) the management of angina pectoris; c) long term management against re-infarction after recovery from acute myocardial infarction; d) the control of most forms of cardiac dysrhythmias; e) the prophylaxis of migraine; f) the management of essential tremor;
h) prophylaxis of upper gastrointestinal bleeding in patients with portal hypertension and oesophageal varices;

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction stated in the UK propranolol 10 mg tablets SmPC.

items.t: Hypertension: start 80 mg twice daily, increase weekly by response; usual 160-320 mg per day.

src.q: A starting dose of 80 mg twice a day may be increased at weekly intervals according to response. The usual dose range is 160 to 320 mg per day.

items.t: Angina, migraine, essential tremor: start 40 mg two or three times daily, increase weekly; usual 80-160 mg/day (migraine, tremor) or 120-240 mg/day (angina).

src.q: A starting dose of 40 mg two or three times daily may be increased by the same amount at weekly intervals according to patient response.
An adequate response in migraine and essential tremor is usually seen in the range 80 to 160 mg/day and in angina in the range 120 to 240 mg/day.

items.t: Anxiety: 40 mg daily for acute situational anxiety; generalised anxiety 40 mg twice daily, up to 40 mg three times daily. Review after 6-12 months.

src.q: A dose of 40 mg daily may provide short term relief of acute situational anxiety.
usually responds adequately to 40 mg twice daily which, in individual cases, may be increased to 40 mg three times daily.
Patients should be reviewed after 6 to 12 months treatment.

items.t: Arrhythmias, anxiety tachycardia, HOCM, thyrotoxicosis: 10-40 mg three or four times daily.

src.q: A dosage range of 10 to 40 mg three or four times a day usually achieves the required response.

items.t: Post-MI: start between day 5 and 21; 40 mg four times daily for 2-3 days, then 80 mg twice daily.

src.q: Treatment should start between days 5 and 21 after myocardial infarction, with an initial dose of 40 mg four times a day for 2 or 3 days.
the total daily dosage may thereafter be given as 80 mg twice a day.

items.t: Portal hypertension: start 40 mg twice daily, increase to 80 mg twice daily by heart rate (aim about 25% reduction); maximum 160 mg twice daily.

src.q: Dosage should begin with 40 mg twice daily, increasing to 80 mg twice daily depending on heart rate response. If necessary, the dose may be increased incrementally to a maximum of 160 mg twice daily.

items.t: Elderly: use with caution; start with the lowest dose.

src.q: Inderal should be used to treat the elderly with caution. It is suggested that treatment should start with the lowest dose.

items.t: Dysrhythmias, phaeochromocytoma, thyrotoxicosis: 0.25-0.5 mg/kg three or four times daily as required (guide only).

src.q: Oral: 0.25 to 0.5 mg/kg three or four times daily as required.

items.t: Migraine: under 12 years 20 mg two or three times daily; over 12 years adult dose.

src.q: Migraine Oral: Under the age of 12: 20 mg two or three times daily. Over the age of 12: The adult dose.

items.t: Fallot's tetralogy: up to 1 mg/kg three or four times daily as required (guide only).

src.q: Oral: Up to 1 mg/kg repeated three or four times daily as required.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to propranolol or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance(s) or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: History of bronchial asthma or bronchospasm.

src.q: Inderal must not be used if there is a history of bronchial asthma or bronchospasm.

items.t: Bradycardia; cardiogenic shock; hypotension; metabolic acidosis; after prolonged fasting; severe peripheral arterial circulatory disturbances; second- or third-degree heart block; sick sinus syndrome; untreated phaeochromocytoma; uncontrolled heart failure; Prinzmetal's angina.

src.q: as with other beta-blockers must not be used in patients with any of the following conditions:

bradycardia; cardiogenic shock; hypotension; metabolic acidosis; after prolonged fasting; severe peripheral arterial circulatory disturbances; second or third degree heart block; sick sinus syndrome; untreated phaeochromocytoma; uncontrolled heart failure or Prinzmetal's angina.

items.t: Patients prone to hypoglycaemia (e.g. after prolonged fasting, or with restricted counter-regulatory reserve: malnutrition, starvation, chronic liver disease, diabetes, drugs blocking catecholamine response).

src.q: Inderal must not be used in patients prone to hypoglycaemia, i.e., patients after prolonged fasting or patients with restricted counter-regulatory reserves.

Patients at risk for an inadequate response to hypoglycaemia includes individuals with malnutrition, prolonged fasting, starvation, chronic liver disease, diabetes and concomitant use of drugs which block the full response to catecholamines.

items.t: Controlled heart failure: may be used; caution with poor cardiac reserve. First-degree heart block: caution.

src.q: may be used in patients whose signs of heart failure have been controlled. Caution must be exercised in patients whose cardiac reserve is poor.
caution must be exercised if it is given to patients with first degree heart block.

items.t: Hypoglycaemia: may mask signs (tachycardia); can cause hypoglycaemia even in non-diabetics (neonates, children, elderly, haemodialysis, chronic liver disease, overdose), rarely with seizures or coma. Caution with hypoglycaemic therapy in diabetes.

src.q: Inderal occasionally causes hypoglycaemia, even in non-diabetic patients
Severe hypoglycaemia associated with Inderal has rarely presented with seizures and/or coma in isolated patients.
Caution must be exercised in the concurrent use of Inderal and hypoglycaemic therapy in diabetic patients.

items.t: Do not stop abruptly: withdraw over 7-14 days, following patients (especially ischaemic heart disease). If stopping before surgery, stop at least 24 hours before.

src.q: Abrupt withdrawal of beta-blockers is to be avoided. The dosage should be withdrawn gradually over a period of 7 to 14 days.
this should be done at least 24 hours prior to the procedure.

items.t: Hepatic or renal impairment: half-life may increase; caution when starting and choosing the first dose. Decompensated cirrhosis: use with caution. Portal hypertension: liver function may worsen and hepatic encephalopathy may develop.

src.q: Since the half-life may be increased in patients with significant hepatic or renal impairment, caution must be exercised when starting treatment and selecting the initial dose.
Inderal must be used with caution in patients with decompensated cirrhosis
In patients with portal hypertension, liver function may deteriorate and hepatic encephalopathy may develop.

items.t: History of anaphylaxis: more severe reactions to allergens; may not respond to usual adrenaline doses.

src.q: may cause a more severe reaction to a variety of allergens when given to patients with a history of anaphylactic reaction to such allergens.

items.t: May aggravate less severe peripheral arterial disease; may mask thyrotoxicosis; in phaeochromocytoma use only with an alpha-blocker.

src.q: may also aggravate less severe peripheral arterial circulatory disturbances.
may mask the signs of thyrotoxicosis.
in patients with phaeochromocytoma, an alpha-blocker may be given concomitantly.

items.t: Galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption: should not take (contains lactose).

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: Verapamil or diltiazem: should not be combined; exaggerated negative inotropic and conduction effects can cause severe hypotension, bradycardia and cardiac failure. Do not give either IV within 48 hours of stopping the other.

src.q: should not be used in combination with calcium channel blockers with negative inotropic effects (e.g. verapamil, diltiazem)
This may result in severe hypotension, bradycardia and cardiac failure.

items.t: Dihydropyridines (e.g. nifedipine): more risk of hypotension; cardiac failure with latent cardiac insufficiency; blood levels of either may change, so dose adjustment may be needed.

src.q: Concomitant therapy with dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, e.g., nifedipine, may increase the risk of hypotension, and cardiac failure may occur in patients with latent cardiac insufficiency.

items.t: Insulin and hypoglycaemic therapy in diabetes: caution; tachycardia of hypoglycaemia is masked and the hypoglycaemic response to insulin may be prolonged.

src.q: Caution must be exercised in the concurrent use of Inderal and hypoglycaemic therapy in diabetic patients. Inderal may prolong the hypoglycaemic response to insulin

items.t: Warfarin, theophylline, rifampicin, quinidine, propafenone, thioridazine, dihydropyridines: hepatic enzyme interactions; blood levels of either medicine may change, so dose adjustment may be needed.

src.q: quinidine, propafenone, rifampicin, theophylline, warfarin, thioridazine and dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
Owing to the fact that blood concentrations of either agent may be affected, dosage adjustments may be needed according to clinical judgement

items.t: NSAIDs (e.g. ibuprofen): may reduce the blood pressure lowering effect.

src.q: Concomitant use of prostaglandin synthetase inhibiting drugs eg, ibuprofen and indometacin, may decrease the hypotensive effects of Inderal.

items.t: IV lidocaine infusion: lidocaine levels rise about 30%; avoid the combination.

src.q: Administration of Inderal during infusion of lidocaine may increase the plasma concentration of lidocaine by approximately 30%.
The combination should be avoided.

items.t: Rizatriptan: exposure rises 70-80%; use rizatriptan 5 mg. Adrenaline/sympathomimetics: may counteract beta-blockade; caution with parenteral adrenaline. Clonidine: withdraw the beta-blocker several days before clonidine. Ergotamine: caution (vasospasm). Cimetidine, hydralazine and alcohol raise propranolol levels. Chlorpromazine: levels of both rise.

src.q: If both drugs are to be used, a rizatriptan dose of 5 mg has been recommended.
Concomitant use of sympathomimetic agents e.g., adrenaline, may counteract the effect of beta-blockers.
Concomitant use of cimetidine or hydralazine will increase plasma levels of propranolol

items.t: Significant renal impairment: half-life may be longer; use caution when starting and choosing the initial dose.

items.t: SmPC: should not be given in pregnancy unless essential. Not teratogenic, but beta-blockers reduce placental perfusion (fetal death, premature delivery); neonatal hypoglycaemia and bradycardia may occur.

src.q: As with all drugs Inderal should not be given during pregnancy unless its use is essential.
However beta-blockers reduce placental perfusion, which may result in intra-uterine foetal death, immature and premature deliveries.
In addition, adverse effects (especially hypoglycaemia and bradycardia in the neonate and bradycardia in the foetus) may occur.

items.t: BUMPS: can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor; no concerns that it causes harm; extra growth scans may be offered.

src.q: Propranolol can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor.
There are no concerns that taking propranolol in pregnancy causes harm.
you may be offered additional scans at around 32 and 36 weeks

src.q: Breast-feeding is therefore not recommended following administration of these compounds.

items.t: SPS: a beta-blocker of choice in breastfeeding (very small amounts in milk); as a precaution monitor the infant for bradycardia or hypoglycaemia.

src.q: Propranolol is a preferred choice due to very small amounts in breast milk and favourable pharmacokinetics although monitoring is still recommended.

items.t: Section 4.4 'must not' statements: infants under 3 months; children with renal or liver impairment of any degree; prolonged or uncontrolled vomiting; restarting after DRESS.

src.q: The product must not be administered to children with renal or liver impairment, whatever the degree of severity, due to a lack of information on these patient populations.
the product must not be administered in cases of prolonged or uncontrolled vomiting.

items.t: Bloody or purulent stools with fever (invasive bacteria or other severe disease) or antibiotic-associated diarrhoea: should not be given.

src.q: The presence of bloody or purulent stools and fever may indicate the presence of invasive bacteria as a reason for diarrhoea, or the presence of other severe disease.
Therefore, racecadotril should not be administered under these conditions.

items.t: Angioedema can occur at any time; airway involvement needs emergency treatment. Stop and supervise closely. Past angioedema not caused by racecadotril may raise the risk.

src.q: Where there is angioedema associated with upper airway obstruction, such as tongue, glottis and/or larynx, emergency therapy should be administered promptly.
Patients with a history of angioedema unrelated to racecadotril therapy may be at increased risk of angioedema.

items.t: Severe skin reactions including DRESS (can be fatal): stop immediately; never restart after DRESS.

src.q: If signs and symptoms suggestive of DRESS appear, racecadotril should be withdrawn immediately and an alternative treatment considered.
treatment with racecadotril must not be restarted in these patients at any time.

items.t: Severe or prolonged diarrhoea with marked vomiting or poor appetite: consider IV rehydration.

src.q: In the event of serious or prolonged diarrhoea with important vomiting or a lack of appetite, intravenous rehydration should be considered.

items.t: Diabetes: count the sucrose content if the daily dose provides more than 5 g sucrose. Chronic diarrhoea not sufficiently studied.

src.q: In patients with diabetes, it should be taken into account that each sachet contains 2.899 g of sucrose.
Chronic diarrhoea has not been sufficiently studied with this product.

items.t: Other medicines that cause bradykinin-mediated angioedema (ACE inhibitors; to a lesser extent angiotensin II antagonists, gliptins, mTOR inhibitors, sacubitril, alteplase, estramustine): combined use may raise angioedema risk and is not recommended.

src.q: The most frequently implicated drugs are ACE inhibitors, and to a lesser extent: angiotensin II antagonists
Concomitant use of racecadotril and other drugs known to cause bradykinin-mediated angioedema may increase the risk of angioedema and are not recommended

items.t: No clinically relevant inhibition or induction of major CYP enzymes in vitro.

src.q: do not inhibit the major CYP enzymes isoforms 3A4, 2D6, 2C9, 1A2 and 2C19 to an extent that would be clinically relevant.

items.t: Must not be given to children with renal impairment of any degree (no data). No eGFR or CrCl threshold given.

src.q: The product must not be administered to children with renal or liver impairment, whatever the degree of severity, due to a lack of information on these patient populations.

items.t: Must not be given to children with liver impairment of any degree (no data).

src.q: The product must not be administered to children with renal or liver impairment, whatever the degree of severity, due to a lack of information on these patient populations.

items.t: No adequate human data; should not be given to pregnant women.

src.q: However, since no specific clinical studies are available, Hidrasec should not be administered to pregnant women.

items.t: No data on excretion in milk: should not be given to breastfeeding women.

src.q: this medicinal product should not be administered to breastfeeding women.

items.t: Rat studies show no effect on fertility.

src.q: Fertility studies conducted with racecadotril on Rats demonstrate no impact on fertility.

items.t: No common adverse effects listed. Uncommon: tonsillitis, rash, erythema.

src.q: Uncommon: tonsillitis.
Uncommon: rash, erythema.

items.t: Angioedema (face, lips, tongue, larynx) and anaphylactic shock: emergency treatment if airway involved; stop racecadotril.

src.q: Racecadotril should be discontinued and the patient should be under close medical supervision
Unknown: anaphylactic shock.

items.t: Severe cutaneous reactions including DRESS (life-threatening or fatal): stop immediately and never restart.

src.q: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs) including drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), which can be life-threatening or fatal, have been reported in association with racecadotril treatment.

items.t: Monitor closely for skin reactions; stop at signs of severe skin reaction or DRESS.

src.q: Patients should be advised of the signs and symptoms and monitored closely for skin reactions.
When experiencing severe skin reactions, the treatment has to be stopped immediately.

items.t: Add the granules to food, or disperse in a glass of water or the feeding bottle; mix well and give immediately.

src.q: The granules can be added to food, dispersed in a glass of water or in the feeding-bottle, mixing well and followed by immediate administration.

items.t: Keep giving oral rehydration solution; racecadotril does not replace it.

src.q: Rehydration is highly important in the management of acute diarrhoea in infants.

items.t: Seek urgent help for swelling of the face, lips or tongue, or a severe rash.

src.q: Angioedema of the face, extremities, lips, mucous membranes may occur.

items.t: Type 2 diabetes in adults not controlled by diet, weight reduction and exercise; also with metformin when metformin alone is not enough. Used with diet and exercise to lower mealtime glucose.

src.q: Repaglinide is indicated in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus whose hyperglycaemia can no longer be controlled satisfactorily by diet, weight reduction and exercise.
Repaglinide is also indicated in combination with metformin in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus who are not satisfactorily controlled on metformin alone.

items.t: Prescribe only if poor glucose control and symptoms persist despite adequate diet, exercise and weight reduction.

src.q: Repaglinide should only be prescribed if poor blood glucose control and symptoms of diabetes persist despite adequate attempts at dieting, exercise and weight reduction.

items.t: Start 0.5 mg before main meals (1 mg if transferring from another oral hypoglycaemic). Titrate by blood glucose, with 1 to 2 weeks between steps. Maximum single dose 4 mg with main meals; maximum 16 mg daily.

src.q: The recommended starting dose is 0.5 mg. One to two weeks should elapse between titration steps (as determined by blood glucose response). If patients are transferred from another oral hypoglycaemic medicinal product, the recommended starting dose is 1 mg.
The recommended maximum single dose is 4 mg taken with main meals. The total maximum daily dose should not exceed 16 mg.

items.t: With metformin: keep the metformin dose; start repaglinide 0.5 mg before main meals and titrate as for monotherapy.

src.q: The starting dose of repaglinide is 0.5 mg, taken before main meals; titration is according to blood glucose response as for monotherapy.

items.t: Debilitated or malnourished: conservative starting and maintenance doses with careful titration.

src.q: In debilitated or malnourished patients the initial and maintenance dosage should be conservative and careful dose titration is required to avoid hypoglycaemic reactions.

items.t: Elderly: no clinical studies over 75 years.

src.q: No clinical studies have been conducted in patients >75 years of age.

items.t: Safety and efficacy below 18 years not established; no data.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of repaglinide in children below 18 years have not been established. No data are available.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to repaglinide or any excipient.

src.q: 4.3 Contraindications Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Type 1 diabetes (C-peptide negative); diabetic ketoacidosis with or without coma.

src.q: Diabetes mellitus type 1, C-peptide negative Diabetic ketoacidosis, with or without coma

items.t: Severe hepatic function disorder.

src.q: Severe hepatic function disorder

items.t: Concomitant gemfibrozil (repaglinide exposure raised about 8-fold).

src.q: Concomitant use of gemfibrozil (see section 4.5).
increased the repaglinide AUC 8.1-fold

items.t: Hypoglycaemia (like other insulin secretagogues); risk is higher in combination with metformin.

src.q: Repaglinide like other insulin secretagogues, is capable of producing hypoglycaemia.
Combination treatment with metformin is associated with an increased risk of hypoglycaemia.

items.t: Stress (fever, trauma, infection, surgery) may cause loss of control; temporary insulin may be needed.

src.q: At such times, it may be necessary to discontinue repaglinide and treat with insulin on a temporary basis.

items.t: Medicines that affect repaglinide metabolism: use with caution or avoid; if needed, monitor blood glucose and the patient closely.

src.q: Repaglinide should be used with caution or be avoided in patients receiving medicinal products which influence repaglinide metabolism

items.t: May be associated with more acute coronary syndrome (e.g. myocardial infarction).

src.q: The use of repaglinide might be associated with an increased incidence of acute coronary syndrome (e.g. myocardial infarction)

items.t: Not studied after secondary failure to other secretagogues or in combination with other secretagogues; benefit-risk with NPH insulin or thiazolidinediones not established.

src.q: Trials investigating the combination with other insulin secretagogues have not been performed.
However, the benefit risk profile remains to be established when comparing to other combination therapies.

items.t: Gemfibrozil (not in this tool's list): contraindicated.

src.q: The concomitant use of gemfibrozil and repaglinide is contraindicated

items.t: Trimethoprim and clopidogrel (CYP2C8 inhibitors): raise repaglinide exposure - avoid; if needed, monitor blood glucose and the patient closely. Also avoid ciclosporin and deferasirox (not in this tool's list).

src.q: the concomitant use of trimethoprim with repaglinide should be avoided. If concomitant use is necessary, careful monitoring of blood glucose and close clinical monitoring should be performed
the concomitant use of clopidogrel and repaglinide should be avoided. If concomitant use is necessary, careful monitoring of blood glucose and close clinical monitoring should be performed

items.t: May enhance or prolong hypoglycaemia: clarithromycin, itraconazole, ketoconazole, other antidiabetics, MAOIs, non-selective beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, salicylates, NSAIDs, octreotide, alcohol, anabolic steroids.

src.q: Gemfibrozil, clarithromycin, itraconazole, ketoconazole, trimethoprim, ciclosporin, deferasirox, clopidogrel, other antidiabetic substances, monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOI), non selective beta blocking substances

items.t: Beta-blockers may mask hypoglycaemia symptoms.

src.q: β-blocking medicinal products may mask the symptoms of hypoglycaemia.

items.t: May reduce the effect: oral contraceptives, rifampicin, barbiturates, carbamazepine, thiazides, corticosteroids, danazol, thyroid hormones, sympathomimetics. Watch glycaemic control closely when starting or stopping them. Rifampicin needs glucose-guided dose adjustment up to about 2 weeks after stopping; other inducers (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, St John's wort) may act similarly.

src.q: Oral contraceptives, rifampicin, barbiturates, carbamazepine, thiazides, corticosteroids, danazol, thyroid hormones and sympathomimetics.
the patient should be observed closely for changes in glycaemic control.
It cannot be excluded that other inducers, e.g. phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, St John's wort, may have a similar effect.

items.t: No relevant effect on digoxin, theophylline or warfarin; cimetidine, nifedipine, oestrogen and simvastatin did not change repaglinide levels.

src.q: Repaglinide had no clinically relevant effect on the pharmacokinetic properties of digoxin, theophylline or warfarin at steady state
Co-administration of cimetidine, nifedipine, oestrogen, or simvastatin with repaglinide, all CYP3A4 substrates, did not significantly alter the pharmacokinetic parameters of repaglinide.

items.t: Not affected by renal disorders (8% renally excreted), but clearance is lower and insulin sensitivity is higher in renal impairment: titrate with caution.

src.q: Repaglinide is not affected by renal disorders
As insulin sensitivity is increased in diabetic patients with renal impairment, caution is advised when titrating these patients.

items.t: Severe hepatic function disorder: contraindicated. No clinical studies in hepatic insufficiency.

src.q: Severe hepatic function disorder
No clinical studies have been conducted in patients with hepatic insufficiency.

items.t: SmPC: no studies in pregnancy; should be avoided.

src.q: There are no studies of repaglinide in pregnant women. Repaglinide should be avoided during pregnancy.

items.t: BUMPS: treat type 2 diabetes in pregnancy with metformin, plus insulin if needed; repaglinide is avoided as a precaution. With an unplanned pregnancy, keep taking it until reviewed promptly.

src.q: Type 2 diabetes during pregnancy should be treated with metformin, as well as insulin if required. Other antidiabetic drugs should not be used.
you should carry on with the drug you are taking until your appointment, as uncontrolled diabetes is risky for you and your baby

items.t: SmPC: no studies; should not be used in breastfeeding women (found in animal milk).

src.q: There are no studies in breast-feeding women. Repaglinide should not be used in breast-feeding women.
Repaglinide was detected in the milk of animals.

items.t: SPS: insulin or metformin are the preferred choices; limited or no published information on other antidiabetic medicines.

src.q: Insulin or metformin are the preferred choices during breastfeeding.
limited or no published information on the use of other antidiabetic (blood-glucose lowering) medicines during breastfeeding.

reproductive.note: The UK repaglinide SmPC checked gives no human fertility or contraception advice; section 4.6 refers only to animal data.

items.t: Common: hypoglycaemia, abdominal pain, diarrhoea.

src.q: Hypoglycaemia Common
Abdominal pain, diarrhoea Common

items.t: Transient visual (refraction) disturbances when starting, from changes in blood glucose (very rare).

src.q: Changes in blood glucose levels have been known to result in transient visual disturbances, especially at the commencement of treatment.

items.t: Hypoglycaemic coma or unconsciousness (frequency not known). Severe hypoglycaemia with seizure, loss of consciousness or coma needs intravenous glucose.

src.q: Hypoglycaemic coma and hypoglycaemic unconsciousness Not known
More severe hypoglycaemia with seizure, loss of consciousness or coma should be treated with intravenous glucose.

items.t: Generalised allergic reactions (e.g. anaphylaxis) and vasculitis (very rare); severe hepatic dysfunction (very rare); cardiovascular disease (rare).

src.q: Generalised hypersensitivity reactions (e.g. anaphylactic reaction), or immunological reactions such as vasculitis.
In very rare cases, severe hepatic dysfunction has been reported.
Cardiovascular disease Rare

items.t: Patient self-monitoring plus periodic blood glucose by the physician to find the minimum effective dose; HbA1c to check response.

src.q: the patient's blood glucose must be monitored periodically by the physician to determine the minimum effective dose for the patient.
Glycosylated haemoglobin levels are also of value in monitoring the patient's response to therapy.

items.t: Periodic review to detect primary or secondary failure.

src.q: Periodic monitoring is necessary to detect inadequate lowering of blood glucose at the recommended maximum dose level (i.e. primary failure)

items.t: Take before main meals, usually within 15 minutes (anywhere from just before to 30 minutes before), 2 to 4 meals a day.

src.q: Doses are usually taken within 15 minutes of the meal but time may vary from immediately preceding the meal to as long as 30 minutes before the meal (i.e. preprandially 2, 3, or 4 meals a day).

items.t: Skip a meal, skip the dose; add a meal, add a dose.

src.q: Patients who skip a meal (or add an extra meal) should be instructed to skip (or add) a dose for that meal.

items.t: One dose per main meal: miss the meal, miss the dose.

src.q: Patients who skip a meal (or add an extra meal) should be instructed to skip (or add) a dose for that meal.

items.t: Take care to avoid low blood sugar when driving, especially with reduced awareness of warning signs.

src.q: Patients should be advised to take precautions to avoid hypoglycaemia whilst driving.

items.t: Treat low blood sugar symptoms (dizziness, sweating, tremor, headache) with oral carbohydrate.

src.q: adequate action should be taken to correct the low blood glucose (oral carbohydrates).

items.t: Primary hypercholesterolaemia (type IIa, including heterozygous familial) or mixed dyslipidaemia (type IIb), and homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, in adults and children aged 6 years or older, as an adjunct to diet.

src.q: Adults, adolescents and children aged 6 years or older with primary hypercholesterolaemia (type IIa including heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia) or mixed dyslipidaemia (type IIb) as an adjunct to diet
Adults, adolescents and children aged 6 years or older with homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia

items.t: Prevention of major cardiovascular events in patients at high estimated risk of a first event, alongside correction of other risk factors.

src.q: Prevention of major cardiovascular events in patients who are estimated to have a high risk for a first cardiovascular event

items.t: 40 mg dose: only for severe hypercholesterolaemia at high cardiovascular risk not at goal on 20 mg, with routine follow-up; specialist supervision recommended when starting 40 mg.

src.q: a final titration to the maximum dose of 40 mg should only be considered in patients with severe hypercholesterolaemia at high cardiovascular risk
Specialist supervision is recommended when the 40 mg dose is initiated.

items.t: Children: use only by specialists.

src.q: Paediatric use should only be carried out by specialists.

items.t: Start 5 mg or 10 mg once daily (statin-naive or switching). May go up one dose level after 4 weeks. Maximum 40 mg only in selected patients (see restrictions).

src.q: The recommended start dose is 5 or 10 mg orally once daily in both statin naïve or patients switched from another HMG CoA reductase inhibitor.
A dose adjustment to the next dose level can be made after 4 weeks, if necessary

items.t: 20 mg daily was the dose used in the risk-reduction study.

src.q: In the cardiovascular events risk reduction study, the dose used was 20 mg daily

items.t: Start 5 mg in: patients over 70 years; moderate renal impairment (CrCl <60 mL/min); Asian ancestry; patients with factors predisposing to myopathy. 40 mg is contraindicated in Asian patients and in moderate renal impairment.

src.q: A start dose of 5 mg is recommended in patients >70 years
The recommended start dose is 5 mg in patients with moderate renal impairment (creatinine clearance <60 ml/min).
The recommended start dose is 5 mg for patients of Asian ancestry. The 40 mg dose is contraindicated in these patients.
The recommended start dose is 5 mg in patients with predisposing factors to myopathy

items.t: Known SLCO1B1 c.521CC or ABCG2 c.421AA genotype: half the usual dose, maximum 20 mg once daily.

src.q: For patients known to have the c.521CC or c.421AA genotype, half of the usually recommended dose and a maximum once daily dose of 20 mg of Crestor is recommended

items.t: With medicines that raise rosuvastatin exposure about 2-fold or more: start 5 mg once daily and limit the maximum dose so exposure does not exceed that of 40 mg alone (e.g. 20 mg with gemfibrozil).

src.q: Start with a 5 mg once daily dose of Crestor if the expected increase in exposure (AUC) is approximately 2-fold or higher.

The maximum daily dose of Crestor should be adjusted so that the expected rosuvastatin exposure would not likely exceed that of a 40 mg daily dose of Crestor taken without interacting medicinal products

items.t: Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, 6-17 years: usual start 5 mg daily. Age 6-9: 5-10 mg once daily (doses above 10 mg not studied). Age 10-17: 5-20 mg once daily (doses above 20 mg not studied).

src.q: In children and adolescents with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia the usual start dose is 5 mg daily.
In children 6 to 9 years of age with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, the usual dose range is 5-10 mg orally once daily.
In children 10 to 17 years of age with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, the usual dose range is 5-20 mg orally once daily.

items.t: Homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, 6-17 years: start 5-10 mg once daily; maximum 20 mg once daily.

src.q: In children 6 to 17 years of age with homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, the recommended maximum dose is 20 mg once daily.
A starting dose of 5 to 10 mg once daily depending on age, weight and prior statin use is advised.

items.t: Not recommended under 6 years. The 40 mg tablet is not suitable for children.

src.q: Crestor is not recommended for use in children younger than 6 years.
The 40 mg tablet is not suitable for use in paediatric patients.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to rosuvastatin or any excipient.

src.q: in patients with hypersensitivity to rosuvastatin or to any of the excipients

items.t: Active liver disease, including unexplained persistent raised transaminases or any transaminase rise above 3 x ULN.

src.q: in patients with active liver disease including unexplained, persistent elevations of serum transaminases and any serum transaminase elevation exceeding 3 times the upper limit of normal (ULN)

items.t: Severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min), all doses.

src.q: in patients with severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance <30 ml/min)

items.t: Myopathy; concomitant ciclosporin; concomitant sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir.

src.q: in patients with myopathy. - in patients receiving concomitant combination of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir (see section 4.5). - in patients receiving concomitant ciclosporin.

items.t: 40 mg dose only: contraindicated with factors predisposing to myopathy/rhabdomyolysis: moderate renal impairment (CrCl <60 mL/min), hypothyroidism, personal or family history of hereditary muscle disorders, previous muscle toxicity with a statin or fibrate, alcohol abuse, situations raising plasma levels, Asian patients, concomitant fibrates.

src.q: The 40 mg dose is contraindicated in patients with pre-disposing factors for myopathy/rhabdomyolysis.

moderate renal impairment (creatinine clearance < 60 ml/min) - hypothyroidism - personal or family history of hereditary muscular disorders - previous history of muscular toxicity with another HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor or fibrate - alcohol abuse
Asian patients - concomitant use of fibrates.

items.t: Muscle: myalgia, myopathy and rarely rhabdomyolysis, especially above 20 mg. Prescribe with caution if predisposed (renal impairment, hypothyroidism, hereditary muscle disorder, previous statin/fibrate muscle toxicity, alcohol abuse, age >70, raised plasma levels, fibrates). Do not start if baseline CK >5 x ULN (confirmed).

src.q: should be prescribed with caution in patients with pre-disposing factors for myopathy/rhabdomyolysis
If the repeat test confirms a baseline CK >5xULN, treatment should not be started.

items.t: Do not use in an acute serious condition suggesting myopathy or predisposing to renal failure from rhabdomyolysis (e.g. sepsis, hypotension, major surgery, trauma, severe metabolic, endocrine or electrolyte disorders, uncontrolled seizures).

src.q: Crestor should not be used in any patient with an acute, serious condition suggestive of myopathy or predisposing to the development of renal failure secondary to rhabdomyolysis

items.t: Liver: caution with excessive alcohol intake or a history of liver disease. Stop or reduce the dose if transaminases exceed 3 x ULN.

src.q: Crestor should be used with caution in patients who consume excessive quantities of alcohol and/or have a history of liver disease.
Crestor should be discontinued or the dose reduced if the level of serum transaminases is greater than 3 times the upper limit of normal.

items.t: Severe cutaneous reactions (SJS, DRESS) reported: stop immediately if signs appear and never restart after SJS or DRESS.

src.q: Crestor should be discontinued immediately and an alternative treatment should be considered
treatment with Crestor must not be restarted in this patient at any time

items.t: Myasthenia gravis may start or worsen with statins; stop if symptoms worsen.

src.q: Crestor should be discontinued in case of aggravation of symptoms.

items.t: Diabetes risk: statins may raise blood glucose; monitor patients at risk (fasting glucose 5.6-6.9 mmol/L, BMI >30 kg/m2, raised triglycerides, hypertension). This is not a reason to stop treatment.

src.q: Patients at risk (fasting glucose 5.6 to 6.9 mmol/l, BMI >30 kg/m2, raised triglycerides, hypertension) should be monitored both clinically and biochemically according to national guidelines.

items.t: Systemic fusidic acid: do not co-administer, or within 7 days of stopping it (rhabdomyolysis, some fatal).

src.q: Crestor must not be co-administered with systemic formulations of fusidic acid or within 7 days of stopping fusidic acid treatment.

items.t: Contains lactose: patients with hereditary galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take it.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, the Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: Fibrates (including fenofibrate): increased risk of myopathy. 40 mg contraindicated with a fibrate; start with 5 mg. Gemfibrozil is not recommended. MHRA: with fibrates start 5 mg and do not exceed 20 mg.

src.q: The 40 mg dose is contraindicated with concomitant use of a fibrate (see sections 4.3 and 4.4). These patients should also start with the 5 mg dose.
the combination of Crestor and gemfibrozil is not recommended
For rosuvastatin, start with 5 mg and do not exceed 20 mg during use with fibrates.

items.t: Warfarin or other vitamin K antagonists: starting or increasing rosuvastatin may raise INR; stopping or reducing it may lower INR. Monitor INR.

src.q: may result in an increase in International Normalised Ratio (INR)
In such situations, appropriate monitoring of INR is desirable.

items.t: Ezetimibe: small rise in rosuvastatin exposure; a pharmacodynamic interaction (muscle adverse effects) cannot be ruled out. Use with caution.

src.q: A pharmacodynamic interaction, in terms of adverse effects, between Crestor and ezetimibe cannot be ruled out
caution should be exercised with their combined use

items.t: Aluminium/magnesium hydroxide antacid: taken at the same time, rosuvastatin levels fall by about 50%; giving the antacid 2 hours after rosuvastatin lessens this.

src.q: The simultaneous dosing of Crestor with an antacid suspension containing aluminium and magnesium hydroxide resulted in a decrease in rosuvastatin plasma concentration of approximately 50%.
This effect was mitigated when the antacid was dosed 2 hours after Crestor.

items.t: Febuxostat: raises rosuvastatin exposure about 1.9-fold. Ciclosporin (7-fold; contraindicated), ticagrelor, certain HIV/hepatitis C protease inhibitors and others in SmPC Table 1 also raise levels: consider alternatives or dose adjustment.

src.q: Febuxostat 120 mg OD 10 mg, single dose 1.9-fold ↑
Whenever possible, alternative medications should be considered, and, if necessary, consider temporarily discontinuing Crestor therapy.

items.t: No clinically relevant interaction with fluconazole; none predicted with clopidogrel (modelling). Not metabolised to a clinically important extent by cytochrome P450.

src.q: No clinically relevant interactions have been observed between rosuvastatin and either fluconazole
predicts no clinically relevant DDI between clopidogrel and rosuvastatin

items.t: SmPC: CrCl <30 mL/min contraindicated (all doses). CrCl <60 mL/min (moderate): start 5 mg; 40 mg contraindicated. Mild to moderate: no other adjustment.

src.q: The use of Crestor in patients with severe renal impairment is contraindicated for all doses
The recommended start dose is 5 mg in patients with moderate renal impairment (creatinine clearance <60 ml/min). The 40 mg dose is contraindicated in patients with moderate renal impairment.

items.t: SPS uses eGFR: rosuvastatin contraindicated if eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m²; 40 mg contraindicated if eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m².

src.q: Rosuvastatin contra-indicated if eGFR less than 30mL/min/1.73m2; 40mg dose contraindicated if eGFR less than 60ml/min/1.73m2.

items.t: 40 mg: consider assessing renal function at routine follow-up (proteinuria and serious renal events reported more at 40 mg).

src.q: An assessment of renal function should be considered during routine follow-up of patients treated with a dose of 40 mg.

items.t: Contraindicated in active liver disease. No increased exposure at Child-Pugh 7 or below; increased exposure at Child-Pugh 8-9 (consider assessing renal function); no experience above 9.

src.q: There was no increase in systemic exposure to rosuvastatin in subjects with Child-Pugh scores of 7 or below.
increased systemic exposure has been observed in subjects with Child-Pugh scores of 8 and 9
There is no experience in subjects with Child-Pugh scores above 9.

items.t: SPS: in stable or chronic liver disease statins can be used with caution; consider a lower starting dose (e.g. rosuvastatin 10 mg daily) with gradual increase.

src.q: available data suggest that statins can be used with caution after assessing individual risks and benefits
consider a lower dose of a high-intensity statin, such as atorvastatin 20 mg daily or rosuvastatin 10 mg daily, with gradual dose escalation

items.t: SmPC: not recommended; stop as soon as pregnancy is recognised, though ongoing need may be considered in very high cardiovascular risk. Potential risk to the fetus.

src.q: Crestor is not recommended for use in pregnant women. Crestor should be discontinued as soon as pregnancy is recognized.
the ongoing therapeutic need and the individual benefit risk in patients with very high risk of cardiovascular events should be considered

items.t: BUMPS: statins are usually avoided in pregnancy; most women are advised to stop three months before trying to conceive and during pregnancy.

src.q: Statins are usually avoided in pregnancy if possible as there is not enough information to say they are safe for the baby.
most women are advised to stop taking statins for three months before trying to conceive, and during pregnancy

items.t: SmPC: breastfeeding not recommended (present in milk; potential risk to the infant).

src.q: Breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment with CRESTOR.

items.t: SPS (differs from SmPC): rosuvastatin is a preferred statin and can be used with caution; monitor the infant's feeding, growth and weight gain, and for constipation, lethargy and irritability. Postponing therapy until after exclusive breastfeeding is preferred if possible.

src.q: Rosuvastatin can be used with caution while breastfeeding, but infant monitoring is still required.
Also monitor the infant for potential side effects including constipation, lethargy, and irritability.
if possible, the preferred option would be to postpone lipid-lowering therapy until after the exclusive breastfeeding period

items.t: Oral contraceptive: rosuvastatin raised ethinylestradiol and norgestrel levels; consider this when choosing the contraceptive dose.

src.q: These increased plasma levels should be considered when selecting oral contraceptive doses.

items.t: BUMPS: no increased risk to the baby expected if the father took a statin around conception.

src.q: We would not expect any increased risk to the baby if the father took a statin before or around the time you became pregnant.

items.t: Common: headache, dizziness, constipation, nausea, abdominal pain, myalgia, asthenia, and diabetes mellitus (depends on risk factors). Adverse effects tend to be dose dependent.

src.q: Nervous system disorders Headache Dizziness
Gastro-intestinal disorders Constipation Nausea Abdominal pain
Musculo-skeletal and connective tissue disorders Myalgia
General disorders and administration site conditions Asthenia
the incidence of adverse drug reactions tends to be dose dependent

items.t: Rare: myopathy, rhabdomyolysis (with or without acute renal failure). Stop if CK >5 x ULN or muscle symptoms are severe. Report unexplained muscle pain, weakness or cramps at once.

src.q: Therapy should be discontinued if CK levels are markedly elevated (>5xULN) or if muscular symptoms are severe and cause daily discomfort
Patients should be asked to report inexplicable muscle pain, weakness or cramps immediately, particularly if associated with malaise or fever.

items.t: Severe skin reactions (SJS, DRESS); hepatitis and jaundice (very rare); pancreatitis (rare); immune-mediated necrotising myopathy; interstitial lung disease (stop the statin if suspected).

src.q: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), which could be life-threatening or fatal, have been reported with rosuvastatin
If it is suspected a patient has developed interstitial lung disease, statin therapy should be discontinued.

items.t: Before starting (SPS): ALT or AST, lipid profile (non-fasting), serum creatinine/eGFR, HbA1c, blood pressure and BMI. CK only if persistent muscle symptoms; TSH if thyroid symptoms.

src.q: Before starting Required Baseline ALT or AST Blood pressure Body mass index HDL cholesterol (non-fasting) non-HDL cholesterol (non-fasting) Serum creatinine (for creatinine clearance) or Estimated glomerular filtration rate
