items.t: SmPC: liver function tests before and 3 months after starting. SPS: ALT/AST and lipids between months 2 and 3; then annual lipids for review.

src.q: It is recommended that liver function tests be carried out prior to, and 3 months following, the initiation of treatment.
Continued until stable Required Between months 2 and 3 ALT or AST

items.t: Stop or do not start if ALT/AST >3 x ULN (repeat in 1 month) or CK >5 x ULN (re-measure after 7 days). Routine CK in symptom-free patients is not needed.

src.q: Stop existing statin or do not initiate new statin if ALT or AST are greater than 3 times upper limit of normal (ULN).
Stop existing statin or do not initiate statin if creatine kinase (CK) greater than 5 times ULN.
Routine monitoring of CK levels in asymptomatic patients is not warranted.

items.t: Once daily at any time of day, with or without food. Continue a cholesterol-lowering diet.

src.q: Crestor may be given at any time of day, with or without food.
Before treatment initiation the patient should be placed on a standard cholesterol-lowering diet that should continue during treatment.

items.t: Report unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, weakness or cramps straight away, especially with fever or feeling unwell.

src.q: Patients should be asked to report inexplicable muscle pain, weakness or cramps immediately
Advise patients to report any unexplained muscle pain.

items.t: Know the signs of severe skin reactions and seek help if they appear.

src.q: patients should be advised of the signs and symptoms of severe skin reactions and be closely monitored

items.t: If taking an aluminium/magnesium antacid, take it at least 2 hours after rosuvastatin.

src.q: This effect was mitigated when the antacid was dosed 2 hours after Crestor.

items.t: Dizziness may occur; take this into account when driving.

src.q: When driving vehicles or operating machines, it should be taken into account that dizziness may occur during treatment.

items.t: Inhaler: short-acting (4-6 hours) relief and prevention of bronchospasm in reversible airways obstruction (e.g. before exercise or allergen exposure); adults, adolescents and children 4-11 years (under 4: see dosing). In asthma, should not be the main or only treatment; prescribe with an inhaled corticosteroid.

src.q: Ventolin Evohaler provides short-acting (4 to 6 hour) bronchodilation with fast onset (within 5 minutes) in reversible airways obstruction.

In asthma, short acting beta-2 agonists including Salbutamol Evohaler should not be the main or only treatment. It is recommended that short acting beta-2 agonists should be prescribed with concomitant inhaled corticosteroid (anti-inflammatory).

items.t: Nebuliser solution: chronic bronchospasm unresponsive to conventional therapy, and acute severe asthma.

src.q: Ventolin Respirator Solution is indicated for use in the routine management of chronic bronchospasm unresponsive to conventional therapy, and in the treatment of acute severe asthma.

items.t: MHRA and NICE: do not prescribe a SABA to anyone with asthma (any age) without an inhaled corticosteroid. Review if as-needed SABA is used more than twice a week; urgently review rising SABA prescriptions or uncollected preventers. For poorly controlled asthma over 12 years, AIR or MART are recommended alternatives.

src.q: do not prescribe SABA to people of any age with asthma without a concomitant prescription of an inhaled corticosteroid
Do not prescribe short-acting beta2 agonists to people of any age with asthma without a concomitant prescription of an ICS.
review and adjust asthma treatment in patients who take more than twice weekly
anti-inflammatory reliever (AIR) therapy and maintenance and reliever therapy (MART) are recommended alternatives for people over 12 years of age with poorly controlled asthma

items.t: Nebuliser in children and adolescents: only specialists should start and manage home nebulised rescue treatment for acute asthma; buying a nebuliser privately for this is not recommended.

src.q: Only specialists in respiratory medicine should initiate and clinically manage use of nebulisers and associated nebulised medicines at home for acute treatment of asthma in children and adolescents.
independent purchase of nebuliser devices outside of medical advice for use at home to deliver rescue therapy for the acute treatment of asthma in children and adolescents is not recommended

items.t: SPS: generic prescribing of inhalers can lead to an unfamiliar device, which could affect use and adherence (no specific brand instruction for salbutamol). NICE: if possible use the same device type for preventer and reliever.

src.q: Generic prescribing of inhalers can lead to people being given an unfamiliar device which could affect usage and adherence.
If possible, prescribe the same type of device to deliver preventer and reliever treatments where more than one inhaler is needed.

items.t: Inhaler, adults: acute symptoms 100 micrograms (1 puff), up to 2 puffs; before exercise/allergen 2 puffs 10-15 minutes before; chronic therapy up to 2 puffs four times a day. On-demand use should not exceed 8 puffs in 24 hours; frequent or increasing need means poorly controlled asthma.

src.q: For the relief of acute asthma symptoms including bronchospasm, one inhalation (100 micrograms) may be administered as a single minimum starting dose. This may be increased to two inhalations if necessary.
To prevent allergen- or exercise-induced symptoms, two inhalations should be taken 10-15 minutes before challenge.
For chronic therapy, two inhalations up to four times a day.
On-demand use of Ventolin Evohaler should not exceed 8 inhalations in any 24 hours.

items.t: Nebuliser, adults (intermittent): 2.5 mg (0.5 ml) diluted to 2 ml with sterile normal saline, may increase to 5 mg (1 ml) diluted to 2.5 ml; can be used undiluted; some adults need up to 10 mg. Continuous: diluted to 50-100 micrograms/ml, usually 1-2 mg per hour.

src.q: Ventolin Respirator solution 0.5 ml (2.5 mg of salbutamol) should be diluted to a final volume of 2 ml with sterile normal saline. This may be increased to 1 ml (5 mg of salbutamol) diluted to a final volume of 2.5 ml.
Some adult patients may require higher doses of salbutamol up to 10 mg
The usual rate of administration is 1-2 mg per hour.

items.t: Inhaler, under 12 years: acute 1 puff (100 micrograms), up to 2; prevention 1 puff before challenge, up to 2; chronic up to 2 puffs four times daily. 12 years and over: adult dose. A spacer can help under 5 years.

src.q: The usual dosage for children under the age of 12 years: one inhalation (100 micrograms). The dose may be increased to two inhalations if required.
The usual dosage for children under the age of 12 years: up to two inhalations 4 times daily.
spacer device may be used to facilitate administration to children under 5 years of age

items.t: Nebuliser, under 12 years: start 2.5 mg diluted to 2-2.5 ml with sterile normal saline; some children over 18 months need up to 5 mg; may repeat up to four times daily. Under 18 months efficacy uncertain (consider oxygen). Home nebuliser use for acute asthma in children only under specialist management.

src.q: The minimum starting dosage for children under the age of 12 years is 0.5 ml (2.5 mg of salbutamol) diluted to 2 to 2.5 ml with sterile normal saline.
Some children (over the age of 18 months) may, however, require higher doses of salbutamol up to 5 mg.
Intermittent treatment may be repeated up to four times daily.
In infants under 18 months the clinical efficacy of nebulised salbutamol is uncertain.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to salbutamol or an excipient. Inhaled and nebulised (non-IV) salbutamol must not be used to stop uncomplicated premature labour or threatened abortion.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.
Non-i.v. formulations of salbutamol must not be used to arrest uncomplicated premature labour or threatened abortion.
Non-IV formulations of salbutamol must not be used to arrest uncomplicated premature labour or threatened abortion.

items.t: Bronchodilators should not be the only or main treatment in severe or unstable asthma. Overuse of SABA can mask disease progression and increases the risk of severe exacerbations and death. Re-evaluate patients using as-needed salbutamol more than twice a week.

src.q: Bronchodilators should not be the only or main treatment in patients with severe or unstable asthma.

Overuse of short-acting beta-agonists may mask the progression of the underlying disease and contribute to deteriorating asthma control, leading to an increased risk of severe asthma exacerbations and mortality.
not counting prophylactic use prior to exercise, should be re-evaluated

items.t: Severe heart disease (ischaemic heart disease, arrhythmia, severe heart failure): warn to seek advice for chest pain or worsening heart symptoms (rare myocardial ischaemia reported). Caution in thyrotoxicosis and diabetes.

src.q: Patients with underlying severe heart disease (e.g. ischaemic heart disease, arrhythmia or severe heart failure) who are receiving salbutamol should be warned to seek medical advice if they experience chest pain or other symptoms of worsening heart disease.
Salbutamol should be administered cautiously to patients with thyrotoxicosis.
Caution is advised when administering this product to patients with a history of diabetes mellitus or hyperglycaemia.

items.t: Serious hypokalaemia can occur, mainly with nebulised or parenteral use; particular caution in acute severe asthma (hypoxia, xanthines, steroids, diuretics); monitor serum potassium.

src.q: Potentially serious hypokalaemia may result from beta-2-agonist therapy, mainly from parenteral and nebulised administration.
Serum potassium levels should be monitored in such situations.

items.t: Nebuliser: lactic acidosis with high-dose nebulised SABA in acute asthma (may be mistaken for treatment failure; monitor lactate); ketoacidosis in diabetes; angle-closure glaucoma with nebulised ipratropium (keep mist out of the eyes); benzalkonium chloride may cause bronchospasm.

src.q: Lactic acidosis has been reported in association with high therapeutic doses of intravenous and nebulised short-acting beta-agonist therapy
It is therefore recommended that patients are monitored for the development of elevated serum lactate and consequent metabolic acidosis in this setting.
A combination of nebulised salbutamol with nebulised anticholinergics should therefore be used cautiously.
Benzalkonium chloride may cause bronchospasm, especially in patients with asthma.

items.t: Inhaler holds 200 puffs; after that it may spray propellant without medicine. Keep a count of puffs used and consider a spare inhaler.

src.q: The inhaler contains enough salbutamol for a total of 200 actuations (puffs) only.
To avoid inadvertent use of an empty inhaler, maintaining a record of the number of actuations (puffs) administered to the patient should be considered.

items.t: Non-selective beta-blockers such as propranolol: should not usually be prescribed together.

src.q: Salbutamol and non-selective β-blocking drugs such as propranolol, should not usually be prescribed together.
Should not normally be prescribed with non-selective β-blocking drugs such as propranolol.

items.t: Xanthines, steroids and diuretics may potentiate hypokalaemia (acute severe asthma): monitor potassium. Nebuliser: corticosteroids can worsen hyperglycaemia/ketoacidosis in diabetes; caution with nebulised anticholinergics (ipratropium) and with large doses of other sympathomimetics.

src.q: Particular caution is advised in acute severe asthma as this effect may be potentiated by hypoxia and by concomitant treatment with xanthine derivatives, steroids and diuretics.
Concurrent administration of corticosteroids can exaggerate this effect.
Ventolin Respirator Solution should be used with care in patients known to have received large doses of other sympathomimetic drugs.

items.t: SPS (QT): beta-2 agonist inhalers alone pose a low risk of clinically significant QT prolongation and a low likelihood of significant interaction with other QT-prolonging medicines; monitor ECG and potassium with high-dose, nebulised, prolonged treatment in people with risk factors or other QT/potassium-lowering medicines.

src.q: When used alone and in the absence of other risk factors, beta agonist inhalers pose a low risk of clinically significant QT interval prolongation.
The likelihood of a clinically significant interaction with other medicines known to prolong QT interval is considered low.

Monitor ECG and potassium before and during high-dose, nebulised, prolonged regular treatment in people with non-modifiable patient risk factors or concurrent medicines known to prolong QT interval or lower potassium.

renal.note: No renal dose advice in the inhaler or nebuliser SmPCs (sections 4.2 and 4.4 checked). BNF not accessed.

hepatic.note: No hepatic dose advice in the inhaler or nebuliser SmPCs (sections 4.2 and 4.4 checked). BNF not accessed.

items.t: Inhaler SmPC: safety not established; rare reports of congenital anomalies (mothers often on several medicines). Should not be used in pregnancy unless clearly necessary.

src.q: Ventolin Evohaler should not be used during pregnancy unless clearly necessary.

items.t: Nebuliser SmPC: consider only if expected benefit to the mother outweighs any possible risk to the foetus.

src.q: Administration of drugs during pregnancy should only be considered if the expected benefit to the mother is greater than any possible risk to the foetus.

items.t: BUMPS: inhaled salbutamol stays mainly in the lungs; very little reaches the baby and no harm has been shown. Continue asthma medicines in pregnancy; no extra scans needed unless asthma is severe.

src.q: Salbutamol from an inhaler stays mainly in the lungs. Very little salbutamol reaches the baby and it has not been shown to cause harm.
Asthma medicines like salbutamol should be continued in pregnancy
Women using salbutamol in pregnancy do not need any additional scans unless their asthma is severe.

items.t: Not for stopping premature labour or threatened abortion (contraindicated for non-IV forms).

src.q: Non-i.v. formulations of salbutamol must not be used to arrest uncomplicated premature labour or threatened abortion.

items.t: Probably passes into breast milk; effect on the neonate unknown. Use only where expected benefit to the mother outweighs any potential risk to the neonate. (No SPS breastfeeding page found for salbutamol.)

src.q: As salbutamol is probably secreted in breast milk, its use in nursing mothers requires careful consideration.
its use should be restricted to situations where it is felt that the expected benefit to the mother is likely to outweigh any potential risk to the neonate

items.t: No information on human fertility; no effect in animals.

src.q: There is no information on the effects of salbutamol on human fertility.

items.t: Common: tremor, headache, tachycardia. Uncommon: palpitations, mouth and throat irritation, muscle cramps. (Both SmPCs list the same effects; frequencies are quoted from the nebuliser SmPC table because the inhaler table text is jumbled.)

src.q: Nervous system disorders Common: Tremor, headache.
Cardiac disorders Common: Tachycardia. Uncommon: Palpitations
Gastrointestinal disorders Uncommon: Mouth and throat irritation.
Musculoskeletal and connective tissue disorders Uncommon: Muscle cramps.

items.t: Paradoxical bronchospasm (wheeze straight after a dose): treat at once with a different fast-acting bronchodilator; stop this product and assess.

src.q: This should be treated immediately with an alternative presentation or a different fast-acting inhaled bronchodilator.
Evohaler should be discontinued immediately, the patient assessed, and if necessary, a different fast-acting bronchodilator instituted for on-going use.

items.t: Very rare hypersensitivity (angioedema, urticaria, bronchospasm, hypotension, collapse); myocardial ischaemia (frequency unknown): seek advice for chest pain. Nebuliser: lactic acidosis (unknown frequency).

src.q: Very rare: Hypersensitivity reactions including angioedema, urticaria, bronchospasm, hypotension and collapse
Myocardial ischaemia* (see section 4.4)
Unknown: Lactic acidosis (see section 4.4)

items.t: If a previously effective dose no longer gives 3 hours of relief, seek medical advice promptly; failure to respond may need urgent treatment.

src.q: If a previously effective dose of inhaled salbutamol no longer provides relief for a duration of three hours following administration, the patient should be advised to promptly seek medical advice.
Failing to respond to treatment with salbutamol may signal a need for urgent medical advice or treatment.

items.t: Review asthma treatment if as-needed SABA is used more than twice a week; urgently review rising SABA prescriptions or failure to collect preventer treatment (MHRA).

src.q: review and adjust asthma treatment in patients who take more than twice weekly

urgently review patients where there has either been an increase in the number of prescriptions requested for SABA reliever inhalers or a failure to collect prescribed anti-inflammatory maintenance treatment

items.t: Serum potassium in acute severe asthma; serum lactate with high-dose nebulised use in acute asthma.

src.q: Serum potassium levels should be monitored in such situations.
It is therefore recommended that patients are monitored for the development of elevated serum lactate and consequent metabolic acidosis in this setting.

items.t: Stop at once if paradoxical bronchospasm.

src.q: Ventolin Respirator Solution should be discontinued immediately, the patient assessed, and if necessary a different fast-acting bronchodilator instituted for on-going use.

items.t: Inhaler: check technique so the puff is synchronised with breathing in; a spacer helps those who find this hard. A different taste from a previous inhaler is possible.

src.q: Patients inhaler technique should be checked to make sure that aerosol actuation is synchronised with inspiration of breath for optimum delivery of drug to the lungs.
Ventolin Evohaler may be used with a Volumatic spacer device by patients who find it difficult to synchronise aerosol actuation with inspiration of breath.

items.t: Nebuliser: breathe in through the mouth via a suitable nebuliser under medical direction; dilute with sterile normal saline as directed; never inject or swallow; keep the mist out of the eyes.

src.q: is for inhalation use only, to be breathed in through the mouth, under the direction of a physician, using a suitable nebuliser
Patients should receive adequate instruction in correct administration and be warned not to let the solution or mist enter the eye.

items.t: MHRA advice for patients: if a blue reliever is prescribed, a separate preventer will also be prescribed for daily use; keep using the preventer even when well; seek urgent help if symptoms are not relieved; ask for a review if the reliever is needed more than twice a week; if there is no dose counter, track doses and keep a spare.

src.q: a separate asthma preventer therapy will always be prescribed for regular daily use as well
seek urgent medical assistance if worsening asthma symptoms (for example, chest tightness, wheezing, coughing, or difficulty breathing) are not relieved
if the blue inhaler does not have a dose counter, manually track the doses used

items.t: Increase the dose or frequency only on medical advice.

src.q: The dosage or frequency of administration should only be increased on medical advice.

restrictions.note: No UK product information found.

hepatic.note: No UK product information found.

items.t: Short-term relief of occasional constipation.

src.q: For the short-term relief of occasional constipation

items.t: MHRA: use stimulant laxatives only if bulk-forming and osmotic laxatives are ineffective. Children under 12 should not use them without advice from a prescriber; 12-17 years can be supplied under pharmacist supervision.

src.q: stimulant laxatives should only be used if other laxatives (bulk-forming and osmotic) are ineffective

Stimulant laxatives should no longer be used in children under 12 years without advice from a prescriber, while products for children aged 12 to 17 years can be supplied under the supervision of a pharmacist.

items.t: Use only if diet change or bulk-forming agents fail.

src.q: This product should only be used if a therapeutic effect cannot be achieved by a change of diet or the administration of bulk forming agents.

items.t: Adults (and over 12 years with the 12-plus product): 1-2 tablets at night; start low and use the smallest dose that gives a soft-formed motion. The 12-plus SmPC: a higher dose may be prescribed under medical guidance, up to a maximum of 30 mg hydroxyanthracene glycosides a day.

src.q: Adults, the elderly and children over 12 years: Swallow one to two tablets at night
A higher dose may be prescribed under medical guidance.
The maximum daily dose of hydroxyanthracene glycosides is 30 mg.
The correct individual dose is the smallest required to produce a comfortable soft-formed motion.

items.t: Duration: one UK SmPC says use for more than 1-2 weeks needs medical supervision; the adult-labelled pack SmPC says not more than 1 week (usually 2-3 doses in that week).

src.q: Use for more than 1-2 weeks requires medical supervision.
Not to be used for more than 1 week. Usually it is sufficient to take this medicinal product up to two to three times during that week.

items.t: If no bowel action after 3 days of increasing dose, consider medical examination.

src.q: If no bowel action has occurred after three days of progressively increased dosage, a medical examination should be considered.

items.t: 12-plus product: contraindicated under 12 years.

src.q: Children under 12 years of age.
Should not be used in children or adolescents under the age of 12 years (see section 4.3).

items.t: Adult-labelled pack: should not be used under 18 years.

src.q: Should not be used in children or adolescents under the age of 18 years.

items.t: MHRA: children under 12 should not use stimulant laxatives unless told to by their prescriber.

src.q: children younger than 12 years should not use stimulant laxatives without advice from a prescriber and clinical guidance should be followed

items.t: Hypersensitivity to senna or any excipient.

src.q: 4.3 Contraindications Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients.

items.t: Use at the same time as other laxatives.

src.q: Not to be used at the same time as other laxative agents.

items.t: Intestinal obstruction and stenosis, atony, appendicitis, inflammatory bowel disease (e.g. Crohn's, ulcerative colitis), abdominal pain of unknown origin, severe dehydration with water and electrolyte depletion.

src.q: Cases of intestinal obstructions and stenosis, atony, appendicitis, inflammatory bowel diseases (e.g Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis), abdominal pain of unknown origin, severe dehydration state with water and electrolyte depletion

items.t: Pregnancy and lactation.

src.q: Pregnancy and lactation (see section 4.6 and 5.3).

items.t: Children under 12 years (12-plus product).

src.q: Children under 12 years of age.

items.t: Patients on cardiac glycosides, antiarrhythmics, QT-prolonging medicines, diuretics, corticosteroids or liquorice root must consult a doctor before use.

src.q: Patients taking cardiac glycosides, antiarrhythmic medicinal products, medicinal products inducing QT-prolongation, diuretics, adrenocorticosteroids or liquorice root, have to consult a doctor before taking senna leaf preparations concomitantly.

items.t: Do not use with faecal impaction or undiagnosed acute or persistent GI complaints (pain, nausea, vomiting) unless advised by a doctor: possible ileus.

src.q: should not be taken by patients suffering from faecal impaction and undiagnosed, acute or persistent gastro-intestinal complaints, e.g. abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting, unless advised by a doctor

items.t: Avoid long-term use: impaired bowel function, laxative dependence, atonic colon; prolonged excessive use can cause fluid/electrolyte imbalance and hypokalaemia.

src.q: Long-term use of stimulant laxatives should be avoided, as use for more than a brief period of treatment may lead to impaired function of the intestine and dependence on laxatives.
Prolonged excessive use may lead to fluid and electrolyte imbalance and hypokalaemia.

items.t: Where dehydration may be harmful (e.g. renal insufficiency, elderly) and fluid is lost: stop and restart only under medical supervision.

src.q: In patients suffering from fluid loss where dehydration may be harmful (e.g. renal insufficiency, elderly patients) Senokot should be discontinued and only be restarted under medical supervision.

items.t: Galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption: should not take (contains lactose).

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, the Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: Stimulant laxatives do not help with weight loss.

src.q: Stimulant laxatives (including Senokot) do not help with weight loss.

items.t: Other laxatives: must not be used at the same time (SmPC 4.3).

src.q: Not to be used at the same time as other laxative agents.

items.t: Hypokalaemia from long-term laxative abuse potentiates cardiac glycosides and interacts with antiarrhythmics and QT-prolonging medicines.

src.q: Hypokalaemia (resulting from long-term laxative abuse) potentiates the action of cardiac glycosides and interacts with antiarrhythmic medicinal products
and with medicinal products inducing QT-prolongation.

items.t: Other hypokalaemia-inducing medicines (e.g. diuretics, corticosteroids, liquorice root) may enhance electrolyte imbalance.

src.q: Concomitant use with other medicinal products inducing hypokalaemia (e.g. diuretics, adrenocorticosteroids and liquorice root) may enhance electrolyte imbalance.

items.t: Kidney disorders: be aware of possible electrolyte imbalance. In renal insufficiency with fluid loss, stop and restart only under medical supervision.

src.q: Patients with kidney disorders should be aware of possible electrolyte imbalance.
(e.g. renal insufficiency, elderly patients) Senokot should be discontinued and only be restarted under medical supervision.

items.t: No hepatic impairment dosing advice. Chronic overdose of anthranoid-containing medicines may cause toxic hepatitis.

src.q: Chronic ingested overdoses of anthranoid containing medicinal products may lead to toxic hepatitis.

items.t: SmPC: contraindicated in pregnancy (genotoxicity data for some anthranoids).

src.q: The use during pregnancy is contraindicated because of experimental data concerning a genotoxic risk of several anthranoids, e.g. emodin and aloe emodin.

items.t: BUMPS (differs from the SmPC): a laxative can be used in pregnancy if diet and lifestyle fail; stimulant laxatives such as senna are tried only when other types have not helped. Concern about womb contractions has not been seen in pregnant women.

src.q: Stimulant laxatives only tend to be tried when those above have not helped.
However, this has not been observed in pregnant women.

items.t: SmPC: contraindicated during lactation (active metabolites such as rhein pass into milk in small amounts).

src.q: The use during lactation is contraindicated because after administration of anthranoids, active metabolites, such as rhein, were excreted in reast milk in small amounts.

items.t: SPS (differs from the SmPC): standardised senna can be used during breastfeeding; as a precaution monitor the infant for diarrhoea or irritability.

src.q: Standardised senna preparations can be used during breastfeeding.
As a precaution monitor the infant for diarrhoea or irritability.

reproductive.note: UK SmPC: no data on fertility.

items.t: Frequency not known: abdominal pain, cramps, diarrhoea (especially with irritable colon; reduce dose); harmless yellow or red-brown urine discolouration.

src.q: Abdominal pain2, abdominal spasm2, diarrhoea2
Yellow or red-brown (pH dependent) discolouration of urine by metabolites, which is not clinically significant, may occur during the treatment.

items.t: Chronic use: colonic mucosal pigmentation (pseudomelanosis coli), usually reversible on stopping.

src.q: Chronic use may cause pigmentation of the intestinal mucosa (pseudomelanosis coli), which usually recedes when the patient stops taking the preparation.

items.t: Hypersensitivity, urticaria, asthma.

src.q: Hypersensitivity, urticaria, asthma, hypogammaglobulinaemia

items.t: Hypokalaemia from prolonged use with diarrhoea; chronic use may cause water/electrolyte disorders, albuminuria and haematuria. Overdose: severe diarrhoea with fluid and potassium loss; replace fluids and monitor potassium.

src.q: Prolonged use of laxatives resulting in diarrhoea and subsequently hypokalaemia.
Electrolytes, especially potassium, should be monitored.

items.t: Daily laxative need or persistent abdominal pain: see a doctor and investigate the cause.

src.q: If laxatives are needed every day, or abdominal pain persists, a doctor should be consulted.

items.t: Overdose or abuse: monitor electrolytes, especially potassium (particularly in the elderly).

src.q: Electrolytes, especially potassium, should be monitored. This is especially important in the elderly.

items.t: Swallow 1-2 tablets at night. Effect usually after 8-12 hours.

src.q: Swallow one to two tablets at night
Defaecation takes place after a delay of 8 - 12 hours

items.t: Do not exceed the stated dose. If no bowel movement after 3 days, or symptoms worsen, see a doctor or pharmacist.

src.q: Do not exceed the stated dose.
If the symptoms worsen during the use of the medicinal product or there is no bowel movement after three days, a doctor or pharmacist should be consulted.

items.t: Does not help with weight loss; overuse can be harmful.

src.q: Does not help with weight loss. Overuse can be harmful.

items.t: Urine may turn yellow or red-brown; this is harmless.

src.q: Yellow or red-brown (pH dependent) discolouration of urine by metabolites, which is not clinically significant

items.t: Major depressive episodes (treatment and prevention of recurrence); panic disorder with or without agoraphobia; OCD in adults and children 6 to 17 years; social anxiety disorder; post-traumatic stress disorder.

src.q: Major depressive episodes. Prevention of recurrence of major depressive episodes. Panic disorder, with or without agoraphobia. Obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) in adults and paediatric patients aged 6-17 years. Social anxiety disorder.

items.t: Not for children and adolescents under 18, except OCD aged 6 to 17. Efficacy not shown in paediatric major depression.

src.q: Sertraline should not be used in the treatment of children and adolescents under the age of 18 years, except for patients with obsessive compulsive disorder aged 6-17 years old.
Efficacy is not shown in paediatric major depressive disorder.

items.t: Start 50 mg once daily. If no response, increase in 50 mg steps at intervals of at least 1 week; maximum 200 mg/day.

src.q: Depression and OCD Sertraline treatment should be started at a dose of 50 mg/day.
Dose changes should be made in steps of 50 mg at intervals of at least one week, up to a maximum of 200 mg/day.

items.t: Start 25 mg once daily; after 1 week increase to 50 mg once daily. Then 50 mg steps at least weekly; maximum 200 mg/day.
items.tag: Panic disorder, PTSD, social anxiety disorder, adults

src.q: Therapy should be initiated at 25 mg/day. After one week, the dose should be increased to 50 mg once daily.

items.t: Maintenance: lowest effective dose. Depression: treat at least 6 months after symptoms resolve; for prevention of recurrence usually the same dose as for the episode. Panic disorder and OCD: review continuation regularly.

src.q: Dosage during long-term therapy should be kept at the lowest effective level
Patients with depression should be treated for a sufficient period of time of at least 6 months to ensure they are free from symptoms.

items.t: Elderly: dose carefully (higher hyponatraemia risk).

src.q: Elderly should be dosed carefully, as elderly may be more at risk for hyponatraemia

items.t: Stopping: avoid abrupt withdrawal; reduce gradually over at least 1 to 2 weeks (4.2), or over several weeks or months according to need (4.4). If intolerable symptoms, resume previous dose and taper more slowly.

src.q: When stopping treatment with sertraline the dose should be gradually reduced over a period of at least one to two weeks in order to reduce the risk of withdrawal reactions
sertraline should be gradually tapered when discontinuing treatment over a period of several weeks or months, according to the patient's needs

items.t: OCD aged 13 to 17: start 50 mg once daily. OCD aged 6 to 12: start 25 mg once daily, increase to 50 mg after 1 week. Further 50 mg increases over weeks if needed (not more often than weekly); maximum 200 mg daily; consider lower body weight.

src.q: Age 13-17 years : Initially 50 mg once daily. Age 6-12 years: Initially 25 mg once daily. The dosage may be increased to 50 mg once daily after one week.
The maximum dosage is 200 mg daily.

items.t: No data under 6 years. Other indications not for under 18. Monitor closely for suicidal behaviour and hostility, and monitor growth and development on long-term treatment.

src.q: No data is available for children under 6 years of age
the patient should be carefully monitored for appearance of suicidal symptoms, especially in early treatment
Physicians must monitor paediatric patients on long term treatment for abnormalities in growth and development.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to sertraline or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Irreversible MAOIs (e.g. selegiline): contraindicated (serotonin syndrome). Do not start sertraline within 14 days of stopping an irreversible MAOI; stop sertraline at least 7 days before starting one.

src.q: Concomitant treatment with irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) is contraindicated due to the risk of serotonin syndrome
Sertraline must not be initiated for at least 14 days after discontinuation of treatment with an irreversible MAOI.

items.t: Pimozide: contraindicated.

src.q: Concomitant intake of pimozide is contraindicated

items.t: Oral concentrate only: disulfiram (alcohol content) - do not use with disulfiram or within 14 days of stopping it.

src.q: sertraline oral solution should not be used in combination with disulfiram or within 14 days of discontinuing treatment with disulfiram

items.t: Serotonin syndrome / neuroleptic malignant syndrome: risk rises with other serotonergic drugs, MAOIs, antipsychotics/dopamine antagonists and opioids. Monitor for signs.

src.q: The risk of SS or NMS with SSRIs is increased with concomitant use of other serotonergic drugs (including other serotonergic antidepressants, amphetamines, triptans)
antipsychotics and other dopamine antagonists, and with opioids.

items.t: QTc prolongation / torsade de pointes: use with caution if cardiac disease, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, family history of long QT, bradycardia or other QT-prolonging drugs.

src.q: sertraline should be used with caution in patients with additional risk factors for QTc prolongation such as cardiac disease, hypokalaemia or hypomagnesemia, familial history of QTc prolongation, bradycardia and concomitant use of medications which prolong QTc interval

items.t: Sources differ on QTc: the SmPC says a QTc effect was confirmed in a thorough QTc study (run at 400 mg/day, twice the maximum dose); SPS says sertraline has no effect on QTc at licensed doses.

src.q: Effect on QTc prolongation was confirmed in a thorough QTc study in healthy volunteers
conducted at steady state at supratherapeutic exposures in healthy volunteers (treated with 400 mg/day, twice the maximum recommended daily dose)
Fluoxetine, paroxetine and sertraline have no effect on QTc at licensed doses

items.t: Bleeding: caution with drugs affecting platelet function (anticoagulants, aspirin, NSAIDs and others) and in bleeding disorders. SSRIs may increase postpartum haemorrhage risk.

src.q: Caution is advised in patients taking SSRIs, particularly in concomitant use with drugs known to affect platelet function
SSRIs/SNRIs may increase the risk of postpartum haemorrhage

items.t: Hyponatraemia (often SIADH; sodium < 110 mmol/L reported): higher risk in elderly, with diuretics or volume depletion. Consider stopping if symptomatic.

src.q: Elderly patients may be at greater risk of developing hyponatraemia with SSRIs and SNRIs. Also patients taking diuretics or who are otherwise volume-depleted may be at greater risk
Discontinuation of sertraline should be considered in patients with symptomatic hyponatraemia and appropriate medical intervention should be instituted.

items.t: Suicidal thoughts/behaviour: monitor closely early in treatment and after dose changes, especially under 25 years and with prior suicidality.

src.q: Close supervision of patients and in particular those at high risk should accompany drug therapy especially in early treatment and following dose changes.

items.t: Mania/hypomania history: caution; stop if a manic phase starts.

src.q: sertraline should be used with caution in patients with a history of mania/hypomania

items.t: Epilepsy: avoid in unstable epilepsy; monitor carefully if controlled; stop if seizures develop.

src.q: sertraline should be avoided in patients with unstable epilepsy and patients with controlled epilepsy should be carefully monitored. Sertraline should be discontinued in any patient who develops seizures.

items.t: Angle-closure glaucoma: mydriasis may raise intraocular pressure - use with caution.

src.q: Sertraline should therefore be used with caution in patients with angle-closure glaucoma or history of glaucoma.

items.t: Diabetes: glycaemic control may change; insulin/oral hypoglycaemic dose may need adjustment.

src.q: In patients with diabetes, treatment with an SSRI may alter glycaemic control. Insulin and/or oral hypoglycaemic dosage may need to be adjusted.

items.t: Sexual dysfunction, sometimes long-lasting after stopping SSRIs.

src.q: There have been reports of long-lasting sexual dysfunction where the symptoms have continued despite discontinuation of SSRIs.

items.t: Akathisia, mostly in the first weeks; increasing the dose may be harmful.

src.q: In patients who develop these symptoms, increasing the dose may be detrimental.

items.t: Schizophrenia: psychotic symptoms may worsen. Grapefruit juice not recommended. False-positive urine benzodiazepine screens.

src.q: Psychotic symptoms might become aggravated in schizophrenic patients.
The administration of sertraline with grapefruit juice is not recommended

items.t: Oral concentrate contains 94.8 mg ethanol per ml.

src.q: This medicine contains 94.8 mg of alcohol (ethanol) in each ml.

items.t: Contraindicated: irreversible MAOIs, pimozide (oral concentrate also disulfiram). Do not give with moclobemide or linezolid.

src.q: the combination of sertraline with a reversible and selective MAOI, such as moclobemide, should not be given
The antibiotic linezolid is a weak reversible and non-selective MAOI and should not be given to patients treated with sertraline

items.t: Other serotonergic drugs (e.g. tryptophan, amphetamines, 5-HT agonists/triptans) and St John's wort: use with caution and avoid whenever possible. Opioids (e.g. fentanyl): caution.

src.q: or the herbal medicine, St John's Wort ( hypericum perforatum ), should be undertaken with caution and avoided whenever possible due to the potential for a pharmacodynamic interaction
Caution is also advised with opioids [e.g. fentanyl (used in general anaesthesia or in the treatment of chronic pain)], and other serotonergic drugs

items.t: Drugs affecting platelet function (NSAIDs, aspirin, anticoagulants) or that raise bleeding risk: increased bleeding risk - caution.

src.q: The risk of bleeding may be increased when medicines acting on platelet function (e.g. NSAIDs, acetylsalicylic acid and ticlopidine) or other medicines that might increase bleeding risk are concomitantly administered with SSRIs, including sertraline

items.t: Warfarin: small rise in prothrombin time - monitor carefully when sertraline is started or stopped.

src.q: Accordingly, prothrombin time should be carefully monitored when sertraline therapy is initiated or stopped.

items.t: QT-prolonging drugs (e.g. some antipsychotics and antibiotics): increased risk of QTc prolongation/TdP.

src.q: The risk of QTc prolongation and/or ventricular arrhythmias (e.g. TdP) may be increased with concomitant use of other drugs which prolong the QTc interval (e.g. some antipsychotics and antibiotics)

items.t: Potent CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. clarithromycin, protease inhibitors, azole antifungals): avoid - may markedly raise sertraline levels. CYP3A4 inducers (e.g. St John's wort, carbamazepine, rifampicin) may lower levels.

src.q: potent CYP3A4 inhibitors, e.g. protease inhibitors, ketoconazole, itraconazole, posaconazole, voriconazole, clarithromycin, telithromycin and nefazodone
The intake of potent CYP3A4 inhibitors should be avoided during treatment with sertraline.

items.t: Strong CYP2C19 inhibitors (e.g. omeprazole, other PPIs, fluoxetine, fluvoxamine): an interaction cannot be excluded.

src.q: Interaction with strong inhibitors of CYP2C19, e.g. omeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole, rabeprazole, fluoxetine, fluvoxamine cannot be excluded.

items.t: Lithium (monitor), phenytoin (monitor levels), CYP2D6 substrates with narrow therapeutic index (e.g. flecainide, propafenone, TCAs), metamizole, alcohol (not recommended).

src.q: When co-administering sertraline with lithium, patients should be appropriately monitored.
the concomitant use of sertraline and alcohol is not recommended

items.t: Levothyroxine: levothyroxine SmPC says its effect may be reduced by sertraline.

src.q: Effects of Levothyroxine may be decreased by concomitant sertraline.

items.t: No dose adjustment needed in renal impairment (no PK difference with CrCl 30-60 ml/min or 10-29 ml/min).

src.q: No dosage adjustment is necessary in patients with renal impairment
(creatinine clearance 30-60 ml/min) or moderate to severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance 10-29 ml/min)

items.t: Hepatic impairment: use with caution and a lower or less frequent dose (about 3-fold higher exposure in mild cirrhosis). Severe hepatic impairment: should not be used (no data).

src.q: A lower or less frequent dose should be used in patients with hepatic impairment
Sertraline should not be used in cases of severe hepatic impairment as no clinical data are available

items.t: SmPC: not recommended in pregnancy unless the woman's clinical condition means benefit is expected to outweigh risk. No evidence of malformations in substantial data.

src.q: Sertraline is not recommended in pregnancy, unless the clinical condition of the woman is such that the benefit of the treatment is expected to outweigh the potential risk.
a substantial amount of data did not reveal evidence of induction of congenital malformations by sertraline

items.t: Late pregnancy/third trimester: observe the neonate (withdrawal or serotonergic symptoms, usually within 24 hours); small increased risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (about 5 per 1000 vs 1-2 per 1000).

src.q: Neonates should be observed if maternal use of sertraline continues into the later stages of pregnancy, particularly the third trimester.
The observed risk was approximately 5 cases per 1000 pregnancies.

items.t: Postpartum haemorrhage: use in the month before delivery may increase risk (less than 2-fold). MHRA: consider individual bleeding/thrombotic risk; do not stop anticoagulants in high-risk women because of this.

src.q: Observational data indicate an increased risk (less than 2-fold) of postpartum haemorrhage following SSRI/SNRI exposure within the month prior to birth
consider the findings of the review in the context of individual patient risk factors for bleeding or thrombotic events

items.t: BUMPS: SSRIs are commonly taken in pregnancy without problems; stopping sertraline can cause relapse and withdrawal - do not stop without advice. Hospital delivery usually advised.

src.q: SSRIs are commonly taken during pregnancy without any problem.
Stopping sertraline can increase the risk of relapse and stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms.
Women taking an SSRI in pregnancy will usually be advised to have a hospital delivery.

items.t: SmPC: small amounts pass into milk; no infant harm reported but risk cannot be excluded - not recommended unless benefit outweighs risk.

src.q: Use in nursing mothers is not recommended unless, in the judgment of the physician, the benefit outweighs the risk.

items.t: SPS (differs from SmPC): sertraline is an SSRI of choice in breastfeeding (very small amounts in milk). As a precaution monitor the infant for agitation, restlessness, sleep disturbance, diarrhoea, poor feeding and weight gain. No need to switch an SSRI used successfully in pregnancy (term, healthy infant).

src.q: Paroxetine and sertraline are the SSRIs of choice during breastfeeding.
As a precaution, monitor for agitation, restlessness, insomnia, drowsiness or other sleep disturbances, diarrhoea, poor feeding and adequate weight-gain.
There is no need to change an SSRI used successfully during pregnancy to a preferred choice in breastfeeding as long as the infant has been born full term and healthy.

items.t: Fertility: no animal effect; SSRI effects on sperm quality are reversible in case reports. Sexual dysfunction (ejaculation failure very common) - can persist after stopping (MHRA 2026: discuss PSSD when starting/changing dose).

src.q: Human case reports with some SSRI's have shown that an effect on sperm quality is reversible.
that there is evidence that some antidepressants [footnote 1] . are associated with a risk of sexual dysfunction and that symptoms may continue after stopping treatment with certain antidepressants

items.t: Very common: nausea, diarrhoea, dry mouth; dizziness, headache, somnolence; insomnia; fatigue; ejaculation failure. Nausea is the most common.

src.q: Nausea is the most common undesirable effect.
Gastrointestinal disorders nausea, diarrhoea, dry mouth
Nervous system disorders dizziness, headache*, somnolence

items.t: Common: dyspepsia, constipation, abdominal pain, vomiting; tremor, paraesthesia; anxiety, agitation, decreased libido; sweating, rash; erectile dysfunction; weight increase; palpitations.

src.q: dyspepsia, constipation*, abdominal pain*, vomiting*, flatulence

items.t: Withdrawal symptoms on stopping are common (dizziness, sensory disturbance, sleep disturbance, anxiety, nausea, tremor, headache).

src.q: Withdrawal symptoms when treatment is discontinued are common, particularly if discontinuation is abrupt

items.t: Serotonin syndrome or NMS (agitation, confusion, sweating, fever, rigidity, tachycardia): potentially life-threatening; risk higher with other serotonergic drugs. Monitor for signs and symptoms.

src.q: The development of potentially life-threatening syndromes like serotonin syndrome (SS) or Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS) has been reported with SSRIs, including treatment with sertraline.
Patients should be monitored for the emergence of signs and symptoms of SS or NMS syndrome

items.t: New or worse suicidal thoughts: seek urgent medical attention (MHRA 2026).

src.q: if you have new or worsening suicidal thoughts, particularly when starting or changing dose of antidepressants, seek urgent medical attention

items.t: Abnormal bleeding (e.g. GI bleeding; uncommon), including fatal haemorrhage reports.

src.q: other haemorrhagic events such as gastrointestinal or gynaecological bleeding, including fatal haemorrhages

items.t: Symptomatic hyponatraemia (rare): headache, confusion, weakness, falls; severe - seizures, coma. Consider stopping.

src.q: Signs and symptoms of hyponatraemia include headache, difficulty concentrating, memory impairment, confusion, weakness and unsteadiness which may lead to falls.
Signs and symptoms associated with more severe and/or acute cases have included hallucination, syncope, seizure, coma, respiratory arrest, and death.
Discontinuation of sertraline should be considered in patients with symptomatic hyponatraemia

items.t: Rare: QTc prolongation/torsade de pointes, seizures, serious liver events, severe skin reactions (SJS/TEN), mania.

src.q: hepatic function abnormal, serious liver events (including hepatitis, jaundice and hepatic failure)

items.t: When starting or changing dose: discuss risk of suicidal thoughts and of sexual dysfunction; monitor regularly after starting (MHRA 2026).

src.q: discuss with patients when starting or changing the dose of an antidepressant or at their next review, the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviours
monitor your patients regularly after starting treatment with an antidepressant

items.t: Close monitoring for clinical worsening and suicidality early in treatment and after dose changes; watch for signs of serotonin syndrome.

src.q: patients should be closely monitored until such improvement occurs
Patients should be monitored for the emergence of signs and symptoms of SS or NMS syndrome

items.t: Warfarin: monitor prothrombin time/INR when sertraline is started or stopped. Children on long-term treatment: monitor growth and development.

src.q: prothrombin time should be carefully monitored when sertraline therapy is initiated or stopped
Physicians must monitor paediatric patients on long term treatment for abnormalities in growth and development.

items.t: Stop if: manic phase, seizures; consider stopping if symptomatic hyponatraemia. Taper when stopping.

src.q: Sertraline should be discontinued in any patient entering a manic phase.
Sertraline should be discontinued in any patient who develops seizures.

items.t: Once daily, morning or evening, with or without food.

src.q: Sertraline should be administered once daily, either in the morning or evening.
Sertraline tablet can be administered with or without food.

items.t: Oral concentrate: measure with the syringe provided and dilute in about 120 ml of water, ginger ale, lemon/lime soda, lemonade or orange juice only; take immediately; do not prepare in advance.

src.q: dilute with approximately 120 ml (one glass) of water, ginger ale, lemon/lime soda, lemonade or orange juice
The dose should be taken immediately after dilution. Do not prepare in advance.

items.t: Seek urgent help (NHS 111, crisis team, Samaritans 116 123) for new or worse suicidal thoughts, especially early or after dose changes.

src.q: You can call NHS 111, or your local mental health crisis team, Samaritans on 116 123

items.t: Sexual problems can occur and may continue after stopping - talk to your prescriber; do not stop without advice.

src.q: do not stop taking your medicine without first speaking to your healthcare professional

items.t: Do not stop suddenly (withdrawal symptoms); effect may take several weeks.

src.q: Abrupt discontinuation should be avoided.
longer periods are usually necessary to demonstrate therapeutic response, especially in OCD

items.t: Avoid alcohol and grapefruit juice. Avoid St John's wort. Be careful driving until you know how you react.

src.q: the concomitant use of sertraline and alcohol is not recommended
the intake of grapefruit juice should be avoided during treatment with sertraline
should be undertaken with caution and avoided whenever possible
the patient should be cautioned accordingly

items.t: Erectile dysfunction in adult men (sexual stimulation needed). Not indicated for women.

src.q: VIAGRA is indicated in adult men with erectile dysfunction, which is the inability to achieve or maintain a penile erection sufficient for satisfactory sexual performance.
VIAGRA is not indicated for use by women.

items.t: Pulmonary arterial hypertension: adults in WHO functional class II-III (to improve exercise capacity); children aged 1-17 years.

src.q: Treatment of adult patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension classified as WHO functional class II and III, to improve exercise capacity.
Treatment of paediatric patients aged 1 year to 17 years old with pulmonary arterial hypertension.

items.t: PAH: initiate and monitor only by a physician experienced in treating pulmonary arterial hypertension.

src.q: Treatment should only be initiated and monitored by a physician experienced in the treatment of pulmonary arterial hypertension.
Treatment should only be initiated and monitored by a physician experienced in the treatment of pulmonary arterial hypertension.

items.t: MHRA: sildenafil is not authorised for intrauterine (fetal) growth restriction and should not be used for it.

src.q: sildenafil should not be used in intrauterine (fetal) growth restriction

items.t: 50 mg as needed about 1 hour before sexual activity; adjust to 25 mg or 100 mg. Maximum 100 mg, no more than once a day. Food may delay onset.

src.q: The recommended dose is 50 mg taken as needed approximately one hour before sexual activity.
The maximum recommended dose is 100 mg. The maximum recommended dosing frequency is once per day.

items.t: ED with CYP3A4 inhibitors: consider a 25 mg starting dose. Ritonavir not advised; if given, never more than 25 mg in 48 hours. Alpha-blockers: stabilise first and consider 25 mg start.

src.q: a starting dose of 25 mg should be considered in patients receiving concomitant treatment with CYP3A4 inhibitors
the maximum dose of sildenafil should under no circumstances exceed 25 mg within 48 hours.

items.t: 20 mg three times a day, about 6-8 hours apart, with or without food. Missed dose: take as soon as possible; do not double.

src.q: The recommended dose is 20 mg three times a day (TID).
Tablets should be taken approximately 6 to 8 hours apart with or without food.

items.t: PAH with CYP3A4 inhibitors: consider 20 mg twice daily with erythromycin or saquinavir-type inhibitors; 20 mg once daily recommended with clarithromycin, telithromycin or nefazodone. Most potent inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir): contraindicated.

src.q: A downward dose adjustment to 20 mg twice daily should be considered when sildenafil is co-administered to patients already receiving CYP3A4 inhibitors like erythromycin or saquinavir.
A downward dose adjustment to 20 mg once daily is recommended in case of co-administration with more potent CYP3A4 inhibitors clarithromycin, telithromycin and nefazodone.

items.t: PAH stopping: consider gradual dose reduction with closer monitoring during withdrawal.

src.q: to avoid the possible occurrence of sudden clinical deterioration during withdrawal, a gradual dose reduction should be considered.

items.t: Elderly: no dose adjustment (ED and PAH).

src.q: Dose adjustments are not required in elderly patients (≥ 65 years old).
Elderly (≥ 65 years) Dose adjustments are not required in elderly patients.

items.t: ED product: not indicated under 18 years.

src.q: VIAGRA is not indicated for individuals below 18 years of age.

items.t: PAH, 1-17 years: 20 kg or less - 10 mg (1 ml suspension) three times a day; over 20 kg - 20 mg (tablet or 2 ml suspension) three times a day. Do not use higher doses (more deaths seen with higher doses). Do not use the 20 mg tablet when 10 mg is needed.

src.q: the recommended dose in patients ≤ 20 kg is 10 mg (1 ml of reconstituted suspension) three times a day and for patients > 20 kg is 20 mg (2 ml of reconstituted suspension) three times a day.
In the long term paediatric extension study, an increase in deaths was observed in patients administered doses higher than the recommended dose.
The 20 mg tablet should not be used in cases where 10 mg TID should be administered in younger patients.

items.t: Under 1 year: safety and efficacy not established. Neonates with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn: should not be used (risks outweigh benefits).

src.q: Outside its authorised indications, sildenafil should not be used in neonates with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn as risks outweigh the benefits
The safety and efficacy of Revatio in other conditions in children below 1 year of age has not been established.

items.t: All: hypersensitivity; nitrates in any form or nitric oxide donors (e.g. amyl nitrite); guanylate cyclase stimulators such as riociguat; loss of vision in one eye from NAION; severe hepatic impairment; recent stroke or myocardial infarction; hypotension below 90/50 mmHg (PAH: severe hypotension at initiation).

src.q: its co-administration with nitric oxide donors (such as amyl nitrite) or nitrates in any form is therefore contraindicated.

The safety of sildenafil has not been studied in the following sub-groups of patients and its use is therefore contraindicated: severe hepatic impairment, hypotension (blood pressure < 90/50 mmHg), recent history of stroke or myocardial infarction
Severe hepatic impairment, Recent history of stroke or myocardial infarction, Severe hypotension (blood pressure < 90/50 mmHg) at initiation.

items.t: ED product: men for whom sexual activity is inadvisable (e.g. unstable angina, severe cardiac failure); hereditary degenerative retinal disorders such as retinitis pigmentosa.

src.q: should not be used in men for whom sexual activity is inadvisable (e.g. patients with severe cardiovascular disorders such as unstable angina or severe cardiac failure).
known hereditary degenerative retinal disorders such as retinitis pigmentosa

items.t: PAH products: combination with the most potent CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir).

src.q: Combination with the most potent of the CYP3A4 inhibitors (eg, ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir)

items.t: Cardiovascular: serious events (MI, unstable angina, sudden cardiac death, arrhythmia, stroke) reported, mostly in men with risk factors. Consider cardiovascular status before ED treatment. Take care with left ventricular outflow obstruction (aortic stenosis, HOCM) or autonomic failure.

src.q: Prior to initiating any treatment for erectile dysfunction, physicians should consider the cardiovascular status of their patients, since there is a degree of cardiac risk associated with sexual activity.
Patients with increased susceptibility to vasodilators include those with left ventricular outflow obstruction (e.g., aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy)

items.t: Priapism risk: use with caution with penile deformity (angulation, cavernosal fibrosis, Peyronie's disease) or conditions predisposing to priapism (sickle cell anaemia, multiple myeloma, leukaemia). Erection lasting over 4 hours needs immediate medical help.

src.q: should be used with caution in patients with anatomical deformation of the penis (such as angulation, cavernosal fibrosis or Peyronie's disease), or in patients who have conditions which may predispose them to priapism (such as sickle cell anaemia, multiple myeloma or leukaemia).
In the event of an erection that persists longer than 4 hours, the patient should seek immediate medical assistance.

items.t: Sudden visual loss (NAION reported): stop and see a doctor at once.

src.q: Patients should be advised that in the event of any sudden visual defect, they should stop taking VIAGRA and consult a physician immediately
In the event of any sudden visual defect, the treatment should be stopped immediately and alternative treatment should be considered

items.t: Bleeding disorders or active peptic ulceration: use only after careful benefit-risk assessment (no safety data).

src.q: There is no safety information on the administration of sildenafil to patients with bleeding disorders or active peptic ulceration. Therefore sildenafil should be administered to these patients only after careful benefit-risk assessment.

items.t: Alpha-blockers: symptomatic hypotension possible (mostly within 4 hours); patient should be stable on the alpha-blocker first.

src.q: Caution is advised when sildenafil is administered to patients taking an alpha-blocker, as the co-administration may lead to symptomatic hypotension in a few susceptible individuals

items.t: PAH: not recommended in retinitis pigmentosa; should not be used in pulmonary hypertension secondary to sickle cell anaemia (vaso-occlusive crises); efficacy not shown in functional class IV; consider veno-occlusive disease if pulmonary oedema occurs.

src.q: and therefore its use is not recommended.
Sildenafil should not be used in patients with pulmonary hypertension secondary to sickle cell anaemia.
should signs of pulmonary oedema occur when sildenafil is administered in patients with pulmonary hypertension, the possibility of associated veno-occlusive disease should be considered.

items.t: PAH: consider carefully whether the vasodilator effect could harm patients with hypotension, fluid depletion, severe left ventricular outflow obstruction or autonomic dysfunction.

src.q: physicians should carefully consider whether patients with certain underlying conditions could be adversely affected by sildenafil's mild to moderate vasodilatory effects
for example patients with hypotension, patients with fluid depletion, severe left ventricular outflow obstruction or autonomic dysfunction

items.t: PAH: possible increased bleeding risk when started in patients on a vitamin K antagonist, particularly PAH from connective tissue disease.

src.q: there may be a potential for increased risk of bleeding when sildenafil is initiated in patients already using a Vitamin K antagonist

items.t: Do not combine with other PDE5 inhibitors or other sildenafil products (e.g. an erectile dysfunction product with a PAH product): not studied, not recommended.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of combinations of sildenafil with other PDE5 Inhibitors, or other pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) treatments containing sildenafil (REVATIO), or other treatments for erectile dysfunction have not been studied. Therefore the use of such combinations is not recommended.

items.t: Excipients: the erectile dysfunction tablets and the PAH tablets contain lactose - patients with hereditary galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take them. The PAH oral suspension contains sorbitol (250 mg/ml) - patients with hereditary fructose intolerance should not take it; it also contains sodium benzoate.

src.q: VIAGRA should not be administered to men with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption.
Lactose monohydrate is present in the tablet film coat.
Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
Each ml of reconstituted oral suspension contains 250 mg sorbitol.
Patients with rare hereditary fructose intolerance (HFI) should not take this medicinal product.

items.t: Nitrates (any form) and nitric oxide donors, including nicorandil (nitrate component): potentiated hypotension - contraindicated.

src.q: sildenafil was shown to potentiate the hypotensive effects of nitrates, and its co-administration with nitric oxide donors or nitrates in any form is therefore contraindicated
Due to the nitrate component it has the potential to result in a serious interaction with sildenafil.

items.t: CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. erythromycin, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, cimetidine): raise sildenafil levels. ED: consider 25 mg start. PAH: reduce dose (see dosing); most potent inhibitors contraindicated.

src.q: when sildenafil is administered concomitantly with CYP3A4 inhibitors, a starting dose of 25 mg should be considered.
Therefore dose adjustments are recommended when using CYP3A4 inhibitors

items.t: PAH: potent CYP3A4 inducers (e.g. carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, St John's wort, rifampicin) lower sildenafil levels; monitor efficacy closely.

src.q: Efficacy of sildenafil should be closely monitored in patients using concomitant potent CYP3A4 inducers, such as carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, St John's wort and rifampicine.

items.t: Amlodipine: extra fall in supine BP of about 8/7 mmHg (similar to sildenafil alone).

src.q: In a specific interaction study, where sildenafil (100 mg) was co-administered with amlodipine in hypertensive patients, there was an additional reduction on supine systolic blood pressure of 8 mmHg.

items.t: Sacubitril/valsartan: greater BP fall; caution when starting sildenafil.

src.q: Therefore, caution should be exercised when sildenafil is initiated in patients treated with sacubitril/valsartan.

items.t: Warfarin and aspirin: no significant interaction in studies; PAH SmPC notes a possible bleeding risk with vitamin K antagonists.

src.q: No significant interactions were shown when sildenafil (50 mg) was co-administered with tolbutamide (250 mg) or warfarin (40 mg)

items.t: Grapefruit juice: modest rise in sildenafil levels; PAH SmPC - not recommended together.

src.q: No dose adjustment is required but the concomitant use of sildenafil and grapefruit juice is not recommended.

items.t: ED: CrCl 30-80 mL/min - usual dosing. CrCl < 30 mL/min - consider 25 mg; increase step-wise to 50-100 mg as needed.

src.q: Since sildenafil clearance is reduced in patients with severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance < 30 mL/min) a 25 mg dose should be considered.

items.t: PAH: no initial adjustment, including CrCl < 30 ml/min; consider 20 mg twice daily only if not well tolerated.

src.q: Initial dose adjustments are not required in patients with renal impairment, including severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance < 30 ml/min ).
A downward dose adjustment to 20 mg twice daily should be considered after a careful benefit-risk assessment only if therapy is not well-tolerated.

items.t: ED: hepatic impairment (e.g. cirrhosis) - consider 25 mg, then step up as needed. Severe hepatic impairment - contraindicated.

src.q: Since sildenafil clearance is reduced in patients with hepatic impairment (e.g. cirrhosis) a 25 mg dose should be considered.

items.t: PAH: Child-Pugh A and B - no initial adjustment (20 mg twice daily only if not tolerated). Child-Pugh C - contraindicated.

src.q: Initial dose adjustments are not required in patients with hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh class A and B).
Revatio is contraindicated in patients with severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh class C)

items.t: ED product: not indicated for women.

src.q: VIAGRA is not indicated for use by women.

items.t: PAH: no human data; should not be used in pregnancy unless strictly necessary (SmPC and MHRA).

src.q: Due to lack of data, Revatio should not be used in pregnant women unless strictly necessary.
Revatio for the treatment of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is not recommended in pregnancy unless strictly necessary

items.t: MHRA: a trial of sildenafil for early-onset fetal growth restriction showed more persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn and neonatal deaths; not authorised for this use.

src.q: data from an independent clinical trial has shown potential harm, including increased risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) and increased mortality, when used in pregnancy for early-onset intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)

items.t: BUMPS: sometimes used in pregnancy for PAH; no clear risks identified. No increased risk expected if the father took sildenafil around conception.

src.q: There are no clear risks of taking sildenafil in pregnancy.
We would not expect any increased risk to your baby if the father took sildenafil before or around the time your baby was conceived

items.t: PAH: one case showed very low milk levels; no infant adverse effects expected. Weigh the mother's need against possible effects on the infant.

src.q: Data from one lactating woman indicate that sildenafil and its active metabolite N-desmethylsildenafil are excreted into breast milk at very low levels.
Prescribers should carefully assess the mother's clinical need for sildenafil and any potential adverse effects on the breast-fed child.

items.t: ED product: not indicated for women. No SPS breastfeeding page for sildenafil was found.

src.q: There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant or breast-feeding women.

items.t: PAH: not recommended for women of childbearing potential unless using appropriate contraception.

src.q: Revatio is not recommended for women of childbearing potential unless also using appropriate contraceptive measures.

items.t: ED: no effect on sperm motility or morphology after single 100 mg doses.

src.q: There was no effect on sperm motility or morphology after single 100 mg oral doses of sildenafil in healthy volunteers

items.t: ED: most common - headache, flushing, dyspepsia, nasal congestion, dizziness, nausea, hot flush, visual disturbance, cyanopsia, blurred vision.

src.q: The most commonly reported adverse reactions in clinical studies among sildenafil treated patients were headache, flushing, dyspepsia, nasal congestion, dizziness, nausea, hot flush, visual disturbance, cyanopsia and vision blurred.

items.t: PAH: very common - headache, flushing, diarrhoea, dyspepsia, pain in extremity. Children: pyrexia, upper respiratory infection, vomiting, increased erections, nausea, bronchitis.

src.q: The most commonly reported adverse reactions that occurred (greater or equal to 10 %) on Revatio compared to placebo were headache, flushing, dyspepsia, diarrhoea and pain in extremity.
were pyrexia, upper respiratory tract infection (each 11.5%), vomiting (10.9%), erection increased (including spontaneous penile erections in male subjects) (9.0%)

items.t: Priapism or erection lasting over 4 hours: seek immediate medical help (risk of permanent damage).

src.q: If priapism is not treated immediately, penile tissue damage and permanent loss of potency could result.

items.t: Sudden loss of vision (NAION, retinal vascular occlusion): stop and see a doctor immediately. Sudden hearing loss reported (PAH).

src.q: Non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (NAION)*, Retinal vascular occlusion*
Not known sudden hearing loss

items.t: Serious cardiovascular events (MI, unstable angina, sudden cardiac death, ventricular arrhythmia, cerebrovascular haemorrhage) reported, often during or after sexual activity. Stevens-Johnson syndrome and TEN reported (ED, rare).

src.q: Serious cardiovascular events, including myocardial infarction, unstable angina, sudden cardiac death, ventricular arrhythmia, cerebrovascular haemorrhage, transient ischaemic attack, hypertension and hypotension have been reported post-marketing
Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS)*, Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN)*

items.t: PAH: specialist initiation and monitoring; closer monitoring when stopping treatment; monitor efficacy with potent CYP3A4 inducers.

src.q: Intensified monitoring is recommended during the discontinuation period.
Efficacy of sildenafil should be closely monitored in patients using concomitant potent CYP3A4 inducers

items.t: ED: assess cardiovascular status and take a history and examination before treatment.

src.q: A medical history and physical examination should be undertaken to diagnose erectile dysfunction and determine potential underlying causes, before pharmacological treatment is considered.

items.t: ED tablets: oral, about 1 hour before sexual activity; food may delay onset.

src.q: If VIAGRA is taken with food, the onset of activity may be delayed compared to the fasted state

items.t: PAH tablets: 6-8 hours apart, with or without food.

src.q: Tablets should be taken approximately 6 to 8 hours apart with or without food.

items.t: PAH suspension: shake the bottle hard for at least 10 seconds before each dose; doses 6-8 hours apart, with or without food.

src.q: Before withdrawing the required dose, shake the bottle vigorously for a minimum of 10 seconds.
should be taken approximately 6 to 8 hours apart with or without food.

items.t: Never take with nitrates (e.g. GTN, isosorbide mononitrate) or amyl nitrite ('poppers').

src.q: its co-administration with nitric oxide donors (such as amyl nitrite) or nitrates in any form is therefore contraindicated.

items.t: Erection lasting more than 4 hours, or sudden loss of vision: get urgent medical help / stop and see a doctor.

src.q: In the event of an erection that persists longer than 4 hours, the patient should seek immediate medical assistance.
they should stop taking VIAGRA and consult a physician immediately

items.t: Dizziness and altered vision can affect driving.

src.q: As dizziness and altered vision were reported in clinical studies with sildenafil, patients should be aware of how they react to VIAGRA, before driving or operating machinery.

items.t: PAH: if a dose is missed take it as soon as possible, then continue; do not double up.

src.q: Patients should not take a double dose to compensate for the missed dose.

items.t: Prevention and treatment of infection in burn wounds.

src.q: is indicated for the prophylaxis and treatment of infection in burn wounds

items.t: Aid to short-term treatment of infection in leg ulcers and pressure sores; aid to infection prevention in skin graft donor sites and extensive abrasions; conservative management of finger-tip injuries.

src.q: as an aid to the short-term treatment of infection in leg ulcers and pressure sores
skin graft donor sites and extensive abrasions
conservative management of finger- tip injuries

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction stated in the UK SPC (MHRA products) accessed; no emc SmPC, MHRA Drug Safety Update, SPS or BUMPS page specific to silver sulfadiazine was found.

items.t: Burns: clean the wound and apply a 3 to 5 mm layer over all affected areas. Re-apply at least every 24 hours, or more often if there is a lot of exudate.

src.q: applied over all the affected areas to a depth of 3-5mm
should be re-applied at least every 24 hours, or more frequently if the volume of exudate is large

items.t: Leg ulcers and pressure sores: clean and debride, fill the cavity to at least 3 to 5 mm, cover with an absorbent dressing; change daily (every 48 hours may be enough for less exudative wounds). Not recommended for very exudative ulcers.

src.q: The cavity of the ulcer should be filled with FLAMAZINE Cream to a depth of at least 3-5mm.
The dressings should normally be changed daily but for wounds which are less exudative, less frequent changes (every 48 hours) may be acceptable.
is not recommended for use in leg or pressure ulcers that are very exudative

items.t: Finger-tip injuries: achieve haemostasis, apply a 3 to 5 mm layer, change dressings every 2 to 3 days.

src.q: Haemostasis of the injury should be achieved prior to the application
Dressings should be changed every 2-3 days.

items.t: Contraindicated in premature infants and newborns in the first months of life; the SPC states contraindicated in children up to 3 months (risk of kernicterus).

src.q: contraindicated in children aged to three months
on premature infants or on newborn infants during the first months of life

items.t: Pregnancy at or near term, premature infants, and newborns in the first months of life (sulfonamides can cause kernicterus).

src.q: As sulphonamides are known to cause kernicterus, FLAMAZINE Cream should not be used at, or near term pregnancy, on premature infants or on newborn infants during the first months of life.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to sulfonamides, silver sulfadiazine, or excipients such as cetyl alcohol or propylene glycol.

src.q: contraindicated in patients known to be hypersensitive to sulphonamides and silver sulfadiazine or to other components of the preparation such as cetyl alcohol or propylene glycol

items.t: Life-threatening skin reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis) have been reported, highest risk in the first weeks. Warn patients, monitor the skin closely, and stop if signs appear (e.g. spreading rash with blisters or mucosal lesions). Never restart after SJS/TEN.

src.q: Life-threatening cutaneous reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN)) have been reported with the use of silver sulfadiazine.
The highest risk for occurrence of SJS or TEN is within the first weeks of treatment.
silver sulfadiazine must not be re-started in this patient at any time

items.t: Use with caution in significant hepatic or renal impairment.

src.q: should be used with caution in the presence of significant hepatic or renal impairment

items.t: Caution in people sensitive to systemic sulfonamides and in G6PD deficiency.

src.q: Caution of use is required in patients known to be sensitive to systemic sulphonamides and in individuals known to have glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency.

items.t: May delay separation of burn eschar and change the appearance of burn wounds.

src.q: may delay separation of burn eschar and may alter the appearance of the burn wounds

items.t: Large-area burns: serum sulfadiazine may approach therapeutic levels and alter the effect of systemic medicines, especially oral antidiabetic medicines and phenytoin. Monitor blood levels, as their effects can be potentiated.

src.q: In large-area burns where serum sulfadiazine levels may approach therapeutic levels, it should be noted that the effects of systemically administered drugs may be altered.
This can especially apply to oral hypoglycaemic agents and to phenytoin.
it is recommended that blood levels should be monitored as their effects can be potentiated

items.t: Enzymatic debriding agents: silver may inactivate them; using both may be inappropriate.

src.q: As silver may inactivate enzymatic debriding agents, concomitant use may be inappropriate.

items.t: Povidone-iodine: the povidone-iodine SPCs say silver-containing products and povidone-iodine reduce each other's effect and should not be used together.

src.q: Products containing mercury, silver, hydrogen peroxide, and taurolidine may interact with povidone-iodine and cause mutual reduction of effects.
Povidone-iodine should not be used together with alkali, hydrogen peroxide, taurolidine, tannic acid, and silver and mercury salts.

items.t: Use with caution in significant renal impairment (no numeric threshold given). Sulfadiazine is absorbed through wounds and excreted in the urine; renal failure is a very rare adverse effect.

src.q: should be used with caution in the presence of significant hepatic or renal impairment
Sulfadiazine is excreted in the urine.
Very rare: Renal failure

items.t: Use with caution in significant hepatic impairment (severity not defined).

src.q: should be used with caution in the presence of significant hepatic or renal impairment

items.t: Contraindicated at or near term (kernicterus risk with sulfonamides). No clinical data on exposed pregnancies; animal studies showed no hazard.

src.q: should not be used in pregnant females at term
no clinical data on exposed pregnancies are available, although animal studies have not shown any hazard

items.t: Caution in breastfeeding: absorbed sulfadiazine passes into milk at 15 to 35% of serum levels.

src.q: caution is required in nursing mothers
