Systemically absorbed sulfadiazine can be excreted in breast milk although at concentrations 15-35% of those found in serum.

reproductive.note: The UK SPC (MHRA products) gives no fertility or contraception statement.

items.t: Common: leucopenia (3 to 5% of burns patients, often 2 to 3 days after starting; usually self-limiting), application-site burning, itching, application-site rash including eczema and contact dermatitis.

src.q: Leukopenia has been reported in 3-5% of burns patients
often manifests itself 2-3 days after treatment has commenced
Common: Application site burning
Common: Application site rash (including eczema and contact dermatitis)

items.t: Very rare Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis: stop treatment and never restart.

src.q: Very rare: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs) Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN)
silver sulfadiazine treatment should be discontinued

items.t: Very rare renal failure. Rare argyria (silver absorption) with large wounds or prolonged use.

src.q: Very rare: Renal failure
Rare: Argyria
in large area wounds and/or after prolonged application,systemic absorption of silver can occur causing clinical argyria

items.t: If leucopenia occurs, monitor the blood count until it returns to normal (treatment usually need not stop).

src.q: the blood count must be monitored to ensure that it returns to normal within a few days
therapy with FLAMAZINE Cream does not usually need to be discontinued

items.t: Monitor closely for skin reactions, especially in the first weeks.

src.q: Patients should be advised of the signs and symptoms and monitored closely for skin reactions.

items.t: Stop if signs of SJS/TEN appear (e.g. progressive rash with blisters or mucosal lesions).

src.q: If symptoms or signs of SJS or TEN (e.g. progressive skin rash often with blisters or mucosal lesions) are present, silver sulfadiazine treatment should be discontinued.

items.t: Large-area burns: monitor blood levels of oral antidiabetic medicines and phenytoin.

src.q: it is recommended that blood levels should be monitored as their effects can be potentiated

items.t: Apply with a sterile gloved hand and/or sterile spatula. Hand burns: apply and enclose the hand in a clear plastic bag or glove closed at the wrist; encourage movement.

src.q: This application is best achieved with a sterile gloved hand and/or sterile spatula.
the whole hand enclosed in a clear plastic bag or glove, which is then closed at the wrist

items.t: Ulcers: keep the cream off surrounding normal skin, as prolonged contact can macerate it.

src.q: can cause maceration of normal skin on prolonged contact

items.t: One container is for one person only. Discard tubes 7 days after opening and large pots 24 hours after opening.

src.q: The contents of one container are for the treatment of one person.
Tubes of FLAMAZINE Cream should be discarded 7 days after opening.
250g and 500g pots should be discarded 24 hours after opening.

items.t: Report any spreading rash, blisters or mouth/eye sores at once.

src.q: Patients should be advised of the signs and symptoms and monitored closely for skin reactions.

items.t: Symptomatic relief of flatulence, wind pains, bloating, abdominal distension and other symptoms of intestinal gas.

src.q: Anti-flatulent defoaming agent for the symptomatic relief of flatulence, wind pains, bloating, abdominal distension and other symptoms associated with intestinal gas

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction stated in the UK SmPC accessed (UK 100 mg capsule SmPC).

items.t: Capsule SmPC: adults, elderly and children, 100-200 mg (one or two 100 mg capsules) 3 or 4 times daily, or as required. No UK dose for the clinic tablet strengths.

src.q: Adults, the elderly and children: One or two capsules taken 3 or 4 times daily or as required for relief

items.t: Capsule SmPC gives the same dose for children as adults; no lower age limit is stated.

src.q: Adults, the elderly and children: One or two capsules taken 3 or 4 times daily or as required for relief

items.t: Hypersensitivity to any of the ingredients.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to any of the ingredients.

cautions.note: The UK 100 mg capsule SmPC section 4.4 states none.

items.t: Capsule SmPC: none reported.

src.q: other forms of interaction None reported.

items.t: Infant oral suspension SmPC: levothyroxine may bind to simeticone; levothyroxine absorption may be reduced if given at the same time to infants treated for thyroid disorders.

src.q: Levothyroxine may bind to simeticone.
Absorption of levothyroxine may be impaired if Dentinox Infant Colic Drops are given concurrently to infants treated for thyroid disorders.

renal.note: No renal impairment advice in the UK SmPC accessed (UK 100 mg capsule SmPC).

hepatic.note: No hepatic impairment advice in the UK SmPC accessed (UK 100 mg capsule SmPC).

items.t: Not absorbed, so no adverse effect on pregnancy is expected; as with all drugs, use with caution. No BUMPS leaflet for simeticone found.

src.q: As dimeticone is not absorbed, it is not anticipated that WindSetlers will have any adverse effects on pregnancy and lactation. However, as with all drugs, caution should be exercised in these conditions.

items.t: SmPC: not absorbed, so no adverse effect expected; use with caution.

src.q: As dimeticone is not absorbed, it is not anticipated that WindSetlers will have any adverse effects on pregnancy and lactation. However, as with all drugs, caution should be exercised in these conditions.

items.t: SPS: preferred choice in breastfeeding; excretion into milk unlikely; no specific infant monitoring usually needed.

src.q: Simeticone can be used during breastfeeding.
Excretion into breast milk is unlikely due to the very high molecular weight.

reproductive.note: No fertility information in the UK SmPC accessed (UK 100 mg capsule SmPC).

items.t: Minor effects: nausea and constipation (frequency not stated).

src.q: Minor adverse effects: nausea and constipation.

items.t: Rare hypersensitivity: rash, pruritus, facial or tongue oedema, breathing difficulty.

src.q: Rarely, hypersensitivity reactions such as rash, pruritis, facial oedema, tongue oedema and respiratory difficulty have been reported.

monitoring.note: No monitoring requirements stated in the UK SmPC accessed (UK 100 mg capsule SmPC).

administration.note: No administration advice beyond oral use in the UK SmPC accessed (UK 100 mg capsule SmPC).

counselling.note: No specific counselling points in the UK SmPC accessed (UK 100 mg capsule SmPC).

items.t: Primary hypercholesterolaemia or mixed dyslipidaemia, as an adjunct to diet when diet and other non-drug measures are not enough.

src.q: Treatment of primary hypercholesterolaemia or mixed dyslipidaemia, as an adjunct to diet

items.t: Homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, as an adjunct to diet and other lipid-lowering treatment (e.g. LDL apheresis).

src.q: Treatment of homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (HoFH) as an adjunct to diet and other lipid-lowering treatments

items.t: Reduction of cardiovascular mortality and morbidity in manifest atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease or diabetes mellitus, with normal or raised cholesterol.

src.q: Reduction of cardiovascular mortality and morbidity in patients with manifest atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease or diabetes mellitus

items.t: 80 mg dose only for severe hypercholesterolaemia at high cardiovascular risk not at goal on lower doses, when benefits are expected to outweigh risks (higher myopathy risk).

src.q: The 80-mg dose is only recommended in patients with severe hypercholesterolaemia and at high risk for cardiovascular complications who have not achieved their treatment goals on lower doses
Simvastatin 80 mg should be considered only in patients with severe hypercholesterolaemia and high risk of cardiovascular complications

items.t: Dose range 5-80 mg/day as a single evening dose; adjust at intervals of not less than 4 weeks; maximum 80 mg/day.

src.q: The dosage range is 5-80 mg/day of simvastatin given orally as a single dose in the evening.
to a maximum of 80 mg/day given as a single dose in the evening

items.t: Hypercholesterolaemia: usual starting dose 10-20 mg/day in the evening; if LDL-C needs to fall by more than 45%, may start at 20-40 mg/day.

src.q: The usual starting dose is 10-20 mg/day given as a single dose in the evening.
Patients who require a large reduction in LDL-C (more than 45 %) may be started at 20-40 mg/day

items.t: Homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia: recommended starting dose 40 mg/day in the evening. With lomitapide, do not exceed 40 mg/day.

src.q: the recommended starting dosage is Zocor 40 mg/day in the evening
In patients taking lomitapide concomitantly with Zocor, the dose of Zocor must not exceed 40 mg/day

items.t: Cardiovascular prevention: usual dose 20 to 40 mg/day as a single evening dose.

src.q: The usual dose of Zocor is 20 to 40 mg/day given as a single dose in the evening in patients at high risk of coronary heart disease

items.t: Dose caps with other medicines: maximum 20 mg/day with amiodarone, amlodipine, verapamil, diltiazem, or elbasvir/grazoprevir; maximum 10 mg/day with fibrates other than gemfibrozil or fenofibrate.

src.q: In patients taking amiodarone, amlodipine, verapamil, diltiazem, or products containing elbasvir or grazoprevir concomitantly with Zocor, the dose of Zocor should not exceed 20 mg/day
the dose of Zocor should not exceed 10 mg/day

items.t: Bile acid sequestrants: give simvastatin more than 2 hours before or more than 4 hours after the sequestrant.

src.q: Dosing should occur either > 2 hours before or > 4 hours after administration of a bile acid sequestrant.

items.t: Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, 10-17 years (boys Tanner Stage II and above; girls at least one year post-menarche): start 10 mg once daily in the evening; range 10-40 mg/day; maximum 40 mg/day; adjust at intervals of 4 weeks or more.

src.q: the recommended usual starting dose is 10 mg once a day in the evening
The recommended dosing range is 10-40 mg/day; the maximum recommended dose is 40 mg/day.

items.t: Not studied in children younger than 10 years, pre-pubertal children or pre-menarchal girls.

src.q: Simvastatin has not been studied in patients younger than 10 years of age, nor in pre-pubertal children and pre-menarchal girls.

items.t: Adolescent girls should be counselled on contraception.

src.q: Adolescent females should be counselled on appropriate contraceptive methods while on simvastatin therapy

items.t: Hypersensitivity to simvastatin or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1. Active liver disease

items.t: Active liver disease or unexplained persistent raised serum transaminases.

src.q: Active liver disease or unexplained persistent elevations of serum transaminases.

items.t: Pregnancy and breastfeeding.

src.q: Pregnancy and lactation (see section 4.6).

items.t: Potent CYP3A4 inhibitors, e.g. itraconazole, ketoconazole, posaconazole, voriconazole, HIV protease inhibitors, boceprevir, telaprevir, erythromycin, clarithromycin, telithromycin, nefazodone, cobicistat-containing products.

src.q: Concomitant administration of potent CYP3A4 inhibitors (agents that increase AUC approximately 5 fold or greater)

items.t: Gemfibrozil, ciclosporin or danazol.

src.q: Concomitant administration of gemfibrozil, ciclosporin, or danazol

items.t: HoFH: lomitapide with simvastatin doses above 40 mg.

src.q: In patients with HoFH, concomitant administration of lomitapide with doses > 40 mg

items.t: Myopathy/rhabdomyolysis risk is dose related and higher at 80 mg. Caution with pre-disposing factors; measure CK before starting if: aged 65 or over, female, renal impairment, uncontrolled hypothyroidism, personal/family history of hereditary muscle disorders, previous statin/fibrate muscle toxicity, alcohol abuse.

src.q: As with other HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, the risk of myopathy/rhabdomyolysis is dose related.
Elderly (age ≥ 65 years). Female gender. Renal impairment. Uncontrolled hypothyroidism.

items.t: Asian patients: caution; use the lowest dose necessary (higher myopathy incidence seen in Chinese patients).

src.q: caution should be used when prescribing simvastatin to Asian patients and the lowest dose necessary should be employed

items.t: SLCO1B1 c.521T>C (CC genotype): higher myopathy risk with 80 mg; where available consider genotyping before 80 mg and avoid high doses in CC carriers.

src.q: high doses avoided in those found to carry the CC genotype

items.t: Stop temporarily a few days before elective major surgery and when any major medical or surgical condition supervenes.

src.q: Therapy with simvastatin should be temporarily stopped a few days prior to elective major surgery and when any major medical or surgical condition supervenes.

items.t: Use with caution in people who drink substantial quantities of alcohol.

src.q: The product should be used with caution in patients who consume substantial quantities of alcohol.

items.t: Systemic fusidic acid: must not be given with simvastatin or within 7 days of stopping it.

src.q: Simvastatin must not be co-administered with systemic formulations of fusidic acid or within 7 days of stopping fusidic acid treatment.

items.t: Statins can raise blood glucose; monitor people at risk of diabetes (fasting glucose 5.6 to 6.9 mmol/L, BMI > 30 kg/m2, raised triglycerides, hypertension). Not a reason to stop.

src.q: Patients at risk (fasting glucose 5.6 to 6.9 mmol/L, BMI > 30 kg/m2, raised triglycerides, hypertension) should be monitored both clinically and biochemically according to national guidelines.

items.t: Myasthenia gravis: may be induced or aggravated; stop if symptoms worsen.

src.q: Zocor should be discontinued in case of aggravation of symptoms.
advise patients with pre-existing myasthenia gravis to be alert to aggravation of symptoms while taking a statin

items.t: Interstitial lung disease: stop if suspected.

src.q: If it is suspected a patient has developed interstitial lung disease, statin therapy should be discontinued.

items.t: Contains lactose: not for rare hereditary galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption.

src.q: This product contains lactose.

items.t: Clarithromycin and other potent CYP3A4 inhibitors: contraindicated. If treatment with a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor is unavoidable, suspend simvastatin for the course (consider an alternative statin). SPS: simvastatin must be stopped while taking clarithromycin.

src.q: If treatment with potent CYP3A4 inhibitors (agents that increase AUC approximately 5 fold or greater) is unavoidable, therapy with simvastatin must be suspended
Clarithromycin is contraindicated with simvastatin.
Contraindicated with simvastatin

items.t: Amlodipine: do not exceed 20 mg simvastatin daily (increased myopathy risk). MHRA: maximum recommended simvastatin dose with amlodipine is 20 mg/day.

src.q: the dose of simvastatin should not exceed 20 mg daily in patients receiving concomitant medication with amlodipine
The maximum recommended dose for simvastatin in conjunction with amlodipine and diltiazem is now 20 mg/day.

items.t: Also maximum 20 mg daily with amiodarone, verapamil, diltiazem; caution with less potent CYP3A4 inhibitors (fluconazole, verapamil, diltiazem).

src.q: The combined use of simvastatin at doses higher than 20 mg daily with amiodarone, amlodipine, verapamil, or diltiazem should be avoided.

items.t: Coumarin anticoagulants (warfarin): simvastatin modestly raises INR; check prothrombin time before starting and often enough in early therapy; repeat if the simvastatin dose changes or stops.

src.q: simvastatin 20-40 mg/day modestly potentiated the effect of coumarin anticoagulants
In patients taking coumarin anticoagulants, prothrombin time should be determined before starting simvastatin

items.t: MHRA: CYP3A4 inducers (e.g. St John's wort) may reduce simvastatin levels.

src.q: Inducers of CYP3A4 (eg, efavirenz, rifampicin, St John's wort) may reduce plasma concentrations of simvastatin and atorvastatin.

items.t: Avoid grapefruit juice.

src.q: Intake of grapefruit juice during treatment with simvastatin should therefore be avoided.

items.t: Ticagrelor: simvastatin doses greater than 40 mg are not recommended.

src.q: The concomitant use of ticagrelor with doses of simvastatin greater than 40 mg is not recommended.

items.t: Moderate renal impairment: no dose change expected. Severe renal impairment (CrCl < 30 ml/min): doses above 10 mg/day should be carefully considered and, if needed, given cautiously.

src.q: No modification of dosage should be necessary in patients with moderate renal impairment.
In patients with severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance < 30 ml/min), dosages above 10 mg/day should be carefully considered and, if deemed necessary, implemented cautiously.

items.t: SPS (all statins): if eGFR is less than 30 mL/min/1.73m2, check the dose with a renal specialist.

src.q: If eGFR less than 30mL/min/1.73m2 check dose with renal specialist.

items.t: Contraindicated in active liver disease or unexplained persistent raised transaminases. Stop if transaminases rise to 3 x ULN and persist; interrupt promptly for serious liver injury.

src.q: Active liver disease or unexplained persistent elevations of serum transaminases.
particularly if they rise to 3 x ULN and are persistent, simvastatin should be discontinued

items.t: SPS: statins are not recommended in unexplained active liver disease or ALT/AST above 3 x ULN; in stable/chronic liver disease they can be used with caution after weighing risks and benefits.

src.q: available data suggest that statins can be used with caution after assessing individual risks and benefits

items.t: Contraindicated; must not be used in women who are pregnant, trying to become pregnant or suspect pregnancy. Suspend for the duration of pregnancy.

src.q: Zocor is contraindicated during pregnancy
Zocor must not be used in women who are pregnant, trying to become pregnant or suspect they are pregnant.

items.t: BUMPS: statins are usually avoided in pregnancy; most women are advised to stop three months before trying to conceive and during pregnancy.

src.q: Statins are usually avoided in pregnancy if possible as there is not enough information to say they are safe for the baby.
As a precaution, most women are advised to stop taking statins for three months before trying to conceive, and during pregnancy.

items.t: SmPC: contraindicated; women taking simvastatin must not breastfeed.

src.q: women taking Zocor must not breast-feed their infants

items.t: SPS (differs from SmPC): simvastatin can be used with caution and infant monitoring, but other statins (rosuvastatin, pravastatin, atorvastatin) are preferred. No published data on milk transfer.

src.q: Simvastatin can be used with caution and infant monitoring during breastfeeding, but other statins are preferred.

items.t: No human fertility data; no effect on fertility in rats. Adolescent girls should be counselled on contraception.

src.q: No clinical trial data are available on the effects of simvastatin on human fertility.
Adolescent females should be counselled on appropriate contraceptive methods while on simvastatin therapy

adverseCommon.note: The simvastatin SmPC (section 4.8) lists no common or very common adverse effects (most listed effects are rare); myopathy occurred commonly only at 80 mg/day in one trial. Source checked: the simvastatin SmPC.

items.t: ACE inhibitors: SmPC - should not routinely be used together, particularly in marked renal impairment. src.q: Since ACE inhibitors decrease aldosterone production they should not routinely be used with Aldactone, particularly in patients with marked renal impairment.
concomitant use of spironolactone with ACEi or ARB increases the risk of severe hyperkalaemia, particularly in patients with marked renal impairment, and should be used with caution

use the lowest effective doses of spironolactone and ACEi or ARB if coadministration is considered essential regularly monitor serum potassium levels and renal function interrupt or discontinue treatment in the event of hyperkalaemia

items.t: NSAIDs (e.g. aspirin, indometacin, mefenamic acid): reduce the diuretic effect, and add to hyperkalaemia risk.

src.q: have been shown to attenuate the diuretic effect of spironolactone.

src.q: In patients receiving digoxin and spironolactone the digoxin response should be monitored by means other than serum digoxin concentrations, unless the digoxin assay used has been proven not to be affected by spironolactone therapy.

items.t: Lithium: risk of lithium toxicity; monitor lithium levels. Abiraterone: not recommended (PSA may rise). Mitotane: do not use together. Carbenoxolone: avoid.

src.q: In adult patients with severe asthma, tiotropium should be used in addition to inhaled corticosteroids (≥ 800 μg budesonide/day or equivalent) and at least one controller.
Spiriva Respimat should not be used as monotherapy for asthma.

items.t: Adults (COPD and asthma): 5 micrograms (two puffs) once daily at the same time each day. Do not exceed; do not use more than once daily.

src.q: The recommended dose for adults is 5 microgram tiotropium given as two puffs from the Respimat inhaler once daily, at the same time of the day. The recommended dose should not be exceeded.
Tiotropium bromide should not be used more frequently than once daily

items.t: Elderly, renal and hepatic impairment: recommended dose can be used (renal CrCl ≤ 50 ml/min: see renal).

src.q: Geriatric patients can use tiotropium bromide at the recommended dose. Renally impaired patients can use tiotropium bromide at the recommended dose.
Hepatically impaired patients can use tiotropium bromide at the recommended dose

items.t: Asthma 6-17 years: 5 micrograms (two puffs) once daily, as add-on to ICS plus controller(s) in severe asthma. Not established in moderate asthma or under 6 years. COPD: no relevant use under 18. Children should use it with an adult's help.

src.q: The recommended dose for patients 6 to 17 years of age is 5 microgram tiotropium given as two puffs from the Respimat inhaler once daily, at the same time of the day.
The safety and efficacy of Spiriva Respimat in children below 6 years of age has not been established.
There is no relevant use of Spiriva Respimat in children and adolescents below 18 years.
Children should use Spiriva Respimat with an adult's assistance.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to tiotropium, any excipient, or atropine and its derivatives (e.g. ipratropium, oxitropium).

src.q: Hypersensitivity to tiotropium bromide or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1 or to atropine or its derivatives, e.g. ipratropium or oxitropium.

items.t: Not for acute bronchospasm or symptom relief (use a rapid-acting beta-2 agonist). Not a monotherapy for asthma: keep the inhaled corticosteroid unchanged.

src.q: should not be used for the initial treatment of acute episodes of bronchospasm, or for the relief of acute symptoms. In the event of an acute attack a rapid-acting beta-2-agonist should be used.
Spiriva Respimat should not be used as monotherapy for asthma.

items.t: Anticholinergic: caution in narrow-angle glaucoma, prostatic hyperplasia or bladder-neck obstruction. Keep spray out of the eyes; if eye pain, blurred vision, halos or red eyes, stop and see a specialist at once.

src.q: tiotropium bromide should be used with caution in patients with narrow-angle glaucoma, prostatic hyperplasia or bladder-neck obstruction.
Should any combination of these eye symptoms develop, patients should stop using tiotropium bromide and consult a specialist immediately.

items.t: Cardiac: caution after MI in the last 6 months, unstable or life-threatening arrhythmia or arrhythmia needing intervention or drug change in the past year, or heart failure admission (NYHA III-IV) in the past year. MHRA: take cardiovascular risk into account and ask these patients to report worsening cardiac symptoms.

src.q: Tiotropium should be used with caution in patients with recent myocardial infarction < 6 months; any unstable or life threatening cardiac arrhythmia or cardiac arrhythmia requiring intervention or a change in drug therapy in the past year
hospitalisation of heart failure (NYHA Class III or IV) within the past year.
take the risk of cardiovascular side effects into account for patients with conditions that may be affected by the anticholinergic action of tiotropium
tell these patients to report any worsening of cardiac symptoms after starting tiotropium

items.t: Renal: CrCl ≤ 50 ml/min, use only if benefit outweighs risk.

src.q: As plasma concentration increases with decreased renal function in patients with moderate to severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance ≤ 50 ml/min) tiotropium bromide should be used only if the expected benefit outweighs the potential risk.

items.t: Not recommended in cystic fibrosis. Contains benzalkonium chloride, which may cause wheeze (higher risk in asthma). Long-term dry mouth may cause dental caries.

src.q: Spiriva Respimat is not recommended in cystic fibrosis (CF).
Benzalkonium chloride may cause wheezing and breathing difficulties. Patients with asthma are at an increased risk for these adverse events.
Dry mouth, which has been observed with anti-cholinergic treatment, may in the long term be associated with dental caries.

items.t: Other anticholinergic medicines: not studied, not recommended.

src.q: The co-administration of tiotropium bromide with other anticholinergic containing drugs has not been studied and therefore is not recommended.

items.t: Used with other common COPD and asthma medicines (sympathomimetic bronchodilators, methylxanthines, oral and inhaled steroids, antihistamines, leukotriene modifiers) without clinical evidence of interactions.

src.q: tiotropium bromide has been used concomitantly with other drugs commonly used in the treatment of COPD and asthma, including sympathomimetic bronchodilators, methylxanthines, oral and inhaled steroids, antihistamines, mucolytics, leukotriene modifiers

items.t: CrCl ≤ 50 ml/min: plasma levels rise; use only if expected benefit outweighs the risk. No long-term experience in severe renal impairment. No dose change stated.

src.q: As plasma concentration increases with decreased renal function in patients with moderate to severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance ≤ 50 ml/min) tiotropium bromide should be used only if the expected benefit outweighs the potential risk.
There is no long term experience in patients with severe renal impairment

items.t: Hepatic impairment: recommended dose can be used.

src.q: Hepatically impaired patients can use tiotropium bromide at the recommended dose

items.t: SmPC: very limited data; as a precaution, preferably avoid in pregnancy.

src.q: There is a very limited amount of data from the use of tiotropium in pregnant women.
As a precautionary measure, it is preferable to avoid the use of Spiriva Respimat during pregnancy.

items.t: BUMPS (asthma): LAMAs such as tiotropium are among asthma medicines; some are less well studied, but benefits of asthma medicines usually outweigh possible risks.

src.q: Long-acting muscarinic antagonists (LAMAs), such as tiotropium
Some asthma medications have not been as well-studied in pregnancy.
For this reason, the benefits of using any asthma medicines during pregnancy will usually outweigh any possible risks.

items.t: Not recommended during breastfeeding (unknown if excreted in human milk; long-acting). Decide whether to continue breastfeeding or therapy.

src.q: use of Spiriva Respimat is not recommended during breast-feeding.
Tiotropium bromide is a long-acting compound.

items.t: No clinical fertility data; no effect in a non-clinical study.

src.q: Clinical data on fertility are not available for tiotropium.

items.t: Common (COPD): dry mouth (uncommon in asthma). Other effects are uncommon or rarer: dizziness, headache, cough, pharyngitis, dysphonia, constipation, oral candidiasis, rash, pruritus; in COPD also urinary retention and dysuria.

src.q: Gastrointestinal disorders Dry Mouth Common Uncommon
Nervous system disorders Dizziness Uncommon Uncommon Headache Uncommon Uncommon
Renal and urinary disorders Urinary retention Uncommon Not known Dysuria Uncommon Not known

items.t: Serious anticholinergic effects: glaucoma, constipation, intestinal obstruction including paralytic ileus, urinary retention.

src.q: Serious undesirable effects consistent with anticholinergic effects include glaucoma, constipation, intestinal obstruction including ileus paralytic and urinary retention.

items.t: Immediate hypersensitivity (angioedema, anaphylaxis) and inhalation-induced bronchospasm can occur.

src.q: Immediate hypersensitivity reactions may occur after administration of tiotropium bromide inhalation solution.
Inhaled medicines may cause inhalation-induced bronchospasm.

items.t: Eye symptoms (pain, blurred vision, halos, red eye): stop and see a specialist immediately.

src.q: Should any combination of these eye symptoms develop, patients should stop using tiotropium bromide and consult a specialist immediately.

items.t: MHRA: review that tiotropium remains appropriate; regularly review patients at high cardiovascular risk.

src.q: regularly review treatment of patients at high risk of cardiovascular events

items.t: Stop and refer urgently if acute glaucoma symptoms.

src.q: Should any combination of these eye symptoms develop, patients should stop using tiotropium bromide and consult a specialist immediately.

items.t: Once a day, two puffs each time. Insert the cartridge and prime until a cloud appears, then 3 more puffs. If unused for more than 7 days, release one puff to the ground; if more than 21 days, prime again. Use the reusable inhaler for no more than one year (up to 6 cartridges).

src.q: Each time used take TWO PUFFS.
If Spiriva Respimat has not been used for more than 7 days release one puff towards the ground.
Do not use the Respimat re-usable inhaler for more than one year, after having inserted the first cartridge.
The Respimat re-usable inhaler allows for replacement of the cartridge, and can be used with up to 6 cartridges.

items.t: This is a daily maintenance inhaler, not a reliever. Do not exceed once daily. Keep the spray out of the eyes. Report any worsening heart symptoms (MHRA).

src.q: remind patients not to exceed the recommended once daily dose
tell these patients to report any worsening of cardiac symptoms after starting tiotropium
Patients should be cautioned to avoid getting the spray into their eyes.

items.t: Moderate to severe pain.

src.q: Treatment of moderate to severe pain.

items.t: MHRA (2025): prolonged-release opioids should not be used for acute pain after surgery; use immediate-release opioids for short-term post-operative pain.

src.q: prolonged-release opioids provide relief from chronic severe pain, however, they should not be used for the treatment of acute pain following surgery

items.t: Not for use in narcotic withdrawal treatment; not a substitute in opioid-dependent patients.

src.q: for use in narcotic withdrawal treatment
Tramadol is not suitable as a substitute in opioid-dependent patients.

items.t: Acute pain (adults and 12 years and over): initial 100 mg, then 50 or 100 mg every 4-6 hours; match duration to clinical need. Maximum 400 mg/day except in special circumstances.

src.q: Acute pain: An initial dose of 100 mg is usually necessary. This can be followed by doses of 50 or 100 mg 4-6 hourly intervals
The total daily dose of 400 mg active substance should not be exceeded, except in special circumstances.

items.t: Pain with chronic conditions: start 50 mg, then titrate to pain severity; reassess need regularly (dependence and withdrawal reported). Maximum 400 mg/day.

src.q: Pain associated with chronic conditions: An initial dose of 50 mg is advised and then titration according to pain severity.

items.t: Prolonged-release (adults and over 12 years): usually 100 mg twice daily (morning and evening); increase to 150 mg or 200 mg twice daily if needed. Interval at least 8 hours. Maximum 400 mg/day except in special clinical circumstances.

src.q: The starting dose is usually 100 mg tramadol hydrochloride as prolonged-release tablet twice daily, in the morning and in the evening. If the pain relief is not sufficient, the dose may be increased to 150 mg twice daily or 200 mg twice daily.
A total daily dose of 400 mg of tramadol hydrochloride should not be exceeded except in special clinical circumstances.
The dose interval must not be less than 8 hours.

items.t: Elderly: no adjustment usually needed up to 75 years without hepatic or renal insufficiency; over 75 years extend the dosing interval if necessary.

src.q: A dose adjustment is not usually necessary in patients up to 75 years without clinically manifest hepatic or renal insufficiency.
Therefore, if necessary the dosage interval is to be extended according to the patient's requirements.

items.t: Use the lowest effective dose; never longer than absolutely necessary. Agree goals and an end-of-treatment plan; taper gradually when stopping.

src.q: Tramadol should under no circumstances be administered for longer than absolutely necessary.
When a patient no longer requires therapy with tramadol, it may be advisable to taper the dose gradually to prevent symptoms of withdrawal.

items.t: Not suitable for children under 12 years (capsules and prolonged-release tablets).

src.q: Tramadol capsules are not suitable for children below the age of 12 years.
Tramadol prolonged-release tablets are not suitable for children under 12 years of age.

items.t: Post-operative use after tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy for obstructive sleep apnoea: rare life-threatening events; extreme caution and close monitoring. Not recommended where respiratory function may be compromised.

src.q: Extreme caution should be exercised when tramadol is administered to children for post-operative pain relief
Tramadol is not recommended for use in children in whom respiratory function might be compromised

items.t: Hypersensitivity; acute intoxication with alcohol, hypnotics, analgesics, opioids or other psychotropic medicines; MAOI now or within 14 days; epilepsy not adequately controlled; narcotic withdrawal treatment.

src.q: in acute intoxication with alcohol, hypnotics, analgesics, opioids, or other psychotropic medicinal products
in patients who are receiving MAO inhibitors or who have taken them within the last 14 days
in patients with epilepsy not adequately controlled by treatment

items.t: Particular caution: opioid dependence, head injury, shock, reduced consciousness of uncertain origin, respiratory centre or function disorders, raised intracranial pressure (MR SmPC also: renal and hepatic impairment).

src.q: Tramadol may only be used with particular caution in opioid-dependent patients, patients with head injury, shock, a reduced level of consciousness of uncertain origin, disorders of the respiratory centre or function, increased intracranial pressure.

items.t: Seizures reported at recommended doses; higher risk above 400 mg/day or with other seizure-threshold-lowering medicines. Epilepsy or seizure susceptibility: only if compelling circumstances.

src.q: Convulsions have been reported in patients receiving tramadol at the recommended dose levels.
Patients with epilepsy or those susceptible to seizures should be only treated with tramadol if there are compelling circumstances.

items.t: Serotonin syndrome (alone or with serotonergic medicines): observe carefully at start and dose increases; reduce or stop if suspected.

src.q: Serotonin syndrome, a potentially life-threatening condition, has been reported in patients receiving tramadol in combination with other serotonergic agents or tramadol alone
If serotonin syndrome is suspected, a dose reduction or discontinuation of therapy should be considered depending on the severity of the symptoms.

items.t: Tolerance, dependence and opioid use disorder can develop even at therapeutic doses; higher risk with personal/family history of substance use disorder, tobacco use or mental health disorders. Monitor for drug-seeking behaviour.

src.q: Repeated use of Tramadol can lead to opioid use disorder (OUD).
Patients will require monitoring for signs of drug-seeking behaviour (e.g. too early requests for refills).

items.t: CYP2D6: poor metabolisers may get inadequate analgesia; ultra-rapid metabolisers risk opioid toxicity even at usual doses.

src.q: If a patient has a deficiency or is completely lacking this enzyme an adequate analgesic effect may not be obtained.
if the patient is an ultra-rapid metaboliser there is a risk of developing <side effects> of opioid toxicity even at commonly prescribed doses

items.t: Opioids may occasionally cause reversible adrenal insufficiency requiring monitoring and glucocorticoid replacement.

src.q: Opioid analgesics may occasionally cause reversible adrenal insufficiency requiring monitoring and glucocorticoid replacement therapy.

items.t: Sleep-related breathing disorders (central sleep apnoea): consider reducing the opioid dose.

src.q: In patients who present with CSA, consider decreasing the total opioid dosage.

items.t: SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics, mirtazapine and MAOIs: serotonin syndrome risk. SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics, antipsychotics and other seizure-threshold-lowering drugs: convulsion risk.

src.q: Concomitant therapeutic use of tramadol and serotonergic medicinal products, such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs), MAO inhibitors (see section 4.3), tricyclic antidepressants and mirtazapine may cause serotonin syndrome
Tramadol can induce convulsions and increase the potential for selective serotonin re-uptake inhibitors (SSRIs)

items.t: Warfarin and other coumarins: increased INR with major bleeding and bruising reported. Use caution; MHRA advises considering extra INR monitoring when starting tramadol and warning patients about bleeding signs.

src.q: Caution should be exercised during concomitant treatment with tramadol and coumarin derivatives (e.g. warfarin) due to reports of increased INR with major bleeding and ecchymoses in some patients.
consider whether additional monitoring of INR is required when starting tramadol or another concomitant medicine

items.t: Benzodiazepines, other opioids, other CNS depressants and alcohol: sedation, respiratory depression, coma and death; lowest dose, shortest duration if combined.

src.q: if a decision is made to prescribe tramadol concomitantly with respiratory or CNS depressants, the lowest effective dose of tramadol should be used, and the duration of the concomitant treatment should be as short as possible

items.t: CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. ketoconazole, ritonavir, erythromycin) might inhibit tramadol metabolism; clinical importance not studied.

src.q: Other medicinal products known to inhibit CYP3A4, such as ketoconazole, ritonavir and erythromycin, might inhibit the metabolism of tramadol
The clinical importance of such an interaction has not been studied

items.t: Carbamazepine may reduce the analgesic effect; ondansetron may increase tramadol requirement; gabapentin/pregabalin increase respiratory depression risk.

src.q: Simultaneous or previous administration of carbamazepine (enzyme inducer) may reduce the analgesic effect and shorten the duration of action.
The concomitant use of Tramadol with gabapentinoids (gabapentin and pregabalin) may result in respiratory depression, hypotension, profound sedation, coma or death.

items.t: St John's wort (THR SPC): reduced tramadol blood levels with risk of therapeutic failure; do not take together.

src.q: Analgesics Tramadol Reduced blood levels with risk Do not take with this product.

items.t: Ciprofloxacin (ciprofloxacin SmPC): avoid combining with tramadol, which lowers the seizure threshold (risk of seizures, including status epilepticus).

src.q: concomitant treatment of ciprofloxacin with drugs known to trigger seizures or lower the seizure threshold, such as but not limited to tramadol, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, should be avoided

items.t: Clopidogrel (clopidogrel SmPC): opioid agonists may delay and reduce clopidogrel absorption (clinical relevance unknown); in acute coronary syndrome consider a parenteral antiplatelet agent.

src.q: co-administration of opioid agonists has the potential to delay and reduce the absorption of clopidogrel presumably because of slowed gastric emptying. The clinical relevance is unknown.
Consider the use of a parenteral antiplatelet agent in acute coronary syndrome patients requiring co-administration of morphine or other opioid agonists.

items.t: Renal insufficiency or dialysis: elimination delayed; carefully consider prolonging the dosing interval (no numeric threshold stated).

src.q: In patients with renal and/or hepatic insufficiency the elimination of tramadol is delayed. In these patients prolongation of the dosage intervals should be carefully considered according to the patient's requirements.

items.t: Prolonged-release tablets: not recommended in severe renal insufficiency.

src.q: In cases of severe renal and/or severe hepatic insufficiency tramadol hydrochloride prolonged-release tablets are not recommended.

items.t: Hepatic insufficiency: elimination delayed; carefully consider prolonging the dosing interval.

src.q: In patients with renal and/or hepatic insufficiency the elimination of tramadol is delayed.

items.t: Prolonged-release tablets: not recommended in severe hepatic insufficiency.

src.q: In cases of severe renal and/or severe hepatic insufficiency tramadol hydrochloride prolonged-release tablets are not recommended.

items.t: SmPCs: inadequate human safety evidence, so tramadol should not be used in pregnant women. Regular use may cause neonatal withdrawal; use in labour may depress neonatal breathing.

src.q: There is inadequate evidence available on the safety of tramadol in human pregnancy. Therefore tramadol should not be used in pregnant women.
Administration during labour may depress respiration in the neonate

items.t: BUMPS (differs from SmPC): take only if recommended by a doctor; studies overall do not show miscarriage or birth defects; use near delivery can cause neonatal withdrawal.

src.q: Tramadol should only be taken during pregnancy if recommended by your doctor.
Studies of pregnant women using tramadol do not, overall, show that it causes miscarriage or birth defects in the baby.

items.t: SPS: reserve tramadol in pregnancy for when other analgesics have been ineffective.

src.q: Reserve tramadol use in pregnancy where other alternative analgesics have been ineffective.

items.t: Capsule SmPC: not recommended (may cause infant respiratory depression).

src.q: Administration to nursing women is not recommended as tramadol may be secreted in breast milk and may cause respiratory depression in the infant.

items.t: Prolonged-release SmPC: should not be used during lactation, or stop breastfeeding during treatment; a single dose usually does not require stopping breastfeeding.

src.q: For this reason tramadol should not be used during lactation or alternatively, breast-feeding should be discontinued during treatment with tramadol.
Discontinuation of breast-feeding is generally not necessary following a single dose of tramadol.

items.t: SPS (differs from SmPCs): can be used short term with caution at the lowest effective dose; monitor the infant (sedation, breathing difficulties, feeding, weight gain); extra caution under 2 months; regular use beyond 3 days under close supervision.

src.q: Tramadol (both oral and intravenous) can be used short-term during breastfeeding with caution and infant monitoring.
Regular use of any opioid in a breastfeeding mother beyond 3 days should be under close medical supervision.

items.t: Post-marketing surveillance does not suggest an effect on fertility.

src.q: Post marketing surveillance does not suggest an effect of tramadol on fertility.

items.t: Very common: nausea, dizziness. Common: headache, somnolence, vomiting, constipation, dry mouth, sweating (hyperhidrosis), fatigue.

src.q: The most commonly reported adverse reactions are nausea and dizziness, both occurring in more than 10% of patients.
Common: vomiting, constipation, dry mouth
Common: headache, somnolence

items.t: Respiratory depression (rare), especially if doses are considerably exceeded or with other CNS depressants.

src.q: Rare: respiratory depression, dyspnoea If the recommended doses are considerably exceeded and other centrally depressant substances are administered concomitantly (see section 4.5), respiratory depression may occur.

items.t: Convulsions (rare), mainly at high doses or with seizure-threshold-lowering drugs.

src.q: Epileptiform convulsions occurred mainly after administration of high doses of tramadol or after concomitant treatment with medicinal products which can lower the seizure threshold

items.t: Serotonin syndrome (frequency not known): reduce dose or stop.

src.q: Frequency not known: serotonin syndrome

items.t: Anaphylaxis and allergic reactions (rare); hypoglycaemia (not known); dependence and withdrawal syndrome.

src.q: Rare: allergic reactions (e.g. dyspnoea, bronchospasm, wheezing, angioneurotic oedema) and anaphylaxis
Frequency not known: hypoglycaemia

items.t: Long-term treatment: careful and regular monitoring (with breaks if needed) to decide whether to continue.

src.q: then careful and regular monitoring should be carried out (if necessary with breaks in treatment) to establish whether and to what extent further treatment is necessary

items.t: With serotonergic medicines: careful observation especially at start and dose increases.

src.q: careful observation of the patient is advised, particularly during treatment initiation and dose escalations

items.t: With warfarin: consider extra INR monitoring when starting tramadol (MHRA).

src.q: consider whether additional monitoring of INR is required when starting tramadol or another concomitant medicine

items.t: Capsules: swallow whole, not divided or chewed, with enough liquid, with or without food.

src.q: The capsules are to be taken whole, not divided or chewed, with sufficient liquid, with or without food.

items.t: Prolonged-release tablets: swallow whole, not divided or chewed, with enough liquid, regardless of meals.

src.q: The prolonged-release tablets must be swallowed whole, not divided or chewed, with sufficient liquid, irrespective of mealtimes.

items.t: May cause drowsiness and dizziness; may affect driving, especially with alcohol.

src.q: Tramadol may cause effects such as somnolence and dizziness and therefore may impair the reactions of drivers and machine operators.

items.t: MHRA: risk of dependence and addiction even at therapeutic doses; learn signs of overdose; do not stop suddenly after long-term use.

src.q: discuss with patients that prolonged use of opioids may lead to drug dependence and addiction, even at therapeutic doses

items.t: If taking warfarin: seek urgent INR test for signs of bleeding (e.g. nosebleed over 10 minutes, blood in urine/stool, severe bruising).

src.q: you should seek medical treatment and have an urgent International Normalised Ratio test should you experience any of the following symptoms

restrictions.note: No UK product information found.

hepatic.note: No UK product information found.

items.t: Treatment of infections caused by trimethoprim-sensitive organisms, including urinary and respiratory tract infections.

src.q: Trimethoprim is indicated for the treatment of susceptible infections caused by trimethoprim - sensitive organisms including urinary tract and respiratory tract infections.

items.t: Prevention of recurrent urinary tract infections.

src.q: Trimethoprim is also indicated for the prevention of recurrent urinary tract infections.

items.t: Prevention and treatment of UTI, and treatment of other susceptible infections, in adults and children.

src.q: Trimethoprim is indicated for the prevention and treatment of urinary tract infections in adults and children

restrictions.note: No specialist-only, shared-care or brand restrictions found in the tablet SmPC, the suspension SmPC, SPS or MHRA pages checked. Dialysis use is specialist-supervised (see renal).

items.t: Adults and children over 12 years: 200 mg TWICE DAILY. Duration 3 days (e.g. uncomplicated cystitis in women) up to 2 weeks, by type and severity of infection. The first dose can be doubled.

src.q: Adults and children over 12 years of age: 200 mg twice daily

Treatment should continue for a period of between 3 days (e.g. uncomplicated bacterial cystitis in women) to 2 weeks depending on the nature and severity of the infection. The first dose can be doubled.

items.t: Adults and children over 12 years: 100 mg ONCE daily AT NIGHT.

src.q: Long-term treatment and prophylactic therapy: Adults and children over 12 years: 100 mg at night

items.t: Adults and children over 12 years: 200 mg (20 ml) TWICE DAILY.

src.q: Treatment of urinary tract infections and all other susceptible infections: 200 mg (20 ml) twice daily.

items.t: Adults and children over 12 years: 100 mg (10 ml) at night.

src.q: Long-term prevention of recurrent urinary tract infections: 100 mg (10 ml) at night.

items.t: Elderly: dose depends on kidney function (see renal).

src.q: Elderly Depending on kidney function, see special dosage schedule.

items.t: Tablets, children 6 to 12 years: 100 mg twice daily for acute infections; 50 mg at night for long-term/prophylaxis.

src.q: Children 6 years to 12 years: 100 mg twice daily
Children 6 years to 12 years of age: 50 mg at night.

items.t: Tablets are not suitable under 6 years; use a suspension. The same SmPC's prophylaxis section also says the tablet is not suitable under 12 years (internal inconsistency in the source).

src.q: This dosage form is not suitable for use in children younger than 6 years; a more suitable dosage form (such as a suspension) should be used in this age group.
This dosage form is not suitable for use in children younger than 12 years; a more suitable dosage form (such as a suspension) should be used in this age group.

items.t: Suspension, children 6 weeks to 12 years, UTI treatment: 8 mg/kg daily in two equal doses. Suggested: 6 weeks-5 months 25 mg (2.5 ml) twice daily; 6 months-5 years 50 mg (5 ml) twice daily; 6-12 years 100 mg (10 ml) twice daily.

src.q: Children 6 weeks to 12 years of age Treatment of urinary tract infections is based on a dosage of 8 mg/kg body weight daily, subdivided into two equal doses.
25 mg (2.5 ml) twice daily 50 mg (5 ml) twice daily 100 mg (10 ml) twice daily

items.t: Suspension, long-term prevention of recurrent UTI: 2 mg/kg daily as a single dose at night. Suggested: 6 months-5 years 25 mg (2.5 ml); 6-12 years 50 mg (5 ml) at night.

src.q: Long-term prevention of recurrent urinary tract infection is based on 2 mg/kg body weight daily given as a single dose at night.
25 mg (2.5 ml) at night 50 mg (5 ml) at night

items.t: Lower age limit differs by SmPC: tablet SmPC says do not give to premature infants or children under 4 months; suspension SmPC says do not give to premature infants and neonates under 6 weeks.

src.q: Trimethoprim should not be administered to pregnant women, premature infants or children under 4 months of age
premature infants and neonates under 6 weeks

items.t: Take particular care with blood monitoring in children on long-term therapy.

src.q: Particular care should be exercised in the haematological monitoring of children on long term therapy.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to trimethoprim or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Severe hepatic insufficiency.

src.q: Trimethoprim is contra-indicated in severe hepatic insufficiency.

items.t: Megaloblastic anaemia and other blood dyscrasias.

src.q: Trimethoprim is contra-indicated in megaloblastic anaemia and other blood dyscrasias.

items.t: First trimester of pregnancy (the tablet SmPC 4.3 also says it should not be given to pregnant women, without naming a trimester).

src.q: Trimethoprim is contra-indicated in first trimester of pregnancy
Trimethoprim should not be administered to pregnant women, premature infants or children under 4 months of age

items.t: Premature infants and young infants - SmPCs differ: tablet SmPC 4.3 says under 4 months; suspension SmPC 4.3 says neonates under 6 weeks.

src.q: Trimethoprim should not be administered to pregnant women, premature infants or children under 4 months of age
Trimethoprim should not be administered to pregnant women (first trimester of pregnancy (see section 4.6)), premature infants and neonates under 6 weeks.

items.t: Hyperkalaemia: closely monitor electrolytes in patients at risk (renal insufficiency, poorly controlled diabetes, potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements or salt substitutes, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, heparin).

src.q: Close monitoring of serum electrolytes is advised in patients at risk for hyperkalaemia (see section 4.8).
Patients at risk for the development of hyperkalaemia include those with renal insufficiency, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus

items.t: Folate deficiency (actual or potential, e.g. elderly): use with caution; consider a folate supplement. Trimethoprim may depress haemopoiesis.

src.q: Caution should be exercised in the administration of trimethoprim to patients with actual or potential folate deficiency (e.g. the elderly). Administration of a folate supplement should be considered.
Trimethoprim may cause depression of haemopoiesis.

items.t: Marked renal impairment: avoid accumulation and haematological toxicity; dialysis patients only under specialist (infection + renal) supervision.

src.q: In patients with marked impairment of renal function, care should be taken to avoid accumulation and resulting adverse haematological effects.
Trimethoprim should only be initiated and used in dialysis patients under close supervision from specialists in both infectious disease and renal medicine.

items.t: Severe cutaneous reactions (SJS, TEN, DRESS): stop immediately if signs appear; never restart after SJS/TEN/DRESS.

src.q: If signs and symptoms suggestive of these reactions appear, trimethoprim should be withdrawn immediately
If the patient has developed a serious reaction such as SJS, TEN or DRESS with the use of trimethoprim, the treatment must not be restarted in this patient at any time.

items.t: Acute porphyria: tablet SmPC says use with caution; suspension SmPC says avoid if known or suspected risk.

src.q: Caution should be used in patients with acute porphyria.
If a patient has a known or suspected risk of acute prophyria, treatment with trimethoprim should be avoided.

items.t: Neonates: use only under careful medical supervision (tablet SmPC).

src.q: Trimethoprim should be used under careful medical supervision in neonates.

items.t: Tablets contain lactose; suspension: patients with hereditary fructose intolerance should not take it.

src.q: Each tablet contains 50 mg lactose
Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance should not take this medicine.

items.t: Methotrexate: tablet SmPC says avoid (increased antifolate effect); suspension SmPC says risk of haematological toxicity. SPS: avoid; if unavoidable, frequent FBC.

src.q: Trimethoprim increases the antifolate effect of methotrexate therefore use should be avoided.
Avoid prescribing co-trimoxazole or trimethoprim with methotrexate, due to the risk of severe bone marrow suppression.

items.t: Potassium-raising medicines (potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, heparin): risk of significant hyperkalaemia; monitor potassium.

src.q: Concomitant use of drugs that may increase serum potassium levels may lead to a significant increase in serum potassium.
Monitoring of potassium should be undertaken as appropriate (see section 4.4).

items.t: Warfarin and other coumarins: trimethoprim may increase the anticoagulant effect.

src.q: Trimethoprim may potentiate the anticoagulant effect of warfarin and other coumarins.

items.t: Dapsone: plasma levels of both drugs may rise.

src.q: Dapsone: Plasma concentrations of trimethoprim and dapsone may increase when taken together.

items.t: Other folate antagonists: may cause folate deficiency in predisposed patients.

src.q: Trimethoprim may induce folate deficiency in patients predisposed to folate deficiency such as those receiving concomitant folate antagonists or anticonvulsants.

items.t: Diuretics (mainly thiazides) in elderly: more thrombocytopenia with purpura.

src.q: In elderly patients concurrently taking diuretics, primarily thiazides, there is an increased incidence of thrombocytopenia with purpura.

items.t: Digoxin, phenytoin (careful monitoring), procainamide, ciclosporin (nephrotoxicity), repaglinide (hypoglycaemia; monitor glucose), rifampicin, pyrimethamine.

src.q: Careful monitoring of patients treated with digoxin or phenytoin is advised
Monitoring of blood glucose is advised if co-administered with repaglinide (see section 4.5).

items.t: eGFR over 30: normal dose. eGFR 15 to 30: normal dose for 3 days, then half dose. eGFR under 15: half the normal dose. Measure: both the tablet and suspension SmPCs name the measure eGFR, but print the unit as "ml/min" (not ml/min/1.73 m2); the thresholds are kept as eGFR because that is the measure the sources name. If only CrCl is known, treat the bands as approximate.

src.q: Dosage advised where there is reduced kidney function: eGFR (ml/min) Dosage advised Over 30 Normal 15- 30 Normal for 3 days then half dose Under 15 Half the normal dose
Dosage advised eGFR (ml/min)

items.t: Consider monitoring renal function and electrolytes, especially with longer use. Dialysis: start and use only under close specialist supervision (infection + renal); trimethoprim is removed by dialysis.

src.q: Monitoring of renal function and serum electrolytes should be considered particularly with longer term use, in patients with impaired renal function.
Trimethoprim is removed by dialysis.

items.t: Contraindicated in severe hepatic insufficiency. Fatal haematological effects have been reported especially in elderly or those with renal or hepatic impairment.

src.q: Trimethoprim is contra-indicated in severe hepatic insufficiency.
Fatalities have been reported (especially in the elderly, or those with impairment of renal or hepatic function in whom careful monitoring is advised

items.t: First trimester: contraindicated (increased risk of miscarriage and malformations, including neural tube defects, oral clefts and heart defects; folate interference).

src.q: Trimethoprim is contraindicated during the first trimester of pregnancy (see section 4.3).
in particular neural tube defects, oral clefts and cardiovascular defects

items.t: Second and third trimesters: avoid unless clinically necessary. Note: both SmPCs also contain a broader line in 4.6 ("contra-indicated in pregnant women"), and the tablet SmPC 4.3 says it should not be given to pregnant women without naming a trimester; the trimester-specific advice is shown here.

src.q: In the second and third trimesters, use should be avoided, unless clinically necessary.
Trimethoprim is contra-indicated in pregnant women, premature infants or infants during the first few weeks of life.
Trimethoprim should not be administered to pregnant women, premature infants or children under 4 months of age

items.t: BUMPS (UKTIS patient leaflet): usually avoided in early pregnancy because it can lower folate; if needed in early pregnancy it is usually given with high-dose folic acid. Other antibiotics are usually used first for UTI.

src.q: Trimethoprim is usually avoided in early pregnancy because it can lower folate levels in your body.
If trimethoprim is needed in early pregnancy, it is usually prescribed with a high-dose folic acid supplement to help maintain folate levels.

items.t: Tablet SmPC: excreted in breast milk but not contraindicated for short-term use.

src.q: Trimethoprim is excreted in breast milk but is not contra-indicated for short term use in lactating mothers.

items.t: Suspension SmPC: effects on the suckling child are likely; contraindicated if the breastfed infant is under 4 months. (The two SmPCs differ; both statements concern trimethoprim in milk, so both are shown whatever the formulation.)

src.q: Effects on the suckling child are likely if therapeutic doses are administered to breast-feeding mothers.
Trimethoprim is contraindicated if the breast fed infant is less than 4 months of age.

items.t: Usual caution when prescribing for women of child-bearing age.

src.q: The usual caution in prescribing any drug for women of child bearing age should be exercised with trimethoprim.

items.t: BUMPS: no evidence that use by the father around conception affects the baby.

src.q: There is no evidence that trimethoprim taken by the father before or around the time of conception affects the baby.

items.t: Very common: hyperkalaemia. Common: headache, nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting, rash, urticaria, candida (monilial) overgrowth.

src.q: Very common: Hyperkalaemia
Common: Nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting.
Common: Skin rashes, urticaria
Common: Monilial overgrowth

items.t: Blood disorders (very rare: neutropenia, agranulocytosis, aplastic anaemia, pancytopenia; megaloblastic anaemia; methaemoglobinaemia). Tell patients to seek immediate help for fever, sore throat, rash, mouth ulcers, purpura, bruising or bleeding.

src.q: Very rare: Leucopenia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, pancytopaenia, bone marrow depression, agranulocytosis, aplastic anaemia
advised to seek immediate medical attention if symptoms such as fever, sore throat, rash, mouth ulcers, purpura, bruising or bleeding develop.

items.t: SJS, TEN, DRESS: stop at once; never restart.

src.q: the treatment must not be restarted in this patient at any time.

items.t: Cholestatic jaundice and hepatic necrosis (very rare, may be fatal); aseptic meningitis (recurs on re-exposure); anaphylaxis, angioedema.

src.q: Cholestatic jaundice and hepatic necrosis may be fatal.
Very rare: Hypersensitivity, anaphylaxis, angioedema

items.t: Long-term treatment or folate-deficiency risk (e.g. elderly): regular blood counts for pancytopenia.

src.q: Regular haematological tests should be undertaken in patients receiving long term treatment and those predisposed to folate deficiency, (e.g. the elderly), to check for possible pancytopaenia.

items.t: Serum potassium if at risk of hyperkalaemia or taking potassium-raising medicines.

src.q: If concomitant use of the above-mentioned agents is deemed appropriate, monitoring of serum potassium is recommended (see section 4.5).

items.t: Folic acid deficiency: give calcium folinate, check response; stopping trimethoprim may be needed.

src.q: If there is evidence of folic acid deficiency, calcium folinate should be administered and response checked by haematologic monitoring. It may be necessary to discontinue trimethoprim.

items.t: Oral. Where a single daily dose is used, taking it at bedtime may maximise urinary concentrations.

src.q: Where a single dose is required, dosage at bedtime may maximise urinary concentrations.

items.t: Tablet breakline is for ease of swallowing only, not for dividing into equal doses.

src.q: The breakline is only to facilitate breaking for ease of swallowing and not to divide into equal doses.

items.t: Seek immediate medical help for fever, sore throat, rash, mouth ulcers, purpura, bruising or bleeding.

src.q: Patients and their carers should be told how to recognise signs of blood disorders

items.t: Know the signs of severe skin reactions and report them.

src.q: Patients should be advised of the signs and symptoms and monitored closely for skin reactions.

items.t: Essential hypertension in adults, and hypertension in children and adolescents 6 to under 18 years.

src.q: Treatment of essential hypertension in adults, and hypertension in children and adolescents 6 to less than 18 years of age.

items.t: Clinically stable adults with symptomatic heart failure or asymptomatic LV systolic dysfunction after a recent (12 hours to 10 days) myocardial infarction.

src.q: Treatment of clinically stable adult patients with symptomatic heart failure or asymptomatic left ventricular systolic dysfunction after a recent (12 hours-10 days) myocardial infarction

items.t: Adult symptomatic heart failure when ACE inhibitors are not tolerated, or (in beta-blocker intolerant patients) as add-on to an ACE inhibitor when mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists cannot be used.

src.q: Treatment of adult patients with symptomatic heart failure when Angiotensin Converting Enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are not tolerated

restrictions.note: No specialist-only or shared-care restriction stated in the valsartan SmPCs. Dual RAAS blockade and the ACE inhibitor + mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist + valsartan triple combination only under specialist supervision (see cautions).

items.t: Hypertension: start 80 mg once daily; may increase to 160 mg and to a maximum of 320 mg. Effect largely within 2 weeks, maximal by 4 weeks.

src.q: The recommended starting dose of Valsartan is 80 mg once daily.
the dose can be increased to 160 mg and to a maximum of 320 mg.

items.t: After recent MI (from 12 hours, clinically stable): 20 mg twice daily, titrated to 40 mg, 80 mg and 160 mg twice daily over the next weeks; aim for 80 mg twice daily by 2 weeks and the target maximum 160 mg twice daily by 3 months. Combination with an ACE inhibitor is not recommended.

src.q: After an initial dose of 20 mg twice daily, valsartan should be titrated to 40 mg, 80 mg, and 160 mg twice daily over the next few weeks.
The target maximum dose is 160 mg twice daily.
The combination with ACE inhibitors is not recommended

items.t: Heart failure: start 40 mg twice daily; increase to 80 mg and 160 mg twice daily at intervals of at least 2 weeks as tolerated (maximum 320 mg daily in divided doses). Consider reducing diuretic doses.

src.q: The recommended starting dose of Valsartan is 40 mg twice daily.
Uptitration to 80 mg and 160 mg twice daily should be done at intervals of at least two weeks
The maximum daily dose administered in clinical trials is 320 mg in divided doses.

items.t: Elderly: no dose adjustment needed.

src.q: No dose adjustment is required in elderly patients.

items.t: Hypertension, 6 to under 18 years: start 40 mg once daily if under 35 kg, 80 mg once daily if 35 kg or more. Maximum doses studied: 18 to under 35 kg 80 mg; 35 to under 80 kg 160 mg; 80 to 160 kg 320 mg. Higher doses not recommended.

src.q: The initial dose is 40 mg once daily for children weighing below 35 kg and 80 mg once daily for those weighing 35 kg or more.
Weight ≥18 kg to <35 kg ≥35 kg to <80 kg ≥80 kg to ≤160 kg Maximum dose studied of tablet in clinical trials 80 mg 160 mg 320 mg
Doses higher than those listed have not been studied and are therefore not recommended.

items.t: Children 1 to 6 years: safety and efficacy not established. Heart failure or recent MI under 18 years: not recommended.

src.q: However safety and efficacy of Valsartan in children aged 1 to 6 years have not been established.
Valsartan is not recommended for the treatment of heart failure or recent myocardial infarction in children and adolescents below the age of 18 years

items.t: Children with CrCl below 30 mL/min or on dialysis: not studied, not recommended. Above 30 mL/min no adjustment; monitor renal function and potassium closely.

src.q: Use in paediatric patients with a creatinine clearance <30 ml/min and paediatric patients undergoing dialysis has not been studied, therefore valsartan is not recommended in these patients.
Renal function and serum potassium should be closely monitored

items.t: Children unable to swallow tablets: oral solution is recommended; exposure is higher with the solution than with tablets.

src.q: For children and adolescents who are unable to swallow tablets, the use of the valsartan oral solution is recommended.
The systemic exposure and peak plasma concentration of valsartan is about 1.7-fold and 2.2-fold higher with the solution compared to the tablets.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to valsartan or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Severe hepatic impairment, biliary cirrhosis and cholestasis.

src.q: Severe hepatic impairment, biliary cirrhosis and cholestasis.

items.t: Second and third trimesters of pregnancy.

src.q: Second and third trimester of pregnancy

items.t: With aliskiren-containing products in patients with diabetes mellitus or renal impairment (GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m²).

src.q: The concomitant use of Valsartan with aliskiren-containing products is contraindicated in patients with diabetes mellitus or renal impairment (GFR < 60 ml/min/1.73 m2)

items.t: Dual RAAS blockade (ACE inhibitor, ARB or aliskiren together) is not recommended; if absolutely necessary, only under specialist supervision with close monitoring. Do not combine an ACE inhibitor and an ARB in diabetic nephropathy.

src.q: Dual blockade of RAAS through the combined use of ACE-inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers or aliskiren is therefore not recommended
ACE-inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers should not be used concomitantly in patients with diabetic nephropathy.

items.t: Post-MI: valsartan with an ACE inhibitor is not recommended. Heart failure: ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker + valsartan, and ACE inhibitor + mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist + valsartan, are not recommended.

src.q: Therefore, the combination of valsartan with an ACE inhibitor is not recommended.
This combination apparently increases the risk for adverse events and is therefore not recommended.
Triple combination of an ACE-inhibitor, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and valsartan is also not recommended.

items.t: Hyperkalaemia: potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium salt substitutes and other potassium-raising drugs (e.g. heparin) are not recommended; monitor potassium.

src.q: Concomitant use with potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics, salt substitutes containing potassium, or other agents that may increase potassium levels (heparin, etc.) is not recommended.

items.t: Sodium/volume depletion (e.g. high-dose diuretics): correct before starting, e.g. by reducing the diuretic dose.

src.q: Sodium and/or volume depletion should be corrected before starting treatment with valsartan, for example by reducing the diuretic dose.

items.t: Renal artery stenosis: safe use not established in bilateral stenosis or solitary kidney; monitor renal function.

src.q: In patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis or stenosis to a solitary kidney, the safe use of valsartan has not been established.
therefore monitoring of renal function is recommended when patients are treated with valsartan

items.t: Primary hyperaldosteronism: should not be treated with valsartan. Aortic or mitral stenosis, HOCM: special caution.

src.q: Patients with primary hyperaldosteronism should not be treated with valsartan as their renin-angiotensin system is not activated.
special caution is indicated in patients suffering from aortic or mitral stenosis, or hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM)

items.t: Angioedema: stop immediately and do not re-administer; some patients had angioedema before with other drugs including ACE inhibitors. Intestinal angioedema: stop and monitor.

src.q: Valsartan should be immediately discontinued in patients who develop angioedema, and Valsartan should not be re-administered
some of these patients previously experienced angioedema with other drugs including ACE inhibitors

items.t: Heart failure or post-MI: caution when starting; always assess renal function. No experience after recent kidney transplantation.

src.q: Caution should be observed when initiating therapy in patients with heart failure.
There is currently no experience on the safe use of valsartan in patients who have recently undergone kidney transplantation.

items.t: ACE inhibitors, other ARBs, aliskiren (dual RAAS blockade): higher rates of hypotension, hyperkalaemia and reduced renal function; not recommended.

src.q: dual blockade of the renin-angiotensin- aldosterone-system (RAAS) through the combined use of ACE-inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers or aliskiren is associated with a higher frequency of adverse events

items.t: Potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements, potassium salt substitutes: concomitant use not recommended; if needed, monitor potassium.

src.q: Potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements, salt substitutes containing potassium and other substances that may increase potassium levels
monitoring of potassium plasma levels is advised

items.t: NSAIDs (including COX-2 inhibitors and aspirin above 3 g/day): caution; reduced antihypertensive effect, worsening renal function, raised potassium. Monitor renal function at the start and keep hydrated.

src.q: Caution required with concomitant use Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medicines (NSAIDs), including selective COX-2 inhibitors, acetylsalicylic acid >3 g/day), and non-selective NSAIDs
Therefore, monitoring of renal function at the beginning of the treatment is recommended, as well as adequate hydration of the patient.

items.t: Lithium: not recommended (raised lithium levels and toxicity); if needed, monitor lithium carefully.

src.q: Concomitant use not recommended Lithium
If the combination proves necessary, careful monitoring of serum lithium levels is recommended

items.t: OATP1B1/OATP1B3 or MRP2 inhibitors (e.g. rifampicin, ciclosporin, ritonavir) may raise valsartan exposure: take care when starting or stopping them. No clinically significant interaction with warfarin, furosemide, digoxin, atenolol, indometacin, hydrochlorothiazide, amlodipine or glibenclamide.

src.q: Exercise appropriate care when initiating or ending concomitant treatment with such drugs.

no interactions of clinical significance have been found with valsartan or any of the following substances: cimetidine, warfarin, furosemide, digoxin, atenolol, indometacin, hydrochlorothiazide, amlodipine, glibenclamide

items.t: Adults with CrCl above 10 mL/min: no dose adjustment.

src.q: No dosage adjustment is required for adult patients with a creatinine clearance >10 ml/min

items.t: CrCl below 10 mL/min or dialysis: no experience; use with caution.

src.q: There is currently no experience on the safe use in patients with a creatinine clearance <10 ml/min and patients undergoing dialysis, therefore valsartan should be used with caution in these patients.

items.t: Children: CrCl below 30 mL/min or dialysis not recommended.

src.q: Use in paediatric patients with a creatinine clearance <30 ml/min and paediatric patients undergoing dialysis has not been studied, therefore valsartan is not recommended in these patients.

items.t: SPS: seek specialist advice before starting if eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73 m².

src.q: Seek specialist advice prior to initiation for patients where there is: severe or unstable heart failure renovascular disease eGFR less than 30ml/min/1.73m2

items.t: Mild to moderate hepatic impairment without cholestasis: use with caution; dose must not exceed 80 mg (adults and children).

src.q: In patients with mild to moderate hepatic impairment without cholestasis, the dose of valsartan should not exceed 80 mg.
In patients with mild to moderate hepatic impairment without cholestasis, valsartan should be used with caution

items.t: Severe hepatic impairment, biliary cirrhosis or cholestasis: contraindicated.

src.q: Valsartan is contraindicated in patients with severe hepatic impairment, biliary cirrhosis and in patients with cholestasis

items.t: First trimester: not recommended. Second and third trimesters: contraindicated (fetotoxicity: reduced renal function, oligohydramnios, skull ossification retardation; neonatal renal failure, hypotension, hyperkalaemia).

src.q: The use of Angiotensin II Receptor Antagonists (AIIRAs) is not recommended during the first trimester of pregnancy
The use of AIIRAs is contra-indicated during the second and third trimester of pregnancy
AIIRAs therapy exposure during the second and third trimesters is known to induce human fetotoxicity

items.t: Do not start in pregnancy; stop immediately on diagnosis and switch if appropriate. After exposure from the second trimester: ultrasound of fetal renal function and skull; observe the infant for hypotension.

src.q: Angiotensin II Receptor Antagonists (AIIRAs) should not be initiated during pregnancy.
Should exposure to AIIRAs have occurred from the second trimester of pregnancy, ultrasound check of renal function and skull is recommended.
Infants whose mothers have taken AIIRAs should be closely observed for hypotension

items.t: MHRA: ACE inhibitors and ARBs should not be used at any stage of pregnancy unless absolutely necessary; stop as soon as possible on diagnosis.

src.q: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor antagonists should not be used at any stage of pregnancy unless absolutely necessary
On diagnosis of pregnancy, treatment with an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin II receptor antagonist should be stopped as soon as possible

items.t: BUMPS: early-pregnancy use is unlikely to harm the baby but the ARB should usually be stopped; use after 20 weeks can cause problems in up to 1 in 3 exposed babies, and needs extra monitoring.

src.q: Taking an ARB in early pregnancy is unlikely to harm your baby.
an ARB should usually be stopped as soon as you find out you are pregnant
Studies show that up to one in every three babies exposed in the womb to an ARB after 20 weeks of pregnancy develop some or all of these problems.
If you take an ARB after around 20 weeks you will require additional monitoring to assess amniotic fluid levels and your baby's growth and wellbeing.

items.t: SmPC: not recommended (no information); prefer alternatives, especially with a newborn or preterm infant. MHRA: not recommended for any ARB.

src.q: Because no information is available regarding the use of valsartan during breastfeeding, Valsartan is not recommended
For all angiotensin II receptor antagonists, use in mothers breastfeeding is not recommended.

items.t: SPS: valsartan can be used with caution if specifically indicated (favourable pharmacokinetics), but another class with more evidence is preferred. Monitor the infant for hypotension and wet nappies; neonates and infants under 2 months are at most risk.

src.q: Valsartan can be used with caution during breastfeeding if it is specifically clinically indicated.
Candesartan, losartan or valsartan have the most favourable pharmacokinetics and would therefore be preferred.
Neonates and infants less than 2 months are at the most risk from the side-effects of angiotensin-II receptor antagonists, particularly hypotension
As a precaution, monitor the infant for hypotension which may manifest as drowsiness, lethargy, looking pale, poor feeding and inadequate weight gain.
