items.t: Patients planning pregnancy should be switched to an alternative with an established pregnancy safety profile unless continued treatment is essential. No effect on fertility in rats.

src.q: patients planning pregnancy should be changed to alternative anti-hypertensive treatments which have an established safety profile for use in pregnancy
Valsartan had no adverse effects on the reproductive performance of male or female rats
women who are planning pregnancy should be switched to alternative antihypertensive treatments that have an established safety profile for use in pregnancy

items.t: Hypertension: no common adverse effects listed; uncommon vertigo, cough, abdominal pain, fatigue.

src.q: Ear and labyrinth system disorders: Uncommon: Vertigo
Respiratory, thoracic and mediastinal disorders: Uncommon: Cough

items.t: Post-MI and/or heart failure: dizziness, postural dizziness, hypotension, orthostatic hypotension, renal failure and impairment (common).

src.q: Nervous system disorders: Common: Dizziness, Postural dizziness
Vascular disorders: Common: Hypotension, Orthostatic hypotension
Renal and urinary disorders: Common: Renal failure and impairment

items.t: Children: headache, dizziness and hyperkalaemia most frequent; hyperkalaemia more often with chronic kidney disease.

src.q: with headache (5.4%), dizziness (2.3%), and hyperkalaemia (2.3%) being the most frequent

items.t: Angioedema (including laryngeal swelling) and intestinal angioedema: stop immediately; do not re-administer.

src.q: Valsartan should be immediately discontinued in patients who develop angioedema, and Valsartan should not be re-administered
If intestinal angioedema is diagnosed, valsartan should be discontinued

items.t: Renal failure, raised potassium, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, serum sickness, vasculitis (frequency not known).

src.q: Not known: Renal failure and impairment, Elevation of serum creatinine
Not known: Decrease in haemoglobin, Decrease in haematocrit, Neutropenia, Thrombocytopenia

items.t: Baseline: blood pressure, eGFR or serum creatinine, potassium, sodium.

src.q: Baseline Blood pressure Estimated glomerular filtration rate or Serum creatinine (for creatinine clearance) Serum potassium Serum sodium

items.t: Hypertension: renal function, sodium and potassium within 1-2 weeks of starting or a dose change; blood pressure within 1 month; then annually.

src.q: Hypertension Within 1 - 2 weeks Estimated glomerular filtration rate or Serum creatinine (for creatinine clearance) Serum sodium Serum potassium Within 1 month Blood pressure
Hypertension Annually Serum sodium Serum potassium Estimated glomerular filtration rate or Serum creatinine (for creatinine clearance)

items.t: Heart failure or post-MI: assess renal function; once stable (heart failure) every 3-6 months.

src.q: Evaluation of post-myocardial infarction patients should always include assessment of renal function
Ongoing once stable Heart failure Every 3 - 6 months Estimated glomerular filtration rate or Serum creatinine (for creatinine clearance) Serum sodium Serum potassium

items.t: Potassium 6.0 mmol/L or above in CKD: stop the ARB after stopping other potassium-raising drugs and seek specialist advice. Sodium below 132 mmol/L: specialist advice. Creatinine rise over 50%: follow local guidelines.

src.q: Value 6.0 mmol/L or above in people with CKD Stop ACEI/ARB after stopping other drugs that may increase potassium and seek specialist advice.
Value is below 132mmol/L Obtain specialist advice
A transient decrease in renal function should not prompt stopping ACEI/ARB
Creatinine increase more than 50% Follow local guidelines

items.t: Take with water, with or without a meal.

src.q: Valsartan may be taken independently of a meal and should be administered with water.

items.t: Dizziness or tiredness may occur; take care when driving or using machines.

src.q: When driving vehicles or operating machines it should be taken into account that occasionally dizziness or weariness may occur.

items.t: Tell the prescriber straight away if pregnant or planning pregnancy.

src.q: When pregnancy is diagnosed, treatment with AIIRAs should be stopped immediately

items.t: Stop and seek help for swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat (angioedema: valsartan is stopped and not given again), or abdominal pain with nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea (intestinal angioedema).

src.q: swelling of the face, lips, pharynx, and/or tongue
Valsartan should be immediately discontinued in patients who develop angioedema
These patients presented with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea.

items.t: Essential hypertension in adults whose blood pressure is not adequately controlled on valsartan or hydrochlorothiazide alone.

src.q: Treatment of essential hypertension in adults.
is indicated in patients whose blood pressure is not adequately controlled on valsartan or hydrochlorothiazide monotherapy.

restrictions.note: No specialist-only or shared-care restriction stated in the SmPC. Fixed-dose combination for patients not controlled on monotherapy (see indications).

items.t: One tablet once daily. Titrate the individual components first (direct switch from monotherapy may be considered). If uncontrolled, increase either component up to a maximum of 320 mg/25 mg. Effect largely within 2 weeks, maximal in about 4 weeks (sometimes 4-8 weeks).

src.q: is one film-coated tablet once daily. Dose titration with the individual components is recommended.
the dose may be increased by increasing either one of the components to a maximum dose of Co-Diovan 320 mg/25 mg
In most patients, maximal effects are observed within 4 weeks.

items.t: Elderly: no dose adjustment needed.

src.q: No dose adjustment is required in elderly patients.

items.t: Not recommended under 18 years (no safety or efficacy data).

src.q: is not recommended for use in children below the age of 18 years due to a lack of data on safety and efficacy.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to valsartan, hydrochlorothiazide, other sulfonamide-derived medicines or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to active substances, other sulfonamide-derived medicinal products or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Second and third trimesters of pregnancy.

src.q: Second and third trimester of pregnancy

items.t: Severe hepatic impairment, biliary cirrhosis and cholestasis.

src.q: Severe hepatic impairment, biliary cirrhosis and cholestasis.

items.t: Severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), anuria.

src.q: Severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance < 30 ml/min), anuria.

items.t: Refractory hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypercalcaemia, and symptomatic hyperuricaemia.

src.q: Refractory hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypercalcaemia, and symptomatic hyperuricaemia.

items.t: With aliskiren-containing products in patients with diabetes mellitus or renal impairment (GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m²).

src.q: with aliskiren containing products in patients with diabetes mellitus or renal impairment (GFR < 60 mL/min/1.73m2)

items.t: Electrolytes: valsartan with potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics or potassium salt substitutes is not recommended. Hydrochlorothiazide can cause hypokalaemia (frequent potassium checks), hyponatraemia, hypomagnesaemia and hypercalcaemia; check electrolytes periodically.

src.q: Frequent monitoring of serum potassium is recommended.
periodic determination of serum electrolytes should be performed at appropriate intervals

items.t: Sodium or volume depletion: correct before starting (symptomatic hypotension).

src.q: Sodium and/or volume depletion should be corrected before starting treatment with Co-Diovan.

items.t: Severe chronic heart failure: should not be used. Renal artery stenosis (unilateral, bilateral or solitary kidney): should not be used for hypertension. Primary hyperaldosteronism: should not be treated with it.

src.q: Co-Diovan should not be used in these patients.
Co-Diovan should not be used to treat hypertension in patients with unilateral or bilateral renal artery stenosis or stenosis of the artery to a solitary kidney
Patients with primary hyperaldosteronism should not be treated with Co-Diovan

items.t: Aortic or mitral stenosis, HOCM: special caution. Mild to moderate hepatic impairment without cholestasis: caution; thiazides may precipitate hepatic coma in liver disease.

src.q: special caution is indicated in patients suffering from aortic or mitral stenosis, or hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM)
Thiazides should be used with caution in patients with impaired hepatic function or progressive liver disease, since minor alterations of fluid and electrolyte balance may precipitate hepatic coma.

items.t: Angioedema: stop immediately and do not re-administer. Caution with previous hypersensitivity to other ARBs; hydrochlorothiazide hypersensitivity more likely with allergy or asthma.

src.q: Co-Diovan should be immediately discontinued in patients who develop angioedema, and Co-Diovan should not be re-administered
Caution should be exercised in patients who have shown prior hypersensitivity to other angiotensin II receptor antagonists.

items.t: Dual RAAS blockade not recommended; ACE inhibitor + ARB should not be used in diabetic nephropathy.

src.q: Dual blockade of the RAAS through the combined use of ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers or aliskiren is therefore not recommended
ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers should not be used concomitantly in patients with diabetic nephropathy.

items.t: Non-melanoma skin cancer: risk rises with cumulative hydrochlorothiazide dose; advise skin checks and sun protection; reconsider use after previous skin cancer (MHRA).

src.q: Patients taking hydrochlorothiazide should be informed of the risk of NMSC and advised to regularly check their skin for any new lesions and promptly report any suspicious skin lesions.
reconsider the use of hydrochlorothiazide in patients who have had previous skin cancer
inform patients taking hydrochlorothiazide-containing products of the risk of non-melanoma skin cancer, particularly in long-term use

items.t: Choroidal effusion, acute myopia and acute angle-closure glaucoma (hours to weeks after starting): stop hydrochlorothiazide as quickly as possible. Risk factors include sulfonamide or penicillin allergy.

src.q: The primary treatment is to discontinue hydrochlorothiazide as rapidly as possible.
Risk factors for developing acute angle closure glaucoma may include a history of sulfonamide or penicillin allergy.

items.t: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (very rare): withdraw; do not give hydrochlorothiazide again after previous ARDS with it.

src.q: Hydrochlorothiazide should not be administered to patients who previously experienced ARDS following hydrochlorothiazide intake.

items.t: Thiazides may worsen glucose tolerance and raise cholesterol, triglycerides and uric acid; may exacerbate or activate SLE; photosensitivity (stop if it occurs); stop before parathyroid function tests.

src.q: may alter glucose tolerance and raise serum levels of cholesterol, triglycerides and uric acid
have been reported to exacerbate or activate systemic lupus erythematosus
Thiazides should be discontinued before carrying out tests for parathyroid function.

items.t: Lithium: not recommended (raised lithium levels and toxicity, increased further by the thiazide); if needed, monitor lithium carefully.

src.q: Since renal clearance of lithium is reduced by thiazides, the risk of lithium toxicity may presumably be increased further with Co-Diovan.

items.t: ACE inhibitors, other ARBs, aliskiren: dual RAAS blockade (more hypotension, hyperkalaemia, renal impairment). Potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements, potassium salt substitutes: not recommended; monitor potassium if needed.

src.q: Concomitant use not recommended Potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements, salt substitutes containing potassium and other substances that may increase potassium levels.

items.t: NSAIDs (including COX-2 inhibitors and aspirin above 3 g/day): reduced antihypertensive effect, worsening renal function, raised potassium; monitor renal function at the start and keep hydrated.

src.q: concomitant use of Co-Diovan and NSAIDs may lead to worsening of renal function and an increase in serum potassium
Therefore, monitoring of renal function at the beginning of the treatment is recommended, as well as adequate hydration of the patient.

items.t: Medicines lowering potassium (other diuretics, corticosteroids, laxatives, amphotericin, salicylates): monitor potassium. Torsades-inducing medicines (class Ia/III antiarrhythmics, some antipsychotics): caution because of hypokalaemia. Digoxin: hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia favour arrhythmias.

src.q: If these medicinal products are to be prescribed with the hydrochlorothiazide-valsartan combination, monitoring of potassium plasma levels is advised
hydrochlorothiazide should be administered with caution when associated with medicinal products that could induce torsades de pointes

items.t: Antidiabetics: dose adjustment may be needed; metformin with caution (lactic acidosis with functional renal failure). Beta-blockers: more hyperglycaemia. Allopurinol: more hypersensitivity reactions. Calcium salts or vitamin D: serum calcium may rise.

src.q: Dose adjustment of the antidiabetic medicinal product may be necessary.
Metformin should be used with caution because of the risk of lactic acidosis induced by possible functional renal failure linked to hydrochlorothiazide.
may increase the incidence of hypersensitivity reactions to allopurinol

items.t: Antidepressants, antipsychotics, antiepileptics: may intensify hyponatraemia; caution in long-term use. Methotrexate and other cytotoxics: reduced renal excretion, more myelosuppression. Methyldopa: isolated haemolytic anaemia. Other antihypertensives: increased effect. Alcohol or opioids: orthostatic hypotension. Colestyramine/colestipol: give hydrochlorothiazide at least 4 h before or 4-6 h after.

src.q: Caution is advised in long-term administration of these drugs.
may reduce renal excretion of cytotoxic agents (e.g. cyclophosamide, methotrexate) and potentiate their myelosuppressive effects
There have been isolated reports of haemolytic anaemia in patients receiving concomitant treatment with methyldopa and hydrochlorothiazide.
hydrochlorothiazide is administered at least 4 h before or 4-6 h after the administration of resins

items.t: Mild to moderate renal impairment (CrCl 30 mL/min or above): no dose adjustment; monitor potassium, creatinine and uric acid periodically.

src.q: No dosage adjustment is required for patients with renal impairment with a creatinine clearance ≥30 ml/min
Periodic monitoring of serum potassium, creatinine and uric acid levels is recommended when Co-Diovan is used in patients with renal impairment.

items.t: Severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min) and anuria: contraindicated (hydrochlorothiazide component). Note: section 4.2 of the same SmPC expresses this as GFR below 30 mL/min.

src.q: Severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance < 30 ml/min), anuria.
Co-Diovan is contraindicated in patients with severe renal impairment (GFR < 30 mL/min) and anuria

items.t: SPS (for ARBs): seek specialist advice before starting if eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73 m².

src.q: Seek specialist advice prior to initiation for patients where there is: severe or unstable heart failure renovascular disease eGFR less than 30ml/min/1.73m2

items.t: Mild to moderate hepatic impairment without cholestasis: valsartan dose must not exceed 80 mg; use with caution (thiazides may precipitate hepatic coma).

src.q: In patients with mild to moderate hepatic impairment without cholestasis the dose of valsartan should not exceed 80 mg
Co-Diovan should be used with caution

items.t: Severe hepatic impairment, biliary cirrhosis or cholestasis: contraindicated.

src.q: Co-Diovan is contraindicated in patients with severe hepatic impairment or with biliary cirrhosis and cholestasis

items.t: ARB component: first trimester not recommended; second and third trimesters contraindicated (fetotoxicity and neonatal toxicity). Stop immediately when pregnancy is diagnosed.

src.q: The use of AIIRAs is contra-indicated during the second and third trimester of pregnancy
When pregnancy is diagnosed, treatment with AIIRAs should be stopped immediately

items.t: Hydrochlorothiazide crosses the placenta; in the second and third trimesters it may reduce feto-placental perfusion and cause neonatal jaundice, electrolyte disturbance and thrombocytopenia.

src.q: Hydrochlorothiazide crosses the placenta.
may cause foetal and neonatal effects like icterus, disturbance of electrolyte balance and thrombocytopenia

items.t: MHRA: ACE inhibitors and ARBs should not be used at any stage of pregnancy unless absolutely necessary; stop as soon as possible on diagnosis.

src.q: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor antagonists should not be used at any stage of pregnancy unless absolutely necessary
On diagnosis of pregnancy, treatment with an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin II receptor antagonist should be stopped as soon as possible

items.t: BUMPS: ARB use after 20 weeks can cause problems in up to 1 in 3 exposed babies; diuretics may reduce placental blood flow and are rarely needed in pregnancy.

src.q: Taking an ARB in early pregnancy is unlikely to harm your baby.
an ARB should usually be stopped as soon as you find out you are pregnant
Studies show that up to one in every three babies exposed in the womb to an ARB after 20 weeks of pregnancy develop some or all of these problems.
If you take an ARB after around 20 weeks you will require additional monitoring to assess amniotic fluid levels and your baby's growth and wellbeing.
Diuretics may reduce blood flow to the placenta.

items.t: SmPC: not recommended (no valsartan data; hydrochlorothiazide passes into milk); prefer alternatives, especially with a newborn or preterm infant. MHRA: not recommended for any ARB.

src.q: Hydrochlorothiazide is excreted in human milk.
Therefore the use of Co-Diovan during breast feeding is not recommended.
For all angiotensin II receptor antagonists, use in mothers breastfeeding is not recommended.

items.t: Patients planning pregnancy should be switched to an alternative with an established pregnancy safety profile unless continued ARB treatment is essential.

src.q: patients planning pregnancy should be changed to alternative anti-hypertensive treatments which have an established safety profile for use in pregnancy
women who are planning pregnancy should be switched to alternative antihypertensive treatments that have an established safety profile for use in pregnancy

items.t: Hydrochlorothiazide: impotence (common).

src.q: Reproductive system and breast disorders Common Impotence

items.t: Hydrochlorothiazide: hypokalaemia and raised blood lipids (very common); hyponatraemia, hypomagnesaemia, hyperuricaemia, postural hypotension, loss of appetite, mild nausea and vomiting, urticaria/rash, impotence (common).

src.q: Very common Hypokalaemia, blood lipids increased (mainly at higher doses) Common Hyponatraemia, hypomagnesaemia, hyperuricaemia
Common Postural hypotension
Common Loss of appetite, mild nausea and vomiting

items.t: Combination: dehydration, paraesthesia, blurred vision, tinnitus, hypotension, cough, myalgia, fatigue (uncommon).

src.q: Uncommon Dehydration Nervous system disorders
Uncommon Hypotension Respiratory, thoracic and mediastinal disorders Uncommon Cough

items.t: Angioedema: stop immediately, do not re-administer. Intestinal angioedema: stop and monitor.

src.q: Co-Diovan should be immediately discontinued in patients who develop angioedema, and Co-Diovan should not be re-administered
If intestinal angioedema is diagnosed, Co-Diovan should be discontinued

items.t: Acute angle-closure glaucoma/choroidal effusion (eye pain, reduced vision): stop hydrochlorothiazide quickly. ARDS/non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema: withdraw.

src.q: Symptoms include acute onset of decreased visual acuity or ocular pain
If diagnosis of ARDS is suspected, Diovan Comp should be withdrawn, and appropriate treatment given.

items.t: Non-melanoma skin cancer (cumulative dose); agranulocytosis, bone marrow failure, haemolytic anaemia, toxic epidermal necrolysis (very rare); renal failure.

src.q: Very rare Agranulocytosis, leucopenia, haemolytic anaemia, bone marrow failure
Very rare Necrotising vasculitis and toxic epidermal necrolysis

items.t: Baseline: blood pressure, eGFR or serum creatinine, potassium, sodium (SPS for ARBs).

src.q: Baseline Blood pressure Estimated glomerular filtration rate or Serum creatinine (for creatinine clearance) Serum potassium Serum sodium

items.t: Serum electrolytes periodically; frequent potassium checks; with renal impairment also creatinine and uric acid. SPS hypertension schedule: renal function, sodium and potassium within 1-2 weeks of a start or dose change, then annually.

src.q: Frequent monitoring of serum potassium is recommended.
periodic determination of serum electrolytes should be performed at appropriate intervals
Hypertension Within 1 - 2 weeks Estimated glomerular filtration rate or Serum creatinine (for creatinine clearance) Serum sodium Serum potassium Within 1 month Blood pressure
Hypertension Annually Serum sodium Serum potassium Estimated glomerular filtration rate or Serum creatinine (for creatinine clearance)

items.t: Check skin regularly for new or changed lesions (non-melanoma skin cancer).

src.q: reconsider the use of hydrochlorothiazide in patients who have had previous skin cancer
inform patients taking hydrochlorothiazide-containing products of the risk of non-melanoma skin cancer, particularly in long-term use

items.t: Potassium 6.0 mmol/L or above in CKD: stop the ARB after stopping other potassium-raising drugs and seek specialist advice. Sodium below 132 mmol/L: specialist advice.

src.q: Value 6.0 mmol/L or above in people with CKD Stop ACEI/ARB after stopping other drugs that may increase potassium and seek specialist advice.
Value is below 132mmol/L Obtain specialist advice

items.t: Once daily, with or without food, with water.

src.q: can be taken with or without food and should be administered with water

items.t: Dizziness or tiredness may occur; take care when driving.

src.q: When driving vehicles or operating machines it should be taken into account that occasionally dizziness or weariness may occur.

items.t: Check skin regularly, report new or changed skin lesions; limit sun and UV exposure and use protection.

src.q: reconsider the use of hydrochlorothiazide in patients who have had previous skin cancer
inform patients taking hydrochlorothiazide-containing products of the risk of non-melanoma skin cancer, particularly in long-term use
Possible preventive measures such as limited exposure to sunlight and UV rays and, in case of exposure, adequate protection should be advised

items.t: Seek urgent help for sudden eye pain or reduced vision, swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, or sudden breathlessness.

src.q: Symptoms include acute onset of decreased visual acuity or ocular pain
At the onset, symptoms include dyspnoea, fever, pulmonary deterioration and hypotension.
swelling of the face, lips, pharynx, and/or tongue

items.t: Tell the prescriber straight away if pregnant or planning pregnancy.

src.q: When pregnancy is diagnosed, treatment with AIIRAs should be stopped immediately

items.t: Major depressive episodes (treatment and prevention of recurrence); generalised anxiety disorder; social anxiety disorder; panic disorder with or without agoraphobia.

src.q: Treatment of major depressive episodes. For prevention of recurrence of major depressive episodes. Treatment of generalised anxiety disorder.
Treatment of social anxiety disorder. Treatment of panic disorder, with or without agoraphobia.

items.t: Not recommended for children and adolescents under 18 years.

src.q: Venlafaxine is not recommended for use in children and adolescents.

items.t: Prescribe the smallest quantity consistent with good patient management, to reduce overdose risk (fatal overdoses reported, mainly with alcohol or other medicines).

src.q: Prescriptions for venlafaxine should be written for the smallest quantity consistent with good patient management, in order to reduce the risk of overdose
Overdose with venlafaxine has been reported predominantly in combination with alcohol and/or other medicinal products, including cases with fatal outcome

items.t: Start 75 mg once daily. If no response, increase up to a maximum of 375 mg/day, at intervals of 2 weeks or more (not less than 4 days if clinically warranted). Increase only after clinical evaluation; keep the lowest effective dose. Continue for at least 6 months after remission.

src.q: The recommended starting dose for prolonged-release venlafaxine is 75 mg given once daily.
may benefit from dose increases up to a maximum dose of 375 mg/day
If clinically warranted due to symptom severity, dose increases can be made at more frequent intervals, but not less than 4 days.
Antidepressive medicinal products should continue for at least six months following remission.

items.t: Start 75 mg once daily. If no response, increase up to a maximum of 225 mg/day, at intervals of 2 weeks or more.

src.q: Generalised anxiety disorder The recommended starting dose for prolonged-release venlafaxine is 75 mg given once daily.
may benefit from dose increases up to a maximum dose of 225 mg/day

items.t: 75 mg once daily. No evidence that higher doses add benefit, but up to a maximum of 225 mg/day may be considered in non-responders (intervals of 2 weeks or more).

src.q: The recommended dose for prolonged-release venlafaxine is 75 mg given once daily. There is no evidence that higher doses confer any additional benefit.
increases up to a maximum dose of 225 mg/day may be considered

items.t: 37.5 mg/day for 7 days, then 75 mg/day. If no response, increase up to a maximum of 225 mg/day (intervals of 2 weeks or more).

src.q: It is recommended that a dose of 37.5 mg/day of prolonged-release venlafaxine be used for 7 days. Dosage should then be increased to 75 mg/day.

items.t: Elderly: no dose change for age alone, but use caution (possible renal impairment, changed sensitivity); use the lowest effective dose and monitor carefully when increasing.

src.q: No specific dose adjustments of venlafaxine are considered necessary based on patient age alone. However, caution should be exercised in treating the elderly
patients should be carefully monitored when an increase in the dose is required

items.t: Switching from immediate-release tablets: use the nearest equivalent daily dose (e.g. 37.5 mg twice daily to 75 mg once daily).

src.q: venlafaxine immediate-release tablets 37.5 mg twice daily may be switched to venlafaxine prolonged-release capsules 75 mg once daily.

items.t: Stopping: avoid abrupt withdrawal. Reduce gradually over at least 1 to 2 weeks; some patients need months or longer. If intolerable symptoms, go back to the previous dose and taper more slowly.

src.q: When stopping treatment with venlafaxine, the dose should be gradually reduced over a period of at least one to two weeks in order to reduce the risk of withdrawal reactions
In some patients, discontinuation may need to occur very gradually over periods of months or longer.

items.t: Not recommended under 18 years. Trials in major depressive disorder did not show efficacy; safety and efficacy for other indications not established. If used on clinical need, monitor carefully for suicidal symptoms.

src.q: Controlled clinical studies in children and adolescents with major depressive disorder failed to demonstrate efficacy
If, based on clinical need, a decision to treat is nevertheless taken, the patient should be carefully monitored for the appearance of suicidal symptoms.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to venlafaxine or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Irreversible MAOIs: contraindicated (serotonin syndrome). Do not start venlafaxine within 14 days of stopping an irreversible MAOI; stop venlafaxine at least 7 days before starting one.

src.q: Concomitant treatment with irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) is contraindicated due to the risk of serotonin syndrome
Venlafaxine must not be initiated for at least 14 days after discontinuation of treatment with an irreversible MAOI.
Venlafaxine must be discontinued for at least 7 days before starting treatment with an irreversible MAOI

items.t: Serotonin syndrome (can resemble NMS), especially with other serotonergic drugs, MAOIs, antipsychotics or other dopamine antagonists. If combined use is needed, observe carefully at start and after dose increases. Tryptophan supplements: not recommended.

src.q: As with other serotonergic agents, serotonin syndrome, a potentially life-threatening condition may occur with venlafaxine treatment
careful observation of the patient is advised, particularly during treatment initiation and dose increases
The concomitant use of venlafaxine with serotonin precursors (such as tryptophan supplements) is not recommended.

items.t: Blood pressure: dose-related rises are common; severe rises needing urgent treatment reported. Screen for and control hypertension before starting; review BP periodically and after dose increases. Caution if raised BP or heart rate could harm (e.g. impaired cardiac function).

src.q: Dose-related increases in blood pressure have been commonly reported with venlafaxine.
All patients should be carefully screened for high blood pressure and pre-existing hypertension should be controlled before initation of treatment.
Blood pressure should be reviewed periodically, after initiation of treatment and after dose increases.
Caution should be exercised in patients whose underlying conditions might be compromised by increases in blood pressure, e.g., those with impaired cardiac function.

items.t: Heart disease and arrhythmia: not studied after recent myocardial infarction or in unstable heart disease (use with caution). QTc prolongation, torsade de pointes and fatal arrhythmias reported; weigh risks and benefits if at high risk of arrhythmia or QTc prolongation.

src.q: Venlafaxine has not been evaluated in patients with a recent history of myocardial infarction or unstable heart disease. Therefore, it should be used with caution in these patients.
The balance of risks and benefits should be considered before prescribing venlafaxine to patients at high risk of serious cardiac arrhythmia or QTc prolongation

items.t: Seizures: introduce with caution if history of convulsions; stop if seizures develop.

src.q: venlafaxine should be introduced with caution in patients with a history of convulsions
Treatment should be discontinued in any patient who develops seizures.

items.t: Hyponatraemia / SIADH: higher risk in elderly, volume-depleted or dehydrated patients and those taking diuretics.

src.q: Cases of hyponatraemia and/or the Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone (SIADH) secretion may occur with venlafaxine.
Elderly patients, patients taking diuretics, and patients who are otherwise volume-depleted may be at greater risk for this event.

items.t: Bleeding (bruising to GI and life-threatening haemorrhage): use cautiously if predisposed to bleeding, including with anticoagulants and platelet inhibitors. May increase postpartum haemorrhage.

src.q: venlafaxine should be used cautiously in patients predisposed to bleeding, including patients on anticoagulants and platelet inhibitors.
SSRIs/SNRIs, including venlafaxine, may increase the risk of postpartum haemorrhage

items.t: Mydriasis: closely monitor patients with raised intraocular pressure or at risk of acute angle-closure glaucoma.

src.q: It is recommended that patients with raised intraocular pressure or patients at risk for acute narrow-angle glaucoma (angle-closure glaucoma) be closely monitored.

items.t: Suicidal thoughts and clinical worsening: monitor closely until improvement, especially early in treatment and after dose changes. Higher risk of suicidal behaviour under 25 years.

src.q: patients should be closely monitored until such improvement occurs
increased risk of suicidal behaviour with antidepressants compared to placebo in patients less than 25 years old

items.t: Mania/hypomania: use cautiously with a history or family history of bipolar disorder. Aggression: use cautiously with a history of aggression.

src.q: venlafaxine should be used cautiously in patients with a history or family history of bipolar disorder.
venlafaxine should be used cautiously in patients with a history of aggression.

items.t: Diabetes: glycaemic control may change; insulin and/or oral antidiabetic doses may need adjusting.

src.q: In patients with diabetes, treatment with an SSRI or venlafaxine may alter glycaemic control. Insulin and/or oral antidiabetic dosage may need to be adjusted.

items.t: Serum cholesterol may rise: consider measuring it during long-term treatment.

src.q: Measurement of serum cholesterol levels should be considered during long-term treatment.

items.t: Sexual dysfunction may occur and can continue after stopping. Akathisia may occur in the first weeks; increasing the dose may be harmful.

src.q: There have been reports of long-lasting sexual dysfunction where the symptoms have continued despite discontinuation of SNRIs
In patients who develop these symptoms, increasing the dose may be detrimental.

items.t: Weight-loss agents (e.g. phentermine): co-administration not recommended.

src.q: Co-administration of venlafaxine and weight loss agents is not recommended.

items.t: False-positive urine immunoassay screens for phencyclidine and amphetamine; confirm with GC/MS.

src.q: False-positive urine immunoassay screening tests for phencyclidine (PCP) and amphetamine have been reported in patients taking venlafaxine.

items.t: Irreversible non-selective MAOIs: contraindicated. Moclobemide: not recommended. Linezolid: should not be given.

src.q: Venlafaxine must not be used in combination with irreversible non-selective MAOIs.
the combination of venlafaxine with a reversible and selective MAOI, such as moclobemide, is not recommended
The antibiotic linezolid is a weak reversible and non-selective MAOI and should not be given to patients treated with venlafaxine

items.t: Serotonergic drugs (triptans, SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics, lithium, St John's wort, opioids such as tramadol and dextromethorphan) and antipsychotics/dopamine antagonists: serotonin syndrome risk; observe carefully, especially at start and after dose increases.

src.q: including triptans, SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclic antidepressants, amphetamines, lithium, sibutramine
opioids [e.g., buprenorphine, fentanyl and its analogues, tramadol, dextromethorphan, tapentadol, pethidine, methadone and pentazocine]
or with antipsychotics or other dopamine antagonists
careful observation of the patient is advised, particularly during treatment initiation and dose increases

items.t: QT-prolonging medicines (class Ia/III antiarrhythmics, some antipsychotics, some macrolides such as erythromycin, some antihistamines, some quinolones such as moxifloxacin): avoid co-administration.

src.q: Co-administration of such medicinal products should be avoided
some macrolides (e.g., erythromycin) some antihistamines some quinolone antibiotics (e.g., moxifloxacin)

items.t: CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. clarithromycin, itraconazole, ketoconazole, ritonavir): may raise venlafaxine levels; caution.

src.q: Concomitant use of CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., atazanavir, clarithromycin, indinavir, itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole,
Therefore, caution is advised if a patient's therapy includes a CYP3A4 inhibitor and venlafaxine concomitantly.

items.t: Other CNS-active drugs: caution. Alcohol: advise patients not to drink.

src.q: caution is advised when venlafaxine is taken in combination with other CNS-active substances
Patients should be advised not to use alcohol

items.t: Anticoagulants and platelet inhibitors: higher bleeding risk; use cautiously.

src.q: venlafaxine should be used cautiously in patients predisposed to bleeding, including patients on anticoagulants and platelet inhibitors.

items.t: Metoprolol (levels up 30 to 40%) and imipramine: caution. Haloperidol levels rise (clinical significance unknown).

src.q: Caution should be exercised with co-administration of venlafaxine and metoprolol.
Caution should be exercised with co-administration of venlafaxine and imipramine.

items.t: GFR 30 to 70 mL/min: no dose change needed, but caution. Severe renal impairment (GFR <30 mL/min) or haemodialysis: reduce dose by 50%; individualise.

src.q: Although no change in dosage is necessary for patients with glomerular filtration rate (GFR) between 30-70 ml/minute, caution is advised.
For patients that require haemodialysis and in patients with severe renal impairment (GFR < 30 ml/min), the dose should be reduced by 50%.

items.t: Mild or moderate hepatic impairment: consider a 50% dose reduction (individualise). Severe: limited data; caution, consider reducing by more than 50%, weigh benefit against risk.

src.q: In patients with mild and moderate hepatic impairment, in general a 50% dose reduction should be considered.
Caution is advised, and a dose reduction by more than 50% should be considered.

items.t: SmPC: no adequate human data; use only if the expected benefit outweighs any possible risk.

src.q: Venlafaxine must only be administered to pregnant women if the expected benefits outweigh any possible risk.

items.t: Use until or shortly before birth: neonatal withdrawal/serotonergic symptoms; some newborns needed tube-feeding, respiratory support or long hospital stay. PPHN risk cannot be ruled out.

src.q: Some newborns exposed to venlafaxine late in the third trimester have developed complications requiring tube-feeding, respiratory support or prolonged hospitalisation.
this potential risk cannot be ruled out with venlafaxine

items.t: Use in the month before delivery: small increased risk (less than 2-fold) of postpartum haemorrhage. MHRA: weigh this against the individual bleeding/thrombotic risk and the benefits of treatment.

src.q: Observational data indicate an increased risk (less than 2-fold) of postpartum haemorrhage following SSRIs/SNRIs exposure within the month prior to birth
consider the findings of the review in the context of individual patient risk factors for bleeding or thrombotic events

items.t: BUMPS (UKTIS): can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor; no good evidence of effects on the baby's development. Late-pregnancy use usually means birth in hospital (neonatal checks).

src.q: Venlafaxine can be used in pregnancy if recommended by your doctor.
There is no good evidence that venlafaxine affects your baby's development.

items.t: SmPC: venlafaxine and its active metabolite pass into milk; infant crying, irritability and abnormal sleep reported. Decide whether to continue breastfeeding or treatment, weighing benefits.

A risk to the suckling child cannot be excluded.

items.t: SPS: can be used with caution and infant monitoring, but SSRIs or tricyclics are preferred. Monitor the infant for irritability, agitation, colic, drowsiness, GI symptoms, poor feeding and weight gain. No need to switch if used successfully in pregnancy (full-term healthy infant).

If duloxetine, mirtazapine, trazodone or venlafaxine have been used successfully during pregnancy, there is no need to switch to a preferred choice in breastfeeding

items.t: Reduced fertility seen in rats exposed to the active metabolite; human relevance unknown. Unintended pregnancies reported with oral contraceptives, with no clear evidence of an interaction (not studied).

items.t: Very common: nausea, dry mouth, headache, sweating (including night sweats).

items.t: Dose-related blood pressure increases are common. Withdrawal symptoms are common on stopping (dizziness, sensory disturbances, sleep disturbance, agitation, nausea, tremor, headache).

src.q: Dose-related increases in blood pressure have been commonly reported with venlafaxine.
Withdrawal symptoms, when treatment is discontinued, are common, particularly if discontinuation is abrupt

items.t: Serotonin syndrome / NMS-like reactions: potentially life-threatening.

src.q: As with other serotonergic agents, serotonin syndrome, a potentially life-threatening condition may occur with venlafaxine treatment

items.t: Severely raised blood pressure needing immediate treatment.

items.t: QTc prolongation, torsade de pointes, ventricular tachycardia, fatal arrhythmias (especially in overdose or with risk factors).

src.q: Treatment should be discontinued in any patient who develops seizures.

items.t: Suicidal thoughts/behaviour and aggression, including on dose reduction or stopping: monitor closely.

src.q: patients should be closely monitored when the dose is reduced or during discontinuation

items.t: Screen for high blood pressure and control hypertension before starting. Discuss the risk of suicidal thoughts and of sexual dysfunction when starting or changing dose (MHRA 2026).

discuss with patients when starting or changing the dose of an antidepressant or at their next review, the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviours

items.t: Blood pressure periodically and after each dose increase. Close monitoring for clinical worsening and suicidality early on, after dose changes and when stopping. Monitor regularly after starting (MHRA). Consider serum cholesterol in long-term use.

monitor your patients regularly after starting treatment with an antidepressant

items.t: Stop if seizures develop. Taper gradually when stopping.

src.q: Use with caution in the presence of diseases in which neuromuscular transmission is affected (myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton syndrome, advanced Duchenne muscular dystrophy).

Intravenous beta-blockers should not be given to patients under treatment with verapamil.

items.t: Simvastatin and atorvastatin: verapamil raises their levels. Start the statin at the lowest dose; if adding verapamil, consider reducing the statin dose. MHRA: do not exceed simvastatin 20 mg daily with verapamil.

consider a reduction in the statin dose and retitrate against serum cholesterol concentrations.

src.q: verapamil should not be given during the first trimester of pregnancy unless, in the clinician's judgement, it is essential for the welfare of the patient.

src.q: Eucreas is not recommended for use in children and adolescents (< 18 years).

src.q: Contraindications - Hypersensitivity to the active substances or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1

items.t: Any acute metabolic acidosis (e.g. lactic acidosis, diabetic ketoacidosis); diabetic pre-coma; severe renal failure (GFR < 30 mL/min).

src.q: Any type of acute metabolic acidosis (such as lactic acidosis, diabetic ketoacidosis) - Diabetic pre-coma - Severe renal failure (GFR < 30 ml/min)

items.t: Acute conditions that may alter renal function: dehydration, severe infection, shock, intravascular iodinated contrast.

src.q: Acute conditions with the potential to alter renal function, such as: - dehydration, - severe infection, - shock, - intravascular administration of iodinated contrast agents

items.t: Acute or chronic disease that may cause tissue hypoxia: cardiac or respiratory failure, recent myocardial infarction, shock.

src.q: Acute or chronic disease which may cause tissue hypoxia, such as: - cardiac or respiratory failure, - recent myocardial infarction, - shock.

items.t: Hepatic impairment; acute alcohol intoxication, alcoholism; breastfeeding.

src.q: Hepatic impairment (see sections 4.2, 4.4 and 4.8) - Acute alcohol intoxication, alcoholism - Breast-feeding (see section 4.6)

items.t: Not a substitute for insulin; should not be used in type 1 diabetes.

src.q: Eucreas is not a substitute for insulin in insulin-requiring patients and should not be used in patients with type 1 diabetes.

items.t: Lactic acidosis (very rare, serious): risk rises with acute worsening of renal function, cardiorespiratory illness or sepsis. Stop temporarily in dehydration. Start medicines that can acutely impair renal function (antihypertensives, diuretics, NSAIDs) with caution.

src.q: Lactic acidosis, a very rare but serious metabolic complication, most often occurs at acute worsening of renal function, or cardiorespiratory illness or sepsis.
In case of dehydration (severe diarrhoea or vomiting, fever or reduced fluid intake), metformin should be temporarily discontinued and contact with a health care professional is recommended.
Medicinal products that can acutely impair renal function (such as antihypertensives, diuretics and NSAIDs) should be initiated with caution in metformin-treated patients.

items.t: Iodinated contrast (intravascular): stop before or at the time of imaging; restart no sooner than 48 hours after, once renal function is re-checked and stable.

src.q: Metformin should be discontinued prior to or at the time of the imaging procedure and not restarted until at least 48 hours after, provided that renal function has been re-evaluated and found to be stable

items.t: Mitochondrial disease (MELAS, MIDD): metformin is not recommended; withdraw immediately if suggestive signs appear.

src.q: metformin is not recommended due to the risk of lactic acidosis exacerbation and neurologic complications which may lead to worsening of the disease

items.t: Hepatic: should not be used in hepatic impairment (including pre-treatment ALT or AST > 3 x ULN). Rare hepatic dysfunction (including hepatitis) with vildagliptin; check liver function before and during treatment.

src.q: Patients with hepatic impairment, including those with pre-treatment ALT or AST > 3x ULN, should not be treated with Eucreas
Rare cases of hepatic dysfunction (including hepatitis) have been reported with vildagliptin.

items.t: Skin: blistering and exfoliative lesions reported; monitor for skin disorders such as blistering or ulceration.

src.q: monitoring for skin disorders, such as blistering or ulceration, is recommended

items.t: Acute pancreatitis: inform patients of the symptoms; stop if suspected; do not restart if confirmed. Caution with a history of acute pancreatitis.

src.q: If pancreatitis is suspected, vildagliptin should be discontinued; if acute pancreatitis is confirmed, vildagliptin should not be restarted.
Caution should be exercised in patients with a history of acute pancreatitis.

items.t: Hypoglycaemia with a sulphonylurea: a lower sulphonylurea dose may be considered.

src.q: Patients receiving vildagliptin in combination with a sulphonylurea may be at risk for hypoglycaemia.

items.t: Surgery under general, spinal or epidural anaesthesia: stop metformin at the time of surgery; restart no earlier than 48 hours after surgery or return to oral nutrition, once renal function is re-checked and stable.

src.q: Metformin must be discontinued at the time of surgery under general, spinal or epidural anaesthesia.
Therapy may be restarted no earlier than 48 hours following surgery or resumption of oral nutrition and provided that renal function has been re-evaluated and found to be stable.

items.t: Alcohol: combination not recommended (lactic acidosis risk).

src.q: Combinations not recommended Alcohol Alcohol intoxication is associated with an increased risk of lactic acidosis

items.t: NSAIDs (including COX-2 inhibitors), ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor antagonists and diuretics (especially loop diuretics): may impair renal function and raise lactic acidosis risk; close monitoring of renal function is necessary.

src.q: e.g. NSAIDs, including selective cyclo-oxygenase (COX) II inhibitors, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor antagonists and diuretics, especially loop diuretics
When starting or using such products in combination with metformin, close monitoring of renal function is necessary.

items.t: Glucocorticoids, beta-2 agonists and diuretics raise blood glucose: inform the patient, monitor blood glucose more often (especially at the start), adjust the dose if needed. Thiazides, corticosteroids, thyroid products and sympathomimetics may reduce the effect of vildagliptin.

src.q: Glucocorticoids, beta-2-agonists, and diuretics have intrinsic hyperglycaemic activity.
The patient should be informed and more frequent blood glucose monitoring performed, especially at the beginning of treatment.
the hypoglycaemic effect of vildagliptin may be reduced by certain active substances, including thiazides, corticosteroids, thyroid products and sympathomimetics

items.t: ACE inhibitors: may lower blood glucose (adjust the antidiabetic dose if necessary); there may also be an increased risk of angioedema with vildagliptin.

src.q: Angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors may decrease the blood glucose levels.
There may be an increased risk of angioedema in patients concomitantly taking ACE inhibitors.

items.t: OCT2/MATE inhibitors (e.g. ranolazine, vandetanib, dolutegravir, cimetidine) could increase metformin exposure.

src.q: transporter-2 [OCT2] / multidrug and toxin extrusion [MATE] inhibitors such as ranolazine, vandetanib, dolutegravir and cimetidine) could increase systemic exposure to metformin

items.t: Vildagliptin: low interaction potential; no clinically relevant pharmacokinetic interactions with pioglitazone, metformin, glibenclamide, digoxin, warfarin, amlodipine, ramipril, valsartan or simvastatin.

src.q: Vildagliptin has a low potential for interactions with co-administered medicinal products.

items.t: Assess GFR before starting and at least annually; every 3 to 6 months in the elderly or if at risk of progression. Review lactic acidosis risk factors before starting if GFR < 60 mL/min.

src.q: A GFR should be assessed before initiation of treatment with metformin-containing products and at least annually thereafter.
Factors that may increase the risk of lactic acidosis (see section 4.4) should be reviewed before considering initiation of metformin in patients with GFR<60 ml/min.

items.t: GFR 60-89 mL/min: metformin maximum 3000 mg/day (dose reduction may be considered); vildagliptin no dose adjustment.

src.q: 60-89 Maximum daily dose is 3000 mg. Dose reduction may be considered in relation to declining renal function. No dose adjustment.

items.t: GFR 45-59 mL/min: metformin maximum 2000 mg/day (start at most half the maximum); vildagliptin maximum 50 mg/day.

src.q: 45-59 Maximum daily dose is 2000 mg. The starting dose is at most half of the maximum dose. Maximal daily dose is 50 mg.

items.t: GFR 30-44 mL/min: metformin maximum 1000 mg/day (start at most half the maximum). The SmPC table text gives no separate vildagliptin figure for this row; the fixed tablet twice daily exceeds these limits, so use the individual medicines if no suitable strength.

src.q: 30-44 Maximum daily dose is 1000 mg. The starting dose is at most half of the maximum dose.
If no adequate strength of Eucreas is available, individual monocomponents should be used instead of the fixed dose combination.

items.t: GFR < 30 mL/min: contraindicated.

src.q: Metformin is contraindicated in patients with GFR < 30 ml/min

items.t: Hepatic impairment: contraindicated (SmPC 4.3); includes pre-treatment ALT or AST > 3 x ULN.

src.q: Hepatic impairment (see sections 4.2, 4.4 and 4.8)

Eucreas should not be used in patients with hepatic impairment, including those with pre-treatment alanine aminotransferase (ALT) or aspartate aminotransferase (AST) > 3 times the upper limit of normal (ULN)

items.t: SmPC: no adequate human data; should not be used in pregnancy.

src.q: There are no adequate data from the use of Eucreas in pregnant women.
Eucreas should not be used during pregnancy.

items.t: BUMPS: type 2 diabetes in pregnancy should be treated with metformin, with insulin if needed; other antidiabetic medicines (including DPP-4 inhibitors) are avoided as a precaution.

src.q: Type 2 diabetes during pregnancy should be treated with metformin, as well as insulin if required. Other antidiabetic drugs should not be used.
As a precaution, they are avoided in pregnancy.

items.t: SmPC: contraindicated in breastfeeding (risk of neonatal hypoglycaemia from metformin; no human data for vildagliptin).

src.q: Due to both the potential risk of neonate hypoglycaemia related to metformin and the lack of human data with vildagliptin, Eucreas should not be used during breast-feeding
Breast-feeding (see section 4.6)

items.t: SPS: metformin (and insulin) are preferred choices in breastfeeding; there is limited or no published information on other antidiabetic medicines such as vildagliptin.

src.q: Insulin or metformin are the preferred choices during breastfeeding.
limited or no published information on the use of other antidiabetic (blood-glucose lowering) medicines during breastfeeding

items.t: Fertility: no human studies.

src.q: No studies on the effect on human fertility have been conducted for Eucreas

items.t: Common: upper respiratory tract infection, nasopharyngitis, dizziness, headache, tremor, vomiting, diarrhoea, nausea, reflux, flatulence, constipation, abdominal pain, sweating, itching, rash, dermatitis, joint pain, weakness.

src.q: Upper respiratory tract infection Common Nasopharyngitis Common
Dizziness Common Headache Common Tremor Common
Vomiting Common Diarrhoea Common Nausea Common Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease Common Flatulence Common Constipation Common Abdominal pain including upper Common
Hyperhidrosis Common Pruritis Common Rash Common Dermatitis Common
Arthalgia Common
Asthenia Common

items.t: Metformin stomach and bowel effects occur mostly at the start and usually settle; taking doses during or after meals helps.

src.q: Gastrointestinal adverse reactions occur most frequently during initiation of therapy and resolve spontaneously in most cases.

items.t: Lactic acidosis: acidotic breathlessness, abdominal pain, muscle cramps, weakness, low temperature, then coma. Stop and seek immediate medical attention.

src.q: Lactic acidosis is characterised by acidotic dyspnoea, abdominal pain, muscle cramps, asthenia and hypothermia followed by coma.
In case of suspected symptoms, the patient should stop taking metformin and seek immediate medical attention.

items.t: Hepatitis (uncommon) or liver dysfunction: stop if jaundice or signs of liver dysfunction; do not restart.

src.q: Hepatitis Uncommon
Patients who develop jaundice or other signs suggestive of liver dysfunction should discontinue Eucreas.

items.t: Pancreatitis (uncommon): stop if suspected; do not restart if confirmed.

src.q: Pancreatitis Uncommon
if pancreatitis is suspected, the DPP-4 inhibitor and other potentially suspect medicines should be discontinued

items.t: Exfoliative and bullous skin lesions including bullous pemphigoid; cutaneous vasculitis; angioedema (rare, more often with ACE inhibitors).

src.q: Exfoliative and bullous skin lesions, including bullous pemphigoid Not known†
A greater proportion of cases were reported when vildagliptin was administered in combination with an ACE inhibitor.

items.t: GFR and liver function tests before starting.

src.q: GFR should be assessed before treatment initiation and regularly thereafter
LFTs should be performed prior to the initiation of treatment with Eucreas in order to know the patient's baseline value.

items.t: GFR at least annually (every 3 to 6 months in the elderly or if at risk); liver function every 3 months in the first year, then periodically.

src.q: In patients at increased risk of further progression of renal impairment and in the elderly, renal function should be assessed more frequently, e.g. every 3-6 months.
Liver function should be monitored during treatment with Eucreas at three-month intervals during the first year and periodically thereafter.

items.t: Withdrawal recommended if AST or ALT ≥ 3 x ULN persists; stop if jaundice (do not restart). Withhold temporarily in dehydration, for surgery and for intravascular iodinated contrast.

src.q: Should an increase in AST or in ALT of 3x ULN or greater persist, withdrawal of Eucreas therapy is recommended.
Following withdrawal of treatment with Eucreas and LFT normalisation, treatment with Eucreas should not be re-initiated.

items.t: Oral, twice daily (morning and evening). Taking with or just after food may reduce stomach and bowel effects.

src.q: Taking Eucreas with or just after food may reduce gastrointestinal symptoms associated with metformin

items.t: Swallowing difficulty (SPS, off-label): film-coated but can be crushed and mixed with water or given with soft food.

src.q: Vildagliptin with metformin tablets Film-coated but can be crushed and mixed with water or given with soft food.

items.t: Know the signs of lactic acidosis; stop and seek immediate help if they occur. If you have severe vomiting, diarrhoea, fever or cannot drink, stop for a while and contact a healthcare professional.

src.q: Patients and/or care-givers should be informed of the risk of lactic acidosis.
metformin should be temporarily discontinued and contact with a health care professional is recommended

items.t: Seek help for persistent, severe abdominal pain (possible pancreatitis) or yellow skin or eyes (possible liver problem).

src.q: persistent, severe abdominal pain (sometimes radiating to the back)
Patients who develop jaundice or other signs suggestive of liver dysfunction should discontinue Eucreas.

items.t: If dizzy, avoid driving or using machines.

src.q: Patients who may experience dizziness as an adverse reaction should avoid driving vehicles or using machines.

items.t: Mild chronic vitamin deficiency; clinical and sub-clinical vitamin B deficiency (e.g. glossitis, stomatitis, cheilosis, beriberi heart signs, pellagra skin signs, corneal vascularisation, polyneuritis).

src.q: For the treatment of mild chronic vitamin deficiency.
For the treatment of clinical and sub-clinical vitamin B deficiency states

restrictions.note: No prescribing restrictions in the UK vitamin B compound strong tablet SmPC (MHRA Products, PL 20416/0410).

items.tag: UK vitamin B compound strong tablet only
items.t: UK vitamin B compound strong tablet: adults and elderly 1-2 tablets three times daily. The clinic tablet has a different make-up: use the clinic label for its dose.

src.q: Adults, elderly and children over 3 years: 1 - 2 tablets three times daily.

items.t: UK vitamin B compound strong tablet: children over 3 years 1-2 tablets three times daily; should not be used in children under 3 years. The clinic tablet has a different make-up: use the clinic label for its dose.

src.q: Adults, elderly and children over 3 years: 1 - 2 tablets three times daily.
Should not be used in children under 3 years.

items.tag: UK vitamin B compound strong tablet only

items.t: Hypersensitivity to thiamine, riboflavin, pyridoxine or nicotinamide.

src.q: Hypersensitivity, to thiamine hydrochloride, riboflavin, pyridoxine hydrochloride and nicotinamide.

cautions.note: The UK vitamin B compound strong SmPC 4.4 lists only lactose-related excipient warnings, which do not apply to the clinic tablet (its excipients are not known). No other warnings.

items.t: Pyridoxine may reduce the effect of plain levodopa: patients with Parkinson's disease on plain levodopa should not take vitamin B6 in doses well above daily needs. Does not apply when levodopa is given with a decarboxylase inhibitor.

src.q: patients with Parkinson's disease who are receiving treatment with plain levodopa should not take vitamin B6 in doses which greatly exceed the daily requirement.
This does not apply when levodopa is combined with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor.

renal.note: No renal impairment advice in the UK vitamin B compound strong tablet SmPC (MHRA Products, PL 20416/0410).

hepatic.note: No hepatic impairment advice in the UK vitamin B compound strong tablet SmPC (MHRA Products, PL 20416/0410).

items.t: Limited data. Can be used if needed to correct deficiency and benefit outweighs risk; caution when prescribing in pregnancy.

src.q: can be used in pregnant women if use is necessary to correct deficiencies and if benefits overweighs risks.
Caution should be exercised when prescribing to pregnant women.

items.t: Excreted in milk; no harm expected at recommended doses. High-dose pyridoxine may reduce milk production (prolactin): use with caution in nursing mothers.

src.q: No harm to suckling infant is expected if used in recommended doses.
In high doses, pyridoxine may interfere with prolactin release and should only be used with caution in nursing mothers.

items.t: No relevant fertility data.

src.q: Fertility: No relevant data is available.

items.t: Side effects are unlikely; excess vitamin B is excreted.

src.q: Vitamin B Compound Strong tablets are unlikely to cause any side effects, as any excess vitamin B is naturally excreted from the body.

items.t: Severe allergic reactions (rash, hives, itching, breathing difficulty, chest tightness, swelling of mouth, face, lips or tongue) or numbness/tingling of the skin: seek medical attention right away.

src.q: Seek medical attention right away if any of these SEVERE side effects like severe allergic reactions
numbness or tingling of the skin occur

monitoring.note: No monitoring requirements in the UK vitamin B compound strong tablet SmPC (MHRA Products, PL 20416/0410).

items.t: Oral.

src.q: Route of administration: Oral

items.t: Get medical help at once for signs of a severe allergic reaction.

src.q: Seek medical attention right away if any of these SEVERE side effects like severe allergic reactions

items.t: Prophylaxis of systemic embolism in rheumatic heart disease and atrial fibrillation; prophylaxis after prosthetic heart valve insertion; prophylaxis and treatment of venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism; transient cerebral ischaemic attacks.

src.q: Prophylaxis of systemic embolism in patients with rheumatic heart disease and atrial fibrillation. Prophylaxis after insertion of prosthetic heart valves. Prophylaxis and treatment of venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.
Transient attacks of cerebral ischaemia.

items.t: Give every patient a patient-held information booklet ('warfarin card') and explain which symptoms need medical attention.

src.q: Patients should be given a patient-held information booklet ('warfarin card') and informed of symptoms for which they should seek medical attention.

items.t: Adults (all indications): typical induction 10 mg daily for 2 days, tailored to the individual; usual maintenance 3 to 9 mg once daily at the same time each day, adjusted to prothrombin time/INR.

src.q: The typical induction dose is 10mg daily for 2 days but this should be tailored to individual requirements.
The daily maintenance dose is usually 3 to 9mg taken at the same time each day.

items.t: Emergencies: start heparin and warfarin together; stop heparin at least six hours before the first control test.

src.q: In emergencies, anticoagulant therapy should be initiated with heparin and warfarin together.
should be discontinued at least six hours before the first test is carried out

items.t: Elderly: as for adults but the dose may need to be lower.

src.q: Elderly: As for adults, but dosage may need to be lowered.

items.t: Protein C deficiency: start without a loading dose (even with heparin); protein S deficiency: start slowly.

src.q: In patients with protein C deficiency, therapy should be introduced without a loading dose of warfarin even if heparin is given.

items.t: Dose may need reducing with weight loss, acute illness or stopping smoking; may need increasing with weight gain, diarrhoea or vomiting.

src.q: Loss of weight Acute illness Cessation of smoking
Weight gain Diarrhoea Vomiting

items.t: No paediatric data are available in the SmPC.

src.q: Paediatric population: No data are available.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to warfarin or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1. Haemorrhagic stroke

items.t: Haemorrhagic stroke; clinically significant bleeding.

src.q: Haemorrhagic stroke (see section 4.4 for further details) Clinically significant bleeding

items.t: Within 72 hours of major surgery with risk of severe bleeding; within 48 hours postpartum.

src.q: Within 72 hours of major surgery with risk of severe bleeding
Within 48 hours postpartum

items.t: Pregnancy (first and third trimesters).

src.q: Pregnancy (first and third trimesters, see section 4.6)

items.t: Drugs whose interaction may significantly increase bleeding risk (e.g. fibrinolytics such as streptokinase and alteplase).

src.q: Drugs where interactions may lead to a significantly increased risk of bleeding
Fibrinolytic drugs such as streptokinase and alteplase are contraindicated in patients receiving warfarin.

items.t: Any condition where bleeding risk may outweigh the benefit of anticoagulation.

src.q: Anticoagulation is contraindicated in any physical condition in which the risk of haemorrhage might be greater that the potential clinical benefits of anticoagulation

items.t: Bleeding is the most frequent adverse effect. Give with caution where there is a risk of serious haemorrhage (e.g. NSAID use, recent ischaemic stroke, bacterial endocarditis, previous GI bleeding). Risk factors include INR >4.0, age ≥65, variable INRs, uncontrolled hypertension, cerebrovascular disease, falls risk, anaemia, malignancy, renal insufficiency, interacting drugs.

src.q: Warfarin should be given with caution to patients where there is a risk of serious haemorrhage (e.g. concomitant NSAID use, recent ischaemic stroke, bacterial endocarditis, previous gastrointestinal bleeding)
Risk factors for bleeding include high intensity of anticoagulation (INR >4.0), age ≥65, highly variable INRs

items.t: Active peptic ulcer: treat with caution, review regularly and teach how to recognise bleeding.

src.q: Due to a high risk of bleeding, patients with active peptic ulcers should be treated with caution.

items.t: Ischaemic stroke: a break is justified; restart 2-14 days after, depending on infarct size and blood pressure; stop for 14 days with large embolic stroke or uncontrolled hypertension.

src.q: Warfarin treatment should be re-started 2-14 days following ischaemic stroke, depending on the size of the infarct and blood pressure.

items.t: Surgery: no severe bleeding risk - operate with INR <2.5. Severe bleeding risk - stop warfarin 3 days before. If warfarin cannot be stopped 3 days before, reverse with low-dose vitamin K. Routine dental surgery (e.g. extraction) does not need warfarin stopped.

src.q: For surgery where there is a risk of severe bleeding, warfarin should be stopped 3 days prior to surgery.
anticoagulation should be reversed with low-dose vitamin K
Warfarin need not be stopped before routine dental surgery, eg, tooth extraction.

items.t: Thyroid disorders: hyper- or hypothyroidism changes warfarin metabolism; monitor closely when starting.

src.q: patients with hyper- or hypo-thyroidism should be closely monitored on starting warfarin therapy

items.t: Protein C deficiency: risk of skin necrosis on starting; start without loading dose.

src.q: Patients with protein C deficiency are at risk of developing skin necrosis when starting warfarin treatment.

items.t: Calciphylaxis (rare): consider stopping warfarin if diagnosed; reported also with normal renal function.

src.q: In case calciphylaxis is diagnosed, appropriate treatment should be started and consideration should be given to stopping treatment with warfarin.
cases have been reported in patients taking warfarin, including those with normal renal function

items.t: Anticoagulant-related nephropathy: acute kidney injury possible, linked to excessive anticoagulation and haematuria; close monitoring including renal function if supratherapeutic INR with haematuria.

src.q: Close monitoring including renal function evaluation is advised in patients with a supratherapeutic INR and hematuria (including microscopic).

items.t: CYP2C9 and VKORC1 genetic variability can significantly affect dose needs.

src.q: Genetic variability particularly in relation to CYP2C9 and VKORC1 can significantly affect dose requirements for warfarin.

items.t: Contains lactose.

src.q: contains 48.350 mg lactose per tablet

items.t: Narrow therapeutic range: care with all concomitant therapy. Any change to medication, including OTC products, warrants more INR monitoring.

src.q: Warfarin has a narrow therapeutic range and care is required with all concomitant therapy.
Any change to medication, including self-medication with OTC products, warrants increased monitoring of the INR.

items.t: Avoid if possible (or give with caution and more clinical and laboratory monitoring): clopidogrel, NSAIDs (including aspirin and COX-2 inhibitors), SSRI and SNRI antidepressants, heparins, other anticoagulants and antiplatelets.

src.q: The following examples should be avoided, or administered with caution with increased clinical and laboratory monitoring: Clopidogrel NSAIDs (including aspirin and cox-2 specific NSAIDS)
SSRI and SNRI antidepressants

items.t: Potentiate warfarin (dose may need reducing, more monitoring): omeprazole, paracetamol (prolonged regular use), statins (not pravastatin; mainly fluvastatin), sulfamethoxazole, erythromycin, metronidazole, azole antifungals, amiodarone, allopurinol and others.

src.q: omeprazole, paracetamol (prolonged regular use)
statins (not pravastatin; predominantly associated with fluvastatin) erythromycin, sulfamethoxazole, metronidazole
When these drugs are co-administered, warfarin dosage may need to be reduced and the level of monitoring increased.

items.t: Broad-spectrum antibiotics may potentiate warfarin by reducing vitamin K-producing gut flora (no specific antibiotic is named in this statement).

src.q: Broad spectrum antibiotics may potentiate the effect of warfarin by reducing the gut flora which produce vitamin K.

items.t: St John's wort: must not be used with warfarin (proven reduced warfarin levels and effect).

src.q: Herbal preparations containing St John's Wort (Hypericum perforatum) must not be used whilst taking warfarin

items.t: Tramadol (MHRA 2024): can raise INR with severe, possibly fatal bleeding; be aware, consider dose adjustment and extra INR monitoring when starting tramadol.

src.q: Taking warfarin and tramadol together can cause harmful drug interactions, which can raise the International Normalised Ratio (INR)
consider whether additional monitoring of INR is required when starting tramadol or another concomitant medicine

items.t: 0.5 mg tablet SmPC only (not in the 5 mg tablet SmPC): oral anti-diabetic agents and diuretics are also listed as potentiating warfarin.

src.q: methylphenidate, diuretics, oral anti-diabetic agents, anabolic steroids

items.t: Corticosteroids: variable effect on INR; increase monitoring when starting and stopping.

src.q: Examples of drugs with variable effect Corticosteroids, nevirapine, ritonavir
in these cases increased monitoring on starting and stopping therapy is advised

items.t: Drugs that reduce warfarin effect include barbiturates, carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampicin, oral contraceptives, oestrogens.

src.q: Examples of drugs which antagonise the effect of warfarin Barbiturates, primidone, carbamazepine, griseofulvin, oral contraceptives, rifampicin

items.t: Miconazole (including oral gel) inhibits CYP2C9: monitor anticoagulant effect; warfarin dose reduction may be needed.

src.q: Miconazole inhibits CYP2C9, caution should be exercised in patients on oral anticoagulants, such as warfarin

items.t: Foods and alcohol: avoid cranberry products; large or sudden diet changes in vitamin K-rich foods (liver, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, green leafy vegetables) can affect control; acute heavy alcohol raises INR; moderate alcohol permitted; avoid herbal medicines/food supplements.

src.q: Patients should be advised to avoid cranberry products.
Moderate alcohol intake can be permitted.
Patients should generally avoid taking any herbal medicines or food supplements whilst taking warfarin

items.t: No dose threshold given. Monitor INR more often in renal disease; renal insufficiency is a bleeding risk factor.

src.q: INR should be monitored more frequently in patients at an increased risk of over coagulation e.g. patients with severe hypertension, liver or renal disease.

items.t: No dose threshold given. Monitor INR more often in liver disease (risk of over-coagulation).

src.q: INR should be monitored more frequently in patients at an increased risk of over coagulation e.g. patients with severe hypertension, liver or renal disease.

items.t: Contraindicated in the first and third trimesters (warfarin embryopathy; fatal bleeding and stillbirth). Rarely prescribed in pregnancy; switch to other anticoagulants during pregnancy or after conception.

src.q: Warfarin is contraindicated in pregnancy in the first and third trimester
patients should be switched on to other anticoagulants during pregnancy or after conception

items.t: BUMPS: avoided in pregnancy where possible (birth defects); may sometimes be recommended with mechanical heart valves. Do not stop without specialist advice; people with a metal valve need urgent specialist advice within a day or two of a positive test.

src.q: Warfarin is avoided in pregnancy where possible as it can cause birth defects.
If you have a metal heart valve you should seek urgent advice from your specialist or GP within a day or two of a positive pregnancy test.

items.t: SmPC: can be used during breastfeeding; no effects expected at therapeutic doses.

src.q: Warfarin can be used during breast-feeding.

items.t: SPS: preferred oral anticoagulant in breastfeeding; monitor the infant for bruising and blood in urine, vomit or stools.

src.q: Warfarin can be used during breastfeeding, although infant monitoring is required.
As a precaution, monitor the infant for bruising on the skin, blood in urine, vomit, or stools.

items.t: Women of child-bearing age should use effective contraception. No fertility data.

src.q: Women of child-bearing age who are taking warfarin tablets should use effective contraception during treatment.
Fertility No data available

adverseCommon.note: One warfarin SmPC (section 4.8) gives all adverse reactions as frequency 'not known'; haemorrhage is the most frequently reported adverse effect (SmPC 4.4). Sources checked: both warfarin SmPCs.

items.t: Haemorrhage (including cerebral haemorrhage, subdural haematoma, GI bleeding): the most frequent adverse effect. Unexpected bleeding at therapeutic INR should be investigated.

src.q: The most frequently reported adverse effect of all oral anticoagulants is haemorrhage.
Unexpected bleeding at therapeutic levels should always be investigated and INR monitored.

items.t: Life-threatening haemorrhage: stop warfarin, give prothrombin complex concentrate 30-50 units/kg (or FFP 15 mL/kg if none); discuss with haematologist/NPIS. Non-life-threatening: slow IV phytomenadione 10-20 mg (adults).

src.q: Stop warfarin treatment, give prothrombin complex concentrate (factors II, VII, IX, and X) 30-50 units/kg
give slow intravenous injection of phytomenadione (vitamin K1) 10-20 mg for adults

items.t: Skin necrosis (rare, mainly with loading doses over 10 mg, within 3-5 days, often obese elderly women); calciphylaxis; 'purple toes'. Discontinuation usually advised.

src.q: Skin necrosis is a rare but potentially serious effect. It is associated with loading doses of over 10mg
Advice on management usually includes discontinuing the warfarin.

items.t: Anticoagulant-related nephropathy (acute kidney injury).

src.q: Anticoagulant-related nephropathy (see section 4.4), haematuria

items.t: Baseline prothrombin time or INR before starting (5 mg tablet SmPC). SPS baseline: clotting screen, FBC, LFTs, serum creatinine or eGFR (ORBIT score); consider TFTs and blood pressure.

src.q: Baseline prothrombin (PT) or INR measurements should be made before beginning therapy with warfarin tablets.
Required Baseline Clotting screening Full blood count Liver function tests

items.t: INR daily or on alternate days early in treatment, then at longer intervals once stable in range. SPS: daily/alternate days, then twice weekly for 1-2 weeks, then weekly; once stable every 12 weeks (more often if high risk, poor control or interacting medicine).

src.q: the INR should be determined daily or on alternate days in the early days of treatment
Daily or on alternate days; then twice weekly for 1-2 weeks; then weekly, depending on local protocol
Every 12 weeks; more frequently if needed INR

items.t: SPS: when a medicine that may interact is started, do an INR test after 3 to 5 days.

src.q: Patients who are prescribed a drug that may interact with warfarin should have an INR test performed after 3 to 5 days.

items.t: High INR: if too high, reduce or stop warfarin and recheck within 2-3 days. SmPC: INR 6.0-8.0 with no or minor bleeding - stop, restart when INR <5.0; INR >8.0 with no or minor bleeding - stop and give phytomenadione 0.5-1 mg IV (adults) or 5 mg by mouth, repeat if still too high after 24 hours.

src.q: If the INR is found to be too high, reduce dose or stop warfarin treatment
INR should be checked within 2-3 days to ensure that it is falling.
INR 6·0-8·0, no bleeding or minor bleeding-stop warfarin, restart when INR <5·0
give phytomenadione (vitamin K1) 0·5-1 mg for adults

items.t: Review regularly whether therapy is still needed and stop when no longer required.

src.q: it is important that the need for therapy is reviewed on a regular basis and therapy discontinued when no longer required

items.t: Oral, once daily at the same time each day. 5 mg tablet SmPC: preferably on an empty stomach.

src.q: taken at the same time each day
Warfarin tablets should be taken at the same time each day, preferably on an empty stomach

items.t: Carry the warfarin alert card; know bleeding signs and report them at once (e.g. nosebleeds over 10 minutes, blood in vomit/sputum/stool/urine, severe bruising, unusual headaches).

src.q: Patients should be instructed on measures to minimise risk of bleeding and to report immediately to physicians signs and symptoms of bleeding.
prolonged nose bleeds (more than 10 minutes)

items.t: Tell the doctor before starting any new medicine, including OTC, herbal remedies or vitamins; avoid St John's wort and cranberry products.

src.q: Patients should be instructed to inform their doctor before they start to take any additional medications including over the counter medicines, herbal remedies or vitamin preparations.

items.t: Avoid sudden big changes in diet (vitamin K-rich foods) and heavy drinking; seek advice before major diet changes.

src.q: Patients should be informed of the need to seek medical advice before undertaking any major changes in diet.
